Victorian Labor pledges $30-a-week public transport fare cap
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
18:57:19 UTC
03:57:19 KST

Premier Ben Carroll has pledged to cap public transport fares at $30 a week if the Labor government is re-elected next month.
The public transport pledge comes hot on the heels of a weekend commitment by Victorian Labor to cap Melbourne freeway tolls at $30 per week.
The Victorian Chamber of Commerce and Industry has expressed concern over the rising tab associated with cost-of-living pledges during the election campaign.
Victoria Premier Ben Carroll has pledged to cap public transport fares at $30 a week if the Labor government is re-elected next month, the second transport capping pledge in as many days.
Half-price fares were introduced by former premier Jacinta Allan at the peak of the fuel price crunch in April, following a short period of free public transport use statewide in the early months of the US-Iran war.
The half-price fare period was scheduled to expire on December 31.
If re-elected next month, Mr Carroll said a Labor government would introduce the $30-a-week fare cap, which would run for two years until December 2028.
"This is real cost-of-living relief that helps a regular commuter save $1,400 a year," the premier said.
"Everyone can benefit, but full-time workers will benefit most."
Victorian Labor estimated the transport fare cap policy would cost $206 million over its two-year duration, which Mr Carroll said would be offset by savings made elsewhere.
The pledge comes only a day after Labor also committed to a $30-a-week freeway toll cap in an election pledge battle with the Coalition, which only months earlier had committed to a $50-a-week toll cap if elected in November.
Victorian Chamber of Commerce and Industry policy and advocacy chief Amelia Bitsis said businesses large and small were concerned about the escalating profligacy of the Victorian election campaign.
"We're asking all major political parties to show some fiscal restraint," she said.
"We simply don't have an accurate enough picture of what the true debt situation is in Victoria.
"What certainly do know is that business is on the hook for that debt, so are Victorian households.
"A lot of the election commitments that we are seeing are lovely nice-to-haves but the question becomes: Can we afford them?"
Public transport affordability was a key feature of the 2022 Victorian election campaign, with then opposition leader Matthew Guy pledging a $2 a day cap on metropolitan train and tram fares.
During the campaign, the Victorian Coalition also pledged to halve V/Line fares.
A political spat later erupted when Labor and the public service came under fire for undertaking a policy costing of an opposition policy proposal, with Coalition MPs arguing it was outside the remit of public servants.
During the same election campaign, then premier Daniel Andrews pledged to cap regional train services at $9.20 a day for full-fare commuters, and $4.60 for concession card holders.

Suncorp borrower's mortgage payments could spike amid transfer to ANZ
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
18:54:39 UTC
03:54:39 KST

ANZ's Suncorp acquisition could see mortgage payments rise upward of $1,000
In short:
Suncorp mortgage customers have been warned their repayments could increase by upwards of $1,000 a month when transferred to ANZ.
Suncorp was bought by ANZ in 2024 after the ACCC initially rejected the acquisition.
Consumer advocates say the way that Suncorp and ANZ are treating people shows how little power borrowers have in Australia.
Suncorp mortgage customers received an alarming email last week advising them that their monthly mortgage repayments could rise by hundreds of dollars.
ANZ Bank bought Suncorp in 2024 and is now logistically transferring hundreds of thousands of borrowers off Suncorp's books and onto the ANZ loan platforms.
The email sent by Suncorp to Suncorp customers on October 13 said: "If you've made advance payments and have funds available in your Cashback/redraw, your minimum loan repayment at ANZ is likely to increase."
One Suncorp customer who contacted the ABC said Suncorp's email indicated home loan repayments could rise by more than $1,000.
Suncorp had previously allowed customers with redraw and cashback facilities to reduce their minimum monthly repayments.
ANZ does not have this policy, so some customers are being warned their minimum repayments will increase if they do nothing.
"This increase could be significant depending on the loan balance, how much is paid in advance and the remaining loan term," Suncorp's email said.
Consumer advocates say the way that Suncorp and ANZ are treating people shows how little power borrowers have in Australia.
"Australians deserve better protections in the mortgage market to give them more certainty about what they will pay and the conditions for their loan," Consumer Policy Research Centre CEO Erin Turner said.
'Unwelcome shock'
The director of data insights at interest rate comparison site Canstar, Sally Tindall, said thousands of Suncorp customers were likely to be in for an "unwelcome shock" when they find out their minimum repayments are set to rise as a result of the changeover to ANZ in June next year.
Suncorp told the ABC its customers could avoid any increase in their home loan repayments.
"For most customers there will be no change to their repayments," Suncorp Bank CEO Malcolm Stedman said.
"Those customers ahead on their repayments may see an increase in their minimum repayments, if they choose to take no action."
Ms Tindall agreed with Mr Stedman's claim if customers followed Suncorp's email instructions.
"This is because Suncorp views extra repayments differently to ANZ when they go to calculate a customer's minimum monthly repayments," she said.
The most common practice across the banks, Ms Tindall said, was to exclude or discount any extra home loan payments made, or available cash, when calculating a person's minimum monthly repayments.
For example, if someone has a $600,000 debt owing on their mortgage, and 25 years remaining, but they have $100,000 in extra sitting in the loan, the bank will calculate the minimum repayment amount on the $600,000 debt owing (they will still, however, only charge you interest on the $500,000).
On the average owner-occupier variable rate of 6.49 per cent, the monthly repayments would be $4,047.
However, Ms Tindall said some banks approached this calculation differently by including the extra repayments a customer has added to their loan.
Using the same example as above, the bank calculates how much you need to repay the $500,000 owing over the 25 years remaining.
In this scenario, the person's minimum repayments would be $3,373.
"Most Australians have a home loan that is "variable at the bank's discretion" where the bank can hike fees or change conditions when it suits them," Ms Turner said.
"This means that most borrowers have little control about how much they are paying for their home.
Banks expected to treat customers fairly
The ANZ Bank's acquisition of Suncorp was originally rejected by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) on the grounds a resulting lack of competition would disadvantage consumers.
"We are not satisfied that the acquisition is not likely to substantially lessen competition in the supply of home loans nationally, small to medium enterprise banking in Queensland, and agribusiness banking in Queensland," ACCC deputy chair Mick Keogh said in August 2023.
"These banking markets are critical for many home owners and for Queensland businesses and farmers in particular.
"Competition being lessened in these markets will lead to customers getting a worse deal."
The Australian Competition Tribunal later set aside the ACCC's decision, leading to the banking acquisition then being approved by both the Queensland and federal governments.
The ABC asked the Queensland Treasury to respond to Suncorp's email to customers asking them to adjust their mortgage repayments to avoid higher costs.
Treasurer David Janetzki told the ABC: "This deal was agreed to by the former Labor government and it is up to former Treasurer Cameron Dick to explain why these protections weren't included in the arrangement."
The ABC has contacted the Queensland deputy opposition leader.
A spokesperson for the Federal Treasurer Jim Chalmers said: "While these are commercial decisions for ANZ we expect the bank to treat its customers fairly and with respect, otherwise they'll look for better deals from others."

Macron condemns "shocking" scenes of violence across France
PARIS, Oct 18 - French President Emmanuel Macron condemned on Sunday what he called the "dissenters" who looted and vandalised cities in "shocking" scenes across France on the sidelines of protests over the cost of living.
"Looking at these images, we have all asked ourselves: what was going through their minds? How can French people do this to France?" Macron said in a televised address to the nation. "Nothing justifies it, nothing explains it, nothing excuses it. Tonight, we all feel anger and shame."
Macron, whose final six months in office are being shaped by mounting political, fiscal and social pressures, said he had ordered a review to determine whether there had been failings in intelligence gathering or police preparedness before protests that were later marred by looting and violence.
He said prefects and mayors would be empowered to ban certain gatherings where necessary.
Macron also said he had asked the government to bring together students, teachers, lawmakers, trade union representatives and business leaders this week to formulate what he described as "concrete proposals" to address the crisis, without providing further details.
"We must sit around the table and build solutions together," he said. REUTERS

Ukraine’s FP-1 drones hit oil and digital infrastructure in St. Petersburg

The St. Petersburg Oil Terminal is one of the region’s largest oil-handling facilities, handling the receipt, storage and shipment of petroleum products, including for export. Its total capacity is 12.5 million tons per year.
The Defense Forces also struck a VKontakte data center near St. Petersburg, Fire Point said. FP-1 drones hit the facility in the settlement of Novosergiivka in the Leningrad region. Paris synagogue, several Jewish-affiliated sites vandalized on weekend, antisemitic motive unlikely
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
18:42:20 UTC
03:42:20 KST

A synagogue in Paris's 19th arrondissement was among several Jewish-affiliated sites reportedly broken into or damaged over the weekend amid widespread riots across France, the Jewish community security organization Service de Protection de la Communauté Juive (SPCJ) said in a statement on Sunday.
The SPCJ issued the statement amid concerns about the spread of misinformation surrounding the incidents, urging France's Jewish community to exercise "caution and responsibility," refrain from circulating unverified reports, and rely on official communications from the organization and authorities.
Members of the Ohalei Yaakov congregation discovered that their temporary prayer space on Rue Burnouf had been ransacked when they arrived on Sunday morning. The congregation has been holding services at the location while its permanent synagogue on Rue Henri Murger undergoes renovations.
Prayer books, tefillin, and the contents of lockers and cupboards were found scattered across the floor following the overnight intrusion, according to the French Jewish news outlet IsraJ. The rabbi's office had also been ransacked.
Synagogue officials suspect attempted theft, do not rule out antisemitism
Although the circumstances and motive remain unclear, members of the congregation believe the intruders may have been searching for money rather than seeking to carry out an explicitly antisemitic attack. No antisemitic graffiti or inscriptions were reported at the scene, and the synagogue's Torah scrolls were left untouched.
"It really looks like an attempted robbery; you can see that those who did this were probably looking for money. The Torah scrolls weren't touched; we just found the items that were in the lockers on the floor," Raphael, a member of the Ohalei Yaakov synagogue committee, told IsraJ.
However, Raphael did not entirely rule out an antisemitic motive, raising the possibility that the intruders had deliberately selected the synagogue because it was a Jewish place of worship.
"Of course, it can't be a coincidence that they chose to target a Jewish place of worship. They must have thought that since it was a Jewish place of worship, there would be money there. Because it's a temporary building, there's no sign outside indicating a synagogue. This leads me to believe that those who broke in last night must have scouted the place, seen that Jews went there for prayers."
Raphael said the congregation observed a peaceful Shabbat, with services proceeding normally and no riots nearby. He suggested that an attack motivated primarily by antisemitism would likely have involved more extensive destruction, including damage to Torah scrolls or antisemitic graffiti.
In a message to congregants, the Ohalei Yaakov committee said there were no signs of forced entry and urged members to be more vigilant about securing the premises.
"We noticed that there was an attempted theft, probably by people looking for money. Some lockers were emptied. NOTHING WAS STOLEN OR VANDALIZED. THERE ARE NO SIGNS OF FORCED ENTRY EITHER," the message read.
Jewish-owned businesses damaged amid nationwide unrest
In Marseille, several businesses sustained damage during Saturday's demonstrations, including some owned by Jewish individuals.
However, there was no evidence indicating that the businesses had been singled out because of their owners' Jewish identities or that the damage was motivated by antisemitism.
The incidents occurred as France experienced some of its most serious civil unrest in years, with demonstrations over rising living costs and deteriorating public services escalating into violence, looting, and attacks on public buildings across the country.

EU, Canada condemn Israeli settler attacks on Palestinians, European diplomats

The EU and Canada have strongly condemned Israeli settler attacks in the occupied West Bank, including those targeting European diplomats, and called for accountability.
In separate statements on Sunday, the EU’s diplomatic service and Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand urged Israel to protect diplomats and Palestinian civilians and prevent further violence.
“The EU strongly condemns the latest attacks by violent settlers in the West Bank, including on European diplomats,” the bloc said.
While acknowledging condemnations by several Israeli representatives, it demanded “full accountability” and effective measures to prevent violence and harassment against Palestinians, including during the olive harvest, as well as against journalists.
The EU also urged Israel to comply fully with international humanitarian and human rights law and halt illegal settlement expansion.
‘Broader pattern of settler violence’

“Canada joins the European Union and our European allies in condemning the latest attack in the West Bank by violent settlers, including on diplomats from Belgium, France, and Poland,” she said.
Welcoming an Israeli police investigation, Anand stressed that Israel, as the occupying power, must ensure accountability and protect diplomats and civilians.
The delegation was visiting the area during the olive harvest and included French and Belgian consuls, a Polish representative and Catholic Church officials.
Masked Israeli settlers confronted the delegation and smashed a window of a Belgian consular vehicle.
Israeli army radio reported that troops and police arrived three hours after receiving the delegation’s location and footage sent within minutes of the incident.
Separately, opposition Yisrael Beiteinu party leader Avigdor Lieberman accused Netanyahu and his defence and national security ministers of failing to curb settler attacks, warning that their inaction was eroding international support for Israel.
Settler attacks on Palestinians and their property have intensified during the olive harvest season, which began earlier this month.

Rabbis for Human Rights files police complaint over Rabbi Lior’s Palestinian olive harvest ruling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
18:42:11 UTC
03:42:11 KST

Rabbis for Human Rights said Sunday it had filed a police complaint against Rabbi Dov Lior over his religious ruling permitting Jews to harvest olives from Palestinian groves, adding to the rabbinical opposition to the ruling amid violence during the West Bank harvest.
The organization said its acting director, Anton Goodman, submitted the complaint on behalf of its 170 rabbinical members, alleging incitement to racism, incitement to violence, and encouraging the theft of property.
The complaint follows reports that the IDF recommended investigating Lior for suspected incitement.
“I am sorry that I have to file a police complaint against a rabbi in Israel, but reality requires us to stand up for the Torah,” Goodman said in the organization’s announcement.
“Entering other people’s land and taking their crops unlawfully is not what God wants from us in this land.”
Lior argued that olive trees remained property of Jewish people
Lior, the former chief rabbi of Kiryat Arba, published the ruling Friday. He argued that the land remained the property of the Jewish people and that Palestinians prevented from harvesting for security reasons could be presumed to have given up on the olives.
He also argued that past harvests had already provided sufficient compensation for planting the trees. His conclusion extended beyond groves near settlements, permitting Jews to harvest in more distant areas to assert Jewish ownership and fulfill what he described as the religious commandment to conquer the land.
The ruling concerns taking the olives; its text does not explicitly authorize physical attacks on Palestinian farmers. The organization’s allegations that it constitutes incitement are part of its complaint, rather than findings by police or a court.
The dispute turns in part on whether farmers barred from reaching their trees can be treated as having relinquished their crops. Rabbis opposing Lior’s position argue that being prevented from harvesting does not mean owners have abandoned their property.
Earlier in the week, a group of Gush Etzion rabbis issued an opinion prohibiting Jews from taking olives from Palestinian-owned groves near settlements, even where the owners were denied access for security reasons.
They argued that the fruit remained the owners’ property and that taking it constituted theft and a desecration of God’s name. One alternative they proposed was arranging for workers or volunteers to harvest under the permitted security arrangements and return the crop to its owners, with harvesting expenses covered.
Tzohar says theft prohibited regardless of owner's religion
The Tzohar rabbinical organization subsequently rejected Lior’s ruling, stressing that theft is prohibited regardless of whether the owner is Jewish.
Tzohar also disputed the assumption that restricted access amounted to abandonment, particularly where owners expressly said they intended to harvest through arrangements allowed by the military. It cited Lior’s own earlier writings in arguing that individuals could not decide for themselves to confiscate property on security grounds.
The religious dispute comes alongside restrictions on access to some harvesting areas.
Rabbis for Human Rights, which brings together rabbis from different Jewish denominations, said its activists accompany Palestinian farmers during the annual harvest both to help pick olives and to deter violence and document incidents.
The organization’s complaint followed a week of reported attacks on Palestinian harvesters, journalists, and European diplomats participating in the harvest.

West Bank attacks on Washington Post journalist, diplomats may signal dangerous trend - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
18:42:10 UTC
03:42:10 KST

The 2023-2026 period is not the first time that a Jewish extremist beat or assaulted a foreign reporter or Western diplomat in the West Bank.
But in the past, when this happened, heads rolled. Whoever was involved was either arrested, fired, or both – and fast.
Often, some of their supervisors were fired or rebuked to make it clear that whoever was managing the area needed to establish a stricter environment to curb such a phenomenon if they wanted to keep their job.
In that sense, the assault on a Washington Post photojournalist in recent days, and what most are reporting as an assault on Western diplomats, is not new.
What is new is that the world assumes that the Israeli government will do nothing other than at most issue condemnations, and that the record of the last three years, and especially the last three months, would suggest they would be right.
Ben-Gvir accused of avoiding crackdown on settler violence
For two years, the IDF and the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) accused National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir of this and of pressuring the police into avoiding cracking down on Jewish extremist violence in the West Bank. Implicitly, they also held Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accountable for not firing Ben-Gvir.
Then, the Shin Bet got quieter for much of 2026 when Netanyahu appointed David Zini, who corralled the agency from involvement against Jewish extremist violence in the West Bank, but the IDF continued its accusations.
And even Zini, after the last few months of a spike in Jewish extremist violence like nothing Israel has seen in decades, recently started to pressure Netanyahu and the government to get more serious about a crackdown.
Yet, despite unanimous, repeated warnings by the defense establishment to Defense Minister Israel Katz and Netanyahu not to suspend the administrative detention of violent extremist Jews, and repeated warnings by the defense establishment to bring it back to get the situation under control, the defense establishment and the prime minister have either said “no” or are waiting until after the elections for any progress.
Their strategy has only encouraged the Jewish extremists to rush to perpetrate more widespread violence in the last three months, as they are concerned that maybe their free hand to attack Palestinians may get rolled back post-elections.
Once the Israeli government does nothing active to truly protect innocent Palestinians for an extended period, such lawlessness was eventually going to impact others in the West Bank, because Jewish extremists realize that the political and defense establishments are intimidated by them.
Netanyahu is afraid that if he confronts Ben-Gvir during election season, he may lose votes to the Otzma Yehudit Party by looking weak.
In this sad state of affairs, enforcing the rule of law in the West Bank has now become associated with looking weak.
Sanctions, US threats have had little effect on Netanyahu, Katz position
What is stunning is that the European and Western sanctions wave in mid-September, and threats from the Trump administration to potentially take some similar actions eventually, have done nothing to change Netanyahu’s and Katz’s position.
Part of this is likely because Netanyahu correctly estimated that Trump would support him in the election. After all, they converge on Iran-related issues, despite their disagreement over the West Bank.
On the same day that US Ambassador Mike Huckabee slammed Israel for mishandling the West Bank, Trump gave Netanyahu a full-throated endorsement because of their joint interests against Iran.
This may or may not decide the election in Netanyahu’s favor.
But whoever is prime minister after October 27, if the situation in the West Bank does not come under control, the defense establishment has warned that violent Jewish extremists, who have already attacked IDF soldiers dozens of times, could become an even greater direct danger to the State of Israel’s ability to function, let alone to its global image.
Palestinian terrorism is still a much bigger threat than Jewish extremist violence and terror. And the West Bank has always been seen as less important than Iran, Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria. But that strategy, or lack thereof, may finally implode with longer-term consequences that will be much harder to fix.

How the weekend’s Jewish extremist violence reverberates through election campaigns - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
18:42:03 UTC
03:42:03 KST

Jewish extremist violence in the West Bank of the kind witnessed over the weekend is, to the country’s discredit, nothing new. Nor is it unprecedented for journalists or foreign dignitaries to be caught up in it.
What is different this time is the timing.
With elections just a week and a half away, incidents involving Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine and a delegation of European diplomats have become another battleground in the campaign. The violence demands attention regardless of the electoral calendar. But that calendar helps explain how the politicians are responding, and which voters they hope are listening.
The shadow of the election is particularly apparent in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s response. He condemned violence in principle while questioning what happened in these cases. His office said the circumstances remained unclear and that investigators needed to establish the facts.
Demanding an investigation before determining individual responsibility is understandable. But the statements went considerably further.
They highlighted the diplomatic delegation’s failure to coordinate its visit with the IDF, the Communist affiliation of a French mayor accompanying it, and reports of Palestinians and far Left activists confronting Jewish youths near Abu Falah. They also warned of a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria.
“The facts must determine the conclusions. Not the headlines,” his office said.
The effect was to shift attention from the alleged perpetrators to the credibility and motives of those accusing them.
Netanyahu's statements deviate from definitive condemnations by US officials
Netanyahu’s qualified statements do not match the unequivocal response of US Ambassador Mike Huckabee, who can hardly be accused of hostility toward the settlement enterprise. Huckabee condemned the assault on Levine as terrorism by “masked cowards” and demanded an investigation, arrests, and prosecution.
Nor was he alone. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was disturbed by the images and had repeatedly asked Israel to crack down.
Huckabee’s statement is significant. When an outspoken friend of the settlements calls such violence terrorism, it becomes harder to portray it as just another predictable attack on settlers. His response demonstrates that defending Jewish settlement and demanding forceful action against Jewish extremists are compatible.
For Netanyahu, however, the violence puts two political assets in tension: his partnership with the hard Right and his claim to be the indispensable manager of Israel’s relationship with Washington.
Netanyahu has several audiences to satisfy.
Washington expects enforcement. His right-wing partners and voters expect him to resist what they see as efforts to exploit confrontations and provocations to discredit the settlements. And mainstream Israelis, including many on the Right, recoil at images of masked Jews rushing civilians with clubs.
His statements try to satisfy all three by condemning the violence, withholding judgment on the incidents, and rejecting collective blame.
Does Netanyahu's response reflect political spin?
The question is how he can sustain that balancing act. Condemning violence is one thing; going after the perpetrators at the risk of antagonizing elements within his own political camp is quite another. Is Netanyahu’s caution just responsible fact-checking, or does it reflect political dependencies that constrain his ability to impose order?
For the opposition leaders, the answer is obvious. But their responses also reveal different electoral calculations.
Yisrael Beytenu’s Avigdor Liberman made the connection to Netanyahu’s political survival most explicitly.
“Bibi is putting out statements in English,” he wrote, while the prime minister and his defense and national security ministers are “doing nothing to stop this madness.”
The reference to English was pointed: Netanyahu’s concern, Liberman was suggesting, is to reassure foreign audiences while avoiding the confrontation at home that effective enforcement would require.
Liberman’s implicit accusation is that Netanyahu’s political dependence on Otzma Yehudit leader Itamar Ben-Gvir and Religious Zionist Party head Bezalel Smotrich limits his willingness to act.
It also challenges Netanyahu’s diplomatic credentials: What good is privileged access to a sympathetic administration in Washington if his coalition’s conduct keeps generating friction with it?
In his social media post on the violent incidents, Gadi Eisenkot placed greater emphasis on security and leadership. He described the violence as Jewish terrorism under government auspices, warning that a handful of criminals were eroding Israel’s legitimacy, endangering security forces, and damaging national security.
He also, notably, identified the settlement enterprise as a victim, saying these acts harm it. By taking this approach, he appeals to voters who support settlements but reject lawlessness. Eisenkot is arguing that tolerating extremists endangers what those voters value, and that protecting the settlement enterprise requires confronting people committing violence in its name.
His final warning carried a clear post-October 7 resonance: “No one in the leadership will be able to claim that they weren’t woken up in time and that they weren’t warned.”
The language evokes the debate over when Netanyahu was awakened on October 7 and reinforces Eisenkot’s broader campaign argument that Israel needs leaders who recognize danger and act before disaster strikes.
Opposition heads speak to settlers, vow to change tide
Naftali Bennett made a similar appeal, but spoke more directly to the settlers themselves.
He stressed that the perpetrators do not represent half a million residents of Judea and Samaria. “This is an un-Jewish, immoral act,” he said, promising that a new government would confront the criminals and “restore governance.”
Bennett’s message is that the government’s self-proclaimed champions of settlement are endangering its future, and that he would protect it more effectively.
There is considerable overlap with Eisenkot, but their emphases differ. Eisenkot speaks as a prospective national leader sounding a security alarm. Bennett speaks more explicitly as a defender of the settler community who would restore order in its interests.
Democrats Party leader Yair Golan, in his response, provided the most detailed account of what a different government would do.
“Jewish terror must be fought with an iron fist, just as Palestinian terror is fought,” he said.
He called for restoring administrative detention for “dangerous Jewish terror activists,” dismantling centers of terrorist activity, evacuating illegal outposts, and arresting and prosecuting offenders. He also promised full government backing for the military, Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) and police.
That specificity may energize his voters. It also gives Netanyahu material to portray the prospective government as a threat to the settlement project, particularly his call to evacuate illegal outposts.
In the immediate aftermath of the weekend’s incidents, Netanyahu tried to prevent the violence from becoming an indictment of his government or the wider settler population. Meanwhile, the leaders of the opposition strove to make Netanyahu’s handling of it a test of his fitness to remain in power.
The prime minister and his opponents – with the exception of Golan – describe the perpetrators as a small minority. But that leaves the question his opponents want voters to ask: If the minority is so small, why has his government been unable – or unwilling – to stop it?

Health staff in Edmonton said a "code orange," or mass-casualty event, was declared to coordinate the medical response for patients being transported from Wainwright, CBC News reported.

Hours after Israeli militants attacked a delegation of European diplomats, French clerics and a visiting mayor in the occupied West Bank, Israel’s leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, responded by questioning the delegation’s account of the assault.

Instead Netanyahu’s team dismissed video of Bernard Baudoux, the mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France, on the ground grimacing in pain and shock, photos of the smashed window of a diplomatic car, and footage of masked men threatening diplomats and activists with sticks.

“We call on the public and responsible journalists to demand verifiable evidence, reject hearsay and refuse to turn unproven allegations into a collective indictment of the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria [the occupied West Bank],” it said.
Guardian footage
Footage below filmed by the Guardian (no audio) shows the moments before Israeli settlers attacked the French mayor Bernard Baudoux, who was in the Palestinian town of Taybeh with a delegation of European diplomats. A second clip shows the immediate aftermath of the attack. The final section shows one group of settlers attacking the car carrying Baudoux and others.
Verifying the details of attacks can be painstaking journalistic work, seeking out eyewitness accounts, photos and videos for confirmation.
But this weekend the Guardian was in Taybeh, and witnessed the masked militants speeding up a hill in order to attack diplomats and French visitors who had spent a morning peacefully harvesting olives with Palestinians who own the groves.
Shortly after 1pm, they were warned that settlers had attacked Palestinians harvesting olives nearby. Keen to avoid confrontation, the group decided to leave and were approaching their vehicles as the militants closed in, masked, menacing and brandishing sticks.
The Guardian filmed the moments before Baudoux was assaulted, showing him approaching an SUV with his wife and Vincent Dollmann, the archbishop of Cambrai, escorted by diplomatic security. Our vehicle pulled away, making room for the two parked by the road to follow.
Moments later the settlers attacked, apparently determined not only to force the foreigners to flee but to extract a price for joining Palestinians on their land.
It was clear the group contained foreign dignitaries because the cars had diplomatic plates, and Baudoux was apparently targeted for his nationality, because he was wearing his mayor’s sash of office. One of the attackers aggressively shouted “France, France” before pushing him to the ground, eyewitnesses said.
Metadata from that video shows there were just 22 seconds between the last shot of Baudoux remonstrating with his attackers and footage of him slumped on the ground taken by activists in the second car.
The embassy security team then helped him into the vehicle but the attack continued as they drove off. Footage filmed from the hillside opposite shows the settlers attacking the SUV as pulls away.
The force of their blows smashed one of the reinforced windows at the back of the car, which can be seen intact in the first video. A photo of the crumpled pane taken minutes later in the relative safety of Taybeh shows the force of the impact.
If the militant settlers had broken one of the windows next to the passengers, it is unlikely those inside would have escaped injuries.

Netanyahu’s office described it as an “alleged assault” and a “disputed incident” adding “the facts … remain unclear and are under investigation”.

It didn’t provide details. El-Sissi on Saturday called for parliament to grant him the authorization to deploy troops and military equipment abroad.
The surge in fighting has threatened civilians in both Saudi Arabia and Yemen, which has seen a return to civil war. The interim capital of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, Aden, has seen its airport and a palace used by the government attacked in the past week.

The unexpected crisis facing our expanding cities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
18:35:08 UTC
03:35:08 KST

In brief
- Some metropolitan cemeteries are expected to run out of burial space by the early 2030s.
- Cremation and alternative forms of deathcare are becoming increasingly common in Australia.
Australians are familiar with the housing crisis, but there's a lesser-known land battle occurring right beneath our feet.
Some metropolitan cemeteries are running out of space, and it's raising questions about the accessibility of burial practices and rise of alternative forms of deathcare.
Among them is Rookwood Cemetery in Sydney's west, which is the largest necropolis in the southern hemisphere.
It rivals the size of many suburbs, spanning more than 280 hectares, and has been operating for almost 160 years.
Rob Smart is the acting CEO of Metropolitan Memorial Parks, which manages eight Crown land cemeteries in NSW, including Rookwood.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
He said the company maximises operating space and is trying to acquire more land but almost all of their cemeteries are expected to reach capacity by the early 2030s.
"As our larger sites do run out of land, that puts pressure on all of the other sites that might still have land," he told SBS News.
It's not just Metropolitan Memorial Parks, with many cemeteries in major cities predicting they will reach capacity within the decade.
That's in part due to the growth of urban areas, according to Ben Kelly, the CEO of the Australasian Cemeteries and Crematoria Association.
"You look at Rookwood in Sydney, that was right on the outskirts, and now, that's almost an inner suburb," he said.
"It's just our cities have grown, we just haven't continued building cemeteries."
Another challenge, Kelly said, is that some residents don't want to live next them, while governments had other funding priorities.
"They're worried, they'll ... reduce house prices, that type of thing or they just find them spooky and they're not," he said.
The NSW government is considering converting Carnarvon Golf Club in the Sydney suburb of Lidcombe into a new cemetery, a proposal criticised by some community members, including Auburn MP Lynda Voltz.
She addressed NSW parliament in May regarding risks of flooding in the area.
"At first glance, this proposal may be presented as a practical response to the growing demand for burial space but when you take a closer look, a different picture emerges," she said.
"The planning falls short, key risks are being brushed over and yet the environmental consequences are hard to ignore ... flooding here is frequent."
The proposal remains under review.
According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, last year there were more than 188,000 registered deaths in the nation. Kelly says roughly 75 to 85 per cent of Australians are now cremated.
But some faith groups, including Islam and Judaism, do not permit the practice.
In 2023, the Vatican updated its guidance on cremation, allowing Catholics to request that a small portion of their relative's ashes be preserved in a "place of significance to them".
Smart believes all Australians should be given the option of a traditional burial.
"Australia is a multicultural country and while we do have a broad range of faiths and cultures within Australia, I think, we need to be able to provide choice," he said.
"To say to people, you can't follow your cultural, your faith-based requirements is very restrictive on the individuals, or the families or the communities."
DIY commemorations
While some cemeteries are running out of space for new burials, Hannah Gould, from the University of Melbourne's DeathTech Research Team, said there is often room to keep cremated remains.
She said the way Australians are approaching death and memorial celebrations is also gradually changing, such as with the rise of 'do it yourself' commemorations.
"When it comes to the handling of the body, the vast majority of those processes need to be done by professionals," she said.
"It's not legal in this country to bury somebody or to cremate somebody yourself but kind of everything else now is is increasingly being done by family members and friends.
"You just organise to like get together at the pub with friends, as opposed to having a formal funeral ceremony that's run by a funeral director."
After cremation, ashes can be kept in a permanent place like a cemetery or scattered on private property or certain public areas with permission.
Ashes can also grow into a living memorial tree, be preserved in a memory rock, turned into jewellery, a diamond or even fireworks.
Alternative forms of disposition including sea burials, green or biodegradable burials and full-body human cryonics have taken place around the world.
Upright burials, where the deceased are buried standing, feet first, are also becoming more popular.
Another space-saving measure is renewable tenure, where burial plots are leased for set amounts of time — usually 25, 50 or 99 years — rather than in perpetuity.
If the grave is not renewed after a grace period, the plot can eventually be reused.
It's widely practised in South Australia, while in Western Australia, graves are sold with a 25-year lease known as a grant of right of burial.
Whether a person wants to be cremated or buried, Kelly believes it's important people have conversations about death and disposition while they're still living.
"Trying to plan after the fact of a loved one dying is so difficult," he said.
"So, if they can get in early and have that conversation, you know, put a note on the fridge, a post-it of 'I want to be cremated', it starts a conversation and gets people talking."

The higher-tax proposal experts say could 'secure' Australia’s future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
18:34:54 UTC
03:34:54 KST

In brief
- The GST increase will raise about $76 billion a year, the Grattan Institute said.
- UNSW found that an increase in GST may not hurt lower-income households than commonly thought.
The last time an Australian government owed this much debt, the country was still paying off a world war — except for the COVID-19 pandemic.
As government debt climbs, the Grattan Institute has proposed a controversial solution in a new report: hike one tax, cut another, and put more money in welfare recipients’ pockets.
The think tank argues that raising the country's Goods and Services Tax (GST) and using the money to cut income taxes and boost welfare payments is a solution to the debt issue.
GST is a flat 10 per cent tax applied to the price of most goods and services sold or consumed in Australia.
According to the report, titled "Budget reboot: How to fund Australia’s future", cost-of-living pressures, growing demand for social services, and higher borrowing costs are the drivers of the Australian government's mounting debt.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
It suggests the situation could worsen in the coming years, with factors such as an ageing population, climate change, and high interest rates forcing the government to spend more.
According to the report, raising GST from 10 per cent to 15 per cent and expanding it to include all food would create a more resilient budget.
Can a GST rise help?
Since its introduction by former prime minister John Howard, which came into effect in July 2000, GST has never increased.
"There are no easy paths back to budget sustainability," Aruna Sathanapally, CEO of Grattan Institute and the report's lead author, said.
"But with smarter spending decisions and a tax system that raises sufficient revenue to care for our ageing population, both current and future generations can be better off.
"Reform on this game-changing scale is challenging, but the prize is worth it: a more secure future for Australia's finances, and for all Australians."
A similar 5 per cent increase plan drafted by economist Richard Holden was pitched by Independent MP Kate Chaney in August 2025.
At the time, Holden told SBS News that compared to other "advanced economies", Australia gets about "twice as much of our revenue from income taxes and about half as much of our income from the GST".
At the time, the Greens labelled the plan "lazy", while the Opposition called it "increasingly brave". Meanwhile, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Labor has not considered a possible GST increase.
"Boosting the GST has become a political no-go zone, in part due to disagreements about how to divvy up the revenue, and concerns it would increase the cost of living," the Grattan Institute report stated.
Where should the revenue go?
The GST increase and expansion will raise about $76 billion a year, according to the Grattan Institute.
The think tank suggests using $58 billion to cut income taxes for low- and middle-income earners and boost welfare payments, which could orchestrate the largest personal income tax cuts in nearly 20 years.
"JobSeeker and Youth Allowance should be raised by 20 per cent, Commonwealth Rent Assistance by 50 per cent, the Parenting Payment by 20 per cent, and pensions by about 8 per cent," the report said.
It suggests allocating the remaining revenue to state governments to shore up their budgets and cut inefficient taxes, such as stamp duty.
It predicts that with the GST increase, most households would pay slightly more in taxes, with larger increases for wealthier and older households.
On the other hand, in estimates, a low-income, single-parent family who rents would be about $150 a week better off, while a higher-income working family would pay $162 a week more in tax.
Will an increase in GST be unfair?
For years, the argument against raising GST was that it would be unfair, particularly to lower-income households.
GST is often described as regressive, in that it takes up a larger share of these households’ income than that of higher-income households' income. This is because higher-income households tend to save more of their income while lower-income households generally spend more of what they earn.
In a July 2025 report, the Australian Council of Social Service argued that increasing the GST to fund income tax cuts "would shift resources from those with the least to those with the most".
However, a recent study by e61–UNSW Policy Research Partnership found that GST may be less regressive than commonly thought. It found households that spend more and those that spend less pay roughly the same share of their spending in GST — about 7.3 per cent.
Examining a household's spending in a year doesn't provide the full picture, the UNSW research partnership says. Instead, it examined the spending of households across a longer time, taking into account changes in people’s circumstances, such as studying, taking parental leave or moving between jobs. Averaging the years, the gap in GST spending between lower-income and higher-income households narrows.
In other words, the perceived fairness of the GST depends not only on how much people earn, but also on how their spending, saving and longer-term financial position are measured, UNSW says.
The research argues that a reform that includes an increase in GST and paying back the revenue to people "through an unconditional income payment" would be "progressive, irrespective of the measure of household resources".

Security forces were already making extensive preparations for Saturday's planned demonstrations, preparations that ultimately proved insufficient to contain the violence. 
The video showed the couple smiling and applauding, prompting accusations that they were completely disconnected from a country increasingly furious over soaring living costs, deteriorating public finances, political paralysis and violence in the streets. Some critics even compared them to Marie Antoinette, the wife of King Louis XVI, who became a symbol of royal extravagance while ordinary French citizens suffered hunger and economic hardship in the years preceding the French Revolution.
Mélenchon's warning to Macron: 'Announce measures or we will lose control'
Even before Macron's address, politicians from both the far right and the far left launched direct attacks on the president and his government. Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who is running in next year's presidential election, said in a video released shortly before the speech that Macron's administration had "run out of steam" and was exhausted, disoriented and seemingly incapable of doing anything beyond commenting on its own impotence and decline.
"We have a government that deplores events without managing to prevent them, control them or even deal with them," Le Pen said. "A minority government that has lost its legitimacy, whose sole concern is no longer governing France but clinging to the last remnants of its fading power." Jordan Bardella, president of Le Pen's National Rally party and her close political ally, said shortly beforehand that Saturday's violence had left "France humiliated" and that "there is no longer any order" in the country.
Far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, whose France Unbowed party (LFI) has been accused by political opponents of inciting protesters and bearing significant responsibility for the violence, also attacked Macron. "I am worried. We had to go through this entire wave of violence before Emmanuel Macron finally made his voice heard," he said. "The government adopted a strategy of letting things deteriorate. Macron is sitting on the fence and playing for time."
Mélenchon has repeatedly accused the government and security forces in recent days of using excessive force against protesters and rioters. On Sunday evening, he again accused the authorities of pursuing a policy of "blind violence." Ahead of Macron's speech, he urged the president to announce concrete measures to address protesters' demands, warning that continuing the political deadlock could cause the situation to spiral out of control.
Édouard Philippe, the former center-right prime minister who also intends to run for president next year and has generally been polling behind Le Pen and Mélenchon, blamed both the far left, particularly LFI, and the current government. He said Saturday's events represented more than a breakdown of public order, describing them as a challenge to the foundations of the French Republic. Philippe also demanded answers about the intelligence assessments and security preparations undertaken before the riots erupted.
The widespread destruction prompted calls from politicians on both the left and right for Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez to resign. Members of the Green party also demanded a parliamentary commission of inquiry into both the violence and the policing methods used to contain it. 
"When a day of demonstrations turns into chaos, we must also examine the responsibility of our leaders, particularly the Interior Ministry, which is responsible for public order and everyone's safety," Green senators wrote. Yaël Braun-Pivet, president of the National Assembly, the lower house of the French parliament, also announced plans to propose a parliamentary inquiry.
30,000 people took part in Marseille looting, authorities say
Macron's address followed a Saturday of widespread violence across France, during which large groups of masked rioters attacked police officers and passersby, set dozens of government buildings on fire and looted hundreds of stores. The unrest erupted after a massive afternoon demonstration against rising living costs and deteriorating public services, attended by hundreds of thousands of people.
Politicians on the right in France and abroad have blamed the violence partly on the far left, which they accuse of fueling the unrest as a show of strength ahead of next year's presidential election. Some have also pointed to immigrants and their descendants, alleging that members of those communities participated heavily in the riots. According to the latest figures cited by French authorities in the report, 2,397 people had been arrested and 997 members of the security forces injured, seven of them seriously.
France's Chamber of Commerce estimated Sunday afternoon that at least 1,500 businesses nationwide had been damaged, with losses running into hundreds of millions of euros. Hundreds of stores were reportedly looted in Paris alone, where Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire said "entire streets were systematically devastated."
Le Parisien described widespread destruction in several neighborhoods. In the 1st arrondissement, rioters reportedly spared virtually no stores around Les Halles. "Tobacco shops, opticians, beauty salons, pharmacies, clothing stores and more were all damaged," the newspaper reported. In the 10th arrondissement, near Porte Saint-Denis, dozens of additional businesses were vandalized.
The newspaper described piles of garbage and burned bicycles scattered across sidewalks, some still smoldering. Sanitation workers dispatched to the scene told its reporters, "It will take us days to clean all this up."
In Marseille in southern France, Lille in the north, Angers in the west and Bordeaux in the southwest, rioters stormed and vandalized city halls and regional government buildings on Saturday. Authorities in Marseille said Sunday evening that their assessment indicated at least 30,000 people had participated in the looting that swept the city.
In Lyon, southeastern France, the city's tourist information office was set on fire Saturday. Footage from the scene showed one rioter waving a Palestinian flag. Local police said "hostile individuals" had obstructed firefighters sent to bring the blaze under control.
An even more devastating incident occurred in Limoges, central France, where masked rioters set fire to the historic city hall. The ornate building, inaugurated in 1883 and having survived both world wars, collapsed and was "largely destroyed," according to authorities. Its bell tower also came crashing down, in dramatic footage circulated on social media and viewed by millions around the world.
The riots left many French citizens in shock Sunday. "It's disgraceful, terrifying, these gangs of young people we saw here yesterday, looting and destroying things with impunity," said Cécile Rogue, 57, in Paris.
Similar emotions were expressed outside the destroyed Limoges city hall. "My children got married here. It's heartbreaking," said Jean-Louis, a retired local resident. "You can make demands without destroying everything."
Volunteers spontaneously turned out to help clear debris from the devastated streets of several city centers, partly to overcome their sense of helplessness. "I woke up this morning, was left speechless and just wanted to feel useful," said Clémentine, 47, from Lyon, who came to help with the cleanup.
Trump to France: 'Immigration has crushed you, close your borders!'
The weekend riots followed a nationwide day of protest against the high cost of living, deteriorating public services and rising fuel prices. High school and university students, labor unions and members of the Yellow Vest movement, which emerged in 2018 in opposition to Macron's economic policies, all joined the demonstrations.
Many view Saturday's protests as a continuation of student demonstrations that began last month in schools in impoverished suburbs north of Paris, where pupils have complained of teacher shortages and poor learning conditions. Those protests also saw numerous incidents of violence, and similar unrest has since spread to other European countries, including Belgium.
In France and abroad, some commentators and politicians have emphasized the involvement of immigrants and their descendants from Africa, Arab countries and Muslim-majority nations in the demonstrations and violence. Marion Maréchal, the niece of far-right leader Marine Le Pen and a politician in her own right, said Saturday night: "The whole world is watching in astonishment and disbelief as the children of Mélenchon's 'New France' destroy our country."
The term "New France" was coined by Mélenchon to describe his vision of a society in which immigrant communities are an integral part of the nation. Maréchal has used it critically to warn against demographic changes that she and other figures on the French right regard as a serious threat to the country's future.
Claims about the role of immigrant communities in the unrest have circulated since the student protests earlier this month, and U.S. President Donald Trump has also weighed in. About two weeks ago, amid a "day of rage" on French streets, Trump wrote on Truth Social that the protests were not really about schools but were a cover for other aims.
"What is happening in France is nothing more than mass immigration that has gotten out of control," he wrote. "This is not about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great country!"
On Sunday, following the weekend's violence, Trump issued another post attacking France's immigration policies. "France is burning!" he wrote. "Immigration of people from a completely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has crushed this once great country. Close your borders and take control before it's too late!"

Cut benefits to fund work support for young people, says Neet review author Alan Milburn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
18:30:19 UTC
03:30:19 KST

Ministers should cut welfare spending to fund more employment support if it wants to end the youth Neet crisis, the author of a government-led review has said.
Alan Milburn, the Tony Blair-era health secretary, told the Guardian he believed ministers should reduce benefits payments to help pay for more employment support, opening a potentially contentious debate within the Labour party over welfare cuts.
His intervention comes in the run-up to John Healey’s first budget, at which the chancellor is under pressure to explain how he will reduce a multibillion-pound black hole in the country’s finances and pay for more cost of living support without increasing borrowing.
“We’ve got to have a different conversation about the welfare system, it just isn’t working for young people,” Milburn told the Guardian. “We need to redistribute money from the welfare system to more employment support if we are going to end the Neet crisis.”
Milburn’s review of why so many 18- to 24-year-olds are not in education, employment or training calculated that a record 1 million young people are now classed as Neet. The former cabinet minister said this was far more than a cyclical youth unemployment problem – it was a “youth detachment” problem, pointing to the fact that 60% of these Neets have never had a job.
Ministers have pushed back Milburn’s final report until after the budget, at which Healey is expected to use a tax raid on banks to help pay for cost of living schemes such as a new energy support package.
The chancellor has signalled his willingness to spend more money on youth unemployment programmes in the short term, however, even if the welfare savings take longer to be realised. He announced a £100m “local apprenticeship service” at last month’s Labour conference, calling it “a downpayment on Alan Milburn’s work”.
In a joint interview with Peter Fonagy, the chair of the government’s landmark independent review of mental health, ADHD and autism, Milburn said his final recommendations were not just about tackling youth unemployment but also improving wellbeing.
“The Neet crisis is a health crisis,” he said. “We’re in this vicious cycle where ill health is driving higher Neet rates. Non-participation is a disaster for young people’s mental health.”
Milburn’s review is likely to recommend that employment, health and benefits support become more integrated. “We have got to change how the wealth, health and welfare systems work and how they interact with each other, because right now they’re plunging far too many young people into a life on benefits, which is ruinous to their life chances, rather than the opportunity to work,” he said.
“No one [in government] is responsible for ensuring that young people both avoid the trap door of becoming Neet and get support to get them out of being Neet.”
Fonagy’s review found that the number of people suffering mental distress has risen significantly across all age groups in England since the 1990s, especially the under-18s. It recommended providing help at the point of need, not after a diagnosis.
“The current system is based on identifying disability, why a person can’t do something,” Fonagy said. “We need a system that actually addresses their potential and what it is that they can do.
“If nothing is done, and the trends go on as up till now, then there will be not one in five young people with diagnosable mental disorders, but one in four,” which, he added, increased the chances of them becoming Neet.
While there will always be a group of young people whose physical or mental health mean work is not an option, “for the vast majority of young people with autism, ADHD, anxiety or depression, the starting point has to be what could you do, what would you like to do, and how can the state help them do it,” Milburn said.
Young people with health needs should get prompt needs assessment, a personalised health plan and a wider “participation plan”, the review is likely to recommend.
The kind of transformation Milburn and Fonagy describe would cost hundreds of millions of pounds in investment, sources believe. While they would not comment on the level of funding required, both were clear that upfront money would be crucial. “I think everybody in government is very, very well aware of the need to invest behind this priority,” Milburn said.
“Over the medium term, it is entirely possible that you can reduce the benefits bill, but in order to do that, you’ve got to provide the support for young people. You’ve got to increase the opportunities that are available for young people and then provide the support for them to enable them to grab those opportunities.”
“This is not a workshy, snowflake generation, you know, who are making mental distress up,” Milburn added. “If we provide more opportunities and we provide more support, the overwhelming majority of young people will take that, because that’s what they want. The system isn’t delivering what young people want, which is a job.”
But Milburn also hinted at possible consequences for those who don’t engage. “Equally, there has got to be an obligation on young people to take up those opportunities, of course,” he said.
The problem with the system was that it was “over-indexed to cash” and didn’t provide enough support, he added. “The consequence is calamitous for young people who could be working and are not being helped to do so, who then end up on a trajectory to a lifetime on benefits.”
But intervening earlier and providing better support would in turn help relieve the pressure on the mental health waiting list. “I would hope that, for the first time, we could also introduce a maximum waiting time for mental health services, particularly for young people,” said Milburn.

At least one person was killed, and five others were wounded in the attack in St. Petersburg, which sparked fires at the Petersburg Oil Terminal and the city's Ruchi oil depot, local Gov. Alexander Beglov said.
A logistics center belonging to Russian retailer Ozon and a data center operated by Russian tech giant VK were also targeted, the companies confirmed.
Russia's Defense Ministry said Sunday that its forces had destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions, the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agency Tass that Kyiv was "resisting" Moscow's invasion but could not "change the current course of events."
Meanwhile, in Ukraine, a woman was killed and a 6-year-old girl was among at least two other people wounded in two Russian attacks on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, local officials said Sunday.
The strikes came as tensions between Ukraine and Washington deepened. President Trump has recently been critical of his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and Kyiv's attacks on Russian oil infrastructure.
Meanwhile, there is still uncertainty about the prospect of further U.S. sanctions on Moscow.

He occupied us. He killed adults and children, his soldiers. He's a terrorist. And that's why I hope that President Trump will be very clear with this position."
Later Sunday, Zelenskyy said on social media that he had spoken with U.S. presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner about the results of an Oct. 9 meeting between U.S. and Ukrainian negotiating teams in Miami, as well as "next steps in diplomacy."
He also accused Moscow of breaking Mr. Trump's "energy ceasefire" 76 times and warned that Russia planned to deprive Ukrainians of heat and electricity before winter.

Energy facilities in four Ukrainian regions were struck overnight, leaving tens of thousands of families without power, he said, accusing Russia of trying to cause a blackout.
"America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements. On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting," he wrote.

Uzbekistan to set up Tashkent International Fashion Academy
A new international fashion academy will be established in Tashkent under a presidential resolution aimed at strengthening education and workforce development for Uzbekistan’s light industry sector, Qazinform News Agency cites UzA.
The Tashkent International Fashion Academy will operate as a state higher education institution under the Agency for the Development of Light Industry. It will be created on the foundation of a joint educational program previously launched by the Tashkent Institute of Textile and Light Industry in partnership with the Paris International Fashion Academy.
Students currently enrolled in the joint program will continue their studies at the new academy and will receive academy-issued diplomas upon graduation. The institution is set to begin classes in the 2026/2027 academic year, with admissions conducted in accordance with existing national regulations.
In addition to joint educational programs, the academy will offer its own bachelor's and master's degree courses. Starting from the 2027/2028 academic year, it will introduce a dual education system to train specialists for the textile, garment, knitwear, leather, and footwear industries in line with labor market needs.
The academy will also support the development of national fashion brands and provide clothing design services for government organizations under state contracts.
Under the new framework, graduates of technical colleges specializing in light industry will be eligible to enter the third year of a bachelor's program on a fee-paying basis, provided they meet academic performance requirements set by the academy.
To attract international talent, foreign faculty, administrative staff, their family members, and international students will be eligible for multiple-entry visas and simplified registration procedures.
The resolution also includes plans to build a 400-bed student dormitory through a public-private partnership by the end of 2028. Until the facility is completed, students transferring from the Tashkent Institute of Textile and Light Industry will be able to use the institute's existing dormitories.

The two people killed on Saturday when a woman in a truck drove through a youth soccer game in north-east Wichita, Kansas, were a six-year-old boy and a 35-year-old man, according to authorities.
Eleven other people between the ages of five and 68 were injured in a case whose possible motivations remained unclear early on Sunday, when it was still capturing widespread attention across the US.
In a news briefing updating initial information, Wichita police said the driver at the center of the case was a 34-year-old woman from Garden City, Kansas, which is about three and a half hours away by car.
Authorities did not immediately release her name any of the victims’ names, including the two killed.
Police said they took the driver into custody after she drove through a field at Stryker Sports Complex during a youth soccer game at about 3.30pm on Saturday.
When police and paramedics arrived in response to emergency calls, they found the truck on the west field of the complex. Two juveniles were inside the truck with the driver, Wichita police captain, Aaron Moses, told news media.
The woman has a valid driver’s license and no outstanding warrants, Moses said.
The boy and man who were killed were both from McPherson, Kansas, about an hour drive north of Wichita. Police said the victims were not related.
Ten of those injured had serious but not life-threatening injuries, police said. Those included children aged five, eight and nine – as well as adults between 28 and 68 years old.
The 11th person reported as injured was a 61-year-old woman who had nontraumatic medical issues, police said.
The competitive youth soccer club McPherson City FC said in a Facebook post on Saturday that it had “suffered an unimaginable tragedy at Stryker Soccer Complex”.
“We ask that you keep all those involved in your thoughts and prayers,” the club’s post continued. “Dealing with a loss of this magnitude also calls for privacy and respect for all our soccer community. Please allow time for healing and grieving to take place and be there for those that seek guidance.”
After saying that McPherson City FC would later post further information in regards to the club and its upcoming events, the post concluded: “Please hold your loved ones tight tonight.”
McPherson’s municipal government wrote in a separate Facebook post: “Our community is hurting, and we stand together, and in support.”
“Stay strong, McPherson,” that post also said. “Be there [and] be kind.”
Stryker Sports Complex announced that all events had been cancelled there until further notice.
“We ask that you keep all individuals and families affected in your thoughts and prayers during this difficult time,” the complex also said in its announcement. “Please avoid the complex to allow emergency personnel to carry out their work.
“Updates regarding future events will be shared as information becomes available.”
Meanwhile, the Kansas State High School Activities Association also suspended its third-place and championship flag football games, which had been scheduled for later on Saturday at the complex.
“The KSHSAA extends our condolences to the families and teams [affected] by the incident,” the association said.
The organization said it planned on providing details about rescheduled games on Monday.
Saturday marked the second time in less than 26 years that the athletic complex near the corner of North Greenwich Road and East 29th Street was at the center of a high-profile, deadly case.
Brothers named Jonathan and Reginald Carr were convicted of shooting five people – including four fatally – on a snow-covered field there in December 2000 during a crime spree that also involved robbery, rape and torture, according to information culled from court filings and media reports.
The Carrs were sentenced to die over what some have referred to as the “Wichita massacre”. And in July, Kansas governor Laura Kelly denied their requests for their death sentences to be commuted to life imprisonment.

Italian police arrest 28 after cost-of-living protests turn violent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
18:17:43 UTC
03:17:43 KST

Italian police have arrested 28 people, including 12 minors, following clashes during cost-of-living protests across several cities.
Tensions continued in central Milan on Sunday after Saturday’s demonstrations, Sky TG24 reported, citing police figures showing 141 law enforcement officers were injured.
Police said 197 people were identified and taken to police stations, while 43 were referred to judicial authorities.
Organised by the Italia in Piazza movement, the protests targeted rising living costs, fuel prices and tax pressures. Police estimated turnout at 5,000 in Milan, 3,000 in Turin, 2,000 in Bologna, 800 in Bergamo and 600 in Brescia.
In Milan, groups threw stones, bottles, firecrackers and barriers at officers, who responded with tear gas and water cannon. Shops in the city centre were damaged and looted, and a Carabinieri vehicle was destroyed.
Police arrested 17 people in the city. Retail association Confcommercio estimated damage to shops and businesses at more than €500,000 ($561,860), according to Sky TG24.
In Turin, officers arrested an adult for resisting police and three minors allegedly carrying Molotov cocktails. A group also entered the Feltrinelli bookstore at Porta Nuova station and threw books onto the floor.
In Bologna, five minors were arrested following clashes near the railway station. Police used tear gas and water cannon after demonstrators threw bottles, stones and barriers.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed solidarity with law enforcement and urged opposition parties to unequivocally condemn the violence, while acknowledging that thousands had protested peacefully.
Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini said his League party would resubmit a parliamentary proposal requiring organisers of demonstrations deemed risky to provide financial guarantees to cover potential damage.
Milan Mayor Giuseppe Sala said protesters’ grievances were understandable, but attacks on officers and extensive damage to the city were unjustifiable.
Bologna Mayor Matteo Lepore also condemned the unrest, urging young people to distance themselves from those using demonstrations as a pretext for violence.
