Language Lab Marks 10 Years With Launch of Ukraine Connected
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
17:59:00 UTC
02:59:00 KST

Language Lab, the Kyiv-based Ukrainian language school, marked its tenth anniversary with an evening at The Last Barricade, the restaurant under Independence Square known for its tribute to Ukraine’s protest movements. The event, held at the beginning of the month, brought together students, teachers and friends of the school. It also served as the launch of Ukraine Connected, a new community for foreigners and Ukrainians that grew out of the informal support the school has long offered its students.
“The 10th anniversary event went wonderfully. And considering the circumstances – the war and constant air-raid alerts – I would even say it was incredible,” said Nataliia Antonenko, one of the school’s teachers. In the days after, she said, the team received many thank-you messages from students.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Ten years ago, Language Lab started as a small school in Kyiv. Today it brings together people from more than 50 countries who have chosen to learn Ukrainian in person or online and connect with Ukraine,” said founder Ksenia Golubytska.
“We have never stopped working, not during COVID and not during the full-scale invasion and ongoing war, because our students needed us,” she said. “Over the years, many of them came to us not just for lessons, but for advice and support with life here. That’s why we chose our 10th birthday to launch Ukraine Connected: a community where everyone who feels connected to Ukraine can find help, friends and a sense of home.”
Kyiv: From Kyivan Rus to Hidden Courtyards
                                                                                                                                                                         Photo of Language Lab’s 10-year-anniversary celebration in Kyiv. (Photo: Language Lab)                              
Grammar at the party
Teachers weren’t sure what guests would want from the evening. Aliona Skliar said she wondered whether students would bother with the Ukrainian-language tasks the teachers had prepared, or would simply want to chat.
“It turned out they were interested in challenging themselves a little,” she said. “Throughout the event, beside networking, many people came to our stand with tasks.”
Teacher Oksana Matii said what struck her most was how naturally people connected. “It reminded us that a language school is not only about learning a language – it is also about creating connections and a sense of community,” she said.
Not everyone remembers the evening for its big moments. Jay Tagliani, a volunteer who has studied with the school for about a month, singled out the food, especially the roast beef appetizers, and the 1,000-hryvnia wine voucher he unexpectedly won.
“It was just a good chance to meet folk and talk,” said James Glennie, a Language Lab student who works in energy and power systems.
                                                                                                                                                                         Photo of Language Lab’s 10-year-anniversary celebration in Kyiv. (Photo: Language Lab)                              
Why learn Ukrainian
For the students, learning Ukrainian is less a hobby than a practical necessity.
“In order to live in a country, one must speak the language,” said Bas, a Language Lab student who declined to give his last name.
Bas said he’s lived in Ukraine since 2012 and has studied with the school for about three years. He listed asking for help, handling documents, contracts and landlords as important reasons for learning Ukrainian.
“You can’t stay ‘the tourist’ forever when you live somewhere.”
Brian True, from Corunna, Michigan, runs a nonprofit that imports human cornea implants and works to develop private eye-banking in Ukraine. He said he has always struggled with languages, but working under Ukrainian laws and regulations made it essential. He wants to speak with people and understand the documents in his daily work.
For Glennie, it pays off “almost every day.” Understanding Ukrainian helps him follow what is happening around him, he said, and lets him keep up in meetings “without having to have every word translated.”
Even a little goes a long way. Tagliani said supermarket trips are now much less stressful. On Ukrainian trains, where he often sits close to strangers who strike up conversations, he has gotten better each time at making himself understood.
Several students said Ukrainians respond warmly to the effort.
“By learning and speaking the language at any level, you show respect for the nation,” True said, “and in return earn and develop both respect and credibility from those who are from here.”
                                                                                                                                                                         Photo of Language Lab’s 10-year-anniversary celebration in Kyiv. (Photo: Language Lab)                              
Help beyond the classroom
Students describe a school that has often helped with life outside lessons.
Glennie said his teacher helps him “constantly with innumerable minor things which locals take for granted.” These include setting up air-raid alerts, finding a vet, dentist or optician, and explaining the mood in Kyiv. The absence of such knowledge, he said, makes life much harder for new arrivals.
Building a social life was the hardest part of arriving, many said. “Everything!” Glennie said. “New country, new town, new apartment, new people, new language and no instant network arising from having a job to go to.”
True said his biggest early hurdle was bureaucracy. He listed four things every foreigner needs to sort out: a temporary residency card, a registered address, a bank account and a work permit. Help with those would have saved him time and stress, he said. He is still building a social circle beyond work contacts, and said Language Lab “has provided a community from which to grow.”
Ukraine Connected aims to formalize that kind of help. Skliar, who also coordinates international volunteers for a charity, said she plans to share the tips she gives foreign volunteers with community members, along with volunteering opportunities.
                                                                                                                                                                         Photo of Language Lab’s 10-year-anniversary celebration in Kyiv. (Photo: Language Lab)                              
“How will UC differentiate itself?”
Not every student is convinced yet. Glennie said he enjoys networking, but warned that any new group “needs to be approached with great care,” with a clear idea of what it offers that others do not.
“There are already some excellent networking organizations out there,” he said. “How will UC differentiate itself?”
Organizers point to one goal: connecting foreigners with Ukrainians, not just with each other.
True said that is often harder than it sounds. “Ukrainians are very private people; yet once they get to know you, they will be open and kind,” he said. Getting established socially, he added, “can take time and patience.”
                                                                                                                                                                         Photo of Language Lab’s 10-year-anniversary celebration in Kyiv. (Photo: Language Lab)                              
Planning for a hard winter
Teachers say the community is being built with the war in mind.
“We hope for the best, but we prepare for the worst,” Antonenko said. She expects the next few months to be difficult. Events may move to shelters when needed, and safety will come first.
Matii said events will be planned around possible air-raid alerts and disruptions, and can move online when necessary. Members may also leave Ukraine, return, or join remotely. “We want it to remain a supportive community where people can stay connected regardless of where they are,” she said.
Antonenko said she hopes Ukraine Connected can become a “Point of Invincibility” for foreigners living and working here. The phrase refers to the heated, powered public shelters Ukraine set up during Russian attacks on the energy grid.
“We want Ukraine Connected to be a place where people can stay connected, support each other, and feel that they are not alone, even in these difficult circumstances,” she said.

“There is no more light in a genius than in any other honest man — but he has a…

"This is because the whole nation is on the streets against the Vote Chors," he claimed, alleging, "Every time Vote Chori is caught, the Modi govt adopts a new tactic: stopping readable voter rolls, fake voter additions, SIR. But not this time."

Stop the politics of shoot & scoot!" he added.This comes after Rahul Gandhi, along with other opposition parties, filed a petition in the Supreme Court on October 12, alleging large-scale voter deletions and irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.

Trump says Washington golf course renovation to start in November, despite judge's order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
17:50:52 UTC
02:50:52 KST

Trump says Washington golf course renovation to start in November, despite judge’s order
WASHINGTON - President Donald Trump on Oct 18 unveiled his plans for overhauling a beloved municipal golf course in the US capital, a project already mired in a contentious legal fight.
On Truth Social, Trump posted a mockup of an 18-hole course which would dramatically change the historic East Potomac Golf Links, saying construction is set to start in November.
“When completed, it will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments such as the US Open, the PGA Championship, the Ryder Cup, and the Presidents Cup,” Trump said.
A federal judge last week excoriated the Trump administration for cutting down hundreds of trees at the golf course with less than a day’s notice, in an apparent circumvention of her previous order requiring prior notification of such work.
Judge Ana Reyes has scheduled a follow-up hearing for Oct 19 and ordered senior officials with the Interior Department, which oversees the property, to testify.
The Trump administration has meanwhile asked for Reyes to recuse herself from the matter, claiming she has shown “animus” toward the government.
The redesign of the East Potomac Golf Links, which has operated for over a century, is just one of Trump’s pet projects to unilaterally remake Washington during his second and final term in office.
Others include the construction of a massive White House ballroom that required demolishing the entire historic East Wing, overhauling the Kennedy Center arts venue and plans for an immense triumphal arch.
Those projects have all similarly been met with various legal challenges, including claims that Congress must give its consent to such large changes.
The course is situated on an island in the Potomac River, and is currently surrounded by roads and paths frequently used by bikers, picnickers and for fishing.
The design Trump posted on Oct 18 appears to eliminate those public areas.
A keen golfer and owner of several golf clubs, Trump has had his eye on overhauling the East Potomac course since returning to office in 2025.
“The current Course is old, broken, dilapidated, and of no further use or effect. It is in very poor condition, with falling, dangerous, and disease infested trees and, importantly, a collapsing and hazardous seawall,” he said on Oct 18.
Work on the new project is set to begin on Nov 15 and take 15 months to complete, Trump said, without commenting on the ongoing legal saga. AFP

Egypt parliament delays vote on military support to Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
17:48:30 UTC
02:48:30 KST

Breadcrumb
Egypt parliament delays vote on military support to Saudi Arabia
Egypt's parliament on Sunday postponed a vote on President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi's request to authorise military support for Saudi Arabia, two lawmakers told AFP, with deliberations set to continue on Monday.
The session was convened after Sisi asked lawmakers to approve support for Saudi Arabia's defence if requested by the kingdom, which has come under near-daily attacks from Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis since early October.
"The session was extended to give all lawmakers the opportunity to speak and express their views," lawmaker Ibrahim Kholeif told AFP, adding that parliamentarians were mostly in support of the move.
Another member, Maha Abdel Nasser, said proceedings would resume Monday "to allow all lawmakers to be heard".
Egyptian media reported that deliberations would continue into Tuesday.
Both lawmakers said no details were being discussed about what form Egypt's military support for Saudi Arabia could take.
Sisi on Saturday requested parliamentary authorisation to help defend Saudi Arabia "if requested", saying it was "inconceivable" for Cairo to stand by as Saudi Arabia's security and stability are threatened.
The decade-plus war between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen's internationally-recognised government reignited in July.
The Houthis seized Yemen's Red Sea coastline in September and have since launched attacks on Saudi Arabia, including state oil giant Aramco and Riyadh's international airport, where 13 people were killed a week ago.
On Saturday, Sisi called for an end to the fighting and said Egypt was not seeking to "confront or attack anyone. We are speaking only about defence".
Houthi threats to Egypt
Egypt's constitution requires the approval of both parliament and the National Defence Council -- which includes the leaders of Egypt's security apparatus -- before troops can be deployed on combat missions abroad.
Shortly before the parliamentary session, the council, chaired by Sisi, approved providing Saudi Arabia with "all necessary and available forms of support" to help defend its security, territorial integrity and Islamic holy sites, the presidency said.
Potential military involvement would constitute a break from Egypt's historically conservative foreign policy, which has prioritised protecting its own national security.
For years Cairo has positioned itself as a regional mediator with channels open across conflict lines, including with Hamas, Israel and Iran.
In response to Sisi's call on Saturday, Houthi parliament speaker Yehia Ali al-Rai addressed a letter of warning to his Egyptian counterpart.
"Egypt's slide down this path would pose a grave danger to its own national security and internal stability before anyone else's," he wrote, according to the Houthis' Saba news agency.
Throughout this year, as its Gulf allies have come under attack in the war between Iran and the US, Cairo has repeatedly preached caution.
The Arab world's largest military did not issue a response even when its own Damietta port was struck by an unidentified drone in July.
It has not joined the Mecca defence pact signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan in August, according to experts to maintain its strategic autonomy.
But Riyadh is one of Cairo's strongest allies, and a key financial backer to Sisi's administration for over a decade.
Egypt joined the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen in 2015, contributing naval and air forces and deploying warships to the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Along with Saudi Arabia, Egypt is hardest hit by disruptions through Bab al-Mandab, the southern gateway to its Suez Canal, revenues from which have not recovered since Houthi attacks began in 2023.
Military expert Samir Farag told AFP that Egyptian assistance could take several forms, ranging from intelligence, military advisers, ammunition and spare parts to weapons and, ultimately, troop deployments.

Milan police clash with protesters on second day of unrest
MILAN, Oct 18 - Milan police clashed on Sunday with protesters throwing stones and looting shops during demonstrations against poor services and the rising cost of living, a day after similar unrest in several Italian cities.
Police in riot gear fired tear gas and used water cannons after several hundred hooded protesters broke shop windows and set bins on fire in the area near central Piazza Duomo, sources with knowledge of the investigation told Reuters.
More than 60 protesters were taken to the police station for further checks, the sources added.
A total of 28 protesters were arrested after similar clashes erupted on Saturday in northern cities including Milan, Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo and Turin, according to a police report on Sunday.
The clashes had echoes of the violence in neighbouring France, where hundreds of thousands of people angered by rising costs and declining public services took to the streets on Saturday in some of the country's most violent protests in years.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, facing an election next year, condemned the violence and announced a government meeting on Monday to discuss how to address the situation. REUTERS

Carney says 4 killed, dozens seriously wounded in fire at Canadian military base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
17:32:17 UTC
02:32:17 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
18 October 2026•Update: 18 October 2026
Four people were killed and dozens more seriously wounded after a fast-moving fire swept through a Canadian military base in Alberta, Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Sunday, describing the incident as one of the worst peacetime tragedies for the country's armed forces.
“I regret that I can confirm at this time that Forest Service members have lost their lives, and their next of kin has been notified. Dozens more are seriously wounded,” Carney told reporters.
The blaze broke out on Saturday afternoon at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, about 200 kilometers (124 miles) southeast of Edmonton, spreading beyond a training area as strong winds hampered firefighting efforts.
“Yesterday afternoon, a violent, fast-moving fire swept through Canadian Armed Forces base in Wainwright, Alberta,” he said. “What followed was one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime.”
Defense Minister David McGuinty confirmed that the incident caused casualties but withheld figures, describing the situation as “active and delicate.”
The Canadian Armed Forces said the fire was first reported at around 4 pm local time (2200GMT) on a training range before spreading beyond its boundaries. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police are investigating, while military and civilian authorities coordinate the response.
Carney said military personnel and civilian crews battled the blaze throughout the night, while air ambulance crews flew in from Edmonton and Saskatoon to assist the wounded.
“The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces we have lost,” he said, adding that flags on federal buildings would be flown at half-mast.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith described the fire as “significant and tragic,” while Chief of the Defence Staff Gen. Jennie Carignan said the military was working closely with authorities to support those affected.
Carney pledged long-term support for victims and their families.
“We will care for the injured through every step of their recovery, and we will stand by the women and men of our armed forces as they bear the weight of this loss,” he said. “They will not carry it alone.”

====================================================================================================

Trump has a chance to unite Saudi Arabia, UAE, and Israel against Iran and the Houthis - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
17:31:24 UTC
02:31:24 KST

Iran’s strongest remaining proxy, Yemen’s Houthis, are doing more than threatening international shipping through the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
They are exposing an uncomfortable reality: Saudi Arabia, despite spending hundreds of billions on defense, remains dangerously vulnerable to an Iranian-backed militia.
The Houthis, radical Shi’ites whose revolutionary zeal mirrors the uncompromising jihadism of Sunni ISIS, harbor ambitions extending beyond Yemen to challenging the Saudi monarchy and seizing Mecca and Medina, Islam’s two holiest sites.
Their attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure, military installations, tankers, and Riyadh’s international airport expose the kingdom’s vulnerability. Threats to its East-West pipeline, a critical alternative to the Iranian-threatened Strait of Hormuz, further underscore the strategic danger.
The question Washington must ask is simple: Why should America continue defending wealthy Gulf allies unwilling or unable to defend themselves?
The Mecca defense pact: An alliance on paper?
The answer should begin with the recently signed Mecca Joint Defense Agreement between Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan.
The agreement declares that an armed attack against one member constitutes an attack against all three.
Yet the Houthi attacks raise a fundamental question: Will this new Muslim defense alliance ever confront an Iranian proxy, or is collective security merely diplomatic theater?
If Turkey and nuclear-armed Pakistan brought their formidable military capabilities to bear alongside Saudi Arabia, the strategic calculations in Yemen and Tehran could change dramatically.
A credible multinational military response might persuade the Houthis that continued attacks carry unacceptable costs, while weakening Iran’s bargaining position with Washington.
Unlike Hezbollah, which operates within Iran’s doctrine of velayat-e faqih (guardianship of the Islamic jurist), the Houthis retain considerable operational independence.
Tehran influences their decisions but does not necessarily dictate every action. That distinction creates opportunities for deterrence and negotiation.
US President Donald Trump believes he has a productive relationship with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and has repeatedly praised Pakistan’s role in facilitating negotiations with Iran.
Now is the time to test those relationships.
Washington should press Ankara and Islamabad to translate their defense commitments into meaningful military cooperation with Riyadh.
Turkey’s possession of Russia’s S-400 air-defense system already raises serious questions about its reliability as a NATO ally. Pakistan, meanwhile, remains a nuclear-armed state whose Islamist currents and strategic interests frequently diverge from Washington’s.
If these countries refuse meaningful assistance, America should reassess how much strategic confidence it places in either.
The Saudi-UAE-Israeli alternative
There is another option, potentially more effective: Saudi Arabia should reconcile with the United Arab Emirates and cooperate militarily with Israel against their common Houthi adversary, under pressure from Trump.
The rivalry between Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) and UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed has complicated regional coordination.
Yet both governments have compelling interests in preventing the Houthis from dominating Yemen and threatening international commerce.
Israel brings intelligence capabilities, operational experience, and demonstrated military effectiveness against Iranian-backed forces.
A coordinated Saudi-Emirati-Israeli strategy, supported by American intelligence and logistics, could significantly strengthen deterrence without requiring another large-scale American commitment.
Trump should make clear to MBS that deeper American security commitments cannot substitute for regional cooperation with the UAE and Israel.
Why should American forces assume risks that regional powers refuse to share?
Unfortunately, Washington helped create this predicament. Some of America’s difficulties are self-inflicted.
In 2021, Joe Biden’s administration ended American support for Saudi-led offensive operations in Yemen and revoked the Houthis’ terrorist designations, citing humanitarian concerns.
Those concerns were legitimate. But the policy also raised questions about whether Washington was underestimating the Houthis’ military ambitions.
This is an organization whose notorious slogan is: “God is the Greatest, Death to America, Death to Israel, Curse be upon the Jews, Victory to Islam.”
The US should never believe humanitarian restraint will be reciprocated in the Middle East. In the region, it is viewed as weakness and an invitation to attack.
Iran today is weaker than most Americans believe, but it is not defeated
America’s approaching midterm elections have made sober, nonpartisan strategic analysis increasingly difficult.
After eight months of war, Iran’s military capabilities have been substantially degraded, its economy is under extraordinary pressure, and its proxies, Hamas and Hezbollah, have suffered devastating losses.
Yet the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps remains the regime’s dominant power center. Iran’s nuclear ambitions, ballistic missile capabilities, and surviving proxies remain unresolved.
Washington has also declined to fully exploit another potential source of pressure: Iran’s deeply disaffected population.
Persians, Kurds, Azeris, Baluchis, Lurs, Arabs, and other communities include millions who reject the Islamic Republic.
Supporting their access to communications, civil organization, strike funds, and arms would enable them to challenge authoritarian rule and increase pressure on Tehran without committing American ground forces.
The objective should be to convince the IRGC that continued confrontation threatens the regime’s survival more than a verifiable agreement limiting its nuclear program, ballistic missiles, and support for terrorism.
Trump still has strategic options.
By pressing Turkey and Pakistan to honor their commitments, encouraging Saudi-UAE-Israeli cooperation, and preserving Israel’s freedom to degrade Iranian proxies, Washington could further weaken Tehran’s leverage.
But the lesson is larger than Yemen: America cannot indefinitely defend Middle Eastern allies who refuse to act collectively against threats to their own survival.
That is the ultimate test for regional security, and whether Trump can turn his Middle East strategic ambitions into lasting achievements.
The writer is the director of MEPIN, the Middle East Political Information Network, and the senior security editor of The Jerusalem Report. He regularly briefs members of Congress and their foreign policy staffers, and the State Department.

Crash-and-burn: Inside Israel’s self-defeating defense against ‘NAZA,’ BBC's war crimes allegations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
17:31:13 UTC
02:31:13 KST

As soon as Hamas succeeded with its October 7 invasion and it became clear how hard Israel would need to come down on the Gaza terror group to restore its security, some significant public relations hit to the Jewish state was inevitable.
However, Israel and the IDF then conducted themselves in such ways that the public relations hit developed into a diplomatic tsunami which has harmed Israel's long-term national security and economic strength.
That is history and cannot be changed.
When the NAZA film came out in mid-September, a week after the EU sanctioned Israel's West Bank, a new chapter started.
Israel was going to take another major hit. But it also had a new opportunity and the world's full attention to set the record straight across the globe over the alleged war crimes and genocide debate.
Unlike earlier in the war, when it was overwhelmed fighting on seven fronts, had tremendous uncertainty about the future, and insufficient time had passed to investigate many incidents – all of these factors, which before delayed Israel providing a detailed response to war crimes allegations, were now more in Israel's favor.
Israel has no major active conflict on any fronts. It has had a ceasefire with Hamas since October 2025. Any incidents since then have been a relatively small number of easily trackable, targeted airstrikes.
If Israel swung and missed big, or did not even bother to swing on the war crimes allegations a year ago and two years ago, now was the chance for Israel to take a more detailed and comprehensive stand. Such a stand would include debunking many false claims, but also admitting in detail to the various errors, which would, in turn, strengthen the defense against the mostly false claims.
Israel is failing to do this. In that failure, Israel and the IDF are bringing about another unnecessary major loss on the public relations front, which will reverberate on the national security, economic, and legal fronts in a much graver way than earlier, because Israel is starting from a much lower point in its international standing.
Will Israel wait until two houses of the US Congress, and possibly in two more years, the occupant of the White House, decide to stop selling Jerusalem the crucial F-35 and other irreplaceable aircraft to realize that holding its cards close to its chest is no longer an option?
What has been held back for nearly three years and is still unconscionably being held back after the NAZA film?
Let's take Israel's response to the NAZA film.
The film is visually powerful, but it has many gaping holes in its specifics.
For example, the film claims that Israel used a 100-to-1 ratio of civilians to combatants when targeting senior Hamas figures and a 201-to-1 ratio when targeting lower Hamas members.
Israel rightly challenged these generalities and asked for specific examples.
Sad, misguided, and self-defeating responses
Last week, the BBC provided those examples with meticulous comprehensiveness.
For several days, The Jerusalem Post spoke to several sources at multiple levels and in different IDF divisions, begging to get specific responses to the examples presented by the BBC.
The sad, misguided, and self-defeating responses of IDF sources were as follows:
1) There is no point. No one believes us anyway, and the whole world is against us anyway.
2) They have given us too many examples to respond to, and we don't have the resources to respond.
3) If we give out the information, it will endanger information security considerations, help the enemy, or be used against us in international judicial war crimes proceedings, or both.
Anyone who says point number one should not handle public relations, as it signals they don't understand the nuances of different sectors of the public in the US, Europe, and elsewhere.
There are absolutely antisemites as well as long-standing "naïve idiots" who are anti-Israel who will never be convinced of Jerusalem's just or complex case.
But there are also tons of people across the West and in other regions of the world who stood with Israel before October 7, after October 7, and for the rest of 2023 and much of 2024, even as the IDF ground parts of Gaza into the sand while fighting Hamas.
For many longtime Israel supporters, the change only came in July 2025 when Israel admitted a major food insecurity crisis in Gaza, and the UN declared that famine had finally occurred.
Subsequently, it became clear that Israel's food surge narrowly avoided famine.
But the stain of the high likelihood of famine, which Israel was forced to admit to (even if it ultimately avoided it) led to a sea change and Israel's European allies finally recognized a Palestinian state, giving Israel nothing in exchange.
In addition, Israel's Western allies lost patience with years of the government, especially the police, failing to rein in Jewish lawlessness and even sometimes terror in the West Bank.
But most importantly, once the invasion of Gaza ended in October 2025, the world's patience in waiting for Israel's answer to war crimes charges was exhausted.
This was a process, and some of these once pro-Israel people might still be retrievable if Jerusalem and the IDF act fast enough with a transparency blitz to confront NAZA and answer the specific charges in the BBC article.
The case is under review
Regarding the IDF claim that the BBC asked for too many responses, the Post then asked the IDF to respond, at a minimum, to the four highly specific cases the BBC flagged.
The first case was from December 2023 when a mother, Nahida Anton, and her daughter, Samar Anton, were killed by sniper fire inside the grounds of the Holy Family church in Gaza, according to the Latin Patriarchate of Jerusalem.
Nearly three years later, the IDF simply states the case is under review.
After three years, it is actually pretty simple: the IDF admits fault and is deciding whether to prosecute or merely discipline the soldiers involved; the IDF denies fault and explains why; or the IDF admits that its record-keeping was faulty and it is not sure who might have been involved and so cannot reach a conclusion. Some of these results could be embarrassing, but after three years, delaying the answer is far worse and makes it look like the NAZA story is true and the IDF's request for specifics a straw man.
In the second case, the IDF struck the Tabaeen school complex and nearby mosque in Gaza in August 2024. Gazan authorities and the BBC claim that at least 93 people were killed, including six women and 11 children. The IDF much earlier in the war responded that 31 Hamas terrorists were killed and that the civilian death estimates were exaggerated.
After over two years, how many civilians does the IDF say were actually killed, if not 62 (93 minus 31)? Once again, the IDF can own up to having made a mistake and killed too many civilians, can defend its claim and say how many civilians actually died, or can share why it thought the civilian death reports were exaggerated, while explaining where some permanent uncertainty will remain.
Possibly embarrassing, but much better than the current silence.
In the third case, just outside of Jenin in September 2024, the IDF reportedly killed 16-year-old Lujain Musleh during an Israeli operation. Lujain's father said she was shot in the head as she looked out of the window at her house in Kafr Dan, after soldiers had surrounded a neighboring house. According to the BBC, the IDF said at the time that armed fighters had fired on the soldiers, who had "fired back at a suspect who observed" them, and that the details of the incident were under review.
How is this still open two years later? There are again three simple choices for the IDF to choose from about how to respond at this point.
The fourth case involves Lebanon. There, an IDF investigation identified by BBC Verify looked into an incident on November 10, 2024, in which an Israeli strike allegedly killed 23 people, including seven children, near the city of Byblos, Lebanon. According to the BBC, the IDF said at the time it had targeted a Hezbollah site, and that it was reviewing the incident.
To be a broken record: How is this still open two years later? There are again three simple choices for the IDF to choose from about how to respond at this point.
What is useful, and devastating, about the BBC article is that it provides both concrete data as an overview, collating all of the 300 or so times when the IDF said it was investigating an incident, with four specific incidents covering the Gaza, West Bank, and Lebanon fronts.
Unlike NAZA, the BBC is being specific. It is basing itself on IDF public data. And then it simply asks the IDF to provide its side of the story.
The IDF provided a bizarre, long-winded, tone-deaf response about the numerous factors it considers when and how to publicize decisions on such incidents.
Here is the bottom line: for nearly three years, until August 19, 2026, the IDF published almost zero public decisions.
On August 19, 2026, to its credit, it finally published five well-reasoned and detailed decisions.
But what about the other 295 decisions?
There are 10 or so other specific decisions which the Post has been requesting responses to for around two years.
The BBC credits the IDF with decisions, or partial decisions, in another 40 or so cases, even if the IDF did a poor job highlighting them and failed to make any major announcement.
To its credit, the IDF has said it is criminally investigating 150 cases and has carried out preliminary reviews of 3,000 cases. To its credit, the BBC acknowledges the IDF has said that it disciplined dozens of soldiers.
But if the IDF got far enough along to need to criminally probe 150 cases, why can it not release some more comprehensive interim findings of where these cases stand – at least after two or three years from when most incidents occurred?
The Post also asked the IDF to release ranks, violation categories, and punishment categories for the dozens of soldiers disciplined, without disclosing the specific soldiers' names or units.
Without doing so, how can any fair-minded Westerner judge what disciplining dozens of soldiers really means?
The BBC also interviewed former IDF international law department chief Col. (res.) Eran Shamir Borer, who encouraged the military to be more transparent.
In fact, in around a dozen conversations with top IDF legal officials over the course of the war, all of them have said the IDF should move faster and be more transparent in publicizing decisions, dating back all the way to summer 2024 when the military first started any public discussion of its probes.
We return to the third reason for not disclosing information: information security and the risk that facts could be abused in international proceedings.
The IDF has launched likely 20,000 or quite a bit more airstrikes on Gaza over the last three years. Hamas has huge data to understand when it will and will not attack regarding civilians.
On top of that, the IDF has killed over 25,000 Hamas terrorists despite the group's human shields strategy.
This is one of the most public wars in history, with the only missing piece being Israel's defensive narrative.
Do Israeli generals really think that anything they put into the public sphere is going to be all that new to Hamas or bring back to life the already killed 25,000 terrorists? The International Criminal Court has already issued arrest warrants in two rounds against Israelis, and it and the International Court of Justice are mainly considering being tougher on Israel in lieu of a comprehensive defense.
How much worse will providing a detailed defense make things?
Israel has lost the Palestinian statehood diplomatic battle, the reputational battle, much of the legal battle, and, recently, a sanctions battle, but still has a chance to hold onto its national security needs with the US.
Will Israel and the IDF wake up in time?

In a London synagogue, a Jewish David stands up to the Green Party’s Goliath - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
17:30:59 UTC
02:30:59 KST

When the Philistines took their turn trying to conquer Israel, Goliath challenged them daily to send a champion to face him.
Though King Saul did not respond, “little” David had had enough of Goliath’s goading and let fly a stone from his sling, felling the giant, whose head he then struck off.
The question has been asked whether the Philistines were the forerunner to the Palestinians. They were not, but the event became a metaphor for the underdog challenging and overcoming the overdog, the little fella defeating the big fella.
Ezekiel prophesied the destruction of the Philistines, and that is what happened.
Probably around 4,000 years later, last week’s Jerusalem Post highlighted the establishment of the Secure Community Network, a safety and security organization for the Jewish community in North America.
“Standing with Strength” is its watchword, with the aim of developing security and training to meet the all-too-common antisemitic attacks.
This now stands as an example to communities in other parts of the world not to lie down and accept the tide of threats, abuse, and violence hurled against them. The UK is one such place that has taken note.
The David vs Goliath fight in the United Kingdom
Another David has come forth to meet the challenge and take on the Goliath of the UK government, and at least one other political party: a small North London synagogue that has a mighty heart. It is probably replicated all over the world.
The antisemites have picked on the wrong Jews, as this synagogue, Highgate United, adopted the hostage Emily Damari and never ended its support for her until she was freed and able to come to London for a joyful visit.
The catalyst for the action of the synagogue comes in the wake of the endless torrent of verbal and physical attacks against the Jewish community, as well as the imposition of sanctions on Israel and the calling for the dismantlement of the state.
The straw that has broken the camel’s back is a motion called by the increasingly popular Green Party, at its conference, to equate Zionism with racism.
The consequence of this is that if they come to power or hold the balance of power, neither inconceivable, the attendance of Jews at a synagogue supporting Israel could be deemed unlawful.
Before this motion, things had already reached a precarious position, with sanctions set by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, while his foreign secretary was telling the Muslim marchers that they were right: Israel is a genocidal state.
The cycle that follows such outrageous acts is the claim that things are not as bad as they seem. Of course, the Holocaust showed us that however alarming the steps are, worse inevitably follows.
Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar has taught that when the aggressor delivers a slap in the face rather than turning the other cheek, a different and stronger response is required.
“Every state that works and acts against the state of Israel must understand that we will take our revenge.”
Hence, following the UK sanctions, Israel’s response has been the closure of the UK consulate in Jerusalem, and while His Majesty’s Government brushes this off as a downgrade, the world sees it for what it is: a humiliation for Britain.
It is not downgrading. It is degrading.
MEANWHILE, THE UK’s “little” David, Highgate Synagogue, steps forward.
The Greens’ Goliath, who passed the Zionism equals racism motion, sent a letter via Councillor Mark Blake, leader of Haringey Green Council, to the rabbi and chairpersons of the synagogue in his area.
He was trying to reassure them about the implications of the party’s disgraceful stance on Zionism and what it means for the local Jewish community. Everything was going to be fine.
This is the usual response of a coward. Having inflicted the blow, the antisemite then goes back to hide behind the parapet with false assurances. This is what Blake did.
Highgate responded with both barrels: “We reject your assurances. You make us unsafe.”
“You may see no connection between the ceaseless vilification of Israel, the blood libels that you and your party regularly trot out, and the hostility to Jews in this country, but we do.”
“We take it from tone and content (of your letter) that you are deeply embarrassed with the decision taken by your party to not only brand Zionism as racism but to call for the eradication by any means necessary, including violence, of the only Jewish state, the only practicing democracy in the Middle East and home to half of the world’s Jewish population…”
“This (motion) has been publicly celebrated by the Haringey branch of the Greens party, aligning itself with Hamas, a genocidal, homophobic, misogynistic, and Islamist terrorist organization.
“This synagogue has had close relatives who were victims of October 7. And let there be no doubt the love of Zion is integral. The threat of the Greens is an ignorant and one-sided view, and we expect you to resign from it.”
The wagons are circled, the war continues.
There is no room for weaseling around, and Highgate Synagogue has sent a message – not just to our enemies who come in many guises, but also to the leaders of the community too often showing themselves inexplicably obsequious. Polite overtures often fall on deaf ears.
During the High Holy Days, government officials were given jars of honey to wish them a sweet new year. Their response was the imposition of sanctions and the desire to disestablish the state of Israel.
Our nation produces brave Davids, not timid Sauls.
As Elie Wiesel said in his oft-repeated guidance: “Stand up, do not stay quiet. Neutrality helps the oppressor, never the victim. Silence encourages the tormentor, never the tormented.”
The writer is a Senior Barrister and retired criminal judge and author of Nothing Like the Truth and co-host of the podcast Shalom from Tel Aviv. He lives between London and Zichron Ya’acov.

Flydubai captain describes blocking axe blows as co-pilot attacked him
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
17:27:17 UTC
02:27:17 KST

The captain of a flydubai flight who was attacked by a co-pilot who intended to crash the plane has described blocking axe blows to his head and screaming for help as he reached to open the cockpit door.
Capt Smit Machchhar has been hailed as a hero for his role in averting disaster on the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv last month, helping to thwart what the UAE attorney general has said was an attempted suicide attack by the co-pilot who had intended to crash the plane into Ben Gurion airport.
Speaking in an interview with The National newspaper from a hospital bed in Abu Dhabi, his head and left arm bandaged, Machchhar said that when the first blow landed, he thought something had gone “horribly wrong with the aircraft structure” before quickly realising he was being attacked and things had “taken a drastic turn”.
“The next thought was I need to get help in here,” he said. “My immediate action was to free myself from the seatbelts and I tried to just block the blows as much as I could.”
He pointed to his arm that was wounded as he defended himself. “The blows were coming on the head. Immediately my hand went to the knob which opens the door and [I was] screaming for my colleagues, screaming his name. I believe that was the first time when I lost my consciousness.”
Flight FZ1073 was in Saudi airspace when the co-pilot attacked Machchhar with a crash axe, an item typically kept in the cockpit for emergency use.
The incident caused the airliner to plunge 16,000 ft (4,900m) in 30 seconds before the attacker was overwhelmed and two other pilots who were on board landed the aircraft safely in Saudi Arabia. The suspect, an Omani national, was transferred to the UAE, flydubai’s home country.
The plan was inspired by the 11 September 2001 attacks on the US, UAE public prosecutors said as a result of their criminal investigation, which was launched on 1 October.
Machchhar said he heard the cockpit door opening and screaming “between my colleague and the guy”. He said the scariest thing he felt was the aircraft nose “steeply going down”.
“I was not very sure that I’ll make it out alive from this. Did I give up? No.”

European diplomats feel the sting of settler violence in West Bank
Shielding Israel from accountability, supplying it with advanced weapons, and turning a blind eye to its unlawful and cruel acts against Palestinians for nearly eight decades have finally come back to haunt Europe and the United States. The consequences have reached a point where even European diplomats, journalists, and other officials are no longer safe from the emboldened Israeli occupiers.
On Saturday, Israeli settler militants attacked European diplomats, a French mayor and the archbishop of Cambrai in Taybeh, in the occupied West Bank, injuring three people and damaging a car, in the latest violent attempt to prevent Palestinians from harvesting olives on their own land, the Guardian reported.
Bernard Baudoux, mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, was wearing his red, white and blue sash of office and attempting to enter a vehicle with diplomatic plates when he was assaulted and knocked to the ground, the Guardian reported.
The masked militant shouted “Vive la France” as he launched the attack, a witness said. Badoux’s wife, and Vincent Dollmann, archbishop of Cambrai, were also threatened by the group of seven men, some armed with clubs.
The group had joined the olive harvest on lands belonging to the Christian town of Taybeh, along with the French consul general in Jerusalem, his wife and other diplomats, and the Belgian and Polish consuls.
Settlers first attacked a group working on the lower slopes of hills near Taybeh. As well as stealing olives, they kicked, abused and assaulted a Palestinian woman in her 70s and beat a man so badly he needed six stitches for a head injury.
Then they approached the diplomats and Badoux, who was in Taybeh for the launch of a twinning agreement with his town in northern France. During the attack, the militants smashed the window of an armored car belonging to the Belgian mission.
Maxime Prévot, Belgium’s deputy prime minister and minister of foreign affairs, condemned the violence against Palestinians, foreign diplomats and journalists, and said his country would continue to push for European Union sanctions on settlers.
“Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack,” he said. “This violence cannot be separated from Israel’s illegal settlement policy … the occupation of the Palestinian territory must end.”
Echoing those sentiments, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot echoed called on Israeli authorities to "urgently halt this criminal violence and guarantee the safety of civilian populations."
Poland's foreign affairs ministry also called for a "firm response" from Israeli authorities and for "an end to the spiral of violence in the West Bank".
The EU condemned the attacks, urged Israel to abide by international and human rights law, and end the expansion of settlements.
To render the incident insignificant, the office of the Prime Minister Benjamin suggesting it was part of a "coordinated campaign to smear Israel."
Palestinian residents of Taybeh have lived with years of escalating attacks from Israeli militants, but settlers had never targeted foreign diplomats there, said Father Bashar Fawadleh, the town’s parish priest.
“What happened today is not an isolated incident. It represents a deeply disturbing escalation in settler violence,” Fawadleh said.
Since the start of the annual olive harvest in late September, Israeli militants have used violence to stop Palestinians bringing in a crop that is economically and culturally vital to their communities.
Since September 27, settlers have launched more than 170 attacks, Israeli rights group Yesh Din said. They killed at least four people, injured more than 100 and damaged thousands of trees, according to Palestinian authorities.
Even the presence of Israeli activists, diplomats, senior clergy and journalists no longer serves as a deterrence to extreme violence.
“If such violence can take place before international witnesses, one must ask what protection remains for local families and farmers when those witnesses are no longer present,” Fawadleh said. “No individual should have to risk physical assault simply to harvest olives from their own land.”
On Friday, Israeli militants attacked and severely injured Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine as she reported on the harvest in the town of Abu Falah. She required surgery on Saturday morning and is now in “moderate” condition, according to a spokesperson for Israel’s Beilinson hospital where she is being treated.
On Oct. 6, Armed Israeli settlers also beat an AFP photographer, leaving him requiring hospital treatment, as he covered ongoing violence by settlers against West Bank olive farmers.
Jaafar Ashtiyeh, 58, a veteran photographer for the international news agency in the Palestinian territory, suffered bruises to his head and torso and was taken by ambulance to a hospital, according to witnesses, his family and fellow journalists.
Israel had already severely restricted the harvest this year by imposing new rules barring Palestinians from trees located in Area C, an area under the Israeli military’s control, which comprises most of the West Bank’s agricultural land.
Gideon Sa'ar, Israel's foreign minister, said the foreign ministry was in contact with the ambassadors of the countries involved.
But he added: "Without detracting from the severity of the incident, it is unfortunate that the visit was not coordinated with the IDF in advance. Such coordination could have helped safeguard the visitors' security."
Demanding diplomats give advance notification of travel violates both diplomatic conventions and international law, said one Western diplomatic source who asked not to be named.
“Israel is in charge of security in Area B and C (the majority of the West Bank), so is obliged to assure safety there for all,” the source said.
A culture of near total impunity for Israeli violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank has prompted former prime minister Ehud Olmert to call for the international criminal court to intervene.
Gadi Eisenkot, an opposition politician and former general hoping to unseat prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu in elections to be held later this month described the attack as “Jewish terror under the auspices of the Israeli government”.
Eisenkot backs Jewish Israeli expansion in occupied Palestine but wants militant violence brought under control because the attackers are “harming the settlement enterprise in [the West Bank] and national security”.

The decline of US dominance in West Asia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
17:12:55 UTC
02:12:55 KST

The decline of US dominance in West Asia
TEHRAN – Several factors have contributed to the decline of U.S. hegemony in West Asia.
For decades, the United States maintained a clear military advantage in air and naval power. Its advanced fighter jets, such as the F-35, and nuclear-powered aircraft carriers, including the USS Abraham Lincoln, gave it a significant technological edge.
But having the most advanced weapons did not necessarily mean being prepared for a prolonged war, particularly one that required weapons and ammunition to be produced and replenished on a mass scale.
This weakness became particularly clear during the illegal war against Iran. The U.S. deployed a massive fleet designed and built during the twentieth century for operations across the open oceans. It was now being drawn into a war in the Persian Gulf, where narrow waterways and shallow coastal waters presented a very different set of challenges.
The U.S. military faces persistent hurdles in maintaining equipment and delivering new weapons on schedule. Its supply chains also depend on foreign sources for certain critical materials. China plays an important role in the supply of gallium and germanium, which are used in military electronics and other advanced technologies. This dependence creates potential vulnerabilities, especially if export restrictions disrupt access to these materials.
These weaknesses expose a fundamental contradiction in American military power: the ability to field sophisticated weapons does not necessarily translate into the ability to sustain a prolonged war.
Iran’s war of attrition
These dependencies make a prolonged conflict increasingly difficult to sustain. U.S. forces risk exhausting their stockpiles faster than they can replenish them, a structural vulnerability that can be exploited through a multidimensional war of attrition.
By deploying large numbers of inexpensive drones and ballistic missiles across land, sea, and air, Iran has confronted U.S. forces with a stark economic imbalance. Tens and billions of dollars’ worth of carrier strike groups and ground-based air-defense systems have been forced to expend scarce interceptor missiles, costing $2 million each against dense waves of Iranian drones no more than $20,000 apiece.
Moreover, because these high-tech interceptors cannot be replaced quickly, every missile fired represents a permanent drain on American combat readiness, opening a direct strategic opportunity for its competitors.
Instruments of financial dominance
The U.S. military presence in West Asia was also only sustainable to the extent that the financial system funding it was sustainable. American regional dominance has long rested largely on monetary control, specifically the petrodollar and central authority over the global banking system through the SWIFT network.
This monetary monopoly gave Washington an influential diplomatic tool, including the ability to freeze foreign central bank reserves, impose unilateral sanctions, and isolate entire countries from international trade.
But the repeated use of these tools has sent a warning far beyond the countries directly targeted. By weaponizing its financial dominance, Washington has demonstrated to the wider international community that dependence on U.S.-controlled financial infrastructure can itself become a sovereign liability.
As Iran sought alternative payment and settlement mechanisms to circumvent sanctions, energy exporters that were not directly targeted, including Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, also began diversifying their options.
By exploring non-dollar arrangements for settling oil and gas transactions, expanding the use of local currencies in trade with major buyers such as China, and participating in multilateral digital-currency initiatives, these countries have begun laying the groundwork for a less dollar-dependent energy trade. Such efforts could gradually reduce the reach of Western financial jurisdiction over strategically important markets.
At the same time, the fiscal foundations of American financial dominance have weakened from within. Decades of overseas military adventures, including spending outside ordinary budgetary channels, have contributed to mounting federal deficits and a rapidly expanding national debt. The annual U.S. budget deficit is just shy of $2 trillion, while the national debt has surpassed $40 trillion.
The collapse of moral authority
Perhaps nothing has damaged U.S. hegemony more profoundly than the erosion of its moral authority.
For decades, Washington, backed by Western media organizations and think tanks, has invoked moral arguments to justify coups, military invasions, and forcible regime change. From the 1953 coup in Iran to the invasions and occupations of Afghanistan in 2001 and Iraq in 2003, and the regime-change campaign in Libya in 2011, the U.S. has repeatedly presented its geopolitical ambitions as moral imperatives. The intervention in Syria in 2024 forms part of this same pattern.
For years, Washington managed to defend its international standing against accusations of hypocrisy. That credibility, however, has been badly damaged by the genocidal war in Gaza.
Washington has shielded the Zionist regime from international accountability.
This has undermined the credibility of the so-called rules-based international order, making it increasingly difficult to distinguish universal principles from policies designed to serve the interests of the U.S. and its allies.
By the time Washington waged an illegal war against Iran, its moral authority had already suffered substantial damage. The legitimacy that once helped underpin U.S. global leadership had lost much of its persuasive force. What remained was a political narrative that increasingly struggled to convince a public audience and Washington’s closest allies.
End of an era?
This does not mean that the U.S. will collapse tomorrow. It remains a global superpower, with formidable military, economic, and technological capabilities.
The more consequential change is that the international order dominated by the West for roughly five centuries, an order that shifted the center of global power away from Asia and toward the West, is now eroding much faster.

4 Dead in ‘Violent’ Fire at a Canadian Military Base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
17:10:14 UTC
02:10:14 KST

Four service members died in a fire that broke out at one of Canada’s main military bases on Oct. 17, according to Prime Minister Mark Carney. Officials are continuing to assess the damage and an investigation is underway to determine the cause of the deadly blaze.
Carney made a statement at midday Sunday about what he described as a “violent, fast-moving fire” that left dozens wounded.
“What followed was one of the worst tragedies for forces on Canadian soil in peacetime,” he said.
Read More: What Happens When the World Is on Fire
Canada Defense Minister David McGuinty similarly underscored the severity of the incident in a video statement on Oct. 17. “I cannot recall an incident like this,” he said, describing the event as “very active and delicate.”
On Sunday, the military said there is no indication that this was an act of terrorism. TIME has reached out to Canada’s Department of National Defence for more information.
Here’s what to know about the event as it unfolds.
What is known about the fire incident at CFB Wainwright
A fire “ignited” within the training area of Canadian Forces Base (CFB) Wainwright in the late afternoon on Oct. 17, according to a statement from the Canadian Armed Forces.
The flames eventually “spread rapidly due to high winds,” the district said in a Facebook post that evening. The fire extended beyond the base and toward the adjacent Municipal District of Wainwright.
In a subsequent update, the district said that the fire was being held. The Canadian Armed Forces said that additional details would be confirmed after next-of-kin have been notified.
McGuinty did not provide details about what might have started the blaze; however, he said that an investigation would be launched.
The Defense Minister is currently en route to Edmonton. He said he had spoken with Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith.
Carney had recently returned to Ottawa after a visit to Alberta as the province prepares to vote on Monday about whether they want to begin the legal process of potentially separating from Canada.
What is CFB Wainwright?
CFB Wainwright is one of the country’s “busiest” army bases, located over 100 miles southeast of the Alberta province capital Edmonton.
The base hosts the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, and it is the “preferred” training ground for army field force units based in Western Canada.
“Our country depends on the women and men of the Canadian Armed Forces,” Carney said on Sunday, “and CFB Wainwright is where the women and men of our armed forces learn to do the hardest things this country can ask of anyone.”
Retired Major-General Denis Thompson spoke to CBC on Sunday about the training he had experienced at Wainwright, which included “large formations … bringing together infantry, foot soldiers, with artillery” in large-scale live-fire training that sometimes include air-dropped munitions.
“You're trying to put that together in order to conduct complex operations in as safe an environment as possible, but remember we're talking about live fire, here, to do things like breaching obstacles, which are extremely difficult,” Thompson said.
Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh told CBC on Sunday that, prior to the incident, he could hear cannon fire and weapons firing, though he noted that the sounds were not unusual for the training base. He said that the base went quiet and then the fire department was activated, and he realized then that something might have happened.
He also explained that weather conditions were a contributing factor. “October has been dry,” he observed, while acknowledging the impact of high winds.
The base employed around 1,300 military and civilian personnel, including roughly 1,070 military members, according to October 2025 figures published by the Town of Wainwright. Wainwright is home to over 6,600 people. That excludes personnel living on the base.
“We have neighbors who are either serving or former members of the Canadian Armed Forces. We’re integrated, our kids playing the same hockey teams, attend the same schools,” Pugh told CBC.
Hospitals declare ‘Code Orange’
According to CBC, Edmonton hospitals have called a code orange alert. The designation is reserved for an external disaster or mass casualty incident.
"This would be the largest mass casualty event that we have seen in this community," Push confirmed to CBC.
He went on to praise first responders working at the local hospital, which served as the initial triage point.
“Our local health care facility was the reception area for those casualties,” he said.
Of the first responders at the scene, Pugh said: “They were witness to things that you would pray that you never see, or that if you do, it would be a once-in-a-lifetime experience of service.”
Alberta Health Services responded to a request from TIME on midday Sunday, saying: "We are working to gather additional information and will provide an update as soon as we can."
“Canadians come together in crisis,” Carney said on Sunday, commending the fast and coordinated response on the ground as the incident unfolded.
The Prime Minister Carney said he is expecting an official statement from leadership in Wainwright by Sunday afternoon.
This is a developing story and will continue to be updated.

France in a web of problems partly fueled by the war on Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
17:08:35 UTC
02:08:35 KST

France in a web of problems partly fueled by the war on Iran
More than 1,800 arrested as police clash with protesters across France
TEHRAN — France spent Sunday sweeping up after its worst street unrest in years. A town hall lies gutted in Limoges, about 1,800 people are under arrest, and as of writing this, the government has yet to say what it will do next.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 550,000 people took part in Saturday’s demonstrations, including 110,000 in Paris, while the CGT (General Confederation of Labor), one of France’s largest trade unions, put the nationwide turnout at 800,000.
Paris police recorded a record 855 arrests. One protester died following a cardiorespiratory arrest north of Paris, according to BFMTV.
The first attack came at dawn, on the shared Paris headquarters of CNews, Europe 1 and the JDD. By afternoon, police faced wildcat groups of 500 to 1,000 people, then waves of looters.
In Marseille, a crowd breached city hall and toppled a bust of Marianne. A tourist office burned in Lyon. In Limoges, a mob that Mayor Guillaume Guerin says used a battering ram set fire to the town hall, opened in 1883 and spared by two world wars. Its 43-meter clock tower fell.
“I had no single national police officer to protect the town hall,” said Guerin, a center-right mayor whose city’s officers were sent to the street march.
A retail trade group counts about 1,500 shops damaged. AFP described looting that looked planned, with crews of about six masked, gloved men disabling security cameras first.
At Place de la République, protesters put a yellow vest on the Marianne statue and hung a banner reading “The police mutilate high-schoolers.”
A school revolt and a fuel revolt merged
Pupils at a Créteil lycée, a French secondary school for students typically aged 15 to 18, began blockading in mid-September over teacher shortages, classes of 32 to 36, deteriorating buildings and stress over Parcoursup, and the university admissions platform.
Classrooms had reached 40 degrees Celsius over the summer. By Oct. 1, 1,027 of roughly 3,700 lycées were affected.
A separate revolt started Sept. 15, when fishermen blocked ports at Nice and Sète. Diesel climbed to a record of about 2.41 euros a liter after the Strait of Hormuz was closed in the war that the United States and Israel launched against Iran on Feb. 28.
On Saturday the two grievances marched together, joined by university students, the CGT, teachers’ unions, former yellow vests, farmers, truckers, nurses and climate activists.
Student representatives want 10 billion euros for education. The unions want a 6 percent public-sector raise after a fourth freeze of the pay index, which has been frozen since July 2023.
La France Insoumise, a left-wing party founded by Jean-Luc Mélenchon that advocates wealth redistribution and expanded public services, says it backs the movement without running it. Matignon, the prime minister’s office, calls the school protests an operation by the party and its allies.
A Le Figaro poll found 62 percent of respondents call the student cause justified, while 61 percent say the party is too involved. The masked groups that have fought police have published no demands.
Police have arrested thousands of minors, maimed some
The Justice Ministry counted 6,877 custodies by Oct. 9, 86 percent of them minors. That is already more than 60 percent of the 11,203 that Amnesty recorded across the entire yellow vest movement. The police watchdog has 24 investigations open.
The injuries are specific. A 15-year-old lost his left hand to a grenade in Lens on Oct. 5. A 16-year-old lost the use of an eye in Tours. A 14-year-old’s jaw was shattered in Saint-Ouen-l’Aumône.
On Saturday, a 17-year-old reportedly lost a hand in Saint-Étienne, and Interior Minister Nuñez declined to confirm what caused it. Amnesty called the force disproportionate.
Nuñez suspended one type of stun grenade at school protests on Oct. 7. He re-authorized them Oct. 16 for “urban violence.”
A government that has routinely lectured nations such as Iran on how to treat young demonstrators now runs the arrest statistics described above. Nuñez himself reports more than 500 injured police, gendarmes and firefighters on Saturday, against the 150 Lecornu cited that night.
A weakened government and protests spreading abroad
President Emmanuel Macron’s approval rating stands at a record low of 15 percent in the Ipsos BVA-CESI poll. Lecornu has 22 percent positive and 69 percent negative, and his government holds 211 of 577 Assembly seats.
The 10-year bond yield touched 5.03 percent in early October, the highest in over two decades. Debt is about 3.6 trillion euros, and interest payments next year will be at least 90 billion. Mujtaba Rahman of Eurasia Group sees a crisis of liberal democracy, a fiscal crisis and a youth crisis arriving together.
Prime Minister Lecornu says France has reached a “point of no return” and told the country it is time to “choose sides.” Jean-Luc Mélenchon replied that the prime minister is “responsible for the chaos.”
Marine Le Pen says social demands were “taken hostage by the extreme left.” She leads the first-round polling for April 18 at 35 percent, ahead of Édouard Philippe at 15 and Mélenchon at 14, according to Ifop.
The remedies so far have been small. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu released 10 million barrels of diesel from reserves after the G7 agreed to free 100 million, and he has promised 3,000 substitute teachers.
Student leaders call it insufficient. The CGT has called an interprofessional strike for Nov. 5, and firefighters have a strike notice running to Oct. 20. AFP judged Saturday more intense than the 2023 riots and the 2018 yellow vest unrest.
Elsewhere in Europe, police fired tear gas and water cannon in Brussels and Liège.
A march against wars and rising living costs in Milan ended in looting and fires, and Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said, “Demonstrating is a right. Setting our cities ablaze is not.”
Tens of thousands marched in Lisbon over housing and wages. HEC Paris professor Alberto Alemanno calls France the epicenter of separate movements with shared grievances, and sees early stirrings in Greece, Germany and Austria.
Donald Trump declared on Truth Social that “France is burning” and blamed immigration, urging Paris to “close your Borders.” He did not mention schools, diesel prices or his own war of choice behind them.
On October 6, Tehran summoned France’s ambassador. Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei pointed to a glaring double standard, noting that while French officials championed unrest in Iran as a “peaceful uprising,” they quickly branded domestic student demonstrations as criminal “urban violence.” While arson and attacks on police cannot be justified, Baqaei emphasized, “The problem is the double standards.”

Today, according to the latest polls, the bloc of the current ruling coalition led by Netanyahu’s Likud party and the united opposition are neck and neck. However, neither side can count on the majority of 61 out of 120 seats in the Knesset required to form a ruling coalition.

28 arrested, 141 officers injured as cost-of-living protests turn violent in Italy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Necva Tastan Sevinc
18 October 2026•Update: 18 October 2026
Italian police arrested 28 people, including 12 minors, following clashes during cost-of-living protests in several cities on Saturday, while tensions continued in central Milan on Sunday, Sky TG24 reported.
Police said 197 people were identified and taken to police stations, while 43 were reported to judicial authorities. Their overall tally listed 141 injured law enforcement officers.
Organized by the Italia in Piazza movement, Saturday’s demonstrations opposed rising living costs, fuel prices and tax pressures. Around 5,000 people participated in Milan, 3,000 in Turin, 2,000 in Bologna, 600 in Brescia and 800 in Bergamo, according to police figures.
In Milan, groups threw stones, bottles, firecrackers and barriers at officers, who responded with tear gas and water cannon. Shops were damaged and looted around the city center, while a Carabinieri vehicle was destroyed.
Police arrested 17 people in Milan. Retail association Confcommercio estimated damage to shops and businesses at more than €500,000 ($561,860), according to the broadcaster.
In Turin, police arrested an adult for resisting an officer and three minors allegedly carrying Molotov cocktails. A group also entered the Feltrinelli bookstore at Porta Nuova station and threw books onto the floor.
In Bologna, police arrested five minors following clashes near the railway station, where demonstrators threw bottles, stones and barriers. Officers used tear gas and water cannon to disperse them.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed solidarity with law enforcement and urged opposition parties to unequivocally condemn the violence, while acknowledging that thousands had demonstrated peacefully.
Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini said his League party would resubmit a parliamentary proposal requiring organizers of demonstrations deemed risky to provide financial guarantees covering potential damage.
Milan Mayor Giuseppe Sala said protesters’ grievances were understandable but violence against officers and extensive damage to the city were unjustifiable.
Bologna Mayor Matteo Lepore similarly condemned the unrest and urged young people to distance themselves from those using demonstrations as a pretext for violence.
