Brazil's Bolsonaro, Lula head into first debate a week before vote
BRASILIA, Oct 18 - Brazilian supporters held rallies for presidential candidates on Sunday as leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro prepared for their first televised debate with just one week left in the campaign.
Pro-Bolsonaro crowds wearing Brazil's national colors of yellow, green and blue packed Paulista Avenue in Sao Paulo's financial center, and the candidate appeared on a float ahead of giving an address.
Lula supporters wearing red, symbolic of his Workers' Party, filled Brasilia's plaza of government buildings and students backing the president protested against Bolsonaro in Rio de Janeiro.
Polls show a close race for the October 25 runoff, with Bolsonaro holding a slight advantage after finishing nearly 2 percentage points ahead of Lula in the election's first round on October 4.
Both candidates hope to engage the 33 million voters who stayed home in the election's first round, equal to about one in five eligible voters.
The debate in Sao Paulo is scheduled to begin at 8 p.m. (2300 GMT) and air on broadcaster Band. The last debate in the election's first round was canceled at the last minute when Lula and Bolsonaro pulled out.
Once a hallmark of Brazilian democracy following the end of the country's 21-year military dictatorship in 1985, televised presidential debates have lost relevance as leading candidates have increasingly chosen to stay away.
A dispute over whether Meta’s platforms, which include Facebook and Instagram, treated the two candidates equally has injected new tension into the campaign's final days.
Lula’s coalition said his Instagram account and posts were restricted, and local newspaper Folha de S.Paulo reported internal Meta messages that acknowledged those restrictions and said the platform had recommended Bolsonaro’s profile and WhatsApp channel to users.
Meta said it had experienced global technical glitches but denied any political bias. “Any suggestion that Meta favors one side is false,” the company said. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

TIME investigation reveals how Israel helped funnel $2 billion in Qatari funds to Hamas-run Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
17:00:47 UTC
02:00:47 KST

Nine days before Israel's October 27 election, a major investigation published Sunday by TIME magazine reveals previously undisclosed documents and correspondence showing Israel's direct involvement in facilitating nearly $2 billion in Qatari payments to the Gaza Strip over more than a decade. 
According to the report, governments led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu did more than authorize the transfers: They encouraged the payments to continue, helped determine how the money would be distributed and worked to preserve the funding arrangements even as Israeli officials publicly accused Qatar of financing Hamas.
An earlier investigation by Ronen Bergman and Yuval Rubovitz, published by ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth, uncovered intelligence documents and testimony showing that Netanyahu had received warnings beginning in 2019 from the Shin Bet domestic security agency, Military Intelligence and Egyptian officials that Qatari money was being diverted to Hamas' military buildup.
The investigation also revealed a separate, covert channel through which Qatar transferred funds directly to Hamas, in addition to the diversion of money originally designated for humanitarian assistance. According to the findings, the combined funding, which Netanyahu was allegedly aware of, covered roughly half the budget of Hamas' entire military wing. Despite explicit warnings and opposition from former Shin Bet directors Nadav Argaman and Ronen Bar, Netanyahu continued the policy, the investigation found.
One of the most striking documents uncovered by TIME is a December 2020 letter from then-Mossad director Yossi Cohen to Qatar's emir, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani. The letter, filled with praise for Doha, was written after Netanyahu had already received warnings that Qatari funds were contributing to Hamas' military capabilities.
In the letter, Cohen expressed Israel's gratitude and appreciation for Qatar's humanitarian assistance to Gaza over the preceding years. He wrote that the efforts had "played a crucial role in improving the humanitarian situation" and contributed to regional stability and security.
The TIME investigation, published amid continuing scrutiny of Netanyahu's policies toward Hamas before the October 7, 2023, massacre, draws on official documents, correspondence between Israeli and Qatari officials and interviews with Israeli, American and diplomatic figures involved in the funding arrangements. The documents suggest that Israel's role was considerably more extensive than Netanyahu has publicly acknowledged. The Prime Minister's Office declined to comment to TIME.
A former Israeli defense official told the magazine that the policy had begun with good intentions but ultimately proved to be a failure that successive prime ministers had perpetuated. The official said Netanyahu was "unquestionably at the center of it," having promoted and accelerated the program while his government oversaw its implementation.
Israel vetted recipients and urged Qatar to keep the money flowing
According to TIME, Qatar began transferring money to Gaza in 2007, after Hamas seized control of the territory, while Ehud Olmert was prime minister. Israel was not initially directly involved in the transfers, but that changed under Netanyahu. Beginning in 2012, his government helped establish a system that involved Israeli authorities in delivering food and medical supplies, determining which Palestinian families qualified for financial assistance and expanding Gaza's electricity supply through Qatari funding.
By 2018, Qatar had transferred approximately $1.1 billion to Gaza, according to figures presented to Israeli ministers and previously reported by Haaretz. The money was designated for humanitarian assistance, fuel purchases and government salaries. That year, Qatar began demanding formal documentation confirming Israel's involvement in the arrangements, partly because Israeli officials were publicly condemning Doha while privately asking it to continue providing the funds.
A senior official in the first Trump administration who was familiar with the negotiations told TIME that the contradiction frustrated the Qataris. Israeli officials would criticize the transfers in public, only to privately approach Doha and request that the payments be renewed.
In October 2018, Israel, Qatar and the United Nations signed an agreement to finance fuel deliveries to Gaza. The arrangement later developed into a three-party mechanism under Israeli and international oversight. Qatar financed fuel and electricity purchases from Israel, funded projects through the United Nations and provided monthly payments to impoverished Palestinian families.
In August 2021, Qatar signed another agreement worth $40 million to provide nearly 100,000 Palestinian households with $100 per month for four months. According to diplomats familiar with the arrangement, Israel vetted the lists of beneficiaries and supervised the distribution mechanism. Funds were transferred through the UN World Food Programme, and eligible families received text messages directing them to locations where they could collect the assistance.
Another document obtained by TIME, dated July 2019, shows Qatar notifying Netanyahu's government of a $6 million transfer to 20,000 Gaza residents, with each beneficiary receiving $300. The magazine said it remained unclear how many recipients selected through the Israeli mechanism were affiliated with Hamas or had relatives belonging to the organization.
In 2020, during the coronavirus pandemic, an Israeli National Security Council official identified as R. L. Maoz contacted Qatari officials to emphasize the importance of maintaining the financial assistance arrangements. The correspondence called for the continued transfer of Qatari humanitarian funds through the established system.
The official also requested that Qatar's assistance not be routed through other countries or intermediaries, but instead continue through Ambassador Mohammed al-Emadi, who headed the Qatari Committee for the Reconstruction of Gaza. The letter expressed appreciation for the cooperation and open dialogue, describing the relationship as important to preserving regional stability and security and bringing the two countries and their peoples closer together.

TPO hosts final session as Vietnamese trade delegation concludes Tehran visit with agricultural MOU

- Dr. Nisi – Director General of the East Asia and Oceania Office, Trade Promotion Organization of Iran.

- Mr. Ravanbakhsh – Director General of the Department of Industry, Mining and Trade of Khuzestan Province.

- Mr. Chenani – CEO of the Khuzestan Province Industrial Park Company.

The two sides signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) for joint-venture cooperation in the agricultural cultivation sector on a land area of 150,000 hectares.
In addition, the two companies signed a cooperation agreement on conducting soil surveys of agricultural land in Ahvaz, the capital of Khuzestan Province, and on sending Vietnamese agricultural experts to conduct trial cultivation of robusta coffee there. The products will serve the local population and the southern provinces, and will be partly exported to Iraq and Kuwait via the Khorramshahr commercial seaport.
The final day of the delegation’s visit, hosted by the TPO, underscored a practical shift from general trade promotion to concrete joint ventures in agriculture. The agreements on soil surveying and trial coffee cultivation in Khuzestan, combined with the 150,000-hectare MOU, provide a measurable follow-up mechanism for the mission’s stated goal of expanding Vietnam’s commercial footprint in the Middle East. The use of Khorramshahr port for exports to Iraq and Kuwait also signals a regional distribution role for Iran beyond bilateral trade.

Paris police in new battles with protesters and looters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:52:11 UTC
01:52:11 KST

Paris police in new battles with protesters and looters
PARIS - French police battled protesters and looters for a second day on Oct 18 as the country reeled from the violent chaos left by a day of cost-of-living demonstrations in which 2,000 people were arrested nationwide.
Paris city workers had not finished clearing up the torched cars, smashed shopfronts and burnt debris from the unrest on Oct 17 when the new troubles started and political recriminations erupted.
AFP journalists said several hundred people gathered in the Republique square in the capital following social media calls for a gathering that the authorities said had not been approved.
Television footage showed the looting of a clothing store and bikes were also set alight nearby.
The Paris police prefecture said security forces moved in when “faced with the initial signs of tension”.
AFP journalists saw police firing tear gas and stun grenades at hundreds of people gathered in the square. Bottles and rocks were hurled at police who made several arrests.
Some 550 people out of 855 arrested in Paris remained in detention from Oct 17’s troubles and police stations were struggling to cope, according to the Legal Team Paris group of lawyers.
Government under pressure
Six months from a presidential election, the government faced opposition attacks over preparations for the nationwide day of action that followed weeks of mounting student protests over conditions in schools.
President Emmanuel Macron, who on Oct 17 vowed that anyone who engaged in vandalism or looting would be prosecuted, was to address the nation on the evening of Oct 18.
Marine Le Pen, the far-right presidential candidate for the National Rally party, said the troubles showed that Macron’s administration was “running on fumes, exhausted and disoriented”.
“We are experiencing a profound crisis of trust and authority, which poses a threat to democracy,” said Le Pen, who leads opinion polls ahead of the election.
Le Pen has blamed ultra-left groups, while Jean-Luc Melenchon head of the far-left France Unbowed party accused authorities of inflaming tensions.
With images of French town halls burning and shops being looted grabbing headlines around the world, US President Donald Trump waded into the debate, blaming immigration for the unrest.
“France is burning! The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country,” Trump said in a social media post.
Looting rampages were reported on Oct 17 in Paris and other cities, including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Strasbourg, on the margins of protests over the cost of living.
Around 1,500 businesses were damaged with losses estimated at hundreds of millions of dollars, according to the Retail and Trade Federation. One person died during the main march in Paris, but officials said the case was health-related.
“It’s like we had a war,” a 78-year-old Paris resident Mehmet Ozeden told AFP amid burnt street barricades from the protests.
‘Animals’
Another resident, Anita Gras, said she saw young men loot a sports shoe retailer.
“It’s appalling, terrifying – groups of young people came here yesterday, looting, smashing everything, with total impunity,” said 57-year-old Cecile Rogue surveying a pile of charred bicycles.
The city of Limoges lost its 19th-century town hall to a fire that local prefect, Maurice Barate, told news channel LCI had been deliberately set by “a wild horde”.
About 7,000 people staged a march in the central city on Oct 18 to show their anger at the devastation.
In Lyon, a store owner, Jean-Christian, said those behind the violence were “animals”.
“We saw them looting, men high on adrenaline.”
A tourist office in the city centre was set ablaze during the protests amid multiple clashes and looting.
On Oct 18, a clothing store was also looted in Lyon.
Tourists stunned
In Paris, startled tourists were seen on Oct 17 running with suitcases along streets filled with tear gas and protesters.
A Danish tourist, Soren Petersen, said it was “sad” to see damage to Paris buildings. “It is not a protest, it’s far beyond a normal protest,” he told AFP.
Around 500 police, firefighters and paramedics were hurt in the protests, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said.
The violence took place on the sidelines of nationwide protests that the interior ministry said drew 550,000 people. The CGT union said 800,000 people participated.
A 17-year-old boy had his right hand blown off by a crowd-control grenade in the southern city of Saint-Etienne. In Mulhouse a 17-year-old girl lost an eye, according to prosecutors.
France’s Yellow Vest movement, which staged street protests eight years ago against Macron’s government over planned fuel-tax hikes, had called Saturday’s “yellow and youth” demonstrations. AFP

Captain of flydubai plane describes blocking axe blows as co-pilot attacked
Oct 18 - The captain of a flydubai flight who was attacked by a co-pilot who intended to crash the plane has described blocking axe blows to the head and screaming for help as he reached for a knob to open the cockpit door.
Captain Smit Machchhar has been hailed as a hero for his role in averting disaster on the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv last month, helping to thwart what the UAE attorney general has said was an attempted suicide attack by the co-pilot who intended to crash the plane into Ben Gurion Airport.
Speaking in an interview with The National newspaper from a hospital bed in Abu Dhabi, his head and left arm bandaged, Machchhar said that when the first blow landed, he thought something had gone "horribly wrong the aircraft structure", before quickly realising he was being attacked and things had "taken a drastic turn".
"The next thought was I need to get help in here," he said in the interview published on Saturday.
"My immediate action was to free myself from the seat belts and I tried to just block the blows as much as I could," he said, pointing to his arm that was wounded as he defended himself. "The blows were coming on the head."
"Immediately my hand went to the knob which opens the door and screaming for my colleagues, screaming his name."
"I believe that was the first time when I lost my consciousness."
The aircraft, flight FZ1073, was in Saudi airspace when the co-pilot attacked Machchhar with a crash axe, typically kept in the cockpit for emergency use.
The incident caused the airliner to plunge 16,000 feet (4,900 meters) in 30 seconds before the attacker was overwhelmed and two other pilots who were on board landed the aircraft safely in Saudi Arabia. The suspect, an Omani national, was transferred to the UAE, flydubai's home country.
The plan was inspired by the September 11, 2001, attacks on the US, UAE public prosecutors say, as a result of their criminal investigation launched on October 1.
Machchhar said he heard the cockpit door opening and screaming "between my colleague and the guy".
He said the scariest thing he felt was the aircraft nose "steeply going down."
"I was not very sure that I'll make it out alive from this. Did I give up? No." REUTERS

Transcript: Sen. Kevin Cramer on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Oct. 18, 2026
The following is the transcript of the interview with Sen. Kevin Cramer, Republican of North Dakota, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Oct. 18, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Welcome back to Face the Nation. We go now to North Dakota Republican Senator Kevin Cramer, who joins us from Bismarck. Good morning to you, Senator.
SENATOR KEVIN CRAMER (R-ND): Good morning. Good to be with you.
MARGARET BRENNAN: I want to ask you about Ukraine. I know you just recently traveled there. A number of your departing, some retiring, Senate Republican colleagues have made clear they were very upset with President Trump's decision to waive the Lindsey Graham sanctions off of Russia and buyers of Russian oil. Senator Cornyn said Lindsey would be appalled. Senator Tillis said it is beyond irresponsible, unconscionable to capitulate to Vladimir Putin. Where do you stand?
SEN. CRAMER: Well, Margaret, on this topic and a whole bunch of others, I think capitulating to a bully generally means they're going to make more demands going forward. That's the problem with taking sort of a business negotiation approach to negotiating with a thug, which is what Vladimir Putin is. So I share those colleagues' positions on it. However, I also have to acknowledge that we are few weeks or a couple weeks from an election. One of the important topics of the election is the cost of diesel fuel. It's really an important issue here in North Dakota.
As Representative Turner pointed out, and I was cheering him on, our allies throughout Europe have been buying energy from Vladimir Putin and funding his war machine for decades and they should stop right now. Having said all of that, I expect this will be a short-term pause, and I certainly hope so, because one of the things that President Zelenskyy asked of us when I was with him on last Thursday, I think it was Thursday or Friday, was that the president would fully enforce the Lindsey Graham sanctions bill. And I still take that position.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah. And some European Union countries do continue to buy fuel products. India and China would be the largest purchasers who would be hit by these tariffs. So do you think the president would actually even post-election trigger the tariffs on China?
SEN. CRAMER: Well, I certainly hope that he does, Margaret. Again, speaking of thugs who will never agree to terms, or at least not continue to agree to terms that would be negotiated, Xi Jinping is another one. I think we have to start approaching our geopolitical negotiations the way that we ought to, and not the way that you do in a boardroom. You know, this is not a finality outcome to a dictator. The outcome of a negotiation with a dictator is more, you know, asking for more demands. And we have to start playing nice with our friends and treating our adversaries like they are adversaries.
MARGARET BRENNAN: You just met with President Zelenskyy. As you know, President Trump publicly blasted him again this week and said Ukraine needs another new president. Let me ask you something specific about how they defend themselves and conduct this war. Starshield is a U.S. military program which Ukraine says that they use to fire into Russian-held territory. Last night, Secretary Rubio said Ukraine does not currently have access to it, but they have asked to use it to fire deep inside of Russia. When you were in Ukraine, as I understand it, you were presenting a proposal to President Zelenskyy to allow for Starshield access expansion if Ukraine stops striking Russian energy assets. What can you tell us about that proposal and what is the status of it?
SEN. CRAMER: So that, you're right, that was a proposal we brought to President Zelenskyy. Senator Wicker, Roger Wicker, the chairman of the Armed Services Committee, came up with that idea. President Zelensky was enthusiastic about it. He said, I'd do that tomorrow. I would absolutely stop attacking Russia's energy facilities if I could have access to targeting capabilities, which is what Starshield would provide them, to go deep into Russia and attack their attackers, in other words, their launch facilities, kill the archer, not the arrows. Of course, the third thing he asked for was the capacity to get licensed to jointly produce, co-produce Patriot missile interceptors, which would help him defend against these much faster now jet-powered drones and missiles coming into Ukraine.
So his requests were three. They were simple. And I agree with all three of them. So I would hope we can get to that point where- remembering that what President Zelenskyy is protecting are civilians. Russia has chosen to go after civilian populations, while President Zelenskyy has simply gone after the launchers and, more importantly, the war machine's funding source, which is energy.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right, bringing us back to where we started here. Ukraine has resumed, just even overnight, hitting Russian oil refineries. They hit the St. Petersburg oil terminal. Russia has been targeting the energy infrastructure inside of Ukraine. Secretary Rubio said there are talks ongoing. Have you talked to Secretary Rubio about your exchange with President Zelenskyy? Who in the administration is actually trying to bring this to a close?
SEN. CRAMER: So I have not talked to Marco, although as I was watching your previous segment, I just said to my staff, I wish I would have called Marco. But obviously he and others are involved with it, including Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. I thin– but I worry, Margaret, that there's a disconnect. Once again, I go back to my earlier illustration. There's a disconnect between traditional, mutually beneficial negotiations between business people and the difference between somebody's protecting humanity itself versus somebody who wants to take humanity down. And so I worry about that. So who exactly is negotiating these things? I don't know who's calling shots. But at the end of the day, I think the president is, you know, it's where the buck stops. And I think he accepts that.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So is Senator Wicker presenting this deal to the White House? What are you doing with what you negotiated?
SEN. CRAMER: Oh yeah, yes, for sure. I mean, we had talked to people in the White House at the Department of War and to the State Department even prior to meeting with President Zelenskyy.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So do you join your colleagues, Senator Tillis and Senator Shaheen, in calling for an investigation of what has happened here in terms of whether U.S. government officials knew that Starlink was going to be interrupted, which impacts Ukraine's ability to use its drones and defend its people?
SEN. CRAMER: Well, I certainly support investigating what was the source of that decision, if in fact it was a decision at all. It may very well have been some sort of a technical glitch. I don't know for sure or whose call it was. So far, nobody's taking credit for making that call or the blame for it. So I do support some sort of an investigation. Certainly Congress itself could and should investigate. I think the letter that Senator Shaheen and Senator Tillis are talking about would be an inspector general investigation, perhaps.
But, sure, we want to get to the bottom of it. In the meantime, what's more important is that that power is put back on full scale and that we actually enhance Ukraine's ability to hit these launch facilities inside of Russia, deeper inside to like 300 kilometers, I think is what President Zelenskyy was asking for.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah. President Zelenskyy said today that it has been restored, but has been throttled back. And in terms of that Starshield expansion, as you say, no deal yet. Let me ask you about something closer to home. You said this summer that you "hate," that was the word you used, President Trump's decision to import foreign beef tariff-free because it's not America first, wrongheaded and threatens the future of U.S. food production. The White House did not reverse course, despite those tough words from you. How negative has that been for your state? And is that going to infect- affect- I should say, the enthusiasm for voters to show up in November? Are these ranchers just so ticked off they're not going to vote?
SEN. CRAMER: Well, first of all, Margaret, it won't have any effect in North Dakota in the election cycle. We don't have a governor up. The president's obviously not up. We don't even have a senator up. And we're gonna have an overwhelming Republican victory here. Having said that, it's very discouraging to our ranchers. Again, I think there's a misunderstanding of commodity cycles, commodity economic cycles. Ranchers rebuild their herds when prices are high. Their herds are obviously made much smaller when prices are low. That's why- that's why the countercyclical effect of commodity prices are well known to us, and why it's discouraging when we reduce or eliminate the barriers to to importing somebody else's beef, which is not nearly as safe or as high quality, at the cost of- at the cost of- our local ranchers. They rely on these higher prices. And by the way, I doubt that bringing in a bunch of Argentine beef is going to bring the price at the grocery store down--
MARGARET BRENNAN: --It hasn't--
SEN. CRAMER: --It has not. But it will hurt the market price of the cattle themselves. Now, ranchers are going up against lots of other problems as well, including the concentration of meat packing in the United States, where about a third or more is literally owned by the Chinese and the Brazilians. So they're going up against a lot of things, but their input costs are also higher. They don't come down because the price of a cow goes down. But yeah, so I still strongly oppose it, and I think it was wrongheaded.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right. Well, I wanted to get your insight on that because we're seeing that dynamic in other states as well, including Kansas. So, Senator, thank you so much for your time today. We're going to have to leave it there. We'll be right back.

Bimol Akoijam willing to contest Manipur Assembly polls if Congress offers ticket

NEW DELHI: Congress MP Angomcha Bimol Akoijam on Sunday said he was willing to contest next year's Manipur Assembly elections from the Keishamthong constituency if the party offered him a ticket, as he faces a sexual harassment case and has been dismissed from Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU).Speaking at an event, the Inner Manipur MP said his decision to enter the electoral contest would be guided by the future of the state."I am ready to fight elections from Keishamthong (in Imphal West district). If the party offers me a ticket, I will contest the Keisamthong assembly constituency. This decision is for the future of the state," Akoijam said, according to news agency PTI.The Manipur Assembly elections are due next year.His remarks come amid an ongoing police investigation into sexual harassment allegations against him and his dismissal from JNU, where he was a professor at the Centre for the Study of Social Systems under the School of Social Sciences.
JNU dismissal and police investigation
Akoijam was dismissed from the university on October 9 following an inquiry into allegations of sexual harassment. He has denied the charges and described the university's action as a "witch hunt", claiming he was not given an opportunity to respond to the inquiry committee's findings.
Delhi Police booked him on October 11 following a complaint by JNU's chief security officer. He recently appeared before investigators at the Vasant Kunj North Police Station in New Delhi in connection with the case.At least 11 female students submitted complaints against Akoijam in May. They alleged that he invited students to his campus residence on the pretext of meetings or gatherings and attempted to harass them. Some students also alleged that he made obscene and inappropriate remarks in class.After appearing before investigators, Akoijam said he intended to challenge his dismissal legally.Speaking to reporters in Imphal on Friday, he said his lawyers were preparing the case and that he would file it within a day or two.He also said he had cooperated with the police and would continue to do so, while requesting adequate notice for any further questioning because of his responsibilities as an MP.
During his remarks to the media, Akoijam also urged greater attention to the wider situation in Manipur, including the plight of internally displaced people, lawlessness and issues surrounding buffer zones."Thousands of people are languishing in relief camps. I don’t think my pain is anything greater than the pain of these people," he said, while alleging that the action against him was an attempt to silence his voice.
The MP had earlier said, "Justice will be done," before travelling to New Delhi to join the police investigation.The allegations have also triggered political reactions in the state. BJP workers staged a protest outside Congress Bhavan in Imphal, demanding Akoijam's resignation and accusing him of bringing disrepute to Manipur. Police prevented the protesters from entering the premises.Congress spokesperson Hareshwar Goshwami described the protest as a diversionary tactic and accused the ruling party of deflecting attention from killings and the crisis in the state.Akoijam has maintained that the allegations against him are false and has challenged the process that led to his dismissal. The sexual harassment allegations remain under investigation.

Exhibition of Farshchian’s works underway in Paris

Exhibition of Farshchian’s works underway in Paris
TEHRAN - An exhibition of images of selected miniature paintings by the late master Mahmoud Farshchian opened on Friday at the Cultural Attaché Office of the Embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in Paris and will run for a week.
It is the fourth and final cultural-artistic event planned by the Iranian embassy as part of the weekly cultural activities for the month of October, ILNA reported.
The opening ceremony was attended by a group of Iranian and international enthusiasts of Iranian art and cultural heritage, as well as the Ambassadors of the Islamic Republic of Iran to France and to the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO).
During the opening day, the historical styles and periods of Iranian miniature art and its great masters were introduced and explained. Additionally, a clip was screened introducing Farshchian’s works, his outstanding artistic characteristics, his widespread fame among Iranians and non-Iranians worldwide, and his unprecedented successes in international circles.
Born in 1930 in Isfahan, Mahmoud Farshchian was celebrated as one of the most prominent figures in contemporary Iranian art, known for his exquisite works inspired by Persian literature and religious texts.
His work is renowned for its intricate craftsmanship, blending traditional Persian miniature techniques with innovative elements that breathe new life into classical themes. His art vividly captures the soul of Persian poetry, religious stories, and spiritual symbolism, creating compositions that are both visually stunning and deeply meaningful. His mastery lies in the delicate balance of tradition and innovation—crafting vibrant, flowing lines, circular motifs, and dynamic colors that evoke emotion and transcend cultural boundaries.
Throughout his illustrious career, Farshchian’s artworks have traveled the globe, exhibited in prestigious cities such as Paris, New York, Chicago, and Tokyo. Many of his pieces have been gifted by Iranian officials as symbols of Iran’s rich cultural heritage. His contributions earned him numerous accolades, reaffirming his status as a national treasure.
With intricate details, dynamic compositions, and a masterful use of color and symbolism, he transforms the canvas into a sacred space where grief and hope intertwine. These paintings not only preserve the historical memory of Karbala but also evoke timeless lessons of faith, justice, and resistance against oppression.
Farshchian’s influence extended beyond his brush. He served as a professor and director at the University of Tehran’s Faculty of Fine Arts, shaping generations of artists who continue to carry forward his artistic vision.
Despite his international recognition, Farshchian remained rooted in his Iranian identity. His art drew inspiration from Persian poetry, the Quran, and sacred texts of Christianity and Judaism, creating a universal language of spiritual artistry. His ability to fuse tradition with modernity has earned him worldwide admiration, with scholars like Umberto Baldini, an Italian art historian, describing him as a “phenomenon and a pivotal point in Iranian art.”
He significantly contributed to promoting Iranian art internationally, often invited to speak at universities and cultural institutions worldwide. Several books and scholarly articles have been published about his works, cementing his legacy as a master artist.
His name has been registered on Britain’s list of 2000 Outstanding Intellectuals of the 21st century, and collectors feel it is a great honor to possess one of his creations.
The previous exhibitions held at the site of the Iranian embassy in Paris included: “Ancient Iran: History and Civilization,” “Today’s Iran: Art, Culture, and Innovation,” and the painting exhibition “Windswept Dreams,” dedicated to commemorating the memory of the children of the Shajareh Tayebeh school in Minab and other martyred children who fell victim to the recent US aggression against Iran.
This series of exhibitions aims to introduce various aspects of Iran’s culture, art, history, and civilization to audiences, while providing an opportunity to develop and deepen dialogue, mutual understanding, and appreciation between the two nations and cultures.

Lesser-known classical music pieces performed at Roudaki Hall
TEHRAN - Tehran’s Roudaki Hall hosted the “Mourning to Dawn” concert, featuring performances of classical music compositions, on Saturday.
Centered around introducing lesser-heard and rarely performed classical music works, the program was staged in two parts with the accompaniment of a piano and a string ensemble, ILNA reported.
The repertoire featured works by composers from various periods of classical music. In the first part, Ahmad Razavi, the piano soloist, performed the second piece from the “Klavierstücke” (3 Piano Pieces), D. 946, in E-flat major by Franz Schubert. Next, Johann Sebastian Bach’s “Harpsichord Concerto No. 7 in G minor, BWV 1058,” was performed in three movements.
The second part was dedicated to works by Julius von Beliczay, Vasily Kalinnikov, Samuel Coleridge-Taylor, Anton Arensky, and Robert Fuchs. Serenades for string instruments, the “Four Novelletten” suite for string orchestra, and variations on a theme by Tchaikovsky were among the pieces in this section.
Mahmoud Mirzaei, the conductor of the “Mourning to Dawn” concert, pointed to the technical difficulty of the performed works, describing the program as comprising seven pieces by various classical composers, noting that many of these works were unfamiliar even to the orchestra’s own musicians.
According to Mirzaei, the technical and performance complexities of the pieces required around 10 to 12 rehearsal sessions to achieve the desired result; nevertheless, the ensemble took the stage with only four rehearsals. Describing the final performance as falling short of his musical ideal, he nevertheless evaluated the musicians’ efforts as acceptable given the time constraints.
The conductor also expressed hope that by maintaining the ensemble’s lineup and allocating sufficient rehearsal time, it would be possible to continue this collaboration and deliver higher-quality performances in future programs.

Iran’s Kanoon nominates two candidates for 2027 Astrid Lindgren Award
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18

Iran’s Kanoon nominates two candidates for 2027 Astrid Lindgren Award
TEHRAN- Iran’s Institute for Intellectual Development of Children and Young Adults (IIDCY-Kanoon) has nominated writer Abbas Jahangirian and illustrator Amir Shabanipour for the 2027 Astrid Lindgren Memorial Award (ALMA), one of the world’s most prestigious honors in children’s literature.
The names of the two Iranian candidates were included in the list of nominees for the award, which recognizes outstanding contributions to literature for children and young adults, Kanoon’s public relations office announced on Saturday.
A total of 277 candidates from 80 countries have been nominated for the 2027 edition in the categories of writing, illustration, oral storytelling and reading promotion. Of these, 85 are appearing on the list for the first time.
Jahangirian, nominated in the writing category, has more than five decades of experience in fiction writing, playwriting, research and education. His works address a range of human and social issues, including environmental protection, peaceful coexistence, intergenerational relationships and the promotion of hope among children and young adults.
His stories also feature children with disabilities as active central characters. Drawing on Iranian history, local culture and national identity, Jahangirian incorporates elements of cinema and theater into storytelling. He has also been involved in teaching fiction writing, playwriting and screenwriting.
His participation in professional organizations concerned with children’s literature and rights, along with the recognition his works have received from festivals and academic researchers, were among the considerations behind his nomination.
Shabanipour has been nominated in the illustration category. His work is distinguished by an independent visual language, creative use of color and composition, and the ability to develop and extend narratives through illustrations.
His illustrations explore children’s emotions, imagination, curiosity and concerns. He has also experimented with different forms of visual storytelling and incorporated Iranian cultural elements to communicate with audiences beyond the country.
Shabanipour has collaborated with publishers and organizations active in children’s literature, contributing to the production of picture books and the promotion of reading. His works have been exhibited at international events, while some of his books have been published abroad. He has also received international awards.
Other Iranian nominees for the 2027 award include writer Atoosa Salehi, illustrators Alireza Goldouzian and Hoda Haddadi, and the “Read with Me” program in the reading promotion category. They were nominated by other Iranian organizations authorized to put forward candidates, including the Children’s Book Council of Iran, the Association of Iranian Children’s Book Writers and the Institute for Research on the History of Children’s Literature.
Atoosa Salehi is an Iranian poet, writer, translator and editor specializing in children’s and young adult literature. She has published more than 100 works across poetry, picture books, graphic novels and fiction. Her 12-volume retelling of Shahnameh for young readers has been reprinted more than 30 times, and some of her works have been translated into several languages.
Alireza Goldouzian is an internationally recognized artist who has illustrated numerous books in Iran, as well as exhibiting his prize-winning children's book art around the world.
Hoda Haddadi’s works highlight her impactful role in creating a feminine, nature-inspired, peace-filled universe influenced by rich Persian literature. Haddadi skillfully employs collage techniques, vibrant colors, and motifs to craft unique visual narratives. Her extensive experience in teaching across various age groups and numerous prestigious awards in illustration further underpin her nomination.
“Read with Me” has been initiated by the Institute for Research on History of Children’s Literature to promote reading for all children, in particular for those living in deprived areas and crisis. The plan promotes the slogan “All children deserve to read quality books”.
Established in 2002 by the Swedish government in memory of Astrid Lindgren, the creator of “Pippi Longstocking”, the Astrid Lindgren Memorial Award aims to promote children’s and young adults’ literature around the world. With a prize of five million Swedish kronor, it is the world’s largest monetary award in the field.
The annual award recognizes authors, illustrators, oral storytellers and reading promoters. Its 12-member jury selects the laureate from the international list of nominees.
The 2027 laureate will be announced on April 6, 2027, during the Bologna Children’s Book Fair in Italy. Canadian illustrator Jon Klassen received the 2026 award.

News from occupied Ukraine: 11 Ukrainians, including 96-year-old woman, evacuated from Russian occupation

News from occupied Ukraine: 11 Ukrainians, including 96-year-old woman, evacuated from Russian occupation
This weekly update from the Kyiv Independent aims to shed light on the situation facing Ukrainians living under Russian occupation and the ever-tightening control of information imposed by the Kremlin.
Key news as of Oct. 17:
- Eleven Ukrainians, including 96-year-old woman, return from Russian-occupied territories, ombudsman says
- Russia sends terrorism case against 6 teenagers in occupied Luhansk Oblast to court
- Ukrainian troops struck Russian drone sites, ammunition depots in occupied territories
- Equipment wear at occupied Donbas coal mines reaches 80–90%
- From Oleshky to Mariupol, crises across Russian-occupied Ukraine deepen
Eleven Ukrainians, including 96-year-old woman, return from Russian-occupied territories, ombudsman says
Eleven Ukrainian citizens have returned to Ukrainian-controlled territory from Russian-occupied areas, including a 96-year-old woman and her son, Ukraine's Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Oct. 16.
One of those evacuated was a man who had remained in occupied Luhansk after his wife died in 2018. His relatives had already left and were waiting for him in Ukrainian-controlled territory, but he had struggled to leave his home. After suffering three heart attacks and developing problems with blood pressure and mobility, he needed specialized transport to make the journey, Lubinets said.
Another case involved a 96-year-old woman and her son from the Russian-occupied village of Tavriiske in Kherson Oblast. The son had been caring for his mother when he was wounded in a Russian air attack in September. He sustained severe injuries, lost an eye, and was hospitalized.
Both needed assistance to return to Ukrainian-controlled territory, as the son was recovering from his injuries and his elderly mother could not travel independently. They returned together on Oct. 15, according to Lubinets.
Separately, Save Ukraine, a Ukrainian humanitarian NGO, said on Oct. 11 that 33 children were returned to Ukraine from the Russian-occupied territories over the past week.
The Volyn humanitarian corridor in Ukraine's northwestern Volyn Oblast is usually used for such evacuations, as it is the only working checkpoint between Ukraine and Belarus. There are currently no functioning checkpoints between Ukraine and Russia.
Given that the territory of Belarus was used by Russia to launch its full-scale invasion, the area around the crossing is heavily fortified with mines and anti-tank hedgehogs.
The last direct route from Russia to Ukraine through a checkpoint in Sumy Oblast was closed in August 2024 amid escalating Russian attacks in the oblast.
The fate of thousands of Ukrainians currently in captivity, as well as those living under occupation, remains uncertain. Between 3.5 million and 5 million Ukrainians remain in Russian-occupied territories and in Russia itself, according to an estimate cited by Lubinets in July.
Many Ukrainians cannot leave for various reasons, such as age, illness, disability, financial constraints, family responsibilities, and the threat of property expropriation by the occupation authorities.

Russia sends terrorism case against 6 teenagers in occupied Luhansk Oblast to court
Russian occupation authorities have sent a criminal case against six teenagers accused of carrying out arson attacks on infrastructure in occupied Luhansk Oblast to court, Russia's Investigative Committee branch in the occupied region claimed on Oct. 6.
According to the statement on Telegram, the teenagers allegedly carried out 20 arson attacks between May and September 2025, targeting electrical substations, gas infrastructure, mobile phone towers, and vehicles in the occupied town of Sverdlovsk and its surrounding area.
The alleged damage exceeded 2.5 million rubles ($32,000), the agency said. The teenagers face charges including terrorism, incitement to commit a terrorist act, and intentional property destruction.
The claims cannot be independently verified.
The case comes amid broader repression in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories. The UN Human Rights Office said in a September 2025 report that Russian authorities have used arbitrary detention and criminal prosecutions against Ukrainian civilians, with frequent violations of procedural safeguards.
read also
Ukrainian troops struck Russian drone sites, ammunition depots in occupied territories
Ukraine's military struck Russian drone launch sites, military supply and ammunition depots, troop concentrations, and communications infrastructure in Russian-occupied parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Crimea between Oct. 11 and Oct. 16, Ukraine's General Staff said.
Donetsk Oblast
Near the occupied city of Donetsk, Ukrainian forces struck a Russian site used to store, prepare, and launch attack drones overnight on Oct. 14. Military supply depots and Russian troop concentrations near several settlements were also targeted, according to the General Staff's Oct. 14 report.
Luhansk Oblast
Ukrainian forces struck a fuel and lubricants depot near Dovzhansk and an ammunition depot near Rubizhne on Oct. 12 and overnight into Oct. 13. Russian troop concentrations near Kuzemivka were also targeted, the General Staff said in its Oct. 13 report.
Zaporizhzhia Oblast
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian troop concentration near Naberezhne on Oct. 12 and overnight into Oct. 13. They also hit a concentration of personnel from the Russian military's Rubikon drone unit near Novokostiantynivka on Oct. 14 and overnight into Oct. 15, according to the General Staff's Oct. 13 and Oct. 15 reports.
Crimea
Ukrainian forces struck four storage facilities for Russian attack drones near occupied Hvardiiske. Damage was confirmed in the General Staff's Oct. 15 report. On Oct. 15 and overnight into Oct. 16, Ukrainian forces also struck two telecommunications towers equipped with antenna systems near Olenivka, according to the General Staff's Oct. 16 report.

Equipment wear at occupied Donbas coal mines reaches 80–90%
Coal mining equipment in Russian-occupied parts of Donbas has deteriorated by 80–90% after 12 years without modernization, Alexander Klimenko, chairman of the board of directors of the Rodina industrial group, said, according to the Russian-backed Luhansk Information Center on Oct. 15.
Rodina, an investor in the coal industry in occupied Luhansk Oblast, has purchased one of only two new mining complexes acquired in Russia this year, the company said. It did not specify where the equipment would be installed or when it would enter operation.
The admission comes amid a wider decline in the region's coal industry. Coal production in occupied Luhansk Oblast fell from 6.7 million metric tons in 2018 to 1.34 million metric tons in 2024, while 68 mines were undergoing liquidation as of July 2026, according to figures cited by Ukrainian media Realna Gazeta.
Donbas was historically central to Ukraine's coal industry, supplying fuel for thermal power plants and coking coal for steel production. The deterioration of mines threatens an industrial sector that once supported regional employment, steelmaking, and energy production.
The 80–90% wear estimate was provided by Rodina's chairman and was not independently verified. The Russian-backed report did not identify the mines assessed or explain how the figure was calculated.
read also
From Oleshky to Mariupol, crises across Russian-occupied Ukraine deepen
While the humanitarian crisis in the Russian-occupied front-line city of Oleshky recently garnered media attention, all regions of occupied Ukraine face worsening humanitarian issues at the hands of Russia's occupation authorities, the Kyiv Independent reported on Oct. 15.
Across all occupied territories, civilians face failing water and electricity systems, shortages of qualified doctors, deteriorating municipal services, and mass depopulation, while specific problems differ from one occupied region to another.
Petro Andriushchenko, head of the Center for the Study of the Occupation, told the Kyiv Independent that the problems are driven by the failure of Russian occupation authorities to maintain basic services, as well as wartime destruction, proximity to the front line, and a lack of qualified personnel.
Russia currently occupies all of Crimea, 99% of Luhansk Oblast, 73% of Donetsk Oblast, 65% of Zaporizhzhia Oblast, and 57% of Kherson Oblast, according to geolocation estimates from the open-source intelligence project DeepState. Crimea, as well as parts of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts, have been under occupation since 2014, while parts of Kherson and Zaporizhzhia oblasts have been under occupation since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.

The U.S. has proposed that European countries unfreeze some Russian assets — turning them over to Washington’s control as part of an effort to get Moscow to resume peace talks — the Financial Times reported on Oct. 15. According to the outlet’s four sources, the proposal was discussed at a meeting in Miami attended by representatives of the U.S., Ukraine, France, Germany, the United Kingdom, the EU, and NATO.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz came out against unfreezing Russian funds. “Those are assets that are frozen in Europe and they should remain frozen in Europe. This is our business and we are deciding over it,” Merz said ahead of the EU leaders’ summit in Brussels.
In response to The Insider’s inquiry, Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that Russia may act through intermediaries in its attempts to convince Belgian authorities to agree to unfreeze the assets.
“As for the frozen assets, I discussed this in detail with Belgium — and I am grateful to the prime minister [Bart De Wever] and his team, and to other EU leaders. Everyone understands that Russia will do everything it can to retrieve the frozen assets through one partner or another. It is a real risk. We have such information, but, again, we have discussed the details with the Europeans. Today the situation remains under Europe’s full control. So as of today, it is safe.”
This past September, the European Commission resumed work on scenarios for seizing the frozen assets of the Russian Central Bank in Europe. One proposed option would involve the creation of a separate structure into which all such assets — including those currently being held at the Belgian depository Euroclear — could be transferred. The previous attempt to approve the use of frozen Russian assets to help Ukraine was blocked by Belgium.
Euroclear holds most of the Russian assets frozen in the EU — €200 billion. Since February 2024, the organization has been using the interest generated by these assets to support the European Fund for Ukraine.
During his visit to Kyiv in mid-August, Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot said that his country is generally open to using frozen Russian assets but that other EU states must share with it all the associated risks. As Prévot previously stated: “If Russia takes us to court it will have every chance of winning and we, Belgium, will not be able to repay those €200 billion, because that represents the equivalent of an entire year of the federal budget. It would mean bankruptcy for Belgium.”

Handala breaches Israeli military’s media intelligence hub, leaks thousands of files
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:44:39 UTC

Handala breaches Israeli military’s media intelligence hub, leaks thousands of files
TEHRAN — Handala said on Sunday that it broke into the Israeli military’s Media Intelligence Monitoring and Analysis Unit and put more than 500 classified documents and tens of thousands of internal messages online.
The unit combs Israeli and foreign media for the army and works alongside Unit 8200 and the military censor.
Handala called the breach “a blow to Israel’s information security infrastructure” and said it will soon publish the unit’s organizational structure and the reach of its access to military intelligence systems.
A small sample from the release, analyzed by the Tehran Times, shows the work itself. It holds 11,275 posts from X, all filed under the label “Israeli Media” and nearly all written in January 2024, the fourth month of the war on Gaza.
Each carries the author’s handle and a “normalized influence” score from zero to 78. About 4,500 accounts appear, roughly four in five posting in Hebrew.
Where a follower count was recorded, the median is 377, and an account with seven followers still earned a 17.
A considerable portion of what the analysts gathered is Israelis arguing and commenting about their own regime. More than 3,000 posts concern the captives.
Ynet Alerts relays the army’s admission that captive Sahar Baruch died in a failed rescue, under the line that living hostages do not return by military means.
Prof. David Pinto’s call to “flood Hamas’s tunnels” is posted again and again. One user writes that the government would not be discussing ethnic cleansing in Gaza, and might stop starving Gazans, if Israelis filled the streets.
Then-war minister Yoav Gallant is named in about 190 posts, and Itamar Ben-Gvir in about 130. Over 400 posts react to the killing of Hamas leader Saleh al-Arouri in Beirut, and a dozen tag Senator Lindsey Graham. Posts demanding the army “crush everyone in Gaza and settle it with Jews” sit in the same file batch, on the same scale.
A smaller batch dates to August 8, 2022, days after Israel’s offensive in Gaza that month. It logs military correspondents Yoav Limor, Amir Bohbot, Yoav Zitun, Yossi Yehoshua, Roy Sharon and Or Heller, plus army-linked pages such as Soldiers Tweeting. Reporter tracking predates October 7 by more than a year.
Handala’s operation places the machinery that records and analyzes those conversations in open view. Handala says the unit’s organizational chart is next.
The Israeli establishment has long claimed technological superiority, backed by steady Western support. Each successful penetration chips at that claim.
Earlier Handala actions already emptied email accounts belonging to Ehud Barak, Gadi Eisenkot, and Benny Gantz, and pulled material from devices linked to Naftali Bennett and Netanyahu’s chief of staff.
In March, it published FBI Director Kash Patel’s personal email, which U.S. officials confirmed. In April came some 19,000 files it attributed to former army chief Herzi Halevi. In September it released selfies of about 700 Israeli security personnel, taken with a tool it called Na’em.
On October 15, it posted 120 pages of contacts belonging to Israeli politician Tzipi Livni, exposing her opposition to Netanyahu as theater.
Naftali Bennett first denied his phone was compromised, then acknowledged unauthorized access to his Telegram account. This month Haaretz said it had verified leaked WhatsApp messages of Netanyahu aide Yonatan Urich, who confirmed his account was hacked.

Tehran slams Macron over ‘Indefensible Double Standards’
TEHRAN – Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei has accused French President Emmanuel Macron of applying double standards to protests in Iran and France, pointing to “a stark contrast” between Macron’s response to unrest in Iran and his stance on attacks against public institutions in France.
In a post on X, Baqaei recalled France’s position on the domestic unrest in Iran in January 2026 and its response to the US-Israeli military aggression against the country, challenging Macron over his approach to the recent protests in France.
“Mr. Macron, do you remember that last January you were advocating ‘peaceful demonstrations without fear of punishment’ for those who, following malicious calls from abroad, attacked our law enforcement centers and public institutions?” Baqaei wrote.
“Now, in your own republic, you say that vandalism and attacks on institutions will not be tolerated and that those responsible will be severely punished!”
Baqaei also recalled a text message Macron sent to US President Donald Trump shortly before the military aggression against Iran, quoting the French president as saying: “We can do great things on Iran.”
The spokesperson argued that subsequent events had revealed the meaning of Macron’s words, accusing France of aligning with the aggression against Iran and the crimes that had consequences extending across the region and beyond.
Addressing Macron directly, Baqaei drew a parallel between the unrest in France and the “No Kings” protests in the United States, warning that alliances formed to advance political agendas could ultimately backfire on those behind them.
“Mr. Macron, now that the fire has reached your own home and ‘No Kings’ is being shouted in America, remember that history does not always watch the world burn through the window opened by ill-fated alliances. Sometimes, it breaks that very window and returns to the homes of those who opened it,” he wrote.
Baqaei concluded his post with a quotation attributed to French fabulist Jean de La Fontaine: “The more artfully a deception is woven, the more damaging it may prove to its author; and treachery may well return to the one who committed it.”

The Tampa Bay Rays on Saturday beat the Cleveland Guardians 7-3 to even the best-of-seven American League Championship Series at two apiece.
Rays pitcher Freddy Peralta affectionately referred to Nick Martinez as “a horse.” Tampa Bay outfielder Chandler Simpson praised him for being “a dog.” By whatever four-legged description, Martinez came through with the terrific start Tampa Bay needed in Game 4.
Pitching for the first time in 10 days, the 36-year-old Martinez threw 5-1/3 strong innings, allowing one run and two hits to earn his first postseason win. He struck out three and walked two, retiring 11 straight batters from the first through fifth to silence a sellout crowd of 33,355 at Progressive Field.
Photo: David Dermer-Imagn Images
“He’s our president. That’s why we call him El Presidente,” Rays reliever Cam Booser said. “Every time Nick goes out there, he gives you everything he has. The guy is an absolute competitor. He brings the energy, he brings the vibes after every play.”
Martinez was amped up to start Friday night in Cleveland before soaking rain postponed the game. The right-hander said, in hindsight, being pushed back another day was a blessing.
Having not pitched since Oct. 7 in Game 3 of the Division Series against the New York Yankees, Martinez said he might have been too excited to be effective after a long layoff.
“I get antsy and was dialed up,” he said. “After you get the body going that much, the central nervous system is fired up, and you’re jacked up. I think my legs would have been heavy if we had started that game at like 9 or 10.”
The Guardians only put Martinez on the ropes once, scoring in the first when Chase DeLauter singled in Steven Kwan, who led off with a single. They did not manage another hit off him, only drawing walks by Travis Bazzana and Petey Halpin before Tampa Bay went to the bullpen.
Martinez threw 79 pitches, 53 of them strikes, to continue his dominance of the AL Central champions. He is 3-0 with a 0.49 ERA over three starts against Cleveland this year.
“Nick rose to the occasion, as I knew he would as someone we have a lot of confidence in,” Rays catcher Liam Hicks said. “He’s pretty easy to catch, because he’s got a lot of pitches and he puts the ball where he wants to.”
Peralta, likely to start Game 6 when the Rays return home Monday, took over for Martinez with one on and one out in the sixth. The trade-deadline acquisition from the New York Mets quelled the threat, needing only nine pitches to get out of the inning and pass the baton.
Thanks to Martinez’s outing, Tampa Bay is lined up nicely with ace Drew Rasmussen starting Game 5 this morning (Taipei time).
“We trust in both guys,” Peralta said. “Nick is always pounding the zone, and he gives us a chance to win, and Drew has been amazing in what he does. Today was amazing. Just a huge game for us.”

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:52 UTC
01:42:52 KST

Taiwanese shuttlers Chen Ping-hsuan and Lee Wei-ting on Saturday won the men’s doubles title at the World Junior Badminton Championships in Cairo, securing Taiwan’s first gold medal in the event.
The top-seeded Taiwanese pair defeated Japan’s Mahiro Oku and Masato Yamashiro in straight games in the final, winning 15-10, 15-9.
Chen and Lee took an early 7-2 lead in the opening game with aggressive play. Although their Japanese opponents narrowed the gap to two points, the Taiwanese duo capitalized on their opponents’ service errors to score three consecutive points and take the game 15-10.
Photo: Lin Chun-yung via CNA
The second game remained closely contested until the score was tied at 6-6. Chen and Lee then pulled ahead with a five-point run before closing out the match 15-9.
The Taiwanese pair did not drop a single game throughout the tournament.
Their coach, Lin Chun-yung, yesterday said that the two players were mentally mature and possessed well-rounded skills.
Although they had partnered for only a little more than a year, in July they won silver at the Badminton Asia Junior Championships, Lin said.
He said he had set a goal for the duo to win a medal at the World Junior Championships, but the pair had exceeded his expectations by taking gold.
He praised their game awareness and ability to dominate the opening and middle stages of the matches.
However, he said that this was the first edition of the junior tournament to use a 15-point game format, adding that the outcome might have been different under the traditional 21-point format.

BOOKMAN BILINGUAL 雙語書林： Chinglish or Natural English? 中式英語或道地英語？
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:51 UTC
01:42:51 KST

1. 他的行為令人無法容忍。
ˇ His conduct is simply intolerable.
χ His conduct is simply intolerant.
Photo: Adobe Stock l 照片:Adobe Stock
註︰intolerant 用於人是指「不能容忍、接受不同意見」、「褊狹的」，例如：
He was so firm in his own belief that he was intolerant of others’ opinions.
或對食物、藥物過敏，有 lactose-intolerant（乳糖不耐症）、gluten-intolerant（麩質不耐症）。intolerable 是「難受的」、「令人受不了的」、「令人無法忍受的」，例如：intolerable heat, intolerable insult 等。
Fashion is a form of ugliness so intolerable that we have to alter it every six months.
2. 這年輕人痛改前非，他的父母非常高興。
ˇ The young man’s parents are extremely happy because he has turned over a new leaf.
χ The young man’s parents are very pleasant because he has turned over a new leaf.
註︰pleasant 表示「（令人） 舒適的」、「（令人感到） 有趣的」 或「令人高興的」，例如：a pleasant companion, a pleasant voice, a pleasant journey 等。說「自己心裏高興」，應用happy 或 pleased，例如：
I’m very pleased with what you have done.
3. 聽了這個消息，他很不愉快。
ˇ He was very displeased when he heard the news.
χ He was very unpleasant when he heard the news.
註：unpleasant 是 pleasant 的反義詞；displeased 是 pleased 的反義詞。
4. 你這個月的工作不能令人滿意。
ˇ Your work this month has not been satisfactory.
χ Your work this month has not been satisfied.
註：satisfactory 表示「令人滿意」，用於事；satisfied 表示「感到滿意」，
用於人。例如：
The student’s answer is quite satisfactory.
He was satisfied with my answer.
5. 這絕不是什麼鑽石，它一文不值。
ˇ This is no diamond! It is valueless / worthless.
χ This is no diamond! It is invaluable.
註：in- 一般是反義詞字首，如 incorrect, indirect，但 valuable 的反義詞不是 invaluable。invaluable 是「無法估價的」或「無價的」、「非常貴重的」。valueless 才是 valuable 的反義詞，作「毫無價值的」解。
Exercises:
A. 這顆頂級鑽石是個無價之寶。
This top-quality diamond is __________ .
1. invaluable
2. nonprice
3. valueless
4. unvaluable
B. 他對自己的信念是如此地堅定，以致於無法容忍別人的意見。
He was so firm in his own belief that he was ______ of others’ opinions.
1. unbearable
2. intolerable
3. unendurable
4. intolerant
Answers: A. 1 B. 4

AI trade reversal pierces star stocks across Asia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:51 UTC
01:42:51 KST

A deepening selloff in US technology stocks is exposing a new vulnerability in Asia’s artificial intelligence (AI) trade: Mounting financing costs could choke off the spending needed to sustain the boom, threatening earnings across a supply chain that has powered the region’s stock market rally.
The pressure intensified last week as oil surged to US$110 a barrel for the first time since May, stoking inflation concerns, and investors turned their attention to the trillions of dollars being borrowed to build AI infrastructure. An eight-session rout in US semiconductor shares — the longest since 2008 — wiped about 16 percent off the Philadelphia semiconductor index, while the NASDAQ 100 suffered its worst week since April last year.
For Asia, where chipmakers and the hardware suppliers that make printed circuit boards, precision components and manufacturing equipment have been among the biggest beneficiaries of the AI frenzy, the implications could be significant heading into today’s open.
Photo: AP
A Goldman Sachs Group Inc basket of regional AI hardware stocks tumbled 11 percent last week, its steepest decline since mid-July. The selloff showed little sign of abating despite an upbeat revenue outlook from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電), underscoring how concerns over AI spending are spreading across the hardware supply chain.
Some of Asia’s standout performers were hit particularly hard in the maelstrom. Nan Ya Plastics Corp (南亞塑膠), a maker of printed circuit board (PCB) materials and the best-performing stock on the MSCI Asia-Pacific Index this year, tumbled 12 percent from a record high. PCB maker Unimicron Technology Corp (欣興電子), the index’s second-best performer, fell 14 percent in a week, while Samsung Electro-Mechanics Co, which makes an array of electronic components, plunged 23 percent.
“Financing costs are like gravity for the AI boom,” GAM Investment Management (Switzerland) AG fund manager Jian Shi Cortesi said. “Rising borrowing costs could make infrastructure projects harder to finance and delay spending. Even a delay could trigger a reset in Asian suppliers’ earnings expectations and valuations.”
The concern is no longer just whether demand for AI chips would hold up. It is whether hyperscalers and neocloud operators can keep financing the infrastructure needed to deploy them — and whether the expected returns would justify the scale of investment.
Bonds of neocloud provider CoreWeave Inc sank to levels signaling distress last week as investors questioned whether AI demand and revenue could support the borrowing behind its expansion. Its shares slumped 12 percent on Friday, resulting in the stock’s worst week since November last year with a 25 percent drop. The episode brought the financing risks of the boom into sharper focus, with surging oil prices adding to worries that inflation could keep borrowing costs elevated.
While TSMC, SK Hynix Inc and Samsung Electronics Co supply the chips and memory needed for AI computing, their earnings depend on continued investment in the infrastructure that uses those products. Component makers and equipment suppliers face the same underlying risk, potentially with less visibility into the timing of individual projects.
Gartner Inc has warned that more than US$3.5 trillion of AI infrastructure spending could be at risk of impairment by 2030 as investment threatens to outpace the revenue needed to justify it.
“If hyperscalers and neoclouds cannot fund their data center investments, that would translate into lower orders for Asia enablers like TSMC, Samsung and SK Hynix,” Union Bancaire Privee SA managing director Vey-Sern Ling (凌煒森) said. “Given how jittery the market is, the read-through would be very negative for the semi picks and shovels.”
The stakes are particularly high for Asian equities, where the AI buildout has become a dominant investment theme. TSMC, Samsung and SK Hynix together account for nearly one-third of the MSCI Asia ex-Japan Index and about one-fifth of the index provider’s broader Asian gauge, with their suppliers adding to the region’s exposure to the same spending cycle, data compiled by Bloomberg showed.
Still, there is little evidence so far that financing strains have translated into weaker orders, and some investors remain confident that robust demand would sustain the sector.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:46 UTC
01:42:46 KST

Dozens of critically endangered orangutans have been rescued in the past few weeks from rampant wildfires burning across Indonesia that have cloaked the region in toxic haze, conservation groups said.
The fires have triggered a months-long pollution spell that has closed schools, fueled a surge in respiratory conditions among humans and animals, and restricted outdoor activities in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and East Timor.
Pollution levels again ranged from unhealthy to very unhealthy across the region on Sunday, cloaking many areas across southern Southeast Asia in toxic haze.
Photo: Reuters
Swiss-based air quality monitor IQAir yesterday again ranked Singapore and Kuala Lumpur among the world’s top ten most polluted major cities.
Fires on Borneo and Sumatra islands, intensified by a turbo-charged El Nino weather phenomenon, continued to emit smoke.
In Indonesia, groups were working to save wildlife from the fires, including orangutans.
Photo: AFP
The West Kalimantan Conservation Agency and Indonesian nonprofit YIARI on Saturday said a team had evacuated 51 orangutans from West Kalimantan since Aug. 6.
Indonesia Ministry of Forestry figures released last week said that as many as 96 orangutans could have been rescued over the past few months in Kalimantan.
On Saturday, three conservation agencies saved a 20-year-old male orangutan in Hampangen in Central Kalimantan on Borneo.
“The evacuation process was carried out with great caution,” the agencies said.
“After the orangutan was sedated, the medical team immediately conducted a health examination before taking the animal to the ... rehabilitation center,” they said.
The Indonesia Ministry of Transportation said that about 2,400 flights across the country have been affected by the haze since the middle of August.
“Haze reduces visibility around airports, which can lead to delays, disruptions, and even flight cancellations,” the ministry said.
In Singapore, concentrations of PM2.5, particulate matter with a diameter of 2.5 micrometers or smaller, remained elevated in western parts yesterday, with the 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) staying in the “very unhealthy” range.
Although PM2.5 is the dominant pollutant during haze episodes and one of six indicators used to calculate Singapore’s overall PSI, it is not the same as the index itself.
Singapore-based atmospheric sciences expert Wang Jingyu (王靖宇) said the region was firmly in the grip of a super El Nino weather phenomenon.
Because “of the super El Nino across the entire Southeast Asia, the sea surface temperature is cooler than normal,” Wang said.
“Under these conditions, cooler sea surface temperature means we do not have enough evaporation from the ocean,” meaning insufficient rain, he said. “We do not have enough rain, the fire cannot be easily put out.”

Eagle-marked bags protect pomelo during season
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:45 UTC
01:42:45 KST

Agricultural workers in Changhua County are using fruit protection bags printed with an eagle to deter Formosan macaques from snatching pomelo fruit ripening on trees.
People passing pomelo orchards in the county’s Baguashan (八卦山) area found that “an army of raptors” had been deployed in the orchard, as almost each fruit was covered with a white bag featuring an eagle’s face.
Ershuei Township Pomelo Production and Marketing Group head Yeh Chiao-lien (葉巧連) yesterday said that damage to fruit from birds has become a serious issue in the area, adding that animals such as macaques or squirrels often nibble at the fruit.
Photo: Chen Kuan-bei, Taipei
During the fruiting period, it is necessary to bag the fruit, she said.
Local pomelo farmers found that, based on their experience, eagle pictures can protect the fruit from such wildlife damage, Yeh said.
The bags also provide a barrier preventing pests such as fruit flies, moths or sting bugs from eating the fruit or laying eggs, she said.
Local pomelo farmer Tsai Cheng-yi (蔡政義) said that bagging has more benefits beyond protecting fruit from bird or macaque damage.
It can also protect fruit from excessive exposure to sunlight, direct contact with rainwater or being bruised by tree branches, he said.
Bagging the fruit can also reduce the accumulation of dust or pesticides, helping the fruit skin stay clean with an even color favorable to the market, Tsai said.
The Ershui Township Farmers’ Association said that some farmers had set up life-like eagle models or flew eagle-shaped kites to keep sparrows away during the rice harvest season.
Pomelo farmers are using the same tactic by printing eagles on the bags, it said.
The bags are made of more wear-resistant fabric with an “observation window” in the bottom of the bag, allowing farmers to check fruit growth without untying the bag, the association said.
While the bags cost nearly NT$2, slightly more than regular bags, the association has provided a NT$1 subsidy on each bag to reduce the financial burden on pomelo farmers, it said.

The day after waiving sanctions and tariffs related to Russian exports, US President Donald Trump on Saturday said he has yet to announce a final decision on the matter as Secretary of State Marco Rubio said officials want more time to evaluate the situation.
Rubio said that the president would use up to 60 days to assess the economic impact of Russia-related sanctions and tariffs that he waived a day earlier.
“A lot of you don’t know what my decision is yet, but we’ll figure it out, and you’ll figure it out,” Trump told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida.
Photo: AP
The waiver came just weeks before November’s midterm elections, with Trump under pressure over high energy prices as war with Iran disrupts global oil supplies.
Trump signed an executive order on Friday waiving key sanctions and tariffs under the law known as the Graham Act, which he signed last month at the urging of lawmakers who want to pressure Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
The measures, including tariffs on Russian goods and penalties on countries buying Russian oil and gas, were due to take effect next week. Friday’s order did not specify how long the waiver would last, but Rubio said Trump opted for a 60-day review.
“I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy,” Rubio told reporters before boarding a plane for a trip to Uzbekistan.
Complicating matters is the Graham Act’s call not only for sanctions on Russia, but also for tariffs on goods from countries that import Russian energy supplies.
Rubio pointed to India, an important US partner that has diversified its energy supplies but remains heavily dependent on Russian oil.
Friday’s executive order drew criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, who warned it would embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin and prolong the war.
Meanwhile, Rubio was scheduled to land in Samarkand yesterday to meet with leaders from the C5+1, a grouping that brings together the US and the Muslim-majority post-Soviet states of Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.
US officials have portrayed resource-rich Central Asia — the region between China, Russia and Iran — as worthy of more attention than it received from Trump’s predecessors.

Rubio has not visited Kyiv or Moscow since becoming secretary of state. He was not present for talks between US and Ukrainian officials in Florida earlier this month, when US officials pressed Ukraine to stop hitting Russian refineries. Vance, not Rubio, represented the US in Pakistan during peace talks with Iran in April.
Rubio’s previous foreign trip, earlier this month, took him to Greece, Portugal and Iceland.

US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau last week wrote on X last week that the idea only certain destinations were worthy of visits from secretaries of state “perfectly encapsulates the decadence and degeneracy of the contemporary US foreign policy establishment.”
One Central Asian diplomat, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said officials in the region are wondering to what extent the US would continue targeting Russian sanctions evasion.
All C5 states, while drawing closer to the US, have deep historical ties with Moscow, and the region has facilitated Russian imports and exports that violate US and EU sanctions, Western officials say.
