Calls for progress on Taichung airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:19 UTC
01:42:19 KST

Taichung International Airport has struggled to keep pace with growing demand for tourism and business travel, while its joint military-civilian use has constrained efforts to expand the airport, legislators said.
The airport is a key gateway for more than 7 million people in central Taiwan. However, of the projects outlined in a development plan five years ago, only improvements to the existing terminal and construction of connecting and apron taxiways have been completed. Plans for a third terminal, remote aprons and an aerospace industry zone remain unrealized.
Taichung airport has more than 30 international routes. Passenger traffic surpassed 2 million in the first seven months of this year, with full-year traffic expected to surpass last year’s 2.75 million passengers.
Photo: Taipei Times
Despite the increase in traffic, the airport has only two baggage carousels, with most international flights arriving in the afternoon. When two flights arrive at the same time, passengers might have to wait about 30 minutes to collect their luggage. Parking is also a major problem, with spaces difficult to find during long weekends and holidays.
Taichung airport is inside the Air Force’s Ching Chuan Kang Air Base, which is divided by the runway into eastern and western areas. The eastern area is used by the military, while civilian aircraft operate in the western area, although most of the land there is also owned by the air force. Restrictions on military land and difficulties developing the western area have become major obstacles to the airport’s expansion, legislators said.
Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator Ho Hsin-chun (何欣純), who is also a candidate for Taichung mayor, said that the airport should add more aircraft stands and baggage carousels in the short term.
In the long term, the central government should coordinate with the Ministry of National Defense over the allocation of military land and restrictions on military flight operations at night, she said.
The Ministry of Transportation and Communications and the Civil Aeronautics Administration should submit a development plan for Taichung Airport through 2045 by the end of the year, Ho said.
Deputy Legislative Speaker Johnny Chiang (江啟臣) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), who is also a candidate for Taichung mayor, said that the third terminal had already been included in the airport’s next phase of construction in 2019.
“The central government must clearly explain what is holding it up,” Chiang said, adding that it should coordinate the competing needs of national defense and aviation safety and present an implementable and trackable construction schedule.
DPP Legislator Tsai Chi-chang (蔡其昌) also said the government should assess options for adding parking spaces, building temporary parking lots or introducing transfer services, while accelerating the Taichung Airport Gateway Project.
Deputy Minister of Transportation and Communications Lin Kuo-hsien (林國顯) said that the civilian airport occupies only 30 hectares of the base’s land, or about 2 percent. The airport would need to expand into the western area to obtain sufficient space, he said, adding that the Civil Aeronautics Administration is working on the airport’s overall development plan through 2045.
Huang Tai-lin (黃泰林), a professor in the Department of Shipping and Transportation Management at Chang Jung Christian University, said that the Civil Aeronautics Administration might be considering a more balanced distribution of airport capacity between northern and southern Taiwan. Taichung and Taoyuan airports have relatively close airspace, while airports in northern and southern Taiwan are farther apart, potentially affecting the order in which projects are developed, he said.
Chaoyang University of Technology Department of Aviation director Lu Yen-liang (盧衍良) said that the development of Taichung airport is also constrained by its role as a regional gateway for central Taiwan, an aircraft maintenance industry cluster and a resilient backup facility, as well as the unique challenges of joint military-civilian use.
He recommended accelerating approval and construction of the Taichung Metro’s orange line, evaluating an elevated access road connecting the airport directly to a national freeway, and building multi-story parking facilities on public land around the airport.
The government should also begin planning and environmental impact assessments for a third terminal and improve operational efficiency, Lu said.
It could also capitalize on central Taiwan’s aerospace and precision machinery clusters to accelerate construction of an aircraft maintenance industrial zone, he said.
Additional reporting by Huang Yi-ching and Ou Su-mei

Japan prepares historic Mars mission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:17 UTC
01:42:17 KST

Japanese scientists are readying a mission to Mars’ moons to retrieve samples that could help unlock the origins of the solar system and life on Earth, in what aims to be the first round trip to the Martian region.
The uncrewed Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) probe, a collaboration with US and European space agencies, as well as numerous universities and tech companies, could also help lay the groundwork for eventual human exploration.
The flagship H3 rocket carrying the MMX is set to blast off from the Tanegashima Space Center tomorrow at 4:41am, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) said.
Photo: AFP
“Being able to be involved in such a grand mission is incredibly exciting,” JAXA’s H3 rocket team project manager Makoto Arita told reporters yesterday.
The spacecraft would arrive near Mars in about August next year, where it would orbit one of its moons, Phobos, before landing and collecting at least 10g of material from the surface during three years of operating within the Martian sphere.
A rover dubbed Idefix — the French name for the comic hero Asterix’s dog — would first conduct surface observations aimed at ensuring a safe landing.
“The sampling [from] Phobos is of course the world’s first, but it means ... this is the first round trip to the Martian system,” MMX project manager Yasuhiro Kawakatsu said.
The mission would also explore the possibility of using Phobos as a “natural space station” by establishing the requirements for a round trip to Mars — something “essential for crewed Mars exploration,” JAXA said.
It would also observe the Red Planet’s moon Deimos, although it would not land on it, before returning to Earth.
JAXA hopes the mission would reveal how Mars and its two moons formed, a key piece of knowledge in working out how the solar system was born.
One theory for the origin of the Martian moons — the “giant impact” hypothesis — is that they formed after a celestial body collided with Mars.
Meanwhile, the “capture” hypothesis postulates that the moons are asteroids captured by Mars’ gravity.
Determining which theory is correct would help reveal “how a habitable environment for life might have arisen on the terrestrial planets,” JAXA said, referring to the four rocky worlds closest to the Sun — Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.
“MMX will shed light on the transport mechanisms that delivered water, volatiles and organic compounds from the outer solar system to the inner rocky planet region — processes that may have played a key role in making these worlds habitable,” said Patrick Michel, a French astrophysicist working on Idefix.
“If Phobos and Deimos are indeed remnants of these early delivery systems, they may hold clues to the origins of life itself, or, to be more correct, to the transport of the materials that were key to the emergence of life on rocky planets,” he said.
MMX is a collaboration with NASA, the European Space Agency, France’s National Center for Space Studies, the German Aerospace Center, and about 20 universities and tech companies.
The development of the spacecraft’s landing legs was particularly difficult, as gravity on Phobos is extremely weak, JAXA scientists said.
Japan’s uncrewed Smart Lander for Investigating Moon — the “Moon Sniper” — tipped over after touching down on Earth’s Moon in 2024, but still transmitted data and survived several two-week lunar nights.
Japan also has experience in bringing back samples from space, including JAXA’s uncrewed Hayabusa-2, which returned 5.4g of rock and dust collected from an asteroid several hundred million kilometers from Earth in 2020.
On the upcoming mission “we have to travel very close to Mars and return,” which means escaping the planet’s heavy gravity, Kawakatsu said.
Phobos orbits about 6,000km above the Martian surface.
“Going deep into what we call the ‘gravity well’ is difficult,” Kawakatsu said.
US and Chinese space agencies have been racing to be the first to return rock samples from Mars’ surface back to Earth.
NASA’s Perseverance rover, which has been roaming the Red Planet since 2021, has already collected samples.
However, the mission was effectively canceled by US President Donald Trump’s administration following a vote by the US Congress in January.
Meanwhile, China has announced its Tianwen-3 spacecraft is scheduled for launch in about 2028 and hopes to return Mars samples to Earth as early as 2031 — potentially before MMX.
Sand and rocks from Phobos might offer a wider variety of samples than those on the planet itself, especially if it was formed by a collision between a celestial body and Mars, JAXA scientists said.

2026 Elections: Election fraud risk rises as voting draws closer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:17 UTC
01:42:17 KST

With the nine-in-one local elections to be held next month, the public should be vigilant against four prevalent types of scams, as fraud rings capitalize on election fever to target voters and businesses, the Criminal Investigation Bureau said yesterday.
The four types of scams are fake giveaways of campaign merchandise, investment fraud involving campaign billboard advertisements, impersonation of candidates and fraudulent political donations, the bureau said in a news release, based on reports received on the 165 anti-fraud hotline.
The first and most common election-related scam involves fake giveaways of campaign merchandise, it said.
Photo courtesy of the Criminal Investigation Bureau
Scammers often pose as merchandise vendors or supporters on social media, offering free campaign items or exchanges among supporters, it said.
Once victims leave comments, they are directed to join Line accounts where scammers request “real-name verification” or “cash-flow verification,” it said.
They would be instructed to use their online banking apps to operate cardless ATM withdrawal services, allowing the scammers to steal their money, it said.
In one case during the Double Ten National Day holiday, a supporter came across a post on Threads offering surplus campaign merchandise, it said.
After clicking a fraudulent link provided by the scammer and following instructions on a fake mobile banking system, the victim gave away over their national ID number, online banking withdrawal code and password, allowing the scammer to withdraw NT$340,000 (US$10,514) from the account within 40 minutes, it said.
The second type of scam involves supposed investments in campaign billboard advertisements, it said.
Scammers claim investors would receive substantial returns once a candidate is elected, or claim to offer insider investment channels with guaranteed profits, it said.
Victims are duped into sending money out of a desire to support the candidate while expecting financial gains, it said.
The third type involves impersonating candidates or public officials on social media, it said.
Scammers first identify staunch supporters on candidate fan pages before impersonating candidates or incumbent officials to send private messages, it said.
Fraud rings claim to be using private accounts and ask supporters to transfer money or provide loans, citing election expenses or the need to raise funds discreetly, it said.
The fourth type involves defrauding businesses under the pretext of political donations, it said.
Scammers place large product orders purportedly to serve as in-kind political donations, paying with post-dated checks, it said, adding that once the merchandise is delivered, the checks bounce.
The bureau urged businesses and the public not to hand over money or goods without first meeting the political figure or campaign team in person and confirming the details.
While the scam tactics are not new and the number of cases reported so far is not high, the public should be vigilant during the final month of the campaign, it said.
People who receive unfamiliar links should verify whether they lead to official Web sites, it said.
If customer service representatives ask them to use online banking apps for real-name or transaction verification, they should immediately halt the process, it said.
Anyone with doubts can call the 165 anti-fraud hotline for assistance, it said.

North, south ports eyed as cruise hubs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:17 UTC
01:42:17 KST

Keelung and Kaohsiung could serve as Taiwan’s northern and southern cruise home ports, with Keelung focusing on routes to Japan and South Korea and Kaohsiung covering the Philippines and Vietnam, the think tank under the Ministry of Transportation and Communications said in a media briefing.
Data collected by the Institute of Transportation (IOT) showed that the number of global cruise ship passengers reached a record-high 37.20 million last year, about 25.3 percent higher than the pre-COVID-19 pandemic level.
Asia had about 3 million cruise ship passengers, about 80 percent of the pre-pandemic level, data showed.
Photo courtesy of Hsieh Chih-huang
However, the number marked a 15 percent increase compared with 2024, the institute said.
IOT deputy director-general Chen Pin-chuan (陳賓權) cited data from the Cruise Lines International Association, showing that Taiwan was the 11th largest cruise ship market from 2016 to 2019 globally, and the second largest market in Asia, preceded by China.
In 2019, Taiwan recorded 671 cruise ship arrivals and 1.06 million cruise ship passengers, Chen said. The Port of Keelung was Asia’s second largest cruise ship port, surpassing the Port of Shanghai and being preceded by the Port of Singapore, he added.
The global cruise ship market was disrupted by the COVID-19 pandemic, with cruise ship passengers in Taiwan reduced to nearly zero in 2022, Chen said.
After the government lifted COVID-19 restrictions in 2023, the number of cruise ship passengers in Taiwan rebounded to 11.57 million last year, surpassing the pre-pandemic level, he said.
However, the number of cruise ship arrivals last year has yet to return to the level in 2019, he said, adding that Taiwan ranked No. 13 in global cruise ship market and No. 4 in Asia.
“This shows the trend toward larger cruise ships, which in turn would optimize the tourism benefits that a cruise ship could bring,” Chen said.
Last year, port-of-call cruises — in which the ship stops at a Taiwanese port as part of its itinerary — accounted for 39 percent, up from 26 percent in 2024, Chen said.
Meanwhile, foreign visitors made up 58 percent of cruise travelers in 2024, with most of them coming from Japan, the US and Germany, he said.
The share of cruise ship passengers arriving through flights and boarding ships in Taiwan — also known as the fly-cruise model — rose to 11 percent by 2023, he added.
More than 64 percent of passengers choose to stay an extra night at the cruise homeport before or after their voyage, generating additional accommodation and tourism spending.
“We recommend that there be more partnerships between the Maritime and Port Bureau and Taiwan International Port Corp (TIPC) to improve port infrastructure and cultivate talents for the cruise ship industry,” Chen said.
International commercial ports in Keelung City and Kaohsiung could take on different roles as Taiwan’s northern and southern cruise homeports, with Keelung covering Japan and South Korea and Kaohsiung expanding routes to the Philippines and Vietnam, Chen said.
“With the increase of fly-cruise travelers, the bureau and the TIPC should work to facilitate the transfer between maritime and air transportation services, including enhancing the baggage handling efficiency,” he said.
TIPC previously estimated that the nation would welcome 605 cruise ships this year, with the number of cruise ship travelers exceeding 1.197 million.

Chinese maritime control a growing issue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:16 UTC
01:42:16 KST

China’s efforts to expand its maritime activities in waters east of Taiwan are a shared concern for Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines, a Japanese specialist on China’s maritime policy said.
The three sides should cooperate to assess Beijing’s intentions and protect their respective interests, Chisako Masuo, a professor at Kyushu University’s Graduate School of Social and Cultural Studies, said in an interview on Wednesday last week.
Masuo said Taiwan and Japan lack close cooperation, while concern in Japan over a contingency involving Taiwan has faded amid growing optimism that an armed invasion would not occur. Such views have spread following the removal of senior Chinese military officers from the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), she said. Attention to maritime issues has also slackened under Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s government.
Photo courtesy of Japan Coast Guard via AFP
However, China’s maritime “law enforcement patrols” east of Taiwan could become more sophisticated and would “absolutely not disappear,” Masuo said.
She added that Japan’s and the Philippines’ exclusive economic zones overlap in the same maritime area, connecting it to Japan’s interests.
Taiwanese and Japanese generally view each other favorably but “surprisingly do not know each other well” and make little effort to understand one another, Masuo said. Both sides assume they understand the other, yet have not exchanged views on some of the most important issues. The two sides need to deepen their mutual understanding, she said.
Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) top priority was domestic politics, while he sought to fulfill two missions: reshaping the international political order and unifying Taiwan with China, Masuo said. Military unification was not a predetermined course of action, she said, but Beijing would “absolutely not abandon this option.”
China would likely increasingly combine “gray zone” tactics that stop short of triggering armed conflict, she added.
Since becoming CCP general secretary and Chinese president, Xi has launched various reforms that have expanded the tools available to him, Masuo said. In maritime policy, these include fisheries reform, port development and marine environmental protection, as well as a system for using people in the fishing industry as maritime militia members.
China has gained new partners by strengthening its scientific and technological capabilities and rebuilding its socialist system, while more people at home have recognized its new missions and fallen in line, she said.
These developments have given Xi more ways to pursue “gray zone” operations, while his growing incentive to use them has made China’s activities increasingly apparent, she added.
Masuo said China wants to break away from the US-centered international system and establish a separate regional order in Asia anchored in Beijing. Its activities in the Pacific suggest it means to bring the western half of the ocean under its hegemony.
To achieve this, China is preparing to respond, even in a worst-case scenario of an armed conflict with the US, she said.
“The Taiwan issue is not an isolated one and could become a flashpoint for a future war between the US and China,” Masuo said.
In the event of a war in Taiwan, the Japanese Self-Defense Forces would have difficulty directly assisting Taiwan under Japanese domestic law. However, Masuo said that “the continued functioning of the Japan-US alliance is also extremely important to Taiwan in practice.”

EDITORIAL: Swing voters could decide election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:15 UTC
01:42:15 KST

With the local elections six weeks out, local daily news and talk shows are being filled with candidates’ campaign events, remarks, interviews, poll numbers, analysis and even fortune tellers making predictions for election results. However, the outcome is still ultimately decided by each citizen’s vote on election day.
The Taipei mayoral election has become a focus of attention this year, as Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) rapidly gained support in an unconventional campaign, sparking a media sensation.
Taipei has about 2 million eligible voters, and with a general turnout of about 70 percent, approximately 1.4 million votes are expected to be cast — 700,000 votes is considered the threshold for candidates to secure a win, with 50 percent of the votes cast.
Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) won the 2022 election with about 575,000 votes (42.29 percent). Without a major third-party candidate this year, many believe the Taipei mayoral election would be a typical showdown between the pan-blue and pan-green camps, with the KMT traditionally enjoying an advantage in the capital.
However, a TVBS poll released earlier this month showed that Shen’s approval ratings are closing on Chiang’s, with only a one-digit percentage point gap between them. Many are saying that whoever can secure the about 342,000 votes (25.14 percent) cast in 2022 for former independent candidate Vivian Huang (黃珊珊), endorsed by the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP), could win this year.
In other words, the “swing voters” could be the decisive factor in this year’s mayoral election.
Shen has been praised for his “crossover appeal” by doing interviews with local media that are generally considered “pro-blue,” including two interviews with long-time political figure and media personality Jaw Shaw-kong (趙少康), who was a KMT vice president candidate in 2024 and head of the KMT’s “blue fighters” group.
Shen’s interviews with long-time TV show producers Wang Wei-chung (王偉忠) and Li Si-duan (李四端) were examples of him reaching out to the other camp. It even prompted calls from KMT members to expel Jaw from the party for promoting Shen, which Jaw rebutted by saying that he had invited both candidates.
As a challenger against an incumbent, and coming from the DPP and its traditionally weaker base in Taipei, Shen has taken every opportunity to go to voters and persuade them of the merit of his campaign.
Shen has been interviewed by a wide variety of people, including travel influencers and literature shows. He has canvassed markets and shopping areas, and even held soapbox sessions to answer questions face-to-face in Taipei’s parks and public spaces.
On the other hand, Chiang has declinined interviews, as Jaw and other media personalities confirmed that they had been repeatedly rejected or ignored, and has avoided public debate with Shen until this month, when poll results started ringing alarm bells for his backers.
Chiang’s first interviews were with former legislator Julien Kuo (郭正亮) and radio host Tang Hsiang-lung (唐湘龍), alleged to have a clear pro-China stance, followed by Anne Wang (王淺秋), a former KMT election campaign spokesperson, and TPP Chairman Huang Kuo-chang (黃國昌).
His selection of venues, only reaching out to the TPP, the KMT’s ally, gives the impression that he is “seeking validation in an echo chamber,” and the TVBS poll indicated that over half of Huang’s former voters are leaning toward Shen.
Chiang came off poorly even in his own echo chamber, with Tang bluntly saying: “If his last name wasn’t Chiang, he might not have been mayor now,” right after Chiang left the interview.
Huang had offered to help Chiang resolve Taipei’s rat infestation during the interview, which some saw as a thinly veiled stab at the mayor.
While there is a vivid difference between the two candidates’ approaches, Vivian Huang on Tuesday last week said in a social media post that the 340,000 votes she received were not hers, but were from “independent-minded city residents” who keep their options open and evaluate whether a candidate can solve problems and deliver on their promises.
“If you do a good job, the people will let you continue; if you do a bad job, the people will replace you,” she said, reminding Shen and Chiang that they must persuade the swing voters of their merit, instead of seeing them merely as numbers up for grabs.
Shen seems to have understood this from the beginning and has said in interviews that his goal is to cross the blue-green divide and persuade as many city residents as he can, even trying to gain support from traditionally pan-blue voters. In contrast, Chiang has not stepped out of his comfort zone, and whether that will change remains to be seen, but voters are certainly evaluating their words and actions.

The most troubling message coming out of Washington for Taipei is not any single statement but the cumulative effect of a series of signals suggesting that US President Donald Trump is rethinking Taiwan’s strategic value while viewing the US-China relationship through the lens of a transactional great-power bargain. The danger behind Trump’s new softness toward Beijing is a potential US-China bargain that undermines Taiwan’s core interests.
During Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) recent state visit to Washington, Trump and Xi appeared to rewrite the history of World War II.
In a Sept. 25 fact sheet on Xi’s visit, the White House said, “The two leaders recalled that the US and China were allies in World War II and fought side by side to win the war.” At a welcome ceremony for Xi on Sept. 24, Trump claimed that the pursuit of “common interests … even made us allies in World War II.” Xi echoed the theme later at the state dinner, contending that China and the US had fought “shoulder to shoulder against fascist aggression” by Japan.
America’s wartime ally, however, was the Republic of China, then governed by Chiang Kai-shek’s (蔣介石) Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT). The communist People’s Republic of China did not emerge until October 1949, more than four years after the war ended. Chinese communists did participate in guerrilla warfare against imperial Japanese forces as part of the nominal “Second United Front” with the KMT. But Washington’s diplomatic recognition, military assistance and formal alliance were with Chiang’s government, which later relocated to Taiwan.
By speaking of America’s wartime alliance in a way that connects it to Chinese communist rule, Trump not only walked into Xi’s diplomatic trap but also is unwittingly helping Beijing appropriate history. Such historical distortion is only one part of the problem. Trump’s inclination to treat Taiwan as a negotiating asset underscores the larger challenge.
Taipei naturally is concerned that Washington has delayed pending foreign military sales to Taiwan, or has discussed the scope of such arms sales with Xi, as leverage in negotiations with Beijing over tariffs, trade, technology and rare earths. No less striking is US Ambassador to China David Perdue’s confirmation that Trump had floated the idea of selling American military equipment to China, America’s principal strategic rival.
The message this sends Taiwan is that US security commitments may no longer be insulated from US-China economic bargaining.
The contrast with the Biden administration is also worth noting. Former US president Joe Biden repeatedly said the US would defend Taiwan militarily if China attacked. Trump has instead emphasized the physical distance separating America from Taiwan, asking why Americans should fight a war “9,500 miles away.” He has also urged Taiwan to “cool it” and warned against steps toward formal independence, effectively echoing Xi’s own rhetoric.
At the same time, Trump’s economic rhetoric has challenged another pillar of Taiwan’s security: its semiconductor industry.
For years, Taiwan’s semiconductor dominance has been described as a “silicon shield.” This is because the global economy’s dependence on Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC) makes Taiwan’s security a vital interest for the US and other democratic nations.
But Trump has repeatedly complained that Taiwan “stole” America’s chip business and has suggested that Taiwan should effectively pay the US for its defense. His administration has also used tariffs to extract trade and investment concessions from Taipei.
Taipei thus faces a jarring paradox: The very economic strength that was supposed to make Taiwan indispensable is increasingly being portrayed in Washington as evidence that Taipei has benefited at America’s expense.
Meanwhile, Trump’s demand that Taipei raise military expenditure dramatically is adding another layer of uncertainty. Taiwan is already starting to do more to defend itself. But when such a demand is accompanied by ambiguity over the durability of US security commitments, it risks creating an impression that American protection is conditional.
These developments point toward “strategic transactionalism” — a shift from viewing Taiwan principally through the prism of democratic values, regional stability and a rules-based order toward seeing its security as one variable in a much broader US negotiation with Beijing.
Trump has already elevated China to America’s peer. By repeatedly framing the US-China relationship as a G2, or Group of Two, Trump is implicitly granting China recognition as an equal great power. Xi has long promoted a “new model of major-country relations” in which the US and China co-manage global affairs while respecting each other’s “core interests,” a term that for Beijing includes Taiwan.
If Washington were to accept such a framework, Taiwan could find itself caught on the wrong side of a great-power bargain. The danger is not an explicit American abandonment of Taiwan but a subtle and gradual normalization of the idea that the US and China have separate spheres of influence.
That scenario could also weaken the coalition on which Taiwan’s security depends. Taiwan’s deterrence depends on the ability of the US, Japan, Australia, European democracies and other partners to convince Beijing that aggression would impose prohibitive costs. If Washington increasingly conducts bilateral deals with Beijing without consulting its allies, those partners may become less certain that their own interests will be protected in a Taiwan crisis.
Against this backdrop, Taipei needs to draw the appropriate lesson and strengthen its own capacity to deter aggression. That means accelerating the implementation of an asymmetric defense strategy built around mobile, survivable and mass-producible systems. It means strengthening reserves, civil defense and critical infrastructure so that Taiwan can withstand a blockade, cyberattacks and other forms of coercion.
Diversifying trade and supply chains, particularly across the Indo-Pacific, can likewise reduce Taiwan’s vulnerability to economic pressures.
If Taiwan is to become less exposed to the vagaries of any one president, whether in Beijing or Washington, it should make itself harder to coerce, harder to isolate and harder to bargain away.
Brahma Chellaney, professor emeritus of strategic studies at the independent Centre for Policy Research in New Delhi, is the author of nine books, including the award-winning Water: Asia’s New Battleground (Georgetown University Press).

In west London, Liverpool were stunned when Brentford defender Keane Lewis-Potter looped a header past Alisson Becker from Igor Thiago’s cross in the 44th minute.
However, the Bees were reduced to 10 men in first half stoppage-time after Yehor Yarmolyuk’s head made contact with Jeremy Jacquet’s face while they waited for a corner.
Liverpool lost Dominik Szoboszlai and Jeremie Frimpong to injuries, but still made their numerical advantage count in the 62nd minute.
Victor Munoz cut inside and slotted a composed equalizer past Brentford’s former Liverpool goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher.
Alexander Isak blasted Liverpool’s winner in the 70th minute after Barcola teed up the Swedish striker for his fifth goal this season.
Brentford finished with nine men following Vitaly Janelt’s second booking in stoppage-time.
Beaten by City in their previous league game, Liverpool are up to fifth place after inflicting Brentford’s first league defeat of the season.
“You see the results of Brentford at home, and you have to be ready for these kinds of battles. We had 45 minutes to do the comeback, and I think we played really well,” Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola said.
Pedro Neto’s double condemned Everton to a first defeat of the season as fourth-placed Chelsea won 2-0 at the Hill Dickinson Stadium despite the loss of goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez to a head injury.
Neto opened the scoring inside the first minute of the second half and secured the points during stoppage-time.
The Argentine shot-stopper was involved in a sickening head clash with Everton defender Jarrad Branthwaite and was taken to hospital.
Fulham won for the first time in the league this season as Alex Iwobi’s 33rd-minute goal clinched a 1-0 victory against Hull City at Craven Cottage.

Villa winger Manzambi headed home from Joao Gomes’ cross in the 33rd minute.
It was a bitter blow to Newcastle, who agreed a deal with Freiburg for Manzambi in the summer before Villa hijacked the deal.

A bruising battle awaits Musk and SpaceX in mobile services
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:42:08 UTC
01:42:08 KST

Elon Musk’s decision to wade into US mobile-phone services sets up a challenge distinct from anything he has previously pursued. This is not a new market or an added twist that fills an industry gap such as his innovations with electric vehicles, low Earth orbit broadband or an online payment system — the areas where Musk made his riches.
This is a dogfight with three entrenched players. It is likely to benefit wireless customers, but for SpaceX investors, it would be expensive and risky, and comes with an uncertain payoff.
The US$240 billion US mobile services market is dominated by AT&T Inc, Verizon Communications Inc and T-Mobile US Inc, all of which spend heavily on the latest technology for their networks to keep ahead of each other and feed consumers’ insatiable demand for bandwidth. It would cost tens of billions of dollars to build Musk’s vision of a hybrid network with 15,000 satellites dedicated to direct-to-device and the ground infrastructure required to compete with the legacy carriers in urban areas. SpaceX’s satellite capacity would broaden coverage to rural and remote areas, but that is not where the people or the profits are concentrated.
This leaves many unanswered questions about the potential return on investment and the time it would take to build the network. You can bet AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile would fight back. All three saw their stocks plummet the day after Musk made firm his intention to become a fourth large mobile service provider. SpaceX has dropped about 9 percent this week.
Musk is planning a major push into a market with little or no subscriber growth because most people already have a phone. Investors need more details on SpaceX’s strategy and the potential returns, especially when the company is already spending so heavily on other projects. There are investments in a data-centers-in-space network and plans to reportedly borrow US$40 billion to purchase Nvidia Corp computer chips for its xAI venture. Many of Musk’s ambitions hinge on the ability to launch Starship frequently and to capture both stages of this massive rocket, which would drive down launch costs.
The opportunity for SpaceX lies with operating margins of more than 20 percent for Verizon and T-Mobile last year, and close to that level for AT&T. If SpaceX is able to offer comparable service at a lower price, it could potentially carve out market share. The incumbents would compete on price, too — a win-win for consumers. If SpaceX’s offering is mostly around extended coverage and zero dead zones, then its appeal would be limited to those customers who live or venture to remote areas — a small addressable market.
Musk advanced his plans last week with the purchase of 14 megahertz of paired low-band spectrum — a premium asset in wireless telephony — and Federal Communications Commission approval to build out his direct-to-device satellite network. SpaceX last year agreed to pay US$17 billion for EchoStar Corp’s medium-band spectrum. Even with these two spectrum purchases, the company is far behind the big three’s capacity and would need to snap up more spectrum in auctions or private deals. Expect the legacy carriers to also gobble up more spectrum to keep their lead.
The investment needed to build out a ground network is hard to nail down. The macro base stations at cell towers can cost as much as US$250,000 each, depending on the area, according to Richard Haas, a spectrum expert with LS Telcom in the UK. SpaceX might need about 50,000 of these sites, which would put the investment at US$12 billion at the upper range, he wrote. That does not seem onerous.
Another indication of the cost of building out the network comes from the bankruptcy filing by Dish DBS Corp, a unit of EchoStar, which attempted to become a fourth carrier with the help of subscribers it picked up as part of an acquisition. EchoStar ended up spending US$30 billion on spectrum and US$16 billion on wireless infrastructure. The network was not fully completed and subscribers had shrunk to about 7.4 million by the June bankruptcy filing from 8.5 million in 2021.
SpaceX is a much more formidable competitor with unique satellite technology and deep pockets, but it is also playing catchup in a mature market, where it would have to wrestle customers away from legacy players. Investors know that whether SpaceX gains traction or not, the battle would first bruise everyone.

Wei Chuan Dragons outfielder Zeng Sheng-an last night hit a three-run homer to power his team to a 3-1 win over the CTBC Brothers at Taipei Dome, giving the Dragons a 2-0 lead in the Chinese Professional Baseball League’s (CPBL) Taiwan Series.
With the Dragons trailing 1-0 in the bottom of the fifth inning, the 20-year-old Zeng, who joined the team last season and was making his Taiwan Series debut, drove a fastball from Brothers starter Felix Pena over the right-field wall.
Zeng became the second-youngest player in CPBL history to hit a home run in the Taiwan Series.
Photo: CNA
The homer came after he committed a fielding error in the top of the inning that ultimately allowed the Brothers to take a 1-0 lead.
In a post-game interview, Zeng said that after making a mistake in the top of the inning, his coaches and veteran teammates told him to put it behind him and focus on what he could do next to help the team. He was glad he was able to bounce back in his next at-bat, he said.
Pena was later pulled from the mound in the same inning after being hit by a batted ball. He gave up four hits and three walks, and struck out three batters over 4.2 innings.
Dragons starter Cristopher Mercedes pitched six innings, allowing one run on five hits and a walk, while striking out three.
The Dragons’ second straight win puts them in a strong position to claim their sixth CPBL championship.
In the CPBL’s 37-year history, teams that have taken a 2-0 lead in a best-of-seven championship series have gone on to win the title 89.5 percent of the time.
After a day off today, the teams are to meet again tomorrow at Taipei Dome for Game 3.
Meanwhile, the CTBC Brothers have condemned threats posted on social media against Venezuelan pitcher Mario Sanchez on Saturday and yesterday.
Sanchez began receiving threatening messages on his social media accounts on Saturday following the loss.
He declined interview requests yesterday, but posted a statement on Instagram.
In the statement, Sanchez said he was willing to put up with complaints about his performance and accept criticism directed at him. However, he said his family was innocent and urged fans and the public not to do anything that would harm them.
Sanchez’s wife, Fabiola San Juan Galue, also responded on Instagram.
Writing in English, she said the couple had recently had a miscarriage and had begun receiving “vulgar and violent” threats on the post they originally shared to celebrate the pregnancy.
The Brothers also expressed support for the pitcher.
Manager Keiichi Hirano said that rather than focusing on negative comments online, the team would be best served by investing in the fans who stick with it through thick and thin.
In a statement, the Brothers said the team and Sanchez’s agency had jointly filed a police report over the threats.
The team said it would pursue all necessary legal action to protect its players and the team’s reputation.

At least 19 people were killed and two dozen more injured on Saturday in eastern India after a stampede that occurred during sudden rainfall at a Hindu religious gathering, officials and Indian media said.
West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari told reporters the fatalities included a seven-year-old girl, adding that 25 other people were injured outside a pavilion “in a stampede” at the Hindu festival of Durga Puja in Kolkata.
“Six bodies have so far been identified,” Adhikari said.
Photo: AFP
A senior police official at the scene said an announcement caused “commotion” after it started raining at night and the “crowd waiting outside the pandal [pavilion] was pushing, pulling and rushing forward and fell on the ground, leading to the stampede.”
Afterward medics were seen moving injured people on stretchers, including a police officer, into a local hospital. Several relatives of victims cried and held one another as they mourned the loss of loved ones.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi addressed the tragedy in a short statement on Facebook.
“The stampede in Kolkata is saddening. Condolences to the bereaved families. Wishing the injured a speedy recovery,” he wrote. “The West Bengal Government is providing all possible help to the affected families.”
Adhikari originally announced 17 fatalities. The Press Trust of India (PTI) reported the death toll rose by two to 19, quoting Adhikari in a later statement. Nine dead bodies have been released to their families, the news agency said.
Police have taken the closed circuit footage of the festival and authorities would initiate action against those seen on it who appeared to fail in their responsibility for crowd control, PTI reported.
Videos shot before the stampede appeared to show large crowds of people waiting to enter the pavilion, in an area with narrow lanes that allow only a few people to walk in at a time, the Indian Express reported.
In a separate incident, a speeding truck killed 13 people when it ploughed into a crowd at a different Hindu festival, officials said yesterday, with Indian President Droupadi Murmu describing the deaths as “heartbreaking.”
The heavily loaded truck reportedly lost control in early yesterday and hit devotees gathered at a temple in Gwalior, in the central state of Madhya Pradesh.
PTI cited hospital officials as saying 13 people had died.
“I express my deepest condolences to the bereaved families and pray for the swift recovery of those injured,” Murmu wrote on social media.

Global uranium production to dip by 50% by 2040 as demand set to double, says IAEA report; forecast could pinch India too
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:40:51 UTC
01:40:51 KST

NEW DELHI: Global uranium supply constraints would witness mining production drop by at least 50% by 2040 even as demand is set to double, according to the latest International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) report. This IAEA forecast on global uranium supply crunch is likely to affect India’s goal to increase its nuclear capacity to 100 GW by 2047.According to publication ‘Uranium 2024: Resources, Production and Demand’, also known as the ‘Red Book’, jointly prepared by Nuclear Energy Agency of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development and the Agency, global uranium requirements are projected to increase to 90,045 tonnes of uranium (tU) in the low-case scenario and up to 1,42,631 tU in the high-case scenario by 2050, which represents a 50% to 144% increase from today’s requirements of approximately 60,000 tU.In contrast to future doubling of uranium requirements, uranium production from existing mines is forecast to decrease by at least 50% by 2040, the report said. “Conversion capacity is already insufficient and is projected to fall further behind demand through 2040, highlighting the need for substantial new investment and facility expansions. While global enrichment capacity currently exceeds demand, it remains unevenly distributed geographically,” it said.
The report suggested new mines and expansion or life extension of existing mines, as well as reopening of idled mines, saying these steps will be required for assurance of supply in the future.Amid the gloomy scenario predicted by IAEA, India has initiated steps to increase nuclear power capacity from current 8,180 MW to 22,480 MW by 2031-32. The expansion includes construction and commissioning of 10 reactors, totalling 8,000 MW, across Gujarat, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Haryana, Karnataka, and MP. Additionally, pre-project activities for 10 more reactors have commenced, with plans for progressive completion by 2031-32. Further, the Modi govt accorded in-principle approval to set up 6 x 1208 MW nuclear power plant in cooperation with the USA at Kovvada in Srikakulam district in Andhra Pradesh.India procures uranium from a combination of domestic mining and international suppliers: Domestic uranium is mined by Uranium Corporation of India Limited (UCIL) from deposits in Jharkhand, Andhra and Karnataka. It relies primarily on natural uranium for its pressurised heavy water reactors and is gradually shifting toward a closed fuel cycle using plutonium-fuelled fast breeder reactors (FBRs) and eventually thorium. To supplement limited domestic reserves and back its expansion targets under HANTI Act, 2025, India imports and has active supply arrangements with Kazakhstan, Russia, Canada, Australia (finalised arrangements under a nuclear cooperation deal), Uzbekistan and France. However, the IAEA prediction of uranium shortfall if drastic steps not taken could pinch India too.Over the next decade, nuclear fuel production will face increasing demand across all nuclear fuel-related segments due to increasing construction programmes in both established and embarking countries, necessitating the development of new fuel types, including for small modular reactors and advanced reactors, it said.
“An increase in uranium production will require sustained investment with positive market conditions, and the discovery of new deposits will require sustained long-term exploration efforts, bearing in mind that the development of new uranium mines takes 10–15 years on average, from deposit discovery to the start of mining operations,” it said.In addition, significant and timely investment in exploration and mining/processing technology will be required, including cost-effective uranium extraction techniques for exploiting unconventional deposit types (for example uranium from phosphate and black shale deposits), some of which may become economic if there is a sustained increase in market prices, it suggested.

No Kings protests shift focus to early voting ahead of US midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:39:40 UTC
01:39:40 KST

No Kings protests shift focus to early voting ahead of US midterms
TEHRAN- The latest round of “No Kings” protests across the United States on Saturday, October 17, focused on a new objective: turning opposition to President Donald Trump’s policies into electoral participation ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
Under the banner “No Kings: Vote Early,” thousands of events were planned across the country, including in all 50 states and Washington, D.C., according to organizers. The demonstrations featured rallies, marches, voter-education activities and efforts to encourage eligible voters to cast their ballots before Election Day.
The October 17 demonstrations marked the fourth nationwide round of the movement, which emerged in opposition to Trump’s presidency and what organizers describe as authoritarian tendencies in his administration.
The organizers framed the latest mobilization as a nonpartisan effort to promote voting and defend democratic participation, while protesters raised concerns ranging from immigration enforcement and the cost of living to the war against Iran.
A movement changes tactics
Earlier No Kings demonstrations emphasized visible opposition to Trump and his policies. This time, organizers placed greater emphasis on early voting, election access and mobilizing voters ahead of the midterms.
The shift reflects a political calculation: demonstrations can express public dissatisfaction, but electoral participation can change the balance of power in Congress and increase pressure on the administration.
According to Newsweek, roughly 3,000 events were planned nationwide, with the focus on early voting and turnout rather than conventional protest alone.
The movement has described its initiative as a nonpartisan effort to bring Americans together in defense of democracy and civil liberties. However, its political character has been contested, with some critics arguing that its activities align closely with Democratic electoral interests.
At local events, some participants openly encouraged opposition to Republican candidates, illustrating the tension between the coalition’s stated nonpartisan approach and the political objectives of some attendees.
Iran war remains among protesters’ concerns
Although early voting was the demonstrations’ central organizing theme, interviews with participants in several states showed that opposition to the war against Iran remained among the grievances motivating some protesters.
In Kalamazoo, Michigan, protester Jared Smith described the range of issues that brought him to the demonstration.
“Everything from Gaza, Iran to gas prices, grocery prices,” he said, according to local television station WWMT.
The remark linked opposition to US foreign policy with concerns about the cost of living, suggesting that some participants viewed domestic economic pressures and overseas military action as interconnected issues.
In Corydon, Indiana, 56-year-old musician Aim Me Smiley said she attended to protest what she called a “rogue” president, data-center expansion and the war in Iran, among other concerns.
Smiley had already voted early and encouraged others to participate in the electoral process, according to the Indiana Capital Chronicle.
Her comments illustrate how some demonstrators viewed the midterm elections as an opportunity to challenge the administration’s domestic and foreign policies.
However, the available interviews do not establish how widely opposition to the Iran war was shared among participants nationwide. It was one of several concerns expressed at the demonstrations rather than the movement’s principal national slogan.
White House challenges movement’s nonpartisan framing
The Trump administration criticized the No Kings movement’s characterization of its activities as nonpartisan.
White House spokesperson Lauren Bis argued that the organizers’ emphasis on voting undermined their claim to political neutrality and criticized the movement’s name.
“The fact that the ‘No Kings’ organizers are talking about voting in the upcoming election proves they should change their name,” Bis said in a statement reported by USA Today. “This November, Americans have a clear choice between President Trump and Republicans’ commonsense policies or the extreme Democrats’ radical socialist, open-border policies.”
The remarks reflect the administration’s broader effort to frame the midterm elections as a choice between Republican policies and the Democratic opposition.
The dispute also highlights a central question surrounding No Kings: whether the movement is primarily a broad-based campaign for democratic participation or an electoral mobilization that could benefit Democratic candidates.
Although organizers describe their activities as nonpartisan, some participants have explicitly called on voters to oppose Republicans. Such statements demonstrate that the movement encompasses a range of political objectives, even as its national campaign emphasizes early voting.
Can street protests translate into political change?
The October 17 demonstrations sought to translate opposition to Trump into greater participation in the midterm elections. Whether that strategy succeeds will depend not only on turnout at rallies but also on whether participants and the communities they reach ultimately cast ballots.
Local reports suggest that attendance varied considerably. In Kalamazoo, Indivisible Greater Kalamazoo estimated that more than 3,000 people attended the demonstration along Drake Road, according to WWMT. In Corydon, Indiana, about 100 people gathered for a local rally, according to the Indiana Capital Chronicle.
These figures illustrate differences between individual events but do not establish a nationwide increase or decline in participation.
The movement’s electoral strategy also raises questions about its longer-term influence. If its activities encourage previously disengaged voters to participate, No Kings could contribute to political pressure on the administration through changes in congressional representation.
Yet demonstrations alone cannot guarantee a change in policy. Their impact will depend on voter participation, electoral outcomes and the ability of activists to sustain public engagement after the rallies end.
For protesters concerned about immigration enforcement, economic pressures and the war against Iran, the immediate objective is to turn dissatisfaction into votes. Whether that translates into a significant shift in US policy will become clearer after the November 3 elections.

Pro-Palestinian student activists disrupted an event held at City St George’s, University of London, featuring human rights barrister Adam Wagner KC, who represented British hostages taken by Hamas during the October 7 massacre.
The incident took place during an event on Thursday, titled “Representing Hostages,” a lecture delivered by Wagner and a visiting professor of law at the university who has advised on key public law and human rights cases, discussing his legal and diplomatic strategy for representing the families of 10 British hostages seized.
During the event, protesters entered the lecture hall chanting “free, free Palestine,” filming attendees, and shouting slogans.
Footage circulating on social media uploaded by the groups City Action for Palestine and the Association of Student Activism for Palestine, who claimed responsibility for the disruption, showed demonstrators confronting organizers and speakers, telling attendees “shame on you” and calling for the event to be shut down.
Wagner recounts protestors storming presentation
Writing in a post on LinkedIn following the incident, Wagner described how a small group of masked individuals entered about halfway through his presentation.
Wagner wrote, “One or two were focused on me, screaming things like ‘WAR CRIMINAL’ and ‘YOU SHOULD BE DISBARRED’. They shouted ‘FREE FREE PALESTINE’ and similar. One was screaming ‘THE ZIONIST HOSTAGES WERE KILLED BY THE ZIONISTS’. They were chanting ‘SETTLERS SETTLERS GO BACK HOME.’”
Wagner said that the protesters left after about 10 minutes, seemingly tipped off that security was arriving, alongside a small group of audience members who also walked out. He noted that he carried on and finished the lecture while the vast majority of the audience stayed.
“The purpose of this protest was not to express an opinion or have a debate, and least of all to listen to my view,” Wagner wrote. “It was to intimidate me, stop me doing my legal work, and try to make it impossible for people who do not share their extremist world view to give lectures and do ordinary things that people at universities do, such as exchange ideas.”
Wagner added, “I will not be intimidated by illiberal people. If I am a threat to them because I make the simple (and unarguable) point that everyone has human rights, and that includes Israeli and British victims of terrorism, and of course Palestinians, then what can I do? This is a point I made in the lecture itself – they just proved it.”
“If these are students then they have a lot to learn. If they think they are helping the cause of Palestinian rights, I very much doubt a single person in the room was convinced,” Wagner added.
Wagner expressed gratitude to City St George’s for facilitating the lecture and remaining supportive during the interruption, noting he was escorted out by the Head of Security after finishing.
In a statement posted on Instagram by City Action for Palestine, organizers defended the disruption.
“City St George’s platformed this event. ‘Representing ‘Hostages,’ our response is: The only hostages are the 10,000 Palestinian hostages unlawfully detained in Zionist detention, without trial,” the group wrote on Instagram.
“The only hostages are the hundreds of Lebanese men, kidnapped by the IOF from their villages in South Lebanon. City St George’s would never platform a discussion on Palestinian and Lebanese suffering. City St George’s prefers to support the IOF, unethical investments and the Jewish-Zionist propaganda machine. Zionism is racism, and Zionism is not welcome and never will be welcome on our campus,” City Action for Palestine.
President of UJS condemns pro-Palestinian student protest
RAPHAEL LEON, the president of the Union of Jewish Students, said in a statement to The Jerusalem Post, “It is astounding that students protested an event about representing hostages abducted by Hamas on October 7.
“This intimidatory behavior, contributing to a chilling effect for Jewish and Israeli students and staff who want to participate in university life in Britain, is another example of extremist student groups positioning themselves outside of the realm of acceptable conduct.”
“The Palestinian cause should not be used to cancel out the pain of the hostages and hostage families. We would have hoped that these students would have the maturity and decency to recognize that. The chants of the protesters further demonstrate their extremism and antisemitism, shouting at Jews to ‘go back home’. This achieves nothing for peace and justice. Society, including universities, must take a stand against hatred,” Leon said.
A spokesperson for City St George’s, University of London said in a statement to the Post, “During yesterday’s public lecture delivered by Adam Wagner KC, visiting professor of law at City St George’s, University of London, a small number of individuals briefly disrupted the event.
“After a few minutes, the individuals left and all planned elements of the event, including the full lecture, Q&A and audience discussion, took place. We understand that the incident may have been unsettling for some attendees.”
“The university is committed to freedom of speech, academic freedom and the right to lawful protest, in line with our Code of Practice. These principles are fundamental to university life and to the open exchange of ideas, including on issues that can generate strongly held and differing views,” the spokesperson said.
“Academic events should be able to proceed in a way that allows speakers and audiences to listen, question and engage with different perspectives. In line with our Code of Practice, whilst disagreement and challenge are a normal part of academic debate, the actions of some should not disrupt the ability of others to participate in that discussion and debate. The university is reviewing the incident,” the spokesperson added.

UK Charity Commission opens case against Restless Beings after UKLFI complaint alleging Hamas ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:39:00 UTC
01:39:00 KST

The UK’s Charity Commission has opened a regulatory compliance case into the human rights charity Restless Beings following a legal complaint by UK Lawyers for Israel (UKLFI) regarding its ties to a Gaza-based organization designated by the United States as controlled by Hamas’s military wing.
The regulatory scrutiny follows a complaint UKLFI submitted detailing extensive evidence of cooperation between Restless Beings and Merciful Hands Gaza, an organization the US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) designated in January as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist entity.
According to the US Treasury, Merciful Hands was owned, controlled, or directed by Hamas and integrated into its military wing, which provided funding and operational instructions.
UKLFI investigation documented overlap between Restless Beings, Merciful Hands
UKLFI's investigation documented overlapping personnel and joint humanitarian projects conducted between 2022 and 2024.
Evidence submitted to regulators included shared personnel such as Nura Barzaq, who was identified as a public relations officer for Merciful Hands and appeared in Restless Beings fundraising videos between 2022 and last year.
The dossier also identified aid workers Alaa al-Tabtibi and Mohammad Abu al-Ouf, who appeared in material published by Merciful Hands while filmed wearing Restless Beings-branded clothing during aid operations.
Additional findings cited joint aid operations during Ramadan 2022 featuring Restless Beings branding on packages, banners, and worker apparel in material published by Merciful Hands, alongside direct funding instances, including a February 2024 distribution of 450 meals funded by Restless Beings.
Senior Hamas figures tied to Merciful Hands administration
The complaint further highlighted connections between Merciful Hands and senior Hamas figures, including Muhammad Abu Nar, who chaired Merciful Hands from approximately 2015 to 2023 and was reportedly a commander within the al-Qassam Brigades.
The dossier pointed to additional archival records, noting that footage from 2017 showed senior Hamas figure Ahmed Behar addressing a Merciful Hands gathering, alongside a local media report attributing the founding of the charity to senior Hamas military commander Ahmed Jabari.
UKLFI contended that these publicly accessible indicators should have prompted rigorous background checks by Restless Beings prior to and throughout their operational partnership.
Restless Beings claims to have provided medical supplies, food to Gaza
According to Restless Beings' 2025 annual filing, the organization stated that it "produced a groundbreaking report on Israel's Genocide in Gaza. Led the calls on UK and EU Governments to impose arms embargo on Israel." The report also claimed that it provides "Food, medicals supplies and life-saving support for victims of Israel's Genocide in Palestine."
The complaint asked the regulator to examine whether charitable assets or funds were channeled to Merciful Hands, whether proper partner-vetting procedures were followed, and whether trustees fulfilled their legal duties.
In response to the submission, the Charity Commission confirmed to UKLFI that it has opened a regulatory compliance case. The regulator emphasized that opening a case does not mean it has reached any findings against Restless Beings, explaining that the process allows the regulator to obtain and assess further information to determine whether regulatory action is required.
A spokesperson for UKLFI said, “We welcome the Charity Commission’s decision to open a regulatory compliance case following our complaint. British donors giving money to humanitarian causes are entitled to know that their donations will not benefit terrorist organizations. Where a charity works with an overseas partner that has been identified by the US Treasury as controlled by Hamas’s military wing, there are extremely serious questions about due diligence, financial oversight and the trustees’ responsibilities.
“Our investigation uncovered substantial evidence of shared personnel, joint operations and funding between Restless Beings and Merciful Hands. We believe these matters demand thorough scrutiny,” the UKLFI spokesperson said.
Restless Beings did not respond to an emailed request for comment by publication time.

The evening will celebrate the unbreakable bonds the girls forged, their private jokes, their creative spirits, and the unique humor that sustained them during their intense military service.
Alongside the musical performances, the festival grounds will feature live art installations and graffiti, honoring the creative passions the soldiers loved most.

Bereaved families seek criminal probe of Netanyahu over October 7 account
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:38:57 UTC
01:38:57 KST

Bereaved families filed a criminal complaint against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday, asking authorities to investigate whether he deliberately misled the state comptroller and the public to distance himself from responsibility for the October 7 disaster.
The complaint is centered on Netanyahu’s 55-page response to the comptroller, submitted in December 2025 and published in February 2026. The families have alleged that it selectively quoted classified documents, omitted warnings, and distorted discussions about Hamas and the threat it posed before the attack.
Addressed to Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara and the head of Israel Police’s Investigations and Intelligence Division, the complaint seeks an investigation into alleged attempted fraud under aggravated circumstances, fraud and breach of trust, and unlawful disclosure of classified information and material from the comptroller’s examination.
The families argue that the benefit Netanyahu sought through the alleged deception was acceptance by the comptroller and the public of his account absolving him of responsibility.
Bereaved families of slain soldiers among complainants
The complainants include Hagit and Ruby Chen, whose son, tank soldier Itay Chen, was killed fighting on October 7 and whose body was taken to Gaza, and Sharon and Eyal Eshel, whose daughter, surveillance soldier Roni Eshel, was killed at the Nahal Oz base.
Lawyers Navot Tel-Zur, Tal Shapira, Ron Berkman and Shoni Albeck submitted the complaint. Retired Jerusalem District Court judge Nava Ben-Or signed a statement endorsing its factual allegations and legal analysis.
The complaint draws on investigations by Ronen Bergman and Yuval Rubovitch published by Ynet and Yediot Aharonot, an October 8 interview with Netanyahu’s former military secretary, Maj.-Gen. (res.) Avi Gil, and a defamation lawsuit filed against Netanyahu by former Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) chief Ronen Bar on Wednesday.
“The document published to the public does not reflect what I saw, heard, or the discussions I attended,” Gil told Channel 12.
Gil also distinguished warnings of weakening deterrence from advance knowledge of the attack, saying there had been no specific, focused warning of such an assault from Gaza.
Netanyahu's Hamas policy central to dispute
One central dispute concerns Netanyahu’s policy toward Hamas. The complaint challenges his assertion that maintaining calm and containing the organization were never part of his directives, citing records that the families say show repeated instructions to preserve quiet in Gaza and postpone confrontations.
It also disputes his presentation of the assessment that Hamas was deterred as a uniform position of the security establishment. The families contend that Netanyahu himself promoted that assessment while his account omitted warnings pointing to growing danger.
Another issue is what Netanyahu knew about Hamas invasion plans. The complaint challenges his denial of receiving or being briefed on the “Jericho Wall” plan, citing earlier descriptions of a large-scale ground assault. Whether he received that specific document is distinct from whether he was briefed on similar plans.
On targeted killings, Netanyahu’s account portrays him as pressing for action that security officials resisted. The complaint argues that the reporting and Bar’s lawsuit show the reverse: proposals were repeatedly brought to Netanyahu, who declined to approve them.
The families also seek scrutiny of his account of Qatari funding diverted to Hamas’s military wing and his handling of warnings before the attack.
Beyond the document’s contents, the complaint alleges that publishing classified material and information from the comptroller’s examination violated restrictions on disclosure.
“We expect the attorney-general to order an immediate criminal investigation and the head of the Investigations Division to launch a comprehensive, impartial investigation as quickly as possible,” the families said in a statement.
The families’ lawyers argued that an investigation would give police access to classified documents needed to test the allegations, including original records establishing what information Netanyahu received and when.

'I will survive!' Disco queen Gloria Gaynor to perform in Tel Aviv in April
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:38:51 UTC
01:38:51 KST

Nearly half a century after her voice defined a generation, the ultimate survivor of the disco era is ready to make Israel dance once again.
Gloria Gaynor, the legendary voice behind the timeless anthem “I Will Survive,” is scheduled to perform at Tel Aviv’s Heichal Hatarbut on April 13.
At 83 years young, the American icon is returning to an Israeli stage for the first time in over a decade, bringing her iconic catalog and a powerful 10-piece band for the single-date engagement.
Following her performance here in 2015, Gaynor received the 2016 Martin Luther King Jr. award the following year, presented annually by the Consulate-General of Israel in New York.
“I fell in love with Israel the first time I went there,” she said at the time. “Now to receive a peace award from a nation that personifies peace in the midst of a raging storm is more humbling than words can express. I am eternally grateful.”
Her highly anticipated return to Israel also caps off a monumental chapter for Gaynor, who recently received one of the highest accolades of her five-decade career with the prestigious Kennedy Center Honors.
Gaynor's 'I Will Survive' has legendary music status
While “I Will Survive” has spent decades as a multi-generational anthem, soundtracking everything from cinematic breakups to LGBTQ+ pride movements, its path to legendary status was entirely accidental.
Written by Freddie Perren and Dino Fekaris, the track was never actually intended for Gaynor. In fact, her record label originally buried it on the B-side of the 1978 single “Substitute.”
It was only when club disc jockeys took matters into their own hands and started spinning the secondary track that the public made its choice clear.
The song skyrocketed to number one on the Billboard charts and earned Gaynor the first and only Grammy Award for Best Disco Recording before the category was permanently retired.
For Gaynor, the song’s themes of resilience were far from abstract.
At the exact moment the song was taking over global airwaves, the singer was facing a severe physical crisis following a near-paralyzing fall on stage that required intensive spinal surgery.
While millions of listeners found comfort in the lyrics as a story of romantic independence, Gaynor has shared that the words took on a profound double meaning for her.
To the artist singing it, “I Will Survive” became a literal testament to her own physical rehabilitation and medical recovery.
Nearly 50 years later, that spirit of endurance remains unbroken.

US researchers identify an effective way to quit smoking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:38:13 UTC
01:38:13 KST

US researchers identify an effective way to quit smoking
The study, led by researchers at the University of Pennsylvania’s Perelman School of Medicine and conducted across four healthcare systems, found that participants offered financial incentives of up to $600 were more likely to stop smoking after six months. The findings were published in the JAMA medical journal on October 3.
The trial focused on patients who continued to smoke and had been referred for low-dose CT scans to screen for lung cancer. Many participants came from medically underserved communities, including people with lower incomes, residents of rural areas, and Black and Hispanic adults.
Researchers compared 4 approaches to smoking cessation: standard care with referrals to support services, standard care combined with free cessation medication, medication plus financial rewards, and the same package supplemented by a text-based behavioral tool called FutureMe. The tool encouraged participants to imagine their lives without smoking.
After six months, the proportion of participants who had quit smoking was 4.3% among those receiving standard care, 5.1% among those offered free medication, 8.8% among those receiving medication and financial incentives, and 7.2% among those who also used FutureMe. Abstinence was verified through blood or urine tests.
Under the incentive programme, participants could receive up to $600 in payments tied to verified smoking cessation: $100 after two weeks, $200 after three months, and $300 after six months.
The results suggest that financial rewards can help people quit smoking more effectively than standard care or free medication alone, particularly among those who have struggled to stop in the past.
“Adding financial incentives increased quit rates in a population that can be especially difficult to reach with traditional smoking cessation approaches,” said Scott D. Halpern, the study’s senior author and director of the Palliative and Advanced Illness Research Center at the University of Pennsylvania.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that regular smoking impacts hair loss and accelerates early graying.

Ukraine and NATO created AI to predict UAV attacks
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine and NATO developed AI models to predict UAV strikes and plan artillery operations. They are being tested and prepared for integration.
Ukraine’s Defense Forces and NATO have developed AI models to forecast enemy UAV strikes and plan artillery operations. This was reported by NATO’s Joint Analysis, Training and Education Centre (JATEC), UNN reports.
Details
These models are designed to forecast enemy UAV strikes near the line of contact and to plan the use of Ukrainian artillery.
As the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine noted, the first model forecasts the use of enemy UAVs based on an analysis of accumulated data, weather conditions, and the current battlefield situation. It has already been tested on real-world datasets, refined, and prepared for integration into the situational-awareness systems of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
The second model helps plan the use of artillery by automatically generating and evaluating possible courses of action. Its prototype was handed over to Ukraine’s Defense Forces for testing and verification.
Provided testing and validation are successful, the model has the potential to be deployed in other combat units of the Armed Forces of Ukraine engaged in fighting the enemy, JATEC noted.

NEW DELHI: The Centre has directed social media giant Meta, which owns Instagram and Facebook, to ensure that its recommendation algorithms do not result in "disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives.""Ensure that recommendation systems do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives, and endeavour to provide appropriate diversity of relevant and credible information," an advisory issued by the ministry of electronics and information technology (MeitY), dated October 10, stated, PTI reported."Also strengthen mechanisms for rapid identification, review and escalation of content, which is gaining significant reach through recommendation systems and has the potential to cause widespread public confusion, apprehension, violence or disturbance of public order," it added.While the advisory does not cite any specific incident that led to its issuance, it comes amid ongoing protests in Delhi demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.MeitY also asked Meta to cooperate with law enforcement and other authorised government agencies by providing information or assistance within the timelines prescribed under the IT Rules, 2021.
The ministry noted that certain content relating to "ongoing public events" was being "prominently displayed and recommended to users" on Meta platforms.Citing the Information Technology Act, 2000, the advisory highlighted the company’s obligation to exercise due diligence under the IT Rules, 2021, which require intermediaries to inform users about prohibited content, including material likely to cause public disorder or incite a cognisable offence.MeitY also flagged content presenting old or selectively edited visuals as current events, misleading claims about emergencies, restrictions or police action, and audio-visual material depicting law-and-order situations without adequate context. It also raised concerns over content likely to incite violence and misleading material receiving disproportionate amplification.
The advisory outlined six requirements for Meta, including measures to identify and address prohibited content and review recommendation and ranking systems to ensure misleading, manipulated or out-of-context material is not "disproportionately amplified or repeatedly recommended to users".MeitY emphasised that the advisory seeks to promote responsible information dissemination while respecting lawful expression and public discourse."Meta is advised to ensure that any action taken pursuant to this advisory is consistent with the Information Technology Act, 2000, the IT Rules, 2021, and other applicable laws," the ministry added.

Instead, he said, she was told she was being dismissed because of her "relationship with people who speak despairingly of Israel". Instead, when pressed by his interviewer, Trump avoided the subject, shifting the focus instead to his own popularity or security in the Middle East.

Trump’s Republican Party is facing a critical midterm election on November 3 that will decide whether it maintains control of the US Congress, as well as other key state and local offices.

“If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so,” Trump wrote.

In response to the post, Netanyahu posted a video on social media expressing gratitude to the US president.
