Iran's response to any new attack will be unpredictable, Basij chief says
TEHRAN – The head of Iran's Basij Organization said one of the factors complicating U.S. calculations is the unpredictability of Iran's response, as Washington does not know where, with what means, or when Tehran would retaliate in any future confrontation.
Hojatoleslam Mahdi Taeb, speaking at a meeting of organizers of nightly public rallies, said the United States and Israel had misjudged Iran's resilience, assuming that a short war of three days to a maximum of six weeks could force the country to surrender.
The enemy expected that after six weeks Iran's missile and munitions stockpiles would dwindle, economic pressure would intensify and domestic insecurity would emerge, pushing Tehran to negotiate from weakness, Taeb said. But the Iranian nation and armed forces stood firm, and the Americans realized their miscalculation, he added.
Reviewing the course of the war, Taeb said that in the early days the IRGC Aerospace Force used complex combined designs of missiles and drones to penetrate Israel's multi-layered air defenses, but in the final days Iranian missiles hit their targets with greater success.
As Iran faced enemy planning for its military endurance, the U.S. and Israel also confronted limitations in munitions stocks and air-defense capacity, he said, adding that their military resilience declined under the pressure of the conflict.
Taeb said Washington and Tel Aviv have shifted strategy from direct war to indirect tools – proxies, regional and international pacts, economic pressure and fomenting insecurity – after failing to achieve their objectives.
Today's competition is a competition of endurance among Iran, the United States, Israel and other countries, he said. While the enemies sought to weaken Iran through sanctions, the Strait of Hormuz has become an effective factor in balancing power and influencing economic resilience, he noted.
He also claimed that psychological referrals among U.S. forces on ships and bases in the region have increased amid fatigue from prolonged confrontation.
U.S. intelligence assessments themselves stress the difficulty of predicting how Iran would respond in any future clash, a factor weighing on American military and security calculations, Taeb said.
The war has challenged U.S. and Israeli positions and interests, he said, claiming that more than 70 percent of Americans believe the war with Iran brought no benefit to their country.
Turning to politics, Taeb said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, eyeing Knesset elections, favors dragging the U.S. back into war with Iran to reshape the political-security environment and preserve his own standing. If electoral conditions do not turn in his favor, security issues could be raised to alter the election process, he said.
On the U.S. midterms, he said the Iran file directly and indirectly affects the American political scene, and President Donald Trump needs a victory to sustain his position. Trump is trying to turn the issue of negotiations with Iran into a symbolic win while using security and economic pressure to challenge Iranian society and foster polarization, he added.
Future developments, Taeb concluded, must be assessed within the framework of competition over national endurance, mutual military and economic constraints, and the interplay of regional dynamics with domestic politics in the U.S. and Israel.

Among the building's tenants are important financial institutions such as the International Monetary Fund, as well as wealth management company Merril Lynch.
At the building's foot is a shopping center, which will remain open for now.

Araghchi’s Baghdad diplomacy: Hormuz, regional security and Muslim unity top Iran’s agenda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:31:37 UTC
01:31:37 KST

Araghchi’s Baghdad diplomacy: Hormuz, regional security and Muslim unity top Iran’s agenda
TEHRAN — Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has used a series of diplomatic meetings in Baghdad to press for an end to military escalation in West Asia, outline Iran’s conditions for restoring security in the Strait of Hormuz and call for a more active role for the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) in addressing disputes among Muslim countries.
Araghchi traveled to the Iraqi capital to attend the 52nd session of the OIC Council of Foreign Ministers, where he held talks with Iraqi officials and counterparts from Lebanon, Egypt and Algeria, as well as the organization’s secretary-general. His engagements focused on regional security, the Palestinian issue, bilateral relations and diplomatic efforts to prevent further escalation.
In remarks on the sidelines of the meeting on Sunday, Araghchi reiterated that Iran remained prepared to defend its national interests while pursuing diplomacy, provided negotiations respected Iran’s rights and were conducted on an appropriate basis.
Strait of Hormuz: Iran sets out seven-point plan for reopening
Araghchi said the insecurity affecting the Strait of Hormuz and its economic consequences for regional countries and the wider international community were a direct result of US-Israeli military aggression against Iran.
He said Tehran had presented Washington with a seven-point plan setting out its conditions for resolving the confrontation. The United States had submitted its own views, which Iran was reviewing, he added.
According to Araghchi, the proposed framework provides a clear path toward restoring security in the strategic waterway if Washington meets Iran’s conditions.
“If our conditions are met, the Strait of Hormuz will reopen on the sixth day, and negotiations will begin on the seventh day,” he said.
The foreign minister stressed that Iran’s conditions were not extraordinary, arguing that they concerned commitments the United States had previously undertaken under an earlier memorandum of understanding and in other negotiations. He said Washington could implement the requirements within days if it genuinely sought to reopen the strait.
Araghchi also briefed Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein on ongoing diplomatic consultations related to regional peace and security. He reiterated that Iran remained committed to diplomacy as a means of preventing further escalation, even as it maintained its readiness to defend its national security.
The issue also featured in Araghchi’s meeting with Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty, during which the two officials discussed bilateral relations, regional and international developments, and diplomatic consultations conducted through mediators.
Araghchi told Abdelatty that Iran had consistently pursued diplomacy with the aim of reducing tensions, while accusing Washington of repeatedly violating its commitments. He cited a US breach of its pledge just two weeks after the signing of a memorandum of understanding intended to end the war.
Iraq ties and the need for regional dialogue
In his meeting with Hussein, Araghchi highlighted the importance of strengthening cooperation between Iran and Iraq, particularly in economic, trade and security affairs.
The two ministers also discussed developments in the Arabian Peninsula and ways to help end regional conflicts. Araghchi emphasized that Iran was prepared to facilitate dialogue between parties involved in regional disputes.
Araghchi also met Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi during his visit to Baghdad. No further details of their discussions were immediately available.
Beyond bilateral ties, Araghchi argued that Muslim countries needed to strengthen dialogue and solidarity to address shared challenges, particularly the Palestinian issue and the continued expansionism of the Israeli regime.
OIC urged to play a stronger role in resolving disputes
Araghchi called on the OIC to play a more effective role in resolving differences among Muslim countries and strengthening cooperation across the Islamic world.
He said he had raised the issue in meetings with the Iraqi prime minister, Hussein, and the organization’s newly appointed Secretary-General Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed.
During his meeting with Cheikh Ahmed, the secretary-general expressed the organization’s interest in drawing on Iran’s experience and capabilities to develop initiatives for mediation and dispute settlement among Muslim countries.
Araghchi welcomed the prospect of a more active OIC role, stressing that the organization’s secretariat should operate professionally and impartially and avoid any perception of bias toward or against member states.
He also emphasized the importance of strengthening solidarity among Muslim countries in confronting common challenges, particularly those arising from developments in occupied Palestine.
The foreign minister noted that the OIC had lost some of its influence in recent years and expressed hope that Iraq’s assumption of the rotating presidency, together with the appointment of a new secretary-general, would help revitalize the organization.
Yemen Resolution: Iran insists on fairness, balance and a political solution
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has warned that Iran will not join the consensus on a proposed resolution on Yemen at the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) unless the final text reflects fairness and balance, stressing that Tehran’s position will depend on the wording ultimately adopted.
Speaking to IRNA on Sunday on the sidelines of the annual session of the OIC Council of Foreign Ministers in Baghdad, Araghchi said the organization’s resolutions had not yet been adopted and that the final communiqué was still being drafted. He noted that Iranian diplomats had engaged in extensive discussions in recent days to ensure that Iran’s views were reflected in the documents, adding that most of the proposed resolutions, with a few exceptions, repeated texts adopted the previous year.
On Yemen, Araghchi said serious discussions had taken place among member states, with Saudi Arabia, Iran and other countries presenting their respective positions. The draft resolution had yet to be finalized, he said, expressing hope that the final text would reflect a fair and balanced approach. If these principles were not upheld, Iran would be unable to join the consensus and would formally register its reservations or reject the resolution, depending on its final wording.
Araghchi acknowledged that countries aligned with Saudi Arabia constituted a sizable bloc within the OIC, but said Tehran had conducted extensive consultations and clearly outlined its position on a just solution to the conflict. He stressed that Yemen’s crisis could not be resolved through military force or blockade, calling instead for a political process grounded in the United Nations Charter, respect for Yemen’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, and protection of the Yemeni people’s human rights. He also offered Iran’s assistance in facilitating dialogue among the parties.
Rejecting allegations that Yemen’s armed forces had attacked Mecca and Medina, Araghchi said repeating such accusations would neither serve the interests of the Muslim world nor strengthen unity among OIC member states. He emphasized that the sanctity of Islamic holy sites must be respected by all.
Lebanon: Iran stresses sovereignty while acknowledging political differences
Araghchi’s meeting with Lebanese Foreign Minister Youssef Rajji focused on bilateral relations, Lebanon’s sovereignty and national security, and regional developments.
Araghchi reaffirmed Iran’s support for Lebanon’s territorial integrity and its efforts to defend its sovereignty and national security against Israeli military action and expansionism.
Speaking separately to reporters, he described his meeting with Rajji as respectful but serious and frank, acknowledging differences between Tehran and the current Lebanese government over approaches to regional and domestic issues.
Nevertheless, he stressed that both countries had an interest in maintaining and developing relations.
“I emphasized that the Islamic Republic of Iran is interested in having comprehensive political, economic and cultural relations with Lebanon as a country,” Araghchi said.
He added that Lebanon’s internal affairs were for the Lebanese people to decide. Referring to Hezbollah, he described the movement as one of Lebanon’s most important political groups and an established part of the country’s political and social landscape.
Araghchi said decisions made by Lebanese political groups, including Hezbollah, should be treated as matters of Lebanon’s domestic affairs.
Algeria: Palestinian issue remains central to Muslim solidarity
In a meeting with Sofiane Chaib, Algeria’s secretary of state to the minister of foreign affairs, Araghchi discussed bilateral relations and developments affecting the Muslim world, with particular emphasis on Palestine.
He described Palestine as the foremost concern facing the Muslim world and humanity, citing the continued Israeli occupation and the situation in the occupied Palestinian territories.
Araghchi called for stronger unity and solidarity among Muslim countries to end Israel’s impunity and to confront its continued expansionism.
He also briefed the Algerian official on developments in West Asia and US interventionist and destabilizing actions in the Persian Gulf region.
Alongside his meetings in Baghdad, Araghchi held a telephone conversation on Sunday with Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar.
According to Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry, the two officials discussed bilateral relations and regional developments and stressed the importance of dialogue and diplomacy amid continuing regional tensions.
The conversation added to the diplomatic contacts surrounding efforts to prevent further escalation and address outstanding regional disputes.
Diplomacy and defense remain parallel priorities
Across his meetings and public remarks in Baghdad, Araghchi presented diplomacy as a central instrument for addressing regional crises, while maintaining that Iran would defend its national interests and security.
His message combined calls for stronger cooperation among neighboring countries, a more active OIC role in resolving disputes, and greater unity among Muslim states over Palestine with a clear warning that progress on the Strait of Hormuz depended on Washington meeting Tehran’s stated conditions.
The meetings also highlighted the range of issues confronting regional diplomacy, from maritime security and the economic repercussions of conflict to Yemen, Lebanon and the future of Palestinian territories.
For Tehran, Araghchi’s Baghdad engagements provided an opportunity to advance bilateral ties, engage regional counterparts and press for diplomatic solutions while reiterating Iran’s position that lasting security requires respect for national sovereignty and the fulfillment of commitments.

The Guardian view on plague in Russia: what is most worrying is the lack of information | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:30:04 UTC
01:30:04 KST

Is there a plague outbreak in Russia? If the answer were a clear yes, there shouldn’t be much reason to worry. With swift medical intervention, plague is treatable. But in the nearly three weeks since a worker at a Siberian plague research unit died of a mysterious respiratory illness, state officials have been consistently tight-lipped about what happened and whether there were any further cases.
It is this uncertainty that has the World Health Organization (WHO) and international community worried: partly because there is a – very small – risk of an outbreak, and partly because it is yet another warning that the international coordination we rely on to prevent pandemics is fraying along with the rest of international politics, and could easily fail to protect us in the future.
The key to containing an outbreak is quick disclosure and open sharing of information. Russia reportedly held high-level meetings about the case, quarantined the hospital where the worker was treated and traced about 200 contacts. That response suggests officials believed the infection was plague, and yet they did not report any of this to the WHO, as international law requires. Russia later revealed that the worker died of a pneumonia of unknown origin – hardly useful information. It undoubtedly gathered lab results and genetic sequences that could shed more light on the case, but has not shared them.
Earlier this year, the hantavirus outbreak originating on the MV Hondius cruise ship was successfully contained, showing that the global health system can still work well when countries cooperate. This latest incident suggests that one recalcitrant nation can jeopardise everyone’s safety. It is not the WHO’s fault that Russia is essentially a rogue state, but the body must be ready for such eventualities. International politics is fragmented, and only becoming more so.
Earlier this year the US left the WHO (though it is still party to some of its treaties). States follow international laws when they believe in them, or when they believe that there will be penalties – reputational or otherwise – for not playing along. The WHO has not attempted to play hardball with Russia, or set off a round of international condemnation from leading member states. Some might be heartened that on 7 October the US state department officially requested that the Russian government share information with the WHO. However, it is likely that this reflects Washington’s increasingly ad hoc approach to international politics – using every lever available as situations arise – rather than a renewed commitment to international law. President Trump said on the same day that he would speak to Vladimir Putin about the issue. If that happened, no one has heard about it or what information may have been revealed.
The keen US interest may give credence to speculation that what in fact happened was some kind of bioweapons research leak. This is thought to be unlikely, but not impossible. The fact that such a scenario can even be plausibly entertained three weeks after the initial event speaks to a serious breakdown in the system. Western states probably do not hold much sway with Russia. But the other Brics nations may have more. The WHO used to rely on US backing for its requests. It may now have to find support among wider, more multipolar coalitions. This potential outbreak may come to nothing, but there will be another soon.

Saudi Arabia unveils $106,000 luxury electric cars as Houthi attacks threaten Vision 2030
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:29:18 UTC
01:29:18 KST

As Houthi attacks continue to disrupt Saudi Arabia's aviation industry and threaten Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's Vision 2030 economic ambitions, another sector of the kingdom's economy is moving forward. Saudi Arabia has unveiled its first homegrown luxury electric cars, marking a significant step in its effort to reduce dependence on oil and establish itself as a global automotive manufacturing hub.
On September 21, Saudi automaker CEER unveiled its first two models, an electric sedan and an SUV, under the EXOBOT name. The company plans to introduce five additional models over the next five years, building a broader range of vehicles aimed at both the domestic and international markets.
Saudi media outlets closely followed the launch, with Al Arabiya describing it as an important milestone in the kingdom's efforts to develop an advanced industrial sector. The project forms part of bin Salman's Vision 2030 strategy, which seeks to diversify Saudi Arabia's oil-dependent economy by expanding manufacturing, attracting investment and creating new sources of economic growth.
According to Al Arabiya, Saudi Arabia is betting on the development of an integrated automotive industry that can strengthen domestic manufacturing, introduce advanced technologies and eventually compete with established automakers across the region and beyond.
"The launch of CEER's first vehicles represents another step forward in Saudi Arabia's progression to build a sustainable and prosperous industrial ecosystem," bin Salman said, describing the automotive sector as a potential engine of economic growth that could establish the kingdom as a leading regional and global manufacturing center.
CEER was established in 2022 as a joint venture between Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, the kingdom's sovereign wealth fund, and Taiwanese technology giant Foxconn. Its stated objectives include developing domestic industry, attracting foreign investment, creating opportunities for private businesses and increasing Saudi Arabia's gross domestic product.
The new vehicles are planned to be manufactured at CEER's production complex in the King Salman Automotive Cluster, located in King Abdullah Economic City, north of Jeddah.
According to Al Arabiya, the complex is expected to become one of the most advanced automotive manufacturing facilities in the Middle East and North Africa. Initial investment in the project stands at approximately $1.3 billion, with a target production capacity of 240,000 vehicles annually once all phases are completed.
The economic expectations are substantial. Saudi projections indicate that CEER could contribute more than $8 billion to the kingdom's GDP by 2034, improve its trade balance by approximately $21 billion and create around 30,000 direct and indirect jobs. The automotive industry also falls under advanced manufacturing and innovation, one of the six main pillars of the Public Investment Fund's strategy for 2026-2030.
Beyond their futuristic appearance, the two EXOBOT models were designed with Saudi Arabia's harsh desert environment in mind. Both feature distinctive doors that open upward, while the vehicles' specially designed glass is intended to significantly reduce heat entering the passenger compartment.
"These vehicles were designed for this climate, these people, this kingdom and the countries of the Middle East," CEER CEO James DeLuca said during the launch. DeLuca, who has more than four decades of experience in the automotive industry, emphasized the company's ambition to create something distinctly Saudi. "We wanted to make sure the world could see what Saudi Arabia is capable of," he said.
Despite the emphasis on Saudi design and manufacturing, the company relies heavily on international partnerships. Its electric drive technology incorporates components supplied by companies including Croatia's Rimac and South Korea's Hyundai Transys, highlighting the role of foreign expertise in developing the kingdom's emerging automotive industry.
On October 8, CEER opened its first mobile showroom in Diriyah, near Riyadh, allowing potential customers to examine the vehicles and place reservations. The company plans to establish additional showrooms across Saudi Arabia as it prepares to bring its first models to market.
According to CEER Chief Commercial Officer Luay Alshurafa, prices begin at 399,000 Saudi riyals, approximately $106,000. The package includes a six-year vehicle warranty or up to 200,000 kilometers, along with scheduled maintenance for the same period and an eight-year battery warranty.
However, customers will still have to wait before taking delivery. The first vehicles are not expected to be handed over before March 2027. In the meantime, CEER plans to open eight additional showrooms across four Saudi cities by the end of 2026.
The company's ambitions extend beyond the Saudi market. CEER ultimately hopes to expand throughout the Middle East and North Africa, positioning itself as a regional competitor in an increasingly crowded global automotive industry.
Yet the challenges remain significant. Despite financial backing from Saudi Arabia's vast oil wealth, CEER must overcome obstacles that have frustrated previous attempts to establish a domestic automotive industry, including shortages of local suppliers and the difficulties of building a manufacturing and distribution network from scratch.
The company also faces logistical and economic uncertainty linked to regional tensions between the United States and Iran, while continuing Houthi attacks have exposed the vulnerability of Saudi Arabia's infrastructure and complicated the broader ambitions of Vision 2030.
For bin Salman, the luxury electric vehicles represent more than a new consumer product. They are part of an effort to transform an oil-producing kingdom into an industrial and technological power. Whether CEER can turn its futuristic designs into a commercially successful automotive industry will be another test of that ambition, at a time when regional conflict is making Saudi Arabia's economic transformation increasingly difficult.

Ballistic missile warnings are back, but the Starlink cap stays, Zelenskyy says: Ukraine’s two US lifelines, one restored
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:28:18 UTC
01:28:18 KST

The US has resumed sharing intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches with Ukraine after a pause of several days, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told NBC News on 18 October. The blackout fell on days when Russia was firing ballistic missiles at Ukraine. Limits on the Starlink satellite service that Ukraine’s forces rely on remain in place, he said.
Russia has leaned on ballistic missiles in this month’s strikes on Ukraine’s grid, firing 39 in a single attack, and Ukraine is short of interceptors to stop them. Washington has used its support as leverage, reportedly telling Kyiv to spare Russian refineries or lose US intelligence and arms.
Three days without warnings
The sharing had been blocked for some period of time before it was restored, Zelenskyy said on Meet the Press.
“We are very thankful for this. Now it works,” he said.
Ukraine gets other intelligence from Europeans and dozens of other partners, he explained. But only the United States has the data that tells Kyiv when Russia launches ballistic missiles.
“We didn’t get it during ballistic attacks during three days,” Zelenskyy said.
A timely warning gives Ukraine’s air defenses extra minutes to prepare and lets authorities alert civilians, Liga noted. Late on 12 October, Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv before the air-raid alert reached people, with no advance data on launches from Russian territory. The next day, US President Donald Trump said Washington was still sharing intelligence. Two days later, Zelenskyy said Kyiv had received no US warnings of incoming ballistic missiles while it paused its strikes on Russian refineries at Washington’s request. That pause followed the energy ceasefire Trump declared on 11 October, which Russia never confirmed.
“He thinks Ukraine is a weak link and that it needs to be squeezed into giving in”: diplomat on why Trump pressures Kyiv, not Moscow
Starlink still capped, Kyiv says
Starshield, the military version of Starlink, still cuts out above 161 km/h, Zelenskyy said, too slow for Ukraine’s interceptor drones to catch Russia’s jet-powered Shahed-type drones. NBC News, which aired the interview, separately reported that Starlink services had resumed at normal speed. He said Ukraine’s generals and government believe the order came from the US government and SpaceX carried it out, though he did not know who exactly made the call. Ukraine had instead asked SpaceX and Trump to open Starlink over Russia so it could hit ballistic missile launchers, he said.
“If [Trump] will personally decide to lift this decision, it will immediately work as it was before,” he said.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who appeared on the same show, called Zelenskyy’s charge “very reckless” and said Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio had denied any administration role. Asked about the break in intelligence sharing, he said he did not know anything about it but that Zelenskyy should be “very careful about making statements like this that aren’t true.” Reuters had reported, citing three officials, that White House officials ordered the Pentagon to limit the service.
Asked whether Ukraine could win without the United States, Zelenskyy said it would be very difficult.
“But if the United States will support Putin, I mean, it’s unbelievable, it’s tragedy. It’s historic mistake and big tragedy,” he said.
He also said his team had received word that US negotiators wanted to meet, and that he had offered to meet in Brussels or London, hoping the US team would be ready this week.
The warnings are back, but they stopped once without explanation. Ukraine’s defense against Russia’s missiles still runs through decisions made in the US.

Ukrainian forces struck an oil terminal, a data center, and a bridge in a large-scale overnight attack on St. Petersburg on Oct. 18, Russian officials and media reported.

Numerous videos appeared to show the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal engulfed in flames. Located in the city's port, the facility is one of Russia's largest fuel storage and export facilities.

Speed caps on Starlink operations in Ukraine remain in place, hindering efforts to counter Russian jet-powered drones, President Zelensky said on Oct. 17.

While Ukraine reported that connectivity was restored by the next day, Zelensky now confirmed that a speed limit of 161 kilometers per hour remains in place.
"Some of our interceptor drones use Starlink to intercept the enemy's fast-moving jet-powered drones," Zelensky said.
But with the current speed cap, Ukrainian interceptor drones cannot down Russian jet-powered drones, the president said, adding that Ukraine "thankfully" also uses other anti-drone air defenses.
The disruptions also complicate other military operations, as some drones rely on Starlink to deliver food, water, and other equipment to soldiers in front-line positions, he added.
The unexpected throttling of Starlink systems sparked a debate about who made the decision, with media reports linking it to SpaceX owner Elon Musk or the White House.
The move came as Ukraine-U.S. ties plummeted with Trump concluding a diesel deal with Russia and publicly lambasting Zelensky.

Ukraine has either received no response from U.S. channels or has been told the problems stem from "technical issues," Zelensky said, dismissing that explanation.
He called the restrictions a "planned operation" targeting Ukraine, noting that the speed limits remain in effect in Ukraine but not in EU countries.
Kyiv sent several vehicles equipped with its Starlink devices to the EU for testing, where they exceeded the speed limit in place in Ukraine, he explained. The president added that European partners are already working on a possible alternative to Starlink.

‘Hybrid warfare’: Taiwan drives away 16 Chinese ships

‘Hybrid warfare’: Taiwan drives away 16 Chinese ships
China is ramping up its presence around Taiwan, in a pattern that Taipei said is designed to ‘alter the status quo’.
Taiwan has confronted and driven away 16 Chinese coastguard, research and fishing vessels that it said were involved in simultaneous “maritime harassment” operations.
An “unusually large” number of Chinese vessels took part in coordinated operations around Taiwan’s main island and Pratas (also known as Dongsha), a disputed island to the southwest, the Taiwanese coastguard said in a statement on Sunday.
The Chinese vessels included four fishing boats, which engaged in “simultaneous operations’ that the coastguard described as “hybrid warfare”.
Taiwan’s coastguard said its vessels took “forceful action immediately to effectively neutralise the threats” and accused Beijing of “attempting to unilaterally alter the status quo” in the Taiwan Strait and give the “false impression of jurisdiction”.
Some of the vessels reportedly entered Taiwan’s restricted waters.
Intensified maritime pressure
Beijing claims Taiwan and Pratas as part of its territory and asserts jurisdiction over the surrounding waters, which Taipei rejects. China has long threatened to use force to regain control of Taiwan.
In an incident on October 1 , Taiwan’s coastguard fired water cannon at a Chinese recreational fishing vessel near Pratas island between Taiwan and mainland China that Beijing claims.
China has intensified its maritime pressure on Taiwan in recent months. Beijing deployed a record 244 coastguard, scientific research and other ships around Taiwan’s main island in July, Taiwanese official data show, compared with just 58 in the same month last year.
In the first 21 days of August, 152 vessels were detected; most were from the Chinese Coastguard, but fishing boats and research vessels were also involved.
China also deploys warships around Taiwan on a near-daily basis, but those are counted separately.

The Guardian view on schools: the hardest questions for Lucy Powell are about priorities | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:25:04 UTC
01:25:04 KST

There is a good case to be made for the increased importance of speaking skills in our new age of machines. With the UK economy’s stronger-than-expected recent performance widely linked to AI investment, it is vital that people are equipped for the kinds of in-person, public-facing jobs that are least likely to be automated. A concerning decline in children’s language development, both in the UK and internationally, has been linked to high screen use. There is a grim irony in a situation where tech companies both compete with humans for contracts and undermine our ability to talk to one other.
The Guardian has previously backed efforts to more strongly embed speaking skills, or oracy, in British schools. In a speech on Thursday, Lucy Powell promised to give them equal status to reading and writing in English (education is devolved, so her main responsibility is for England, but there are parallel initiatives in the other nations). Yet with promised updates to the national curriculum postponed, and plans for special educational needs reform causing deep anxiety to families, schools and councils, the hardest questions for the education secretary are about priorities. Following negative feedback from schools, she has also asked Ofsted to look again at its new inspection framework.
The curriculum review completed last year was deliberately cautious, reflecting the Starmer administration’s overall tone. Since then, England’s high scores in maths and science, in international tests, have shown that standards in some subjects have risen. But in English, an overly prescriptive and grammar-obsessed curriculum is putting pupils off. This is the obvious place to start with new speaking skills. The delayed curriculum revisions should set out how it is going to be done.
The energy that Ms Powell brings to the education brief is welcome. She is right to refuse to “sit still and polish the status quo”, especially as the Conservative party seeks to take credit for improvements to English schools that were a legacy of New Labour. The decline of the arts in schools must also be tackled. An improved vocational offer is arguably most urgent of all.
But there is no point denying the challenges around implementation. The government is already committed to the introduction of new maths and English qualifications, to replace demoralising GCSE resits. Reform of the special educational needs system will need to be carefully monitored. Many experts in the college sector believe that the scrapping of BTec qualifications, in favour of T-levels and V-levels, is a mistake. This too needs to be closely watched. A stronger steer from government on universities is also needed. Bridget Phillipson’s decision to unfreeze fees after eight years has only slightly eased their funding difficulties. Reform of unfair student loan terms must come sooner rather than later.
Ms Powell is not unique, among Andy Burnham’s new brooms, in facing a daunting set of challenges. Her pledge to go “further and deeper on curriculum reform” is welcome; the world is changing fast and schools need help to keep up. A strengthened emphasis on the spoken word is just one part of this. But in the coming months, she will need to make decisions about where to put her energies. There are only so many changes, on top of special educational needs reforms, that schools can be expected to cope with.

Trump endorses embattled Israeli PM Netanyahu ahead of October 27 election
US President Donald Trump on Sunday endorsed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of Israel's October 27 elections. It was not clear what impact the endorsement would have on voters, since many Israelis have expressed disappointment with Trump over the outcome of the Iran war and the US president's ceasefire proposal.
President Donald Trump on Sunday endorsed embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu late in his reelection campaign, a coveted boost because of Trump’s popularity but one that the American had withheld for months as the vote neared and the leaders' strategies in the Middle East diverged.
Trump said in a post on social media that Netanyahu “has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combating the Islamic Republic of Iran”.
Read moreHow Netanyahu survived the political fallout from the October 7 attacks
Israelis are set to vote October 27, in the first national elections since Hamas attacked Israel on October 7, 2023.
The absence of an endorsement was a setback for the Likud politician, who had billed his tight ties to the Republican president as a selling point for staying in power.
“Thank you, President Trump, for the tremendous support and work together,” Netanyahu said in a statement in Hebrew posted on X. “Together we will complete the mission!”
His Likud Party attached to the statement a 35-second video showing clips of the two leaders together and Trump praising Netanyahu.
It was not immediately clear what impact the endorsement would have on what is expected to be a tight race. Trump is still popular in Israel, but many Israelis, including leading commentators, have expressed disappointment over the inconclusive outcome of the Iran war and Trump’s ceasefire proposal, which fell short of many of the countries’ key goals when they jointly launched the war in February.
In his post, Trump again threatened to “soon finish the job” against Iran “unless they change their ways, rapidly”, but added he might not want to if Netanyahu loses the election. “If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so,” Trump said.
He said Netanyahu had been “Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself.”
The main election rival to Netanyahu responded to Trump's endorsement of the incumbent premier, saying "only Israelis can choose their leader".
Speaking at a conference in Tel Aviv ahead of upcoming elections, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot said he "admires" Trump, but "Israel is a democratic country: only Israelis can choose their leader".
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Trump endorsed Netanyahu in past elections and in November he sent a letter to Israeli President Isaac Herzog asking him to pardon Netanyahu on corruption charges.
But Trump's comments about Netanyahu in recent months had been much more subdued, and he repeatedly demurred when asked if he would back the prime minister. The president, when asked in a Time magazine interview published this month about backing the Israeli leader, said, ”I’m not involved in politics anymore,” despite his campaigning for and endorsing US politicians.
Trump, especially in his second term, has sought to give his stamp of approval to candidates in foreign elections and claimed credit when they have been successful. He endorsed Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán in his unsuccessful bid for a fifth term, as well as Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Polish President Karol Nawrocki, and several Latin American leaders.
Trump and Netanyahu have been close allies and seemed more aligned than ever in the wake of the joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran's nuclear facilities in 2025. But over the course of the nearly eight-month war with Iran this year, they have had disagreements.
Trump criticised Israel’s decision to attack a key Iranian gas field in the first weeks of the war. In June, he called Netanyahu “crazy." Trump also said that he was “a little bit perturbed” as Israel’s fighting with Hezbollah militants in Lebanon was holding back peace talks with Iran.
Beyond Iran, Netanyahu in August rejected Trump’s latest plan to advance a stalled ceasefire in Gaza, pushing back on the US administration’s call for Israel to withdraw from territory it controls in Gaza until Hamas has been disarmed.

Gaza: Bodies of 75 killed by Israel recovered, buried after three years
Palestinians on Sunday held funerals for the bodies of 75 people killed by Israel in the genocide in Gaza, which comes after civil defence teams worked for three years to retrieve the bodies from under the rubble despite a lack of specialised equipment.
The families of those killed gathered in Gaza City in a mass funeral organised by the Martyrs’ Families’ Association and in coordination with the General Directorate of the Civil Defence.
The mass funeral was held inside the al-Daraj Sports Stadium, with prayers offered for the deceased before the bodies were carried to the Sheikh Radwan Cemetery in northern Gaza.
Kamal Hijazi, whose loved ones were among those killed, told The New Arab that being able to hold a funeral was somewhat a relief.
“The rubble formed a barrier between us and giving the dead a proper farewell, in a way that was dignified and befitting of them. The Israeli occupation does not recognise the dignity of Palestinians, whether they are dead or alive- but we will not allow the rubble to be the grave of our martyrs,” he said.
He also called on the relevant authorities in Gaza to preserve and document the data of those killed and recovered in the hopes that “there will be justice in Gaza”.
“We will not ask anything of the international community, as we have no confidence in it,” he continued.
Civil defence spokesman Mahmoud Basal confirmed that around 8,000 Palestinians remain buried under the rubble, with teams unable to recover their remains due to a lack of resources.
“Civil defence teams are working under extremely difficult conditions without heavy machinery to remove the rubble burying the bodies. Children, women and the elderly are dying, and no one is able to retrieve their bodies from under the rubble, all while the world, human rights groups, all while Arab and Western countries stand by and watch without lifting a finger,” he said.
One of the people who attended the funeral procession, Najat Abdel Aaal, told The New Arab, said 10 of her family members were among those recovered, noting that most of them were women and children.
She said during the time of the bombing when they were killed, she screamed and cried out for help.
“But at the time, crews were only able to pull out a few people from under the rubble, and the bodies of my family and relatives were buried for three years,” she explained.
“Retrieving the bodies after three years has reopened the wounds we all feel. It has brought up a mixture of relief and pain, but families have finally been able to bid farewell to their loved ones and lay them to rest,” she added.
Israel’s war on Gaza, which commenced in October 2023, has killed over 74,000 Palestinians and has been determined to be a genocide by leading international rights groups and scholars.
The war has levelled entire neighbourhoods, devastated the healthcare system, and destroyed many civilian buildings, including residential blocks, places of worship and schools.
Despite a ceasefire agreed in October 2025, with the terms demanding that aid deliveries are made daily, Israel has obstructed scores of items from entering the enclave, including heavy machinery and specialised tools used to find and recover the dead from beneath the rubble.
A report from Euro-Med Human Rights Monitors states there is approximately 68 million tonnes of rubble across the Gaza Strip.
The lack of equipment has raised concerns that without forensic surveys, any efforts to recover bodies could result in the crushing or scattering of remains.
According to human rights group Gisha, Israel continues to define thousands of critical emergency humanitarian items as “dual use”, and blocks them from entering the enclave.
The listed items, ranging from construction materials to wheelchairs, sleeping bags, and portable toilets, have hindered Gaza's reconstruction.

No crew, a cargo bed, and pontoons: Ukraine’s MAT1LDA robot is built to cross water with 400 kg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:19:48 UTC
01:19:48 KST

Ukrainian company Nodrics has developed MAT1LDA, an eight-wheeled amphibious ground robot that can carry supplies across water, swamps, and rough terrain, robot-maker Tencore said, Ukrainian military outlet Militarnyi reported on 17 October. The machine joins Tencore’s new family of ground robots, which the company has also shown in the US.
Ukraine’s ground robots now haul supplies and evacuate wounded soldiers through zones where drones make every move deadly, and the Defense Ministry has launched its first competitive tender for them.
500 kg on land, 400 kg afloat
A petrol engine drives MAT1LDA’s eight wheels, and side pontoons keep it afloat, so it can cross water, marshland, and rough ground without preparation, Militarnyi said. Its makers claim it carries up to 500 kg on land and 400 kg on water, with a range of up to 160 km on land and 50 km on water.
Its open frame lets crews swap equipment quickly to suit the task, fitting cargo containers or evacuation stretchers.
Robots won’t replace armored vehicles, says Ukrainian company that builds both. It reveals one job they can’t do
Four robots, one system
MAT1LDA is part of the Tencore Ecosystem, which brings together four classes of ground robots for military and civilian work, Militarnyi reported earlier. Besides the amphibious eight-wheeler, it includes the tracked TerMIT, the wheeled TOR 4×4, and the TRAX Utility firefighting and rescue robot. The company says it has delivered more than 4,000 robots to Ukraine’s armed forces since the full-scale invasion, used across more than 50 brigades.
Tencore calls it Ukraine’s first integrated ecosystem of its kind. Putting the platforms into one system is meant to make them easier to use, maintain, and fit with extra equipment. One of the first shared add-ons is AI KIT, a hardware and software module that lets a robot keep to its route or drive back on its own after losing contact with its operator.
On show in Washington
Tencore displayed MAT1LDA carrying a TerMIT robot at the Association of the US Army’s annual trade show in Washington this month, Breaking Defense reported.
Other Ukrainian makers have built swimming ground robots too: one switches from land to water in seconds, and another can tow 10 tons, its maker says. In April, Tencore formed a joint venture with France’s Shark Robotics.

What gets in the way of prisoners’ rehabilitation | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:18:58 UTC
01:18:58 KST

Your editorial on overcrowded prisons and probation (13 October) was most welcome as it highlights a crisis in community justice that shows little sign of abating. You say that problems date back to the failed part-privatisation of the probation service, but in reality political interference has been happening for far longer than that.
Having worked for years as a prison probation officer and then in an aftercare and resettlement unit for ex-offenders, I saw good practice and ongoing practical and emotional support that demonstrated all the important points raised by Enver Solomon in his recent Guardian article.
Staff visited prisons and got to know inmates before they were released, which involved in-depth discussions of their offending history and what was needed for successful resettlement. Staff visited wet day centres for problem drinkers and established links with community organisations. They did not see themselves as the exclusive purveyors of rehabilitation.
In 1984 the government produced a “statement of national objectives and priorities” that made work with prisoners low-profile, and the aftercare unit closed a few years later. When I tried, as part of my doctoral research, to interview probation staff in the 1990s about their role in prison resettlement, I found that such work had stopped.
Since then, probation officers have increasingly lost their autonomy – and the opportunity and permission to get to know the people they supervise. Risk has become the driving force, resulting in an incredible rate of offenders breaching their licence conditions and being returned to prison.
Probation staff are told to be more professionally curious and to give hope to offenders. The service has struggled to hit its targets, but has surely lost the point of its work, which is not the fault of its hard‑working staff. Action is required, now.
 
Anthony Goodman
 
Professor of community justice, Middlesex University
Your editorial on rehabilitation in prison makes some important points. It is also worth noting the political hypocrisy around this issue. The Barlinnie Special Unit, which did change people in prison, was closed in 1994, while the rehabilitation policies pursued in Grendon Underwood, which opened in 1962, have rarely been extended into the main system.
Why? Because these places challenged the decades‑long political obsession with punishment and deterrence. Whether or not the “Scandi” units at Wandsworth and Pentonville in London, which pursue a similar philosophy to Barlinnie and Grendon, will also be marginalised and ignored remains to be seen.
More broadly, rehabilitation will not work in a society divided by brutal social divisions, a point made by Victoria Law in her book “Prisons Make Us Safer”: And 20 Other Myths About Mass Incarceration: “What does it mean to rehabilitate a person to their former state if that state involves poverty, racism, unemployment, unstable housing, and/or violence? Can a person be rehabilitated if they have never been habilitated (or made fit or capable for society)?”
We must address these issues, stop prison building, redirect the billions wasted on prisons towards probation and other radical alternatives, and reduce sentence lengths, or the devastating cycle of crisis/reform/crisis will only continue and intensify inside.
 
Joe Sim
 
Emeritus professor of criminology, Liverpool John Moores University
Your editorial rightly highlights that the government must prove community supervision works to win support for early releases, while calling for a “person-centred” approach and noting the value of “purposeful activity”.
At LandWorks, a charity providing intensive placements for people on licence or serving community sentences, we see every day that community projects can deliver powerful results. By providing person-centred support wrapped around meaningful, purposeful work and the building of trust, real change can and does happen.
There are many men and women in the system who want to change their lives but face huge hurdles – addiction issues, chaotic home lives, little or no employment history and failed relationships. Providing consistent support can transform lives and reduce the likelihood of further offending. Our independently analysed reoffending rates can attest to that.
The voluntary sector already holds blueprints for breaking the cycles of prison overcrowding, recall and reoffending. A commitment from the government to learn from these existing successful models could transform our criminal justice system and improve public confidence. Rehabilitation and resettlement support makes a huge difference when delivered effectively.
 
Chris Parsons
 
Project director, LandWorks
The debate over early release from prison masks a deeper issue. The underlying problem is a failure to invest properly in early intervention and prevention.
The prison governor Polly Toynbee spoke with was right to highlight the need for early-years support (Britain is addicted to prisons. Our crumbling probation service proves they don’t work, 16 October). School exclusion, episodes of going missing and disruption in childhood are often warning signs of the harm and offending that may follow.
Trusted-adult mentoring can make a decisive difference. Giving a young person someone to turn to in a moment of stress can help prevent that moment from ending with a weapon being picked up.
St Giles and other like-minded organisations provide this support in schools, with positive results: a 21% reduction in violence and a 14% decrease in offending, according to the Youth Endowment Fund.
The same approach can support people serving sentences in the community, helping them to access services that address the root causes of offending while strengthening the effectiveness of community sentences.
But investment alone is not enough. We must also rethink our justice system and ask who genuinely needs to be in prison. Effective community-based solutions already exist; expanding them would tackle the causes of offending, while easing the intense pressure on prisons and probation staff.
 
Tracey Burley
 
Chief executive, St Giles

RJ Mitte’s story offers insight into life with cerebral palsy and mental health issues | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:18:53 UTC
01:18:53 KST

The sudden passing of RJ Mitte has deeply affected many people in the cerebral palsy community (RJ Mitte, actor best known for Breaking Bad, dies aged 34, 12 October). His success challenged assumptions and showed what can be achieved when people are given opportunities and support.
Yet the 165,000 people with cerebral palsy in the UK are too often underestimated. Others frequently decide what we can and cannot do without recognising our abilities, ambitions or potential.
With the right support, we can live fulfilling, successful and meaningful lives. For that reason, the reported circumstances surrounding RJ’s death may surprise some people. Unfortunately, mental health is often overlooked. People with cerebral palsy are more likely to develop mental health conditions and experience poor wellbeing.
We continue to face prejudice, low expectations and barriers that others rarely encounter. We are often excluded from opportunities, left feeling isolated, and denied the support needed to reach our full potential. As a result, many of us are required to build far greater resilience and self-confidence than our able-bodied peers.
People with cerebral palsy can and do thrive. We build careers, contribute to our communities and achieve remarkable things. But success should not depend on resilience alone. We need support to help us get there.
In the UK, many people with cerebral palsy – a lifelong condition – face a cliff edge when they turn 18. The care and support they received as children often disappears as they transition into adulthood.
We deserve lifelong support and an integrated care pathway that recognises the physical and mental health impacts of cerebral palsy, including access to specialist mental health services.
 
Dr Denise Al Mari-de Waal and Aaron Hume
 
UP – The Adult Cerebral Palsy Movement

Looming Medicaid cuts mean that US hospitals must prepare for a perfect storm | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:18:41 UTC
01:18:41 KST

Your report (Millions of Medicaid recipients to face draconian requirements as of 1 January, 13 October) warns that millions may lose Medicaid coverage just as hospitals face rising uncompensated care and growing emergency department demand.
Protecting eligible patients from losing coverage through paperwork must remain the first priority. But hospitals also have a responsibility to prepare operationally for 1 January. They should not compound the coming increase in emergency demand with avoidable peaks they create themselves.
My colleagues and I analysed 1,692,090 hospital admissions across New York State. Emergency admissions varied relatively little across the week, while scheduled admissions were concentrated early in the week. For a representative 500-bed hospital, the resulting pattern was equivalent to needing 103 additional beds on Monday and having 160 fewer patients on Friday. Hospitals cannot schedule heart attacks, strokes or uninsured patients’ emergencies. They can, however, schedule most elective admissions. By distributing them evenly across weekdays, hospitals can reduce competition for the same beds and nurses.
Smoothing scheduled admissions cannot prevent coverage losses or eliminate every cause of emergency department crowding. It can, however, help hospitals absorb the added pressure with less avoidable boarding, delay, and patient harm. Before building more beds or accepting five-hour waits as inevitable, every hospital should determine how much usable capacity its own scheduling practices are wasting.
 
Eugene Litvak
 
President and CEO, Institute for Healthcare Optimization; adjunct professor of operations management, Harvard TH Chan School of Public Health

Fire at Canadian military base kills seven, CBC reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:15:53 UTC
01:15:53 KST

At least 4 killed in major fire at Canadian military base
CALGARY - The Canadian government said on Oct 18 that a weekend fire at an Alberta military base killed at least four people and seriously injured dozens in what Prime Minister Mark Carney called one of the worst peacetime tragedies ever for Canada’s armed forces on home soil.
“The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our Armed Forces whom we have lost,” Carney said on Oct 18, adding that he had ordered flags on federal buildings across the country to be lowered to half-staff to honour the victims.
CBC, the government-funded national broadcaster, previously reported seven deaths at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, citing unnamed sources.
The Canadian authorities have said the situation continues to evolve, and that they will not confirm casualty figures until next of kin have been notified.
CFB Wainwright had 1,310 military and civilian personnel stationed there as of 2021, according to census data. The base, one of Canada’s largest, is about 210km east of Edmonton in Alberta. National Defence Minister David McGuinty said on Oct 18 he would go to the city for briefings on the situation.
The base houses the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which runs training scenarios and exercises for the army. Carney said those affected in the fire on Oct 17 came from military bases across the country.
Few details have been released about the cause of the fire, which took place at about 4pm local time on Oct 17 (6am on Oct 18, Singapore time) in a training area at the base as winds gusted up to 96kmh.
Military and civilian firefighters fought the fire through the night in “some of the worst conditions imaginable,” Carney said.
Canadian officials are expected to address the public from Wainwright, which is located in a largely rural area, later on Oct 18 afternoon.
Air ambulances from Edmonton and Saskatoon, which is about 300km from Wainwright, flew to the military base on Oct 17, Carney said. Patients are being treated in Edmonton, Wainwright, Calgary and Red Deer, he said.
Health staff in Edmonton said a “code orange,” or mass-casualty event, was declared to coordinate the medical response for patients being transported from Wainwright, CBC News reported.
The town of Wainwright, with a population of about 6,600, is just north of the base.
The municipality posted on social media that the fire had crossed the base fence into the nearby district but no evacuation orders had been issued. It said on Oct 18 that the fire is not expected to spread beyond its current boundaries. REUTERS

The peak of this new DANA will come between Sunday and Monday, bringing heavy rain to Ibiza and Formentera and also to Alicante, Murcia and Almeria.
Spain's State Meteorological Agency has issued a special warning for "very heavy and persistent" showers and thunderstorms in Spain's Levante region and parts of the Balearic Islands, from this Sunday and over the next 48 hours.
The combination of the DANA Adam, cut off and isolated from the general atmospheric circulation, together with a very humid easterly flow, will bring widespread rainfall to four provinces (southern Valencia, Alicante, the Region of Murcia and the Almería coastline) and up to three of the Balearic Islands, with a particular impact on the Pityusic Islands (Ibiza and Formentera) but also leaving significant totals in Mallorca.
Aemet's information note refers to the possibility that the showers could become "torrential", but specifies that it is difficult to calculate exactly where in these regions the highest totals will be recorded. At the time of writing, the agency is maintaining red alerts only along the southern Valencian coast and in the north of Alicante and, in addition to the Mediterranean areas mentioned, orange alerts in the Seville lowlands, Ronda and the Sierra de Grazalema in the province of Cádiz.
"The most likely scenario indicates that the highest accumulations may occur along the southern coast of Valencia and around Cape La Nao, where amounts in excess of 60-90 millimetres in one hour and up to 200-300 mm in 12 hours are expected, with the possibility that they may extend to adjacent areas; as well as in the Pityusic Islands, where more than 160 mm could accumulate in 12 hours," the agency's statement says.
"From late in the day, rainfall could also be significant in coastal and pre-coastal areas of Alicante, Murcia and Almería, and across the Balearics spreading to the island of Mallorca, with totals above 50 mm in one hour and 100-140 mm in 12 hours," it adds. The impact on this latter island will be much more pronounced along its southern coast, where the Balearic capital, Palma, is located.
Aemet warns that late on Monday the episode could shift towards the north of the Valencia region and even reach Tarragona, before finally losing strength as Tuesday approaches.

Lavrov’s pivotal Monday visit to Tehran with a mediation flavor
Unknown

Lavrov’s pivotal Monday visit to Tehran with a mediation flavor
Arman-e-Emrooz analyzed Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov’s upcoming visit to Tehran on Monday. Reports suggest that the trip is part of Russia’s ongoing mediation efforts between Iran and the United States. In recent months, Moscow has sought to position itself as a facilitator in reducing tensions between Tehran and Washington.
The timing of the visit coincides with US review of sanctions and measures related to the so-called shadow fleet, highlighting the complexity of the current situation. On one hand, the United States faces domestic pressure to lower energy prices ahead of elections. On the other, Iran is seeking meaningful economic relief. These circumstances have created an environment in which both sides may be inclined toward tactical flexibility. The meeting between Lavrov and Araghchi could represent an important step in that direction, provided both parties enter discussions with a shared understanding of existing realities and align their expectations with practical possibilities. The outcome of the visit could influence developments in the coming weeks.
Khorasan: Trump, the mother of all lies
Khorasan addressed Trump’s recent claim about using the “Mother of All Bombs” in a future strike against Iran. Trump is making such threats at a time when the economic consequences of tensions in the region have significantly increased costs related to energy and essential goods for American families and other countries, putting additional pressure on his administration. The paper described Trump as a gambler seeking a face-saving exit from the Iran war quagmire. After previous efforts, including military deployments to the region and severe economic pressure campaigns that were expected to quickly force Iran into submission, failed to achieve their goals, Trump has now turned to the rhetoric of the “Mother of All Bombs.” The article contends that the purpose of such statements is to create psychological pressure inside Iran and gain leverage in ongoing exchanges of messages between the two sides.
Shargh: An open-ended American policy or an open-ended Iranian one?
Shargh devoted its editorial to decision-making regarding the current conflict. The newspaper argued that decisions made today are linked not only to the future of 90 million Iranians but, in some respects, to global developments as well. The editorial proposed moving beyond the simple pro-war versus pro-peace divide and distinguishing among three separate positions: first, ending the war at any cost; second, negotiating an end to the conflict while preserving core national red lines; and third, continuing resistance until specific political and security conditions are achieved. This conceptual distinction is important for policymaking. A person who favors negotiations does not necessarily support surrender or territorial fragmentation, just as someone who considers resistance necessary is not necessarily indifferent to its human and economic costs. The paper argues that recognizing this distinction prevents an “open-ended American policy” from automatically being interpreted as an “open-ended Iranian policy,” which it describes as the key issue.
Ettelaat: Possibility of a longer conflict process
Ettelaat examined possible future scenarios for the conflict. US demands have shifted from redefining Iran’s regional role to focusing on the nuclear issue and the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, Iran’s demands have reportedly evolved from direct compensation by Washington to a conditional investment fund financed by other parties. Nevertheless, the newspaper argued that two major ambiguities remain unresolved and may even have deepened as a result of the conflict. Continued American pressure is said to intensify divisions among Iranian elites and increase their reluctance to take the first step. Washington, however, may interpret this hesitation as evidence that pressure is working and therefore warrants further action. According to the analysis, diplomacy has reached a deadlock. As US midterm elections draw closer, there remains a possibility that the conflict will add another chapter to the historical memories each side holds of the other, extending a process that has already lasted for more than four decades.
Hamshahri: The impact of war and economic tensions on US elections
Hamshahri focused on concerns influencing American voters. The newspaper argued that economic conditions and the conflict involving Iran have become major public concerns. Rising prices for gasoline, diesel fuel, and essential goods, along with inflation and growing concerns about living costs, have increased pressure on the Trump administration. The paper noted that these concerns are reflected in public opinion polls and political analyses. At the same time, the Iran conflict remains among voters’ principal worries. Hamshahri also linked these concerns to allegations regarding corruption and the financial interests of individuals close to Trump in connection with the conflict. As a result, the newspaper concluded that the economic pressures associated with the conflict cannot be ignored in assessing the US political climate. According to its analysis, these pressures have fueled public dissatisfaction and could present a significant challenge for Republicans in upcoming elections.

18 octobre 2026 - Seul le prononcé fait foi
Allocution du Président de la République.
Mes chers compatriotes, je m'adresse à vous ce soir dans un moment d'une extrême gravité, après ce que nous avons vécu hier dans de nombreuses villes de France, en hexagone comme dans nos Outre-mer. Hier, samedi 17 octobre, des factieux, issus de groupuscules d'ultra-gauche, rejoints par de nombreux délinquants, se sont livrés à une violence débridée dans nos villes. Des commerces ont été pillés, des bâtiments publics, des magasins, des mairies ont été attaqués et pour certains détruits. Plusieurs centaines de policiers et de gendarmes ont été blessés.
En regardant ces images, nous nous sommes tous demandé, qu'ont-ils dans la tête ? Comment des Français peuvent faire cela à la France ? Pourquoi brûler la mairie de Limoges, l'office de tourisme à Lyon, envahir la mairie à Marseille ou attaquer la résidence du préfet à Bordeaux ? Comment peuvent-ils en arriver là ? Rien ne le justifie, rien ne l'explique, rien ne l'excuse.
Nous ressentons tous ce soir de la colère, de la honte. V oir les rues de nos villes ainsi saccagées est insupportable. En votre nom, j'exprime le soutien de la nation à nos forces de l'ordre et à nos forces de sécurité intérieure. Elles ont tenu et ont fait de leur mieux. Nous pensons aux nombreux blessés ainsi qu'à leurs familles. J'exprime aussi notre soutien à tous nos maires et tous nos élus. Je veux dire aussi notre soutien aux nombreux commerçants, artisans, acteurs économiques qui ont subi les conséquences de ces violences et qui sont aujourd'hui dans le désarroi. Certains ont défendu eux-mêmes leurs magasins et leurs vitrines face aux délinquants. Je veux leur dire qu'ils ne seront pas laissés seuls face à ces difficultés. Le gouvernement leur apportera des réponses. Dès demain, le Premier ministre présidera une cellule de crise pour mobiliser les aides les plus rapides possibles et accompagner celles et ceux qui traversent ces heures si difficiles.
Il faut être lucide. Hier, nos forces de l'ordre, malgré leur professionnalisme, ont eu à subir une violence inouïe dans de nombreuses villes à plusieurs reprises. J'ai demandé au gouvernement d'en tirer toutes les leçons en matière de renseignement et d'anticipation et faire en sorte que cela ne puisse pas se reproduire. J'attends des réponses claires et toute la transparence sera faite. C'est ce que j'ai demandé au ministre de l'Intérieur. Les enquêtes seront conduites avec toute la diligence nécessaire le plus rapidement possible et la plus grande fermeté a été demandée au procureur par le garde des Sceaux. Le suivi judiciaire doit être exemplaire. Nos juges rendent la justice en votre nom et ils savent ce que vous attendez. Chaque fois que des infractions sont commises, elles doivent donner lieu à des suites judiciaires appropriées. Ceux qui ont détruit doivent payer. Ceux qui ont pillé doivent rembourser. Ceux qui ont cherché à faire tomber la République auront à en répondre.
Il faut aussi regarder lucidement ce qui s'exprime dans le pays. Hier, plusieurs centaines de milliers de nos compatriotes ont manifesté avec la volonté de porter des revendications légitimes. Jamais nous ne devons confondre ces derniers avec ceux qui ont détruit, cassé, pillé. Ces manifestants ont fait part d'une inquiétude sur le coût de la vie, sur le prix des carburants, qui trouvent leur source dans le conflit lancé dans le golfe Persique, auquel la France n'a pas pris part et dont nous subissons les conséquences. Je comprends parfaitement leur inquiétude. Elle s'exprime d'ailleurs aussi dans plusieurs autres capitales en Europe. A ce titre, j'ai pris plusieurs initiatives au niveau international pour garantir notre carburant, notre gaz et agir sur les marchés de l'énergie. Je poursuivrai ces actions dès demain matin, en allant dans les pays du Golfe pour sécuriser nos approvisionnements. Le Premier ministre et le gouvernement ont également pris des décisions en lien avec les distributeurs de carburant pour que ces efforts se répercutent concrètement sur les prix. Le gouvernement fait le maximum pour que cette question essentielle du pouvoir d'achat soit traitée. Je sais que les Français attendent des résultats concrets et nous continuerons à agir.
Depuis plusieurs semaines aussi, notre jeunesse exprime une angoisse profonde dans les lycées comme dans les universités. Une inquiétude sur l'avenir, sur les conditions de vie et d'études, sur la capacité à s'orienter, à se projeter, à trouver sa place dans la société. L'idée qu'il n'y aurait pas de futur désirable en quelque sorte. Je comprends nos lycéens et nos étudiants. Ils sont au cœur de mon engagement politique depuis plus de dix ans. Leur parole doit être entendue, sans a priori et sans minimiser les difficultés. Le travail est déjà engagé par le gouvernement. Le ministre de l'Education nationale s’est mobilisé et a mis en place une plateforme qui a recueilli plus de 100 000 contributions qui s'ajoutent aux réunions tenues au niveau des académies et des lycées. Cela nous permettra de construire avec notre jeunesse des réponses adaptées.
Notre responsabilité est donc double. Entendre la colère et agir sur ses causes et faire respecter fermement l'ordre républicain. Nous ne devons ni confondre les revendications légitimes avec les violences, ni laisser les violences empêcher que ces revendications soient entendues. C'est pourquoi je veux ce soir donner une méthode claire. Premièrement, dans le contexte actuel, les préfets prendront les décisions en lien avec les maires pour protéger nos villes, nos bâtiments publics et nos commerces, y compris en allant jusqu'à interdire quand il le faut certains rassemblements et en prenant toute action nécessaire. Deuxièmement, j'appelle l'ensemble des partis politiques, des organisations professionnelles et syndicales à condamner sans ambiguïté toutes les violences et à appeler au calme. Chacun doit prendre ses responsabilités. Le pays a besoin d'ordre, d'apaisement et pas d'une escalade. Le Premier ministre réunira dans les prochains jours ces formations afin d'obtenir des positions claires et publiques. Troisièmement, Nous ne pouvons pas demander à notre jeunesse de croire en l'avenir sans lui donner la possibilité de construire les réponses et d'être autour de la table. Oui, il nous faut nous asseoir autour de la table et construire ensemble des solutions. Élèves, étudiants, enseignants, représentants des organisations patronales et syndicales, collectivités territoriales, parlementaires travailleront dès cette semaine avec le gouvernement à des propositions concrètes. Le Premier ministre les réunira dans les prochains jours à cet effet. Je veux être ici très clair, À l'égard des casseurs et de tous ceux qui se livrent à des violences, nous serons intraitables. L'écoute et le dialogue ne signifient ni la faiblesse, ni l'impunité.
Mes chers compatriotes, nous sommes à six mois de notre élection présidentielle. À six mois. Et donc tous ceux qui aujourd'hui vous expliquent que l'urgence est d'aller dans la rue, de manifester, de créer le désordre, n'ont qu'un but. Abîmer la République et voler le débat. Les choix d'avenir que vous aurez, que nous aurons à faire dans six mois, ils sont essentiels. La France est une grande force démocratique. Elle mérite ces débats. Ils doivent se faire dans les réunions publiques. Ils doivent se faire avec les partis, et non pas dans la rue par la violence. Ils doivent se faire dans les journaux, sur les plateaux de télévision, dans les rassemblements pacifiques, où l'on parle et l'on s'explique dans le respect, jamais dans le désordre et dans la casse. Notre pays mérite une belle élection présidentielle dans six mois. C'est aussi maintenant qu'elle se joue, par l'esprit de responsabilité. Oui au dialogue, oui à la réponse concrète de court terme et à la préparation des décisions futures. Mais non toujours à la violence quelle qu'elle soit. Nous avons besoin d'unité, de calme et de respect.
Vive la République et vive la France.

Belarus Could Enter War Against Ukraine by Deploying Ballistic Missiles at Russia’s Request, Zelenskyy Says
Russia is considering deploying additional ballistic missile systems in Belarus, potentially expanding its ability to strike western Ukraine, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned on October 17.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Zelenskyy’s remarks to journalists on October 17, Moscow is seeking Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko’s cooperation to expand its military infrastructure in the country and support further attacks against Ukraine.
The Ukrainian president said Russia has already positioned communications relay equipment in Belarus to facilitate drone operations, but Moscow appears interested in expanding its capabilities beyond unmanned aerial systems.
Zelenskyy warned that deploying ballistic missiles on Belarusian territory would create an additional threat to Ukraine’s western regions, potentially allowing Russian forces to launch attacks from another direction.
He also emphasized that such a move would further involve Belarus in Russia’s full-scale invasion, exposing the country to additional security risks.
The president said Ukraine intends to strengthen its air defenses in response to the evolving threat. This includes increasing production of turret-mounted defensive systems and distributing them across regions based on the intensity of Russian attacks.
Belarus has played a supporting role in Russia’s invasion since February 2022, when Russian troops used its territory to launch an offensive toward Kyiv. Moscow has also used Belarusian airfields, military facilities, and airspace to support operations against Ukraine.
Although Belarusian armed forces have not formally entered the fighting as a separate combat force, the Lukashenko government continues to provide Russia with logistical support, access to infrastructure, and military-industrial assistance.
Earlier, on October 16, Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko ordered the creation of “people’s militia” units in every village council across the country, expanding local defense structures amid growing concerns over Belarus’s potential deeper involvement in Russia’s war against Ukraine.
