Trump endorses Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of reelection bid
President Trump on Sunday endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection, saying on social media that he "has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran."
This is a coveted boost for Netanyahu because of Mr. Trump's popularity in Israel but one that the U.S. leader withheld for months as their strategies in the Middle East diverged.
Netanyahu's government, the most nationalist and far-right in Israel's history, faces domestic criticism over security failures and international criticism over the treatment of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza. Some of the government's senior officials are settlers themselves.
"Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself. Despite all of that, he has endured and, in fact, he has thrived!" Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social.
Netanyahu, on X, thanked Mr. Trump for his "tremendous support and the joint work."
"Together we will complete the mission!" he added.
Netanyahu's Likud Party attached to the statement a 35-second video showing clips of the two leaders together and Mr. Trump praising the prime minister.
In a separate video message shared on social media, Netanyahu said he was "honored and humbled" by Mr. Trump's endorsement and that there has "never been a greater friend of Israel in the White House."
In the video, he also sent a message to the American people about the importance of not letting Iran have a nuclear weapon.
"If you're worried about today's gas prices, think of what will happen if Iran gets nuclear weapons — something that Donald Trump and I will never allow," Netanyahu said. "And when that happens, when that regime disappears, gas prices will go down, and how? But only under Trump."

"If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Mr. Trump said.
The U.S. leader and Netanyahu have been close allies and seem more aligned than ever in the wake of the joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran's nuclear facilities in 2025. But over the course of the nearly eight-month war with Iran this year, they have had disagreements.
Israelis are set to vote on Oct. 27, which will be the first national elections since the 2023 Hamas attack on Israel.

Upgraded military capabilities have changed adversaries’ calculations: minister

Upgraded military capabilities have changed adversaries’ calculations: minister
TEHRAN — Iran’s newly appointed Defense Minister Mehrdad Akhlaghi Ketabchi says the country has upgraded and modernized its defense capabilities since the 12-day war imposed on Iran by the United States and Israel, changing adversaries’ military calculations and raising doubts about the prospects of further confrontation.
Addressing an open session of the Iranian Parliament on Sunday, after lawmakers approved his appointment as minister of defense and armed forces logistics, Akhlaghi said Iran had strengthened its defensive preparedness in response to the conflict, creating new uncertainties for those considering further military action against the country.
“Following the 12-day war waged jointly by the United States and Israel against Iran, our defensive capabilities have been upgraded in ways that have changed the enemy’s assessments and calculations and created deep doubts among our adversaries about continuing the war,” he said.
 
Akhlaghi also warned US President Donald Trump against translating military threats into action, saying Iran had put the necessary countermeasures in place.
“We have taken all necessary measures to counter the ‘Mother of All Bombs’ and are confident in our preparations. We are carrying out our duties with complete confidence,” he said, referring to the US president’s threats involving the powerful conventional bomb.
Warning of the potential consequences for US forces, the defense minister said Washington should consider the risks of escalating a confrontation with Iran.
“If he drops a bomb, he should consider how many of his troops might have to be carried out in body bags,” Akhlaghi said. “If he follows through on his threats, he will have to face the dire consequences.”
Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of the parliamentary session, he reiterated that Iran had devised the measures needed to respond to potential threats and said Trump should consider how to withdraw US forces from the region safely.
 
“If his slogans turn into action, he will have to suffer the consequences,” he said.
Strategic deterrence in a changing threat environment
Ketabchi argued that the strategic environment confronting Iran was undergoing fundamental changes, encompassing the nature of threats, the logic of military power, technological developments and the regional security order.
He described these shifts as contributing to a strategic deadlock for Iran’s adversaries, emphasizing that defensive strength depended not only on operational capabilities but also on an accurate understanding of the wider strategic environment.
The defense minister also highlighted the increasingly hybrid nature of modern warfare, in which conventional military operations are combined with economic sanctions, cyber operations, disruptions to supply chains, information warfare and restrictions on access to advanced technologies.
Such a threat environment, he said, requires a comprehensive defense strategy capable of addressing multiple forms of pressure simultaneously rather than relying exclusively on conventional military strength.
His remarks underscore the importance Tehran places on modernizing its defense capabilities while adapting to technological advances and evolving methods of military and economic confrontation.
Parliament approves new defense minister
Iranian lawmakers approved Akhlaghi’s appointment on Sunday following a review of his qualifications and policy plans. He was nominated by President Masoud Pezeshkian on October 5, 2026.
According to the vote announced in parliament, 237 lawmakers voted in favor of his appointment, while 15 opposed it, out of 277 members present.
He succeeds Major General Aziz Nasirzadeh, the previous defense minister, who was martyred during criminal attacks by the United States and the Zionist regime.
Born in 1958 in the northern Iranian city of Rasht, Akhlaghi has held senior positions in the country’s defense industries, including heading the Shahid Bakeri Industrial Group and serving as managing director of the Aerospace Industries Organization.
He takes over the Ministry of Defense and Armed Forces Logistics following the tenure of Brigadier General Majid Ibn al-Reza, who served as acting defense minister after the killing of his predecessor, Major General Aziz Nasirzadeh, in US-Israeli attacks on Tehran on February 28, 2026.
His appointment comes as Iran continues to prioritize the modernization of its defense infrastructure and preparedness to respond to potential military threats, with the new minister placing deterrence, technological adaptation, and readiness across multiple domains at the center of his stated approach.

Italy: Clashes erupt at cost-of-living protests
October 18, 2026
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni on Sunday condemned rioting during cost-of-living protests, expressing solidarity with police after clashes in several cities.
The violence broke out during cost-of-living demonstrations on Saturday, leaving at least four police officers and 20 demonstrators injured in Milan.
The unrest comes amid anger over high prices, stagnant real wages and a shortage of affordable housing in major cities.
What happened during the protests?
In Milan, black-clad, masked youths threw fireworks and bottles at police and erected barricades in the central Piazza Duomo, the Italian news agency ANSA reported.
Police initially withdrew to await reinforcements and later used tear gas to clear the square. Some 50 young people were arrested, about half of them minors, according to ANSA.
Clashes also broke out in Turin, Bologna and Bergamo. Police in Bologna used water cannon and made four arrests, all minors, with seven people reported to prosecutors.
How did Italy's PM Meloni respond?
Meloni expressed solidarity with police on Sunday, condemning criminals who she said exploited demonstrations to provoke confrontations and "sow chaos."
"Demonstrating is a right, but setting our cities on fire is not," she said.
Milan Mayor Giuseppe Sala also condemned the violence while acknowledging the grievances behind the demonstrations.
"The reasons for the protest were understandable. The violence against police and the serious damage to the city, however, cannot be justified," he said.
Why were people demonstrating?
Protesters rallied against high living costs and low wages, with households facing expensive fuel and difficulty finding affordable housing.
In Rome, thousands joined a demonstration organized by the Italian General Confederation of Labour (CGIL). Its leader, Maurizio Landini, announced a general strike for November 20.
The violence came as similar demonstrations in France descended into rioting, arson and looting, with more than 1,800 people arrested nationwide.

Why Ukraine’s freedom-loving Cossacks chose the Russian tsar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:00:57 UTC
01:00:57 KST

Why Ukraine’s freedom-loving Cossacks chose the Russian tsar
On January 8, 1654, drums resounded in the town square of Pereiaslav. Cossacks, townsfolk, and commanders formed a large circle and Hetman Bogdan Khmelnitsky stepped into the center. This was a man who had seen it all: six years of war, stunning victories and crushing defeats, burned cities and villages, and the betrayal of allies. On that day, he offered the people a choice that would shape their future.
He told the people that four figures could potentially rule over them. The first option was the Turkish Sultan – a Muslim who was known to oppress Orthodox Christians in Greece. Then, there was the Crimean Khan – also a Muslim who couldn’t really be trusted since he often betrayed allies. The Polish king was not a viable option, since everyone remembered how the Polish lords had oppressed the population. And finally, there was a fourth option: the Tsar of the East, a fellow Orthodox Christian.
The people responded with a cry, “We want to serve the Eastern Orthodox Tsar!”
The choice between the West and Russia is often considered a recent phenomenon. Yet for the inhabitants of Ukraine, this choice first presented itself 400 years ago – and it was made not by politicians behind closed doors, but by the public in the middle of a town square. Why did these free Cossacks, accustomed to electing their own hetmans and exercising self-governance, choose to serve the Russian tsars? And why did many Cossacks remain loyal to Russia time and again, even when their hetmans betrayed their oath to the tsar?
This week, the Day of the Ukrainian Cossacks was observed, and RT remembers how they first made the choice to join Russia.
17th-century-style Eurointegration
By the mid-17th century, much of present-day Ukraine was under the control of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. And this was far from an appealing image.
The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth was governed by the Polish Catholic nobility, many of whom viewed the local Orthodox population as second-class citizens. They referred to Orthodox Ukrainians as ‘bydlo’ (cattle), stripping them of all rights.
The Orthodox population was barred from professional guilds and faced restrictions in holding municipal offices. Peasants were effectively enslaved, while many Orthodox churches and monasteries were seized and shut down. Priests and monks suffered persecution, humiliation, and violence.
The common people lost many of their defenders. Many noble Orthodox families converted to Catholicism en masse – not out of conviction, but to ‘become Polish’. For example, Ieremiah Vishnevetsky, a man from an Orthodox family whose ‘conversion’ was driven by a desire for status and career advancement, became one of the primary oppressors and tormentors of the Orthodox people.
At the same time, the southern territories of what is now Ukraine faced regular raids by the Crimean Tatars, who pillaged border settlements, capturing people and enslaving them. Fleeing from the oppressive rule of the Polish on one side and seeking protection from the constant invasions of the Tatars on the other, Ukraine’s Orthodox population retreated into the so-called Wild Field. In the expansive, fertile steppes stretching from the Dniester to the Don rivers, there was no authority to govern them. These people established their own communities and formed self-defense groups; they became known as Cossacks. Living on the frontier, in conditions far harsher than those of America’s Wild West, they always had their weapons at hand.
The Cossacks launched campaigns against the Crimean Khanate and the Ottoman Empire, but their primary focus was on preserving their Orthodox faith and resisting Polish oppression. Throughout the first half of the 17th century, uprisings frequently erupted across Ukraine, but due to the Cossacks’ poor organization and the superior military training of the Poles, these rebellions were consistently crushed with brutal force.
By 1648, it seemed that the Poles had eradicated all the rebellious Cossacks and subjugated the populace. For the Polish, it seemed like there was nothing more to worry about. However, this was a grave mistake.
Unity of faith
Against the background of the horrifying national and religious oppression raging in Ukraine, the neighboring Orthodox Russian Tsardom presented a stark contrast. At the beginning of the 17th century, Russia had endured a brutal civil war and foreign intervention known as the Time of Troubles. Nevertheless, it had managed to repel external foes and was steadily regaining its strength. This powerful, centralized Orthodox state naturally drew the attention of the Cossacks.
During this period, identity was largely defined by faith, and the terms ‘Orthodox’ and ‘Russian’ were nearly interchangeable. At that time, there was no clear distinction between Russians and Ukrainians; both identified as Russian, viewing themselves as heirs to the medieval state of Kievan Rus’.
While people in the Russian Tsardom and modern-day Ukraine had their linguistic and regional differences, they had a lot more in common with each other than with the Poles. National and religious identities were intertwined, which is why Cossack leader Bogdan Khmelnitsky, in his speech at the Pereiaslav Council emphasized this unity by saying, “We share the same faith.”
However, a shared faith and identity didn’t automatically translate into political decisions. Whenever uprisings happened, Cossack delegations went to Moscow seeking assistance. In 1620, Cossack Hetman Pyotr Sagaidachny wrote to Tsar Mikhail Fyodorovich, expressing the Cossacks’ readiness to serve him. In 1624, Metropolitan Iov Boretsky of Kiev directly appealed to the Russian tsar, asking him to protect the “brotherly people” and to incorporate Malorossiya (literally, Little Russia – one of Ukraine’s historical names) into Russia. But at the beginning of the 17th century, Russia was just recovering from the turmoil of the Time of Troubles and was not prepared for a new war with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, so it responded to these appeals with caution.
Nonetheless, this did not deter the people of modern-day Ukraine. In the 1630s, thousands of Cossacks migrated to the Russian Tsardom, settling along its southern borders. After the defeat of the 1638 uprising, Hetman Yakov Ostrianin led 1,000 Cossacks and their families into Russia. He settled in Chuguev (present-day Kharkov region), where the tsarist government was constructing a new fortress, and helped repel Tatar raids on the southern frontiers alongside Russian troops. Thus, the historical region known as Slobozhanshchina emerged, which encompassed the modern-day Ukrainian cities of Sumy, Kharkov, Izium, and others. Cossacks who served the Tsar settled there, living next to the Russian forces that were stationed in the area.
Ultimately, the unity between the Russian Tsardom and Orthodox Ukrainians was sealed by Bogdan Khmelnitsky.
Free choice
Bogdan Khmelnitsky knew from personal experience the futility of seeking peaceful and respectful relations with the Poles. By age 50, he had a successful military career, numerous campaigns, and years of loyal service to the Polish king behind his back. In 1648, he held the rank of Cossack hundredman (similar to a company commander) in Chigirin. However, taking advantage of Khmelnitsky’s absence, the nobleman Chaplinsky seized his family estate, kidnapped his wife, and assaulted (or, according to some reports, killed) his son. When Khmelnitsky sought justice in the Polish court, he was laughed at. From then on, Khmelnitsky sought both personal and national revenge.
Khmelnitsky sparked a Cossack uprising that quickly gained popular support. As a gifted military leader, he won several battles, decimating the Polish army in Ukraine and capturing its commanders. Following initial victories in the summer of 1648, Khmelnitsky reached out to Tsar Alexei Mikhailovich of Russia, requesting that the Cossacks and their lands be placed “under the tsar’s high hand.” However, accepting the Cossacks as subjects meant Russia would have to engage in war with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, something Moscow wasn’t prepared for at that time.
The next five years of war were incredibly tough for the Cossacks: victories were interspersed with defeats, and their allies – the Crimean Tatars – often betrayed them. The conflict devastated fertile lands and claimed an increasing number of lives. The Cossacks realized that alone, they wouldn’t be able to stand up to the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, then the strongest player in the region. If they were defeated, the Polish nobles would return to Ukraine and exact revenge. Therefore, Khmelnitsky continued his diplomatic outreach to Moscow.
Eventually, the Russian Tsardom recognized that it was ready for a big war. In late 1653, the Zemsky Sobor, a representative assembly, decided to accept the Zaporozhian Host under the “high hand” of the tsar. A large embassy headed by Boyar Vasily Buturlin was dispatched to Ukraine.
In January 1654, a Cossack council convened in Pereiaslav. It was attended by Ukraine’s leaders of the time: Khmelnitsky himself, renowned commanders, colonels, judges, and representatives from 14 of the 17 Cossack regiments.
According to Cossack tradition, however, such a pivotal decision could not rest solely with the elites. So, Khmelnitsky and his comrades went to the town square and addressed the people, who eagerly embraced the news, shouting their desire to be ruled by the “Eastern Orthodox tsar.” The Cossack commanders unanimously agreed to ally with Russia and accepted the Russian tsar as their sovereign.
Following this, Cossack and Russian diplomats traveled throughout Ukraine, and in just the first two months of 1654, over 120,000 people pledged allegiance to the Russian tsar in 183 towns and settlements – a staggering figure considering the logistical challenges of the era. Accounts of those who witnessed these events, both on the Russian and Ukrainian side, reveal that in most cases, Cossacks, townsfolk, and peasants enthusiastically swore loyalty to the Russian tsar, with refusals being exceedingly rare.
The formal incorporation of the Cossack Hetmanate into the Russian Tsardom was sealed by the March Articles of 1654. The Zaporozhian Host found itself under a kind of protectorate of the Russian Tsardom, while enjoying extensive internal freedom. The agreement, ratified by Tsar Alexei Mikhailovich, affirmed the election of the Hetman and Cossack elders, protected the rights and liberties of the Cossacks, townspeople, and Orthodox clergy, ensured the autonomy of local courts and the freedom of tax collection, and allowed the Hetman to establish diplomatic relations with other peoples, except for Poland and the Ottoman Empire. In return, the Russian Tsardom guaranteed military protection for the Cossacks and committed to fighting against the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.
At that time, Ukraine enjoyed a remarkably privileged position. Just a short while before, Polish nobles had treated the Cossacks as “cattle,” humiliating and oppressing them. Now, however, the Cossacks had freedom and were backed by the tsar’s mighty army.
But comfort can breed complacency, and some Cossack leaders came to believe that their oaths to the Russian tsar didn’t amount to much.
The Ruin
Three years after the Pereiaslav Council, Khmelnitsky died, and Ivan Vygovsky took over. A man of incredibly flexible views, he initially built his career in the service of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth but later switched sides to become the personal secretary of Bogdan Khmelnitsky.
Vygovsky was a key advocate for joining Russia, yet upon becoming hetman, he reversed his stance and forgot his oath of loyalty to Moscow. Just a year after taking power in 1658, he signed the Treaty of Hadiach with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, which aimed to reincorporate Ukrainian lands into Poland.
However, it soon became apparent that the decision of 1654 wasn’t made solely by the Cossack leadership. Early on, at the stage of negotiations with Poland, figures like Colonel Martyn Pushkar and Zaporozhian Otaman Yakov Barabash opposed the decision to defect to the Polish side and betray their Orthodox brethren. Many Cossacks and townsfolk rallied behind them. For these individuals, returning to Polish rule meant a return to oppression and humiliation. Vygovsky managed to suppress this particular uprising, and commanders loyal to Russia were killed.
After Vygovsky’s open betrayal, however, many prominent Cossack leaders – including those now celebrated as Ukrainian national heroes, such as Ivan Bogun and Ivan Sirko – rose against him. For them, as for the hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians at the time, treason against the Russian tsar and submission to the Polish were intolerable.
Consequently, the Cossacks united with Russian forces against the traitors. Notably, in 1658, Kiev was defended from Vygovsky’s troops by the combined forces of Tsarist voivode Vasily Sheremetev and Kiev colonel Vasily Dvoretsky. As the conflict escalated, not only Cossacks but even townspeople and ordinary peasants turned against Vygovsky’s allies. Those who had betrayed their oath to the tsar were often punished or killed by the people.
Pro-Russian Cossacks and Tsarist troops united to inflict a series of defeats upon Vygovsky; he lost power and fled to Poland, where he was ultimately executed without trial, since he was no longer needed. This stands in stark contrast to Dvoretsky, whose descendants remained influential members of the local Malorossian elite until 1917.
This story illustrated that Russia’s influence in Ukraine rested not on fleeting decisions made by individual commanders but on the overwhelming support of the populace. However, at that point, Ukraine plunged into decades of civil strife.
In 1659, Yuriy Khmelnitsky, the son of Bogdan Khmelnitsky, became hetman and signed new agreements with Russia. By then, Russia had begun to grasp the unique political culture of the Ukrainian elites and started to curb Cossack independence. Under the new terms, electing a hetman or making international decisions required the tsar’s approval, and the presence of Russian garrisons increased in Ukrainian cities.
However, soon after signing the treaty with Moscow, Yuriy Khmelnitsky launched a war against the Poles. Having lost this war, he ended up signing another agreement with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.
Yet another Cossack hetman had ‘outplayed’ himself, negotiating worse terms with the Poles than with the Russians. As a result, Cossack autonomy was curbed and they were obligated to fight alongside the Poles against the Russian Tsardom.
The Cossack regiments stationed on the eastern bank of the Dnieper river rejected this betrayal, leading to a de facto split of Ukraine into Left and Right Banks. This marked the beginning of Ukraine’s own ‘game of thrones’. Subsequent hetmans and atamans followed a familiar pattern: from declarations of loyalty to Russia to restrictions on Cossack autonomy; from formal allegiance to betrayal and eventual death or exile.
Russia managed to put an end to this chaotic cycle of conflict only by signing the Truce of Andrusovo with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1667, which divided Ukraine along the Dnieper River.
Mazepa’s betrayal and the people’s loyalty
One of the most dramatic tests of the Cossacks’ loyalty to Russia unfolded during the Great Northern War. Russia was fighting Sweden for access to the Baltic Sea, as Sweden was the dominant power in Northern Europe at the time. In the early years, the war proved challenging for Russia, prompting Hetman Ivan Mazepa, who had been in power for over 20 years, to betray his old ally, Tsar Peter the Great, and ally himself with Swedish King Charles XII (whom he believed would emerge as the victor).
In the summer of 1708, General Judge Vasily Kochubey and Colonel Ivan Iskra reported Mazepa’s secret contacts with the Swedes. However, Peter the Great trusted his old friend so much that he dismissed their warnings. Kochubey and Iskra were executed, but once Mazepa’s treachery came to light, they were posthumously rehabilitated; the Kochubey family later received a noble title and several military and state leaders of the Russian Empire were descended from it.
In late autumn 1708, Mazepa finally defected to Charles XII’s side. Notably, only a few thousand people followed him. When it became clear that this was not merely a campaign but outright betrayal, the ranks of Mazepa’s supporters dwindled even further.
The vast majority of Cossacks remained loyal to Russia. They fought alongside Russian troops against the Swedes. Being Orthodox Christians, they could not fathom the idea of siding with the enemies who were, moreover, Protestants. Similarly, ordinary townspeople and peasants stayed true to Russia.
In his first address to the Cossacks, the new hetman Ivan Skoropadsky asserted that “All of Ukraine must be loyal to Moscow, and must not be seduced by the friendship of the Swedes, who, aside from being entirely foreign to Ukraine, are not even neighbors.”
Modern Ukrainian historians tend to romanticize Mazepa as a champion of freedom and independence, but this portrayal is misleading. Mazepa and his circle were simply looking for a new master, driven by a false sense of Russia’s vulnerability. In reality, the people of Ukraine remained steadfastly loyal to Russia and the Orthodox Tsar, with Cossack regiments fighting side by side with tsarist forces during the legendary Battle of Poltava.
From maces to ministerial positions
Following Mazepa’s betrayal, Russia systematically curtailed Cossack autonomy. Despite the unwavering loyalty of the vast majority of Cossacks, the treachery of their leaders became increasingly audacious. In 1722, Peter the Great established the Collegium of Little Russia, essentially a ministry for Ukrainian affairs.
The position of hetman was alternately abolished and reinstated, but the Cossacks’ autonomy was steadily curbed. Those who failed to grasp that times had changed, like the appointed hetman Pavel Polubotok, found themselves imprisoned in the Peter and Paul Fortress.
Concurrently, another trend emerged. Cossack leaders began integrating into the imperial elite, a shift that, for many of them, proved more beneficial than the semblance of freedom.
Alexei Razumovsky, the son of a humble Cossack, arrived in St. Petersburg as a singer in the court chapel and eventually became the favorite (and according to some accounts, the secret husband) of Empress Elizabeth. His brother, Kirill, headed the Russian Academy of Sciences and served as the last hetman. Alexander Bezborodko, the son of a general scribe, rose to become Chancellor of the Russian Empire. Pyotr Zavadovsky became the first Minister of Public Education in Russia. Victor Kochubey, a descendant of the executed judge, served as Minister of Internal Affairs and Chairman of the State Council of the Russian Empire. The list of the descendants of the Cossacks who achieved high office in the Russian Empire goes on and on.
The era of the Cossacks eventually faded into history.
In 1764, Razumovsky laid down his mace. Cossack regiments were transformed into regular hussar and carabiner regiments. The Charter of 1785 equalized the rights of Cossack leaders with those of the Russian nobility.
A century and a half earlier, in 1648, the Cossacks had launched a rebellion against the Poles, fighting for their own rights, laws, and the Orthodox faith. In 1654, they pledged allegiance to the Russian Tsar in Pereiaslav. Later on, many events unfolded: the Cossacks oscillated between Poland, Turkey, and Sweden, yet the majority remained loyal to Russia.
There were numerous reasons for this loyalty. A shared identity and faith made rapprochement with Moscow natural; fear of foreign lords, khans, and sultans united the Cossacks under Russian banners. Moreover, social interests and career aspirations made serving the empire appealing. Some were driven by sincere motives; others acted out of fear or personal gain.
Ultimately, those who remained loyal to the Orthodox Russian Tsar emerged as the winners, exchanging their former unprivileged status for the right to build the empire alongside the Russians.

Does medical transition help young transgender people’s mental health? A Finnish study sparks a battle over the answer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:00:49 UTC
01:00:49 KST

A nationwide study from Finland indicates that adolescents and young adults referred to specialized gender identity services were far more likely than their peers to receive specialist psychiatric care, both before and after their first clinic visit. The research, published in Acta Paediatrica, found that rates of specialist psychiatric care did not decline among those who went on to receive hormones or surgery, and that in this group they rose sharply from pre-referral levels. The study cannot show whether the treatments caused that rise, but it has quickly become a flashpoint in one of medicine’s most heated debates.
Gender dysphoria is a condition characterized by psychological distress or impaired daily functioning resulting from a mismatch between a person’s biological sex and their internal sense of gender. To alleviate this distress, individuals often seek medical gender reassignment, which involves cross-sex hormone therapies and surgeries designed to align their physical bodies with their experienced gender. Over the past 15 years, clinics across the Western world have seen a sharp rise in the number of teenagers and young adults seeking these evaluations, accompanied by a demographic shift toward adolescents who are biologically female.
Young people seeking gender care frequently experience co-occurring mental health difficulties, particularly depression and anxiety. For example, a 2018 study of children and adolescents in the United States found that transgender and gender-nonconforming youth were several times more likely to have a recorded psychiatric diagnosis or hospital admission than their cisgender peers in the months before their gender identity was first documented in their medical records.
Proponents of early medical intervention suggest that providing hormones and surgery during adolescence can improve mental health by easing gender dysphoria. Supporting this view, a 2023 observational study of transgender youth in the United States reported improvements in life satisfaction and reductions in depression and anxiety symptoms over two years of hormone therapy.
Other analyses, however, indicate that the long-term mental health outcomes of medical transition remain uncertain. Many existing studies lack comparison groups from the general population, rely on small sample sizes, or track patients for only brief periods. In a 2023 study using the same Finnish registry data, members of the current research team observed that the psychiatric care rates of people seeking gender care had grown substantially alongside the post-2010 surge in referrals.
To build on that work, study lead author Sami-Matti Ruuska, a medical doctor and specialist in adolescent psychiatry at Tampere University and the University of Eastern Finland, and his colleagues examined nationwide health records to see how rates of specialist psychiatric care develop over time among young people who undergo medical gender reassignment compared to those who do not, and whether these patterns differ by sex.
“There is a dearth of high-quality research in pediatric gender medicine,” Ruuska told PsyPost. “Previous studies suffer from, for example, small sample sizes, short follow-up times, and lack of control groups. These things leave room for chance variation, i.e., observed findings can be due only to chance, not a real effect or phenomenon.”
“At the same time, medical gender reassignment (hormonal and surgical treatments) for youth suffering from gender dysphoria is oftentimes suggested to be beneficial, even vital, for their mental wellbeing, and has been quickly adopted as the so-called golden standard treatment for gender dysphoria in adolescence,” Ruuska explained.
“To adopt so widely something with so little high-quality evidence could be considered an outlier in medicine. Medical gender reassignment also carries health risks regarding, for example, fertility, bone density, surgical complications, and even possibly neurocognition. For these reasons it is important to conduct high-quality research on the topic.”
The researchers analyzed comprehensive national registry data covering every resident in Finland. In Finland, gender identity assessments that can lead to medical reassignment are centralized at two university hospitals. The team identified all 2,083 individuals under the age of 23 who attended these specialized clinics between 1996 and 2019, who had an average age of 18.5 years at their first visit; more than half were already 18 or older. Each clinic patient was matched by birth year and birth municipality with eight individuals from the general population, four males and four females, resulting in a control group of 16,643 peers.
The authors tracked every participant from their initial gender clinic appointment, or the corresponding date for matched controls, until death or June 2022, yielding an average follow-up period of roughly 5.5 years and a maximum of 25 years. By linking unique personal identification numbers across national databases, the team gathered records on prescription hormone purchases, gender-affirming surgeries, and visits to specialist-level psychiatric services. According to the authors, specialist psychiatric care in Finland requires an accepted medical referral and is reserved for severe disorders rather than mild distress.
The main outcome was whether a person had any specialist psychiatric contact in a given period, and when measuring care after the initial gender clinic visit, the researchers excluded routine assessment appointments and focused on treatment occurring two or more years later.
Among the 2,083 young people referred to the gender clinics, 1,602 were biological females seeking masculinizing transitions, and 481 were biological males seeking feminizing transitions. Overall, 38.2 percent (796 individuals) went on to receive medical gender reassignment through hormones, surgery, or both. Before ever contacting the gender clinics, 45.7 percent of the gender-referred group had already received specialist-level psychiatric treatment, compared to 15.0 percent of the matched control group.
This disparity widened when looking at the years following the initial clinic appointment. Two or more years after their first visit, 61.7 percent of the gender-referred youth received specialist psychiatric care, while the rate among the control group remained steady at 14.6 percent. The intensity of care was also much higher among the gender-referred group: 27.6 percent had more than 100 lifetime psychiatric contacts, compared to 4.3 percent of controls.
When the researchers split the data by time period to examine generational shifts, they found a pronounced change in pre-referral care after 2010, coinciding with the rapid rise in clinic referrals. Among young people referred between 1996 and 2010, 23.7 percent had received specialist psychiatric care prior to their gender clinic visit, compared to 11.8 percent of controls, a difference that did not meet the study’s strict threshold for statistical significance.
For those referred between 2011 and 2019, however, the proportion with prior psychiatric treatment doubled to 47.9 percent, compared to 15.3 percent of controls. By two or more years after their first visit, though, the two groups looked similar: 66.1 percent of the earlier group and 61.3 percent of the later group had received specialist psychiatric care.
The researchers next examined trajectories based on whether patients underwent medical gender reassignment. Before visiting the gender clinic, individuals who eventually received medical reassignment had much lower rates of prior psychiatric treatment than those who did not proceed with medical transition. Specifically, 9.8 percent of biological males who later underwent feminizing reassignment and 21.6 percent of biological females who later underwent masculinizing reassignment had prior psychiatric care, compared to 53.1 percent and 65.0 percent of their counterparts who did not medically transition. The authors noted that this baseline difference likely reflects clinical screening, as severe, unstable psychiatric illness serves as a reason to delay or withhold medical transition in Finland.
Despite starting with lower rates of prior psychiatric care, the young people who underwent medical gender reassignment experienced sharp increases in specialist psychiatric care two or more years after their initial clinic contact. Among those who underwent feminizing reassignment, the proportion receiving specialist psychiatric treatment rose from 9.8 percent before the clinic visit to 60.7 percent during follow-up, and among those who underwent masculinizing reassignment, the rate increased from 21.6 percent to 54.5 percent.
During follow-up, rates were broadly similar across all four gender-referred groups, ranging from about 55 to 67 percent. By contrast, psychiatric care rates remained relatively stable for controls and showed only slight increases from baseline for gender-referred youth who did not medically transition.
To account for these baseline differences, the researchers used statistical models that controlled for birth year, the year of the initial clinic visit, and whether the person had received psychiatric treatment beforehand. These models estimate hazard ratios, which compare how often an event occurs in one group versus another over time. Without any statistical adjustments, the gender-referred youth who did not receive medical treatment had the highest risk of later specialist care. Once prior psychiatric treatment was taken into account, all four gender-referred groups had similarly elevated risk, roughly 4.7 to 6.1 times that of male controls and 3.0 to 3.7 times that of female controls.
The authors suggested two possible explanations for the rise in psychiatric care among those who underwent medical transition: estrogen therapy may contribute to depressive symptoms in some people, and the treatments may not have met the expectations patients placed on them.
“Severe mental health problems are very common in adolescents suffering from gender dysphoria, and regardless of proceeding to medical gender reassignment, the need for psychiatric treatment due to these disorders does not subside,” Ruuska said. “This does not support the aforementioned suggestion that medical gender reassignment would improve the mental health of these youth. In addition, at least severe mental health disorders do not seem to be explained by gender dysphoria.”
“In fact, the finding that these youth suffer from severe mental health problems even before the first contact with the gender clinics, and that these problems increase over time, suggest that for some of these adolescents, gender dysphoria may be attributable to other mental health challenges,” he added. “In addition, in some, the need for psychiatric treatment emerges only after medical gender reassignment, which may suggest that medical gender reassignment might even have a negative impact on some of these youth’s mental health. The results highlight the need to thoroughly assess these youth’s mental health before and throughout potential medical gender reassignment. Medical gender reassignment is not timely when a youth suffers from concurrent severe mental health problems.”
These findings are broadly in line with a 2020 study covered by PsyPost, which tracked suicide deaths across stages of transition rather than psychiatric care and found that risk remained elevated at every stage, although it did not rise over time and declined among trans women. They stand in contrast to the 2023 U.S. study described earlier, though that study tracked self-reported symptoms and life satisfaction rather than use of psychiatric services.
Outside researchers asked to comment on the study pointed to both the strengths of the nationwide dataset and the need for caution when interpreting observational records. “This is a registry-based observational study, with nationwide coverage, a large sample, matched population controls, substantial follow-up, and virtually no loss to follow-up,” Marie-Claude Geoffroy, an associate professor in the Department of Psychiatry at McGill University and the Douglas Mental Health University Institute, Canada Research Chair in Youth Suicide Prevention, and a clinical psychologist who was not involved in the research, told PsyPost.
“The higher use of specialist psychiatric services among gender-referred youth compared with matched controls is important, but it should not be interpreted causally. Other factors such as residual confounding, selection into treatment, and closer mental health monitoring could also have contributed to the observed differences.”
Residual confounding refers to differences between groups that statistical adjustments did not fully capture, while selection into treatment refers to the possibility that the people who received hormones or surgery differed from those who did not in ways that affected their later care. Geoffroy also situated the results within broader research on self-harm, including non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI), which refers to deliberately hurting oneself without intending to die.
“A recent meta-analysis found that approximately 1 in 2 transgender and gender-diverse youth experience suicidal ideation or NSSI, and 1 in 4 have attempted suicide,” Geoffroy added. “Such findings, together with those of Ruuska et al., however point to the urgent need to invest in prevention and mental health support—all youth deserve the opportunity for positive mental health.”
Since its publication, the study has been widely shared on social media and Substack and was cited in by the Wall Street Journal editorial board as evidence against gender transitions for youth. The study also prompted several letters to the editor in Acta Paediatrica from international researchers and clinicians debating its methodology and interpretation.
In one commentary, Swedish psychiatrist Mikael Landén wrote that the study’s nationwide coverage and long follow-up challenge the assumption that medical transition reliably resolves mental health struggles, while reminding readers that observational registry data cannot prove that the medical treatments themselves caused the increase in psychiatric care.
Other researchers raised sharper criticisms in a letter signed by nearly 50 researchers and clinicians, which asked the journal to reconsider the paper, and in letters from E. Kale Edmiston and colleagues and Federico Sandri and colleagues. These critics argued that counting specialist psychiatric visits measures healthcare use rather than mental illness, that a yes-or-no measure treats a single visit the same as years of care, and that because Finnish clinics require mental health conditions to be stabilized before approving medical transition, patients might hide symptoms beforehand and seek help only afterward.
They also contended that the two-year window was too short to separate assessment-related visits from post-treatment outcomes, and suggested that stress from discrimination could contribute to later psychiatric care.
In one response and a later reply, Ruuska and his colleagues defended their approach and presented additional analyses to test the critics’ concerns. They argued that in Finland’s public healthcare system, specialist psychiatric care is strictly reserved for severe mental disorders and ends once a patient is in remission, making it a reliable indicator of severe illness. The authors also stated that their study does not claim definitive causality, while maintaining that the underlying mechanisms, including potential adverse effects of treatment, require careful examination.
To address concerns about the two-year timeline, the authors re-analyzed the data looking at five or more years after the initial clinic visit, with similar results, and conducted a separate analysis tracking patients only after their final hormone or surgical milestone was completed. In that milestone analysis, the proportion of patients receiving specialist psychiatric care rose from 19.2 percent before their first clinic contact to 48.9 percent after their last medical reassignment procedure, while rates among matched controls went from 14.4 percent before to 13.2 percent after, resulting in a sixfold elevated risk compared to male peers.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these results. Because the study relied on national administrative registries, the researchers could not examine the specific personal reasons why individual patients sought psychiatric care, nor could they measure direct patient-reported outcomes like body satisfaction, relief from gender dysphoria, or subtler changes in quality of life. The registries also lacked data on family support, trauma history, and socioeconomic status, all of which can influence youth mental health.
Most importantly, the study is observational, so it cannot show whether hormones or surgery caused the rise in psychiatric care among those who received them. Because people with recent severe psychiatric problems were less likely to be approved for treatment, the group that went on to receive hormones or surgery began with much lower rates of psychiatric care than other referred youth, which makes before-and-after comparisons within that group difficult to interpret.
Annie Pullen Sansfaçon, a full professor at the University of Montreal’s School of Social Work and researcher for the UdeM Institute for Public Health, who co-signed one of the critical letters to the editor, emphasized the role of social and environmental factors. “Gender affirming medical care can help improve mental health, but mental health is also influenced by other factors such as levels of parental and peer support or experiences of violence and bullying,” Pullen Sansfaçon told PsyPost.
“Furthermore, qualitative longitudinal and prospective research involving youth who have accessed gender affirming medical care, as well as with those who later detransition, suggest that gender affirming medical care can also shape many aspects of their lives, from the level of discrimination or affirmation they experience, their feeling of dysphoria, as well as some of their resilience factors such as their feeling of pride, affirmation, and connectedness,” Pullen Sansfaçon said. “As such, Ruuska et al.’s study needs to be interpreted with caution because it does not account for the person-environment interaction, which may severely limit the findings and what we can conclude from them.”
In their published response, the authors acknowledged that quality of life, family support, and socioeconomic status were not available in the registries, but argued that these missing factors were unlikely to fully explain the rise in psychiatric care.
Ruuska stressed that the findings describe group-level patterns. “The results should not be interpreted in a way that there wouldn’t be any adolescents suffering from gender dysphoria who could benefit from medical gender reassignment,” Ruuska noted. “There are, but the difficulty in clinical work is to recognize these youth. It is much easier to recognize when these interventions are not timely (i.e., concurrent severe mental health issues).”
“And even in some of these youth, they could be timely later on if the gender dysphoria persists and their mental health ameliorates,” Ruuska continued. “This is to underline the take-home message of the study: mental health needs of these adolescents need to be recognized and treated.”
The research group plans further studies using the same dataset.
The study, “Psychiatric Morbidity Among Adolescents and Young Adults Who Contacted Specialised Gender Identity Services in Finland in 1996–2019: A Register Study,” was authored by Sami-Matti Ruuska, Katinka Tuisku, Timo Holttinen, and Riittakerttu Kaltiala.

Fresh clashes erupt in Paris as France protest arrests exceed 2,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:00:13 UTC
01:00:13 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
18 October 2026•Update: 18 October 2026
French police used tear gas and a water cannon against protesters in central Paris on Sunday, a day after nationwide cost-of-living demonstrations were marred by violence that resulted in more than 2,000 arrests.
Fresh tensions erupted at Place de la Republique following social media calls for a gathering, Le Parisien reported. Police made several arrests, while some protesters erected barricades and firefighters tackled a blaze on nearby Rue Yves-Toudic.
The Paris police prefecture said officers were deployed to disperse the gathering and make arrests after initial tensions.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez announced an updated nationwide tally of more than 2,000 arrests following Saturday’s unrest, during which over 600 police officers, gendarmes and firefighters were injured.
He said the injury toll remained provisional and investigations were continuing to identify those responsible for violence and considerable damage to businesses.
President Emmanuel Macron will address the nation at 8 pm Sunday, the Elysee announced. He is also scheduled to meet Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu and relevant ministers beforehand.
An interministerial crisis meeting chaired by Lecornu, initially planned for Sunday evening, has been postponed until 10 am Monday.
Saturday’s demonstrations brought together trade unions, Yellow Vest collectives, students and farmers. The Interior Ministry recorded 550,000 participants nationwide, while the CGT trade union claimed nearly 800,000.
A demonstrator died after suffering cardiorespiratory arrest in Paris, while public buildings and businesses were attacked in several cities.
In Limoges, Haute-Vienne Prefect Maurice Barate said the fire at the historic city hall was virtually extinguished, but almost the entire historic section had been lost.
Lecornu pledged state financial support, continuity of public services and accelerated reconstruction procedures for the city.
The Association of Mayors of France called for gatherings outside town halls at noon Monday to condemn attacks on public buildings.
Meanwhile, police and gendarmerie watchdogs are investigating after a minor lost a hand to a grenade in Saint-Etienne during Saturday’s protests, local authorities said.

Pezeshkian: Iran ends gasoline imports, will stand against coercion with people's support

Pezeshkian: Iran ends gasoline imports, will stand against coercion with people's support
TEHRAN – President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran has become self-sufficient in gasoline supply through consumption management and public cooperation, stressing that the government will stand against US and Israeli plots with the support of the people.
Speaking at the eighth meeting of the Government Information Council, held in his presence, Pezeshkian said the administration has used all its capacities to prevent disruption to people's livelihoods, with basic and essential goods supplied through round-the-clock efforts.
 
According to ISNA, the session reviewed the actions and programs of the council for using the capacity of media outlets and public relations departments to explain the government's achievements and measures to resolve the country's crises and problems.
Standing with people against US military and economic war
Emphasizing the full and targeted use of media capacity to realize justice in various fields and continuous all-out efforts to solve people's problems, the president said the main goal and plan of Iran's enemies through military aggression, economic pressure and sanctions, and media onslaught is to create and deepen division among the people and strata of society.
"We must all join hands to solve the country's and people's problems and use all capacities, including the media, to strengthen unity and cohesion in the country," Pezeshkian said.
Referring to the difficulties caused by the enemy's military aggression and economic blockade, he said that despite all the problems, the government has done and will do its utmost to resolve people's problems, and in this path, securing people's livelihood must be the first and main priority for all of us.
"If we gain people's trust and have people with us, no power will be able to harm our country," the president added. "Despite all the pressure and hardships caused by the enemy's military and economic war, the government has used all its capacities to ensure people's livelihood is not disrupted."
From $12 billion in imports to gasoline self-sufficiency despite US blockade
Pezeshkian also addressed high energy consumption and fuel supply under the economic blockade, saying the administration put saving and consumption management on its agenda to prevent further problems in energy and fuel, which led to significant savings with public cooperation.
"Today we have become needless of gasoline imports, whereas we had to spend 12 billion dollars for importing needed gasoline," he said.
Stressing that all revenues from fuel price adjustments, savings and consumption management will be paid back to the people themselves, the president said media capacity must be used to accompany people on important issues such as energy consumption management, gasoline saving, and strengthening national unity and social cohesion.
He called on managers in administrative bodies and organizations to work with empathy to encourage government employees, including through plans such as car-free Tuesdays, reduced use of personal cars, increased productivity, and use of teleworking capacity, to control and manage excessive energy and fuel consumption.
Describing the neighborhood-based plan and greater use of public participation, the Basij, benefactors and charities as ways to solve problems and strengthen society's resilience against enemy aggression, Pezeshkian said the government, with people's help and accompaniment, will stand against all conspiracies and sinister plans of the US and the Zionist regime and will not allow Iran's enemies to achieve their objectives.
The president said the 500,000-toman increase in the electronic coupon will definitely be implemented. On the coupon scheme, he said today those with more capital benefit from more subsidies, but the program and goal is to take subsidies from the affluent and financially capable and give more help to the needy.
Continuing his remarks, Pezeshkian stressed the need for all administrative bodies and organizations, as well as companies and the private sector, to strengthen production and increase productivity.
"I invite anyone who can help in this field to cooperate. The country's managers must use expert and experienced forces to improve the country's difficult conditions, solve people's problems and increase productivity," he said.
Referring to major actions in education, including the inauguration of educational projects and smart schools on Saturday morning, the president said he was very pleased with the major measures taken in a short time, noting that the increase in educational spaces, reform of teaching methods, and development of cultural and sports spaces in educational complexes have been remarkable, with benefactors playing an important role through 48,000 billion tomans in contributions.
On ethnic and gender justice, Pezeshkian stressed continued government efforts, saying the administration seeks to further increase the participation of ethnic groups and women in decision-making and policy implementation.
Media must build unity and trust, not praise the government
"To increase consonance in society and people's resilience against hardships, pressure and enemy threats, we must all join hands, and media and public relations must accompany with all capacity and strength," he noted.
Stressing that the accompaniment of media and public relations departments by no means praising government actions, the president said: "I do not like anyone to praise me, tell us our faults and shortcomings so we can work to fix and reform them."
At the beginning of the session, council members expressed views on the importance and role of media and public relations in explaining the government's achievements and actions to the people and society.
Among the key points raised were the need for comprehensive understanding of the enemy's different dimensions and use of all national capacities to neutralize plots against Iran, gaining public trust and aligning people with governance, designing a think tank alongside a narrative room in the government's media apparatus, strengthening content production by all government pillars and managers along with accountability to public opinion, building hope through respect and continuous engagement with people, having a media engine alongside a media annex for executive plans, avoiding polarization, efforts for social reconstruction and addressing people's concerns, proper use of cyberspace to foster hope, the need for re-engineering media architecture under military and economic war conditions, effective use of media persons and influential figures, and avoiding ineffective mass production in favor of limited but effective content.

Trump endorses Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s October elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
15:56:10 UTC
00:56:10 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
18 October 2026•Update: 18 October 2026
US President Donald Trump on Sunday threw his support behind Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s Oct. 27 elections, declaring his “Complete and Total Endorsement” of the longtime leader’s bid for re-election.
In a lengthy post on his Truth Social platform, Trump praised Netanyahu’s leadership and his partnership with Washington, particularly in confronting Iran, warning that the US could be forced to take on the burden itself if Israelis choose another leader.
“If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so,” Trump wrote.
He described Netanyahu as “Strong, Brave, and Brilliant,” adding that the Israeli leader had grown stronger despite mounting pressure, including opposition within Israel itself.
Following the endorsement, Trump told Israel’s Channel 12 that he “was always going to do that,” but “just didn’t want to do it too soon.”
Trump stressed the “good relationship” he has with Netanyahu, saying: “It is important that Israel has a person they can count on.”
Asked whether he could work with an alternative Israeli leader, Trump replied: “Maybe I will, maybe I won’t. Who wants to take the chance?”
The endorsement comes as Netanyahu faces a politically sensitive election campaign, with his leadership scrutinized over security, the war in Gaza and his handling of Israel’s international standing.
Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 in Gaza since October 2023, most of them women and children, while around 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed, according to Palestinian authorities.
In November 2024, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
The International Court of Justice is also hearing a case brought by South Africa and joined by several countries that accuses Israel of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

Mass funeral for 75 recovered from under rubble in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
15:54:47 UTC
00:54:47 KST

Breadcrumb
Gaza: Bodies of 75 killed by Israel recovered, buried after three years
Palestinians on Sunday held funerals for the bodies of 75 people killed by Israel in the genocide in Gaza, after civil defence teams worked for three years to retrieve the bodies from under the rubble despite a lack of specialised equipment.
The families of those killed gathered in Gaza City in a mass funeral organised by the Martyrs’ Families’ Association and in coordination with the General Directorate of the Civil Defence.
The mass funeral was held inside the al-Daraj Sports Stadium, with prayers offered for the deceased before the bodies were carried to the Sheikh Radwan Cemetery in northern Gaza.
Kamal Hijazi, whose loved ones were among those killed, told The New Arab that being able to hold a funeral was somewhat a relief.
“The rubble formed a barrier between us and giving the dead a proper farewell, in a way that was dignified and befitting of them. The Israeli occupation does not recognise the dignity of Palestinians, whether they are dead or alive- but we will not allow the rubble to be the grave of our martyrs,” he said.
He also called on the relevant authorities in Gaza to preserve and document the data of those killed and recovered in the hopes that “there will be justice in Gaza”.
“We will not ask anything of the international community, as we have no confidence in it,” he continued.
Civil defence spokesman Mahmoud Basal confirmed that around 8,000 Palestinians remain buried under the rubble, with teams unable to recover their remains due to a lack of resources.
“Civil defence teams are working under extremely difficult conditions without heavy machinery to remove the rubble burying the bodies. Children, women and the elderly are dying, and no one is able to retrieve their bodies from under the rubble, all while the world, human rights groups, all while Arab and Western countries stand by and watch without lifting a finger,” he said.
One of the people who attended the funeral procession, Najat Abdel Aaal, told The New Arab that 10 of her family members were among those recovered, noting that most of them were women and children.
She said during the time of the bombing when they were killed, she screamed and cried out for help.
“But at the time, crews were only able to pull out a few people from under the rubble, and the bodies of my family and relatives were buried for three years,” she explained.
“Retrieving the bodies after three years has reopened the wounds we all feel. It has brought up a mixture of relief and pain, but families have finally been able to bid farewell to their loved ones and lay them to rest,” she added.
Israel’s war on Gaza, which commenced in October 2023, has killed over 74,000 Palestinians and has been determined to be a genocide by leading international rights groups and scholars.
The war has levelled entire neighbourhoods, devastated the healthcare system, and destroyed many civilian buildings, including residential blocks, places of worship and schools.
Despite a ceasefire agreed in October 2025, with the terms demanding that aid deliveries are made daily, Israel has obstructed scores of items from entering the enclave, including heavy machinery and specialised tools used to find and recover the dead from beneath the rubble.
A report from Euro-Med Human Rights Monitors states there is approximately 68 million tonnes of rubble across the Gaza Strip.
The lack of equipment has raised concerns that without forensic surveys, any efforts to recover bodies could result in the crushing or scattering of remains.
According to human rights group Gisha, Israel continues to define thousands of critical emergency humanitarian items as “dual use” and blocks them from entering the enclave.
The listed items, ranging from construction materials to wheelchairs, sleeping bags, and portable toilets, have hindered the reconstruction of Gaza.

'Cockroach' party founder released from Indian police custody
India's youth-led Cockroach Janata Party founder Abhijeet Dipke was released from detention on Saturday, a day after his arrest during a police crackdown on protests against the election authority.
Dipke, 31, was detained Friday in New Delhi as he headed to join a rally that the CJP protest movement had called in the capital's central Connaught Place district.
An AFP photographer saw him walk out of a police station Saturday afternoon, wave to the media, and give a thumbs-up as he was driven away.
"Abhijeet Dipke released," CJP legal affairs chief Ratna Singh said on social media.
Opposition parties and CJP activists have defied a security crackdown, rallying to demand the resignation of India's chief election commissioner after accusing the poll body of manipulating voter rolls to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling party.
The commission, which oversees voting in the world's most populous nation, has denied any wrongdoing.
Police arrested two other senior CJP leaders, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, on 14 October after they entered Jantar Mantar, a decades-old protest site police have declared off-limits for demonstrations. They remain in custody.
"Now just waiting for my brothers to be free", Dipke said in a post on X that included a photo of Ranka and Das.
In a separate Instagram post, Dipke said he "knew going to jail was inevitable" and was ready to face "whatever comes my way".
"Because the day I decided to come back to India, I placed my fate in the hands of the people of India and the Constitution of this country."
Members of Modi's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India's electoral rolls.
Rights groups and critics, however, say the Modi government has eroded democratic freedoms over more than a decade in power, citing pressure on journalists, civil society groups, and political opponents, allegations the government rejects.

According to the department, 150 of the affected premises are private residential or commercial buildings, while the remaining two are public housing estates under the Tenants Purchase Scheme.

Japan expected to rank sixth in Global GDP Rankings by 2027, IMF
Japan is projected to slip to sixth place in the world in terms of nominal gross domestic product (GDP) by 2027, as India and the United Kingdom are expected to overtake it, according to the latest International Monetary Fund (IMF) World Economic Outlook report, Qazinform News Agency cites Jiji Press.
The decline in Japan's GDP ranking is largely attributed to the depreciation of the yen against the U.S. dollar, although slower economic growth has also contributed to the weakening position.
Japan ranked as the world's fourth-largest economy in 2025, behind the United States, China and Germany.
The IMF forecasts Japan's nominal GDP at $4.34 trillion in 2026, rising to $4.47 trillion in 2027. Despite the increase in economic output, the country is expected to be surpassed by India, whose nominal GDP is projected to reach $4.52 trillion in 2027.
If the forecast proves accurate, India would become the world's fourth-largest economy, pushing Japan further down the global rankings.

Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama on Sunday rejected calls to step down and said street protests, which continued for a sixth day, were a threat not to his government but to Albania's hopes of joining the European Union.
Student-led demonstrations, fuelled by anger over perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards, have engulfed central Tirana and spread to other cities in the past week.
Demonstrators demanding Rama's resignation have set fire to government buildings as well as banks, smashed shop windows and pulled up paving stones to throw at police.
Violence erupted again on Sunday when thousands gathered outside the Education Ministry and hurled rocks at riot police who responded with tear gas, water cannon and rubber bullets.
The unrest, which followed months of largely peaceful protests over the summer against a luxury coastal development backed by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, poses the biggest challenge yet to Rama, who has governed since 2013 and last year won a fourth term in office.
Rama says protests challenge his government's vision, not its legitimacy
"I am not being challenged, the government is not being challenged, a government majority or a winning party in the elections is not being challenged, but a path is being challenged, a mission is being challenged," Rama said in a live address on Facebook.
“Albanians need to think very clearly: Do they want this, do they want that, or do they want the EU?”
Rama invited students to dialogue as excavators dug up and removed the paving outside his office in central Tirana before protests started on Sunday.
The US embassy in Tirana urged protesters to refrain from violence.
"Violence, rioting, physically injuring others, and the destruction of property are not civic engagement," it said on X.
Corruption scandals have tarnished Albania's image over the years, and analysts say the country is a hub for gangs seeking to launder money from drugs and weapons trafficking.
However, Rama has said his government is tackling corruption as never before. Along with Montenegro, Albania is currently leading the group of Balkan countries seeking to join the EU and aims to enter by 2030.
Rama accuses foreign interests of fueling protests, alleged drone attack
Rama blamed unspecified foreign interests for the protests and for what he said was an attempted drone attack at his office this week.
"God knows what the consequences will be. There are no young people, no students, and no minors who would even think of implementing this plan. This is a foreign hand," he said.
Police said 388 people had been charged with criminal offenses during the demonstrations. Scores of police officers and protesters have been injured.

US officials visit Palestinian village after settler attacks on diplomats
TAYBEH, West Bank/JERUSALEM, Oct 18 - US diplomats visited a Christian Palestinian town in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on Sunday following attacks by militant Israeli settlers on European diplomats and an American photojournalist in the previous two days.
Riley Barnes, assistant secretary of state for democracy, human rights and labor, Brian Burch, US ambassador to the Holy See, and a number of other diplomats visited the Latin Convent church and were expected to meet with members of the Christian community in Taybeh.
Belgian, French and Polish diplomats, along with a French mayor and Palestinian civilians, had been attacked near Taybeh on Saturday by masked Israeli settlers.
The previous day, Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine was taken to hospital after being assaulted while covering a Palestinian olive harvest near another West Bank village.
The diplomats' visit coincided with US President Donald Trump endorsing his ally, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, for Israel's parliamentary election on October 27.
NETANYAHU CIRCUMSPECT ON SETTLER VIOLENCE
Trump has this year expressed his opposition to settlement expansion, but his administration has put little pressure on Netanyahu's right-wing, pro-settler government to change its policy.
UN bodies and most countries deem the settlements illegal under international law, but Israel rejects this, viewing the territory as disputed rather than occupied.
While Foreign Minister Gideon Saar and the Israeli military (IDF) both blamed "Israeli rioters" for the attack on the diplomats, Netanyahu, whose coalition is projected to lose its governing majority, has been more circumspect.
He has said the diplomats entered a "sensitive area with a history of confrontations without prior coordination with the IDF", and that the facts of the attack on Levine are "unclear".
France urged Israeli authorities to arrest Saturday's attackers and to end criminal violence in the West Bank, but by Sunday there was no announcement from Israeli authorities of any arrests in either of the two latest incidents.
The West Bank is home to some 500,000 settlers and at least 3 million Palestinians.
Settler attacks on the Palestinians are surging, with at least 170 since September 27, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli human rights group. Journalists, activists and foreign observers have also been targeted.
Yet prosecutions of Israeli settlers are rare.

National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir claimed Sunday that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office had secretly assured several European Union countries that he would not be included in Israel's next government, escalating tensions between the two coalition partners just nine days before the October 27 election.
In a special statement to the media, the far-right Otzma Yehudit party leader said he had received verified information in recent days indicating that Netanyahu's office had made formal commitments to European governments to exclude him from the next cabinet. The allegation has not been independently confirmed.
"I say these things with deep sorrow," Ben-Gvir said. "For a long time, I heard such reports, but I prayed they were not true." He claimed that explicit assurances had been conveyed to European foreign ministers and more senior officials that Netanyahu had no intention of bringing him into the next government.
Addressing Netanyahu directly, Ben-Gvir warned him against seeking international or domestic political legitimacy at his expense. "Don't count on legitimacy from the left," he said. "Don't count on the left that has been after you for decades. They will hate you forever."
He argued that Netanyahu's political future depended on maintaining a strong right-wing coalition rather than bringing in centrist parties. "Bibi needs a strong Ben-Gvir, not a strong Eisenkot," he declared, referring to former IDF chief of staff and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot.
Growing tensions ahead of election
The accusations follow a series of confrontations between Netanyahu and Ben-Gvir over the composition of the next government. On Thursday, Netanyahu said the Defense Ministry and National Security Ministry would remain under Likud control if he wins reelection, effectively ruling out Ben-Gvir's ambitions to obtain the defense portfolio. Otzma Yehudit accused Netanyahu of preparing to replace it with Eisenkot's party. 
The latest claims also contrast with earlier assurances Netanyahu reportedly gave Ben-Gvir. As ynet reported last month, Netanyahu personally sought to reassure his coalition partner that any future government he formed would be based on the current coalition and its principles, despite calls for a broader alliance. 
Ben-Gvir accused Likud of deliberately trying to reduce Otzma Yehudit's representation to five Knesset seats, warning that weakening his party could ultimately cost the right-wing bloc its majority.
"If you hurt Otzma Yehudit, you could cause our voters to stay home," he said, insisting his supporters would not automatically switch to other right-wing parties.
The relationship between the two leaders has been marked by repeated confrontations. Ben-Gvir resigned from Netanyahu's government in January 2025 over the Gaza ceasefire and hostage agreement, only to return two months later following the resumption of Israeli military operations. 
Despite the latest dispute, Ben-Gvir insisted he remained committed to Netanyahu becoming prime minister. He reminded Netanyahu that he had previously defended him against efforts within Likud to remove him, claiming the prime minister had once told him he trusted Ben-Gvir more than members of his own party.
"Every vote for Otzma Yehudit is automatically a vote for Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister," Ben-Gvir said. "But to have a real, strong right-wing government, rather than a weak centrist government, Bibi needs a strong Ben-Gvir."
