BEIJING, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- The first round of the 2026-27 Chinese Basketball Association (CBA) League regular season concluded on Sunday, with defending champion Shanghai Sharks cruising past the Shenzhen Aviators 102-68, while the Sichuan Blue Whales defeated the Tianjin Pioneers 97-85 to end the longest losing streak in league history.
The CBA regular season will feature 460 games across 46 rounds, up from 420 last season. The playoffs will return to a 3-5-5-7 format, replacing last season's 3-3-5-7 system.
The most notable structural change this season is the return of promotion and relegation, which was abandoned after the 2003-04 season. The bottom two CBA teams after the regular season will face the top two sides from the National Basketball League (NBL) in home-and-away playoffs in April 2027.
Facing the threat of relegation, Sichuan snapped its 47-game losing streak across two seasons with a 97-85 victory over Tianjin, powered by Jaden Shackelford's game-high 38 points. Sichuan's previous win came on March 16, 2025, and its 47-game skid was the longest losing streak in CBA history.
Blue Whales head coach Simon Petrov said after the game that his team had a bright future, adding that he was very happy with the group as it stands.
"My biggest hope is to help all the players become better players, so they can contribute more to the team, become responsible players and play smart basketball," he said.
Defending champion Shanghai opened its season with a convincing win on Friday despite an inefficient shooting performance from newcomer and former NBA All-Star D'Angelo Russell, who scored 21 points on 7-of-23 shooting. Shanghai center Wang Zhelin added 14 points and 18 rebounds, while forward Zhang Zhenlin contributed 16 points.
Shenzhen was outrebounded 59-35 by Shanghai, while its leading scorer Terquavion Smith struggled from the field, making just five of 22 attempts to finish with 18 points.
Sunday featured two games that went down to the wire. Barry Brown Jr., who finished with 31 points, hit a game-winning three-pointer to lift the Beijing Ducks to an 84-82 victory over the Jilin Northeast Tigers. In another thriller, Xu Jie missed a potential game-winning baseline jumper as the Guangdong Southern Tigers narrowly fell 96-95 to the Nanjing Monkey Kings.
Elsewhere, the Fujian Sturgeons edged the Jiangsu Dragons 89-85, the Beijing Royal Fighters cruised past the Ningbo Rockets 95-71, and the Zhejiang Lions outlasted the Shanxi Loongs 115-109 in double overtime. The Xinjiang Flying Tigers narrowly beat the Qingdao Eagles 82-80, while the Guangzhou Loong Lions defeated the Zhejiang Golden Bulls 90-79 and the Liaoning Flying Leopards overcame the Shandong Heroes 95-84. ■

HANGZHOU, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- The Council of the Alliance for Cultural Heritage in Asia (ACHA) on Sunday approved Egypt as a partner state and Kazakhstan as an observer state at its fourth meeting in Hangzhou, east China's Zhejiang Province, bringing the total number of member states, partner states and observer states to 26.
Over the past year, the ACHA has achieved fruitful cooperation and a steady stream of tangible outcomes, and has made a key leap toward becoming an institutionalized and standardized intergovernmental organization, according to the meeting.
Through regional consensus and joint research, the alliance has turned practical cooperation into concrete results. It has also promoted the development of young talent in cultural heritage protection, injecting new vigor and vitality into exchanges and mutual learning among Asian civilizations.
Participants at the meeting said the alliance should build momentum for capacity building, improve the effectiveness of cooperation and stimulate innovation, while expanding the breadth and depth of its cooperation. They said the ACHA should become an important force in promoting the inheritance and development of civilizations.
The alliance launched its official website at the meeting, providing a digital platform for information sharing and collaboration.
Established in 2023, the ACHA is committed to implementing the Asian Initiative for Cultural Heritage Conservation.
The alliance aims to promote conservation standards and cooperation models for cultural heritage conservation in Asia through scientific conservation and innovative use, enhance connectivity, and promote shared values of cultural heritage within the region.
It seeks to safeguard Asia's cultural heritage and sustain the roots of diverse civilizations, expand global partnerships for cultural heritage conservation, and advance the Global Civilization Initiative with the power of cultural heritage. ■

US ambassador to Israel calls West Bank settler attack on American photojournalist ‘terror’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
15:33:38 UTC
00:33:38 KST

The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, has denounced the settler attack that left the Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine badly beaten and needing surgery as a “despicable act of terror” and called for the arrest and prosecution of those responsible.
Levine, 63, an award-winning journalist who lives in Israel, was set upon last Friday by masked Israeli settlers who used clubs and other weapons to attack Palestinian people attempting to harvest their olives in occupied West Bank towns.
The photographer, who is in a hospital in Petah Tikva near Tel Aviv recovering from hand surgery, broken ribs and other injuries she sustained in the attack, said she was beaten for more than 10 minutes by the settlers, who also stole her camera, passport and phone.
“I was attacked, pushed to the ground,” Levine said. “Luckily, I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn’t even be here, because they just kept kicking and kicking me.” She said the attack ended when her Palestinian colleagues intervened to save her.
Huckabee, a rightwing ally of President Donald Trump with a track record of hardline, pro-Israel rhetoric, was notably blunt in his condemnation of what he called the “vicious and cowardly attack” on Levine. In a post on X on Saturday, he noted that she was a US citizen who had been clearly identifiable as a journalist.
“We have called for a full investigation, arrest, and prosecution to the fullest extent of the law to whoever participated in this,” Huckabee added. “Attacking a female photographer is despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards. Dishonorable act of senseless violence.”
Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has been ambiguous in addressing Levine’s assault, condemning “violence against anyone” but referring to the attack as “alleged” and saying its circumstances remain unclear.
In an interview with the Associated Press on Sunday, Levine said she had been “shocked and insulted” to hear that Netanyahu referred to the attack on her and others as “alleged”, adding that the prime minister “had all the evidence on the table”.
But she described the sharp condemnation of settler violence expressed to her in a call from Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, and in a letter signed by several of the country’s top former security and intelligence officials, in which they all expressed shame over the attack.
Levine blamed “Jewish terrorists” for Thursday’s attack and added: “I’ve been covering this region for over 40 years, and I have never seen this country in such a state as it is today.”
The photojournalist also said she was planning to return to work when she had recovered from her injuries. “I’ve invested decades of blood, sweat and tears into this,” she said. “They cracked my bones, they haven’t cracked my spirit.”
The attack on the Palestinian farmers and Levine was followed on Saturday by another outbreak of settler violence directed against European diplomats, a French mayor and the archbishop of the French city of Cambrai, who were visiting the occupied West Bank.
Bernard Baudoux, the mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, was wearing his red, white and blue sash of office and attempting to enter a vehicle with diplomatic plates when he was assaulted and knocked to the ground. A masked militant shouted “Vive la France!” as he launched the attack, a witness said. Badoux’s wife and Vincent Dollmann, the archbishop of Cambrai, were also threatened by the group of seven men, some armed with clubs.
The group had joined the olive harvest on lands belonging to the Christian town of Taybeh, along with the French consul general in Jerusalem, his wife and other diplomats, and the Belgian and Polish consuls.
“I think that if settlers are behaving like this, there is a tolerance on the part of the Israeli government,” Baudoux told Agence France-Presse after he was attacked. “The whole world needs to know what’s happening. For me, I’ll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here.”
Violence is surging ahead of bitterly fought elections to be held on 27 October, with Palestinians’ annual olive harvest being repeatedly disrupted by Israeli settlers as Netanyahu seeks to shore up his pro-settlement rightwing base.
France’s foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, has called on Israel to “urgently halt criminal violence” and to arrest those responsible for attacking Baudoux. The EU has condemned the attack and urged “full accountability as well as effective measures to prevent continued acts of violence and violent harassment against Palestinians, including during the ongoing olive harvest season, as well as against journalists”.
The European Commission executive vice-president, Teresa Ribera, went further, posting an interview with Levine in hospital and adding the caption: “They want no witnesses.”
Israel’s foreign ministry has condemned the attack on the diplomats and Israeli police promised to open an investigation.
Herzog, who holds a mostly ceremonial role, called Levine in hospital on Saturday, saying the attack was “outrageous and shocking” and was weighing on his conscience.
Netanyahu’s main rival in the elections, the former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, criticised the prime minister over the violence, saying it was “burning away the little legitimacy the state of Israel still possesses”. He described the attacks as “Jewish terrorism, under the auspices of the Israeli government”.
Trump endorsed Netanyahu for re-election in a post on his Truth Social network on Sunday, hailing him as “a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran”. He added: “Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself.”
The Washington Post has reiterated its call for a full and transparent investigation into the attack on Levine, even though Israel rarely investigates settler violence fully.
Yesh Din, an Israeli rights group, says about 94% of investigations into settler violence since 2005 have ended without an indictment, with just 3% leading to full or partial convictions.
The Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

We are also defending the areas near Kramatorsk and destroying Russian forces 20 km from Zaporizhzhia, not 5, as someone over there in Russia is snowing Putin."

A month before the diesel waiver, Trump’s envoys had already pitched Kyiv on Russian gas, NYT says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
15:31:37 UTC
00:31:37 KST

During their visit to Kyiv in September, US President Donald Trump’s envoys urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to consider restarting the pipelines that once carried Russian gas to Europe, The New York Times reported on 17 October. They presented it as part of a peace deal with Russia. In the weeks that followed, they pressed the idea with European officials, while Washington freed Russian diesel and spared Russia’s oil buyers from new US penalties.
Energy sales fund Russia’s war, and Ukraine’s halt of transit in January 2025 left TurkStream as Gazprom’s only pipeline route into the EU. Meanwhile, Russia has kept bombing Ukraine’s grid through the energy truce Washington declared on 11 October.
The pitch in Kyiv
Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner put the idea to Zelenskyy when they met him in Kyiv, the newspaper reported, citing people familiar with the talks. Trump officials argued that transit fees, which Ukraine gave up at about $1 billion a year, would benefit Kyiv, and that European voters would eventually want cheaper energy. Russia’s share of EU gas imports had fallen from 45% in 2021 to 13% last year.
The envoys presented renewed Russian gas sales as one of the economic incentives in a wider settlement covering Russia’s relationship with NATO, security guarantees for Ukraine, and territorial control. Some European and Ukrainian officials suspected Washington would seek a cut of the profits. The White House denied that the Nord Stream pipeline had been a subject of recent discussions. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov claimed that resuming energy cooperation is in Russia’s interest and, right now, even more in Europe’s.
Germany pushes back
At Ukraine talks the envoys hosted in Florida last week, Günter Sautter, security adviser to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, forcefully opposed the idea. German lawmakers have called a return to Russian deliveries a disaster for European security, even treason, as the far-right AfD courts Gazprom to bring the gas back. Former Economy Minister Robert Habeck, who steered Germany off Russian gas after 2022, said Trump “seems to have more sympathies with Vladimir Putin than he has with the Ukrainians.”
Congress gave Trump 30 days to hit Russia’s oil buyers with 100% tariffs. He waives them two days before deadline, citing US interests. Moscow calls it historic
One concession after another
Rather than pressure Putin or strengthen Ukraine, the administration has spent much of its peace effort on economic incentives for Russia, the newspaper wrote. The US Treasury cleared imports of Russian diesel on 9 October. On 16 October, Trump waived the penalties on Russia’s oil buyers that Congress had passed in the Graham Act. Washington is also weighing relief for sanctioned shadow fleet tankers. And the White House ordered limits on the military satellite service Ukraine’s forces rely on, Reuters reported.
Putin’s economic envoy Kirill Dmitriev claimed the ice had broken and more joint initiatives would follow, including data centers powered by Russian nuclear energy. The talks also cover the sale of Lukoil’s foreign assets to a group that includes the US government, the newspaper reported earlier this month. Zelenskyy, who had heard the pitch in Kyiv, alluded to it in a Financial Times interview this week.
“The question will be when will the next deal be? Maybe it will be gas. Definitely it will be gas,” he said.
Reopening the pipelines could hand Moscow back significant revenue and strengthen its sway over Europe’s energy market, Liga noted. Each new concession lowers the price Russia pays for continuing the war.

- Musk pushed Trump to slow Starlink in Ukraine, weakening air defenses as Russian drones attacked cities – The Telegraph

TikTok permanently suspends advertising account for Elon Musk documentary: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
15:23:34 UTC
00:23:34 KST

Halis Sunnetci
18 October 2026•Update: 18 October 2026
By Halis Sunnetci
ISTANBUL (AA) – TikTok has permanently suspended the advertising account promoting Musk, a documentary about billionaire Elon Musk, citing repeated violations of its political-content policies, The Hollywood Reporter reported Saturday.
Distributor Bleecker Street was informed Friday afternoon that its advertising account would face a permanent suspension, preventing the company from purchasing ads or paying to promote content about the film.
The documentary's regular, unpaid TikTok account remains active, but Bleecker Street can no longer purchase advertisements or pay to boost its posts, according to the report.
A Bleecker Street spokesperson confirmed the suspension and expressed disappointment over its timing, as the documentary expanded to more than 470 theaters across North America. The company is appealing the decision.
TikTok cited a "level of severity with political-policy violations" in correspondence with the distributor, warning that "some violations trigger immediate suspension."
The platform had previously rejected paid advertising for the documentary's trailer, while Meta and Google-owned YouTube initially rejected similar ads before reversing their decisions. Musk-owned X has also refused to carry advertising for the film.
Directed by Oscar-winning filmmaker Alex Gibney, Musk examines the billionaire's business empire, his acquisition of Twitter and his political activities, including his involvement with the US Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).
The nearly four-hour documentary earned $70,000 from four theaters in New York and Los Angeles during its opening weekend before expanding to dozens of cities across North America.
The film is also scheduled to stream on HBO in 2027.

Netanyahu warns Israel could lose US support, seeks 450 billion shekels in extra defense spending
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
15:23:17 UTC
00:23:17 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned Sunday that Israel could face a hostile U.S. administration in the future, potentially threatening its military assistance and strategic relationship with Washington, and said the country must develop new international alliances. At the same time, he announced plans to allocate approximately 450 billion shekels in additional defense spending over the next decade.
Netanyahu made the remarks during an event at which he presented his security doctrine, nine days before Israel's October 27 election. Just hours later, U.S. President Donald Trump publicly endorsed Netanyahu's reelection bid for the first time during the current campaign.
"In two years, a president, man or woman, could come to power who is very hostile to Israel," Netanyahu said. "How would you deal with that? How would you operate in relation to the United States? And beyond that, what solutions would be necessary?"
His remarks came against the possibility that a future U.S. administration could suspend military assistance to Israel or even join international sanctions and an arms embargo against the country.
Netanyahu said Israel must use the remaining years of Trump's presidency to strengthen its position while preparing for a potentially dramatic shift in American policy.
"First, we must do everything we can during these two years, and during the following two years, in the American arena, through good times and bad," he said. "The second thing is to create other alliances. That is what I am working on now with many countries in our region and outside it. India is not a small country, and there are many others."
He pointed to political developments in Latin America as another opportunity to expand Israel's network of allies.
"There is a major shift in Latin America, and there could be an enormous change in Brazil in just a few days," Netanyahu said. "We must expand our pool of alliances and develop capabilities that make us valuable to everyone."
He also addressed Israel's strained relations with European countries, accusing some governments of publicly condemning Israel while continuing to seek cooperation with it.
"Countries that condemn us, and they have some nerve, by the way, condemn us and then come to us," he said. "I tell them: It depends on you. It depends on how you behave."
Netanyahu argued that Israel still possesses diplomatic leverage but would need considerable international expertise to navigate changes in Washington and other capitals.
In a separate social media post Sunday, Netanyahu appeared to acknowledge the possibility of a change in U.S. leadership, describing Trump's remaining time in office as an opportunity to advance Israel's strategic objectives.
"We have another two years of my friend President Trump's term, and this is exactly the time to complete our major missions on every front," he wrote.
On defense spending, Netanyahu said he intended to allocate approximately 450 billion shekels over the coming decade to strengthen Israel's military capabilities. An additional defense spending package of approximately 350 billion shekels had previously been agreed upon, according to earlier reports.
Addressing the future size of the Israel Defense Forces, Netanyahu said the military would have to expand, although technological advances, particularly artificial intelligence, could reduce some of its manpower requirements.
"As for a large army or a small army, the IDF definitely needs to grow," he said. "It will grow, but not at the rate we might have expected because AI reduces many requirements. Still, it needs to grow, and for that, of course, you need to allocate both funding and personnel."
He added: "I am putting about 450 billion shekels into this so that we have the capabilities and the teeth."
Turning to Iran, Netanyahu said the regime remained a threat despite what he described as severe military and economic damage inflicted on it. He warned that Tehran would seek to rebuild its nuclear program, develop other unconventional weapons and restore its regional network of allied armed groups.
"Like cancer, this will not end as long as that regime remains in place," he said. "It will try to recover, renew its nuclear program, renew other unconventional weapons programs and rebuild the axis."
Netanyahu claimed that Israel had already accomplished approximately 90% of its objectives against Iran and described the Iranian leadership as severely weakened.
"Why aren't people taking to the streets? Because right now they are being killed. Simply killed. They are killing or wounding tens of thousands of their own people. That is the nature of this regime," he said.
He then explicitly stated that his policy was aimed at bringing down the Iranian government. "Our plan is very comprehensive and very determined, to bring about the downfall of the regime," Netanyahu said. "That is my plan. That is the directive I have given all the security agencies, and that is what will happen."
Netanyahu also discussed Israel's relationship with Russia, describing it as one based on competing national interests rather than consistent cooperation.
"We speak when necessary," he said. "But Russia has its interests, and we have the interests of the State of Israel, and they do not always overlap. Sometimes they even clash."
He cited Russia's cooperation with Iran during the war in Ukraine as an example of conflicting interests and also raised the issue of anti-Israel bot networks spreading what he described as extreme antisemitic content.
"We raise all these issues, and we do so very clearly," Netanyahu said. "And when there is an opportunity to cooperate, we do that as well."
Gadi Eisenkot, chairman of the opposition Yashar! party and a former IDF chief of staff, sharply criticized Netanyahu's presentation, describing it as an empty political exercise rather than a serious national security strategy.
"Nine days before the election and three years after the gravest failure and disaster in Israel's history, with every war front still open, Netanyahu decided to present his 'security doctrine' to the public," Eisenkot said.
"Two hollow pages, full of slogans that have nothing whatsoever to do with a security doctrine, reveal more than anything the strategic vacuum Netanyahu has left the State of Israel in and his disregard for the security of Israeli citizens."
Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of attempting to manipulate public opinion and spread fear ahead of the election.
"This is Netanyahu's method: manipulating perceptions, frightening people and trying to divert attention from the parade of lies and racism surrounding his campaign tonight," he said.

WATCH smashed storefronts, burned buildings as Europe faces aftermath of latest violent protests
Tens of thousands took to the streets of European cities over the weekend to protest rising living costs, housing shortages and government policies, with demonstrations escalating into violent clashes, looting and arson in several countries. The unrest left smashed storefronts, damaged public buildings and burned-out vehicles in its wake.

In Portugal, tens of thousands also demonstrated, although no comparable scale of violence or damage was reported.
Footage from across Europe showed smashed shop windows, looted stores, burning vehicles and fires near public buildings.
In Limoges, France, flames engulfed the historic town hall, while masked demonstrators in Milan hurled stones at riot police near the Gothic cathedral and set fire to street barricades. In Brussels, protesters overturned a car, while in Tirana, demonstrators threw rocks and petrol bombs at police near the Education Ministry. Riot police in several cities used tear gas and water cannons to disperse crowds.
The massive rallies reflect a range of national grievances rather than a coordinated movement. In France, demonstrations took place in Marseille, Strasbourg, Nantes, Lyon and other cities.

'A great deal depends on America's position' — Zelensky holds call with Trump's peace envoys as US pivots to Moscow's side
Editor's Note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
President Volodymyr Zelensky held a phone conversation on Oct. 18 with U.S. President Donald Trump's special envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who have been tasked with leading peace talks between Kyiv and Moscow.
The call comes as Ukraine faces severe challenges in its relationship with Washington, once its strongest partner in defense against Russia's full-scale invasion. But in recent days, Trump has waived sanctions on Russia, demanded Ukraine halt attacks on oil refineries, and reportedly ordered restrictions on Ukrainian forces' access to vital Starlink services on the front lines.
Zelensky said his conversation with Kushner and Witkoff on Oct. 18 focused mainly on the results of their teams' latest diplomatic talks in Miami.
According to the president, the U.S. and Ukraine are in "constant communication" and are preparing their "next steps in diplomacy."
"We are constantly informing our partners about the real situation with the ongoing Russian shelling, which does not stop for a minute, and the issue of air defense," Zelensky said.
"A great deal depends on America's position here. Ukraine remains ready to work constructively, honestly, and for real results."
Later in his evening address on Oct. 18, Zelensky said the call also included discussion of Patriot air defense systems, critical for intercepting Russian ballistic missiles.
In an interview with NBC's "Meet the Press" published Oct. 18, Zelensky said he hoped Ukraine would be able to hold talks with the U.S. as early as next week. He also said Washington had resumed sharing intelligence with Kyiv regarding Russian missile launches.
The pause in missile warnings was just one of multiple blows to U.S. support for Ukraine the White House has dealt in the days since Trump abruptly announced a plan to purchase diesel from Russia to offset domestic fuel prices.
Trump on Oct. 9 said he'd made a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, shocking not only Ukraine but also many U.S. lawmakers from both parties. When questioned about helping fund Russia's ongoing war, Trump doubled down, saying Zelensky was making problems for the world by attacking refineries and that Ukraine should get a new president.
Then, on Oct. 11, Trump unilaterally declared an "energy ceasefire" between Ukraine and Russia. The truce appeared to be a surprise to both Kyiv and the Kremlin, but Zelensky said Ukraine was prepared to suspend attacks on Russian oil refineries if Moscow stopped battering Ukraine's power grid.
The Kyiv Independent reported on Oct. 12 that the Trump administration had threatened senior Ukrainian military and government officials in a push to protect Russian oil refineries. The U.S. warned it would suspend intelligence sharing and weapons support through NATO's PURL program if Ukraine refused to comply.
While Ukraine paused strikes on refineries, Russia made no such concessions. Zelensky revealed on Oct. 18 that Russia has attacked Ukrainian oil and gas facilities 76 times since Trump's energy ceasefire announcement the week before.
Trump has refused to blame Russia for breaking the truce, and Kyiv has resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Troubles mounted for Ukraine on Oct. 14, when the sudden introduction of a speed cap on Starlink systems disrupted multiple battlefield operations, including mid-range drone strikes and air defense.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk reportedly proposed the restriction to Trump, who agreed with the plan — though both have dodged responsibility for the move.
Zelensky has confirmed that the speed limit remains in place, hindering the efficacy of Ukraine's middle-strike campaign and the ability of interceptors to stop Russian high-speed jet drones.
A week after announcing the diesel deal with Putin, Trump issued a broad waiver of sanctions against Moscow under the Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act on Oct. 16.
Despite the devastating turn in U.S. policy, Zelensky said on Oct. 18 that Ukraine was still working with Washington to bring about an end to the war.
"Peace comes only through strength and cooperation built on trust," the president said.
"We are doing everything on our part to make this happen, and to ensure that America's position is strong and helps bring peace closer."

Trump endorses Netanyahu in Israeli election
WASHINGTON - US President Donald Trump on Oct 18 endorsed his ally Benjamin Netanyahu as the longtime Israeli prime minister struggles for an edge in next week’s parliamentary election.
Trump praised Netanyahu as a “great warrior prime minister” and peace partner, crediting him with joining the United States in launching strikes on Iran in February.
The conflict, in its seventh month, has disrupted energy markets globally and wreaked havoc across the Middle East, damaging critical infrastructure and destabilising regional economies.
“Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social.
“Despite all of that, he has endured and, in fact, he has thrived! I have watched Bibi under the most trying of times. Normal men or women in such situations would have wilted under the pressure – But Bibi did not wilt, he actually got stronger, and maintains that same Strength today.”
In his message, addressed to “the Great People of Israel,” Trump added, “Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel.”
The Trump endorsement is not certain to give Netanyahu and his right-wing Likud party a boost in the Oct 27 national election, as Israeli public support for Trump has diminished amid Israeli-US disagreements over Iran.
Polls have suggested no candidate has a clear path to power. Israel’s prime minister is chosen through coalition-building in Parliament rather than by direct popular vote.
It will be Israel’s first vote since the Hamas attack on Oct 7, 2023, that shook the country and plunged the Middle East into turmoil, as Israel went to war in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
The election could determine whether Netanyahu remains in power after one of the most consequential periods in Israel’s history, or is defeated by centrist rivals promising to usher in a new era.
Netanyahu promptly expressed his thanks to Trump on X, saying, “Together we will complete the mission!”
Trump has broken with longtime US tradition by endorsing candidates in elections in foreign countries, including Hungary, Colombia, Argentina, Japan and Honduras.
Endorsement might help
Trump’s relationship with Netanyahu has been close but also fractious, with the president at times publicly and privately criticising Israel’s longest-serving prime minister.
The war that the US and Israel launched against Iran is unpopular with Americans, who vote Nov 3 in congressional elections, while support for Israel among Americans has also decreased over the Iran war and Israel’s conduct in the three-year war in Gaza that Trump has promised to end. Both leaders on Sunday mentioned finishing the job in Iran.
Tamar Hermann, a senior research fellow at the non-partisan Israel Democracy Institute in Jerusalem, said Trump’s late endorsement could help win back wavering Netanyahu voters but was unlikely to draw widespread support.
Most Israelis, even those who are critical of Netanyahu and his government, were largely in favour of the Iran war.
In an election this close, “it couldn’t hurt him, and it might help,” said analyst Aaron David Miller of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace in Washington.
Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist coalition is projected to lose its governing majority, although the opposition may also struggle to form a government, opinion polls show. That could lead to Netanyahu serving as a caretaker prime minister while another election is held.
The US president passed up earlier opportunities to endorse Netanyahu, perhaps because he wanted to see what leverage he could exercise on issues like Gaza or Lebanon, said Miller. In the end, he said, Trump sided with a leader he sees as strong and unfairly persecuted.
“However angry Trump may be at Netanyahu for pushing this Iran war, this in the end was a Trump decision,” Miller added.
A Trump decision not to endorse Netanyahu would have raised “legitimate questions about whether or not the whole Iran venture was in fact something Trump should have done,” he said. REUTERS

Russian Military Satellite Stalks Ukraine-Linked Spy Satellite in Orbit, Closing In to Just 5 Km
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
15:14:19 UTC
00:14:19 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russian Military Satellite Stalks Ukraine-Linked Spy Satellite in Orbit, Closing In to Just 5 Km
A Russian military satellite has approached within approximately 5 kilometers (3 miles) of a commercial radar satellite operated by ICEYE, a company providing satellite imagery used by Ukraine’s military.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Tracking data suggests the Russian spacecraft is maintaining its position nearby, potentially marking an unprecedented maneuver involving two active satellites in low Earth orbit.
According to Defence Blog on October 18, Russian satellite Kosmos 2612 adjusted its orbit on October 16 to approach ICEYE-X36, a synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellite operated by the Finnish-founded company’s US division.
Astrophysicist and independent satellite tracker Jonathan McDowell identified the maneuver using updated orbital data. He said the Russian spacecraft appeared to be maintaining a position within 5 kilometers of ICEYE-X36, although further observations were needed for confirmation.
“New TLEs show that K2612 made a manuever on Oct 16 and is now stationkeeping within 5 km or less of ICEYE X36. To my knowledge this is the first LEO rendezvous of two active satellites where the owner of one of the sats did not give approval,” McDowell wrote on X.
Space surveillance company LeoLabs separately told Axios that the Russian satellite’s movement appeared deliberate, placing Kosmos 2612 approximately three miles from ICEYE-X36 as of October 17. ICEYE declined to comment.
The company operates radar imaging satellites capable of observing Earth’s surface regardless of cloud cover or daylight conditions. Ukraine has used ICEYE imagery since 2022, including data from a satellite purchased through crowdfunding.
A Ukrainian official confirmed to Axios that the country’s military cooperates with ICEYE but could not establish whether ICEYE-X36 specifically supports Ukrainian operations.
As reported by Defence Blog, Kosmos 2612 was launched in April 2026 aboard a Soyuz-2.1b rocket from Russia’s Plesetsk Cosmodrome alongside five other military satellites.
According to the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), five satellites from that launch conducted orbital adjustments in May, bringing them into the same orbital plane as ICEYE-X36.
One reportedly passed within approximately 2.5 kilometers (1.6 miles) of the commercial satellite on May 26. ICEYE CEO Rafal Modrzewski later told that the company had maneuvered its satellite in response.
Previously, in March 2026, reports revealed that Russia’s Luch-2 military satellite had been shadowing European communications satellites, including Intelsat-39, which is also used by Germany’s Bundeswehr. The spacecraft’s proximity reportedly raised concerns about intercepted communications and potential interference with satellite operations.

Love, Loathing and the Zionist Underground: A Novel in Which Everything Happens
Early on while reading "Fate," Zeruya Shalev's 2021 novel released in Joanna Chen's English translation this week, I realized that I've read a lot of contemporary literary fiction lately where nothing much happens. This is not a slight against the slightly plotted novel, but a note on the abundant action of Shalev's work, which explodes and melts in your hands.
In "Fate," everything happens: love, secrets, divorce, infidelity, fevered deathbed declarations, guerilla warfare, religious epiphany, Oedipal-adjacent dynamics, momentary necrophilia, spaghetti Bolognese. "Fate" is not for the faint of heart.
The novel begins within the long-ago memories of Rachel, a Jewish freedom fighter – or terrorist, depending who you ask – who has braved sniper fire traveling from Tel Aviv to bang the door of her mother-in-law's Jerusalem home when her young husband, Mano, suddenly leaves her. It is the dawn of Israel's independence, and everything but her convictions are provisional. Moving forward to the present day, elderly Rachel is at her own home in a West Bank settlement, awaiting an introductory visit from Atara, the daughter eventually born to this man who would blockade and divorce her decades earlier. Atara has come because Mano mentioned Rachel – actually, mistook Atara for Rachel – only as he lay dying.
From here the story proceeds, shifting between the poles of these two women, Rachel and Atara, both tied to one another by forces beyond their wills, both facing the vicissitudes of life in Israel from the vantage points of different politics and generations. "This is a different country," Rachel notes of Israel today, "gray and crowded, hiding behind walls and barbed wire fences, a land that has lost faith in its righteousness." She is cranky, tired, a patriot bewildered by her nation's evolution and bitter, still, over the British overlords who killed her friends: "Boaz and Arieh and Yisrael and Uri and Elhanan and Shlomo and Gedalia and Zvi and Haim and Uzi and Yosef and Shmuel and Hemda and Ruth and Meir and Shemesh," a line she recites often, like prayer or meditation.

Two Romanian F-16s shot down two jet-powered Russian Geran attack drones over Romania’s territorial waters near Sulina on the evening of 17 October, Romania’s Defense Ministry said. The ministry released cockpit images of the mission the next day, as NATO allies prepare to discuss Black Sea security at a special session Romania requested.
This comes as Moscow continues its air attacks on Ukraine, while the US is trying to make deals with Russia over its diesel and lift sanctions. Russia keeps striking Ukraine’s energy system and cities, while its drones and suspected saboteurs keep turning up inside NATO, from tankers hit off Romania to a foiled arson attempt at a Starlink site in Lithuania.
Down within minutes
The F-16s took off from the 86th Air Base at Borcea at 17:43 after radar detected a group of air targets about 120 km east of Zmiinyi (Snake) Island, flying southwest, Ukrainian military outlet Militarnyi reported, citing the ministry. The first drone entered Romanian airspace at 17:59 and was shot down at 18:01 southeast of Sulina. The second entered at 18:01 and was downed at 18:05 east of Sulina.
Both were jet-powered attack drones of the Geran family, the ministry said. The Geran is Russia’s version of the Iranian-designed Shahed. When first detected, the drones were about 65 km from the coast of Russian-occupied Crimea and 140 km from the Ukrainian-held shore, and their southwest course may point to Russian origin, Militarnyi calculated.
Congress gave Trump 30 days to hit Russia’s oil buyers with 100% tariffs. He waives them two days before deadline, citing US interests. Moscow calls it historic
The ministry posted the cockpit images on 18 October, showing a missile launch and a fireball over the sea. “Targets spotted, identified, engaged and neutralized!” it wrote.
Allies to meet on the Black Sea
A special session of the North Atlantic Council, NATO’s top decision-making body, will discuss defense and deterrence in the Black Sea on 20 October at Romania’s request. Romanian President Nicușor Dan has confirmed that the two tankers that caught fire near Sulina last week were hit by drones, and a NATO military source told Reuters they were Russian.
Romanian radar has logged 54 drone intrusions into the country’s air and sea space since Russia’s full-scale invasion, 35 of them this year, and the military has shot down six such targets in 2026, Defense Ministry data show.
Searches in Poland and Lithuania
Within hours, Poland’s Operational Command said it was checking a possible airspace violation by an unknown object overnight into 18 October. Troops, police, and military police searched for a possible crash site south of Lublin after residents reported the loud sound of a flying object around 02:00, Militarnyi reported.
On the morning of 18 October, an unknown drone entered Lithuania’s airspace and triggered air raid alerts, the country’s crisis management center said. NATO jets accompanied it but could not shoot it down because of bad weather, Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said. Debris preliminarily identified as drone parts was later found in the village of Juodžioniai in Pasvalys district, and the army said the drone may have entered from the direction of Poland.
Romania moved from escorting Russia’s stray drones to firing on them in July, when its F-16s downed three in 72 hours.

French government in crisis talks after ‘colossal failure of the state’

The French president, Emmanuel Macron, has criticised “unbridled violence” after one of the most violent days of unrest in years left public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted and more than 2,000 people arrested in cities across the country.
“Watching these images, we have all asked ourselves how could French people do this to France?” he said in a televised address.
Macron said “nothing justifies” violence and that local state officials would be able to ban certain street gatherings if they deemed it necessary.
He said a distinction must be drawn between what he called genuine, peaceful demonstrators making demands over the cost of living and the education system, and others who “destroy, ransack and loot”. He criticised what he called “factious groups from the ultra-left, joined by numerous delinquents.”
Politicians on the left and right called for the resignation of the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, after the government appeared to have been caught by surprise by the scale of violence on Saturday as state buildings were stormed and torched, bus stops smashed, roads barricaded and shops broken into and destroyed. Protests also took place in Spain, Italy and Portugal.
Crowds clashed with police at Place de la République in central Paris on Sunday afternoon as violence flared for a second day. Electric bikes were piled in some streets and set alight. Bottles and rocks were thrown and thick plumes of smoke rose from burning bins. Police responded with teargas and stun grenades.
Police and officials faced challenges of different types on Saturday. First, tens of thousands of peaceful protesters attended calm marches through major cities including Paris, supporting schoolchildren’s demands for more teachers and repairs to decrepit schools. Those marches, which came after four weeks of street marches and barricades of schools, were attended by parents, teachers and grandparents as well as students and workers protesting over the high cost of living. The demonstrators carried banners saying the government was not listening to them and calling for more money for public services.
But separately to those peaceful demonstrations, different groups caught police and officials by surprise with moving gatherings, sporadic burning, the barricading of streets and clashes with police in cities including Paris, Bordeaux, Nice and Marseille.
Finally, masked looters took advantage of what French media called the “chaos” on the streets to smash shopfronts and grab goods. In Paris, groups of looters, some of whom appeared to be children, were seen running through the night with clothes and shoeboxes after masked adult men smashed shopfronts.
In Paris, where police said a record 855 people had been arrested, the burnt-out remains of barricades built using bikes, bins and other materials littered streets on Sunday. Several streets had smashed shop windows and the remains of torched cars. The capital had experienced “a level of violence that we have never seen before, I believe”, said the Socialist deputy mayor, Lamia El Aaraje.
In Limoges in central France, where the 19th-century town hall was burned down, the mayor, Guillaume Guérin, said the people who stormed his building “were not demonstrators that defend causes” but “people organised for war”. He said those who stormed and torched the town hall had told a building caretaker he would be killed, and told elected officials they would “burn”. He said there had been a failure of the state to deal with the crisis.
“Around 3.30pm our municipal police, although present in number, found themselves no longer able to fight against the violence of rioters because they had run out of ammunition,” Guérin said. He called this “a colossal failure of the state”.
In Marseille, where masked groups stormed the city hall and a police station, the Socialist mayor, Benoît Payan, told BFMTV: “I have no words … I never thought I’d ever live through something like this. Hordes of rioters and looters attacked our common [state] buildings … with no real demands, but with the sole aim to wreck the demands of those who had demonstrated legitimately.”
Payan said questions must be asked about policing tactics, as other town hall buildings, for example in Lille, were also targeted.
Grégory Doucet, the Green mayor of Lyon, said he had never seen such violence in his city, including the torching of the historic tourist office. He told Le Monde: “I’m stunned by the violence against public and state property. I saw and heard fear and anger. Shop owners felt abandoned.”
Doucet said the government must find a “sense of nuance” in properly examining what happened and “avoiding stereotypes”. He said the government needed to give a political response to long-running societal demands from peaceful demonstrators on one hand, and also examine the roots of violence.
Traders’ unions said more than 1,500 shops and businesses had been ransacked, with the cost running into tens of millions of euros. “This had nothing to do with the peaceful protesters,” said one shoe shop owner in Paris. “These were organised groups who were breaking things and looting. We’d never seen anything like it.”
Opposition politicians questioned the government’s policing tactics, saying there had been a lack of state intelligence.
The interior ministry said there had been more than 2,000 arrests and about 600 police, firefighters and paramedics had been hurt. A 17-year-old boy had his right hand blown off by a crowd-control grenade in the eastern-central city of Saint-Étienne. A 17-year-old girl lost an eye in Mulhouse and a policing investigation was opened into the circumstances.
Macron’s centrist government and the far-right frontrunner for the presidential election, Marine Le Pen, both blamed what they called “ultra-left” groups for the violence. The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said the government would not be “intimidated” by violence, and blamed the unrest on the “ultra-left” and criminals.
The radical-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who attended the peaceful street demonstration in Paris on Saturday, accused the government of organisational failings that had “opened the door to chaos”.
Lecornu replied on social media: “Laying the responsibility for violence on heads of police is a dangerous and cynical reversal of responsibilities.”

Drones don’t sell on need. They sell on value - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
15:08:36 UTC
00:08:36 KST

Every sales manual says the same thing: find the pain, sell the cure. In my industry, that advice is half right, and the wrong half is expensive.
A drone produces a dozen different kinds of value. It surveys a highway interchange in an hour, to the centimeter, where a crew once stood in traffic for days. It collects in one day the thermal data on a solar field of 20,000 panels. It patrols a fence at two in the morning without a car, and puts live video in a control room before a guard has found his keys.
Increasingly, it is sold not as hardware but as a service. In drone-as-a-service, the customer buys no aircraft, holds no license, and does not need to know how to fly. The operator installs the station, holds the approvals, trains the dispatchers, maintains the fleet, and carries the responsibility. The customer pays monthly for an outcome: a patrol, a survey, a defect list.
Autonomy is what makes that model work. A drone that lives on site in a weatherproof dock, charges itself, launches on an alarm or a schedule, and lands without anyone beside it turns a drone service from a visit into a utility. Our stations put a drone in the air within 15 seconds of a call; it flies for 54 minutes, recharges in 27, and is directed by a dispatcher who never leaves the control room.
Here is my argument: the urgency of a customer’s need decides how fast he arrives, but only visible value decides whether he signs and whether he stays, and making that value visible, to customers who do not yet feel the need, is the burden of the operators.
One morning near Lod
At about 6:30 a.m. on September 15, 2024, a missile fired from Yemen fell in open ground near Lod, in central Israel. Six weeks earlier, we had installed an autonomous drone at a power station in the area. It was airborne within seconds. The control room had live video of the impact area before anyone had left the gate, and the response teams drove out knowing what was waiting for them.
Nobody in that control room needed to be told afterwards what the drone was for.
That is what need does: it accelerates. But mornings like that are rare. What a customer pays for in every other month is the routine, patrols flown on schedule, alarms verified from the air before anyone is dispatched, every event on video. Need opened the door. Value is the rent.
Now consider a customer with no need at all. This summer, our analysis of an 88-megawatt solar field in the South found dozens of dead strings, rows of panels producing nothing, while the site’s monitoring reported normal operation. The owner felt no pain; the dashboard was green. The loss was invisible, and worth well over $100,000 a year. Need would never have brought that customer to us. Only a number could.
The clearest proof comes from California. Since 2018, police in Chula Vista have sent drones to more than 25,000 emergency calls. The drone arrived first on 17,170 of them, in an average of 97 seconds, and on 4,629 calls, no officer had to be sent at all. A city council does not need to have suffered a slow response to understand that number.
Why the value has outrun the market
None of this is Israeli. In 2016, PwC put the value of business services and labor that drones could replace at more than $127 billion. Nearly a decade later, Drone Industry Insights sizes the entire commercial drone-services market at about $29b. The value was always there. Few customers could see it in their own numbers.
The European Union Aviation Safety Agency's figures from November 2025 count 2.5 million registered drone operators across 31 states, and 4,226 operational authorizations, the permits behind serious commercial flying. In the United States, the rule for routine flight beyond visual line of sight, the rule that makes docked autonomy ordinary, was proposed in August 2025 and, as of early October, was still unpublished. Israel has allowed docked flight without a pilot on site since 2022. Regulation is moving; customers are slower.
Who teaches, and who collects
So who makes the value visible? Not the manufacturer, who meets the customer once, at the sale. In a service model, the operator meets him every day. We fly more than 15,000 drone missions a year for more than 200 business customers, and each arrives at a different distance from his own need: defense with the need already sharp, infrastructure security after an event, solar slowly, surveyors on cost. All of them sign for the same reason, a value they can measure. That is why our process starts with the customer’s own baseline, not a demonstration flight: a site visit, a survey, a pilot with metrics agreed in advance, and a decision taken on the data.
It is also why autonomy is the core of our business and the center of its future. A crew-based service sells a day of flying. A stationed drone sells every day. Once the station, the certification, and the control room exist, each additional mission, a patrol, a thermal scan, a check after a storm, costs almost nothing, and each one adds a line to the customer’s baseline. The next step is already visible: control centers running many stations at once under airspace-management systems, and the same network carrying urgent medical supplies and deliveries. We are starting urban delivery work with Israel’s Innovation Authority.
The economic conclusion follows. In drone-as-a-service, value goes to whoever owns the measurement, the company that set the baseline and reports against it every month. Flight hours are already a commodity; the dock is becoming one. The network of stations, and the baseline behind each of them, is not. So the education that builds it has to carry a price: our academy, which trains close to 1,000 commercial operators a year, is a business; dispatcher training is a line on the quote; implementation is a phase with a fee.
What still has to be fixed
Let me name where we got it wrong.
Too often we sold the capability we found impressive rather than the value the customer could measure. A thermal map is beautiful. A site manager wants to know what Monday’s repairs are worth. Every time we led with the technology, the sale got longer.
Early this year, we planned to sell autonomy through security companies, as a back office behind their brands. Within months, we reversed it. A service sold on value needs the operator in the room when the baseline is set. We now sell directly.
And “autonomous” still carries more people than the word suggests. The aircraft flies itself; the service does not run itself. Anyone promising an asset owner a lights-out operation today is selling something.
A customer who needs a drone will eventually find one. A customer who can see what a drone is worth will pay for it every month. The first is a sale. The second is a business, and autonomy is how it scales.
The writer, a colonel in the reserves, is founder and CEO of Propeller Drones Ltd., Israel’s largest drone services provider.
This was written in collaboration with Propeller Drones.

Tirana sees sixth day of violent protests as Albania’s PM refuses to resign
At this moment, no one is clear on what tomorrow will bring, says Albanian journalist Lindita Karadaku.
Violent protests have rocked Albania’s capital Tirana for the sixth consecutive day as Prime Minister Edi Rama, who is serving his fourth term, ruled out resigning.
Hundreds of protesters gathered again on Sunday in front of the Ministry of Education, chanting “Rama, resign” in a tense standoff with the police, who later used rubber bullets, water cannons and tear gas to hold back the crowds.
Shops and institutions in the centre of the city have secured their doors and windows with metal shutters, while city workers removed paving stones to prevent their use by protesters.
Lindita Karadaku, a journalist for Albanian news outlet TV Klan, told Al Jazeera on Sunday that it was difficult to see how the unrest could unfold or how long it could last.
“Prime Minister Rama is determined and has made it very clear that he will not resign, but also the young people who are protesting are determined and make it clear that they will not give up so easily,” she said. “At this moment, no one is clear what tomorrow will bring.”
Rama said during a live social media stream on Sunday that “the government is not being challenged” but implied that ongoing unrest in the country might affect Albania’s path towards European Union membership.
“Albanians need to think very clearly,” Rama said. “Do they want this, or do they want the EU?”
Albania is hoping to achieve membership status by 2030.
Key demands
Protesters are demanding better education, more jobs, a stop to alleged ongoing corruption, and Rama’s resignation.
According to local media reports, demonstrators in Tirana were primarily attacking government institutions and the police, including the Ministry of Education building and the area around Rama’s office.
The prime minister, who has been in office since 2013, blamed the involvement of a “foreign hand” for the surge in protests and said his government is doing its best to address corruption.
At the same time, he said that he was ready to listen to the justified demands of students and discuss the costs of education. But he insisted that those responsible for the destruction of property must be held accountable.
In an interview with Al Jazeera, a political analyst from Tirana, Mentor Nazarko, said Rama does not seem to understand “the depth of the problem, has not found solutions and has lost a lot of time”.
“His legitimacy has melted away. Between him and the citizens there is almost nothing but the police: untrained for protests, poorly paid, with segments that collaborate with crime and corruption,” he said.
According to a Ministry of Health report issued on Sunday morning, 65 people were injured, of which 37 were police officers, while 12 were hospitalised. Since Tuesday, 272 people have been injured in the clashes, including 169 police officers, the ministry said.
Discontent in Albania has been growing for months. The first protests in the country this year were called the “Flamingo Revolution” and began in May. Demonstrators rebelled against the controversial project of a luxury tourist complex in the south of Albania, affiliated with Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of US President Donald Trump.

I saw rioting, looting, above all, anger. If French leaders think more violence will solve this, they’re mistaken | Oliver Haynes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
15:06:42 UTC
00:06:42 KST

The first thing I learned on the streets of Paris this weekend is that there is no arguing with teargas. I arrived at Place de la République just after 1pm yesterday. The mood was festive until police started firing volleys of teargas into the square from Rue du Faubourg-du-Temple.
I didn’t see the inciting incident – if there even was one – and tried walking into the cloud of CS gas hanging in the air. It was impossible. The gas clings to your nose and burns your eyes, and you quickly start struggling to breathe. I retreated towards the Boulevard de Magenta, blinking furiously to stop the stinging.
This approach to the crowd had been adopted by the authorities early in the day, causing chaos across the city and setting the tone for what would follow. A friend had to return to her home with her elderly parents because police had fired teargas “at random” at a crowd of young people in Strasbourg-Saint-Denis in the 10th arrondissement.
I headed back up the Boulevard de Magenta. There I met protesters including a student at the Sorbonne, who had come to “support the highschoolers first and foremost, and to demand more money in public schools, from primary schools to universities”. Another major factor that he said had motivated him to come out on to the street “was the repression faced by highschoolers, who are under 18”, such as an incident in Lens, where a police grenade blew a 15-year-old’s hand to bits.
Other protesters I spoke to came from various sections of society: young, old, white and from ethnic minority backgrounds. People were there in their capacity as workers in a union, students in a lycée or individual citizens who had come out in anger at the rising cost of living. The price of petrol, the original motivating factor behind the 2018 gilets jaunes (yellow vest) movement, had prompted several people to come out after it hit a record €2.4 per litre at the end of last month.
This section of the protest was completely peaceful, marching away from République, making lots of noise and climbing on scaffolding to fly flags, but otherwise doing nothing beyond articulating political demands. Between 550,000 and 800,000 people took to the streets across France as part of protests like these.
When I returned to République around 4pm, I saw that the situation had descended into chaos. Stun grenades were exploding everywhere, and protesters were throwing bottles at the police. Smoke from a blazing car filled the air. A branch of Nicolas, a chain wine shop, had its window smashed in and black-clad protesters looted it – not for the wine but for missiles to throw at police in retaliation for the stun grenades.
I was unable to stop and talk to people amid this fury, but my sense was that this was a combination of black bloc – anarchists who come out to many protests to cause trouble – gilets jaunes, young and middle-aged people who were furious at the government and the police, and, of course, opportunistic young men looking for a scrap. As ever with street protests, many people, many motivations.
There were cries of the old gilets jaunes slogan Macron Démission (“Resign Macron”). Beyond the organised group of hobbyist rioters, the dominant emotions seemed to be fear and rage. With each stun grenade the non-violent parts of the crowd were thrown into panic, but would then regroup and stand their ground while the rioters continued throwing missiles. Perhaps the feeling could be summed up by a poster I saw the day before the protest: “Lost hope, 17/10 to find it again. Fuck just about everything 17/10. We are already in hell meet on 17/10”.
So what next? With more than 1,800 arrests, what will become of these people, this movement, these riots?
There is a sense among certain parts of the French population that making enough noise, including acts of vandalism, sends a signal to power. And indeed, there is some evidence to suggest this is the case. Neoliberal reforms have been rebuffed successfully on several occasions in France, primarily through strike waves or roundabout blockades – though these too had the presence of a radical fringe, willing to set fire to things.
As the dust settles, what will be the political repercussions? Marine Le Pen, attempting to profit from the situation, has positioned herself on the side of those angry at the cost of living, while condemning the looters. In a statement she described the French people as caught between the “austerity and fiscal hammering of those in power and the insurrectionary activists”. She promised to “free” the French “from Macronist toxic policies and protect them from the violence of the far left”. Carefully omitted was the fact that her party is proposing deeper austerity than even the Macronists, but the images of fire and looting that will be broadcast on every news channel reinforce her narrative of restoration of order to the streets.
Meanwhile, the French left, chiefly represented by Jean-Luc Mélenchon, is defending the protesters and seeking to channel their anger into the presidential campaign, focusing on the violence of the police over that of the rioters. The left may also be able to make gains from this tense situation.
While the government seems determined to continue with its budget unimpeded, it may only be a matter of time before another such explosion occurs. You can’t argue with teargas, but it will only hold the inevitable at bay for so long.
- Oliver Haynes is a journalist and co-host of Sacré Bleu: the French presidential election podcast

Americans increasingly dissatisfied with Trump as midterms approach: Poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
15:04:01 UTC
00:04:01 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
18 October 2026•Update: 18 October 2026
By Berk Kutay Gokmen
ISTANBUL (AA) - A growing number of Americans believe the country is heading in the wrong direction, with President Donald Trump’s approval rating falling to a second-term low as Republicans face mounting challenges ahead of November’s midterm elections, according to a new poll.
The NBC News poll showed Saturday that 71% of US adults believe the country is on the “wrong track,” the highest percentage recorded during Trump’s second term.
Trump’s approval rating dropped to 34%, while 66% disapproved of his performance. The proportion of respondents who strongly disapprove of the president reached 51%, marking a new high for his second term.
Economic dissatisfaction appears to be a major factor behind the negative public mood. The economy ranked as the most important issue for 31% of respondents, while 44% said their financial situation had worsened over the past year.
Rising living costs are also weighing on households, with 67% describing gasoline prices as a serious problem. Many respondents said they had changed grocery purchases or reduced spending to cover essential expenses.
The survey also revealed growing political challenges for Republicans. Among registered voters, 55% preferred Democrats to control Congress, compared with 45% who favored Republicans, signaling potential difficulties for the party in power in the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
A majority of respondents, 58%, said Trump’s policies were hurting the country, while 28% believed they were helping.
Trump received his lowest approval ratings for his handling of the cost of living, at 27%, and the war with Iran, at 29%. Immigration and border security remained his strongest issue, with 43% approving of his approach.

Pope Leo XIV after his hospital stay: "I feel closer to those who suffer illness"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
15:02:19 UTC
00:02:19 KST

Discharged on Saturday after surgery for a malignant tumour in his right lung, Pope Leo led the Angelus from the Apostolic Palace and thanked doctors, saying he will gradually resume duties.
Met with warm applause from the crowd of faithful who had gathered in St Peter’s Square in the Vatican on Sunday morning, Pope Leo XIV appeared punctually at noon at the window of the Apostolic Palace to lead the Angelus prayer.
Leo XIV was discharged on Saturday from Rome’s Gemelli hospital after a five‑day stay following the removal of the lower lobe of his right lung, due to the presence of a pulmonary adenocarcinoma.
"I want to thank all those who have prayed for me in these days. I really felt your support, thank you!" the Pontiff said. "I am particularly grateful to the doctors, nurses and all the staff of the Gemelli Polyclinic," the Pope continued, before describing how he experienced his time in hospital: "It made me feel in a special way close to all those who are going through illness and a condition of infirmity."
Leo XVI then said that in "this delicate phase" he will gradually resume his activities. The Pontiff is expected to travel to Latin America in the coming weeks.
How is Pope Leo? Professor Margaritora: "An ideal patient"
Professor Stefano Margaritora, the surgeon who operated on Leo XIV’s lung on Tuesday 13 October, spoke about the upcoming apostolic journey. In an interview with Vatican media he explained that there are no clinical reasons why this trip should not take place.
According to Margaritoria, at the time he was discharged from hospital the Pope was in "satisfactory" clinical condition. "The re‑expansion of the lung after the operation is progressing according to the time frame normally expected. Overall, therefore, his condition is good," the professor added.
He also said the discovery of the malignant tumour was accidental. "As unfortunately often happens, while carrying out routine abdominal tests, this small spot was found in the chest, at the base of the lungs. This is fairly common, because when radiological examinations of the abdomen are done, since the diaphragm is a kind of parachute, the lung bases are normally visible. But certainly, if this small spot had been a little higher, it would not have been seen," Margaritoria added.
The professor said he was satisfied with the operation and recounted how, in his post‑operative recovery, the Pope put "heart and soul" into it. "His determination to recover within a very short time is extremely effective from every point of view: it has truly been exemplary," he added.
"Pope Leo was an ideal patient. I don’t say that to flatter him, but he really was a patient who did not cause the slightest problem for the team looking after him," he also said.
Margaritoria then said that convalescence will take a couple of weeks and, for this reason, he believes the Pope’s trip to Latin America, scheduled to start on 6 November, can go ahead. "I would say there are no clinical reasons why this journey should not take place," the professor said.

Israel’s current government is failing. The next one must do better - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

As we approach election day a week from tomorrow, it is worth taking a look at our 37th government, which has probably been the most unstable and malfunctioning government Israel has ever had. Israel’s interest is undoubtedly that its next government will be better, in all respects.
When the government was formed on December 29, 2022, it was supported by the 64 MKs of the Likud, the Religious Zionist Party and Otzma Yehudit union, United Torah Judaism, Shas, and Noam. Soon after being established, it included 32 ministers, some of whom (for example Ron Dermer, who later left the government) were not MKs, while others left the Knesset on the basis of the “Norwegian Law,” to enable other members of their respective parties to enter the Knesset.
In a study about the government soon after it was formed, Prof. Ofer Kenig of the Israel Democracy Institute pointed out that most of the ministers in the new government lacked ministerial experience. In retrospect, we can add that quite a few of the ministers appointed were also unsuitable from a professional point of view, such as Education Minister Yoav Kisch (Likud), and former construction and housing minister Yitzhak Goldknopf (United Torah Judaism).
Several other appointments were of persons prone to be problematic because of their extreme positions and/or conduct, such as Itamar Ben-Gvir (Otzma Yehudit) and Bezalel Smotrich (Religious Zionist Party), who were appointed to the National Security Ministry and the Finance Ministry, respectively (Smotrich was also appointed as an additional minister in the Defense Ministry on Judea and Samaria affairs).
Though there are limits to which a prospective prime minister can decide on the ministers from parties other than his own, and sometimes even on the ministers from his own party, we should at least expect that he will seek to establish the best possible government to serve the state, rather than his own political survival.
In the second half of the government’s term, Netanyahu’s appointment of Israel Katz on November 7, 2024, as defense minister, to replace Yoav Gallant, was undoubtedly based on the latter consideration. Of the eight defense ministers who served under Netanyahu since 1996, Katz is undoubtedly the least suitable from a professional point of view.
When the government was formed at the end of 2022, it was the second largest government Israel had ever had – the largest was the short-lived Netanyahu-Gantz government (Israel’s 35th government), which included 34 ministers. Both governments included many superfluous small ministries.
On October 12, 2023, Benny Gantz’s National Unity Party joined the government following the outbreak of war in the Gaza Strip, and three of its members – Gantz, Gadi Eisenkot, and Gideon Sa’ar – became ministers-without-portfolio. All the components of the National Unity Party resigned on June 9, 2024, against the background of their rejected demand that the government adopt a strategic plan for the war, and delays in bringing back all the hostages.
However, on September 29, 2024, Sa’ar and his newly established United Right party, rejoined the government, with Sa’ar being appointed foreign affairs minister. At this stage, the coalition’s majority rose to 68.
TODAY, MORE than two years later, the coalition includes only 60 members, after Noam left on March 25, 2025, and Torah Judaism left on July 14, 2025. Shas has not formally left the coalition, but has resigned from all its coalition positions in the government and the Knesset.
Noam left because its leader and only MK, Avi Maoz, claimed that most of the promises he had received upon joining were not kept, while the two haredi parties quit against the background of the non-passage of a law for the full exemption of the haredim from military service, which Netanyahu had promised them.
Though Netanyahu failed to give the haredi parties what they demanded, it was another case of Netanyahu putting his own political survival before the national interest.
What this means in practice is that besides being justice minister, Yariv Levin also serves as acting labor minister, Jerusalem and Jewish tradition minister, and religious services minister, while Tourism Minister Haim Katz also serves as health minister, construction and housing minister, and welfare and social security minister.
All these extra ministerial positions were held by the two haredi parties, and Netanyahu decided not to appoint full-time replacements because he needs the haredi parties for his political survival.
One may argue about Levin’s quality as justice minister – depending on whether one supports or opposes the plans he put forward for a legal reform/revolution of Israel’s justice system in January, 2023. But given the major manual labor shortage that Israel is suffering, the absence of a full-time labor minister is no joke.
It could be argued that even though these days, when foreign tourism to Israel is down to a trickle, leaving Israel’s health, construction and housing, and welfare and social security in the hands of Tourism Minister Katz is tantamount to neglect in these fields.
The problem is especially severe in the case of health, which is in a serious crisis due to the results of the unending war, and the vast numbers of physically and mentally injured military personnel. Add to this a growing shortage of doctors and other medical personnel, due to the departure from Israel of over 4,000 doctors in the years 2023-2025.
Experts on Israel’s political system argue that today there isn’t a single ministry that is run efficiently and fulfills its tasks satisfactorily. It is also a statistical fact that coalition funds – money provided by the government to the parties that are members of the coalition for distribution to their specific sectors without Knesset approval – are much higher today than since the system began in the 1980s.
From 2023-2026, coalition funds reached NIS 20.1 billion, while the ministerial budgets for education, health, welfare, and employment for the population at large were cut by NIS 11.7 billion.
Why is this important in regard to the elections to the 26th Knesset?
Because, should Netanyahu once again emerge victorious, the government he will form in its aftermath might be even worse than the outgoing government. Voters should certainly take this into account.
However, at the moment it looks as if the best the Likud and its political bloc can hope for is that the opposing political bloc will fail to form a government like themselves, and Netanyahu will remain the prime minister of a transition government for several months, until new elections take place for the 27th Knesset.
Should the political bloc that opposes the current government, either headed by Yashar’s Gadi Eisenkot or someone else, manage to form a new coalition after the elections, constructing a more stable and properly functioning government will undoubtedly be one of its first goals.
The writer has written journalistic and academic articles, as well as several books, on international relations, Zionism, Israeli politics, and parliamentarism. From 1994 to 2010, she worked at the Knesset Library and the Knesset Research and Information Center.
