The Israeli blockade constricts the dining tables of Gazans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
14:59:11 UTC
23:59:11 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel's blockade leaves hungry Gazans facing astronomical prices, unhealthy food choices
Israel's devastating war and blockade on the Gaza Strip have left many Palestinians struggling not only to find food, but also to afford the variety needed to maintain a healthy diet.
Despite the availability of some products in local markets, soaring prices, diminished purchasing power and restrictions on the entry of goods have left families relying on whatever they can obtain to stave off hunger.
For Umm Hadi al-Arja, a displaced mother of four from Beit Lahia in northern Gaza, feeding her children means baking bread in a clay oven fuelled by scraps of cardboard and making do with whatever supplies she can obtain.
The family lives in a dilapidated tent near Gaza City's coastline, relying partly on canned goods distributed through World Food Programme (WFP) food parcels.
Meat, chicken and fish have become unaffordable luxuries, leaving her struggling to provide her children with a balanced diet.
"I have four children, and I try to provide them with whatever food is available to us," al-Arja told The New Arab. "We bake bread and serve it with oil, za'atar or cheese. We do everything we can to ensure they don't go hungry, but I simply cannot provide everything they need."
Israeli restrictions on food supplies and soaring market prices have further narrowed her family's choices, she said.
"Despite the so-called ceasefire, we cannot obtain healthy, nutritious food. Even when items are available in the markets, they are unaffordable," she said. "We eat whatever we can manage to get, not what our bodies actually require."
High prices deepen the food crisis
Mahdi Shomer, who lives with his six children in a tent in Gaza City, faces the same dilemma.
He visits markets where many essential products are displayed, but often returns without buying what his family needs because he cannot afford the prices.
"When I go to the market, I see many of the items we need, but I cannot afford to buy them," Shomer told TNA. "The issue isn't always the availability of food, but rather our ability to pay for it."
His purchases are increasingly dictated by necessity rather than nutritional value.
"I now only buy enough to stave off hunger, rather than what the body actually needs," he said. "Sometimes we make do with just bread and a few simple items. We are forced to go without meat, chicken and fruit because they are too expensive."
The gap between food availability and purchasing power remains a major obstacle for households already dependent on humanitarian assistance.
According to Gaza's Government Media Office, 74,855 humanitarian aid trucks had entered the Strip out of the 219,000 expected under the ceasefire agreement that took effect on 10 October 2025, representing approximately 34 per cent of the agreed total.
A joint food security analysis by the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), the WFP and UNICEF found that approximately 1.4 million people, or nearly 67 per cent of Gaza's population, were facing critical or worse levels of acute food insecurity. This compared with approximately 1.6 million people, or 77 per cent of the population, at the end of 2025.
The analysis also found that approximately 212,000 people were experiencing emergency-level food insecurity.
Although some indicators had improved, the agencies warned that the situation remained fragile and that assistance did not always provide sufficient quantities or diversity to meet nutritional needs.
The destruction and restricted accessibility of agricultural land have further undermined local food production.
According to the analysis, more than 70 per cent of agricultural land was inaccessible, leaving only about 3 per cent usable and limiting farmers' ability to supply fresh vegetables and other produce.
Malnutrition risks extend beyond hunger
Palestinian nutritionist Mahmoud al-Saqqa warns that high food prices and limited choices are forcing Gaza's residents to rely on diets lacking essential nutrients.
"Many families depend on canned food and products high in salt, sugar and fat because fresh produce has become too expensive," he told TNA.
"People may eat enough to satisfy their hunger but still lack the proteins, vitamins and minerals their bodies need to stay healthy," he said, warning that poor nutrition could weaken immunity, particularly among children, older people and those with chronic illnesses.
"Malnutrition does not always mean being underweight. A person can consume enough calories but still lack essential nutrients because their diet is not varied," he added.
Children are particularly vulnerable, with some also forced to take on adult responsibilities.
Fourteen-year-old Mohammed al-Yazji lost his mother during the war, while his father was detained by the Israeli army, leaving him to care for his younger siblings.
"Every day, I think about what we will eat and how I will provide food for my siblings," Mohammed told TNA. "They are young and need many things. I try not to let them feel that we cannot meet their needs, but the situation is extremely difficult."
"We need a variety of food, not just bread and a few basic items. I wish I could provide meat and fruit, but sometimes we have to make do with whatever is available," he said.
Al-Saqqa explained that improving nutrition required access to affordable fresh food, including vegetables, fruits and protein-rich products, as well as targeted support for those at risk of malnutrition.
While humanitarian aid remains essential, addressing the crisis also requires allowing sufficient food supplies into Gaza, supporting local agriculture and making nutritious food affordable for families.

Ukraine Graduate Fellowship Group Fund to Support HKS MC/MPA Students from Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
14:58:00 UTC
23:58:00 KST

The Ukraine Graduate Fellowship Group Fund (UGFGF) has been launched this month to support students from Ukraine pursuing a Mid-Career Master in Public Administration (MC/MPA) at the Harvard Kennedy School (HKS).
The effort was spearheaded by Niels Planel, an HKS alumnus who helped establish the fund in coordination with HKS to create new opportunities for Ukrainians committed to leadership and public service. “In the current context, I saw the creation of such a Fellowship as a meaningful way to contribute to Ukraine’s future,” said Planel, a French national.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The fund establishes and supports the Ukraine Graduate Fellowship, which will be open to admitted HKS MC/MPA Program students from Ukraine with a demonstrated interest in leadership and public service. The Fellowship will be awarded to a minimum of one student annually on a competitive, merit basis, with preference given to students with demonstrated financial need. Recipients will receive up to $100,000 for tuition, fees, and living expenses.
The initiative’s first donor is Gérard Wormser, founder of international review Sens Public. Reflecting on the importance of the effort, Wormser, also a French national, stated: “The next chapter in Europe’s history is the democratic transformation of a friendly nation, thereby shaping a better century.”
Founded in 1936, the Harvard Kennedy School is considered the world’s premier leadership and public policy school. Its alumni worldwide include heads of state and government, cabinet ministers, legislators, and leaders across the business, military, media, finance, nonprofit, arts, and technology sectors.
US Resumes Intelligence Sharing With Ukraine, Zelensky Says
The Fellowship will be awarded at the discretion of Harvard Kennedy School’s Degree Programs and Student Affairs office. All admissions and fellowship decisions will be made solely by Harvard Kennedy School in accordance with its established policies and procedures.
HKS considers the following attributes when evaluating applications for admission: Strong academic achievement and intellectual distinction, leadership capabilities and personal character, quantitative proficiency, commitment to public service, diverse experiences and backgrounds.
The program’s length is one year, and on average, the entering age in the MC/MPA program is 38 and students have 14 years of work experience. The admission application deadline for the next school year is Dec. 1, 2026.
Says Planel: “I am hopeful that this Fellowship will create new opportunities for Ukrainians to gain the skills, networks, and experience needed to help shape their country’s future. I encourage Ukrainians committed to leadership and public service to apply.”
More information about the MC/MPA program and admissions process is available through the Harvard Kennedy School’s website.

California wildfire forces thousands to evacuate, burns 570 acres
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
14:54:45 UTC
23:54:45 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
18 October 2026•Update: 18 October 2026
A wildfire in Orange County in US State of California, burned 570 acres and damaged or destroyed seven homes before firefighters made progress in containing the blaze.
All evacuation orders were lifted Saturday night as crews continued battling the Norte Fire, which was 25% contained, according to the Orange County Fire Authority.
The fire broke out around midday Friday in San Clemente, spreading rapidly and forcing thousands of residents to leave their homes. At its peak, approximately 4,600 homes and nearly 16,000 people were within the evacuation zone, fire officials said.
As conditions improved, officials lifted evacuation orders in parts of San Clemente and allowed residents to gradually return to a zone in San Juan Capistrano.
Orange County Fire Authority Fire Chief T.J. McGovern described the challenging conditions at a news conference Friday evening.
"Due to weather and topography, this fire moved fast," McGovern said, describing the wind as "relentless."
No injuries among residents had been reported as of Friday, although two firefighters were hurt, according to officials. The cause of the fire remains under investigation.
The wildfire erupted amid dangerous weather conditions, including high temperatures and strong Santa Ana winds. Red flag warnings remained in effect for Los Angeles and Ventura counties and the Antelope Valley foothills through Saturday night.
Fire crews also faced the challenge of containing another major blaze nearby. The Norte Fire was burning about 20 miles (32 km) north of the Henderson Fire at Camp Pendleton in San Diego County, which had scorched 2,079 acres.
On Friday, officials said around 400 firefighters were working to contain the Norte Fire, with another 400 expected to join the effort.

CISF to reorganise eight territorial sectors into specialised functional units from November 1
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
14:53:33 UTC
23:53:33 KST

NEW DELHI: Come November 1, the Central Industrial Security Force (CISF) will transition from a region-specific administrative and operational control structure to a purely functional one, ensuring that each of its reorganised sectors caters to the specialised requirements of the industries and establishments secured by it.CISF officials said 8 its 11 territorial sectors spread across the country will be reorganised into functional sectors dedicated to govt installations and museums in Delhi, coal industries, power plants, petroleum and natural gas units, and steel industry etc.The National Capital Region (NCR) region, New Delhi will thus become the Govt Buildings, Museums & Monuments and Mass Rapid Transit System (GBMM & MRTS) sector, New Delhi. The North sector, New Delhi will be reorganised as Power-I sector, Delhi and the North Eastern-II sector, Kolkata as Power-II sector, Kolkata. The Eastern sector, Ranchi will be rechristened as Coal Sector, Ranchi and cater to the security needs of the coalfields guarded by CISF.Similarly, the Central sector will become the dedicated Steel sector based at Bhilai. The North Eastern sector at Guwahati has been transformed into the Petroleum and Natural Gas sector, Guwahati.
To fortify India's maritime trade infrastructure, the Western Sector (Mumbai) and South Sector (Chennai) have been respectively transformed into the West Coast Port Sector and the East Coast Port Sector.The existing Department of Atomic Energy and Department of Space sector headquartered at Bengaluru as well as the Airport-I sector, New Delhi and Airport-II sector, Bengaluru, will continue under their respective functional arrangements.“The revised structure, approved by CISF DG Praveer Ranjan with the concurrence of ministry of home affairs (MHA), will come into effect from Nov 1, 2026, a CISF spokesperson said on Sunday. Apart from aligning the supervisory structure of the force more closely with the specific security requirements of different sectors, the new arrangement aims to improve operational oversight, promote sector-specific expertise, ensure greater uniformity insecurity practices and strengthen coordination with the concerned ministries, departments and installation managements.
Over the past 25 years, CISF has progressively adopted a functional approach in selected sectors, including aviation.The experience gained from this approach has highlighted the advantages of specialised supervision, focused training, sector-specific standard operating procedures (SOPs), better utilisation of specialised personnel and closer coordination with the concerned organisations.

Mercedes-Benz to develop self-driving cars with NVIDIA
Mercedes-Benz and NVIDIA will extend their strategic partnership to develop advanced driver assistance and autonomous driving systems, including future Level 4 vehicles, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
The expanded collaboration will combine Mercedes-Benz's automotive engineering and safety expertise with NVIDIA's AI technology and computing platforms to accelerate the development of highly automated vehicles.
The partnership will build on Mercedes-Benz's MB.OS operating system and NVIDIA's Hyperion computing and sensor architecture. NVIDIA's Alpamayo Stack software will provide AI-powered driving capabilities, supporting urban point-to-point navigation, active safety functions and automated parking.
The companies also plan to use NVIDIA's Halos safety system to strengthen vehicle safety through additional safeguards and redundant systems.
The technologies are expected to support the development of vehicles with SAE Level 4 automation, which allows a car to perform all driving tasks within designated conditions or areas without requiring human intervention. Potential applications include autonomous limousine services.
“NVIDIA is our most important strategic partner in automated driving,” said Jörg Burzer, a member of the Mercedes-Benz Group AG management board and its chief technology officer for development and procurement.
He said the expanded partnership builds on years of cooperation and aims to deliver new driving technologies while maintaining the safety standards expected by Mercedes-Benz customers.
Beyond self-driving technology, the companies will continue using NVIDIA's computing capabilities in vehicle engineering simulations and Mercedes-Benz's MO360 digital production ecosystem. The work aims to improve efficiency, flexibility and quality across the automaker's global manufacturing network.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported on NVIDIA’s Rev Lebaredian discussing the potential of digital twins in Kazakhstan and the challenges of implementing the technology.

Belgian police arrested 195 people during demonstrations against education policies and budget cuts in Brussels and Liege on Saturday, with clashes, fires and vandalism reported in both cities, according to police statements released on Sunday.
Authorities reported 150 arrests in Brussels and 45 in Liège, as officers deployed tear gas and water cannons to disperse protesters and restore order.
Barricades and clashes in Brussels
Brussels police recorded 118 administrative detentions and 32 judicial arrests, including 15 minors among those arrested under judicial procedures.
The judicial arrests were linked to alleged offences including throwing objects at police officers, resisting arrest and deliberate arson, police said.
Investigators continued identifying suspects, and the figures could change.
Five officers sustained minor injuries, while unrest caused significant damage in central Brussels. Protesters used electric scooters and construction materials to build barricades, police said.
Officers repeatedly resorted to tear gas and water cannons during the demonstrations.
Fires and arrests in Liege
In Liege, police reported 40 administrative detentions and five judicial arrests, including 12 minors among those detained, according to the Belga news agency.
Vandalism and fires were reported in public areas on Saturday evening. Around 50 protesters gathered at Place Saint-Lambert and fired pyrotechnic mortars at the Prince-Bishops’ Palace, prompting police to use a water cannon and tear gas to disperse the crowd.
People gathered nearby chanted demands for the release of their friends. Police said calm appeared to have returned by the evening.
The demonstration had begun peacefully, with between 200 and 250 people gathering outside Guillemins railway station at around 10 am before marching to Place Saint-Lambert, where a sit-in blocked bus traffic.
Protesters later blocked roads near Le Cadran, including access to the motorway towards Burenville, with some moving barriers to construct barricades, Belga reported.
Student protests spread from France
Student demonstrations that began in France over education conditions spread to French-speaking Belgium on 1 October.
Previous protests have led to numerous detentions, with some suspects subsequently remanded in custody.
Saturday’s arrests underline the tensions surrounding demonstrations against education policies and budget reductions, although police said investigations into the latest incidents were continuing.

Rubio arrives in Samarkand as Washington seeks closer ties with Central Asia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
14:45:23 UTC
23:45:23 KST

The US secretary of state will meet the foreign ministers of five Central Asian countries on Monday under the C5+1 format. Trade, investment, critical minerals and security are expected to feature in discussions, while more than 200 American business executives accompany the visit.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, on Sunday evening ahead of talks with representatives of five Central Asian countries, as Washington seeks to expand diplomatic, economic and security cooperation with the region.
Rubio will attend a ministerial meeting under the C5+1 format, bringing together the United States and Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan. He is also scheduled to hold bilateral talks with senior officials from all five countries.
The visit has a significant commercial dimension. According to the US State Department, Rubio is accompanied by a delegation of more than 200 American business leaders, with discussions expected to focus on opportunities for trade, investment and economic cooperation.
Speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews on Saturday, before leaving Washington, Rubio was asked why he had chosen to visit Uzbekistan while several international crises demand American diplomatic attention.
"This is an important relationship," Rubio said, explaining that the timing had been chosen to bring together the foreign ministers of all five Central Asian countries.
"One of the things that suffers is the strategic business," he said, referring to the tendency for diplomatic visits to focus on immediate crises. "But there's countries you'd like to get to because we want to build our relationships with them."
C5+1: From Samarkand to the White House
The C5+1 framework was established in Samarkand in November 2015, when then-US Secretary of State John Kerry met his counterparts from the five Central Asian republics.
The dialogue subsequently expanded to presidential level, with meetings hosted by Joe Biden in 2023 and Donald Trump in November 2025.
The most recent summit in Washington placed particular emphasis on trade, investment and critical minerals.
According to the US Department of Commerce, more than $25bn (approximately €22bn) in commercial agreements and commitments were announced during the November 2025 C5+1 meetings, covering aviation, agricultural equipment, railway infrastructure and mineral development.
These included agreements at different stages of development rather than investments already completed.
Trade, investment and strategic cooperation
Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan are among Washington's main economic partners in the region. According to US government figures, bilateral trade in goods and services reached $7.1bn (approxiametely €6.3bn) with Kazakhstan and $1.7bn (€1.5bn) with Uzbekistan in 2025, while American companies have also announced agreements covering aircraft, agricultural machinery and mineral development.
Central Asia offers Washington opportunities to diversify critical mineral supply chains and develop partnerships in energy, transport infrastructure and technology.
The region has substantial oil, natural gas and uranium resources, alongside deposits of other minerals used in manufacturing, advanced technologies and energy systems.
For Central Asian governments, closer ties with the United States offer additional sources of investment, technology and access to international markets, while they maintain extensive economic relationships with Russia and China.
The European Union is also seeking closer economic ties with Central Asia. At a summit in Samarkand in April 2025, Brussels announced a €12bn Global Gateway investment package covering transport, critical raw materials, energy and digital connectivity.
The American delegation includes representatives of companies such as Boeing, Citibank and Franklin Templeton.
American development finance and export credit institutions are also expected to participate in business discussions.
Security cooperation is another element of the agenda, with US officials identifying counterterrorism as an area for closer cooperation with some countries in the region.
Bilateral talks with Uzbekistan
The programme also includes the first round of an expanded strategic partnership dialogue between Rubio and Uzbekistan's Foreign Minister Bakhtiyor Saidov on Monday.
According to the Uzbek Foreign Ministry, the discussions will cover political relations, trade, investment and regional and international developments.
On 16 October, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev met US Special Envoy for South and Central Asia Sergio Gor to review preparations for Rubio's visit, the C5+1 meeting and the second session of the Uzbekistan–US Business and Investment Council.
President Mirziyoyev is scheduled to attend the Council's meeting in Samarkand on Monday.
The Council, co-chaired by Saida Mirziyoyeva, Head of Uzbekistan's Presidential Administration, and Sergio Gor, was established to promote bilateral investment, commercial partnerships and joint projects.
Security has been tightened in Samarkand, where Uzbekistan's Interior Ministry has announced temporary traffic restrictions on roads leading into the city and several central streets from 18 to 22 October.
Following his meetings in Uzbekistan, Rubio is scheduled to travel to India, visiting Mumbai and Jamnagar for discussions with government officials and business leaders, including talks on trade and energy cooperation.
His Asian tour is expected to conclude on Thursday.

Hungary breaks ranks with EU over US-Russia diesel deal

The deal faced harsh criticism in the EU, with Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni labeling it a “very risky” gamble that could undermine the whole Western sanctions policy towards Russia. The exemption was agreed between Trump and Magyar’s predecessor, Viktor Orban, who was a harsh critic of Western economic restrictions on Moscow over the Ukraine conflict.
Due to being a landlocked country, Hungary remains heavily dependent on deliveries of Russian pipeline oil and gas. Some 90% of its crude oil in 2025 had been provided by Moscow, according to S&P Global data.
The Hungarian prime minister stressed that he understood that the Russia-US diesel deal was “not welcome from Ukraine’s point of view.”
After it was announced, Vladimir Zelensky lashed out at Trump, calling the agreement “weak” and insisting that the actual reason for the global energy shortage was not Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries as the US president claimed, but the American war on Iran.
Following his address at the EU summit in Brussels on Friday, Zelensky told journalists that “we cannot accept these agreements [between Washington and Moscow]. Because gas deals will follow. And I am absolutely certain of this. After gas, they will lift sanctions on other things as well.”
On Saturday, Trump also signed an executive order to waive “the bone-crushing” sanctions, championed by the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, which proposed 500% tariffs on imports from Russia and 100% tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.
White House Deputy Press Secretary Taylor Rogers defended the move, saying that it “provides the president with additional authorities to pursue a peaceful resolution” of the Ukraine conflict. “Enforcing the sanctions provisions now would impede ongoing US efforts to negotiate a durable and comprehensive peace agreement,” she explained.

China Focus: From smart sensors to AI robots, technology transforming China's elderly care
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
22:42:36 CST
23:42:36 KST

HEFEI, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- A mobile phone alert warns a community worker that no door activity has been detected at an elderly resident's home for more than 24 hours. Another alert reports that a smoke detector has been triggered.
The notifications come from smart devices installed in the homes of over 600 elderly people living alone, mostly aged 80 or above, in Luyang District of Hefei, the capital of Anhui Province in east China. The devices, including door sensors and smoke detectors, help community workers identify potential emergencies and respond more quickly.
The smart early-warning system is part of a government-funded elderly care program launched in 2025, according to Zhao Fei, director of the Luyang district office of the committee on aging.
When an alert is triggered, a three-tier response mechanism involving family members, community workers and community officials is activated to ensure each warning receives appropriate follow-up, Zhao said.
"The combination of smart early warnings and human intervention builds a safety net for elderly people living alone at home," Zhao said.
Around a dozen alerts are generated and handled each day. "It would be nearly impossible to identify such risks through human inspections alone," Zhao said.
The initiative is part of broader efforts to harness intelligent technologies and high-tech products to improve elderly care as China faces a rapidly growing elderly population.
Official data shows that China's population aged 60 and above exceeded 323 million by the end of 2025, accounting for about 23 percent of the national total population.
In addition to smart devices such as millimeter-wave fall detectors, the Shulu Community Service Center in Hefei high-tech zone has introduced a robot to assess the mental health of elderly people, said Liu Li, head of the center's social affairs department.
Equipped with cameras and powered by large AI models, the robot analyzes facial expressions, eye features and subtle body movements, conducts noninvasive screening, and by combining these observations with physiological signals generates a report on a person's mental state.
China's rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and advanced manufacturing are encouraging technology companies to develop products for the expanding elderly care market.
Anhui Sanlian Robot Technology Co., Ltd. has introduced its fourth-generation lower-limb exoskeleton, which uses AI to adapt the level of assistance according to users' movements.
The device can detect when users need extra support as they lift their legs and reduce assistance when they stop moving, allowing people with walking difficulties to move more naturally, said Wu Xianchun, the company's marketing director.
The company's exoskeletons were initially developed mainly for postoperative leg rehabilitation and activities such as mountain climbing. They are now used primarily in elderly care facilities, with demand increasingly shifting toward helping older people exercise their legs and improve everyday mobility, Wu said.
Advances in AI and manufacturing are helping improve the performance and affordability of elderly care products, Wu said. Better algorithms make devices smarter, while improved manufacturing processes and mass production help enhance quality and reduce the cost of components such as batteries and motors.
"Affordable, high-quality elderly care tech products will better serve senior citizens," Wu said.
Smart technologies are also gaining ground in other Chinese cities. In Beijing, intelligent massage and companion robots are being used for physical therapy and companionship. Some nursing homes in Shanghai have adopted smart mattresses to monitor residents' health, while virtual reality devices are being used for rehabilitation training among older people in Shenzhen.
China's market for elderly care service robots is expected to exceed 10 billion yuan (about 1.5 billion U.S. dollars) in 2026, according to a research report released by the China Software Testing Center this year.
The growing market is also driving more young entrepreneurs to tap opportunities in the elderly care industry.
Liu Sizhe, an 18-year-old student at the University of Science and Technology of China, launched a startup this year and led a team in developing an AI-based system for preliminary screening for Alzheimer's disease.
Users can have casual conversations with the system via a mobile phone or a tablet, while the technology analyzes their speech rate and responses to identify potential signs of cognitive impairment.
Liu said his grandparents inspired the project. Watching them grow older prompted him to consider how he could use technology to help elderly people.
"I do not want the elderly to be left behind by technological advances," Liu said. ■

China Focus: When family is out of reach, paid companionship fills a gap in China's elder care
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
22:42:23 CST
23:42:23 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Mrs. Zhou, an 82-year-old widow, lives alone and has no children in Nanjing, the provincial capital of Jiangsu in east China. Her daily life has brightened up since a 24-year-old man began visiting her home to chat, teach her how to use a smartphone and warn her about scams.
The visits are part of a growing practice in China known as "shared children," in which young people are paid to keep elderly people company -- a service seen as filling a gap in emotional support for the country's aging population.
Late last year, the man, Heng Mengyu, first knocked on Zhou's door and soon became a regular visitor. Zhou had no relatives or friends nearby and rarely left her apartment. She was depressed and pessimistic, and had repeatedly mentioned writing a suicide note. After several months, her outlook on life began to change.
One afternoon, Heng arrived at Zhou's apartment as scheduled. He checked for safety hazards -- inspecting kitchen outlets and the gas valve, looking through the refrigerator and clearing out expired food -- while Zhou offered him fruit.
Heng did not try to talk her out of her feelings. Instead, he listened. Over repeated visits, he helped Zhou identify telecom fraud schemes, corrected her health misconceptions, and encouraged a regular routine and a better diet. Zhou gradually opened up, sharing her thoughts and daily life, and regained confidence.
The service is Heng's own venture. He became interested in elder care in college and has worked in the field since graduation. Late last year, he came up with the idea of "doorstep companionship services" and developed a detailed checklist covering home safety inspections, organizing supplies, clearing expired food, smartphone tutorials, anti-fraud education, emotional support, and recording the elderly person's condition.
"Our service isn't just simple care," Heng said. "It focuses on the life and psychological blind spots that the elderly often overlook." After each visit, he records the client's physical condition, emotional state and living situation, and reports back to their children or community.
Heng's visits last at least two hours and start at 200 yuan (about 30 U.S. dollars). His team has grown from one person to nine, including stay-at-home mothers, working teachers, nursing graduates and psychological counselors.
Most "shared children" providers nationwide are young. A post-90s graduate of a Shanghai university, surnamed Qiu, provides weekend visit services, such as chatting with elderly clients, or accompanying them to get haircuts. One client treats him like her own child.
Many individuals and organizations advertise "shared children" services online. Rates are usually hourly, with a single two-to-four-hour visit costing from several hundred to over 1,000 yuan.
The rise of "shared children" reflects a demand driven by population aging. At the end of 2025, China had over 323 million people aged 60 or above, accounting for 23 percent of the population. The figure is projected to surpass 400 million around 2035.
Surveys show the elderly prefer to live at home, and the country has large numbers of empty-nest and disadvantaged elderly, with a high old-age dependency ratio. The fifth sample survey on the living conditions of China's urban and rural elderly found that in 2021, 14.2 percent of elderly Chinese lived alone, while empty-nest elderly -- those living alone or only with a spouse -- accounted for nearly 60 percent.
Mental health needs are equally acute. A blue book on elderly mental health published by the China Research Center on Aging found that 23.76 percent of elderly Chinese experience loneliness to varying degrees, while 26.4 percent show depressive symptoms, including 6.2 percent with moderate to severe depression.
Ye Qing, president of the Wuhan Filial Piety Culture Promotion Association, said increased population mobility has made empty-nest households the norm. Among urban families of only children, the "4-2-1" structure -- four grandparents, two parents and one child -- accounts for 62.3 percent, steadily weakening the traditional family's care-giving role. Children far from home may want to fulfill their filial duties but are constrained by distance and limited energy. The rise of "shared children" responds to this reality, Ye said.
Clients of such services are mostly elderly people who live alone, are socially isolated and emotionally low. Long periods of solitude breed negativity, and with no one nearby to confide in, what they want most is someone to listen to them.
Heng said this is a key difference between "shared children" and ordinary domestic help. "We don't do assembly-line service. We only do companionship with warmth." The core of his team's work is not completing tasks but sensing changes in the elderly person's mood and inner needs, easing loneliness through companionship.
The doorstep model is flexible and customizable to each family's situation, suiting the realities of home-based elder care. Market demand has also created a new employment field, allowing people with a passion for elder care and flexible schedules to work through companionship and care-giving.
Ye and other experts believe the new sector fills part of the gap in emotional elder care, but needs guidance to become standardized and institutionalized. They suggest building efficient supply-demand matching mechanisms through internet platforms, improving user review and credit systems, and refining income distribution and incentive mechanisms -- stabilizing the workforce and ensuring sustainable and quality service over the long term. ■

Xinhua Headlines: Inside China's "unlikely" AI computing hub
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
22:42:19 CST
23:42:19 KST

* In less than two years, Inner Mongolia's computing capacity has nearly quadrupled, reaching 363,000 petaflops by August 2026, as large-scale data centers have sprung up across the region.
* However, the region is not content to remain a mere "landlord of data centers." It is striving to move up the value chain, reinventing itself not only as a hub for green computing but also for token trading and AI applications.
* With the influx comes new challenges. Computing facilities require enormous amounts of electricity to run and water to keep server racks from overheating. Inner Mongolia, a frontrunner in China's green energy transition, is charting a course of green computing.
HOHHOT, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- A four-hour drive northwest of Beijing takes one across the Great Wall and into the grasslands of Inner Mongolia, seemingly a world away from China's booming coastal towns.
Yet here, in a city once known as China's "potato capital," data centers are rising from the grasslands, towering cranes fill the skyline, and some of the country's biggest tech companies are moving in.
The city is Ulanqab, in the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, which has emerged as a new frontier in the global race for computing power. Ulanqab is a poster child for this rise. In less than two years, Inner Mongolia's computing capacity has nearly quadrupled, reaching 363,000 petaflops by August 2026, as large-scale data centers have sprung up across the region.
A combination of factors helped fuel this transformation. Its climate allows natural cooling of AI server racks for nearly ten months a year. The windswept steppes offer a massive volume of wind and solar power, driving rates down to as low as around 0.35 yuan (about 5.2 U.S. cents) per kWh. Moreover, its proximity to Beijing ensures an ultra-low latency of under 5 milliseconds, facilitating seamless model training and real-time inference.
However, the region is not content to remain a mere "landlord of data centers." It is striving to move up the value chain, reinventing itself not only as a hub for green computing but also for token trading and AI applications.
RISING ABOVE GRASSLAND
At the Ulanqab Chahar High Tech Development Zone, the epicenter of the city's newfound buzz, an "Apple Boulevard" runs alongside an "Alibaba Boulevard" and a "Huawei Boulevard" -- named after three of the major companies that have set up a presence here. Other tech giants, including ByteDance, Kuaishou and VNET Group, have also moved in.
Vehicles from across China line the roads, and workers speak in accents from every corner of the country. Around lunchtime, food stalls spring up around the construction sites, selling boxed meals, fruit and drinks.
"Within the high-tech zone alone, 22 computing-power projects are currently under construction, involving nearly 30,000 construction workers," said Liu Junping, deputy director of the administrative committee of the development zone.
"When I came here to scout the site in 2022, it was still pretty desolate, and sandstorms would sometimes sweep through," recalled Zhou Yiguang, an executive with the VNET Group's Ulanqab base. The group has planned a computing cluster covering 1,100 mu (about 73 hectares) of land in Ulanqab, and the first phase has been in operation since October 2024.
In fact, it is not just Ulanqab. Inner Mongolia has emerged as a hub for computing power, with its regional capital Hohhot as another high ground. As of the first half of 2026, roughly 20 of China's 30 leading private computing companies had established a presence in the region, with combined investment exceeding 200 billion yuan (around 29.75 billion U.S. dollars). In addition, nine of the country's top 10 computing service providers had also set up operations there.
GREEN COMPUTING
With the influx comes new challenges. Computing facilities require enormous amounts of electricity to run and water to keep server racks from overheating. Inner Mongolia, a frontrunner in China's green energy transition, is charting a course of green computing.
In 2025, the computing industry in Ulanqab alone consumed 4.3 billion kWh of electricity. That figure is estimated to reach 9 billion kWh in 2026 and will continue to surge as more computing centers are expected to start operating over the next two to three years.
Globally, tech giants are moving beyond simply "buying power" to "competing for power" and even "generating their own power." China, however, has leveraged its world-leading power grid, renewable energy and energy storage industries to pioneer the integration of computing power and electricity supply, known as "computing-electricity coordination."
In the Ulanqab Chahar High Tech Development Zone, a zero-carbon industrial park is taking shape. The park will be managed as a unified power distribution unit, with wind and solar infrastructure developed collectively by the government, then distributed to individual computing centers across the park.
Chen Zhigang, deputy director of the Ulanqab municipal development and reform commission, said that the park's surrounding areas have about 10 gigawatts of wind and solar development capacity available. Once tapped, these resources could generate more than 30 billion kWh of electricity annually, enough to cover future increases in demand.
After the zero-carbon industrial park is completed, more than 80 percent of the park's electricity will come directly from renewable energy. In the Horinger New Area in Hohhot, computing centers in operation source 85 percent of their power consumption from green energy.
Water poses another potential constraint. However, widespread adoption of water-conserving cooling equipment, such as waterless fluorine-pump air conditioning systems and closed cooling towers, helped ease the high demand for cooling water.
Moreover, take VNET Group's cloud computing center in Ulanqab for example: here, outdoor cold air is directly used for cooling for nearly 10 months of the year, with spray systems activated only during the hottest summer days.
"All the water used for cooling at the computing center is reclaimed water. It does not affect local natural water resources or groundwater," said Li Yi, technical director of VNET Group's Ulanqab base.
According to the Ulanqab water resources bureau, under the regional regulations, data centers are prohibited from using groundwater as cooling water. In 2025, big data companies across the city consumed 1.54 million cubic meters of water, accounting for only 0.33 percent of the city's total water consumption. Meanwhile, the city produces about 72 million tonnes of reclaimed water annually.
TOKEN HUB
Building computing capacity is one thing, yet turning it into a high-value AI economy is another. "If we rely solely on cheap electricity and low land costs, we risk becoming little more than 'landlords of server rooms,'" Liu Huansuo, deputy director of the Ulanqab big data administration, warned.
The concern is well-founded. The high-value segments of the computing economy -- chips, algorithms and models -- remain largely beyond Inner Mongolia's reach.
According to economic data from Ulanqab, the city's computing-power industry generated 6.835 billion yuan in revenue in 2025, with 368 million yuan in tax revenue. A computing center is estimated to create about 100 jobs per 100 mu (about 6.7 hectares) of land.
Yet these returns remain modest relative to the massive upfront investment in infrastructure and the enormous computing capacity that is being developed.
To address the challenge, Inner Mongolia strives to move up the value chain -- evolving from a "server-room landlord" to a "token capital," and cultivating its own ecosystem of AI applications.
On May 30, Inner Mongolia's Token Trading Platform, billed as the country's first green-computing full-stack AI platform, went into operation in the Horinger New Area, positioning Hohhot to become a major token-trading hub in northern China.
The goal is to turn raw computing power into a tradable commodity that can be measured, priced and ultimately converted into higher-value AI services, said Guo Juying, deputy director of the Horinger New Area Administrative Committee. She described the transition as a shift from "selling electricity" to "selling tokens," as every AI conversation or model inference can ultimately be measured in terms of tokens generated and consumed.
Ulanqab has its own plan. At the end of 2025, the city released a three-year action plan for building a "Token Capital" for 2026-2028, envisioning a new economic chain spanning the production, trading and application of tokens.
The application ecosystem is also expanding. Hohhot has developed nearly 100 application scenarios in sectors such as dairy, new energy and biomedicine. A facial recognition database for cattle is already widely used on smart pastures.
For a region that has built its computing infrastructure at remarkable speed, the next challenge may be harder. But overcoming it will open up a whole new horizon across China's economic landscape. ■
(Video reporter:Zhang Sheng; Video editors: Hong Ling, Zhang Mocheng and Hong Yan)

A timeline of West Bank attacks on Palestinians and foreign officials

2026-10-18
14:42:01 UTC
23:42:01 KST

A timeline of West Bank attacks on Palestinians and foreign officials
Settler pogroms have escalated, coinciding with the annual olive harvest season in the occupied West Bank.
European diplomats and officials were attacked on Saturday amid a surge in settler pogroms across the occupied West Bank in recent weeks, coinciding with olive harvest season.
The settler pogroms have escalated just weeks before Israel heads to the polls on October 27.
The European Union (EU) on Sunday condemned settler attacks on European diplomats and Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. A day earlier, a veteran American journalist working for the Washington Post was also brutally attacked.
But this is not the first time Israeli settlers have assaulted foreign officials or prominent Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
Here’s a timeline of some of the recent and past attacks:
October 17, 2026
Israeli settlers assaulted European diplomats, including a French mayor, near the Palestinian village of Taybeh in the occupied West Bank.
The delegation was visiting Palestinian olive harvesters on Saturday when the Israeli attackers confronted the group.
In Saturday’s incident, the settlers targeted Belgium’s consul general, French and Polish diplomats, and Catholic representatives, Belgian Minister of Foreign Affairs Maxime Prevot said.
“A French mayor was assaulted and a Belgian vehicle damaged,” Prevot said, linking the incident to Israel’s “illegal settlement policy” and pledging to push for further EU sanctions.
Bernard Baudoux, the French mayor who was assaulted, told the AFP news agency the attack suggests that “there is a tolerance on the part of the Israeli government” towards settler violence.
Video shared by an activist at the scene, Amit Orfali, shows Baudoux leaning against a vehicle while sitting on the dusty ground. Other clips showed young masked men knocking insistently on a driver’s side window and asking for identification, while other masked men carrying sticks advanced in the distance. Orfali said the masked men “threatened to kill us”.
France’s Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot called on Israel to arrest the “extremist settlers” who “violently assaulted” Baudoux, and bring them to justice. “They must urgently halt this criminal violence and guarantee the safety of civilian populations, as they are compelled to do under international law,” he said in a post on X.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office has, however, appeared to question the reports of the attack on the Europeans, saying on X that they are “alleged” and require “compelling evidence”, despite acknowledging that published footage of the incident exists.
“We take positive note of statements by several Israeli representatives who condemned the attacks,” the EU said in a statement on Sunday. “But we expect full accountability as well as effective measures to prevent continued acts of violence and violent harassment against Palestinians, including during the ongoing olive harvest season, as well as against journalists.”
October 16, 2026
Palestinian farmers harvesting olives and veteran American journalist Heidi Levine, 64, who freelances for the Washington Post, were brutally attacked by settlers.
Levine fell to the ground during the assault before she was set upon, witnesses said. “We looked and saw that there was a journalist … on the ground with people surrounding her, beating her, clubbing her, robbing her, pulling her up, beating her again and kicking her,” Jasper Nathaniel, an independent journalist who witnessed the attack, told Al Jazeera.

Manchester City owner’s £55m housing loan while Burnham was mayor investigated
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
14:41:15 UTC
23:41:15 KST

A £55m loan to Manchester City’s Abu Dhabi owner will be investigated as part of a review into a fund for housing projects while Andy Burnham was mayor.
The prime minister has faced weeks of scrutiny over his links to Manchester City’s super-rich owners after the club was found guilty of boosting its income by £900m in a nine-year breach of financial rules.
Burnham, the former Greater Manchester mayor, was accused of siding with the Abu Dhabi owners after the “unprecedented” rule breach, when he said they had been “such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester” and that he would be “really concerned” to lose them from the sport.
He could now face more uncomfortable questions after councillors in Greater Manchester said they planned to investigate loans made to property companies while he was mayor.
In 2017, three companies ultimately controlled by the Manchester City owner, Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan, the vice-president and deputy prime minister of the United Arab Emirates, were loaned £55m as part of a fund operated by Burnham’s Greater Manchester combined authority (GMCA).
The loans were to help finance a major housing development called Manchester Life, which promised to create 6,000 homes in an “unprecedented” opportunity for the city. GMCA said the loans had been repaid in full but has not disclosed the interest rate or why Sheikh Mansour, as a scion of one of the world’s wealthiest families, would have been eligible.
It emerged last week that Burnham had met City’s owners while enjoying hospitality from the club at its Etihad Stadium weeks before the loans were approved. That meeting later disappeared from public records before it came to light last week, prompting the prime minister to ask GMCA to carry out a “manual trawl” of his meetings to ensure “full transparency”.
John Leech, a Liberal Democrat councillor in Manchester, said the fund – which has handed out £1bn to 50 separate developers since 2015 – would be investigated by GMCA’s overview and scrutiny committee, which he chairs.
Leech told the BBC the approval process for loans had been criticised as “very opaque in the past and that it’s not necessarily been clearly understood why X was successful and Y wasn’t”.
He said it was “not unreasonable” to ask why seemingly successful businesses needed to borrow public money through this loan scheme. “In the case of Abu Dhabi, you would imagine that they wouldn’t have any problem accessing funds from elsewhere as well,” he said.
“And so the process clearly does seem to be out of kilter with what the original stated aims were back in 2015.”
He added: “We just want to be clear that there is a transparent rather than an opaque process”.
Downing Street declined to comment. A GMCA spokesperson said it was supporting Leech’s overview and scrutiny committee with its inquiries. They said the fund had built 11,000 new homes and was contributing “billions of pounds worth of development at no cost to the taxpayer”.
GMCA added: “Decisions to grant loans from the fund are taken publicly. Not a single viable scheme was ever turned down and funds were lent to around 50 different developers.
“The fund is open to all developers, with lending criteria based on parameters set by the government and developed with external financial experts to reflect due diligence standards in the private sector.”

Egypt says ready to give Saudi Arabia necessary support amid Houthi conflict
Oct 18 - Egypt is ready to provide Saudi Arabia with the support it needs to defend its security and stability, the presidency said on Sunday, as Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis intensify their attacks on the world's largest oil exporter.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi requested an urgent parliament session to authorise the military, one of the Arab world's largest, to help defend Saudi Arabia if the kingdom requested its support.
A parliamentary vote had been expected on authorizing the request for military support on Sunday, but discussions were due to continue on Monday, two lawmakers and local media reports said.
HOUTHIS RAMP UP ATTACKS ON SAUDI ARABIA
The Houthis have in recent days attacked Riyadh's international airport and the state oil giant Saudi Aramco, amid renewed fighting with the Saudi-backed forces of the internationally recognised government following the collapse of a truce.
"Egypt will provide Saudi Arabia with all necessary and possible forms of support to defend its security and stability, protect its resources, territorial integrity and Islamic holy sites," the Egyptian presidency said in a statement.
It followed a meeting of Egypt's National Defence Council chaired by Sisi and attended by the parliamentary speaker, the prime minister and the army chief.
Sisi said in a speech on Saturday that Egypt would act in accordance with guidance from Saudi King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who visited Sisi on September 15, after fighting in Yemen reignited.
Egypt and Saudi Arabia are close strategic and economic partners. Saudi Arabia and other oil-rich Gulf states provided Egypt with billions of dollars in aid, central-bank deposits and investments after the military ouster of Islamist President Mohamed Morsi in 2013.
Egypt had previously joined the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in Yemen in 2015 to support the government against the Houthis, but played a limited combat role. REUTERS

'France is burning!': Trump blames immigrants as riots devastate Paris and other cities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
14:31:53 UTC
23:31:53 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump intervened again Sunday in the violent unrest sweeping France, blaming immigration for the destruction and looting that have devastated parts of Paris and other major cities. "France is burning!" Trump wrote on Truth Social. "The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country. Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late!"
His remarks followed a day of widespread violence Saturday in which masked rioters attacked police officers and bystanders, set government buildings ablaze and looted hundreds of stores. The violence erupted following nationwide demonstrations against the rising cost of living and deteriorating public services, drawing hundreds of thousands of participants. French authorities reported at least 2,000 arrests and approximately 600 injured police and security personnel, according to the latest figures released Sunday.
The full extent of the destruction remains unclear, but French business representatives estimated that at least 1,500 businesses had been damaged, with losses running into hundreds of millions of euros. In Paris alone, hundreds of stores were looted. Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire said "entire streets were systematically destroyed," while Le Parisien described extensive damage in neighborhoods across the capital.
In the central Les Halles district, rioters targeted virtually every type of business, including pharmacies, clothing stores, beauty salons, tobacco shops and opticians. Similar scenes unfolded near Porte Saint-Denis, where dozens of businesses were vandalized. Burned bicycles, broken glass and piles of debris littered the streets. Sanitation workers told Le Parisien that clearing the wreckage would take days.
According to AFP, some looting appeared organized and coordinated. Small groups of masked young people wearing gloves reportedly disabled security cameras before smashing storefront windows and stealing merchandise. In one widely circulated video said to have been filmed in Paris, a woman desperately tried to stop masked looters from entering a supermarket. "Why are you doing this?" she shouted before being pushed aside. "Stop! That's not the point!"
Another video from Nice showed a video game store employee trying to protect a Micromania branch from looters before being kicked in the back and knocked to the ground. In Paris, groups were filmed emptying cellphone stores and passing stolen merchandise to accomplices outside. AFP described scenes resembling an uprising, with protesters shouting "Revolution!" The agency said the scale and intensity of the violence appeared to exceed previous waves of unrest in France, including the 2023 riots following the police killing of teenager Nahel Merzouk and the Yellow Vest protests of 2018 and 2019.
Historic city hall goes up in flames
Some of the most dramatic scenes came from Limoges in central France, where masked rioters set fire to the historic city hall, a building inaugurated in 1883 that had survived both world wars. Flames engulfed the structure, and its bell tower collapsed in footage circulated widely online. Authorities said much of the building had been destroyed.
Government buildings were also attacked in Marseille, Lille, Angers and Bordeaux, where protesters broke into municipal offices and regional administrative buildings. In Lyon, the local tourist office was set ablaze, and police reported that hostile crowds interfered with firefighters attempting to extinguish the flames. Footage from the city showed one rioter waving a Palestinian flag.
The weekend's violence followed weeks of growing frustration over inflation, fuel prices, declining public services and deteriorating conditions in French schools. Students, labor unions and members of the Yellow Vest movement, which emerged in 2018 in opposition to President Emmanuel Macron's economic policies, joined Saturday's demonstrations.
The unrest also follows student protests that began last month in poorer suburbs north of Paris over teacher shortages and inadequate school conditions. Those demonstrations were accompanied by violence that subsequently spread to other European countries, including Belgium.
Macron's government and figures on the French right have accused far-left groups of hijacking legitimate social grievances and turning the demonstrations into violent confrontations ahead of next year's presidential election. The political tensions come as France prepares to choose a successor to Macron, who is barred from seeking a third consecutive term. Polls cited in French political coverage have pointed to a possible contest between far-right leader Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the far-left France Unbowed party.
Trump and Vance blame immigration
The unrest has also reignited fierce arguments over immigration and integration, with French right-wing politicians and prominent conservative figures abroad blaming immigrants and their descendants for a significant share of the violence. These accusations have become central to the political debate, although the broader demonstrations have involved people from different backgrounds and political movements.
Marion Maréchal, the niece of far-right leader Marine Le Pen, accused supporters of left-wing politician Jean-Luc Mélenchon's vision of a "new France" of destroying the country. "The whole world is watching in astonishment and disbelief as the children of Mélenchon's 'new France' destroy their country," she wrote.
The phrase refers to Mélenchon's vision of a French society in which immigrant communities are an integral part of national identity, but Maréchal and other right-wing figures have adopted it as a warning about demographic change.
Nice Mayor Éric Ciotti expressed outrage over the destruction in Limoges, calling the burning city hall a symbol of a republic in decline. "This is an allegory of our republic going up in flames and dying," he wrote. "We will not allow our country to die without a response. Millions will reject chaos. We will win!"
Trump had already linked the unrest to immigration earlier this month, arguing that student demonstrations were a cover for broader political and cultural aims. In a Truth Social post about two weeks ago, he claimed that the protests had nothing to do with schools and instead reflected mass immigration that had spiraled out of control. He also accused Islam of seeking to take over France.
Vice President JD Vance echoed those accusations Sunday, sharing footage of the destruction in Limoges. "Liberals in the West imported the Third World into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion," he wrote, accusing political leaders of ignoring questions about integration and cultural compatibility. He said Western governments had been warned about the consequences but had refused to listen.
Vance also connected the violence to the upcoming U.S. midterm elections, as Trump and Republicans seek to maintain control of Congress. "I hope Americans are paying attention," he wrote. "This is the future congressional Democrats want for your country."
Palestinian flags displayed during some of the demonstrations have drawn particular attention from conservative commentators, who linked them to the broader pro-Palestinian protest movement. American commentator Meghan McCain, daughter of the late Republican senator John McCain, shared footage of the burning Limoges city hall and wrote: "This is what 'globalize the intifada' means."
The slogan, heard frequently at anti-Israel demonstrations in Europe and the United States in recent years, is defended by supporters as a call for Palestinian liberation but criticized by opponents as an endorsement of violence against Jews and Israelis.
Macron faces criticism over response
Macron, meanwhile, was preparing to address the nation at 9 p.m. Israel time Sunday following mounting criticism of his response to the unrest. Opponents of the violence accuse him of failing to take sufficiently decisive action, while supporters of the protests argue that his government has failed to address their demands and restrain police tactics.
In recent weeks, Macron has largely responded with statements acknowledging public anger while condemning violence. Critics have called for stronger measures, including emergency powers that could allow authorities to deploy additional security forces and impose tighter restrictions on rioters. The government has so far avoided declaring a state of emergency.
The president also faced criticism over footage showing him and his wife, Brigitte, dancing and enjoying a Céline Dion concert Friday night, just hours before the unrest erupted. The video circulated widely over the weekend, with critics accusing the couple of appearing detached from growing public frustration over rising living costs, pressure on public finances, political paralysis and violence in the streets.
Some compared the images to Marie Antoinette, the French queen who became a symbol of royal excess during the economic crisis preceding the French Revolution. Critics argued that Macron's appearance at the concert reflected a disconnect between the presidency and the mood of a country facing deepening social and economic tensions.
Macron, whose second term ends next May, cannot run for another consecutive term. The unrest has added to the political pressure on his administration at a time when France is already grappling with economic uncertainty and divisions over immigration, public services and national identity.
With damaged businesses counting their losses, historic buildings in ruins and security forces facing questions about their preparedness, Macron must now contend with both the immediate consequences of the violence and the wider political crisis ahead of France's presidential election.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday thanked the Trump administration for resuming intelligence sharing between the two countries, but maintained the US had intentionally throttled its Starlink satellite internet access so that Donald Trump could send a “message” in his ongoing feud with the Ukrainian president.
In an interview on NBC, Zelenskyy said the US had “unblocked” intelligence on impending Russian ballistic missile strikes, which have pounded the country’s energy infrastructure as winter draws in.
“It was blocked for some period of time. And then it was deblocked by the American side. We are very thankful for this. Now it works,” Zelenskyy told NBC’s Meet the Press. “Only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles. And we didn’t get it during ballistic attacks during three days.”
Zelenskyy also said that Elon Musk’s SpaceX was responsible for suddenly limiting the speed at which Starlink terminals worked in Ukraine, hampering drone operations on the frontlines as well as some air defence missions.
“It was a message from American government to limit the speed,” he said. “And technically, SpaceX did it.”
Two people were killed and at least 17 injured as Russia and Ukraine continued to trade strikes on each other’s power infrastructure, after the breakdown of Trump’s short-lived and unilaterally declared “energy ceasefire”.
Trump has increasingly sought a detente with Moscow, inking a deal to import diesel fuel from Russia and waiving sanctions voted for overwhelmingly by both houses of Congress. Zelenskyy has become increasingly critical of Trump’s actions as the US has piled pressure on Ukraine to cease striking refineries in Russia and end the war quickly on Putin’s terms.
“We want to trust him and I hope that he will change his decisions,” Zelenskyy said of Trump. “Because I think that it’s all mistakes and it will not help us. And it will not help [the] United States.”
Zelenskyy on Sunday said that he had spoken with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the two Trump envoys charged with ending the war in Ukraine, as part of Ukraine’s “virtually nonstop communication” with the Trump administration.
But the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, in a separate interview on NBC on Sunday said that Zelenskyy had been “reckless” to accuse the Trump administration of standing behind the throttling of Starlink.
“President Trump and Secretary Rubio have categorically said that no one in the Trump administration did that,” said Bessent. “And I think it is very reckless for President Zelenskyy to make such a charge.”
He added: “President Zelenskyy should be very careful about making statements like this that aren’t true.”
Ukraine has resumed striking refineries in Russia and on Sunday attacked one of the country’s main oil terminals.
One person was killed and 15 wounded overnight after Ukraine used more than 1,000 drones to target Russian oil depots, logistics facilities and datacentres in one of its largest ever aerial bombardments.
St Petersburg’s governor, Alexander Beglov, said on Sunday that fires had broken out overnight at the city’s oil terminal, an oil depot and industrial warehouses. A logistics centre belonging to the Russian retailer Ozon and a datacentre for the local tech company VK were also targeted, both companies confirmed.
Alexander Drozdenko, the governor of the Leningrad region that surrounds St Petersburg, said 145 drones had been shot down and about 20,000 people were without electricity after the raid. “A large-scale [unmanned aerial vehicle] attack continues to be repelled,” he wrote on Telegram.
Fears that the conflict could be spilling over into Nato’s borders were stoked again on Sunday morning after Lithuania told residents in central and northern parts of the country to seek shelter for about an hour after an unidentified flying object entered its airspace.
During the red alert, Nato fighter jets were scrambled to the area, and Kaunas airport, near Lithuania’s second largest city, was temporarily closed, the national crisis management centre said.
The Nato aircraft were unable to visually identify the object due to cloudy weather and did not attempt to shoot it down, the centre said.
Ukraine’s foreign ministry later said it regretted the possible diversion of its drones into Lithuanian airspace on Sunday, which it said may have been caused by Russian electronic warfare.
“We apologise for any disruption, risks and concern this may have caused,” a spokesperson, Heorhii Tykhyi, wrote on X. “We are committed to sharing all relevant information with our Lithuanian partners to establish the full circumstances of the incident.”
Meanwhile, local officials in the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia said Russian strikes had killed a woman and wounded at least two other people, including a six-year-old girl. Two apartment buildings, 18 cars and an educational institution had been damaged by the attack, according to Mykhailo Semikin, the head of the Zaporizhzhia regional military administration.
Tensions are deepening between Kyiv and Washington, with the US president criticising Ukraine for its strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, despite continued Russian aggression.
Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” last week – which neither side said they agreed to beforehand – that quickly collapsed as Moscow continued its strikes on Ukraine’s power grid and Kyiv eventually resumed its hits on Russian oil refineries.
The Russian defence ministry said its air defence units had downed 1,015 Ukrainian drones around the country overnight. The Tass news agency quoted the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, who said Russia was responding with systematic, large-scale strikes.
“The Kyiv regime is resisting, but this cannot change the course of events,” he said, answering a question about how Russia might respond to Kyiv’s attack on St Petersburg.
On Saturday, Russia said it had carried out a major overnight attack, targeting Ukraine’s largest steelworks in the city of Kryvyi Rih and vessels using the port of Odesa. In a statement, Russia’s defence ministry said its forces had also hit an electricity substation in the north-western city of Zhytomyr and another steel plant in Zaporizhzhia.
In the Trump administration’s latest effort to reduce tensions with Russia, the US president announced on Friday that he would put a hold on a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause on the legislation passed by both chambers was in the national interest.
Trump has yet to give details about what he has decided regarding further sanctions on Russia.
“We’ll figure it out, and you’ll figure it out,” he told reporters at a fundraising dinner at his Florida estate on Saturday. “But it’s a very good decision, and it’s going to be a decision that’s good for the country, and I think good for the world.”
In a post on X on Sunday, Zelenskyy said in the week since Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire Russia had attacked Ukraine’s energy, oil and gas sectors 76 times.
He also said that the previous night alone, energy facilities in four Ukrainian regions had been attacked and tens of thousands of families were still without power. He accused Russia of trying to cause a blackout.
“America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements,” he said. “On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting.”
Zelenskyy also stressed that the war was continuing due to Russia’s invasion – not because Ukraine was defending itself. “It is Russia that must face pressure for peace to have a chance. Thank you to everyone who understands this and helps,” he said.
Ukrainian drones have repeatedly entered Nato airspace in the Baltic region in recent months. Kyiv has said they were steered off course by Russian signal jamming. Such incidents have stoked concerns that Russia’s war in Ukraine could spread.

Syria names Omar al-Halabi as chairman of sovereign wealth fund
Unknown

2026-10-18

Breadcrumb
Syria names Omar al-Halabi as chairman of sovereign wealth fund
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa on Sunday appointed Omar al-Halabi as chairman of the country's sovereign wealth fund, created by the transitional authorities but criticised by experts as lacking transparency.
Syria's sovereign fund sits at the heart of the country's efforts to attract foreign capital after 13 years of war, and was created to oversee investment projects and manage state assets.
It also manages assets confiscated from businessmen close to the government of longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad, whom the new authorities ousted in December 2024.
In a decree published by state media, Sharaa appointed Halabi "as adviser for economic affairs to the presidency of the republic" and as "chairman of the board of directors of the sovereign fund".
According to state news agency SANA, Halabi has "more than 20 years of professional experience working with governments, sovereign institutions and the private sector in the Middle East and international markets in the fields of economic policy and institution building and sovereign investment".
It said Halabi previously headed economics and public policy advisory for the Middle East at accounting firm KPMG and also worked with Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund.
After establishing Syria's sovereign fund in June 2025, authorities have not announced its director.
But several people who requested anonymity told AFP in July that they met the director and identified him as Abu Maryam al-Australi, a former jihadist whose surname means "the Australian".
Australi is sanctioned by Canberra and was close to Sharaa when the now-president led a rebel group in northwest Syria that went on to spearhead the offensive that toppled Assad.
Syria's authorities, who inherited an economy shattered by years of war and economic sanctions, have been intensifying efforts to speed up reconstruction, with the sovereign fund a key part of the process.
According to official estimates, the fund controls assets whose value exceeds Syria's GDP.
Experts, however, had previously criticised what they said was the fund's lack of transparency, with economist Karam Shaar calling it "a black box".
The fund also manages assets confiscated from businessmen close to the former authorities, including Mohammad Hamsho, who was sanctioned by the European Union and the United States and who has reached a settlement with the new authorities.
Most Syrians live in poverty, while the World Bank has estimated that rebuilding the country will cost more than $216 billion.

Check your wallet: some 2-euro coins are worth far more
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
14:27:15 UTC
23:27:15 KST

They may say two euros, but collectors sometimes pay many times that amount: rare editions and striking minting errors can turn small change into sought-after treasures.
At the bakery, at the parking meter or in the supermarket, coins usually change hands without anyone checking them. Yet it can be worth taking a closer look at your change: some 2-euro pieces have a collector value that far exceeds their face value. What matters, however, are specific features. An unusual design alone does not turn a coin into a rarity.
Grace Kelly: From two euros to 3,000
One of the best-known treasures is a 2-euro commemorative coin from Monaco issued in 2007. It marks the 25th anniversary of the death of Princess Gracia Patricia, formerly Hollywood actress Grace Kelly. The European Central Bank puts the mintage at just 20,001 copies. The coin can be recognised by the portrait of the princess, the country name "MONACO" and the year 2007. To the right of the effigy is the artist's name, "R.B. BARON".
Experts estimate this coin to be worth around 3,100 euros.
There is a big catch, though: it was sold directly to collectors and was not released into normal circulation. Finding one in your change would therefore be extremely unlikely. In principle it is a valid 2-euro coin and could be used for payments, but hardly anyone would do so deliberately.
When a mistake makes a coin interesting
Alongside rare issues, errors can also increase a coin's value, and making such a find would be more realistic. A striking example is the so-called fried-egg strike: the differently coloured inner part of a 1- or 2-euro coin is not seated correctly, so its metal is pressed partly into the outer ring. The irregular shape resembles a fried egg.
A pronounced rotation of the two sides of the coin relative to each other or striking on the wrong blank can also be of interest. Business magazine "WirtschaftsWoche" cites possible values of up to 100 euros for fried-egg strikes, up to 200 euros for rotated dies and up to 650 euros for pieces struck on the wrong blanks.
When coins are produced, two different metal parts are joined and struck under high pressure. Despite precise technology and careful checks, faulty specimens occasionally make their way into circulation.
In this case, the German 2-euro commemorative coin "Saxony-Anhalt" from 2021 was struck on a 1-euro blank. As a result, the colours are reversed compared with a normal 2-euro piece: the outer ring is gold-coloured, the inner part silver-coloured. The specimen also weighs only 7.50 grams instead of the usual 8.50 grams.
Coin dealer Münzen Müller values a comparable minting error at 1,200 euros.
This tiny "S" won't make you rich
How quickly an ordinary coin can turn into an alleged sensation on the internet is illustrated by examples of Greek coins with a small "S" in one of the stars, which are repeatedly offered as valuable minting errors, reports zwei-euro.com.
In reality the letter stands for "Suomi", meaning Finland, where part of the Greek coins were produced. According to coin experts, this is a regular variety with a mintage of 70 million pieces. The "S" alone therefore does not justify any exceptional value.
Found a valuable coin? Don't polish it!
If you spot an unusual coin, you should first identify the issuing country, year and motif. The ECB documents the official 2-euro commemorative issues on its website.
If you then believe you have discovered a valuable specimen, you should have it assessed by a specialist coin dealer or auction house. If the find is confirmed, a direct sale or an auction may be possible. Make sure you ask in advance about any fees, and do not clean or polish the coin, as this can reduce its value to collectors. Rubbing or polishing can cause the finest scratches and strip away the original mint lustre.
