UN sec-gen frontrunner Rebeca Grynspan’s Jewish roots, record on Israel - explainer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:41:17 UTC
22:41:17 KST

Jewish former vice president of Costa Rica Rebeca Grynspan is leading the straw poll for the next UN secretary-general. If she successfully replaces Antonio Guterres when he finishes his term on December 31, she will become the first Jewish UN secretary-general in the body’s history.
Grynspan, 70, was born to Jewish parents Manuel Grynspan Burstin and Sara Mayufis Schapiro in San José. Her parents fled Poland in 1936 due to Nazi persecution, while her maternal grandparents stayed behind and were killed during the Holocaust.
Grynspan’s husband – Saul Weisleder – is also Jewish, and they have two children. Her sister, Frida, lives in Israel, and Grynspan has a niece and nephew who served in the IDF. In a 2014 interview with the Tico Times, Frida referred to herself as a “lifelong Zionist.”
After obtaining a bachelor’s degree in economics from the University of Costa Rica and a master’s degree in economics from the University of Sussex in England, Grynspan became a professor and researcher at the Economic Science Research Institute of the University of Costa Rica.
She served as vice finance minister from 1986 to 1988, and as the second vice president of Costa Rica from 1994 to 1998. She then became the first woman to serve as the secretary-general of the Ibero-American General Secretariat from 2014 to 2021 and then the first woman to become the secretary-general of UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) in 2021. She currently holds this position.
In a video explaining why she chose to run for secretary-general, Grynspan said: “Conflicts are going up, trust in international law in the organization is going down, and time is running out.”
“I am a daughter of peace; my parents were refugees of the Second World War. I know what wars take away and what peace makes possible; that’s why I’m running.”
Grynspan's stance on Israel, Palestine
The Jerusalem Post’s research into Grynspan’s Israel and Palestine stances found that she has not maintained a public stance on either matter.
She did not post to social media on or immediately after the October 7 attacks. Her first post was on October 21, 2023, on X/Twitter, when she wrote, “Horrified by the tragic loss of life in Israel & Gaza. All civilians must be protected & we must work for peace in the region so people can have the future they want for themselves & their children. Hatred, terrorism, violence & war are not the way.”
On November 9, 2023, she wrote on Instagram, “I echo the call made by the highest-level humanitarian coordination forum of the @UnitedNations system: Respect for international humanitarian and human rights law; Immediate and unconditional release of civilians held hostage; Civilians must be protected.”
On 21 November 2023, at a UN Trade and Development Board executive session meeting in Geneva, Grynspan “echoed the call of the UN’s Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, condemning the horrific loss of civilian lives on both sides, the attack perpetrated by Hamas on October 7 and the continued bombardment of the IDF hitting civilians, hospitals, shelters, schools, and UN facilities in Gaza.”
“The protection of civilians must be paramount, as you correctly said, dear president, no party to an armed conflict is above international humanitarian law,” she added.
In 2017, she was the keynote speaker at a B’nai B’rith Uruguay memorial event.
Aside from that, the Post could find very few posts where she mentioned Israel, Palestinians, Gaza, Jews, or any related topics.
Grynspan viewed as relatively Israel-friendly candidate
Under Grynspan, the UNCTAD has adopted a seemingly Israel-critical line, publishing several unfavorable reports on the collapse of the Palestinian economy “as a result of the Israeli occupation and bombings.”
Grynspan is nevertheless seen as a more Israel-friendly candidate, given her family ties and relative public neutrality. She is running against outspoken anti-Israel candidates, such as former Chilean president Michelle Bachelet.
In an interview with Reuters last week, Grynspan said “the UN has become too risk-averse” and said the organization must cut jobs, curb bureaucracy and stop agencies duplicating work.
During Antonio Guterres’s tenure as UN secretary-general, the organization has faced renewed criticism over what Israel and pro-Israel watchdogs have described as its disproportionate focus on Israel.
In 2024, the UN General Assembly adopted 17 resolutions concerning Israel, compared with seven addressing the rest of the world combined, according to UN Watch.
Critics also point to UN bodies’ repeated condemnations of Israeli settlement policy and their scrutiny of Israel’s conduct in Gaza.

Tomer Caspi, Tomer Zaltzman crowned Winner Epic Israel bike race champs in Western Galilee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:41:10 UTC
22:41:10 KST

Tomer Caspi and Tomer Zaltzman were crowned the men’s champions of Winner Epic Israel 2026 after four days of demanding mountain biking in the Western Galilee, as Israel’s largest mountain bike race returned to the north for the first time since the war forced trails and forests in the region to close.
The 11th edition of the race, held in partnership with the Jewish National Fund (KKL-JNF) and sponsored by Specialized, concluded Saturday after bringing approximately 500 riders to Mateh Asher Regional Council and Nahariya for a challenging competition covering more than 300 kilometers and approximately 3,000 meters of cumulative climbing.
Caspi and Zaltzman, competing for Tomer’s team, won the men’s overall title with a combined time of 9:52:12 across the three competitive stages. Their victory capped an event that combined elite competition with a broader message of recovery and renewal for communities that endured years of disruption during the war.
The race, held in memory of its founder’s father, Giora Tzachor, was particularly meaningful this year because of its return to trails that had been inaccessible to the public for approximately three years.
Reopening of routes was made possible in part by KKL-JNF
The reopening of the routes was made possible in part by KKL-JNF’s restoration and upgrading work across the north, including hundreds of kilometers of mountain biking trails in Hanita, Kabri, Yehiam and Matzuba. Several of those routes were incorporated into this year’s course.
For race founder and producer Gal Tzachor, the return was about far more than the competition itself.
“To see hundreds of riders crossing the finish line here in the Western Galilee, after three years in which we could not return to the area, is an especially moving moment for me,” Tzachor said. “This year, the race was much more than a cycling competition. We returned to trails that had been closed, forests that had undergone rehabilitation and an area we all love so much.
“Over four days, we saw competitive sport at the highest level, but also an entire community returning to the north and bringing life back to the region. This race was born out of a love for the land, cycling and people, and it continues the legacy of my father, Giora Tzachor. I am proud of everyone who took part in this special edition.”
The competition began Wednesday, Oct. 14, with a 10.5-kilometer prologue in the Mateh Asher area. Amos Girani and Ronen Shirazi finished first in the opening event before the riders embarked on three demanding stages that determined the overall standings.
On Thursday, the first stage covered approximately 82 kilometers and included 1,150 meters of climbing. Caspi and Zaltzman finished at the top of the standings, establishing themselves as contenders for the overall title.
The pair strengthened their position Friday during the second stage, the most demanding single-day course of this year’s race. The route covered approximately 86.5 kilometers and featured 1,730 meters of climbing, placing significant physical demands on the competitors.
Saturday’s final stage took the riders across another 74 kilometers, with approximately 800 meters of climbing, before the overall champions were confirmed.
While the men’s competition attracted much of the attention, trophies were also awarded across several other categories.
Luba Bernstein and Helen Mora won the women’s division in 15:18:47 for Helen & Luba. Noam Strasnov and Yuval Friedman of NYCC Specialized took the men’s Masters title in 11:08:49, while Abigail Louis Yaavetz and Shahar Tamir of The Buttons-MIX won the mixed category in 12:30:58.
Sharon Pe’er and Erez Shaked of Team Specialized claimed the Grand Masters title in 11:21:44, while Eli Cohen and Eitan Medina of Team Bulthaup won the Super Grand Masters division in 12:36:00.
Race provides an important boost to local economy
The return of the race also provided an important boost to the local economy. Riders were joined by family members, professional support crews and spectators who stayed in the area and visited local hotels, restaurants and businesses.
For communities in the Western Galilee that have faced the consequences of the war, the event offered another opportunity to welcome visitors and restore the region’s sporting and tourism activities.
KKL-JNF Chairman Eyal Ostrinsky described the race’s return as a victory for the entire country.
“It feels like a victory for all the people of Israel,” Ostrinsky said. “At KKL-JNF, we are proud and excited, together with the residents of the north, to see Winner Epic Israel return to the Western Galilee after three years in which the trails were closed because of the war. This is a victory in its own right, another symbol of the return to life in the north, a region that is so dear to every citizen of Israel.
“Alongside our investment in the land, we believe it is important to strengthen communities, tourism and the local economy. We will continue working for and alongside the people of the north to rehabilitate what was damaged and help build and strengthen the region.”
The event also highlighted the role of sport in rehabilitation and community support. Wounded Israeli military veterans from Brothers for Life, an organization that assists injured soldiers throughout their recovery, took part alongside young cyclists from the Bartali Youth Cycling Club, which empowers teenagers through the sport.
Their participation added another dimension to an event centered on perseverance, recovery, and a return to normal life.
Toto Chairman and CEO Meir Bardugo said the organization was proud to support the race as part of its broader commitment to Israeli sport.
“The Toto is proud to partner with Winner Epic Israel again this year, in cooperation with KKL-JNF,” Bardugo said. “The riders and spectators enjoyed a high-quality and moving sporting experience, delivered to particularly high professional standards, that presented Israel in a positive light.
“As we approach the Toto’s 60th anniversary, Winner Epic Israel is another way for us to demonstrate our commitment to supporting Israeli sport in all its forms and to take part in the process of rehabilitation and the return to routine life in Israel.”
Nahariya Mayor Ronen Marley, whose city hosted the competition for the first time, welcomed the opportunity to showcase the area to riders and visitors.
“We were delighted to host Winner Epic Israel for the first time in our city, which is known as the city of bicycles, in partnership with KKL-JNF and the Toto,” Marley said. “The atmosphere was excellent, the riders enjoyed themselves, and the spectators had a great time cheering them on throughout the course.
“Hosting this international competition is part of our municipal efforts to promote sport and tourism, and it allowed us to introduce participants and visitors to our unique coastline and promenade. I am confident that this cooperation will expand in the coming years and contribute to strengthening the north in particular and Israel as a whole.”
Event brought renewed energy to communities still recovering
Mateh Asher Regional Council head and Confrontation Line Forum chairman Moshe Davidovich said the event had brought renewed energy to communities still recovering from the difficult years.
“We are concluding the Epic Israel competition with an enormous sense of pride and excitement,” Davidovich said. “The energy, determination and sporting spirit you brought with you, precisely here and precisely now, after the difficult years we have endured, have breathed new life into Mateh Asher and the entire Western Galilee.
“I congratulate the winners and thank all the participants and the production team for being genuine partners on the road to rehabilitation and growth. We have shown that the Galilee has come alive again. We will continue to rebuild and grow, and we look forward to welcoming you back next year.”
Aviad Friedman, head of the Northern Renewal Administration, also emphasized the significance of restoring major sporting events to the region, describing the race as a meeting point for people, communities and landscapes that demonstrated the north’s potential.
The administration, he said, would continue promoting initiatives that strengthen communities, encourage tourism and create opportunities for local residents and businesses as the region rebuilds.
For Caspi and Zaltzman, the return to the Western Galilee ended with a championship. For the communities that hosted the riders, the event offered a different kind of victory: the reopening of beloved trails, the return of visitors and another step toward restoring the north’s sporting, cultural and economic life.
After three years of disruption, Winner Epic Israel’s 2026 edition demonstrated that the roads to recovery can sometimes be found on two wheels.

Poland, Bulgaria, now Lithuania: Russia’s suspected arson campaign reaches a third Starlink site serving Ukraine

Unknown Publisher

22:40:51 KST

Someone tried to set fire overnight to a Lithuanian company that stores Starlink communication equipment, but tipped-off guards foiled the attempt, Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said. He linked the attack to Russia’s hybrid war against Europe. It is the third suspected sabotage of Starlink infrastructure in Europe in under a month.
Russia keeps attacking Ukraine at the front and from the air while running a sabotage campaign behind the lines in Europe, which ISW has linked into one pattern. Starlink keeps Ukraine’s drone units and front-line troops connected, and Poland pays for much of that service.
Fuel canisters and a control unit
The attack came just after midnight, the prime minister wrote. Security services had warned the company about possible attacks, security was stepped up, and the attempt failed.
The company provides connectivity through nine Starlink satellite antennas used by Ukraine, Sinkevičius told Lithuanian public radio LRT. At almost 2 a.m., intruders tried to burn the antennas and their control unit, leaving behind incendiary liquid in canisters of 3 to 10 liters.
“It is obvious that this is part of Russia’s hybrid war with elements of sabotage,” he said, adding that the client was likely “the Russian side.”
He said he believes the people involved, and how many there were, are known, but gave no details, citing the investigation.
Police Commissioner General Arūnas Paulauskas said no suspects had been detained, any damage was minimal, and the company kept working. A pretrial investigation is under way.
New Starlink restrictions disrupt Ukrainian drone missions. Kyiv adviser says move is tied to “political situation”
A drone the same morning
Hours later, an object that apparently entered from Poland crossed northern Lithuania, and NATO jets failed to identify it, Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said. Possible fragments were found in the Pasvalys district near the Latvian border. Latvia’s military said the object may have blown itself up on a course toward Latvia.
Sinkevičius said the sabotage version had to be checked for the drone too. He called the National Security Commission for Monday, 19 October, to examine both incidents and consider giving services more powers to neutralize drones.
The third Starlink site
In September, a fire destroyed the distribution panel at a Starlink ground station in Wola Krobowska, Poland. Germany detained two Turkish nationals on 12 October, and Warsaw blamed Russian intelligence. In Bulgaria, masked intruders burned 11 of 17 Starlink antennas near Sofia.

Mamdani, Paris already knows where 'globalize the intifada' ends up - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:40:21 UTC
22:40:21 KST

Some of the protesters in Paris on Saturday didn’t stay on the ground. They climbed the Monument to the Republic, the bronze Marianne at the center of Place de la République, and stood above a crowd of tens of thousands.
Reuters photographer Jack Taylor caught them up there. In his picture, two flags fly side by side over the square: the French tricolor and the Palestinian flag.
The people below had come to protest the cost of living, worsening public services, and the state of French schools. Those are French problems, and serious ones. So what was the Palestinian flag doing up there next to the tricolor?
Saturday’s demonstrations turned into some of the worst violence France has seen in years. Rioters burned cars, looted shops, and attacked police officers. By Sunday, nearly 1,800 people had been arrested across the country, according to Reuters.
More than half a million people took part in the demonstrations, the overwhelming majority of them peacefully, over real problems: French classrooms are short of teachers, and families are struggling with living costs.
I want to be careful with the answer. The flag proves less than some people were already claiming. It shows that protesters brought the Palestinian cause to a demonstration about French problems. It doesn’t tell us whether anyone carrying it had a hand in the arson or the attacks, and we don’t know that yet.
On Sunday, the Combat Antisemitism Movement shared a video it said showed a Paris synagogue vandalized during the unrest. It opens on what looks like a small prayer room. The Torah scroll is still standing in its wooden ark. Around it, the furniture has been shoved out of place, and things are lying all over the floor.
The synagogue was reported to be in the 19th arrondissement, a district in northeastern Paris. Nobody has independently confirmed what happened there, when the video was filmed, or whether it had anything to do with Saturday’s riots. I’ve watched too many frightening clips get treated as fact before anyone bothered to ask what happened, and I don’t want to add another one.
Still, it bothered me. On Saturday, the Shabbat, a synagogue is a pretty ordinary place. People pray, complain that the rabbi’s sermon ran long, and ask about each other’s kids. Nobody there should have to wonder what happened at a political demonstration earlier that day.
This is how the conflict travels. When it reaches Paris or New York, it rarely finds an Israeli official to shout at. It finds Jews, and it works on them in two steps. First they’re made to stand in for Israel. Then they’re made to answer for it. I learned how the first step works on a Paris street in 2015.
Ten hours in Paris after 2015 terrorist attacks
In February 2015, I spent 10 hours walking through Paris and its suburbs in a kippah and tzitzit, the ritual fringes worn by observant Jewish men. It was a few weeks after the terrorist attacks at the satirical magazine Charlie Hebdo and at the Hypercacher kosher supermarket, where four Jews were murdered. A photographer followed me with a hidden camera. A security guard came along and stayed out of sight.
I was covering the Jewish world for the Israeli news website NRG and the newspaper Makor Rishon at the time, and we wanted to see what ordinary Jewish life felt like on the streets of Paris.
We started in the center of Paris, where the worst I got was the occasional stare. Then we headed into other neighborhoods and out to the suburbs, and the mood changed. People cursed at me and threatened me, and some spat. Someone shouted “Viva Palestine” as I walked past. In one neighborhood, our security guard, who had been keeping out of sight, decided it was getting dangerous, and we got out.
I hadn’t said a word about Israel or carried a flag, and nobody asked what I thought of the Israeli government. Apparently my kippah had already answered for me. That’s the first step: to the people shouting at me, a Jew walking down a Paris street had become Israel.
What still gets me is how young some of them were, teenagers barely older than children, who seemed to know almost nothing about Jews except what they’d picked up on the street.
The video went viral. Millions of people watched it, and for a while I was the guy explaining on television around the world what it felt like to walk through Paris in a kippah.
Attacking a synagogue to send a message to Israel
One Saturday morning in August 2024, two cars went up in flames outside the Beth Yaacov synagogue in La Grande-Motte, a seaside town near Montpellier in southern France. One of them had a propane tank inside.
Firefighters found more fires at two of the synagogue’s entrances. Five people were inside, including the rabbi, and none of them were hurt. A police officer who walked up to the scene was injured when the tank exploded.
French prosecutors later said the suspect had admitted carrying out the attack to support the Palestinian cause and to provoke a reaction from the Israeli authorities. He denied wanting to kill anyone, though he acknowledged he had wanted to frighten people.
I still find the logic hard to follow. A man angry at Israel set fire to a synagogue in southern France and expected it to influence decisions made in Jerusalem. The people who prayed there had no say over Israeli policy and no special line to the prime minister’s office. They were Jews, and as far as he was concerned, that was enough. It was the same first step I met on the street in 2015, this time carried out with fire.
After the attack, Yonathan Arfi, president of CRIF, the body that represents French Jewish institutions, spoke to my colleague Michael Starr. He said French Jews lived with the knowledge that some people saw them as legitimate targets in a battle being fought thousands of kilometers away.
French Jews have lived with this since the Second Intifada, which began in 2000, long before October 7, 2023. In those years, attacks on Jewish schools, synagogues, and individuals became common for Europe’s largest Jewish community.
Ilan Halimi was kidnapped, tortured, and murdered in 2006 because he was Jewish. In 2012, a terrorist murdered Rabbi Jonathan Sandler, his two sons, and 8-year-old Myriam Monsonego at a Jewish school in Toulouse. In 2025, France recorded 1,320 antisemitic incidents, according to the Interior Ministry. That was down from the year before and still historically high.
The second step does its damage more quietly. A CRIF study published in July looked at the experiences of 30 Jewish schoolchildren interviewed in 2024. Many said they felt pressured to answer for Israeli policies, sometimes by classmates who barely understood the conflict. Some hid that they were Jewish or avoided talking about Israel at all.
These are teenagers worried about grades and friends, and they’re being asked to defend decisions made by the Israeli cabinet. I’m not sure most of the ministers could explain all of those decisions. A Jewish kid in a Paris classroom is expected to.
What a rabbi told New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani
Early in his campaign, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani resisted calls to condemn the slogan “globalize the intifada.” Intifada, he argued, means uprising, and some activists use the word to describe resistance to oppression.
In September 2025, he told MSNBC’s Al Sharpton that his views had changed. A rabbi, he said, had told him the slogan reminded her of bus bombings in Haifa, and that she feared extremists could terrorize Jews in New York.
She was describing exactly how the intifada travels. He said he now saw a gap between what some people meant by the phrase and its impact on Jewish New Yorkers, and that he would discourage its use.
I’ll give him credit for that. It means he can’t say nobody explained it to him. The rabbi could have added the Park Hotel in Netanya, where a Palestinian suicide bomber walked into a Passover Seder in March 2002 and murdered 30 people.
For Israelis who lived through the Second Intifada, the word means buses blown up in Jerusalem and Haifa and restaurants turned into murder scenes. So when someone calls for that to be globalized, I’d like to know what exactly they’re planning to export.
Mamdani’s supporters may mean demonstrations, civil disobedience, or solidarity with Palestinians. Fine, that’s politics. But we hear the bombings, and calling it an “uprising” doesn’t change what we hear.
Last month, his administration announced a strategy to combat antisemitism, including $6.4 million in grants for hate-crime prevention and support for victims, along with more money for security at synagogues and other houses of worship. I hope it helps.
Earlier this month, I wrote that his security grants and cultural programs would leave a central part of the problem untouched: the hostility Jews face over their attachment to Israel. That part depends on Mamdani himself, and on whether he tells people on his own side when their language or behavior has crossed a line.
On a Wednesday evening in November 2025, two weeks after Mamdani won the election, Nefesh B’Nefesh, which helps Jews move to Israel, was holding an event at Park East Synagogue on Manhattan’s Upper East Side.
Outside, police put up barricades between protesters and a group of counterprotesters. Some of the protesters chanted “globalize the intifada” and “make them scared.” Inside, the event went on.
The next day, his press secretary said he had discouraged the language and would continue to do so. The same statement said sacred spaces “should not be used to promote activities in violation of international law.”
When the news site Jewish Insider pressed his team on what that meant, it said it was referring to the organization’s promotion of settlement activity beyond the Green Line, the pre-1967 armistice line.
So the Jews inside heard a crowd chanting about making them scared, and the next day the mayor-elect’s office suggested they’d misused their own synagogue by promoting settlements.
The protesters had made them stand in for Israel. The incoming mayor’s office then asked them to answer for it. Which part of that evening, exactly, was their fault?
Even the Union for Reform Judaism, whose leaders are hardly automatic supporters of every Israeli government, condemned the intimidation and criticized his response.
Anyone can protest Israel’s policies. Jews going into a synagogue should be able to get there without being threatened, and a mayor should be able to say so without adding a “but.” It isn’t a hard sentence to write.
Young child in Paris understood the presence of antisemitism
The Israeli-Palestinian conflict is part of ordinary life in France now. It comes up in classrooms and neighborhood conversations, and in arguments between people who have never been to Israel.
I have plenty of disagreements with my own government, as regular readers of this column know. A Jew in France or New York should be able to hold any opinion about Israel, or none, without being tested on it before walking into a synagogue.
One moment from those 10 hours in Paris is stuck in my head, much more than the insults.
A young boy saw me walking by in my kippah and asked his mother what I was doing there. Didn’t I know I might be killed?
He seemed genuinely worried about me. The boy knew nothing about the hidden camera or the security guard. All he saw was a Jew walking through his neighborhood. Young as he was, he already understood what that could mean there, and he was afraid of what might happen to me.
He’d be a young man now, and I wonder whether he remembers that afternoon as well as I do.
As for the teenagers who spat at me, I’d like to know whether any of them ever got to know a Jewish person, learned something about Jewish history, or rethought what they had been taught.
Eleven years later, there’s violence in France’s streets again, and French Jews are looking at videos like the one from the 19th arrondissement.
Mamdani has said he wants Jewish New Yorkers to feel safe. I hope he means it. He can show it the next time someone chants “globalize the intifada” outside a synagogue, by condemning it plainly, with no second sentence about the people inside.
People can support Palestinians without reaching for the worst years of the Second Intifada. And kids in Paris and New York deserve to meet Jews as neighbors before anyone teaches them that every Jew is a stand-in for Israel.
I still wonder what that boy’s mother told him. I hope it was something kind.

"France is burning!" Trump wrote, accusing immigrants from vastly different cultural backgrounds of contributing to the country's decline.
"The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country," he continued.
Trump urged French authorities to act immediately, writing, "Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late!"
His remarks followed one of France's most violent days of civil unrest in recent years, as demonstrations that had continued for weeks descended into rioting on Saturday, with government buildings set ablaze, stores looted and protesters clashing with police.
Government buildings torched as protests turn violent
In the central French city of Limoges, a fire engulfed the 143-year-old city hall on Saturday, with footage showing the building's spire collapsing, CNN reported Sunday, and in Marseille, masked individuals dressed in black forced their way into city hall and vandalized the property.
In another incident, CNN reported the city's tourist office was set on fire in Lyon as violence spread through the streets,
The protest movement began last month among high school students in Paris's economically disadvantaged northern suburbs, where frustration over teacher shortages and deteriorating school facilities developed into a broader campaign against inequality, rising living costs and declining public services.
Although most demonstrators protested peacefully, smaller groups engaged in violent confrontations with police, vandalized public buildings and looted stores, including luxury boutiques and supermarkets.
French authorities reported attacks targeting police officers, media personnel and government property in several cities, as security forces struggled to contain the violence.
French government vows crackdown on rioters
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu condemned the destruction and said the government would not be "intimidated" by those responsible. He blamed the violence on the "ultra-left" and criminals, warning against attempts to exploit the unrest for political purposes ahead of next year's presidential election.
"To those who clearly want to use this violence as a 'warm-up' before the presidential election, I say clearly: We will not let ourselves be intimidated. No one will impose their political agenda through violence," he wrote in a post on X/Twitter.
Lecornu said approximately 1,200 people had been arrested during the unrest while visiting affected areas Saturday evening.
The demonstrations drew hundreds of thousands of participants nationwide. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez estimated the turnout at approximately 550,000, while the CGT labor union and other organizers placed the figure at 800,000.
French President Emmanuel Macron also condemned the attacks, pledging to prosecute those responsible for the destruction.
"We will all stand united against the sowers of chaos, who only seek to undermine our institutions and prevent those who peacefully express their demands from doing so," he wrote on X.
Macron is to address the nation in a televised broadcast on Sunday evening.

Ukraine Peace Prospects – Q&amp;A
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Q? Do you think the Trump–Putin “deal” will see diesel and global energy prices fall?
Answer - No. I don’t see Russia as having much spare diesel capacity to export. Recent Ukrainian deep-strike drone attacks have been successful, forcing shortages at home and forcing the Russian authorities to impose an export ban. I do not expect Ukraine’s deep-strike drone attacks to stop, as they are having an effect. Why would Ukraine stop?
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Q? So what is Trump trying to achieve?
Answer - I assume that someone in the US administration understands the Russian economy and has told Trump my answer to the first point above. If that is the case, then I think Trump’s messaging around the Russian diesel deal is more to create a scapegoat for the fact that energy prices have remained elevated after Trump’s Iran war. He is seeking to portray Zelensky as the recalcitrant party and responsible for higher global energy prices - even though the evidence still suggests that the biggest driver of higher global energy prices is the Iran war, not the war in Ukraine. Clearly, Trump is trying to change the pitch around midterms, which look increasingly difficult for Trump and the GOP.
Q? Is there an actual energy deal behind the scenes?
Answer - No. Neither the Russian nor Ukrainian side seems to know of any behind-the-scenes deal. One is tempted to think that Trump is making this up as he goes along. Trump seems to think that just by him saying something makes it happen. That’s not the case with Putin and Zelensky. I think Putin and Zelensky have other interests and drivers.
4 New Air Defense Towers Built Near Putin’s Valdai Residence
Q? Will Putin accept an energy deal?
Answer - I think Putin has zero interest in accepting any energy deal right now. His agenda will be focused on the French elections in May 2027, and he will be eager to escalate until then and through the winter. The aim will be to cripple the Ukrainian economy and increase the costs to Europe of supporting Ukraine, to the point that in mid 2027 Europe will have to decide whether and how it continues to support Ukraine.
Putin will offer Trump warm words but deliver nothing. He will take any concessions from Trump, and expect and demand more. The more he holds out for more, the weaker Trump and the Western alliance look. He likely sees Trump as increasingly desperate and incoherent, and he will exploit this by stringing Trump along and, in doing so, further pushing Europe away from the U.S.
Q? Will Putin test NATO Article 5?
Answer - Very likely; actually, he is already doing that. The question is how far he will go in risking a kinetic attack on NATO. As the US backstop for Europe is threadbare, few people trust that Trump would commit US forces to defend Europe. The question is whether this an opportunity that Putin can resist - to test, and diminish NATO’s article 5, while the opportunity is there. Expect more Russian cyberattacks, drone strikes, attacks on European critical infrastructure, assassination attempts against Western industrials, and election meddling, et al.
Q? Will Ukraine agree to an energy deal?
Answer - Only if Russia agrees, which it is unlikely to do. With that in mind, Ukraine has an interest in continuing to hit Russian energy sector assets - in order to bring the war to Russia. And increasingly it has the autonomous capability to do so.
Q? Will Europe pull the plug on support for Ukraine, if demanded by Trump as the price for a Ukraine peace deal?
Answer - Not for a bad deal. Europe increasingly realizes that a) Russia is an existential threat; b) the US backstop to Europe is no longer there; c) European security depends on Ukraine surviving as long as possible against Russia to allow time for Europe to develop an independent defense capability from the US. When push comes to shove, Europe will choose Ukraine over the US.

Ukraine retook Kolodiazi north of Lyman as its drones hit 200-plus Russian vehicles in Operation Vivaldi’s last phase, Ukrainian drone officer says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:39:09 UTC
22:39:09 KST

Ukrainian infantry encircled and retook the village of Kolodiazi north of Lyman without getting drawn into street fighting, while a drone battalion kept the sky above them shut, the battalion’s chief of staff told Suspilne on 18 October. The village fell during the fourth and final phase of Operation Vivaldi, Ukraine’s counteroffensive in northern Donetsk Oblast.
For years now, Russia has aimed to seize Lyman and cross the Siverskyi Donets River. It needs this area to encircle Ukraine’s fortress belt of Donetsk Oblast cities from the northwest, ISW assesses. Vivaldi’s four phases retook 277 km² and 16 settlements on that approach, and a veteran of the operation has said Ukraine’s assault troops suffered more than ten times fewer casualties than Russian forces doing it.
Drones over the infantry
The 60th Mechanized Brigade fought in all four phases of Vivaldi and took Kolodiazi in the last one, said the chief of staff of the brigade’s Fatum unmanned systems battalion, callsign Krash.
“Our task, as an unmanned systems battalion, was to escort and ‘close’ the air in front of our infantry to make it impossible for the enemy to hit it. To suppress all the firing assets possible,” he said.
The brigade’s 3rd Mechanized Battalion, the main striking force, encircled Kolodiazi and retook it without getting drawn into street fighting, Krash said. The 1st Mechanized Battalion kept Russian reinforcements out of the area, while drone crews suppressed artillery, hit supply runs, and worked against Russian drone operators.
Vivaldi counteroffensive advanced after Ukraine took Russia’s drones out of the fight, ISW assesses
500 troops and 200-plus vehicles
The drone battalion killed or wounded about 500 Russian troops during the fourth phase and struck Russian armored vehicles, trucks, and motorbikes, its chief of staff said.
“More than two hundred pieces of various equipment: Grad and Uragan multiple rocket launchers, various armored vehicles, tanks, armored combat vehicles. Most of all motorbikes and quad bikes, there the count runs into the hundreds. This is our enemy’s main logistics tool,” he said.
Ghost villages
The villages retaken in northern Donetsk Oblast are nearly empty of civilians, Krash said.
“It’s very typical for de-occupied settlements: these are ghost towns. You can see right away where the occupier stepped. All the settlements are under the control of the Third Army Corps, our forces stand there and prevent enemy infiltration. But civilian life in these towns is either absent or very scarce,” he said.
Third Army Corps commander Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi reported Kolodiazi’s liberation, along with Zelena Dolyna and Lypove, when he summed up Vivaldi’s fourth phase, which secured 101 km².

Physicists create a bizarre new quantum state called a fractional fermi sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:37:21 UTC
22:37:21 KST

Physicists create a bizarre new quantum state called a fractional fermi sea
- Date:
- October 18, 2026
- Source:
- University of Innsbruck
- Summary:
- Physicists have discovered a strange new state of quantum matter in which ultracold atoms defy familiar organizational rules, forming a highly excited yet surprisingly orderly configuration called a "fractional Fermi sea." The discovery challenges established quantum theories and hints at exotic quasiparticles that scientists have dubbed potential "super-Fermions."
- Share:
Physicists have uncovered a strange new form of quantum behavior in which particles organize themselves in ways that challenge established theories. Even more surprising, the particles maintain a remarkable hidden order despite being driven into an extremely energetic state.
In a study published in Physical Review Letters, researchers from the group led by Hanns-Christoph Nägerl, working with theoretical physicist Alvise Bastianello of the CNRS and Université Paris-Dauphine, describe how to engineer an exotic quantum state known as a "fractional Fermi sea."
The breakthrough involves pushing ultracold cesium atoms far beyond their normal conditions by repeatedly changing how strongly they attract or repel one another. Rather than simply becoming disordered, the particles rearrange themselves into an unusual configuration that behaves differently from the quantum systems scientists have traditionally studied.
The theoretical findings provide the foundation for recent experimental research conducted by Nägerl's team at the Department of Experimental Physics.
Pushing Quantum Particles Beyond Their Normal Limits
Under ordinary conditions, quantum particles follow well-established rules that determine how they arrange themselves, particularly at extremely low temperatures.
One important example involves fermions, a category of particles that includes electrons. These particles cannot all occupy the same quantum state, so they fill available energy levels according to specific restrictions. At very low temperatures, this arrangement produces what physicists call a Fermi sea.
But what happens when researchers deliberately disrupt the conditions that normally govern how particles behave?
As Alvise Bastianello explains: "Fermions, for instance, stack neatly into the available energy states to form the so-called 'Fermi sea'. But what happens if one forces interacting atoms to continuously cycle through extreme conditions, smoothly shifting them from strongly repelling each other to strongly attracting each other?"
To investigate this possibility, the researchers studied ultracold cesium atoms confined to a one-dimensional system. This means the atoms are restricted to moving along a single direction, creating an environment in which their quantum interactions can be studied with exceptional control.
The team examined what happens when the interactions between these atoms are repeatedly adjusted, cycling between powerful repulsion and attraction.
Their calculations revealed something unexpected. Starting from the ground state, the lowest energy configuration available to the system, the atoms could be driven into a highly excited state without losing their underlying organization.
The researchers call this unusual arrangement a fractional Fermi sea because its particles appear to obey a modified rule governing how quantum states are occupied.
"Instead of simply heating the system, the interaction cycle reorganizes the atoms into a new many-body state," says Yi Zeng, the leading author of this study. "This gives us a controlled way to explore quantum matter beyond the usual equilibrium paradigms."
A Strange New Quantum State With Hidden Order
One of the most intriguing features of the fractional Fermi sea is that its particles remain organized even though the system has been pushed far from equilibrium.
In physics, equilibrium describes a condition in which a system's overall properties have settled into a stable balance. Systems driven far from equilibrium can behave in complicated and unexpected ways, making them particularly challenging to understand.
Yet the fractional Fermi sea is not simply a collection of excited particles behaving randomly. Instead, it contains distinctive mathematical patterns that reveal a deeper structure.
Among these patterns are pronounced ripples called Friedel oscillations. These are wave-like variations associated with the way quantum particles influence one another. The researchers also identified unusual patterns in how correlations between particles weaken with increasing distance, even when the repulsive interactions are relatively weak.
These signatures are important because they differ from predictions associated with Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid theory, a long-established framework for describing how interacting quantum particles behave in one-dimensional systems.
The findings therefore point toward a previously unexplored type of quantum behavior that cannot be fully described using this familiar theoretical picture.
"This state is highly excited, but it is not random," says Hanns-Christoph Nägerl, the group leader. "It has a hidden order that becomes visible in its correlations."
The strange behavior also raises questions about the effective particles that emerge within the system. Physicists call these collective excitations quasiparticles because they can behave like individual particles even though they arise from the coordinated motion of many interacting particles.
Nägerl suggests that the unusual excitations might eventually deserve a name of their own.
"We are not yet sure how we should name these new quasiparticles. Perhaps 'super-Fermions'?"
Opening a New Frontier in Quantum Physics
The discovery suggests that fractional Fermi seas represent an exotic critical phase of quantum matter, with characteristic patterns of particle correlations that extend beyond existing descriptions of one-dimensional quantum systems.
It also demonstrates the growing power of quantum simulation, a technique that allows scientists to use carefully controlled quantum systems to investigate physical behavior that would otherwise be difficult to reproduce or study.
Ultracold atoms are particularly useful for this purpose because researchers can precisely adjust their interactions and observe how the resulting quantum states change.
Rather than limiting these experiments to recreating phenomena already understood through established theories, scientists can now explore deliberately engineered states that reveal entirely new possibilities.
As Hanns-Christoph Nägerl says: "The discovery of fractional Fermi seas shows how far we can push quantum simulation: not only reproducing known models, but creating and probing states that go beyond established paradigms."
The current publication establishes the theoretical framework for fractional Fermi seas. A companion study describing their experimental realization through quantum simulation is undergoing peer review.
Together, the research points toward new ways of investigating the fundamental behavior of quantum matter, including unusual collective excitations and hidden forms of order that emerge only when particles are pushed far outside their normal conditions.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Innsbruck. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal References:
- Alvise Bastianello, Yi Zeng, Sudipta Dhar, Zekui Wang, Xudong Yu, Milena Horvath, Grigori E. Astrakharchik, Yanliang Guo, Hanns-Christoph Nägerl, Manuele Landini. Exotic Critical States as Fractional Fermi Seas in the One-Dimensional Bose Gas. Physical Review Letters, 2026; 136 (23) DOI: 10.1103/j3s5-gjpf
- Yi Zeng, Alvise Bastianello, Sudipta Dhar, Zekui Wang, Xudong Yu, Milena Horvath, Grigori E. Astrakharchik, Yanliang Guo, Hanns-Christoph Nägerl, Manuele Landini. Realization of fractional Fermi seas. arXiv, 19 May 2026 DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2602.17657

Tallinn, Tartu and Pärnu: cities must be involved in shaping the EU’s next funding period
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:35:08 UTC
22:35:08 KST

Tallinn, Tartu and Pärnu believe that greater consideration must be given to the needs of urban regions when planning the European Union’s next funding period. To this end, the three cities will submit a joint appeal to Estonia’s Ministry of Finance, emphasising that cities’ practical experience must be reflected in decision-making before priorities and funding measures are finalised.
At a joint press conference held today in Tallinn, the mayors of the three cities stressed that funding in the next period must enable interconnected challenges to be addressed comprehensively. They also called for more flexible funding opportunities and a reduced administrative burden.
According to Tallinn Mayor Peeter Raudsepp, the issue is not only how much EU funding Estonia receives, but also how effectively it can be used.
“Cities have practical experience of which investments are genuinely needed and where they can have the greatest impact. This knowledge must be taken into account when defining the objectives and measures for the next funding period, rather than only when the funds are being distributed,” Raudsepp said.
Tartu Mayor Urmas Klaas emphasised the need for investments with a long-term impact.
“For Tartu, this primarily means comprehensive renovation of educational buildings, the development of sustainable mobility, and investment in urban infrastructure, including connections across the Emajõgi River. The needs of Estonia’s larger cities must be clearly reflected in the national plan for the next EU budget period, and cities should be partners to the state in shaping that plan.”
Pärnu Mayor Siim Suursild said that cities must be involved as partners from the very beginning of the funding planning process.
“Pärnu serves a much wider area than its administrative boundaries alone, and this must also be taken into account when designing support measures. Projects need to be considered as a whole. Currently, funding often covers only one narrow component, while everything else required must be financed entirely from the city’s own budget,” Suursild said.
The influence of larger cities extends well beyond their administrative boundaries. Jobs, schools, services and infrastructure in Tallinn, Tartu and Pärnu are also used daily by residents of neighbouring municipalities. Therefore, the actual role of urban regions must be taken into account when planning funding for the next period.
In their joint appeal, Tallinn, Tartu and Pärnu identify several priorities: the development of a knowledge-based economy and entrepreneurship, crisis resilience and security, energy efficiency and climate change adaptation, digital development, and sustainable mobility.
The three cities also propose making funding more flexible, reducing administrative burdens, and improving municipalities’ ability to prepare and implement projects.
The needs of larger cities and urban regions must be clearly reflected in the national partnership plan, while interconnected investments should be planned and implemented as integrated projects.
Earlier involvement of cities would help improve funding decisions and direct investments to where they can deliver the greatest benefits for Estonia.

Fires broke out at the oil terminal and the oil depot, and serious damage to the data centre was also reported.
Background:
- On the night of 17-18 October, more than 100 drones attacked Leningrad Oblast. The St Petersburg Oil Terminal caught fire and power supply disruptions were recorded.
- Russian online marketplace Ozon reported an attack on one of its logistics centres in St Petersburg overnight.

Iran appointed Mehrdad Akhlaqi, a longtime senior figure in the Islamic Republic's missile industry, as its new defense minister on Sunday, replacing an acting minister who had served since his predecessor was killed in an Israeli strike in February. Hours after his appointment, Akhlaqi threatened the United States and Israel with a sweeping military response, warning President Donald Trump that any renewed attack on Iran could leave American forces facing heavy casualties.
Akhlaqi, 68, succeeds Majid Ebn al-Reza, who had served as acting defense minister following the killing of Aziz Nasirzadeh in Israel's opening strikes on February 28, at the start of Operation Roaring Lion. Iranian lawmakers approved his appointment by a large majority after he presented a plan to rebuild military-industrial infrastructure damaged during the war, accelerate the development of defense technologies and expand cooperation with private-sector companies. 
The new minister has spent decades in Iran's defense industry, particularly its ballistic missile program, and has been subject to American and European sanctions for his activities. He previously headed the Shahid Bagheri Industrial Group, a subsidiary of Iran's Aerospace Industries Organization responsible for ballistic missile production. The UN Security Council placed him under sanctions in March 2007, followed by the U.S. Treasury in 2008, which accused him of overseeing the group's daily operations and participating in negotiations to acquire equipment.
In November 2014, Akhlaqi was appointed head of Iran's Aerospace Industries Organization, which operates under the Defense Ministry. European Union documents also link him to senior management roles in Iran's Defense Industries Organization and to the development of missiles, drones and other military technologies. He holds a degree in chemical engineering from Amirkabir University and a master's degree in strategic management from Malek Ashtar University. Despite his extensive career, he has maintained a relatively low public profile, with much of the available information about him appearing in military records and sanctions documents.
'Let's see how many bodies Trump evacuates'
Addressing lawmakers following his appointment, Akhlaqi declared that he had been a potential assassination target for decades. "I have been on the enemy's assassination list for 35 years," he said, warning that if the "American-Israeli enemy makes another mistake," Iran's response would be "surprising and extensive."
He pledged to strengthen Iran's regional network of allied armed groups, known by Tehran as the "axis of resistance," and restructure the Defense Ministry to meet what he described as daily security threats.
Akhlaqi also claimed that Iran had already taken measures to counter a potential American attack involving the GBU-43/B, commonly known as the "Mother of All Bombs," the most powerful conventional bomb in the U.S. arsenal. His remarks followed reports that Trump was considering using the weapon in a future strike against Iran.
"Trump should be thinking about how to get his people out of the region safe and sound," Akhlaqi warned. "Let him try dropping one bomb, and then we'll see how many bodies he has to evacuate."
The new defense minister also claimed that Iran was relocating its military production facilities to more heavily protected locations. "We are not building new factories in their previous locations. Instead, we are building them inside mountains and fortified, secure structures," he said. "With our fingers on the trigger, we are prepared for war against the Zionists."
He further promised that an Iranian-made heavy fighter jet would take flight next year, describing it as an entirely domestically produced aircraft.
Iran says seven-day Hormuz deal remains on the table
Alongside the military threats, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that Tehran's proposal to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz under a seven-day framework remained on the table, despite Trump's rejection of the plan last month.
"Our position is completely clear. We presented it to the United States in the form of a seven-day plan," Araghchi said. "If there is any sincerity on the American side, the path forward is clear: If the conditions are met, the strait will reopen on the sixth day and negotiations will resume on the seventh."
Iran's conditions include lifting the U.S. blockade of its ports, removing oil sanctions, releasing frozen Iranian funds and ending hostilities on all fronts, including Lebanon. Tehran is effectively seeking a return to the framework of a June memorandum of understanding under which Washington offered significant concessions. Trump, however, has shown no interest in returning to that arrangement and is demanding immediate nuclear concessions that Iran has refused to provide.
Amid the diplomatic deadlock, Iran has intensified attacks this month on oil tankers and commercial vessels crossing the Strait of Hormuz under an American-led protection operation, seeking to disrupt traffic through the strategic waterway. Fuel prices have remained elevated despite Trump's statements that the strait is fully open.
The U.S. blockade of Iranian ports also remains in place, further straining an already deteriorating Iranian economy. Trump has signaled that he could resume military strikes after the November 3 U.S. midterm elections, raising the prospect of renewed fighting if negotiations fail.
Araghchi insisted Sunday that Tehran would not surrender in such a scenario. "We are better prepared for self-defense than ever before," he said. "At the same time, we remain open to the diplomatic path, provided it is conducted with respect and dignity and guarantees the rights of the Iranian nation."

Feast of grapes: A harvest tradition and travel experience in Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:31:00 UTC
22:31:00 KST

Feast of grapes: A harvest tradition and travel experience in Iran
TEHRAN - Held between August 21 and September 21 in different grape-growing regions of Iran, the feast of grapes is a traditional harvest celebration with roots believed to date back around 3,000 years.
When grapes reach full ripeness, the festival offers travelers an opportunity to experience Iran’s agricultural traditions, folk culture and living intangible heritage.
The celebration is particularly associated with Urmia and villages across West Azarbaijan province, where the traditional grape feast and Doushab-pazan --the preparation of grape juice and doushab, a thick grape syrup, have been registered as national intangible cultural heritage.
The tradition is believed to have originated in the ancient times as an expression of gratitude for the grape harvest. It later continued among Christian and Armenian communities in the region.
As mentioned by Visit Iran, the festival has been held in villages including Gerdabad, Digaleh, Resimanabad, Ghoshchi, Jamalabad and Goulan, with local communities maintaining their own customs.
Historically, grapes were regarded as a blessing, and some communities avoided eating the first grapes of the harvest before the ceremony. Care was also taken during harvesting to prevent grapes from falling to the ground, reflecting the belief that wasting the fruit was an act of ingratitude.
In the Urmia area, festivities traditionally take place around the vineyards and Lake Urmia. A central figure is the Il Bashi, or tribal leader, who opens the ceremony with words of thanks and a special prayer in Azarbaijani, followed by a Persian translation. Traditionally, the leader is accompanied by four women representing earth, water, air and fire, as well as a young boy and girl symbolizing the continuation of life.
The children distribute grapes to participants as a blessing. Prayers are offered for the protection of vineyards and crops from hail, storms and floods, followed by the traditional extraction of grape juice using specialized tools and equipment.
The festival then becomes a lively community celebration. Local wrestling competitions, Azerbaijani folk songs such as Qushmaja and Bayati, and traditional dances form part of the festivities. The collective Yali dance, performed by participants standing in a line, represents unity and togetherness.
Visitors may also encounter displays and competitions involving dried grapes and other products, including grape juice, vinegar and raisins.
For travelers, the feast of grapes provides more than a seasonal festival. It is an opportunity to enter the vineyards, meet local communities and observe traditions that connect agriculture with music, food, belief and collective memory. Held during the transition from summer to autumn, the celebration offers a distinctive way to discover the cultural landscape of northwestern Iran and the enduring traditions of the communities around Urmia.

France: Young voters blase about Glucksmann's Socialists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:31:00 UTC
22:31:00 KST

France: Young voters blase about Glucksmann's Socialists
October 18, 2026
The historically working-class Parisian neighborhood of Belleville has gentrified in recent years. It was here that Raphael Glucksmann, a member of the European Parliament for France's center-left Socialists, celebrated his victory in the party's presidential primary on October 11.
Two rounds of voting had been anticipated, but the 46-year-old son of philosopher and essayist Andre Glucksmann triumphed in the first round with a convincing 66% of the vote and will be the Socialist candidate in France's 2027 presidential election.
As he left the Cantine de Belleville restaurant, Glucksmann was flour-bombed by an unidentified assailant. The following morning, he called on his rival, the left-wing French populist Jean-Luc Melenchon, to condemn attacks carried out by his supporters, though it is not clear that the attacker was indeed a supporter of Melenchon's La France Insoumise (LFI).
The incident has highlighted the issue set to dog Glucksmann's presidential candidacy over the coming weeks: How can he win over Melenchon's supporters if he refuses to work with their candidate?
Gluckmann's rapid rise
"Where do you stand on Melenchon?" That was the question that dominated much of the Socialists' primary campaign. Party leader Olivier Faure spoke in favor of leaving the door open for cooperation with the LFI, but Glucksmann called for a clear break with the far left. His decisive victory is therefore also seen as a vote in favor of a clear demarcation.
The other primary candidates questioned Glucksmann's political experience. Segolene Royal, a previous presidential candidate, compared his bid for the Elysee with that of an "intern" wanting to take charge of a company. She said Glucksmann had no experience in government or even running a local authority.
Despite Glucksmann's victory in the primary, his starting position is a difficult one. A poll by Toluna Harris Interactive, published the day after his win, projects that he would win 10–11% of the vote. The same poll put Melenchon on 18%, meaning the far-left man would be much more likely to reach the runoff. But the survey was conducted before Glucksmann won the primary, and so does not take into account any potential boost the nomination may give him. Still, 10% would be an improvement on the Socialists' performance in the last presidential election in 2022, when their candidate Anne Hidalgo won just 1.75% of the national vote.
There is also the complication that the Socialists are banking on a man who is not even a party member to lead them from irrelevance. Raphael Glucksmann actually belongs to a small center-left party called Place Publique.
Melenchon's youth appeal
Glucksmann has his work cut out for him — especially with young people. In an Ipsos survey in September, which posited Glucksmann as the social-democratic candidate and Edouard Philippe as the only candidate from the political center, Melenchon scored 41% among the under-25s. Meanwhile, 20% of this age group supported the far-right nationalist Marine Le Pen. France's young electorate is politically divided, but Melenchon still dominates on the left.
The 75-year-old is currently rallying alongside the students whose protests have drawn international attention. At a rally near Clermont-Ferrand in central France , he expressed solidarity with their movement and reiterated his calls for lowering the voting age to 16 and abolishing Parcoursup, France's national admissions procedure for higher education.
In an analysis for the Fondation Jean-Jaures, a Socialist-aligned think tank, the political scientist Antoine Bristielle distinguishes between a core group of committed LFI voters and the broader left. Melenchon's most loyal supporters, he says, are often young, educated city-dwellers, and many are under a lot of financial pressure. Four in ten households in this group live on a net monthly income of less than €2,000 ($2,200).
Bristielle estimates that just under a third of the left-wing electorate in his study care more about a left-wing victory than their allegiance to any particular party. Almost half of the people in this group are younger than 35, and would consider voting for the Socialists, the Greens, or LFI. Redistribution and an active government are important to them, but most would prefer politicians who are willing to compromise.
Glucksmann's youth efforts
The pattern recently observed in Germany, where young women are more likely to vote for the left and young men for the right, does not apply in France. Political scientists Anja Durovic, Nonna Mayer and Noemie Piolat found that in the 2024 European and parliamentary elections, young French women were not significantly more likely to vote for the left, or less likely to vote for the far right, than men of the same age. It remains to be seen whether this pattern will be replicated in the 2027 presidential election.
Glucksmann says he would ease the burden on earned income by reducing France's CSG social security tax while increasing taxes on inheritances worth more than €2 million. He also presents himself as a committed supporter of European integration, while Melenchon has called the EU a neoliberal institution. Glucksmann's political profile combines social policy demands with foreign policy positions that could also appeal to voters from the camp of the current president, Emmanuel Macron.
France's Ukraine policy is one such issue. Glucksmann favors decisive support for Kyiv. Manon Aubry, a member of the European Parliament for Melenchon's LFI, says her party supports military assistance only under certain conditions, namely: The provision of aid to Ukraine must first be subject to democratic debate; it must not enable attacks deep inside Russian territory; and it must not weaken France's own defense capabilities. In 2024, LFI MPs voted against the French–Ukrainian security agreement.
The tension between the parties of the left was once again apparent in the aftermath of the flour attack in Belleville. The LFI MP Sebastien Delogu posted a declaration of support on X for the taxi driver who was going to have to clean his car.
Glucksmann must win over a lot of voters from Melenchon's camp if he is to have a chance of winning the presidency. This is likely to prove a much more difficult task than simply distancing himself from Melenchon.

New customs instructions drafted to reduce goods stoppage at borders

Unknown Publisher

New customs instructions drafted to reduce goods stoppage at borders
TEHRAN- The Head of Iran Customs Administration announced the drafting of an executive instruction for customs facilitations aimed at speeding up goods clearance, reducing duplicate procedures, and smoothing truck movement at the country’s borders.
According to Mehr News Agency, Foroud Asgari, Head of Iran Customs Administration, speaking on the sidelines of a meeting at the Iran Chamber of Commerce, referred to the issues raised there regarding smoothing the entry and exit of goods, truck traffic at borders, goods valuation, guarantees, and percentage-based clearance of goods. He stated: “During the war period, we obtained a set of customs facilitations from authorized authorities, took them to the government, and had them approved. The President signed these approvals on 16 Mehr, and we are now preparing their executive instruction so that the provisions of the approval are implemented uniformly in customs offices across the country.”
Stating that the main focus of this instruction is preventing goods from stopping at the country’s entry and exit points, he added: “In the export area, we are seeking to have goods assessed using the capacity of inland customs offices so that shipments, after going through assessment procedures, are not stopped again at the borders.”
The Head of Iran Customs Administration, explaining the mechanism envisaged for controlling shipments at borders, said: “Risk management is applied at border entry points, and shipments that require further control based on risk assessment will be directed to the docks for necessary checks; but other goods should pass through the green lane based on mutual trust and the seal affixed by the customs of origin, in order to prevent duplicate controls and unnecessary stoppage.”
Asgari emphasized: “The goal is for customs controls to be carried out in proportion to the risk level of each shipment, and for goods that do not need re-examination to cross the border without imposing extra procedures and stoppage.”
Referring to the envisaged timing mechanism in the import area, he stated: “A specific time has been considered for the various agencies involved in the import process, and the agencies responsible for issuing permits must issue the relevant permits within the set deadline.”
The Head of Iran Customs Administration continued: “The responsible agencies must decide on imported goods and related processes within a specified timetable. If an agency does not act within the stipulated deadline, it must be accountable to the relevant authorities.”
Asgari added: “Customs will also extract information on the timing of processes and permit issuance and will provide performance reports on the agencies to the country’s authorities so that obstacles in the path of goods clearance are identified and followed up.”
Referring to the problems existing in the order registration and goods sampling processes, he said: “In drafting this approval, attention was paid to issues related to order registration, repeated sampling, and measures that were unnecessary but caused rework and increased process time, and we tried to envisage the necessary solutions to resolve these problems.”
The Head of Iran Customs Administration expressed hope that with the implementation of the new instruction, a significant change will occur in the process of goods entering and exiting the country’s customs points, and economic actors will be able to clear their goods more quickly and easily.
Asgari, in response to the issue of truck stoppage and traffic at the country’s borders and the measures taken to resolve this problem, stated: “Part of the existing issues must be followed up by Customs itself. In this regard, we have held border meetings with the heads of customs administrations of neighboring countries to achieve greater coordination for removing obstacles and increasing truck transit capacity.”
He added: “Meetings have been held with the heads of customs administrations of Armenia and the Republic of Azerbaijan, and this week the head of Turkmenistan’s customs administration was present on the soil of the Islamic Republic of Iran and negotiations were held in this regard. The other sides have also announced readiness to cooperate and increase truck transit capacity.”
The Head of Iran Customs Administration, referring to operational visits to important border customs offices of the country, said: “In these visits, problems related to various agencies and obstacles in the process of transit and goods clearance were examined. A significant part of these issues was raised in last week’s meeting with the Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance, many of which were solvable, and a number have also been resolved.”

What are self-replicating ‘AI worms’, and why is Anthropic worried about them?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

Warnings about what artificial intelligence might do in the future – together with alarming reports of what it has gotten up to already – are being issued so quickly that even security experts have difficulty triaging what to worry about.
Yet a report this week from Anthropic’s offensive research team grabbed attention by describing a new, practical threat, one devoid of human characteristics or apocalyptic musings. The red team, as such internal testers are called, said it created a malicious AI program that spread autonomously through internet-connected “smart” televisions and could do the same inside other ordinary devices. While machines running AI usually need a fair amount of computing power, the researchers said that their program split parts of itself among 15 televisions and was still able to function by using a bit of power from each.
In addition to evoking the horcruxes that kept pieces of Lord Voldemort’s soul alive within objects in the Harry Potter series, the report alarmed some professionals because the generally weak security of smart televisions and many other “internet of things” devices would be very hard to correct, even with a concerted effort.
“It’s something to worry about just like every other wave of cyber-attacks. We need to mitigate the possible effects,” said Joshua Saxe, who led development of Meta’s AI security effort. “I’m concerned right now that folks in the cybersecurity community are not taking these kinds of real risks as seriously as they should be.”
The damage of such “AI worms” could be astonishingly large. Self-replicating computer viruses, which need not trick a human to propagate, are known as worms, and earlier worms have wreaked some of the worst havoc in the history of the internet.
That legacy includes the Morris worm of 1988, which arrived before the mainstream consumer internet, when a graduate student released a program that took advantage of various software flaws and weak passwords, copying itself so rapidly that many infected machines slowed to a stop. The US and Israel brought worms into international espionage with the stealthy Stuxnet in the lat 2000s, which sabotaged Iranian nuclear centrifuges. Other worms like the Russian NotPetya and North Korean-attributed WannaCry have caused tens of billions of dollars’ worth of damage worldwide.
Many of the world’s most destructive worms have depended on known vulnerabilities that device owners have not patched, sometimes months after patches became available. The Anthropic team predicted that a worm like theirs could function in the same way and be harder to stop, because smart devices receive patches less often than phones or laptops. Worse, they theorized that an AI worm could keep adapting to other types of hardware by researching newly disclosed vulnerabilities.
What differentiates AI worms from typical reproducing viruses is that AI models can learn as they go, said Ariel Herbert-Voss, an early security expert at OpenAI who now runs AI security startup RunSybil. Existing cybersecurity infrastructure is not ready for the proliferation of such threats, Herbert-Voss said. “We need to better enable our security teams. We need to be giving them more resources to fix problems.”
Worms could also be used for benevolent purposes, suggested Chris Inglis, a former deputy director of the National Security Agency who served as National Cyber Director in the Biden White House.
“The question of whether AI worms are plausible has been settled by several breakout events over the past six months,” Inglis said by digital message. “The better question is how we will employ them, counter them, and/or combine them with other emerging technologies.”
Anthropic researchers said a successful AI worm would need to have more capability on less powerful devices than is possible right now – but they added that current trends will make that feasible by year’s end. Their research follows a paper published by experts at the University of Toronto a few months ago, which infected a full-size computer and could spread to similar machines more rapidly than the television worm.
“The capabilities have been developing very rapidly,” said co-author and Toronto PhD student Jonas Guan.
Guan and other experts said that, as a practical matter, an AI worm should not top anyone’s list of AI fears. The Anthropic version moves very slowly, Guan said, and worms have predictable and detectable actions that can be blocked at multiple layers. Basic security hygiene, including requiring strong passwords and two-factor authentication, would stop most worms and other hacking, experts said.
“Nothing about this is truly feasible or impactful,” said Juan Andres Guerrero-Saade, vice-president of research at security firm SentinelOne. “It’s nifty stunt hacking that’s getting way more amplification in service of the ridiculous doomer narratives that suggest models have a mind and will of their own.”
Anthropic did not respond to an interview request.
Outside Washington, many in the AI and security worlds believe greater government oversight of AI is now essential. But members of Congress have introduced mutually conflicting bills, while the White House has so far created only a small review board.
Security researchers and laypeople alike find themselves weighing the motivations behind fearful prognostications from AI companies, which range from espousing quasi-religious beliefs, to seeking legislation to exclude rivals or save money, to hyping the anticipated multi-trillion-dollar public valuations of the San Francisco AI giants.
“The claim that a lot of this is marketing is correct, but the reality dwarfs any PR,” said Gadi Evron, who is running a conference on AI security in San Francisco this month called Unprompted. “Whatever claims the labs are making, they are not warning us enough. We need to understand that nobody can stop the AI storm.”

Mladenov made the demand in a letter to Yoram Halevi, the Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT), in response to Halevi's announcement of the suspension of goods entering Gaza through private traders—the channel by which most goods enter—"until further notice", according to Haaretz.
