The UN envoy also called on the Israeli government to immediately approve the implementation of the pilot project, under which the Palestinian technocratic committee and the international stabilisation force would begin operating in a limited area of Rafah, in the southern Gaza Strip, currently under the control of the Israeli army and where Hamas has no presence.
The new message came after the Israeli Security Cabinet, in late July, on the eve of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's trip to Washington, approved the deployment of a limited number of international peacekeeping troops to Rafah. However, the decision was later reversed under pressure from ministers of the religious Zionist movement, and Netanyahu announced in late August that the deployment had not been approved.
Mladenov concluded his demands by calling on the Israel to cooperate with the self-styled Peace Board in establishing a new mechanism for managing the supply of goods to the Gaza Strip. According to him, this matter is currently under discussion between the board's staff and Israel.
On Friday, Hamas criticized Mladenov's statements, accusing him of "aligning himself with Israel's pretexts for obstructing the entry of goods into the Gaza Strip and deepening the humanitarian crisis there". This came in a statement issued by the movement in response to what it described as Mladenov's adoption of the Israeli narrative regarding the decision by Netanyahu's government to suspend the entry of goods designated for the private sector into Gaza.
It considered Mladenov's position to be "blatant bias and alignment with the occupation and its pretexts aimed at obstructing the entry of goods, in order to deepen the humanitarian crisis for our besieged Palestinian people in the Gaza Strip".
The movement denied Israeli accusations of interfering in the mechanisms for bringing goods destined for the private sector into Gaza, imposing taxes, and threatening merchants. It asserted that these accusations were "baseless", describing them as "a repeated and blatant Zionist attempt to exacerbate and deepen the humanitarian crisis and evade the obligations of the ceasefire agreement".
Since the beginning of the war, the United Nations and humanitarian organisations have emphasised that the humanitarian corridor, which includes aid organizations and governments, cannot meet the long-term needs of Gaza's population, and that there is a need to strengthen the commercial corridor.
Since the ceasefire, Israel has only allowed eight merchants to submit applications to bring goods into the Gaza Strip, compared to approximately 1,500 before the war.

Crafting and playing the oud: A living musical heritage in Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:29:00 UTC
22:29:00 KST

Crafting and playing the oud: A living musical heritage in Iran
TEHRAN – With its resonant melodies and distinctive pear-shaped body, the oud has long been part of the musical traditions of Iran and the wider West Aisa. Its craftsmanship and performance, sustained through generations of makers and musicians, received international recognition in 2022 when Iran and Syria jointly inscribed the tradition on UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
The inscription was approved during the 17th session of the Intergovernmental Committee for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, held in Rabat, Morocco, from Nov. 28 to Dec. 3, 2022. At the time, the addition brought the number of Iran’s inscribed intangible cultural heritage elements to 18.
The oud is a lute-like string instrument known for its warm, expressive sound. Musicians play it by resting the instrument on their leg, fingering the strings with one hand and plucking them with the other. Its ability to produce rich melodic and harmonic tones makes it suitable for solo performances as well as ensembles accompanying traditional songs and dances.
Crafting an oud requires patience and specialized woodworking skills. Its most distinctive component is a pear-shaped sound box, commonly made of walnut wood, which plays a central role in shaping the instrument’s resonance. According to the traditional methods described in Iran’s nomination, making an oud can take about 25 days, including stages of wood preparation and treatment. Water and steam are used to improve the wood’s durability and workability.
A typical oud has five pairs of strings, although some versions include a sixth string. Variations in construction and stringing allow musicians to produce a broad range of tones and adapt the instrument to different musical styles.
Beyond its physical form, the oud represents a body of knowledge encompassing material selection, woodworking, instrument construction and musical performance. Its historical presence is reflected in artistic depictions, literary works and miniature paintings, offering evidence of its place in the region’s cultural memory.
In southern Iran, the instrument and related musical traditions have particular significance among some Arab and Bakhtiari communities, especially in Khuzestan, Bushehr and Hormozgan provinces. Oud music is also practiced and appreciated in other parts of the country, including Tehran, Kurdistan, Shiraz, Isfahan and Khorasan.
The tradition continues through formal education and apprenticeship. Music schools, art centres, colleges and universities teach oud performance, while experienced musicians pass on their knowledge through direct instruction. Oud making, traditionally practiced predominantly by men, has also attracted increasing numbers of women, broadening participation in the craft.
Iran included the tradition on its National Heritage List in 2018, before submitting the multinational nomination with Syria for UNESCO recognition.
The inscription adds to Iran’s extensive record of intangible cultural heritage, which includes the Radif of Iranian music, the music of the Bakhshis of Khorasan, the art of crafting and playing the kamantcheh, traditional dotar craftsmanship, carpet weaving, Ta’zieh, Naqqali storytelling and the art of miniature.
The joint recognition of oud craftsmanship and performance highlights the importance of safeguarding living traditions that transcend national borders. Their continuity depends not only on preserving techniques and instruments but also on ensuring that the knowledge, music and cultural practices associated with them remain part of everyday life for future generations.

Drone Strikes Major St. Petersburg Bridge, Hitting Key Highway Connecting City’s North and South
A drone reportedly struck a major eight-lane bridge in Russia’s St. Petersburg overnight on October 18, targeting a key section of the Western High-Speed Diameter highway that connects the northern and southern parts of the city. The extent of the damage remains unclear.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to OSINT investigations by ASTRA and Exilenova+ on October 18, the drone struck the cable-stayed bridge spanning the Korabelny Fairway, a major crossing linking two districts of Russia’s second-largest city.
Eyewitness footage reportedly captured an explosion on the bridge, allowing OSINT analysts to geolocate the incident to coordinates 59.919637° N, 30.209319° E. The precise extent of the structural damage has not yet been established.
The bridge connects Bely Island in St. Petersburg’s Kirovsky district with Vasilyevsky Island, forming part of the southern section of the Western High-Speed Diameter, a toll highway providing a major transport connection across the city.
Measuring 622 meters in length and 39 meters in width, the bridge carries eight lanes of traffic. Construction began in 2013, and the crossing officially opened in December 2016.
The reported strike occurred approximately 4.5 kilometers from the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal, where a fire broke out following the same overnight drone attack. Russian authorities also reported disruptions at Pulkovo Airport, where flight operations were temporarily suspended.
The strikes extended beyond the bridge and oil terminal. A VKontakte data center and the nearby Vostochnaya electrical substation in the Leningrad region were also hit, coinciding with power outages and disruptions to the Russian social media platform.

Ryanair’s 'Moroccan adventure' advert for Western Sahara found misleading
Ireland’s advertising watchdog has provisionally found that Ryanair misled customers by promoting flights to Dakhla, a city in Moroccan-occupied Western Sahara, as a "Moroccan adventure".
The Advertising Standards Authority said Dakhla was "not a part of Morocco" and recommended that the campaign should not appear again as it is framed currently, according to a preliminary decision dated 12 October seen by The Irish Times.
In promotional emails sent by the Irish budget airline in March, Dakhla was described as a destination "where ocean, desert, and culture come together" and a place where visitors can “explore Moroccan culture up close".
The findings still require approval from the authority’s independent council, which will decide whether to uphold a complaint brought by Sinn Féin MEP Lynn Boylan.
Boylan had complained that presenting the coastal city as Moroccan was misleading, saying it "erases indigenous people by showing the city as belonging to Morocco".
According to The Irish Times, Ryanair’s submission read it did not intend to describe the destination as "expressing any political stance".
Dakhla is a city on the Atlantic coast of Western Sahara, a former Spanish colony that remains listed by the United Nations as a non-self-governing territory. Its unresolved status is at the heart of a decades-long conflict between Morocco and the Sahrawi independence movement, the Polisario Front.
Morocco has occupied most of Western Sahara since 1975 and considers it part of its national territory.
The Algeria-backed Polisario Front seeks independence and a referendum allowing the indigenous Sahrawi people to determine the territory’s future.

Eating blueberries every day may have a surprising effect on your mood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:22:24 UTC
22:22:24 KST

Eating blueberries every day may have a surprising effect on your mood
A new study hints that eating blueberries daily could help improve mood in older adults, potentially through surprising effects on the gut microbiome.
- Date:
- October 18, 2026
- Source:
- Hebrew SeniorLife Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research
- Summary:
- Eating blueberries every day could have surprising effects on mood, according to a small study that found greater reductions in depressive symptoms among older adults who consumed the fruit for three months. Researchers also detected changes in gut microbial enzymes, suggesting a possible gut-brain connection, although the mood benefits were not statistically significant compared with a placebo.
- Share:
A small pilot study suggests that eating blueberries every day may influence gut bacteria and potentially affect mood in older adults. Participants who consumed blueberries regularly experienced a greater and more consistent reduction in depressive symptoms, along with subtle changes in genes associated with gut microbial enzymes.
However, the improvements in depressive symptoms were not statistically significant when compared with the placebo group. Although the findings do not establish that blueberries can relieve depression, they offer preliminary clues about a possible connection between blueberry consumption, the gut microbiome, and mental health.
"Fiber and anthocyanins in blueberries have potential to modify the gut microbiome and metabolites that are relevant to depression in older adults," said lead author Courtney L. Millar, PhD, assistant scientist II at Hebrew SeniorLife's Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research and assistant professor of medicine at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School. "Our objective was to preliminarily determine the effect of blueberry consumption on the gut microbiome, metabolites, and depressive symptoms."
Testing the Effects of Daily Blueberry Consumption
To investigate the potential connection, researchers recruited adults aged 65 and older who were physically inactive and experiencing mild depressive symptoms. The pilot study used a randomized, double-blind, parallel-arm, placebo-controlled design to evaluate whether consuming blueberries could influence gut microbes and mood.
Over three months, participants consumed either 48 grams of blueberry powder each day (approximately two cups of fresh berries) or a matching placebo powder.
Researchers examined the participants' gut microbiomes using metagenomic sequencing, which allowed them to measure the abundance of different microbial species and genes. They also used liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry to analyze gut-derived fecal short-chain fatty acids, compounds produced through microbial activity. Depressive symptoms were assessed using validated questionnaires administered before and after the three-month intervention.
Blueberries Linked to Subtle Changes in Gut Microbial Activity
A total of 18 participants completed the study. Most were women, and the group was predominantly white (placebo group, n = 8; mean age: 75 ± 6; blueberry group, n = 10; mean age: 71 ± 4).
Despite the encouraging pattern in depressive symptoms among participants consuming blueberries, the researchers found no statistically significant difference in mood improvements between the blueberry and placebo groups.
The gut microbiome results also revealed a mixed picture. The overall abundance of microbial species, MetaCyc metabolic pathways, and short-chain fatty acid metabolites remained unchanged.
However, researchers identified statistically significant changes within the blueberry group in the abundance of genes associated with several gut microbial enzymes. One of these was EC 3.6.3.31 Polyamine Transporting ATPase, which is involved in the production of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), a neurotransmitter that plays a role in brain signaling.
These findings suggest that blueberries may influence specific aspects of gut microbial function even without producing measurable changes in the overall composition of the microbiome. Larger studies will be needed to determine whether these changes are connected to meaningful improvements in mood or depressive symptoms.
The study, "A pilot study of daily blueberry intake modulates the gut microbiota enzyme commissions in older, sedentary adults with mild depressive symptoms," was published in the Journal of Nutrition, Health and Aging.
Other contributors included Mohit P. Chopra, MD, of the Deanna and Sidney Wolk Center for Memory Health at Hebrew SeniorLife and the Department of Psychiatry at UMass Chan Medical School; Xochitl Morgan, PhD, and Emily A. Green, PhD, of the Department of Biostatistics at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health; Alex Wolfe of the Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research at Hebrew SeniorLife; Kerry A. Pierce of the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard; and Lidan Gao, PhD, and Christopher N. Blesso, PhD, of the Department of Nutritional Sciences at the University of Connecticut.
Additional contributors were Alyssa B. Dufour, PhD, of the Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research at Hebrew SeniorLife and the Department of Medicine at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School; Douglas P. Kiel, MD, MPH, of the Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research at Hebrew SeniorLife, Harvard Medical School, and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center; and Lewis A. Lipsitz, MD, of the Hinda and Arthur Marcus Institute for Aging Research at Hebrew SeniorLife and professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School.
Story Source:

New corridors help preserve country’s trade capacity: TPO official

Unknown Publisher

New corridors help preserve country’s trade capacity: TPO official
TEHRAN- Deputy Head of the Trade Promotion Organization (TPO) said: With the cooperation of various sectors and the creation of new infrastructure and corridors, part of the country’s trade capacity was preserved and it became possible for activities to continue.
According to the Mehr News Agency, Amir Roshanbakhsh, Deputy for Promotion of International Businesses of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization, said: In the current conditions, the most important challenge facing Iran’s foreign trade is transportation and the movement of goods along export and import routes—a problem that has intensified following the siege.
He stated: In the last year, about 75 percent of the country’s goods trade was conducted through the Sea of Oman and the Persian Gulf. The initial estimate was that, with the imposition of the siege, this capacity would be completely lost; however, statistics for the first six months of the year disprove this claim.
Roshanbakhsh, referring to efforts made to maintain the flow of foreign trade, added: With the cooperation of various sectors and the creation of new infrastructure and corridors, part of the country’s trade capacity was preserved and it became possible for activities to continue.
However, he emphasized that the current problems of foreign trade are not solely caused by crisis conditions, but are rooted in policymaking and the approach to economic governance—issues that existed even under normal conditions and have now become more visible during the crisis period.
In another part of his remarks, Roshanbakhsh addressed the role of economic associations in pursuing the demands of private-sector actors and said: Associations have been formed with the aim of securing the rights of various economic guilds and groups and can be the voice of the private sector.
Referring to the Iran Chamber’s more than one-century history of activity, he added: The country’s private-sector parliament can play the role of intermediary and facilitator between the government, as the legislator, and economic actors, and can provide the ground for more effective interaction between the two.
According to Roshanbakhsh, strengthening the role of economic associations can help increase private-sector participation in decision-making and regulatory processes and reduce harmful government intervention in economic activities.
In conclusion, referring to the legal capacities of economic associations in the country, he emphasized: Existing laws in this area have suitable capacities, and the Iran Chamber can, by playing an advisory role and addressing association-related issues, provide the ground for strengthening associations and more effective reflection of the private sector’s demands.

France was reeling on Sunday from widespread damage caused by violent protests the day before that saw 1,800 people arrested, a historic town hall torched and widespread looting.

The convulsion raised the stakes for President Emmanuel Macron, who is in his final months in power before elections to replace him in six months’ time. It followed weeks of student protests that had also turned violent at times.
Macron was to address the nation Sunday evening at 6 p.m. GMT, his office said, after meeting key ministers.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said 1,800 people were arrested over the protests and looting, with investigations under way “to identify the perpetrators of these acts so they can be brought to justice”.
Torched cars, smashed shopfronts and burnt debris scarred numerous streets in Paris, where officials said 557 people were in custody after a “record” number of arrests.
The capital experienced “a level of violence that we have never, I believe, seen before”, said Paris deputy mayor Lamia El Aaraje.
Hundreds of shops were looted in Paris and other cities, including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Strasbourg, during the protests over the cost of living.

Around 1,500 businesses were damaged, causing losses estimated in the hundreds of millions of euros, according to the Retail and Trade Federation.

“They stayed until 1:00 am, we were afraid they were going to throw things at us,” she said.

Paris’s Socialist deputy mayor El Aaraje accused Le Pen’s party of “acting like a pyromaniac firefighter”, using the protests to further her presidential ambitions.
US Vice President JD Vance also waded in, implying on X that the unrest was because France had “imported the third world”.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu was to chair a crisis meeting of ministers at 0800 GMT on Monday, his office said. They were to look at the insurance and help for impacted shops as well as the prosecution of perpetrators of the violence.
Half a million demonstrators

An American tourist, Jill Burns, said “we were scared”.
Around 500 police, firefighters and paramedics were hurt in the protests, the interior minister said.
The violence took place on the sidelines of nationwide protests that the interior ministry said were attended by 550,000 people. The CGT union said 800,000 people participated.

“All good news for Marine Le Pen,” he said.
France’s Yellow Vest movement, which staged street protests eight years ago against Macron’s government over planned fuel-tax hikes, had called Saturday’s “yellow and youth” demonstrations.
The principal grievance was the cost of living, pushed up in part by the war in the Middle East, which has helped send inflation soaring in Europe as elsewhere.

The 25th-seeded Davidovich Fokina is set to climb 13 places to a career-high world number 13 when the rankings are released on Monday.
Jodar, playing in his first Masters 1000 final and the youngest Shanghai finalist in tournament history, made a blistering start, broke for a 2-0 lead and again to take the opening set.
Davidovich Fokina recovered from a break down in the second set and saved break points in three successive service games before edging a tight tiebreak to force a decider.
The momentum swung decisively in Davidovich Fokina's favour when he broke the 12th-seeded Jodar twice and sealed victory in two hours and 27 minutes.
"I have a blank mind," Davidovich Fokina said. "I don't know what to say and I don't know how I feel. Just a huge relief.
"After the first set I had to keep trying, keep pushing. In the tiebreak, I believed in myself again. In the third set, maybe I had a bit more fitness physically."
It's the third ATP singles title of the 27-year-old's career, adding to his ATP 250 triumphs in Chengdu and Mallorca this season.
The first meeting between the two Spaniards pitted one of the ATP Tour's rising talents against a player enjoying the best season of his career.
The 20-year-old Jodar, who was ranked outside the world's top 900 little more than a year ago, strengthened his bid to qualify for the ATP Finals in Turin in his first full season on tour. (Reuters)

Police pass the buck, IDF can't stop it: why settler violence goes unchecked in the West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:18:00 UTC
22:18:00 KST

"It is important to understand the situation on the ground. Against Palestinian terrorists, we use every tool available, from M16 rifles to F16 fighter jets, and gather extensive intelligence. But when it comes to the 'blue side,' meaning Jews, the IDF is prohibited from gathering intelligence, and the tools at our disposal are far more limited," a security official told ynet just last week.
Two violent incidents over the weekend once again exposed the difficulties Israeli authorities face in confronting Jewish extremist violence in the West Bank. A Washington Post photographer was attacked during the olive harvest in Abu Falah, while diplomats from France and Belgium visiting the predominantly Christian Palestinian village of Taybeh were attacked on Saturday afternoon. The European Union condemned the incidents, demanding accountability and effective measures to prevent continued violence against Palestinians and journalists.
After months of attacks by Jewish extremists, the latest incidents have renewed questions about who is responsible for preventing the violence, why suspects repeatedly escape before security forces arrive and whether Israeli authorities have the resources and political backing to bring offenders to justice. Security officials sharply criticized the support extremists receive from elected officials. "There are members of Knesset and ministers who visit illegal outposts and give them their full support," one official said.
Police point to jurisdictional restrictions that complicate enforcement. Officers cannot operate independently in Area B of the West Bank, where many confrontations occur, without accompanying IDF forces. The weekend's attacks also took place in areas where Palestinian farmers were not required to coordinate their olive harvest with Israeli authorities, meaning security forces had not been deployed there beforehand. Police said they learned of the incidents only afterward, and no arrests were made because the suspects had fled before officers arrived. Police also cited insufficient cooperation involving the Foreign Ministry and the investigation as an obstacle to progress.
A police official told ynet that several agencies operate in the West Bank, each with different responsibilities. "Responsibility for preventing incidents on the ground is determined according to the law, the area and the missions assigned to each agency," the official said. "The police's responsibility for investigations and enforcement is not in question, but the distinction between that responsibility and the operational responsibility for prevention must not be blurred."
When security forces arrive at confrontations between Jewish extremists and Palestinians, their immediate priority is restoring order. By the time the situation is under control, many of those involved have escaped. Police stress that operational responsibility for Area B rests with the military, but the division of responsibilities has long been identified as a problem. In 2018, Israel's state comptroller urged police and the IDF to clarify their respective duties before and after police arrive at an incident and warned that poor coordination between police, the military and the Shin Bet could undermine law enforcement.
The IDF acknowledges the seriousness of the violence but says it cannot station troops at every potential flashpoint. Military officials estimate that doing so would require at least 10 additional battalions, diverting forces from other operational fronts. The military has already added two regular battalions, the headquarters of the 98th Division and Border Police companies, but officials say significant personnel shortages remain.
Investigations continue as suspects evade arrest
Police say investigations into the attacks on the Washington Post photographer and European diplomats remain in their early stages. Officers are working to identify suspects, collect evidence and prepare arrests. More than 70 indictments have been filed over Jewish nationalist violence in the past year, but security officials say closer coordination is still needed to ensure those responsible face justice. In some cases, arrested suspects have been released to house arrest or without restrictive conditions.
Security officials also criticized the judiciary's handling of certain cases. "There are judges who do not understand the gravity of the situation and release rioters who committed serious offenses, including attacking security personnel or violating orders," one official said. "On the other hand, there are judges who take a much tougher approach."
The latest violence occurred during the annual olive harvest, a period that regularly brings tensions over Palestinian access to agricultural land. Security officials pointed to messages circulated among West Bank residents ahead of the harvest, warning of olive-picking activities and military preparations, which they said were subsequently identified as part of a campaign. Over the weekend, Rabbi Dov Lior also published a letter declaring olive harvesting on Palestinian land permissible and even a religious obligation.
The attacks on a journalist and foreign diplomats have added an international dimension to a longstanding enforcement problem. When foreign nationals and diplomatic representatives are targeted, the consequences extend beyond the West Bank, potentially intensifying criticism of Israel and increasing pressure on its government to demonstrate concrete results.
For Israel, the challenge is twofold: preventing Jewish extremist violence and containing its diplomatic consequences. Without clearer responsibility, better coordination and sufficient forces on the ground, the gap between official condemnations and effective enforcement is likely to persist.

University lecturer Kostiantyn Chub killed in Russian attack on Poltava
Dr Kostiantyn Chub, who held a PhD in physics and mathematics and lectured at V.G. Korolenko National Pedagogical University in Poltava, was killed in a Russian attack on Poltava on 17 October.
Source: Dr Chub's ex-wife, as reported by Suspilne Poltava, a local branch of the Ukrainian public broadcaster
Details: Born in 1967, Kostiantyn Chub studied at Poltava Pedagogical University before completing postgraduate studies at the Faculty of Cybernetics at Taras Shevchenko National University in Kyiv. He later earned a master's degree in primary education.
In 2002, Kostiantyn was awarded a PhD in physics and mathematics.
Kostiantyn began his career teaching mathematics and computer science at Secondary School No. 37 in Poltava, where he worked for several years. He later joined the Department of Mathematical Analysis and Computer Science at the Pedagogical University.
From September 2004, Kostiantyn worked at the same university's Faculty of Pedagogical and Art Education. He taught for 35 years in total.
For 18 years, Kostiantyn served as the faculty's deputy dean for academic affairs. He also authored more than 80 academic publications.
Background:
- On the evening of 17 October, the Russians attacked Poltava. A Russian UAV hit a residential area, damaging four buildings.
- One person was killed and four others were injured as a result of the attack.
- A drone was also recorded as having crashed in Poltava Oblast, damaging five houses.
- A Russian strike on Zaporizhzhia killed Zoia Samofal, who was known for the beautiful knitted dolls she made, dedicated mathematics teacher Bronislava Tumanska, and two families.
- A total of 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 injured in Russian attacks on Ukraine in September, the UN reported.

Gaza families fear food shortages as Israel halts commercial shipments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:16:13 UTC
22:16:13 KST

Gaza families fear food shortages as Israel halts commercial shipments
Gaza residents report rising prices after commercial shipments stopped, while families unable to afford extra supplies fear further shortages if the closure continues.
Gaza City, Gaza — Prices of basic goods are rising rapidly in Gaza, where Israeli restrictions on the import of commercial goods are in their fifth consecutive day.
Families already suffering from the siege on the enclave have started stocking up on goods they can still find, for fear of imminent shortages and continued price increases.
The cost of flour, eggs, onions and other staples has sharply increased since Wednesday, when Israel said that commercial goods would no longer enter Gaza. This comes amid a dispute over fees involving Palestinian merchants and Hamas, which still has some authority in the strip.
Hundreds of thousands of Palestinians in Gaza have been plunged into poverty since Israel began its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023. The price of basic goods has soared, as incomes have shrunk due to the war and Israel’s tightened siege.
Residents without the means to buy in bulk will have to continue to purchase food when they can. They will be worst hit by the daily price rises if the border remains closed.
Food shortages
The impact of the Israeli import restrictions is playing out in marketplaces, which are slightly busier than usual.
Ismail al-Barawi, 52, from Jabalia in northern Gaza, noticed a significant rise in prices within two or three days of the crossings being closed on Wednesday.
He described a recurring cycle of uncertainty in Gaza over the status of the crossings, which is usually followed by higher prices.
Al-Barawi said a carton of eggs that had cost 35 shekels ($11.34) was now selling for between 60 and 70 shekels ($18 to $21). The price of a kilogramme of onions had risen from five or six shekels ($1.50–$1.80) to between eight and 10 shekels ($2.40–$3), while a kilogramme of avocados had increased from seven or eight shekels ($2.10–$2.40) to around 15 shekels ($4.50).
“These increases happened in just two or three days,” he said, voicing concern about what prices would be if the crossings remain closed for another 10 to 15 days.
The increases have forced him to buy smaller quantities of what he needs. Instead of a full carton of 30 eggs, he might buy only four or five.
“Today, everyone is trading at the expense of the people. There is no mercy,” he said. He expressed frustration at traders, saying they raise prices as soon as they hear that crossings may remain closed, adding to the problem of real shortages.
Al-Barawi predicted that a 50 kg sack of flour could end up costing 200 or even 300 shekels ($60–$90), if the crossings remained closed.
Al-Barawi is responsible for providing food to his extended family of about 11 or 12 people, including his married daughters and their children. Whenever he has money, he prioritises basic goods such as flour, rice, cooking oil, onions and potatoes.
Given the uncertainty, it makes sense for Palestinians to stock up now before prices increase further. But many families in Gaza have no money to spare, he added.
“Some people cannot even afford to feed themselves for a day. How much can they save or store when they have no money?” he said.
But stockpiling also has its limits. Fresh vegetables can spoil within days, he said. Unreliable electricity supplies make it difficult to store meat for more than a brief period.
Questions on the suspension
Gaza’s Government Media Office on Thursday rejected Israel’s explanation for the suspension, denying that authorities in the territory had imposed taxes or government fees on commercial trucks.
The office said the 10,000-shekel ($3,242) amount cited by Israel was linked to a voluntary community fund intended to support vulnerable families and financial relief projects.
It also said measures requiring a 30 percent rate for cash transactions had been introduced in agreement with the Chamber of Commerce to address a shortage of cash liquidity and the circulation of worn-out banknotes.
The office accused Israel of using the dispute to impose further restrictions on supplies entering Gaza, which has been under an Israeli blockade since 2007.
Gaza authorities were not to blame for the reduction of trucks entering the enclave, it said, and called on mediators and international parties to push for the entry of 600 trucks a day, in line with existing agreements with Israel.
The office warned that continued restrictions would worsen the humanitarian and economic crisis in Gaza.
Food remains unaffordable for many households in Gaza. The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported that food prices in Gaza in September 2026 averaged 204 percent above pre-October 2023 levels, when the genocidal war on Gaza began and Israel tightened restrictions on goods entering the enclave. OCHA’s October 2 situation report, before the new border restrictions were imposed, documented the wider humanitarian pressures facing residents.
No money
Iman Atallah, a 50-year-old displaced woman living in Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza, said the suspension of food deliveries has brought back memories of the man-made famine which hit the enclave in 2025.
Atallah said the price of a sack of flour had already risen from between 25 and 35 shekels ($7.50–$10.50) before the closure to about 80 shekels ($24). With little income and a family to support, she said that even buying basic food had become increasingly difficult.
“Before the crossings closed, flour was affordable. We could somehow manage to buy it. Now it costs 80 shekels ($24),” she said.
The flour her family receives through aid distributions lasts less than a month. Fresh fruit and eggs are not completely unaffordable.
“We used to eat more, and we could buy eggs for the children. Now we’ve had to give those things up,” she said.
Her family now relies on rice and lentils, and they can afford only a little bread. Atallah said they sometimes skip breakfast or dinner, with lunch as their main meal of the day.
Atallah’s family is one of the many in Gaza unable to afford extra supplies and facing a bleak outlook if the crisis continues.
“We cannot stock up because we have no income,” she said. “If the crossings remain closed for 10 or 15 days, everything will become extremely expensive. Those who have money will stock up, while those who do not will just have to watch.”

Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas also confirmed the information, but stressed that he could not provide further details at this time.

During the Parade of Nations, Kazakhstan's flag was carried by Dastan Mukashbekov, a bronze medalist at the Paris 2024 Paralympics and Asian Para Games champion, and Ayala Mereke, a multiple-time World Para Judo Championships medalist.
Kazakhstan has participated in the Asian Para Games since the event's inception, with the national team continuing to grow. While 131 Kazakh athletes competed at the previous Games in Hangzhou, this year's delegation includes 150 competitors.
Kazakh athletes will compete in para athletics, para swimming, para judo, para taekwondo, para powerlifting, para table tennis, para shooting, para archery, para cycling, sitting volleyball, boccia, and wheelchair tennis.
This year's Games mark a milestone for Kazakhstan, which is represented in wheelchair tennis for the first time. National team athlete Aizhan Butimbayeva described the debut as a significant achievement, noting that the sport has been developing in Kazakhstan since 2022 and that local athletes have already earned medals at international competitions.
A total of 18 sports are included in the Games program, with 502 medal events scheduled.
The competition will run through October 24 at venues across Aichi Prefecture and Nagoya, with Kazakh athletes' performances broadcast on the Qazsport television channel.
Noteworthy, Kazakhstan claims 10 victories ahead of Asian Para Games opening ceremony.

Paris left reeling as student-led protests turn chaotic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:08:06 UTC
22:08:06 KST

Paris left reeling as student-led protests turn chaotic
Some 1,800 people arrested and hundreds injured during nationwide demonstrations attended by hundreds of thousands.
Paris residents tell Al Jazeera they’re dismayed by protest damage
Paris, France – France is counting the cost of a day of unrest after hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets nationwide, in the largest mobilisation since protests over education reforms and rising prices began last month.
At Place de la Republique, in the heart of the French capital, people on Sunday surveyed the previous day’s destruction in dismay: smashed windows, gutted buildings, looted shops.
“I find it unacceptable – absolutely unacceptable,” said Rabah, who has been living in Paris for more than 70 years. “Back in the day, we also demonstrated, but peacefully,” he said.
Staring at the burned skeleton of what used to be a newspaper stand, 56-year-old Claire was also shaken. “I love Paris so much, and seeing it like this makes me furious,” she said. “It’s absolutely appalling. I’m actually quite overcome with emotion.”
Nearby, the statue of Marianne, the symbol of the French Republic, was covered in graffiti. “Those who sow misery reap anger,” read one inscription.
The student-led protests began in mid-September, caused by grievances ranging from overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages to systemic inequality and a lack of opportunity.
The movement quickly spilled out of the schoolyards and into the streets, tapping into broader social and economic anxieties.
On Saturday, these complaints converged in a mobilisation that saw a nationwide turnout of 550,000 people, according to authorities; unions and organisers put the estimate at 800,000.
But while the vast majority of demonstrators rallied peacefully, the scale of the violent unrest threatened to eclipse their message. In Paris, there was also heavy use of tear gas and stun grenades by the police, including before the start of the march, which set the tone for a tense day.
“I marched from the 10th arrondissement town hall to Place de Clichy. I was there from start to finish, and it was very peaceful – just all kinds of people, all of them nonviolent,” said Stephanie, a 23-year-old Parisian student.
“But once again, the violence was so spectacular that the actual message – the reasons behind the protesters’ grievances – was never conveyed,” she said.
Macron to address nation
French President Emmanuel Macron, whose second and final term ends next year, will give a televised address to the nation at 18:00 GMT on Sunday after meeting government ministers, his office announced.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said nearly 1,800 people had been arrested – almost half of them in Paris – and more than 500 police officers, gendarmes and firefighters had been injured in the unrest.
“Protesting is a fundamental right. Causing disorder through violence and in a concerted manner is not,” he said on Sunday.
During Saturday’s protest in Paris, Al Jazeera saw groups of black-clad, masked young men smashing shop windows with what appeared to be golf clubs before fleeing with bags of stolen goods.
In Marseille, France’s second-largest city, dozens of shops were looted and a group of people broke into the city hall before being forced out.
“Students and others have real claims they want to air which no one is listening to now because idiots are smashing everything,” said Benoit Payan, the city’s mayor.
In Limoges, footage showed flames engulfing the city hall as the fire spread through the historic building. Public buildings were also damaged in Bordeaux and other cities.
Police conduct has also come under scrutiny. France’s police inspectorate, the IGPN, had opened 36 investigations into alleged police violence since the high-school protests began, according to figures released by the Ministry of the Interior on October 13. The figure predates Saturday’s demonstrations.
Human rights lawyers have described some of their clients’ injuries as comparable to those seen in conflict zones. These include a minor who has lost his hand, another with his jaw smashed and a third pupil who lost sight in one eye.
“There is an increasingly systematic use of crowd-control measures that would normally be reserved for much more serious situations,” said Christophe Calvao, president of the Paris Young Lawyers’ Union. “This only serves to inflame tensions and make people even angrier.”
The government now faces the challenge of responding to widespread social discontent while trying to pass a budget aimed at bringing France’s public finances under control.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu wants to reduce the country’s deficit through spending restraint and tax measures – a move that will likely deepen public anger. Cuts to France’s generous welfare system have traditionally faced strong public resistance.
All of this takes place in a highly toxic political environment as parties harden their positions ahead of next year’s presidential election.
Jean-Luc Melenchon, the leader of the left-wing France Unbowed party and potential presidential contender who has sought to appeal to young voters, accused the government of fuelling the unrest.
“In Paris, aberrant leadership has opened the door to chaos. Those in charge no longer know what to do; the rank and file are afraid and are running wild,” he said.
Lecornu hit back. “This is YOUR political responsibility,” said the prime minister on social media, accusing far-left groups of orchestrating the violence.

Nearly NIS 800 for a family outing: Israel’s Hanukkah Festigal ticket prices skyrocketing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:06:12 UTC
22:06:12 KST

An Israeli family buying four full-price main-hall tickets to Festigal, one of the country’s best-known Hanukkah children’s shows, would pay NIS 796 this year, after prices rose by up to 7.8%.
That bill covers admission alone, before transportation, food, or other expenses associated with a family outing.
Hanukkah is a busy season for children’s entertainment in Israel. During the school holiday, theaters and entertainment venues stage musicals, plays, and other family performances. Festigal is among the most prominent productions, bringing together Israeli singers and actors in an annual musical built around a new storyline.
This year’s production, Top Secret Festigal, is scheduled to open on November 28 at Expo Tel Aviv. Its cast includes Israeli pop singer Noa Kirel, entertainer Ran Danker, and actress Eliana Tidhar, with Eden Ben Zaken appearing as a guest singer.
According to a price comparison compiled by Shelcha, an Israeli consumer benefits club, Festigal’s full ticket prices increased by NIS 10 in each of its three seating categories compared with 2025.
Main-hall seats rose from NIS 189 to NIS 199, an increase of approximately 5.3%. Lower-tier seats increased from NIS 159 to NIS 169, or 6.3%, while upper-tier tickets rose from NIS 129 to NIS 139, a 7.8% increase.
Holiday attractions becoming financially challenging for families
“Hanukkah is a holiday of light and miracles, but for many families, spending on outings and attractions also becomes a financial challenge,” said Sigalit Cohen-Baruch, CEO of Shelcha.
“When you add the costs of other outings throughout the holiday, you realize that every purchasing decision can affect the family budget,” she said.
The comparison also showed how membership benefits can change the cost of the same show. Consumer clubs and bank-card programs offer eligible customers discounted tickets, with prices and purchase limits varying by program.
Shelcha said its members could buy main-hall tickets for NIS 95 and upper-tier seats for NIS 45. The latter price represented a discount of approximately 67.6% from the full price.
Hever, a benefits organization serving career military personnel and retirees, offered still lower prices in the comparison: NIS 69 for the main hall and NIS 29 for the upper tier.
Bank customers may also qualify for discounts. Mizrahi-Tefahot advertised Festigal tickets ranging from NIS 59 to NIS 119 through its cardholder benefits program, with a limit of two tickets per code and eligibility tied to qualifying card spending.
Holiday children's entertainment shows similar price gaps
Similar price gaps appeared elsewhere in the holiday entertainment market. Motek Forever, a separate production aimed at younger children, was listed at a full price of NIS 159, compared with NIS 59 through Shelcha and NIS 39 through Hever.
In a response published by the Hebrew-language newspaper Israel Hayom, Festigal’s organizers said they offered several price tiers and special arrangements through organizations and workers’ committees to help families afford tickets.
Cohen-Baruch recommended setting a holiday budget before booking and comparing offers across ticket sellers and membership programs. The final cost depends on which performances and seats are available, how many discounted tickets a family is entitled to buy, and whether it meets the program’s conditions.

IRGC profiting from sex trafficking of Iranian women, using children for proxy wars - JCFA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:06:03 UTC
22:06:03 KST

Iranian women trafficked for sex, undocumented migrants, children, and refugees are being exploited by the Islamic Republic, and specifically the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), to finance and support its proxy wars across the region, according to a new analysis published last week by the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs.
Ella Rosenberg, a senior research fellow at the JCFA and a member of the Dvorah Forum, said Iran’s legal framework allows the regime to project an image of compliance with international anti-trafficking regulations while relying on flawed legislation that falls short of international standards and fails to adequately protect victims.
She noted specifically that the Islamic Republic conflates human trafficking with migrant smuggling, and the regime has consistently refused to ratify the 2000 United Nations Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish Trafficking in Persons (the Palermo Protocol).
IRGC directly benefiting from sex trafficking, Israeli study finds
Beyond failing to protect victims, Rosenberg assessed that the IRGC directly benefits from human trafficking. She noted that the IRGC uses the sex trafficking sector, often facilitated by the regime through temporary marriages, as a major source of income.
Rosenberg described Iran as a source, transit, and destination country for the sex trafficking of women and girls, citing widespread poverty, systemic corruption, and economic mismanagement as contributing factors.
She argued that Article 1041 of Iran’s Civil Code, which permits girls to marry at 13 and younger girls to marry with parental permission and court approval, has helped normalize the sexual exploitation of minors. Rosenberg also linked the practice of nikah mut’ah, a temporary marriage contract agreed upon for a predetermined period, to the exploitation of women and girls and their vulnerability to organized trafficking networks.
Trafficking networks move victims within Iran and across its borders into neighboring countries, including Iraq, with the alleged support of the IRGC, according to Rosenberg. She argued that the scale of cross-border sex trafficking could not be sustained without the corps’ complicity, given its role in border control and the intelligence apparatus’s oversight of internal security checkpoints and airports.
Adding more weight to her analysis, Human rights groups, including IHR Monitor and HRANA, have documented allegations that IRGC commanders accepted bribes to facilitate the passage of trafficking victims. Rosenberg added that the IRGC profits directly from the exploitation of Iranian women by taxing the commercial sex trade.
IRGC exploiting Afghan, Pakistani refugees
In addition to financially benefiting from human trafficking, the JCFA report claimed that the IRGC’s Quds Force and the Basij systematically traffic undocumented migrants, refugees, and children to “sustain their proxy wars across the Middle East.”
The IRGC exploits vulnerable populations, particularly Afghan and Pakistani refugees, to recruit fighters through deception, financial coercion, and threats of deportation, she argued. Individuals harvested from these communities are coerced into joining proxy militias like the Fatemiyoun and the Zainabiyoun brigades, for deployment in foreign countries like Iraq.
Additionally, in violation of international law, the Basij systematically recruits and coerces Iranian children as young as 12 into military indoctrination and combat support roles. This was argued to be a severe form of human trafficking, as the recruitment exploits children’s vulnerability to coerce them into hazardous, involuntary servitude in military environments. Though JCFA warns of the abuse of children aged 12 and up, The Jerusalem Post has previously reported on the death of an 11-year-old Basij member who was killed at a checkpoint in Iran.
Rather than directly profiting from the trafficking of vulnerable individuals into the IRGC, Rosenberg put that the financial gain can be categorized as cost avoidance rather than revenue. She argued that rather than deploying trained members of the IRGC, which the regime would have to pay and has invested in, the revolutionary guards can deploy underpaid or unpaid vulnerable groups who are deemed disposable because of their lack of funded training.
Such deployments were estimated to save the Islamic Republic billions of dollars in military expenditure, freeing funds to be redirected into the IRGC’s domestic corporate monopolies and regional terror financing networks.
Again, Iran’s “tax” system also allows it to benefit from migrants transiting from Pakistan and Afghanistan hoping to reach Europe through Iran and Turkey.
The migrants are also routinely subjected to debt bondage, extortion, and forced labor in Iran’s informal agricultural and construction sectors to pay off exorbitant smuggling fees by criminal networks who pay protection money to the IRGC. This alone is estimated to generate billions of dollars for Iran’s shadow economy. creates a multi-billion-dollar shadow economy.
Focus on Iran's nuclear program may distract from IRGC human trafficking
Rosenberg shared that Iran was able to continue to exploit these systems as sanctions from the EU and US have primarily focused on Tehran’s nuclear proliferation, ballistic missile development, support for regional terrorism, and suppression of domestic dissent. Failing to also sanction the IRGC and the front companies it uses for human trafficking continues to provide Tehran a lifeline.
Given that the funds raised by human trafficking are often liquid, Rosenberg also alerted to the fact that it was hard for international systems to monitor how much wealth Iran is accumulating through these streams. Individuals involved in facilitating or covering for the regime-backed smuggling networks are therefore allowed to continue to travel, utilize regional banks, and manage front companies without fear of asset freezes or international arrest warrants.
To prevent Iran from continuing to profit from human trafficking, Rosenberg advised that the US Treasury Department should utilize the Global Magnitsky Human Rights Accountability Act specifically to designate IRGC border commanders, Basij recruitment officers, and complicit Iranian law enforcement officials for their roles in labor and sex trafficking.
She added that the European Commission must also leverage the Sixth Anti-Money Laundering Directive (AMLD6) to require European financial institutions to monitor illicit financial flows generated by Iranian trafficking networks aggressively.

It is therefore trying to shore up its defenses at home and prepare for operations in the region.

The Iranian parliament widely supported Akhlaghi's appointment. He has said he will rebuild the country’s defense sector.

Iranian state media provided a short bio, noting that “his previous positions include heading the Shahid Bakeri Industrial Group and serving as managing director of the Aerospace Industries Organization.”
Akhlaghi worked in Iranian defense industries for over four decades

New Iranian defense minister sanctioned by UN for involvement in missile program
The new defense minister was sanctioned for his role in the missile program. In 2007, the UN listed Akhlaghi on a sanctions list “as an individual involved in nuclear or ballistic missile activities.”

The US Treasury Department also sanctioned Akhlaghi in 2008. He is well known for his role in Iran’s missile program. He has also been involved in procuring items for the program.
The person now in charge of Iran’s defense ministry is uniquely positioned to try to rebuild its missile program.

Recent reports, however, indicate that Iran is rebuilding its missile program and has also repaired many missile launchers.

An Algerian national formerly found to be in possession of an al-Qaeda training manual and who was later sentenced to nine months in prison for immigration offenses is now the BBC’s principal data scientist in the Responsible AI division.
This was first reported by The Telegraph on Saturday, and then independently confirmed by The Jerusalem Post.
The case involves Hicham Yezza, who was working in an administrative role at the University of Nottingham when, in May 2008, university staff discovered a copy of an al-Qaeda training manual on his work computer and alerted the authorities.
The document had been sent to him by his friend, postgraduate student Rizwaan Sabir, who was researching Islamist terrorism and allegedly wanted help printing it.
On May 14, 2008, both men were arrested under the Terrorism Act 2000 and detained for around six days. They were released without charge, after Yezza maintained that he had no involvement in terrorism and said the document had been sent to him for printing, not for operational purposes.
The Nottingham Two arrests and immigration conviction
The case sparked outrage from academics and civil-liberties campaigners, and the case became known as the “Nottingham Two” arrests.
Following his release from the terrorism investigation, Yezza was immediately rearrested under immigration legislation, and authorities sought to deport him to Algeria.
In 2009, Yezza was sentenced to nine months in prison for an immigration-related offence involving his claim to have valid permission to remain in Britain. He was released after five months, and is now a British citizen.
On returning from prison, Yezza launched Ceasefire Magazine, which describes itself as an independent political and cultural publication motivated by “a belief in the free exchange of radical and ground-breaking ideas.”
On his LinkedIn, Yezza listed himself as editor-in-chief of the magazine from September 2010 to September 2021. Since his departure, the magazine has become significantly less active. Its most recent article appears to be a May 2025 Comment piece titled “Dispossession resistance is a natural law right of the Palestinian people.”
The piece, by Asim Qureshi, refers to Hamas as a “faith-based movement” and said, “Until the entirety of the Zionist colonial entity and all its settlements are dismantled, the Palestinians will be entitled to exercise their natural law right to resist their dispossession and recover what was unlawfully stolen.” However, as Yezza has apparently taken a step back from the magazine, no relationship can be drawn between him and its current content.
Yezza's BBC career and previous anti-Israel statements
Outside of Ceasefire Magazine, Yezza served as an editorial consultant for Al Jazeera from November 2017 to June 2019. He then spent three years and 10 months at the BBC in an editorial capacity, first as a Middle East and North Africa (MENA) expert and then as a senior journalist in BBC Monitoring’s central editorial Data Hub team.
In his time as a MENA expert, Yezza reported on the war in Gaza despite his previous anti-Israel stances.
As of July 2025, he is the principal data scientist for Responsible AI at the BBC, “helping guide and shape how the BBC approaches and applies responsible AI use across the organization.”
Prior to his employment with the BBC in 2021, Yezza was an active commenter on social media, frequently speaking about the “occupation and apartheid” in Israel.
Many of his posts in the year 2018 revolved around Israel, his support for Palestinian resistance, and his defense of Jeremy Corbyn against accusations of antisemitism.
He also tweeted that rockets being fired from Gaza into Israel were “resist[ance].”
The Post reached out to the BBC for comment.

Israeli court orders seven to repay NIS 1.85m in misused cancer donations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:05:23 UTC
22:05:23 KST

The Haifa District Court has ordered seven people who ran two linked charities to personally repay NIS 1.85 million after finding that a donation intended to help children and teenagers with cancer was diverted to another organization and spent outside its approved purpose.
Senior Judge Ron Sokol ruled that the officials breached their duties by allowing the transfer, submitting misleading reports and failing to account adequately for the money. His October 8 decision also found that substantial sums were paid unlawfully to the charities’ leading figure, attorney Galit Pauker Shemesh, as salary and rent.
The ruling, announced by the Justice Ministry on Sunday, concerns the charities, Keren L’Chaim and Keren L’Chaim L’Yeladim V’Noar (for children and youth), both ordered by the court to close in 2024.
All seven must repay the money, and any one of them can be required to cover the full amount still owed. Interest and inflation adjustments will be added from April 2019. They were also ordered to pay a total of NIS 20,000 in legal costs.
Donation intended to support children with cancer
The money came from the estate of Helen Hatab. Her estate administrator told the court that she had been a teacher and had suffered from cancer, leading him to propose using part of her estate to support children and teenagers with the disease.
A family court approved the arrangement in March 2019. The program was to provide educational support during illness, guidance for recovering patients and funding for equipment, medicines and treatment through the original Keren L’Chaim charity.
But the bank details supplied for the transfer belonged to the newer organization, Keren L’Chaim L’Yeladim V’Noar. The family court did not approve transferring the donation to a different charity or using it for a different purpose.
The First International Bank of Israel (FIBI) initially refused to transfer the money after identifying the mismatch between the approved recipient and the account. The charities subsequently opened accounts at Bank Mizrahi-Tefahot, where the donation was deposited in the newer charity’s account in April 2019.
Sokol also found that a document submitted to FIBI had been altered to replace the original charity’s registration number with that of the newer organization.
Charity officials defend spending on hostel renovations
The seven argued that the money had supported legitimate charitable work, principally renovations at Beit Keren, a hostel for at-risk girls in Hadera. Pauker Shemesh maintained that the estate administrator had approved redirecting funds, that she had provided evidence of the renovation costs and other expenses, and that her salary and rent payments were justified and approved.
The other six argued that they had volunteered, received no personal benefit, and relied on Pauker Shemesh and professional advisers to oversee the finances.
The court rejected those defenses. The approved cancer-support program could not simply be replaced with another charitable project without the required approval, Sokol found. He concluded that transferring the donation and changing its purpose were intended to evade scrutiny of the original charity and allow the officials to continue handling donations without restrictions.
The officials said that roughly NIS 1m. had been spent on the hostel, but did not provide sufficient invoices, plans or other evidence to establish that expenditure. A promised expert assessment of the work’s value was never submitted.
Sokol accepted that some renovation work had taken place. In calculating the repayment, he deducted NIS 41,621 for that work, using the amount recorded in the charity’s financial report.
Court orders repayment of salary and rent
Pauker Shemesh was separately ordered to return NIS 180,390 in salary and NIS 112,110 in rent, plus interest and inflation adjustments. Any salary and rent she returns will reduce the total amount the seven must repay.
Sokol acknowledged that the officials had genuinely wanted to help people in need and had done so for years. But he found that the money had also been used improperly for personal benefits, mainly for Pauker Shemesh, and that the other officials’ failure to oversee spending had allowed this to happen.
“We cannot accept the respondents’ claim that they are exempt from any duty merely because they acted as volunteers,” Sokol wrote.
Trusting that nobody was pocketing money was no substitute for checking that donations were used for their intended purpose, he added.

The world does not realize that it is approaching World War III - FT
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:01:58 EEST
22:01:58 KST

The world does not realize that it is approaching World War III - FT
Kyiv • UNN
The International Crisis Group has counted 65 conflicts around the world — the highest number since World War II. FT warns of the risk of a global confrontation.
The number of armed conflicts has already reached its highest level since World War II. Russia’s war against Ukraine, the confrontation between the United States and Iran, and tensions surrounding Taiwan could escalate into a global clash. The Financial Times writes, reports UNN.
Details
As FT columnist Gideon Rachman writes, the wars in Iran and Ukraine dominate global news headlines, but the International Crisis Group recently counted 65 ongoing conflicts around the world—the highest number since the end of World War II.
The conflict in Sudan, fueled by external forces, is particularly bloody—it is punctuated by massacres of civilians and the displacement of more than 14 million people.
One important factor is the changing global balance of power, which is encouraging revisionist states to challenge the global dominance of the United States and its allies.
The relative decline in the power of the Western alliance has created opportunities for revisionist states dissatisfied with the current world order. So has the rise of anti-war sentiment in the United States, driven by disappointment with the outcomes of the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq.
This shift in the international balance of power has prompted Russia, Iran, and China to take greater risks. Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine did not come out of nowhere; it was preceded by Russian military aggression against Georgia in 2008, as well as the annexation of Crimea in 2014 and military intervention in Syria in 2015.
Meanwhile, China has built military bases on artificial islands that it created in the South China Sea and pushed the Philippines out of Scarborough Shoal, which is much closer to the Philippine coast than to China.
The emergence of a new generation of strongman leaders has contributed to this new atmosphere of international instability. Leaders such as Putin, Xi, Trump, and Benjamin Netanyahu are nationalists and self-proclaimed men of destiny.
However, there is a theory of peace underlying some of Trump’s proclamations, as well as Putin’s and Xi’s territorial ambitions. It is the idea that great powers should be allowed to dominate a "sphere of influence" over their immediate neighbors. Their smaller neighbors, such as Ukraine, Taiwan, Canada, or Cuba, should accept the dominance of a regional hegemon. Moreover, if all great powers respect one another’s spheres of influence, then global peace can be maintained.
According to this theory, this brutal realpolitik, rather than some imagined rules-based order, is the best guarantee of peace in the world. The idea may seem superficially plausible, but in reality it does not stand up to scrutiny. It ignores the views and interests of neighboring countries.
Previously
Head of the Office of the President Kyrylo Budanov stated that World War III has been underway for a long time already and, in his view, began in Ukraine.
