Why have settler pogroms surged during olive harvest season in West Bank?
France and Belgium condemn settler attack on diplomats, but critics say the EU needs to act beyond words of condemnation.
The European Union has condemned Israeli settler attacks on EU diplomats and Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, amid unprecedented settler pogroms during the Palestinian olive harvest.
“We expect full accountability as well as effective measures to prevent continued acts of violence and violent harassment against Palestinians, including during the ongoing olive harvest season, as well as against journalists,” the EU said in a statement on Sunday.
“We urge Israel to fully abide by International Humanitarian and Human Rights Law, and to cease the expansion of settlements.”
Israeli settler attacks during this year’s olive harvest season have already surpassed 2025 totals, with critics pointing out that mere condemnations by the EU and member states without holding Israel to account will not deter settler pogroms, which are granted impunity by the Israeli authorities.
Saturday’s incident is the latest in weeks of intensifying pogroms against local communities in the occupied West Bank by Israelis from illegal settlements who are largely protected – or at least unrestricted – by Israeli forces.
On Friday, Israeli settlers also attacked Palestinian olive pickers and a veteran photojournalist.
Why have settler pogroms surged during olive harvest season in the occupied West Bank?
Here’s what we know:
What has been the response?
Belgium’s Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said the country’s consul general to the Palestinians, as well as French and Polish diplomats and Catholic representatives, were also among those attacked.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot called on the Israeli government to arrest the settlers who assaulted Bernard Baudoux, the mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, and said on X it must “urgently put an end to this criminal violence and ensure the safety of the civilian population”.
The assault has prompted an Israeli police investigation, as settler pogroms disrupt the Palestinian harvest across the occupied territory.
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the Trump administration is “very disturbed” by the images of the settler attack on American photojournalist Heidi Levine, 64, who works as a freelance photojournalist for The Washington Post, in the occupied West Bank on Friday.
Speaking to reporters at the Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, Rubio said he was yet to receive an official briefing on Friday’s incident, but what he saw “didn’t look good”.
He urged Israel to “crack down” on the violence and said President Donald Trump does not want to see “friction” or “a crisis” in the West Bank.
Ahmed Najar, a Palestinian political analyst and playwright, told Al Jazeera that condemnation without consequences is not accountability.
“Western governments continue to arm, fund and diplomatically protect Israel while treating settler attacks as isolated acts by a few extremists. But this violence flourishes within a wider system of occupation, settlement expansion and impunity,” he said.
“The West cannot claim to oppose settler violence while continuing to support the state and policies that enable it,” he added.
Sven Kuhn von Burgsdorff, former EU representative to the occupied West Bank and Gaza, had a similar view.
“The lame protests issued by the European chancelleries in response to these terrorist acts of Israeli settlers are pathetic since they are not followed up by concrete punitive measures,” he said.
“This is especially disgraceful considering that this settler terrorism has been going on for years with full impunity. At the last Foreign Affairs Council meeting in Brussels on October 12, the EU ministers were still unable to decide on sanctioning the violent settlers and/or its enablers, the annexationist apartheid government of PM Netanyahu,” he added.
What happened on Saturday?
On Saturday, Israeli settlers attacked vehicles belonging to diplomats from France, Belgium and Poland near the Palestinian Christian village of Taybeh in the occupied West Bank.
At least seven masked settlers surrounded the vehicles, demanded identification documents, smashed the window of a vehicle belonging to the Belgian consulate and assaulted the French mayor, according to witnesses and media reports.
The 78-year-old told the Reuters news agency that he was “a bit shaken” by the event.
“I had my mayor’s sash on, with the blue, white and red colours, which clearly represent the symbol of France, in an attempt to protect the people around me. Well, that was not enough, and I was attacked, violently attacked, protected by the people who were there to try and limit things,” Baudoux said.
He said the settlers threw him to the ground, after which his group rushed back into their vehicles to leave.
“I didn’t think something like this could happen to me coming here as a pacifist to celebrate a ‘twinning’ — friendship between two cities,” he added.
However, refusing to be terrified by the attack, Baudoux said, “I think we need to go back to the olive plantations because they have great significance for the Palestinian people.”
Former EU diplomat Burgsdorff told Al Jazeera these attacks are not new, saying he witnessed “thugs attacking peaceful Palestinian farmers and citizens” during his visits to the occupied Palestinian territory between January 2020 and July 2023.
“Once a settler mob even threw stones at us – but we were already in our vehicles. Since we couldn’t count on protection by Israeli police or military, we left the scene of confrontation as soon as possible,” he added.
Where else have settlers attacked olive pickers?
In recent weeks, Israeli settlers have intensified pogroms against Palestinians picking olives in the region.
Earlier on Saturday, settlers injured six Palestinians as Israeli forces arrested farmers during pogroms across the occupied West Bank.
Four women and a child were among the injured when Israeli settlers attacked residents in Ma’in village in the Masafer Yatta area, south of Hebron, according to the Palestine Red Crescent Society (PRCS).
In Deir Ammar town, west of Ramallah, Israeli forces opened fire on farmers picking olives, forcing them to leave their land, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa. Israeli settlers also injured two Palestinians as they opened fire in the area.
In the village of Kafr Malek, northeast of Ramallah, settlers raided a farm at dawn and killed about 20 sheep, Mayor Najeh Rustum told Al Jazeera.
Reporting from Ramallah, Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh said settlers destroyed olive trees across the Beit Furik plain, east of Nablus, in the northern West Bank, while Israeli forces arrested landowners and olive pickers.
In Deir Jarir village, east of Ramallah, she said, settlers under army protection fired live ammunition at farmers in the al-Hariq area to prevent them from harvesting, forcing them off their land.
Settlers also smashed the vehicle of international activist Jonathan Budlak in the village and threw stones at a farmer’s vehicle.
On Friday, dozens of masked settlers attacked Palestinian farmers harvesting olives, throwing stones, using slingshots and setting trees on fire.
Friday’s and Saturday’s attacks follow the killing of Ali Hassan Yasser al-Bazzari, 44, during an assault on Palestinians picking olives near Burqa, northwest of Nablus, on October 7. Witnesses reported that settlers and Israeli soldiers attacked the harvesters.
Journalists documenting the violence have also been targeted.
Veteran freelance journalist Levine was attacked near Abu Falah on Friday. She fell to the ground during the attack before she was set upon, witnesses said.
Levine, who was taken to a hospital northeast of Ramallah after the attack, later told reporters that her attackers “just kept kicking me and kicking me, like probably 50 times”.
Levine was wearing a protective vest marked “PRESS” on the front and back. Her cameras and phone were taken from her during the assault, The Washington Post reported.
On October 6, armed settlers beat Palestinian photographer for the AFP news agency Jaafar Ashtiyeh, 58, with rifle butts near Aqraba, south of Nablus. He was taken to hospital with injuries to his head and torso, according to witnesses, relatives and colleagues.
Why have settler pogroms surged during olive harvest season?
The Israeli settler pogroms have been going on for many weeks and have increased during the ongoing olive harvest season.
Israeli rights group Yesh Din has documented 377 incidents of violence involving occupiers and soldiers in two weeks through October 10.
According to the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), “So far this year, nearly 200 settler attacks linked to the olive harvest have caused casualties or property damage. That is already more than the 185 incidents recorded during the entire 2025 season.”
But the attacks are not new. Every year, Israeli settlers and hardline groups use the olive harvest period to assert control over valuable agricultural lands, often blocking Palestinians from reaching their groves, stealing crops, or building illegal settlement outposts and roads on private Palestinian property.
The olive harvest is also a critical economic lifeline for roughly 80,000 to 100,000 Palestinian families in the occupied West Bank. Intimidating, injuring, or barring farmers from picking their olives, as well as uprooting or burning thousands of olive trees, inflict serious financial damage and force families off their land.
“The olive harvest is not simply an agricultural season for Palestinians; it is a vital source of income and a powerful expression of their connection to the land. Settlers target this period because Palestinian families are gathered in exposed groves, often close to settlements and outposts,” Najar told Al Jazeera.
“By assaulting farmers, burning or uprooting trees and stealing crops, they are not merely disrupting a harvest – they are making it increasingly dangerous for Palestinians to reach and remain on their own land,” he said.
“The violence is also intended to deter international campaigners from accompanying Palestinian farmers, standing with them against settler violence and documenting the atrocities being committed … The objective is not only to dispossess Palestinians, but to ensure that their dispossession happens without witnesses,” he added.
According to Al Jazeera’s Odeh, this year, due to the upcoming elections, which are crucial for right-wing parties, Israeli settlers are more emboldened.
“In fact, they have received even a religious edict telling them that stealing the olive harvest was not just permissible; it was the right thing to do,” she said.
What has Israel said about the attacks?
The Israeli military has condemned Saturday’s attack on the EU diplomats and said it has opened an investigation into the incident. It said its soldiers were not present during the attack.
Settler attacks over the years have also occurred under the protection or passive stance of the Israeli army, which often declares Palestinian farming areas “closed military zones” or coordinates with settlers to restrict landowner access.
Meanwhile, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office has appeared to question the reports of the attack on the Europeans, saying on X that they are “alleged” and require “compelling evidence”, despite acknowledging that published footage of the incident exists.
Al Jazeera’s Odeh noted that while the prime minister downplays violence, Israeli opposition figures are attacking Netanyahu, saying it undermines the standing of Israel.
“They vow to protect the illegal settlements while trying to curb settler violence,” she added.

Microsoft pulls out of AI datacentre project in Essex over power supply concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:28:45 UTC
21:28:45 KST

The development of a huge AI datacentre hailed by the UK government has received a fresh setback after Microsoft pulled out of the project over concerns about power supplies.
The development by the British company Nscale, heralded by ministers as the country’s largest AI datacentre when it was announced in 2025, was planned to open at Loughton in Essex next year.
Doubts had already emerged about the scheme after the Guardian revealed in March that the location was still an operational scaffolding yard.
Now there are further concerns after Microsoft, one of its largest planned customers and expected to have been the anchor tenant, informed the company that it was pulling the plug on its agreement.
It comes a month after it emerged that power supply problems meant the project would face a lengthy wait before coming online.
Keir Starmer’s government had highlighted the Loughton project when announcing the UK’s AI strategy in 2025, describing it as the “largest UK sovereign AI datacentre”. Datacentres are the central nervous system of AI technology such as chatbots.
The end of the deal with Microsoft, first reported in the Telegraph, means Nscale has lost its only publicly announced customer for the Essex datacentre. It is understood that Microsoft remains on board for another project the company has in Norway.
Nscale, which is backed by tech companies including Nvidia, has positioned itself as Britain’s “sovereign” datacentre provider but the loss of an anchor tenant for its Loughton project could undermine its ambition to float on Wall Street this year with a potential valuation of $35bn (£26bn).
Targeting the rapid growth of AI to boost the economy, the UK government’s proposals to harness the technology have focused on two Nvidia-backed companies: the London-based Nscale and the US company CoreWeave.
Official figures show investments in AI are among the factors helping Britain’s economy to beat expectations of a weaker growth performance this year as the war in the Middle East rattles global business activity.
Nscale is a “neocloud”, one of a number of companies with deep ties to Nvidia that are building the key infrastructure for the AI boom. It is this relationship with Nvidia that meant it and CoreWeave were chosen as key players in the UK’s sovereign AI push, which happened under Starmer.
There is, however, a growing chorus of voices which suggest that neoclouds may be a vulnerability in the broader AI economy, especially as delays pile up across partners.
Driven by hopes of an economic transformation, many are taking on increasingly risky debt, including companies vital to the AI boom. If Nscale pushes back its initial public offering in New York, these vulnerabilities may come into sharper focus.
The former UK deputy prime minister Nick Clegg and the former Meta chief operating officer Sheryl Sandberg are board members at the company. Clegg holds a 0.25% stake that could be worth $88m if the company floats at a $35bn valuation.
It emerged earlier this month that UK Power Networks (UKPN), which owns and maintains the electricity grid across London and the south-east of England, had informed Nscale that it would not be able to supply enough power to the company’s Loughton datacentre until the early to mid-2030s.
Nscale said it was “committed to the project” but the failure to find a quick fix to the power supply issue underlines how much energy has become a hindrance to datacentre development.
The scaffolding yard site has been cleared by Nscale, and the company is investigating whether it can generate power onsite and whether it can speed up the connection process.
An Nscale spokesperson said: “We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK, and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK.
“Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts.”

On Sunday morning, broken glass and litter filled the streets as Parisians emerged from their apartment blocks to be greeted by the aftermath of the destruction.
Alexandre Bompard, the Chairman and CEO of the Carrefour Group, said on Sunday that a "total of 50 shops" had been targeted, "including 19 Carrefour convenience stores and supermarkets."
He said the affected locations included premises in Paris, Rennes, Lille, and Bordeaux, among others.
"My thoughts are also with the 1,500 shops belonging to all the other retail chains and with all the shopkeepers who have suffered the same unacceptable violence," Bompard continued, adding that the destruction would have "considerable human and economic consequences.
"Dozens of employees at our franchise partners will be forced onto short-time working," he said. "The cost of the repairs will run to well over ten million euros."
One store owner near the Place de la République whose shop had been wrecked by rioters told the Brut outlet that he had put all his savings into the business and that he felt like he'd lost everything.
"I don't know how I'll get by or how I'll live with my family," he said.
Brut said a neighbour had decided to set up a fundraiser to help the man get back on his feet.
Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire has also pledged to offer his full support to businesses affected in the capital and announced that he had requested the creation of an "emergency task force to support shopkeepers who have been victims of vandalism."
"Its role will be to assess the damage, support affected shopkeepers, and assist them with administrative and insurance procedures," he said. "You bring Paris to life every day. Today, it's Paris' turn to stand by your side."
Looters assault Euronews crew
A Euronews crew were assaulted by looters in Paris on Saturday, near the Place de la République, as they reported on the situation.
The crew were making their way to another location when they were confronted by masked individuals looting a nearby Intermarché Express supermarket.
"We were standing on Boulevard de Magenta, not far from a supermarket that was being looted by young people, young adults, teenagers. When they saw we were filming, they started hitting my cameraman and attempted to take his microphone and they encircled us," Estelle Nilsson-Julien, Euronews’ correspondent in Paris, said.
"They then pushed him against the wall and started hitting and punching him. They also hit me. They punched him in the face, but because he was wearing goggles and a mask, he was not harmed," she added.
A march moving along the Boulevard de Clichy towards the Place de Clichy across the other side of Paris remained peaceful, another Euronews journalist on the ground reported.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said in an update on Sunday that more than 600 police officers, gendarmes, and firefighters had been injured on Saturday, with more than 2,000 people arrested.

Riots break out after unauthorised rally in Bern
Riots broke out in Bern during an unauthorised demonstration on Saturday night. Emergency services were attacked with fireworks and dangerous objects. The police used rubber pellets and rubber bullets. No one was injured.
The Bern Cantonal Police reported on Sunday that, shortly after 11:20 pm on Saturday evening, a large number of people had gathered at the Schützenmatte in Bern for an unauthorised spontaneous demonstration. A procession subsequently formed and made its way towards the Lorraine quarter.
During the march, the demonstrators – some of whom were masked – set off pyrotechnics on several occasions. At the end of the Lorraine Bridge, police officers issued verbal warnings to the participants and ordered them to turn back. Despite police barrier tape and clear signals from the police, this order was not obeyed, the statement continued.
More
The Reitschule: past and present
The demonstrators removed the barrier tape and continued on their way towards the police forces at the Känzeli. The police then deployed force for the first time. Pyrotechnics were immediately fired directly at the officers, who were also attacked with projectiles. According to the statement, the officers were then forced to use rubber pellets and rubber bullets in self-defence.
The procession then retreated via the Lorrainebrücke to the Schützenmatte. There, the demonstrators remained on the forecourt of the Reitschule for some time, while police forces remained on the scene.
At around 2:00 am, a group attacked the officers at the Henkerbrünnli via Neubrückstrasse with objects. This necessitated the police using rubber pellets once again. Shortly after 3:40 am, the rally on the Schützenmatte finally dispersed. The affected sections of road were closed for around three hours during the rally. Numerous officers from the Bern Cantonal Police were deployed.
According to current information, no one was injured. An investigation has been launched.

Typhoon Champi could bring heavy rain to Taiwan later this week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:19:33 UTC
21:19:33 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — A sea warning for Typhoon Champi could be issued as early as Wednesday night, with a land warning possible Thursday, according to the Central Weather Administration.
The typhoon could have its greatest impact on Taiwan on Friday and Saturday, bringing heavy to torrential rain to central and northern Taiwan. Forecast models differ on its path, however, and the storm requires continued monitoring, per CNA.
CWA forecaster Liu Pei-teng (劉沛滕) said Champi, the year’s 29th typhoon, was about 2,470 km southeast of Eluanbi on Sunday afternoon, moving west-northwest at 20 km per hour. Maximum sustained winds near its center reached 53 meters per second, with a 200 km radius for winds of at least 7 on the Beaufort scale.
Liu said the storm could approach eastern Taiwan as a strong typhoon, although some forecast models suggest it could make landfall in Hualien or Taitung. Its eventual path will depend partly on changes in the Pacific high-pressure system.
Some models indicate it could turn north before reaching Taiwan, while others suggest it could move farther south through the Bashi Channel.
Liu said the weather would remain relatively stable early in the week, with mostly cloudy to sunny skies and highs of 33–34 C in western Taiwan. As the northeast monsoon strengthens midweek, temperatures in northern and northeastern Taiwan are expected to fall, with scattered showers in some areas.
The typhoon’s outer circulation could bring heavier rain to central and northern Taiwan from Friday. Its subsequent movement and intensity remain uncertain, the CWA said.

Scientists uncover 3 key brain pathways linked to lasting depression relief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:19:08 UTC
21:19:08 KST

Scientists uncover 3 key brain pathways linked to lasting depression relief
- Date:
- October 18, 2026
- Source:
- The Mount Sinai Hospital / Mount Sinai School of Medicine
- Summary:
- Researchers have uncovered three brain pathways linked to lasting improvements in people receiving deep brain stimulation for severe, treatment-resistant depression. They also discovered that patients who failed to improve after two years shared a striking pattern: insufficient stimulation of a crucial brain connection. The findings suggest that millimeters in electrode placement could make a major difference in treatment outcomes.
- Share:
Scientists at Mount Sinai have identified three important brain connections associated with long-term improvement in patients receiving deep brain stimulation (DBS) for severe depression that has not responded to conventional treatments. The discovery could help researchers make this experimental therapy more precise and effective.
Published October 1 in the American Journal of Psychiatry, the research examined the largest group of patients assembled across multiple independent cohorts to date who had received subcallosal cingulate deep brain stimulation (SCC DBS) for treatment-resistant depression.
The researchers found that lasting improvements were consistently associated with electrical stimulation reaching three specific white matter pathways: the cingulum bundle, forceps minor, and medial uncinate fasciculus/ventral amygdalofugal pathways.
These findings strengthen the case for using detailed maps of the brain's connections to determine exactly where electrodes should be implanted, rather than choosing their positions based primarily on anatomical landmarks. Known as connectome-based targeting, this strategy has already helped shape the ongoing Abbott TRANSCEND clinical trial, a randomized, controlled study that uses individualized brain connectivity maps to guide SCC DBS treatment.
"This study underscores the importance of individualized surgical targeting for achieving optimal outcomes with deep brain stimulation for depression," said Helen Mayberg, MD, Mount Sinai Professor in Neurotherapeutics and founding Director of the Nash Family Center for Advanced Circuit Therapeutics at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai. "In any randomized controlled trial of a neuromodulation treatment, precise lead placement and confirmation that the intended brain target has been engaged are essential first steps. We still have much to learn about which patients are most likely to benefit from stimulation of this particular target, but developing imaging-based signatures that can match patients to their optimal treatment remains a central goal of our research."
How Deep Brain Stimulation Targets Severe Depression
For people with treatment-resistant depression, standard therapies have failed to provide adequate relief. Researchers are investigating deep brain stimulation as a possible treatment for individuals living with severe, persistent symptoms.
The procedure involves surgically placing electrodes inside the brain to deliver controlled electrical signals to circuits involved in depression. However, positioning the electrodes correctly remains one of the greatest challenges.
Electrical stimulation does not simply affect the brain tissue closest to an implanted electrode. It can also influence larger networks through the white matter pathways that connect different brain regions. As a result, two patients with electrodes implanted in nearly identical locations may experience very different outcomes depending on which connections are actually stimulated.
Earlier research from Mount Sinai and Emory University helped establish the importance of these networks. In studies published between 2014 and 2023 in Biological Psychiatry, Molecular Psychiatry, and Nature, the teams identified white matter pathways associated with successful SCC DBS treatment and developed a method for planning electrode placement using brain connectivity maps.
The latest investigation sought to determine whether those connections were also important in patients treated at other research centers. Scientists also wanted to understand whether differences in the pathways reached by stimulation could help account for patients who did not benefit.
Three Brain Connections Linked to Lasting Improvement
To investigate, the researchers examined information from several clinical studies, including the BROADEN trial and a patient cohort at the University of Toronto, where SCC DBS was originally developed.
They used computer models of the electrical fields generated by implanted electrodes alongside maps of brain connectivity. This allowed them to estimate which pathways received stimulation and compare those patterns across different patient groups.
The results showed a consistent relationship between sustained improvement and stimulation of the cingulum bundle, forceps minor, and medial uncinate fasciculus/ventral amygdalofugal pathways.
One finding was especially notable. Across the study sites, patients who had not responded to treatment after two years showed a lack of stimulation engagement with the left cingulum bundle.
The researchers did not investigate whether moving electrodes to reach this pathway would improve those patients' symptoms. Nevertheless, the pattern offers a possible explanation for why apparently similar electrode placements can produce different results. An electrode might be positioned in the correct general region but still fail to activate all the connections associated with lasting improvement.
"This study addresses an important question in DBS: not simply which area of the brain to stimulate, but which connections within that area need to be engaged," said Brian Kopell, MD, Director of the Center for Neuromodulation at Mount Sinai. "For a network disorder such as depression, millimeters can determine whether stimulation reaches the pathways we intend to modulate. Identifying and reproducibly engaging those pathways gives us a more precise surgical target and a framework for understanding why otherwise similar electrode placements may produce different clinical outcomes."
Toward More Personalized Depression Treatments
Although reaching these three pathways appears important, the researchers emphasize that electrode placement alone is unlikely to determine whether a patient improves.
The investigation concentrated on identifying the brain connections that should receive stimulation. Additional studies are needed to determine which individuals are most likely to benefit from SCC DBS and how electrical stimulation should be adjusted as treatment continues.
There were also limitations to the brain imaging data. Individual diffusion MRI scans, which can provide information about a person's white matter connections, were not available for every participant. Consequently, much of the analysis used generalized maps of brain connectivity rather than maps created specifically for each patient.
For the Emory patient group, the researchers were able to compare results obtained from generalized connectivity maps with those based on individual diffusion imaging. Both approaches produced consistent findings, providing further support for the importance of the identified pathways. However, more research is needed to establish the value of patient-specific imaging.
Future investigations will explore whether additional brain imaging measurements, including white matter integrity and functional connectivity, can help identify suitable patients, improve electrode placement, and guide treatment settings.
"Our findings show precisely engaging these white matter pathways is a critical first step toward sustained response," said Ki Sueng Choi, PhD, Associate Professor, Imaging Core Leader at the Center for Advanced Circuit Therapeutics at Mount Sinai, and corresponding author of the study. "The next step is to characterize abnormal functional and structural brain states along these pathways to build more detailed models for setting patient-specific stimulation parameters, including amplitude, frequency, and pulse width, for precision medicine."
By combining increasingly detailed brain maps with personalized stimulation settings, scientists hope to better understand why some people experience lasting relief while others do not. The findings represent another step toward developing more targeted treatments for severe depression, although further clinical research is necessary to establish how much these approaches can improve outcomes.
Research Funding and Disclosures
The research received support from the National Institutes of Health BRAIN Initiative through grant UH3NS103550, the Hope for Depression Research Foundation, and the DANA Foundation.
Abbott's Neuromodulation business supplied data from the BROADEN clinical trial but did not participate in designing or analyzing the current study.
Conflict of Interest Disclosures: Dr. Brian Kopell serves as a paid consultant to Abbott Laboratories.
Dr. Helen Mayberg is a named co-inventor of a method that uses deep brain stimulation (DBS) in a particular brain region (the subcallosal cingulate area) to treat treatment-resistant depression. The method was licensed to Abbott Laboratories. Dr. Mayberg has received royalty payments from Functional Neuroscience related to this technology and is eligible to receive additional payments in the future. She also serves as a paid consultant to Abbott Laboratories in connection with its clinical trials involving DBS for depression.
Dr. Ki Sueng Choi and Dr. Martijn Figee are also paid consultants to Abbott Laboratories.
Dr. Mayberg, Dr. Kopell, and Dr. Choi are named co-inventors on a patent application covering a technique for identifying optimal electrode placement in deep brain stimulation for depression. The patent application was filed through Mount Sinai, and the technology remains unlicensed. However, the approach has been used in the TRANSCEND clinical trial.

Russian ‘Matryoshka’ Bot Farm Targets US Midterms With AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:19:00 UTC
21:19:00 KST

Russian state-backed disinformation operators are deploying automated bot networks to artificially inflate view counts for fabricated videos targeting Democratic candidates and Hollywood celebrities ahead of the US midterm elections, Bloomberg News reported.
The digital influence campaign – identified by social media researchers as “Matryoshka” or “Operation Overload” – relies on artificial intelligence to generate counterfeit news broadcasts and deepfakes designed to erode public trust in electoral integrity and undermine political support for Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
A review by Bloomberg of 130 fabricated videos and doctored newspaper front pages circulated between Sept. 10 and Oct. 9 revealed a systematic campaign focused almost exclusively on Democratic contenders across the country.
The findings were documented by the anonymous research group Antibot4Navalny and corroborated by US-based open-source intelligence firms Graphika and dTeam.
AI-generated celebrity fakes
The operation began circulating AI-manipulated video clips across social media platform X in early September. The media files featured synthetic likenesses of high-profile actors and musicians – including Robert De Niro, Julia Roberts, and Cher – falsely depicted as attacking Democratic politicians or encouraging viewers to join an online campaign labeled “#AllDemocratsAreCriminals.”
Additional fabricated materials mimicked established American broadcast networks to distribute unsubstantiated allegations against prominent candidates.
Trump Envoys Push Russian Gas Transit in Ukraine Peace Talks
One video carrying a counterfeit ABC News digital banner claimed that James Talarico, the Democratic nominee contesting a US Senate seat in Texas, made payments to OnlyFans models.
A spokesperson for Talarico firmly denied the assertion. Another video mimicking CBS News alleged that the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) uncovered eight undeclared real estate properties owned by Georgia Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff. No public records or official disclosures substantiate the claim.
Researchers observed that Matryoshka-linked posts frequently accumulated hundreds of thousands of impressions on X within their first hour of publication. However, digital forensic data shared by Antibot4Navalny demonstrated that view counts were systematically manipulated by automated bot networks to project artificial virality.
“The number of views for Matryoshka posts can jump as high as 200,000 within the first hour but then quickly plateau,” researchers observed, noting that organic engagement follows a steady growth curve rather than a sudden spike followed by an abrupt flatline.
Forensic analysis established that the amplifying accounts had been dormant for years, possessed few followers, and generated virtually no genuine reposts or likes relative to recorded views.
Strategic shift to down-ballot races and midterms
The operational footprint of the campaign reflects a tactical evolution from previous Russian influence efforts. While past operations focused predominantly on high-stakes presidential contests, Matryoshka has broadened its parameters to target down-ballot congressional and gubernatorial races.
According to Bloomberg’s analysis, the network disseminated targeted disinformation against Democratic candidates in 20 of the 35 US Senate races and 29 of the 36 gubernatorial contests scheduled for the Nov. 3 ballot.
US intelligence agencies have warned Congress of the escalating deployment of synthetic media by foreign adversaries.
A recent assessment by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) identified Russia as the primary foreign actor deploying artificial intelligence to degrade public confidence in American democratic institutions ahead of the midterm vote.
Antibot4Navalny, which has monitored Kremlin-aligned digital networks since 2018, initially identified the Matryoshka apparatus in September 2023 as it attempted to undermine Western military assistance for Ukraine.
The operation was named after traditional Russian nesting dolls due to its operational pattern: accounts distributing one fabricated narrative frequently pivot to distributing fresh fabrications on successive days.
French government monitoring agency Viginum confirmed in early 2024 that initial seeds of Matryoshka content were routed through Russian-language channels on Telegram before migrating to Western social networks.
“It’s evolving with the technology and is more sophisticated as a result,” said Darren Linvill, professor at Clemson University and co-director of its Media Forensics Hub. “They’re actively trying to fish for more engagement.”
Disinformation backbones and physical infrastructure hits
The exposure of the Matryoshka campaign coincides with growing scrutiny of the physical and digital infrastructure that underwrites Russian computational influence operations.
Between Oct. 8 and Oct. 11, Ukrainian precision drone strikes disabled three major data centers owned by Russian technology giant Yandex in the Vladimir, Kaluga, and Ryazan regions.
The kinetic disruptions caused widespread server outages across Russian enterprise networks and triggered a sharp reduction in automated web requests originating from Russian server clusters.
According to network intelligence provider Cloudflare Radar, automated bot traffic from Yandex’s sovereign network plunged immediately following the facility strikes.
The computational downtime was followed by reports from digital monitors across Europe describing a marked decline in automated polarization.
Polish open-source defense analyst Jarosław Wolski observed a noticeable contraction in coordinated online attacks pitting Polish citizens against Ukrainian refugees, alongside a temporary drop in bot-driven engagement boosting fringe political parties in Germany.
President Volodymyr Zelensky referenced the operational ripple effects on Oct. 12, noting that precision interdiction against Russian digital nodes resulted in “less hatred, less discord, and fewer provocations because there were fewer bots.”
Western security agencies maintain that Moscow’s influence operations increasingly blur the boundary between cognitive warfare and algorithmic manipulation.
Previous legal actions by the US Department of Justice disrupted 968 AI-powered bot profiles operated under the direction of state broadcaster RT and the Russian Federal Security Service (FSB), alongside the “Doppelganger” network of cloned media domains, underscoring allied efforts to dismantle coordinated influence operations ahead of the November vote.

Kabir Adeniyi

The European Union has pledged €20 million ($23 million) in defense assistance to Nigeria’s armed forces to strengthen security cooperation and support efforts to tackle persistent insecurity across the country.
The proposed assistance was discussed during a meeting in Abuja between Nigerian Defense Minister Christopher Musa and Gautier Mignot, the EU ambassador to Nigeria and the Economic Community of West African States, according to a statement by Leah Katung-Babatunde, the minister’s media aid.
The support will be provided under the EU’s European Peace Facility, with an EU technical delegation expected to visit Nigeria in November to agree on the arrangements for its delivery, the statement said.

He said security operations were gradually restoring relative peace in some troubled areas, although kidnappings along major highways and attacks on isolated communities remained serious challenges.
The minister also said Nigeria was expecting 10 attack helicopters, unmanned aerial vehicles and other military equipment to strengthen ongoing security operations.
On regional security, Musa identified the shrinking Lake Chad Basin, which supports more than 50 million people, as a source of potential instability.
He said preventing terrorists from using islands in Lake Chad as operational bases remained a key priority for the Multinational Joint Task Force, which coordinates regional efforts against insurgency.
Musa also stressed that Nigeria’s disarmament, demobilization and reintegration program should prioritize victims of conflict, including military personnel affected by the insurgency.
Nigeria has battled a long-running insurgency in the northeast, alongside banditry, kidnappings and other forms of violence in different parts of the country.

The Gaida: Bulgaria’s traditional bagpipe and the voice of centuries

2026-10-18

Tsvetana Toncheva
Article
The Gaida: Bulgaria’s traditional bagpipe and the voice of centuries
Sunday 18 October 2026 14:15
Sunday, 18 October 2026, 14:15
PHOTO Bozhidar Cholakov
Font size
From the village square to the grand concert stage, the Bulgarian bagpipe known as "gaida" has accompanied songs, festivities and rituals for centuries. Today, it is not only one of Bulgaria’s most recognisable folk instruments, but also a living tradition recognised by UNESCO.
Powerful, rich, resonant and deeply moving, the voice of the Bulgarian "gaida" is part of Bulgaria’s sonic memory. For Bulgarians, it symbolises home and the place where we come from. For centuries, its sound has been an integral part of our festive and ritual life. Today, the bagpipe is not merely part of the country's folk heritage, but one of the most vivid emblems of Bulgarian culture.
Part of the bagpipe ensemble from the "Hristo Botev-1869" Community Center in Kalofer at the Koprivshtitsa Festival, 2010
PHOTO Georgi Stoyanov
The craft of making a bagpipe and the skill of playing it are arts passed down through generations. Many Bulgarians think of it as a traditional Bulgarian instrument, yet it is by no means unique to Bulgaria. The most familiar form of the bagpipe has been widespread throughout Europe since the Middle Ages.
Almost every European nation has developed its own version of the instrument, and similar instruments can be found in other parts of the world.
Today, bagpipes are particularly popular in the Balkans, including Bulgaria, Serbia, North Macedonia, Greece, Albania and Türkiye.
In Scotland, they are a symbol of national identity. Irish and Spanish traditional bagpipes are also well known. The instrument is found in North Africa, Western Asia and the Caucasus as well.
PHOTO Radostina Chernokova
The history of the bagpipe stretches far back into antiquity and is difficult to trace. It is believed that the first instruments of this kind appeared at least 1,000 years before Christ, although some sources place their origins as far back as the sixth millennium BC.
According to historical accounts, the Roman emperor Nero, a passionate lover of music and theatre, played the bagpipe. In Rome, however, the instrument had actually been introduced from Ancient Greece, and the Greeks may have borrowed it from the Hittites.
Some researchers believe that the bagpipe was part of the musical culture of the ancient Thracians. Even Herodotus, the “Father of History”, wrote that the Thracian people used the instrument “only for praise”.
PHOTO Ani Petrova
The Bulgarian bagpipe ("gaida") is a bag-powered wind instrument consisting of a leather bag ("meh"), a blowpipe ("duhalo"), a chanter ("gaidunitsa"), a drone pipe ("ruchilo"), reeds ("piskuni") and connecting stocks ("glavini").
Traditionally, the bag is made from treated goat or lamb skin and serves as an air reservoir. The piper blows air into it through the blowpipe and regulates the air pressure with the help of the elbow.
The chanter is the melodic part of the instrument. It has finger holes that allow the player to produce notes of different pitches.
The drone pipe provides a continuous, low fundamental tone over which the melody unfolds, giving the bagpipe its distinctive sound.
Particularly important are the reeds ("piskuni"), small vibrating components that turn the flow of air into sound.
PHOTO BNR
Making a bagpipe requires exceptional craftsmanship. Its wooden parts are traditionally made from dogwood, plum and other hardwoods, while tuning the instrument calls for precision and experience. A fine bagpipe is the result not only of good materials, but also of the maker’s skill.
Two main types of bagpipe are known in Bulgarian musical tradition: the djura gaida, which is smaller, and the kaba gaida, which is larger. A Macedonian bagpipe is also found in the southwestern regions. 
The djura gaida has a higher, clear and powerful sound. It is widespread throughout Bulgaria, from Moesia, Deliorman and Dobrudzha to the Balkan Mountains, Sredna Gora, Northern, Eastern and Western Thrace, Strandzha, the Shopluk region, Graovo, the Western Outlands and Pirin Macedonia. It is played both as a solo instrument and in ensembles, accompanying songs and dances.
The Macedonian gaida is found in the southwestern part of Pirin Macedonia, as well as in Vardar and Aegean Macedonia. Its tuning lies between that of the dzhura and kaba bagpipes, giving it a medium-high pitch.
The kaba gaida is the musical voice of the Rhodope Mountains. Larger in size, it has a lower, deeper, softer and fuller timbre, and is closely tied to the region’s folk traditions. Rhodope traditional round dances ("horo") are performed to its accompaniment, while the slow melodies played on the kaba bagpipe are among the most emblematic treasures of Bulgarian folk music.
A museum in the Rhodopes tells the story of the Bulgarian bagpipe
An ensemble of several kaba bagpipes creates a striking soundscape. Over the past half-century, the celebrated orchestra 100 Kaba Bagpipes has become a symbol of Bulgarian ensemble playing on this instrument. Founded in 1961 by folklorist Apostol Kisyov, the orchestra gave its first concert performance that same year at the Rozhen folk gathering, held in the village of the same name in the Rhodope Mountain in southwestern Bulgaria.
On 16 May 2012, in the National Palace of Culture in Sofia, 333 Rhodope kaba bagpipers, representing four generations of musicians from across Bulgaria, played fragments of traditional Rhodope melodies together for nine minutes and thirteen seconds. Their performance set an official mass-participation record recognised by Guinness World Records, surpassing the previous record held by 240 Scottish bagpipers playing simultaneously.
When "100 kaba bagpipes" play together, time comes to a standstill
The bagpipe is not merely an artefact of the past. Knowledge of how to make the instrument and the skills needed to play it are passed from one generation to the next, from master to apprentice, within families, at community cultural centres, in music schools and in folk ensembles. This living bond between generations has helped bring international recognition to the Bulgarian bagpipe.
In 2025, UNESCO inscribed “Bagpipes and Bagpipe Playing in Bulgaria: Transmission of Knowledge and Skills” on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The decision highlights the importance of the practices that allow the tradition to evolve and be passed on to future generations.
The Bulgarian bagpipe has also made its mark beyond the country’s borders. One of the most powerful symbols of the international reach of Bulgarian musical tradition is the song Izlel e Delyo Haydutin, performed by Valya Balkanska with bagpipers Stefan Zahmanov and Lazar Kanevski. The recording is included in the musical selection on the Golden Record carried aboard Voyager 1, the spacecraft launched from Cape Canaveral in 1977 and reported to have left the Solar System in 2004. The record, which contains images and sounds from Earth, was designed to preserve a part of our planet’s heritage for future generations and to serve as a message to extraterrestrial civilisations. In this way, the voice of Bulgaria's Rhodope musical tradition became part of a message from Earth to the cosmos.
PHOTO Facebook /gaidari.varna
A number of performers and teachers have helped popularise the Bulgarian bagpipe. Among them is Kostadin Varimezov from Strandzha, one of Bulgaria’s most celebrated bagpipers, known as the “king of the Bulgarian bagpipe” and “Saint Kostadin of folk music”. He was among the artists who brought the Bulgarian bagpipe into the world’s musical encyclopaedias.
He performed across Europe, Asia and America and was one of the first Bulgarian musicians not only to present the country’s folk music at concerts and festivals around the world, but also to live abroad for extended periods and teach Bulgarian folklore there.
Today, the bagpipe continues to sound out at folk festivals and gatherings, in community cultural centres and music schools, on concert stages and in contemporary musical projects. For Bulgarians, it is neither a museum relic nor simply an ancient instrument preserved as a keepsake. It is a living body of knowledge, continually passed on, developed and heard.
The bagpipe is made of wood, skin and air. But what makes it a symbol is human memory. As long as there are children learning to play, craftspeople making instruments and audiences who recognise and cherish this sound, Bulgaria’s bagpipe tradition will remain a vibrant part of the country’s cultural identity.

Hurricane Trudy may bring "life-threatening" flooding, mudslides to Mexico's Pacific coast
Hurricane Trudy brought heavy rain and powerful winds to parts of Mexico's Pacific coast on Sunday, impacting sections of the country's western and southwestern states that were already targeted by Hurricane Simon last week. 
The National Hurricane Center, which is based in Miami, warned that hurricane and tropical storm conditions could materialize in areas under weather alerts Sunday morning and afternoon. The center also urged people in coastal regions of Michoacán, Colima and Jalisco to prepare for potentially life-threatening flooding and mudslides as a result of the impending rain.
A hurricane warning remained in effect from Manzanillo in Colima state to Cabo Corrientes in Jalisco. As of the hurricane center's latest update, issued in the early hours of Sunday, Trudy had maximum sustained winds of 105 mph, making it a Category 2 hurricane. The storm had strengthened into a major Category 3 hurricane as it tracked toward Mexico late last week, but it has since weakened.
On Sunday, Trudy was about 135 miles west-southwest of Manzanillo and moving northwest at 10 mph.
Trudy's center was expected to remain near the Mexican coast through Sunday evening before moving south of the Baja California Peninsula. A tropical storm warning remained in effect for Las Islas Marias. A warning for the coast east of Punta San Telmo to Lazaro Cardenas was discontinued.
The Mexican Navy urged mariners and coastal residents to exercise extreme caution because of high waves, heavy rain and the risk of rising rivers, flooding and landslides in vulnerable areas.
Colima authorities said the risks remained low, but warned that heavy rainfall could cause damage because the ground was already saturated by successive storms along the Pacific coast.
Trudy was expected to bring 4 to 8 inches of rain through the weekend, with isolated totals of around 12 inches along and near the coast in Michoacán, Colima and Jalisco. The hurricane center said areas with steep terrain were particularly vulnerable to serious flooding and mudslides.
Other Pacific storms
Elsewhere in the Pacific, Typhoon Champi was passing Guam as a massive super typhoon, with fierce winds strong enough to be classified as Category 4. It was getting farther away from the island on Sunday after traveling near Guam's southern tip, with sustained winds of 150 mph.
As of Sunday afternoon, local time, Champi was 200 miles west of Guam and moving westward at 14 mph, according to the National Weather Service.
The storm could strengthen into a Category 5 super typhoon early Monday local time. Guam and Rota remained under a typhoon warning, while the tropical storm warning and typhoon watch for Tinian and Saipan were canceled.
The governors of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands both requested emergency disaster declarations on Friday.
On Saturday, President Trump approved an emergency declaration for Guam authorizing the Federal Emergency Management Agency to coordinate all federal disaster relief efforts. FEMA announced that federal disaster assistance was available for the territory of Guam to supplement local response efforts following Typhoon Champi.
Airports, harbors and some health facilities in the territories were closed. Resources were unlikely to reach the islands for three to five days, according to Saturday updates from FEMA.
The territories are still recovering from super typhoons Sinlaku and Bavi, which struck in April and July, respectively.

Feature: Indian-controlled Kashmir's traditional musical instrument makers strive to keep vanishing craft alive
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
20:06:13 CST
21:06:13 KST

A musician examines a rabab before purchasing it at the workshop of Mushtaq Ahmad Dar in the outskirts of Srinagar city, the summer capital of Indian-controlled Kashmir, Oct. 12, 2026. (Xinhua/Javed Dar)
by Peerzada Arshad Hamid
NEW DELHI, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Inside the courtyard workshop of his two-story home, Mushtaq Ahmad Dar examines each chisel with meticulous attention. Holding one in his left hand, he runs his right index finger along the bevel, then reaches into a water-filled jug for a soaking whetstone. He hones the blade until a faint smile crosses his face, then braces another dull chisel and rubs it steadily across the stone.
"My father says that it is always the tools that work wonders," said Dar, a traditional Kashmiri musical instrument maker.
At 10 a.m., his apprentice places a half-done Kashmiri rabab, an ancient, plectrum-plucked stringed instrument carved from a single piece of mulberry wood, before him. Dar drives a sharpened chisel into the wood, hammering its butt with his adze as shavings curl away, gradually shaping the rabab's deep, concave bowl.
Dar tells Xinhua that he learned the craft as a boy from his father, continuing a tradition dating back to his grandfather, a locally renowned singer.
"Not only am I, but my three brothers are also well-versed in the craft," Dar said. "We live in a joint family, and I am hopeful our children too will carry forward this legacy."
Among his brothers, Dar has perfected the skill and now often discusses the instruments' intricacies with clients on behalf of his father, who, because of his advanced age, can no longer devote himself fully to the trade.
At Dar's workshop in Budgam district, a 25-minute drive northwest of Srinagar city, the summer capital of Indian-controlled Kashmir, traditional string instruments, including the rabab, santoor, sarangi, Kashmiri sitar, and Sikh rabab, are being made.
Dar spends months crafting a single instrument, carefully selecting mulberry and walnut wood and prioritizing quality over speed. His instruments are in demand across India.
"For most of the instruments, we use mulberry wood, but for santoor, we use walnut wood," he said. "I am lucky enough that I have a good clientele. This craft has given us everything we have today. People place orders at my workshop in advance for the instruments of their choice."
"The music runs in our blood, as our forefathers have been associated with it for generations," he said. "I know how to play every instrument that I make. These objects communicate with me."
Dar is seen as one of the torchbearers of a craft many feared would die with the Indian-controlled Kashmir's last santoor maker, 85-year-old Ghulam Mohamed Zaz of Srinagar.
Surrounded by the vibrant walls of his room, Zaz ran his frail fingers across the sharp edges of a newly fashioned, trapezoidal box of walnut wood. He checked its precision with a scale, his movements slow and deliberate.
"A craft doesn't simply die -- it endures," he said. "What kills a craft is the flood of fakes and inferior copies replacing the authentic work. I hold the line for this art today, but I do not know who will carry it into tomorrow."
He is the last of the eighth generation in his family to carve the classical instrument and claims that all the acclaimed artists of the region played on the santoors made by them.
The word santoor in Persian means "a hundred strings." The traditional Kashmiri santoor typically has 100 strings. Worldwide, santoor varieties differ mostly in their string count.
In his uptown Srinagar office, Nazir Ganaie, the founder of Kashmir Rabab Academy, an institute that works to preserve the region's musical heritage, is busy putting the final touches on an upcoming concert schedule. The event offers a rare chance to hear a performance played entirely on traditional Kashmiri instruments.
Driven by a passion to protect these indigenous folk traditions, Ganaie built this platform to bring local artists together and showcase their talents.
"For me, the rabab is not merely a musical instrument. It is an emotion deeply etched into our collective soul. The moment I strike its strings, I am transported to the mountains and valleys of Kashmir, where every note carries a story, a memory and a sense of belonging," Ganaie said.
His love for playing the Kashmiri rabab took him to Dar some years back to place an order in bulk for Kashmiri handmade rababs.
Ganaie often visits Indian-controlled Kashmir's master instrument makers to chronicle their personal histories and the resilient spirit driving them to preserve their craft.
"Today Kashmiri rabab, santoor, and sarangi stand distinct from their global counterparts," said Muzaffar Ahmad Bhat, a Srinagar-based musicologist. "They are now deeply woven into the region's folklore, defining the vibrant rhythm of folk songs and the spiritual depth of classical Sufiana Mausiqi, a centuries-old classical choral ensemble music. Far more than mere tools for performance, these instruments have become inseparable fragments of Kashmiri society, culture, and identity."
The traditional craftsmanship required to make these instruments is rapidly vanishing. At the heart of this decline is the loss of aging master craftsmen, with few apprentices stepping up to fill the void.
"Low financial returns and shrinking demand make it difficult for remaining artisans to earn a living. Ultimately, the shift toward electronic music and cheap, machine-made instruments has severely threatened a legacy that once thrived on human hands," he said.
Ganaie, however, feels the internet and social media have opened up avenues for the musicians as well as makers of the musical instruments to keep the art thriving and prevent it from vanishing into the thin air.
"It is heartening to see rabab and santoor makers and other traditional instrument artisans finding renewed hope as online orders and social media open up new markets for their craft. The growing visibility of these instruments in major productions of Bollywood and music platforms has also helped introduce the region's rich musical heritage to wider national and international audiences," he said.
Meanwhile, a young musical instrument maker Altaf Ahmad Sheikh is hard at work in another Srinagar neighborhood. His hands steady, engraving delicate floral and foliage designs that weave gracefully between the bird motifs on a sarangi. The design has transformed a plain wooden instrument into an ornate work of art.
He has spent months crafting this sarangi, an instrument that represents not just his devotion to the craft, but his very livelihood.
Sheikh, a school dropout, learned the craft from his father, a renowned sarangi maker.
"I am striving hard to keep the craft alive," Sheikh said as his young son sat in front of him, perhaps trying to imbibe the skill. ■

"Iran's plan is still on the table," Araghchi said. "If they (the United States) meet those conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will be reopened on the sixth day, and negotiations will resume on the seventh."
He said that Iran's conditions were neither extraordinary nor unusual, adding that they were the same commitments "the United States had already committed itself in the peace memorandum of understanding (MoU) and other negotiations."
Araghchi emphasized that Iran will not bow to threats and is prepared to defend itself, while remaining ready to pursue diplomacy.
On Feb. 28, Israel and the United States launched joint attacks on Tehran and other Iranian cities. Iran responded with waves of missile and drone attacks targeting Israel and U.S. bases and assets in the region, and tightened its grip on the Strait of Hormuz.
A ceasefire was achieved between the warring parties on April 8. On June 18, Iran and the United States signed a MoU on ending the war in the region on all fronts.
Under the MoU, the two countries were scheduled to hold negotiations within 60 days, ending on Aug. 17, to reach a final agreement on Iran's nuclear program and the removal of sanctions. However, they failed to make sufficient progress toward a deal. ■

Montenegrin President Jakov Milatovic meets with visiting Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, in Cetinje, a city near Montenegro's capital, Podgorica, Oct. 17, 2026. (Xinhua/Shi Zhongyu)

Milatovic asked Wang to convey his sincere greetings to Chinese President Xi Jinping, and welcomed the first-ever visit by a Chinese foreign minister to Montenegro.
Noting that this year marks the 20th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Montenegro and China, Milatovic said the visit holds important symbolic significance.
Recalling his experience studying in China, Milatovic said he had gained a deeper understanding of China's economic and social development and the lives of its people, as well as the importance of cooperation with China.
Noting that European Union (EU) accession is currently a priority on Montenegro's foreign policy agenda, Milatovic said the country also attaches great importance to relations with China, with Montenegro firmly adhering to the one-China principle and remaining committed to friendly and mutually beneficial cooperation with China.

Researchers in Australia develop AI tool to assess stroke risk
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
20:05:19 CST
21:05:19 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have developed an artificial intelligence (AI) model that analyzes DNA to identify genetic risk factors for stroke, paving the way for more personalized risk assessments and prevention.
The study identified 18 genetic variants linked to ischemic stroke, the most common type of stroke. People in the highest genetic risk group had a 22 percent higher chance of stroke than those in the lower-risk group, according to a statement released recently by Australia's University of Technology Sydney (UTS).
The team used a type of AI known as a transformer to train the model on thousands of genetic variations and identify links to ischemic stroke. Researchers tested the AI model using genetic and health data from the UK Biobank and a large U.S. database. The model was more accurate than previous genetic risk tools at distinguishing people who had suffered a stroke from those who had not.
The study also identified the gene EDEM2 in brain cortex tissue as a key contributor to stroke susceptibility, providing a target for further research.
Researchers are now developing a multimodal AI tool that combines genetic assessments with other modes of data, including health and lifestyle surveys, scans and imaging, to improve risk assessment for stroke and other diseases. ■

The maneuver saw the Russian satellite reduce the separation to the NATO nation’s orbiter from about 320 kilometers (200 miles) to around five kilometers (three miles) in less than 24 hours. Two monster black holes could collide in just 100 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:03:18 UTC
21:03:18 KST

Two monster black holes could collide in just 100 years
- Date:
- October 18, 2026
- Source:
- Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy
- Summary:
- Astronomers have uncovered compelling evidence of two supermassive black holes spiraling toward a potentially spectacular collision at the center of galaxy Mrk 501. A previously unseen jet of particles revealed the likely presence of a second black hole, with observations suggesting the pair completes an orbit every 121 days. Depending on their masses, these cosmic giants could merge in as little as 100 years.
- Share:
Supermassive black holes are thought to exist at the centers of nearly all large galaxies. These enormous objects can weigh millions or even billions of times as much as the Sun, but scientists still do not fully understand how they grow to such extraordinary sizes. Pulling in (accreting) gas from their surroundings is one way they gain mass, although this process alone may be too slow to explain the largest examples. Merging with other massive black holes could provide the missing explanation.
Galaxy collisions are common throughout the universe, making it likely that their central black holes also eventually come together. As two galaxies merge, their black holes are expected to move closer, begin orbiting one another, and gradually spiral inward until they combine into a single object.
Despite this expectation, scientists still struggle to model the final stages of these mergers. Even more puzzling, astronomers have not reliably identified a pair of supermassive black holes orbiting extremely close together, despite abundant evidence of colliding galaxies.
A Second Jet Reveals a Hidden Black Hole
An international research team led by Silke Britzen of the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy (MPIfR) in Bonn has now uncovered direct observational evidence suggesting that such a pair exists at the center of the galaxy Mrk 501. The findings have been accepted for publication in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society and are scheduled to appear in an upcoming issue.
Astronomers have long known that the central black hole in Mrk 501 produces an intense jet of particles that shoots into space at nearly the speed of light. These jets arise from the extreme conditions surrounding black holes, where powerful magnetic fields help accelerate material outward.
To investigate the system, researchers examined detailed radio observations collected at multiple frequencies on dozens of separate days over approximately 23 years. The extensive dataset revealed something remarkable: alongside the familiar jet was a second jet whose movement could also be tracked.
The observations provide what the researchers describe as the first direct imaging evidence of such a system at the center of a galaxy, strongly suggesting that a second supermassive black hole is present. The black holes themselves, however, remain too close together in the sky to be individually resolved.
"We searched for it for so long, and then it came as a complete surprise that we could not only see a second jet, but even track its movement," reports Silke Britzen.
Two Supermassive Black Holes in a Cosmic Dance
The previously known jet is aimed toward Earth, making it appear exceptionally bright and relatively easy to observe. The newly identified jet points in a different direction, which helps explain why it remained hidden for so long.
Over just a few weeks of observations, astronomers noticed dramatic changes in the second jet's position. It appeared to emerge from behind the larger black hole and sweep counterclockwise around it. The movement repeated, suggesting that the entire system was undergoing a regular orbital motion.
"Evaluating the data felt like being on a ship. The entire jet system is in motion. A system of two black holes can explain this: The orbital plane sways," explains Silke Britzen.
The researchers also identified an unusual event in June 2022, when radiation from the system appeared to form a ring. This phenomenon, known as an Einstein ring, occurs when gravity bends light in a way that creates a ringlike appearance.
One possible explanation is that the two black holes and Earth were briefly aligned in just the right way. In that configuration, the gravity of the foreground black hole could have acted like a lens, bending light from the second jet behind it. This effect, called gravitational lensing, offers another potential clue to the nature of the system.
Two Black Holes Could Merge in Just 100 Years
By examining changes in the jets and repeating patterns in their brightness, the team calculated that the two black holes appear to complete an orbit around each other approximately every 121 days.
Their estimated separation is just 250 to 540 times the distance between Earth and the Sun. Although that might sound enormous, it is remarkably small for objects with masses ranging from 100 million to a billion times that of our Sun.
Such a tight orbit could have dramatic consequences. Depending on the black holes' actual masses, their separation may shrink rapidly enough for them to merge in as little as 100 years.
That would be an exceptionally short countdown by astronomical standards, potentially giving researchers an extraordinary opportunity to investigate how supermassive black holes approach their final collision.
Gravitational Waves Could Reveal an Approaching Merger
Unfortunately, Mrk 501 is so distant that even today's most powerful instruments cannot distinguish the two black holes as separate objects. The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT), which produced the first images of black holes in 2019 and 2022, also lacks the resolution needed to capture this particular pair individually.
As a result, astronomers will not be able to directly watch the distance between the black holes decrease. However, another method could reveal their approach.
As massive objects orbit one another, they generate gravitational waves, tiny distortions in spacetime that travel outward through the universe. The proposed black hole pair in Mrk 501 should produce extremely low-frequency gravitational waves that could be detected using pulsar timing arrays (PTAs).
These arrays use the remarkably regular radio pulses emitted by rapidly rotating neutron stars, known as pulsars, as precise cosmic clocks. By measuring subtle changes in when those pulses arrive at Earth, scientists can search for the influence of passing gravitational waves.
Supermassive black hole binaries (SMBHBs) are already considered the leading explanation for the gravitational wave background, a persistent signal thought to arise from many distant sources across the universe. In 2023, the European Pulsar Timing Array and other research collaborations reported evidence of this background.
The discovery in Mrk 501 now makes the galaxy a particularly promising target for connecting a gravitational wave signal to an individual pair of supermassive black holes.
Such a detection could do more than confirm the system's existence. It might allow scientists to measure how the pair's orbit evolves and determine whether the black holes are approaching their final merger.
"If gravitational waves are detected, we may even see their frequency steadily rise as the two giants spiral toward collision, offering a rare chance to watch a supermassive black hole merger unfold," notes co-author Héctor Olivares.

Journal Reference:
- S Britzen, H Olivares, Gopal-Krishna, F Jaron, I N Pashchenko, E Kun, F K Schinzel, J Becerra González, D Paneque, N R MacDonald. Detection of a second jet within the nuclear core of Mrk 501. Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, 2026; 548 (4) DOI: 10.1093/mnras/stag291

Netanyahu suggests anti-Israel conspiracy behind outrage over attack on European diplomats
Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu alleged a 'smear' campaign against Israeli settlers on Saturday, attempting to cast doubt on accounts of a settler attack on European diplomats visiting the occupied West Bank during the olive harvest.
In a statement published on the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) social media account on Saturday evening, Netanyahu’s office described the assault as an "alleged" attack and suggested reporting on settler violence was part of a coordinated effort to discredit Israel.
The delegation included representatives from the French and Belgian consulates and the Polish representative to the Palestinian Authority. Taybeh’s mayor, Khoury, told The New Arab that the visitors had attended an event marking a twinning agreement between the Palestinian town and the French town of Aulnoye-Aymeries.
When members of the delegation accompanied Palestinians to harvest olives nearby, a group of around 10 Israeli settlers attacked their convoy. The attackers reportedly threatened those present and smashed the windows of a Belgian consular vehicle, injuring Aulnoye-Aymeries mayor Bernard Baudoux and two Palestinians.
The PMO referred to the attackers as "masked Israelis in Judea and Samaria", using Israel’s term for the occupied West Bank, and alleged that the diplomats had entered a "sensitive area" without prior coordination with the Israeli military.
Khoury disputed that account, telling The New Arab that the delegation had been taken to an area west of Taybeh, near homes that Palestinians considered safe. The settlers, he said, arrived from several settlement outposts surrounding the town.
Rather than unequivocally condemning the assault, Netanyahu’s office placed the reports "amid concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest, relying on sensational headlines before the full facts emerge".
"These images alone do not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility," the PMO said, adding that Israeli police and forensic investigators had opened an investigation.
The statement urged journalists and the public not to turn "unproven allegations" into a "collective indictment" of Israeli settlers.
It also sought to undermine Baudoux’s account by highlighting his support for Palestinians, noting that he had "previously raised the Palestinian flag over his municipal building, prompting French authorities to order its removal". The statement offered no explanation of how that episode cast doubt on his account of the attack.
Speaking after the attack on Saturday, Baudoux said the assault demonstrated Israel’s "tolerance" of settler violence.
"I had on my mayor’s sash with the blue, white and red colours, which clearly represent the symbol of France, in an attempt to protect the people around me. Well that was not enough and I was attacked, violently attacked, and … thrown to the ground," he said.
The attack drew criticism from a number of diplomats, including in Washington. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that US officials were "very disturbed by those images and what we’re seeing".
He added that Washington had "asked the Israelis and continue to ask them to crack down on that stuff".
