Brain iron levels in children with ADHD may depend on when they start medication
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:00:23 UTC
21:00:23 KST

Children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder who begin taking stimulant medications at a younger age may develop different brain iron levels than those who start treatment later. A new analysis of brain imaging data suggests that starting medication by age eight is associated with higher iron concentrations in dopamine-rich brain regions compared to starting at age nine or later. The research was published in the journal Brain Research.
Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, commonly known as ADHD, is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by inattention, impulsivity, and hyperactivity. These symptoms often create challenges with everyday tasks and social interactions. The condition is closely tied to reduced signaling of dopamine, a chemical messenger in the brain that helps regulate movement, attention, and reward. To manage symptoms, doctors routinely prescribe psychostimulants, which work by increasing the amount of dopamine available in the central nervous system.
Brain iron plays an essential role in this process because it is a necessary ingredient for the brain to manufacture dopamine. Tyrosine hydroxylase, the enzyme responsible for creating dopamine, relies entirely on iron to function properly. Iron also aids in the production of myelin, the protective sheath that insulates nerve fibers and speeds up communication between brain cells.
Because of this relationship, iron tends to concentrate heavily in dopamine-rich regions, such as the basal ganglia and the substantia nigra. These deep brain structures are heavily involved in motor control and learning. As a child grows into adolescence, iron levels in these areas typically increase alongside the maturation of the dopamine system.
Prior research has shown that children with ADHD who have never taken medication often have lower levels of brain iron compared to their peers without the condition. At the same time, some brain imaging research suggests that children treated with psychostimulants have iron levels similar to those of neurotypical children. This pattern raised the question of whether stimulant medications directly influence brain iron levels over time.
Hugo A.E. Morandini, a researcher at the Child and Adolescent Health Service in Perth, Australia, along with a team of colleagues, wanted to better understand how psychostimulant treatment relates to brain iron. They designed a study to track iron levels over a two-year period. They specifically looked at how both the duration of treatment and the age a child started taking medication might relate to iron concentrations.
To conduct the research, Morandini and his team used brain imaging data from the Oregon ADHD-1000 dataset, a public repository of clinical information. They identified 29 children with ADHD who were consistently taking psychostimulant medications and 38 neurotypical children with no psychiatric diagnoses. The children underwent magnetic resonance imaging scans at the beginning of the study and again two years later.
The researchers used a specific type of scan called functional magnetic resonance imaging. While this technology is often used to map blood flow, the team analyzed the data using a specialized technique that estimates the concentration of iron in brain tissue based on its magnetic properties. They focused their analysis on several brain regions rich in dopamine and iron, including the globus pallidus, putamen, caudate nucleus, thalamus, and substantia nigra.
First, the team compared the iron levels of the children with ADHD to the neurotypical children across the two-year period. The researchers adjusted their statistical models to account for variables like age, sex, and intelligence quotient. They found that differences in iron levels in the substantia nigra, thalamus, and most of the basal ganglia were not statistically significant between the two groups.
However, the children with ADHD had lower iron content in the globus pallidus. This structure is a key part of the basal ganglia that helps regulate dopamine circuitry and reward behaviors. The authors noted that a shorter average duration of medication exposure in their study compared to past research might explain why globus pallidus iron had not reached the levels seen in neurotypical children.
Next, the researchers looked exclusively at the 29 children with ADHD to see how their medication histories related to their brain iron. They calculated the total time each child had been taking psychostimulants and noted the age at which they first started the treatment. The researchers then tested whether these factors predicted iron levels across the different brain regions.
The length of time a child had been taking stimulants had almost no statistical relationship with brain iron. The researchers found a very small negative association between treatment duration and iron in the thalamus, but they noted this effect was so minor it is unlikely to have any clinical meaning. In all other regions, the models for treatment duration were not statistically significant.
The age at which a child began treatment showed a different pattern. The team split the children with ADHD into two subgroups based on when they started medication. One group began treatment at age eight or younger, while the other began at age nine or older.
The analysis revealed that children who started taking psychostimulants at an earlier age had higher iron content in the thalamus, caudate nucleus, putamen, and globus pallidus. The researchers noted that the brain undergoes rapid developmental changes in iron and dopamine during childhood. They proposed that starting medication earlier in childhood might intersect with these developmental windows, making the dopamine system more sensitive to external influences.
The findings come with several limitations that affect how the results should be interpreted. The analysis relied on a relatively small number of participants, meaning the patterns observed need to be confirmed in larger populations. A larger study could provide more precise estimates of how medication timing interacts with brain development.
The researchers also had to rely on parent reports to determine when the children began taking medication and how long they had been treated. Parent recall can sometimes be imprecise, which could introduce errors into the timelines. The study also lacked information on the exact dosages the children were taking and how strictly they adhered to their daily medication schedules.
Because the researchers observed existing medication habits rather than assigning treatments, the results establish an association rather than a direct cause and effect. It is possible that children prescribed medication at a younger age have more severe symptoms, which could be tied to underlying differences in brain biology. The researchers could not measure the children’s brain iron before treatment started, making it difficult to isolate the exact impact of the drugs.
Future research will need to follow patients from before they start medication into adulthood to fully chart the effects of early treatment. Tracking these changes over a longer lifespan could help researchers understand whether the differences in brain iron persist as patients grow older.
The study, “Neurochemical impact of psychostimulants: Longitudinal MRI analysis of brain iron content in children with ADHD,” was authored by Hugo A.E. Morandini, Sjoerd B. Vos, Paola Chivers, Tim J. Silk, and Pradeep Rao.

Who is Mehrdad Akhlaghi, Iran’s new tech-focused defence minister?

12:00:04 UTC

Who is Mehrdad Akhlaghi, Iran’s new tech-focused defence minister?
Akhlaghi’s experience centres on ballistic missiles, aerospace technology and defence-industrial production.
Tehran, Iran – Mehrdad Akhlaghi Ketabchi has been appointed Iran’s defence minister at a time when the war with the United States is expected to escalate.
The 68-year-old was approved on Sunday by parliament, which has convened online since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran on February 28, to assume leadership of the Ministry of Defence and Armed Forces Logistics. In total, 237 lawmakers voted in favour of Akhlaghi’s appointment and 15 against.
Former Defence Minister Aziz Nasirzadeh was killed along with a large number of other senior figures, including Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, on the opening day of the war.
The position was filled temporarily by Majid Ebn-e Reza, who will now become Akhlaghi’s deputy.
Akhlaghi will be responsible for rebuilding and expanding Iran’s military-industrial infrastructure, which has been heavily targeted by the US and Israel.
The new minister’s defence plans were approved earlier by senior military authorities, President Masoud Pezeshkian and parliament’s Commission on National Security and Foreign Policy.
“The Islamic Republic of Iran will not be the instigator of aggression against any country but will defend the territorial integrity of the country strongly and to the death against any aggression,” Pezeshkian said.
The president said Akhlaghi has more than 42 years of experience in the Defence Ministry and related organisations.
His principal expertise is in ballistic missiles, solid-fuel propulsion, aerospace technology and military-industrial production, according to state media.
Previously, he served as the head of the Shahid Bagheri Industrial Group, the Aerospace Industries Organization and the Defence Industries Organization. Akhlaghi and these entities are all subject to sanctions by the US. He is also under United Nations sanctions.
He has been associated with developing several missile types and related weapons-development projects over the past decades, according to Tasnim, a newspaper linked with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC),
Akhlaghi reportedly played a role in expanding the major Sejjil and Zolfaghar family of Iranian ballistic missiles as well as precision-guided weapons, such as the Almas missiles and Yasin guided bombs.
He is also said to have expertise in space launchers, research rockets and infrastructure associated with the Imam Khomeini Space Center in Semnan. These have all been critical elements in Iran’s wars against Israel and the US.
This month, Iran’s Defence Ministry spokesman, Brigadier General Reza Talaei-Nik, told reporters that Akhlaghi’s nomination reflected Iran’s need to increase the quantity and quality of strategic weapons, particularly missiles and drones.
“Offensive arms are being actively improved,” the spokesman said.
The US has repeatedly claimed that it has destroyed most of Iran’s military-industrial capacities, but Tehran has maintained it continues to have considerable offensive and defensive capabilities outside the reach of US and Israeli bombs. These weapons have been upgraded based on Iran’s new war experience, it has insisted.
Akhlaghi told members of parliament this month that he had met with senior military commanders, including the commander-in-chief of the IRGC, Brigadier General Ahmad Vahidi, to develop a better understanding of their requirements during and after the war.
His priorities as defence minister would be faster military-industrial development, air defences, incorporation of emerging technologies using government and private sector firms, improvements in armed-forces welfare and development of international military cooperation, according to reports.
In his first comments as defence minister on Sunday, Akhlaghi taunted the administration of US President Donald Trump, which this month threatened to use the “mother of all bombs” on Iran’s nuclear and energy infrastructure.
“We have made preparations and continue our work with ease of mind,” he told reporters. “The US president must think of getting his forces out of our region in one piece. If he drops one bomb, he must see how many of his troops he will have to evacuate horizontally.”

New NHS England policy for trans people could have ‘a number of adverse impacts’, report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:00:03 UTC
21:00:03 KST

Trans people could face delays and a greater risk of “corridor care” under new NHS England guidance that means they will no longer be able to use same-sex wards, according to an internal report.
An NHS England impact assessment, seen by the Guardian, stated that trans people may also potentially experience discrimination and this could lead to them “avoiding accessing healthcare at all”.
The document considered the impact of new NHS guidance on single-sex spaces across all protected characteristics, including age, disability and sex. It said the policy’s focus on “privacy, dignity and safety for men and women” would have a positive impact, as would the legal accuracy in guidance on single-sex spaces.
It also highlighted benefits for women who are pregnant or breastfeeding, people with certain religious beliefs and minority-ethnic groups.
But it said there were a “number of potential adverse impacts for trans people”, adding: “There may be delays and a greater risk of ‘corridor care’ for trans people with a negative impact on their physical and mental health and wellbeing if side rooms are not available.
“Trans people may fear and potentially experience discrimination by being ‘outed’ as trans through not being accommodated in a ward that aligns with their lived gender or being placed in a side room.”
It said there was a risk that hospitals would not have the capacity to provide side rooms when needed, “forcing trans people into the potentially distressing situation of being accommodated on wards aligned with their biological sex”.
It said the new policy might have a “negative impact on fostering good relations” between cisgender and transgender people, as staff may need to “balance the needs of one group against the other” and this could create animosity and division.
It also said some women who did not “present in line with general societal expectations” could be subjected to questioning around their sex in order to access single-sex wards.
NHS England published new guidance for trusts on Thursday stating that single-sex wards, toilets and changing rooms should be used by people based on their biological sex, not their gender identity.
It stated that trans people should be “accommodated in line with their biological sex” while ensuring their clinical needs were met and their “privacy, dignity and safety are maintained”, along with other patients sharing their accommodation.
A supreme court ruling in 2025 that stated the terms “woman” and “sex” in the Equality Act referred only to a biological woman and to biological sex, and did not include transgender women with gender recognition certificates.
The updated Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) code of practice for services said they must be used on the basis of biological sex, and acknowledged that “trans people are likely to be disadvantaged by this, by comparison to people who are not trans”.
The NHS England impact assessment said negative impacts of the new policy could be mitigated by ensuring clinical need was always prioritised, and it highlighted how the new policy did not apply in A&E or intensive care.
It said the delivery of same-sex accommodation should not be a reason for patients to receive “corridor care”, and that decisions on where to place trans people should be made on a “case-by-case basis”.
NHS England declined to comment.

How to make the perfect poires belle Hélène – recipe | Felicity Cloake's How to make the perfect …
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:00:03 UTC
21:00:03 KST

It’s always slightly embarrassing to realise that you’ve missed a pop culture reference, even if it’s 162 years old, so I won’t dwell on the fact that until last week I was unaware of the existence of Offenbach’s 1864 operetta about Helen of Troy, La Belle Hélène, after which today’s dish is named. In any case, the great French chef Escoffier was so moved by it, or perhaps by its popularity among Parisian diners, to name this simple dessert of vanilla-scented poached pears topped with hot chocolate sauce after the work’s heroine, played by the comely Hortense Schneider.
Though other homages (he includes no fewer than five dishes with that name in his 1907 Guide Culinaire, none of which involve pears) may, like the music, have faded from public consciousness, this particular pairing, if you’ll forgive the pun, has stood the test of time. As Nigel Slater observes in Tender: Volume 2, “The marriage of pears and chocolate is extraordinary. It is as if they were made for each other.” This, I think, is the duo at its “most sumptuous”.
The pears
Everyone is agreed that, for best results when poaching pears, you need them to be firm. As Nigella Lawson writes in How to Eat, “In fact, it is a positive advantage to use what would in other circumstances seem rebarbatively firm fruit” (extra points if, unlike my spellcheck, you were already familiar with the word “rebarbative”). Squidgy fruit of the kind that runs down your chin will fall apart during cooking; turn those into cake instead.
As far as I can tell from the recipe included in François-Régis Gaudry’s magisterial Let’s Eat France, which claims to have respected “the proportions of the era”, Escoffier poached the fruit in a vanilla syrup, a tradition most versions honour. However, Max Rocha of Cafe Cecilia in London eschews the pod in favour of citrus zest (lemon and orange), rosemary and a stick of cinnamon. (Also, to be fair, Rocha, like Slater, does not claim to be making poires belle helene, but simply poached pears with chocolate sauce). Very nice it is, too, and I would encourage you to experiment, but, out of deference to the dessert’s creator, I’ve stuck with vanilla.
Under-ripe pears tend to be willing recipients of help in the flavour department, so for once I’m in favour of dialling up the sugar, because the pears need to be robust enough to stand up to the intense chocolate sauce. I’ll also be adding the juice of a whole lemon, as Jane Grigson and chef Alain Benech, whose recipe is featured on Delia Smith’s website, suggests. I’ll include the finely grated zest, too; the acidity not only helps the fruit retain its colour, but brings out its perfume as well.
Though everyone uses a slightly different cooking method, from a brief boil (Grigson’s Fruit Book) to keeping the liquid at a very gentle heat throughout (Slater), none proves disastrous; what is key is to keep the pears submerged so they cook evenly (Benech recommends topping them with a cartouche of baking paper, which sounds a faff but really isn’t, especially compared with constantly turning the fruit in the pan once they bob up to the top) and to leave them ever so slightly harder than you’d like them, because they will continue to cook as they cool in the syrup.
Grigson and Slater both halve their pears, which, while it does speed up the cooking time, looks less fun on the plate, which feels a shame – this is definitely a show-off sort of dessert. Do, as Benech suggests, remove a little of the stringy core from the base, however – it’ll make them a lot easier to eat with a modicum of decorum.
The sauce
Without sauce, the dish would just be fruit, which, as I never tire of reminding my mum, is not a proper pudding. That said, Grigson notes that this is a dish that “has had much criticism from some food writers, for the combination of delicate pears with chocolate sauce … the secret lies in taking very little sauce”. She has a point: chocolate, like tomato ketchup, is a flavour bully – let it in, and it tends to take over – so I would suggest moderating things to an artful drip, or allowing your guests to serve themselves at the table. After all, if they overdo it, they only have themselves to blame.
Rocha is the only one to use cocoa powder and water rather than melted chocolate and dairy, which results in an intensely flavoured but thin sauce. Initially, I’m quite taken by the idea; it feels a nice counterpoint to any creamy things you might be serving with your pears, but it does mean serving the pear in a puddle of chocolate sauce, rather than allowing it to drip glossily down from its stem (a sentence I have rewritten more than once), so, in the end, I’ve stuck with the traditional melted chocolate. Grigson and Slater both add black coffee, which feels like overcomplicating things (even though it goes well with chocolate), as does Benech’s dash of poire william and the kirschwasser that’s in Grigson’s box of tricks. By all means pop them in, if you like, especially if your sauce needs thinning down a little, but a dash of vanilla extract and a pinch of salt should be quite sufficient.
Gaudry makes the sauce with milk, Grigson and Slater whipping cream, and Lawson and Benech double cream. The fattier the dairy, of course, the richer and thicker the result – and double cream tends to be easier to get hold of than whipping, which is another point in its favour – but some double cream is so lusciously dense that it forms an unattractive brown lump, rather than the silky stream I’m after. Give it a good stir first, and loosen the finished sauce with a little milk or water, or even liqueur, if necessary. For extra shine, stir in a knob of butter or a spoonful of golden syrup at the end, but with this proportion of chocolate to dairy, you probably won’t need any help in that department. Do serve the sauce warm and the pears cold, though, because much of this dish’s charm lies in contrast.
The dairy
Rocha and Slater, classy chaps that they are, serve the pear and chocolate sauce au naturel, but it’s hard to argue that this isn’t improved by an elegant scoop of vanilla ice-cream (what isn’t?) or a billowing spoonful of Benech’s creme chantilly (cream whipped with sugar and vanilla seeds). Whichever you go for, however, don’t overlook one final contrast. A sprinkling of flaked almonds (Benech) or crystallised violets (Grigson) leaves you with cold ice-cream or cream, cool, juicy pears, hot chocolate sauce and a crunchy garnish. Perfection in a dish.
Perfect poires belle helene
Prep 20 min
 
Cook 30 min
 
Serves 4
4 firm, not-too-ripe pears
  
1 unwaxed lemon
  
1 vanilla pod
  
200g white sugar, or golden sugar
 
¼ tsp salt (optional)
 
1 tbsp flaked almonds, toasted, or crystallised violets, to serve
 
4 scoops vanilla ice-cream, or 150ml double or whipping cream, whipped with 1 tbsp caster or icing sugar and ¼ tsp vanilla extract or paste, or the seeds from ½ vanilla pod, to serve
For the sauce
 
150g dark chocolate
  
200ml double or whipping cream
 
Pinch of salt
  
Milk, or water or liqueur of your choice (optional)
Prepare the pears some hours before you’re intending to eat. Find a wide, fairly deep pan and cut out a circle of greaseproof paper of the same diameter. Fold this in half then in quarters, then in eighths, and cut a small hole in the centre to let out steam.
Add the lemon zest and juice to the pan. Split open the vanilla pod, scrape out the vanilla seeds and add these to the pan with the empty pod, sugar and salt, if using. Pour in a litre of water and bring to a simmer, stirring to dissolve the sugar.
Peel the pears, leaving the stalks intact, and cut a small slice off their bottoms so they’ll stand up straight later. Scoop out some of the woody core from the bases, then lay down the pears in the pan
Unfold the paper cartouche, use to cover the fruit, then leave the pears to simmer gently for about 25 minutes, until cooked through but not too soft. Take off the heat, leave to cool in the poaching liquid, then put in the fridge to chill.
When you’re ready to eat, chop up the chocolate. Put the cream in a small pan, heat to a bare simmer, then take off the heat and add the chocolate. Leave to sit for a couple of minutes, then stir until melted and smooth.
Add the salt, if using, and if the chocolate mix feels too thick to pour easily, stir in a dash of milk, water or liqueur, too.
To assemble, drain the pears and pat them dry with kitchen paper (the poaching liquid makes a lovely drink, or reduce it to make a syrup to drizzle over future desserts). Divide the fruit between shallow bowls, standing them upright.
Either pour a spoonful of chocolate sauce down one flank, or serve the sauce separately for everyone to pour their own. Add a spoonful of ice-cream or chantilly cream, scatter with toasted nuts or violets, and serve immediately.
- Poires belle helene: is this the most beautiful of pear-based desserts or have you fallen for something less operatic – an upside-down cake, perhaps, or a boozy sorbet?

Forty years on from the tragic killing of Ahmed Iqbal Ullah, activists call for renewed fight against the far right
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:00:01 UTC
21:00:01 KST

“For my brother Ahmed, British values meant standing up for others. It was doing right. It was supporting and looking after the underdog, whoever that may be, regardless of their colour or background,” Selina Ullah says, of the brother she lost to a senseless act of violence 40 years ago.
Ahmed Iqbal Ullah, a British Bengali schoolboy, was 13 when he was murdered in a racist attack in the playground of Burnage high school, in south Manchester, in 1986, after defending young pupils from bullying.
Ahmed’s murder – by a 13-year-old white British pupil who was sentenced to the youth equivalent of life, was a landmark moment. The Macdonald inquiry into the racism and racial violence in Manchester schools that surrounded Ahmed’s death sparked a national debate about antiracism in education.
Forty years on, Ahmed’s memory is at the heart of the Ahmed Iqbal Ullah RACE Centre (AIU), which houses archives on Black figures in Manchester, community history on events such as Manchester carnival, and pan-African activism in the city and beyond.
The 1970s concept of “political Blackness” – the idea of a strategic multiracial alliance across groups affected by racism – fell out of favour in the 1990s, as it became seen as an inadequate reflection of differing experiences.
But the story of AIU speaks to the power of solidarity across communities. Since it was founded in 1987 in Ahmed’s memory by Lou Kushnick, a Jewish-American professor at theUniversity of Manchester – with teacher Jackie Ould as its education co-ordinator – it has provided archivists, teachers and campaigners with the inspiration and resources to document under-recorded Black, antiracist and migration histories, fight social injustice and push for greater representation in education.
A memorial event, The Legacy of Ahmed: 40 years on, was held last month. It was attended by Ahmed’s family, AIU’s head, Maya Sharma, justice campaigners from 1986, including lawyer Robert Lizar, and a new generation of antiracism activists.
At the event it was argued that “political Blackness” – the framework in which AIU was founded – had a new relevance in the face of a resurgent far right.
Zara Manoehoetoe, a youth worker with Manchester antiracism organisation Kids of Colour, said: “Politically black is the note that we have to ground ourselves in, because anti-blackness manifests for all of us.
“We are working with young people from across Greater Manchester … The international context lives in their DNA, it lives in their homes, it lives at the kitchen table, it lives in the food that their mothers and their nanas are putting on their plates.”
The writer and film-maker Tariq Mehmood was a speaker on the panel alongside Manoehoetoe.
In 1986 Mehmood joined the justice campaign, spearheaded by Selina Ullah, which preceded the Macdonald inquiry.
Mehmood urged activists today to move offline and into grassroots organising across communities, amid a “continuing struggle” against racism in the UK and genocide in Gaza.
He added: “We were not victims [in the 1980s]. We educated ourselves. We organised youth movements. We organised workers’ organisations. That’s Indians, that’s Pakistanis, that’s Bangladeshis, that’s Africans, a whole plethora of anti-imperialist organisations … and in that context, we were Black.”
Prof Gus John, who served on the panel for the Macdonald inquiry and co-authored the book of the report, Murder in the Playground, was among speakers at the memorial event.
John said of the inquiry and the book: “What we were saying was it was important that schools have a responsibility to teach children and enable them to understand racism, how it operates in society and how they could be implicated in perpetuating it.
“Kenneth Baker [then education secretary] refused to accept the report, refused to raise the matter in parliament, and refused to put this book in the House of Commons library. Roll on 40 years … and every day, we hear more and more stories of racist incidents.”
Nika Muthra-Shah, the director of educational innovation at the Rekindle Collective, the Black-led supplementary schools programme, spoke of how young people are “feeling a lot of anger and a lot of fear about the rise of the far right”, and how the collective was countering it through youth empowerment, education in critical thinking and encouraging dialogue.
The memories of speakers who were at school with Ahmed highlighted how racism – and the fight against it – shape young lives.
From the audience at the memorial event Naeem, who was in the playground the day Ahmed was stabbed, said: “Ahmed was a very good friend. I was sometimes jealous of him because he used to wear the best clobber – Adidas tracksuits, like Run DMC!
“[When Ahmed was killed] we didn’t get any help or support from nobody, and we just got on with our life. After then, my life just deteriorated, I wasn’t bothered with school, I was fighting, I was suspended, I became racially abusive towards people. I turned my life around, [but] it’s always in my heart.”
Pervez Iqbal, who was a year older than Ahmed at Burnage High and part of the original justice campaign, was inspired by the tragedy to pursue a career in education.
He said: “We grew up very quickly when in reality we were still children who needed some guidance. Those experiences eventually gave me the determination to do something positive in my life. I studied, became a teacher and eventually I returned back to Burnage where I worked for 23 years.
“Schools and communities can change, education can change attitudes, and people working together can create something better for the next generation. My message for today is simple. Never forget Ahmed [or] our responsibility to educate, guide, and protect people.”
In October, Home Office figures revealed racially and religiously motivated offences have reached record highs in the UK. Police recorded 146,825 hate crimes in the year ending March 2026 – a rise of 7% in the past year. Offences targeting Muslims increased the most – up 15%, from 4,479 to 5,132.

Czech companies interested in Ukraine's reconstruction – Chamber of Commerce representative
Tomas Kopecny, Special Representative for Ukraine at the Czech Chamber of Commerce, said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
"Czech exports to Ukraine are growing and will continue to grow. Exports also essentially mean participation in reconstruction projects. This means that Czech companies are getting involved and investing in Ukraine," Kopecny said.
According to him, Czech businesses are showing considerable interest in Ukraine's reconstruction, despite the fact that Czech partners do not expect peace or a ceasefire agreement in the near future.
Kopecny noted that during the first four years of Russia's full-scale war, Czech entrepreneurs had repeatedly visited Ukraine on business missions. Several such visits have also taken place this year, including a business mission to Dnipro focused on the construction of shelters.
At the same time, Czech companies are developing partnerships with Ukrainian businesses in the Czech Republic itself, he said. In October, a delegation representing more than ten Ukrainian technology and industrial companies, universities, research institutions and clusters took part in the MSV 2026 International Engineering Fair in Brno.
By the end of the year, the Czech Chamber of Commerce plans to organize two more large-scale missions involving dozens of entrepreneurs from several cities.
A major business mission to Ukraine led by Czech Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Industry and Trade Karel Havlicek is scheduled for November.
"This mission is the culmination of previous initiatives, while also involving state representatives at the highest possible level. […] Dozens of entrepreneurs are expected to take part in the mission," Kopecny said.
He identified energy, infrastructure and agriculture as the main areas of cooperation.
The delegation will include companies that are major producers and investors in the energy sector, including Moravske naftove doly (MND), RSJ, Gentec and Agregat. Skoda Transportation is actively involved in infrastructure projects, while Czech company Agromino operates in Ukraine's agricultural sector.
Kopecny also noted that earlier this year, Deputy Prime Minister Havlicek described Ukraine as an important partner for the Czech Republic, and that these statements have been accompanied by concrete steps. He expressed hope that the security situation would allow the planned events to go ahead.
"The government is taking only slightly fewer practical steps than its predecessor. For example, the budget for funds intended to help rebuild Ukraine has been increased, whether through guarantee programs or export insurance. […] The Czech government is actually supporting these companies when it comes to civilian cooperation. They simply do not talk about it because they have chosen this policy," he said.
As previously reported, Ukraine and the Czech Republic remain in contact on further steps to develop cooperation, particularly in infrastructure reconstruction and joint projects to restore local communities.

Russia hit Ukraine’s energy 76 times during a US-declared truce—and tens of thousands lost power overnight. Civilians killed and injured
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:55:21 UTC
20:55:21 KST

Russia has kept striking Ukraine’s energy sector throughout the week since US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 18 October. From overnight into Sunday, Russian drones and a ballistic missile hit substations, homes, and industrial sites from Odesa to Volyn. They killed civilians and left tens of thousands of families without power.
Russia fights along the front line while hitting cities and the grid behind it with drones, missiles, and glide bombs. Ukraine says Moscow plans up to 1,000 such munitions against 60 key infrastructure sites this winter, and jet-powered drones partly free it to concentrate missiles on fewer targets, the Institute for the Study of War assessed. With Graham Act penalties on hold and US sanctions on Russian diesel suspended, Russia faces no new US cost for its strikes on Ukraine’s grid. Protecting and restoring the grid falls to Ukraine’s air defenses and repair crews.
Russia hit energy sites 76 times in a week
Zelenskyy counted 76 deliberate Russian strikes on energy and oil-and-gas facilities since Trump’s announcement. Overnight, Russia hit substations in Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, and Odesa oblasts, he said. In the past week, Russia fired almost 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 66 missiles, most of them ballistic, mainly to cause a blackout. His message was aimed at Washington.
“America must see that Russia is not taking steps in return for the lifting of sanctions or deals. On the contrary, they take every signal that they can make money as proof that their bet on war is working and they can keep fighting,” Zelenskyy wrote.
22 House lawmakers press Trump to implement Russia sanctions law. Diesel deal draws bipartisan backlash
Overnight, Russia launched one Iskander-M ballistic missile and 180 Shahed-type drones, 26 of them jet-powered, the Air Force reported. Air defenses downed or suppressed 152 drones, but strikes hit 20 locations.
Power cuts from Odesa to Ternopil
Strikes left about 24,000 consumers in Odesa Oblast without power, oblast head Oleh Kiper said. In Vinnytsia Oblast, the attack damaged critical infrastructure and forced emergency outages, oblast head Natalia Zabolotna wrote. Drones hit three energy facilities in Ternopil Oblast, one of them for the second time, and cut power to some consumers, oblast head Taras Pastukh said.
Civilians killed and injured
A Russian strike on Zaporizhzhia killed a 27-year-old woman and injured two others, including a 16-year-old, the State Emergency Service reported. In Poltava, an evening attack killed one person, injured four, and damaged 10 detached houses, city council secretary Kateryna Yamshchykova said.
Five Russian bombs kill 17 in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia next day after Trump lets Russia ship first 300,000 tonnes of its diesel
A drone hit a high-rise in Odesa and set its roof on fire. A 13-year-old girl was hurt, city military administration head Serhii Lysak said, and Kiper put the number of injured at two.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, Russian drones and artillery injured three people, oblast head Oleksandr Hanzha said. In Donetsk Oblast, Russian attacks killed seven civilians on Saturday, six of them in Sloviansk, oblast head Vadym Filashkin reported.
Fires in the west, alerts across the border
A morning drone strike set warehouse and production buildings ablaze at an enterprise in Manevychi, Volyn Oblast, oblast head Roman Romaniuk said. With heavy smoke blowing toward the town, Romaniuk urged residents to stay indoors, shut windows and doors, and switch off ventilation. A repeat strike set an enterprise in the district on fire again, the State Emergency Service said, adding that air tests found no dangerous concentrations outside the site. In Lviv Oblast, drone debris damaged a logistics warehouse and two houses, oblast head Maksym Kozytskyi said.
Polish military aircraft operated in Poland’s airspace twice during the attack, as the Government Security Centre warned residents of Lublin Voivodeship and later alerted Subcarpathian Voivodeship. In Lithuania, NATO jets failed to identify an object that apparently entered from Poland, Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said.
A ceasefire Moscow never confirmed
Trump announced the energy ceasefire on 11 October, news that surprised Zelenskyy. A White House official said Russia was still weighing it. Hours later, Russia hit a Kharkiv power plant, and on 14 October it fired 39 ballistic missiles at the grid. Then Trump waived Graham Act penalties on buyers of Russian oil, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the administration wants 60 days to weigh the economic effects.

Midterm melee: Americans in the Netherlands gear up to vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:55:18 UTC
20:55:18 KST

Midterm melee: Americans in the Netherlands gear up to vote
Brandon Hartley
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Americans living abroad can often feel like they’re stuck on the political sidelines of their native land. With one of the most contentious midterm elections in US history coming up next month, we spoke with the Netherlands’ American community about how they’re getting involved in the race and the challenges they face.
For the past two years, Donald Trump has dominated headlines around the world. It seems like there’s little the divisive president and his administration haven’t disrupted within and well beyond US borders.
There’s no denying that much is riding on the country’s midterms on November 3 and that the result will have a defining impact on the course of global politics over the next few years.
As with prior elections, Americans living in the Netherlands may feel there’s little they can do besides mail in their absentee ballots – and even that is an often complicated process that many fail to complete.
Each state sets its own deadlines and decides whether ballots can go back by email, fax or post. A ballot posted from the Netherlands also has to cross the Atlantic in time to be counted.
Some don’t bother at all, and some feel they shouldn’t. “One of the reasons why many in the Netherlands don’t vote is because they’ve been here for a very long time,” said Tre’ Shawn Griffin-Noordermeer, vice chair of the Netherlands chapter of Democrats Abroad. “They feel like they shouldn’t be voting because they’ve lived outside the US for so long.”
In fact, federal law lets US citizens abroad keep voting in federal elections in the state where they last lived, however long they have been away.
To help get that message out, various groups here have been volunteering and hosting events in the days leading up to the midterms.
Reaching out to voters
Members of campaign group Democrats Abroad in the Netherlands have spent recent weeks running an email campaign and arranging “Vote From Abroad” gatherings on Zoom.
They’ve also been hosting lunches and other events in cities around the country to discuss the midterms along with putting up fliers and getting the word out on social media and via phone banking.
“We’ve got hundreds of volunteers here in the Netherlands who have been helping with this,” Griffin-Noordermeer told Dutch News. “A few weekends ago, we called over 13,000 people.”
Originally founded in 1964, Democrats Abroad serves as the Democratic party’s official organisation for American citizens living overseas. One of its primary tasks is encouraging its members and other voters, who are spread across 197 countries, to cast their ballots.
And that’s more difficult than it might seem.
Counting the voters
Nobody knows exactly how many Americans in the Netherlands can vote. The US does not require citizens to register with the government when they move abroad, and some states drop overseas voters from their rolls when they stop responding to election mail. That leaves neither the State Department nor voter lists with a reliable count.
The national statistics office CBS puts the number of US nationals living in the Netherlands at just over 27,000 in 2026 – though not all are old enough to vote, and Dutch-Americans with both passports are counted as Dutch, so aren’t included.
Worldwide, about 2.2 million Americans of voting age live abroad, according to the Federal Voting Assistance Program (FVAP), the US defence department office that helps military and overseas citizens vote. FVAP estimates only about 11% of them voted in the 2024 presidential election. Even fewer typically take part in midterms.
FVAP says 14.8% of eligible voters in Europe voted in 2024.
Preparing for the worst
Despite Trump’s low approval ratings, the path to a “blue wave” for the Democrats won’t necessarily be an easy one.
His administration also continues to meddle with the midterms. In August, the Pentagon, which runs FVAP, made last-minute changes to the Federal Post Card Application (the form overseas voters use to register and request ballots), removing the checkbox for US citizens who were born abroad and have never lived in the US. The Democratic National Committee has gone to court over the change.
That followed a March 2025 executive order in which Trump sought to add proof-of-citizenship requirements to the same form, parts of which federal courts have blocked. The order also aimed to stop states counting mail ballots that arrive after Election Day.
In June, the US Supreme Court ruled 5-4 that states can keep counting ballots postmarked by Election Day that arrive later. That matters for voters whose ballots travel by international post.
Hayley Hughes, the co-founder of the Netherlands chapter of Indivisible, admitted she’s worried about how things might go.
She has already had discussions with the leads of other chapters about what to do if the administration interferes with ballot counts or sends government agents to polling stations.
Trump has said Republicans should “take over the voting” in at least 15 places, and his former adviser Steve Bannon has welcomed the idea of immigration agents at the polls.
“We’re already thinking we might have to mobilise,” Hughes told Dutch News.
“We’re looking at a protest here that week, if needed. In the US, there could be a mass mobilisation of peaceful protests and a general strike where people don’t go to work or school. We all hope that won’t be needed.”
The week of the midterms
Several midterm events are scheduled for the week of the elections. The Atlantische Commissie in The Hague is hosting an “American midterm election breakfast” on 4 November.
In Amsterdam, the commission is also helping with the John Adams Institute’s “Midterm Madness” event on November 6. It’s set to serve as an afterparty with a ‘festival-style experience’ featuring live music along with discussions and lectures about the results featuring Mark Leibovich, a staff writer at The Atlantic, and others.
Comedian Greg Shapiro is once again teaming up with Pep Rosenfeld for an Election Night Party at Boom Chicago. They’ve hosted these events since the ‘00s and are once again prepared to stay up late. The comedy club has vowed to remain open past 4:00 “if things get crazy.”
“How late, well, we’ll wait and see,” Shapiro told Dutch News. “I’ve got performances the next day. At some point I’ll have to get some sleep.”
Shapiro will be taking a break from his ongoing ‘KING ME: 250 Years of Donald Trump’ comedy tour for the Boom Chicago gathering. He’s worried about how much rewriting he’ll have to do for subsequent performances after the midterms.
“There’s no telling what could happen,” he said. “It could become January 6th on a national scale.”
If you’re an American living overseas and haven’t voted yet, there could still be time based on where you’re registered. Visit votefromabroad.org for further assistance.

Türkiye solves 60 cold-case murders in 9 months of this year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:54:45 UTC
20:54:45 KST

Turkish police and gendarmerie forces have solved 60 murders committed between 2004 and 2024 in the first nine months of this year by re-examining evidence from cold cases using modern forensic technology and pursuing new leads, Interior Ministry sources said on Oct. 18.
Of the cases solved, 35 fell under the jurisdiction of the police and 25 under the gendarmerie, with the oldest dating back to 2004, the sources told the Turkish state-run Anadolu Agency.
Re-examinations of evidence from past investigations, assessed alongside newly obtained material, have played a key role in identifying suspects, according to the sources.
Investigators have been analyzing DNA profiles, surveillance footage, telephone records, traffic data, mobile phone base station records and witness statements.
They have also traced physical evidence, including vehicle fragments recovered at crime scenes, while examining similarities between separate cases for potential links.
“Those who think they can commit murder and cover their tracks, believing they will never be found because time has passed, are gravely mistaken,” Interior Minister Mustafa Çiftçi said.
He stressed that police and gendarmerie units were continuing their investigations in coordination with chief public prosecutors’ offices and relevant institutions.
The Justice Ministry recently established a bureau tasked with investigating several high-profile unsolved cases.
Meanwhile, law enforcement agencies continue to pursue cold cases, including those that have received little or no media attention, in an effort to identify perpetrators and bring them to justice.

How Israeli support could most effectively aid Saudi Arabia against the Houthis - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:50:52 UTC
20:50:52 KST

There is increased discussion about how Israel might help Saudi Arabia against the Iranian-backed Houthis. How might such help take shape, and what might be most effective?
This comes amid wider questions about whether Saudi Arabia will join the Abraham Accords. Questions about this have come up since the accords began in 2020. So far, Riyadh has taken a wait-and-see approach, preferring that Israel make positive moves on the Palestinian issue.
Now, US President Donald Trump has said that Saudi Arabia may be accepting help from Israel. Asked about whether he thought Saudi Arabia might normalize ties with Israel, he said, “I think they will. Israel’s been very helpful to Saudi Arabia.” The comments were made days after Saudi Arabia appeared to downplay whether Israel would support them.
The context for this latest development is the Houthis’ increased attacks on Saudi Arabia. America has not joined the fighting but may be supporting the Saudis in various ways, such as via intelligence.
The US has so far chosen not to join strikes on the Houthis. The Trump administration carried out strikes on the Houthis in March and April 2025. The administration eventually concluded that it was better to do a deal with the Houthis than continue strikes.
On Sunday, Walla had a piece by Amir Bohbot, asking whether Israeli aid to Saudi Arabia would be an opportunity or a potential powder keg.
“Security sources confirmed to Walla that the quality of Israeli intelligence is improving, but at the same time the Houthis are causing heavy damage. The security establishment is aware that there is an opportunity to strengthen relations, but is not addressing the issue for fear of inflaming the situation,” Bohbot reported.
The Turkish pro-government media outlet Anadolu Agency noted on October 13 that “Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has rejected an Israeli push to join the military campaign against Yemen’s Houthi group, despite efforts to secure Riyadh’s approval through US mediation.”
Anadolu Agency said it based this on a report in Haaretz. “Another source familiar with the matter said Israel hoped military cooperation with Saudi Arabia would strengthen bilateral ties and pave the way for a future normalization agreement,” the report said. “There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the report.”
Saudi Arabia needs Israeli aerial defense systems
Ynet noted on Sunday, in a piece by Ron Ben-Yishai, that “the Saudis urgently need early-warning radar systems and air defense batteries capable of countering different types of aerial threats, including Iron Dome, David’s Sling, and even Arrow 2 interceptors.”
“The Houthis are attacking Saudi Arabia with ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and explosive-laden drones, requiring a combination of defensive capabilities,” he added.
This analysis noted that “Trump sees a chance to revive Saudi-Israel normalization as the Houthis strike Riyadh; Israel is sharing intelligence, but Riyadh’s demand for Palestinian statehood talks and Israel’s need for its own defenses make a deal far from certain.”
It also added that Trump may see an “opportunity for greater Israeli assistance, potentially generating enough goodwill in Riyadh to persuade the Saudis to abandon their longstanding condition for normalization: negotiations with the Palestinians toward a two-state solution. For now, however, there is good reason to doubt that Trump’s comments signal a meaningful breakthrough in Israeli-Saudi relations.”
Walla noted that “security sources confirmed that as time goes by, the contribution of Israeli intelligence is increasing, with the Houthis in the background causing heavy damage to the Saudis throughout the country.”
The report goes on to say that “as first published in Walla, the IDF is assisting Saudi Arabia on the intelligence front in the fight against the Houthis in aspects of warning, target banking, and building a situational picture.”
“Israel sees this as a positive process that will intensify once the US decides how it will decide on the Iranian issue,” it said.
America, Walla said, is facing this dilemma: “If the US attacks Iran, the latter may attack the countries of the region, including Israel. If America continues with the economic sanctions (there is a slim chance of a political agreement without further conflict), this could also lead to escalation in the region.”
Houthis targeted shipping they claimed was linked to Israel after Oct. 7
The overall story now points to potential increased Israeli involvement and support. It’s worth noting that the Houthis began attacks on Israel soon after October 7. The Houthis began by attacking ships they claimed were linked to Israel.
The Iranian-backed group said that it was targeting Israeli ships and vessels linked to Israel, although many of the ships attacked had no direct Israeli ownership or operational connection.
One of the most prominent incidents occurred on November 19, 2023, when Houthi forces seized the Galaxy Leader, a vehicle carrier, in the Red Sea.
Armed men boarded the ship from a helicopter and diverted it to Yemen. A Japanese company operated the vessel and, through its ownership structure, was linked to Israeli businessman Abraham Ungar. None of its 25 crew members were Israeli nationals. They remained detained until January 2025, when the Houthis released them following the Gaza ceasefire agreement.
The seizure marked the beginning of a wider campaign against international shipping. The Houthis subsequently expanded their declared targets to include vessels traveling to Israeli ports and ships associated with American and British interests.
The Houthis also carried out ballistic missile attacks on Israel. Israel responded by striking dozens of Houthi targets in 2025. This shows that Israel has already launched a campaign against the Houthis. The US has also carried out a campaign.
Notably, Saudi Arabia has fought the Houthis since 2015. That means that all the players know the Houthi threat and capabilities. The Saudis have worked with Egypt, the UAE, and others in the past against the Houthis.
It appears that Riyadh will work again with Egypt and the UAE. Israel has ties with the UAE and Egypt via peace treaties. Israel also already works closely with the US Central Command.
Any cooperation against the Houthis can strengthen regional defense ties and infrastructure. This helps defend against Iranian-backed threats and Iran’s direct threats. For instance, when Iran carried out large missile attacks on Israel in 2024, many countries cooperated against the threat.

LIMOGES, France – Residents in Limoges recoiled in horror on Oct 18 at the city’s fire-ravaged town hall, an ornate 19th-century neo-Renaissance building that survived both world wars but was torched by a masked mob during the worst unrest to convulse France in years.
Stunned onlookers watched helplessly the previous evening as the blaze tore through the roof, felling the building’s clock tower in scenes that revived haunting memories of the collapse of the Notre Dame cathedral’s spire in a 2019 fire.
“It broke my heart. I saw Notre Dame all over again, except this time it was our town,” said Francoise Faurie, who witnessed the fire consume Limoges’ town hall.
Faurie’s family had been due to celebrate her granddaughter’s baptism at the town hall in a month.
“What kind of country are we living in? What are we leaving our children?” she said. “There’s no reason to touch that building. You can have demands, you have the right to protest, but not the right to violence.”
The local prefect, Maurice Barate, said the roof had caved in to the lower floors, sparing only the west wing and destroying large parts of the exterior.
The destruction of the building – a listed monument opened in 1883 and inspired by Paris’ city hall – was a “heritage catastrophe”, he said.
Its central clock tower and belfry towered 43m over the square below.
“It’s inadmissible to have burned down the town hall!” said one resident, Gilbert. “Those who did this need to be punished. They need to pay out of their own pocket; it’s not for the state to pay.”
The town’s shaken mayor, Guillaume Guerin, described how the local police force had quickly been overwhelmed by a several hundred-strong mob that he said smashed windows and used a battering ram to break down the main door.
“The logistics, the organisation, the premeditation behind the attack on the town hall is something I find unbearable,” he told reporters.
Guerin said there had been insufficient police numbers to protect the building since officers from the national force had been deployed to the street protest.
“I had no single national police officer to protect the town hall,” the centre-right mayor continued. “This country is doing badly. This country is doing very badly, and it’s a small provincial mayor telling you so.”
Crowds gathered under blue skies as specialists surveyed the damage.
Edith Lorcen, a retired nurse, expressed her shock at the malice of those behind the attack.
“I’m disgusted. I’m hurting,” Lorcen said. “But it does nothing to add hate on top of hate.” REUTERS

The government approved on Sunday the allocation of NIS 2.5 billion for "urgent defense procurement," to be funded through across-the-board cuts to government ministries’ budgets, less than two weeks before the October 27 elections.
The funds will be allocated through across-the-board cuts of 4.9 percent to government ministries’ budgets, rather than coalition funds.
The cuts will affect key ministries such as the education, health, welfare and social affairs ministries, the proposal shows. 
A legal opinion attached to the government proposal warned of the implications of the cuts to government ministries and noted the need for the government to exercise restraint in making decisions during the election period.
The legal opinion also raised concerns that approving the funds so close to the elections could create an irreversible situation for the incoming government and risk prioritizing party interests over the public interest.
However, the document also acknowledged the need for the defense procurement, stating that it was required urgently.
Reason for urgency classified, will be presented to the Ministerial Committee on Procurement
The reasons for the urgency of the classified procurement, as well as the details of the security needs, will be presented as part of the classified proposals submitted to the Ministerial Committee on Procurement, the document added.
The government's decision on the funds comes after an additional NIS 3.5 billion was approved on Wednesday for further urgent defense procurement, including a roughly NIS 1 billion deal to purchase Apache helicopters.
The Finance Ministry told The Jerusalem Post that close to NIS 1 billion used for the Apache helicopter purchase would be diverted from funds earmarked for a five-year plan to develop Israel’s Arab sector. The remaining NIS 68 million would come from the 2026 state budget.
Lapid criticizes decision to cut government ministries
Opposition leader Yair Lapid on Sunday sharply criticized the defense procurement being funded by making cuts to government ministries.
"Defense procurement is essential, but it can be funded without cutting money for the poor or for our children’s education," he stated.
"There are billions of shekels sitting in coalition funds. Instead of the money going to the corrupt, draft dodgers, and deserters, it could be used to buy Apache helicopters."
"The cuts to the welfare and education budgets are yet another crime by the government against the productive, serving public," Lapid added.
MK Oded Forer (Yisrael Beytenu) accused the government of prioritizing political interests ahead of the elections.
“The Israeli government continues, even in its final days, to put political interests above the public interest," he stated.
"It is cutting the budget for the rehabilitation of the North, as well as health and welfare services in the periphery."
“But there is always money for draft dodgers and yeshivas. Netanyahu and [Finance Minister Bezalel] Smotrich will not touch their funding."
“Instead of harming essential services for Israeli citizens, it is time to cut the coalition funds that finance draft evasion and buy political loyalty," Forer added.

World leaders must wise up to threat of cyber-attacks or rogue fridges will be least of their worries | Heather Stewart
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:46:50 UTC
20:46:50 KST

Rogue French fridges were an unlikely talking point for the world’s leading economists, central bankers and finance chiefs meeting in a sultry Bangkok last week – helping to underline the spiralling cost of cyber-attacks.
Kristalina Georgieva, the managing director of the International Monetary Fund, seized on news that supermarket chains across France had to chuck out piles of spoiled food after hackers accessed their fridge controls and turned up the temperature to 50C.
Speaking at the fund’s annual meetings in the Thai capital, she was keen to hammer home the importance of guarding against “bad actors” in a rapidly changing, interconnected world – especially now that AI was “putting the potential of digital fraud on steroids”.
Policymakers have been warning for some time that the AI boom could at some point threaten financial stability via a share price crash – a “correction”, as it is euphemistically called.
But a different, related threat came into sharp focus in Bangkok. Georgieva said she was concerned that cybercrime, turbocharged by AI, could undermine trust in the financial system altogether.
Social media feeds are rife with adverts using celebrity fakes to punt cryptocurrencies or gold, and even the old-school email-style scams can be generated far more prolifically.
Just as a sea of AI slop has the potential to undermine trust in fact-based reporting and send people down political rabbit holes, Georgieva fretted that cyber-fraud could knock consumer confidence in mainstream banks.
Recalling her own childhood behind the iron curtain in Bulgaria, she said many people did not trust the system, and kept their cash in a shoebox under the bed. “I worry, today, that unless we figure out how to get ahead of this curve … we may end up with lots of people with shoeboxes under their beds,” she said.
It might not even take a cybercrime wave. This week the JP Morgan chief executive, Jamie Dimon, warned that the bank would not allow digital agents to operate on its customers’ behalf. “You don’t want rogue agents, and there could be thousands of them,” he said.
AI agents, including Meta’s Muse, are starting to offer their users the opportunity to hand over their financial details. The agents will then scout for the highest savings rates and shift the user’s money accordingly.
Financial regulators fret about this for a number of reasons. One is that if such services become widely used, they could have destabilising herding effects. With deposits able to be moved around the financial system at a moment’s notice, it could accelerate a bank run in times of uncertainty.
A second worry is that highlighted by Dimon: who is responsible if your AI agent makes a financial decision on your behalf that turns out to be disastrous – or even criminal?
The answer is probably that we will need case law to find out, which will only come when something goes badly awry.
That is alarming because legal ambiguity about who owes what to whom when things go wrong can be an accelerant to financial instability.
We learned that lesson back in the 2008 financial crisis, when it turned out that some banks had built financial products with such fiendishly complex liability structures that they were effectively impossible to value – unleashing panic.
Speaking alongside Georgieva, the Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, who chairs the Financial Stability Board of global central bankers, pointed to another arresting news story from this week – that Anthropic had warned AI models might soon be able to “self-replicate” in domestic devices. Who should bear the responsibility – and the costs – if your internet-enabled oven, or telly, blows up as a result?
One entirely prudent response might be for consumers to reject internet-enabled devices and stick to “dumb” appliances instead that can’t be hijacked by self-replicating bots. This month, some of those French supermarkets rushed to take their fridges offline to avoid the hack.
While it may not be much of a loss to society if internet-enabled kettles and fridges do not take off, the financial analogue to a dumb appliance would be Georgieva’s shoeboxes – and that would have costs for those consumers, and the smooth running of the economy as a whole.
As Bailey somewhat apocalyptically put it: “If we don’t have trust in money, we don’t operate as a society.”
Senior financial policymakers are genuinely disturbed at the collision between rapidly developing AI and the global financial system – which now extends well beyond heavily regulated banks – to embrace social media platforms, payments apps and other financial tools.
It is unfortunate this moment comes as the US – the crucible of the AI boom – is governed by a man whose main contribution to the debate has been to seek to rename AI “superintelligence”.
At the Bangkok meetings this week, Kevin Warsh, the chair of the US Federal Reserve, obediently used Donald Trump’s phrase on stage – as all US government agencies have been ordered to.
There has been some progress in acknowledging the risks. Trump’s superintelligence taskforce, chaired by the director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, is setting up mechanisms for AI labs to report “breaches, hacks, jailbreaks, and other issues” – although not, it seems, to submit their models for pre-launch testing.
The UK has pledged to take up the issue of AI safety as part of its agenda for the G20 presidency next year, and G7 finance ministers announced in Bangkok that they would carry out simulations to test the resilience of the global financial system to cyber-attacks.
That could help to highlight vulnerabilities, but the questions at stake are much wider and more complex than whether criminals can hack the banks – and are urgent now, just as the prospects for international cooperation seem bleak. Superintelligence will seem anything but super if its misuse becomes a trigger for financial chaos.

Ukraine Strikes Deep Into St. Petersburg, Setting Major Russian Oil Export Terminal on Fire
Ukrainian long-range drones struck one of Russia’s major oil export terminals in St. Petersburg overnight on October 18, igniting a fire at the facility as a large-scale drone attack targeted energy infrastructure across the city and surrounding Leningrad region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukrainian drone manufacturer Fire Point on October 18, its FP-1 long-range attack drones were used to strike the Petersburg Oil Terminal, a major petroleum export facility on Russia’s Baltic coast. St. Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov confirmed that the terminal had been hit, with a fire breaking out in its oil storage area.
The Petersburg Oil Terminal is one of the region’s largest facilities for receiving, storing, and exporting petroleum products, with an annual handling capacity of approximately 12.5 million tons.
The complex contains 32 storage tanks with a combined capacity of approximately 442,000 cubic meters, making it an important component of Russia’s petroleum logistics and export infrastructure.
Footage published by the Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ showed flames and smoke rising from the facility following the overnight strike. Reports indicated that the fire was still burning at approximately 7:30 a.m. local time.
The extent of the damage to the terminal’s storage infrastructure and its potential impact on petroleum exports have not yet been independently established.
The Petersburg Oil Terminal was not the only infrastructure facility targeted during the overnight attacks. Drones also struck a data center operated by VKontakte, Russia’s largest domestic social networking platform, near St. Petersburg.
The attack coincided with disruptions to VKontakte services and electricity outages in parts of the city and surrounding Leningrad region. The nearby 330-kilovolt Vostochnaya electrical substation was also targeted.

Drone Strike Hits Russia’s VKontakte Data Center, Knocking Services Offline as St. Petersburg Faces Blackouts
Russia’s digital infrastructure came under fire as an overnight drone attack reportedly hit a major VKontakte data center, exposing the vulnerability of the servers and power networks supporting one of the country’s most widely used online platforms.
A major overnight drone attack struck a data center belonging to Russia’s largest social network, VKontakte (VK), near St. Petersburg on October 18, disrupting digital services and coinciding with widespread power outages across parts of the city and surrounding Leningrad region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The attack targeted VKontakte’s data infrastructure alongside several other facilities in the region, including a major electrical substation and an oil terminal. Russian users subsequently reported significant disruptions to the social network and related online services.
The targeted data center is located in Novosergievka, in the Vsevolozhsky district of Russia’s Leningrad region, just outside St. Petersburg. The facility contains four server halls, approximately 640 server racks, and more than 20,000 servers, making it a significant component of VKontakte’s digital infrastructure.
The complex is located next to the 330-kilovolt Vostochnaya electrical substation, which was also reportedly struck during the attack.
Following the overnight strikes, parts of St. Petersburg and the surrounding Leningrad region experienced electricity outages, raising questions about the extent of the damage to the area’s power infrastructure.
At the same time, users across Russia began reporting problems accessing VKontakte and associated services. According to data from the Russian outage-monitoring platform Sboy.RF, complaints about VKontakte increased sharply between 3:00 a.m. and 5:00 a.m. local time on October 18.
The exact scale of the disruption remains unclear, and it has not been independently established whether the reported outages resulted from direct damage to the data center, interruptions to its electricity supply, or other technical failures.
VKontakte is Russia’s largest domestic social networking platform and a central part of the country’s digital ecosystem, serving tens of millions of users. Its parent company, VK, also operates a range of digital products, cloud services, and online platforms.
The reported attack on VKontakte’s infrastructure was part of a broader overnight wave of drone strikes around St. Petersburg. St. Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov confirmed that the Petersburg Oil Terminal had been hit, with a fire breaking out in its oil storage area.
The terminal is a major facility for handling and storing petroleum products, with 32 storage tanks and a combined capacity of approximately 442,000 cubic meters.
The reported strike follows earlier attacks on three Yandex data centers in Russia between October 8 and 11. According to Ukraine’s Center for Countering Disinformation, activity among suspected Russian disinformation accounts dropped by nearly 84% following the first strike, highlighting the potential impact of data center disruptions on Moscow’s online influence operations.

“A Kazan-Mumbai connection is worth exploring, provided a detailed assessment confirms sustainable passenger demand, commercial viability and the necessary regulatory clearances. With the right cooperation between governments, airlines and the tourism industry, such initiatives could create meaningful benefits for both sides,” Synghal said.
Asked about India’s efforts to diversify trade in response to tariff pressure from key trading partners, Synghal said diversification was “a strategic necessity for India,” adding that “our objective should not be to replace one market with another, but to build a broader, more balanced and sustainable network of international trade partnerships.” He said he sees potential in tourism, civil aviation, pharmaceuticals, agriculture and food processing, information technology, engineering, and transport and logistics.
Synghal emphasized that Russia’s regions offer major opportunities beyond the country’s main commercial centers. “For Indian businesses, the priority is to develop a deeper understanding of regional demand and local regulations, identify reliable partners, and establish commercially viable, long-term projects,” he said.
Trade between India and Russia reached $38 billion in the first half of this year and remains on course toward the annual target of $100 billion by 2030 set by the leaders of the two countries, Indian Ambassador to Russia Vinay Kumar told the media on the sidelines of the forum. “We think we are on the right path to achieve the target,” Kumar said, explaining that further focus areas would include boosting Indian pharmaceutical exports to Russia and expanding opportunities for India’s skilled workers, who are increasingly being hired by Russian companies.

Pope Leo to gradually resume papal activities since removal of cancerous tumour
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:40:25 UTC
20:40:25 KST

Pope Leo told a crowd gathered in St Peter’s Square on Sunday that he would “gradually resume” his activities, at his first appearance before the faithful since undergoing an operation to remove a cancerous tumour from his lung.
The Catholic leader, 71, was greeted with applause as he appeared unaided at the window of the Vatican’s Apostolic Palace to deliver his Sunday angelus. It was his first public appearance since making the shock announcement at the previous Sunday’s address that a small nodule had been found on his lung.
Leo was diagnosed with the most common kind of lung cancer – adenocarcinoma – on Tuesday, after doctors removed part of his right lung to extract the tumour.
He thanked those who had prayed for him in recent days, saying that he appreciated the support while adding that the experience had made him feel especially close “to all those who are going through illness or a state of infirmity”.
“Now that this delicate phase has passed … I will gradually resume my activities, always with the help of God and your prayers,” he said.
Leo left Gemelli hospital in Rome on Saturday, where doctors deemed him “fit for discharge” after undergoing blood tests and a chest X-ray that morning.
Doctors said on Wednesday that Leo’s recovery from the operation was progressing normally. They said they were waiting for the results of tests to determine whether the cancer had spread and if more treatment would be needed.
The Vatican had originally estimated a week-long stay in hospital.
The pope undertook some work duties in hospital, including making a phone call on Friday to Vladimir Putin, during which he urged the Russian president to call a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky.
There have been questions over whether Leo would be able to manage a gruelling 12-day trip to South America in November. However, his surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, said on Saturday that there were “no clinical reasons” to prevent him from travelling.
“The Holy Father has put his heart and soul into his recovery,” Margaritora told Vatican News, adding that he expected the pope to fully recover from the operation “in another 10 days or so”.
Before the cancer diagnosis, Leo, who enjoys sports, especially tennis, was generally believed to be in good health. He often makes use of the papal retreat in Castel Gandolfo, close to Rome.
The Gemelli, located in the north-west of the Italian capital, is renowned for treating reigning popes. Pope John Paul II stayed there so many times that the Vatican worked with the hospital to establish a high-security papal suite.

Swiss railways records fourfold rise in heat-related track warping
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:35:41 UTC
20:35:41 KST

Swiss railways records fourfold rise in heat-related track warping
Due to the summer heatwave, Swiss Federal Railways (SBB) has recorded nearly 100 cases of track warping and compression deformation. In response to the exceptional heat of summer 2026, the company set up a working group.
When asked about this, SBB confirmed the figure of 97 cases of warping and compression-induced deformation reported in the SonntagsZeitung. According to the newspaper, this figure is nearly four times higher than that of the previous year.
The railway company emphasised that the increase in the number of deformations or settlement had no impact on safety. Patrick Braess, an expert from the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology ETH Zurich, however, warned in the newspaper of the risk of heat-related derailments.
+ Extreme heat impacts train travel in Switzerland
SBB regularly inspects its tracks using measurement and diagnostic vehicles. Given last summer’s exceptional heat, SBB set up a working group tasked with identifying additional measures where necessary. But there is no such thing as zero risk.
SBB is focusing above all on targeted and effective long-term measures. These include, in particular, the use of concrete sleepers, which offer greater stability than wooden sleepers, as well as increasing the neutralisation temperature during welding, so that the rails can better withstand the generally higher temperatures.
White paint – a solution?
SBB has tested white paint as a measure against heat. The cooling effect was initially around 4.5 degrees on average. After two years, this effect had diminished to around half due to soiling, reported SBB. The heavier the traffic, the more rapidly the effect diminishes.
However, as part of an ongoing analysis, the SBB is examining whether white coatings could be a suitable measure in certain specific cases.

Egyptian parliament begins emergency session on possible troop deployment to defend Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
