'Jews see us as Arabs, and some Arabs see us as traitors': SLA family's daughter becomes student leader
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:12:41 UTC
20:12:41 KST

In the living room of the Joubran family home in Nahariya stands a display cabinet filled with figurines of Christian saints, photographs of bearded Maronite clergymen, a depiction of the Last Supper and a Lebanese flag. Among these objects, which reflect the family's faith and origins, lies something you might not expect to find there: a booklet of teachings by Rabbi Nachman of Breslov.
But perhaps that should not be surprising. The family of George Joubran, a former artillery officer in the South Lebanon Army (SLA), navigates several identities. They are Lebanese, but also Israeli Christians who attend church while remaining deeply rooted in Jewish society.
Sometimes, those identities clash. "Jews see us as Arabs, and some Arabs see us as traitors," explains Sonia Joubran, 24, the eldest daughter of Adeline and George, who was elected chair of the student union at Kiryat Shmona University about three months ago.
Like her younger sisters, Lia, 22, and Joelle, 20, Sonia was born in Israel and has never visited her family's homeland. Yet she is convinced that peace is within reach.
"Most Lebanese want peace, and I believe that within a year I'll be able to visit. And who knows, maybe one day I'll be Israel's ambassador to Lebanon," Sonia told ynet.
We met Sonia and her mother ahead of the start of the academic year at Israel's northernmost, and newest, university.
George, 58, owns a company that brings workers from Jordan to Israel. He spends most of his time in Eilat and returns home every two weeks. He grew up in the village of Mazraat al-Mathaneh, near the Christian town of Jezzine. The Jezzine enclave was not part of Israel's security zone in southern Lebanon, but it was controlled by an SLA battalion that cooperated with Israel and fought Hezbollah.
Adeline, 48, a medical secretary at the Galilee Medical Center in Nahariya, grew up in Beirut. When she was 12, she moved with her family to the village of Burj al-Muluk (al-Khirbeh), along the road between Marjayoun and Metula. Her father worked as a cook, preparing meals for IDF and SLA soldiers, which made him, in Hezbollah's eyes, a collaborator with Israel.
'We thought we'd be back in two weeks. We've been here 26 years'
Adeline remembers May 24, 2000, the day the IDF withdrew from Lebanon, as though it were yesterday.
"I was 21, a psychology student and a teacher at a school in the village of Houla," she recalls. "In the middle of class, the principal came into the room and said, 'What are you doing here? Get out now! Hezbollah has entered the village.'
"I started fleeing on foot. My father picked me up along the way, and when we got home, he said, 'We're leaving for Israel.' I said, 'What do you mean, leaving? I have an exam at university.' And my father said, 'Forget the exam. We're leaving.' Hezbollah had threatened that the moment the IDF withdrew, they would enter our homes and slaughter us in our beds."
Just four kilometers separate Burj al-Muluk from the border crossing at Metula. "We waited there for seven or eight hours before they let us enter. We thought we'd be back home within two weeks, a month at most. And here we are, 26 years later."
Adeline met George at Kibbutz Shomrat, where she lived with her parents. Their eldest daughter was born in Nahariya, and when she was a baby, the family moved to Eilat. They returned north when Sonia was 4.
"There's an SLA community in Nahariya, and it was easier to adjust here. In Eilat, my kindergarten teacher didn't know how to deal with me because I didn't speak Hebrew," Sonia recalls. "Here, I learned the language, and my mother learned alongside me."
At elementary school, however, she once again felt like an outsider. "I was subjected to a kind of social boycott. I was the only SLA child in the class, and the other children didn't know what that meant. There was a Druze boy in my class, and they would always push us toward each other and shout, 'Arabs!' at us. Instead of dealing with it, the principal would remove both of us from the classroom."
In high school, Sonia studied Arabic in an intelligence-track program whose graduates are intended for IDF Unit 8200. "I also attended an 8200 preparatory program, but in the end I didn't enlist and received an exemption because I was the daughter of an SLA veteran.
"I have family in Lebanon, my paternal grandmother in Jezzine and an aunt on my mother's side in Beirut, and I was afraid that if Hezbollah discovered I had joined the IDF, they would harm them. Instead, I did national service at the hospital in Nahariya as a medical assistant," she said.
'They crossed out Israel and wrote Palestine instead'
After completing her national service, Sonia was accepted to study medicine at New Vision University in Tbilisi, Georgia, alongside students from around the world. She enjoyed her studies and made friends, but on the morning of October 7, 2023, during the second semester of her first year, everything changed.
"I found out about October 7 from an Instagram Story posted by an Arab Israeli student who uploaded videos of Hamas terrorists inside Israel and mockingly wrote, 'They're playing PUBG with them.' That's a game about shooting and killing. I'm not saying everyone is like that. There are extremists on every side."
The atmosphere on campus suddenly became hostile. "They turned the library into a mosque. There was a map of the world's countries at the university, and suddenly I saw that someone had put an X over Israel and written 'Palestine' instead.
"No matter how hard I tried to explain that our people had been massacred and murdered, they didn't understand. I had friends who were murdered, and I have friends who survived the Nova festival. It was difficult. I decided to stop studying and return to Israel," Sonia said.
Wanting to continue in a field involving care and treatment, she decided to enroll in psychology studies at Tel-Hai College, shortly before it became Tel-Hai Kiryat Shmona University.
Alongside her studies, she volunteered with the Rashi Foundation's Ma'aleh initiative, supporting the Ma'alot-Tarshiha municipality and helping develop strategic plans and programs for young people. She was also active in the Rothschild Foundation Ambassadors program, which trains young social leaders. Becoming involved in student leadership was therefore a natural next step.
Elections for the Kiryat Shmona University student union were held in June. "I decided to run at the very last minute and registered just a few hours before the deadline. I was stunned when I was elected because I hadn't run a major campaign, and I'm not Jewish," Sonia explains.
As chair of the student union at Tel-Hai Kiryat Shmona University, Sonia also serves on the general assembly of the National Union of Israeli Students.
Although she entered the race at the last minute, she has a clear vision. "It's important to me to work toward the rehabilitation, development and strengthening of communities in the Upper Galilee, especially Kiryat Shmona, after three difficult years of war. Twenty percent of our students are Arabs, Druze and Circassians, and it's important to me that minority populations feel part of the community and contribute to it.
"We met with Mayor Avichai Stern, and we're advancing social initiatives that will turn Kiryat Shmona into a vibrant city where young people choose to live."
One of the most significant days for Sonia in the past three years was September 27, 2024, when Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah was killed.
"We were so happy. We opened champagne and put up a sign downstairs for all our religious neighbors announcing that Nasrallah had been killed, because it was Shabbat. It was a moment of closure for my parents and the entire SLA community. But there's still a lot of work to be done to rid Lebanon of terrorist strongholds."
So far, Sonia has met her relatives from Lebanon mainly at the home of her uncle, who lives in Canada, or in nearby countries such as Jordan. But she believes that one day, and not in the distant future, visiting her aunt in Beirut will require nothing more than a 90-minute drive.

The Cabinet of Ministers has established a commission to sell the state-owned stakes in Sense Bank and Ukrgasbank - Koretskyi

20:11:58 KST

The Cabinet of Ministers has established a commission to sell the state-owned stakes in Sense Bank and Ukrgasbank - Koretskyi
Kyiv • UNN
The commission will determine the terms of the tenders, the starting price, and the winners of the sale of shares in Sense Bank and Ukrgasbank. International partners may join the work.
The Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine established a commission for the sale of the state-owned shares in Sense Bank and Ukrgasbank. Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi reported this, according to UNN.
Details
He noted that this commission would determine the procedure for holding the tenders, decide on the admission of participants, approve the starting auction price, taking into account the adviser’s recommendations, determine the winners and the sale price, and submit the relevant decisions for approval by the Government.
Representatives of international financial organizations and EU institutions may join its work. The task is to create the proper conditions for the transparent and competitive sale of the state-owned shares in both banks
Context
The National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office released a video with more complete audio recordings and details of the case as part of a special operation dubbed "Forrest Gump" aimed at exposing a criminal organization. Among those involved in the case are current and former MPs and senior officials of the Office of the President.
The SAPO stated that, according to the investigation, the purpose of creating and operating the said criminal organization was to seize real estate and other assets of legal entities by unauthorized interference in the operation of information (automated) networks of the Ministry of Justice of Ukraine, falsifying court rulings, title documents, and more.
Later, the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine decided to suspend Mykola Hladyshenko, Chairman of the Supervisory Board of JSC Sense Bank, from exercising his powers.
To remind you
The High Anti-Corruption Court ordered a preventive measure in the form of a UAH 15 million bail for Oleksii Stupak, Chairman of the Management Board of state-owned Sense Bank.

What help can Egypt offer Saudi Arabia in the war against the Houthis?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:11:26 UTC
20:11:26 KST

What help can Egypt offer Saudi Arabia in the war against the Houthis?
Analysts say that any move from Egypt will remain ‘strictly defensive’, as the conflict in Yemen intensifies.
Egypt’s parliament is convening on Sunday after President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi requested an emergency session to approve defensive military aid to Saudi Arabia, if Riyadh asks for support in its war with Yemen’s Houthis.
The request comes as the Iran-backed armed group continues attacks on Saudi Arabia, including the capital, Riyadh, and its airports and oil facilities.
El-Sisi declared that Egypt will “carry out any measure to protect” Saudi Arabia, in a speech on Saturday, but said that he “hopes” the parliament will give him authorisation to proceed.
On Sunday, Egypt said it would provide “all necessary and possible support to Saudi Arabia to defend its safety and stability”. The National Defence Council, chaired by President el-Sisi, said it “stands fully with” Saudi Arabia to defend its resources, territorial integrity and Islamic holy sites.
But what would Egyptian assistance look like? And what capacity does it have to “protect” Saudi Arabia in its war with the Houthis?
Here is what we know.
What’s behind el-Sisi’s decision to offer help to Saudi Arabia?
Saudi Arabia has long been a strategic and economic partner of Egypt, and el-Sisi said in a statement last month that Saudi security is “integral” to Egypt’s security.
Political analyst and Gulf studies expert Thomas Bonnie James told Al Jazeera that the Houthi security threat to the kingdom is one of the “converging” pressures that have led to this decision. The other one, is economics.
“Houthi pressure on [Bab] al-Mandeb threatens the Suez Canal, which Egypt’s foreign minister says has lost about $11bn since the attacks began in 2023,” he said, referring to Houthi attacks on Israeli-linked ships passing through the narrow strait, carried out in solidarity with Gaza.
James suggested that the decision is also important to Cairo, because “millions of Egyptians live and work in Saudi Arabia, which is Egypt’s largest single source of remittances. An Egyptian resident was killed, and others were injured in the attacks on Riyadh’s airport.”
He also said that Egypt does not want to be seen as the regional ally that “stood aside while others defended the kingdom,” as Turkiye and Pakistan have made their own pledges after activating the Mecca defence pact signed in August amid the deteriorating security situation in the Middle East.
What’s the latest on the Yemen war?
Hostilities in Yemen continue to escalate. Two air raids by the Saudi-led coalition hit Hodeidah in the southwest on Sunday.
Saudi forces also intercepted drones near Riyadh and Eastern provinces. The capital’s King Khalid international airport has come under attack at least 20 times since fighting flared between the internationally recognised government and the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah – Arabic for Supporters of God.
The Saudi-backed forces are fighting the Houthis on several fronts, including Taiz and Marib, and some analysts argue the Houthis are stretched thin after their summer gains.
But James told Al Jazeera “that defeating them outright is a tall order”.
“Ground forces backed by air power can retake the coastline; stopping missiles launched from the mountains is much harder,” he said.
When will the Egyptian parliament convene?
They will be convening on Sunday at 1pm local time (10am GMT).
Under the Egyptian law, the President cannot declare war or send the military on foreign missions without the approval from the parliament.
For the authorisation to be granted, at least two-thirds of the politicians in the House of Representatives must vote in favour of the proposal.
Does Egypt have security cooperation with Saudi Arabia?
Not exactly. Egypt and Saudi Arabia have not signed a formal bilateral or multilateral pact on defence cooperation. But Cairo has a long history of cooperation with Riyadh.
Egypt is a founding member of the Multinational Maritime Defense Coalition, which Saudi Arabia launched in July. It aims to protect shipping in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb – territories on Yemen’s coastline. Houthis captured towns and cities near Bab al-Mandeb last month, but the internationally recognised government has since wrested control of some of the areas from the Iran-backed group.
Egypt also participated in joint military exercises with Saudi Arabia in 2024.
Cairo was also part of a 2015 coalition, cobled together after the Houthi group captured large areas of north and western Yemen, including the capital Sanaa in September 2024. Egypt contributed naval and air forces to help secure maritime corridors in the Red Sea against the Houthis.
But James, the Gulf studies expert, told Al Jazeera that what el-Sisi is proposing is different from the maritime defence coalition Egypt recently joined.
“He is hoping for authorisation to deploy Egyptian forces to help defend Saudi territory itself,” he said. “It would move Egypt from a multilateral maritime framework to a bilateral military commitment.”
What will be the nature of Egyptian assistance to Saudi Arabia?
El-Sisi explicitly said that he is only proposing “defence” and that he isn’t “speaking in order for us to fight anyone or attack anyone”.
Military Defence Analyst Alexandru Hudisteanu said that the use of counter-drones and anti-missile support is a high probability if the decision is authorised.
“It would be the most urgent need at this point to make sure that the defence of Saudi Arabia is backed up and reinforced,” he told Al Jazeera.
Simultaneously, he added that the request itself is also a strategic move of deterrence.
“We know Saudi Arabia has one of the most prolific militaries out there in terms of capacities and capabilities. It’s a matter of the territory which Saudi Arabia needs to cover at any given moment,” Hudisteanu said.
James said that any contribution by Egypt would focus on the protection of Saudi territory, using “air and missile defence around critical infrastructure, intercepting drones, naval escort and intelligence sharing”.
James said that it is unlikely Egypt will deploy troops to Yemen’s front lines.
In the 1960s, former Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser deployed tens of thousands of troops in the Yemen Civil War. Saudi Arabia backed the rival side. Egypt suffered heavy casualties and Saudi-Egyptian ties were strained.
“What Egypt will not want is to send troops into Yemen. Nasser’s intervention there in the 1960s sends a clear message: defend the kingdom, don’t take ownership of Yemen,” he told Al Jazeera.

Ebola outbreak spreads to 8th province in DR Congo
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
19:11:14 CST
20:11:14 KST

KINSHASA, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- The ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has spread to an eighth province, with new cases confirmed in Nord-Ubangi Province in the north, according to the latest health ministry report released Sunday.
Two men in their 20s were reported infected in the Wapinda health zone, one of whom has died. The report did not specify the source of infection.
As of Friday, the country had recorded 9,415 confirmed cases, including 4,536 deaths, since the outbreak began in May, representing a case fatality rate of 48.2 percent.
The eastern province of Ituri remains the epicenter, accounting for more than 73 percent of all confirmed cases nationwide, followed by neighboring North Kivu Province. The outbreak has now affected 66 health zones across eight provinces.
The Ebola outbreak declared in May has become the largest and deadliest ever recorded in the DRC and the second-largest Ebola outbreak globally, after the 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic. ■

Researchers for 1st time observe solar-storm-like eruptions near black hole
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
19:10:56 CST
20:10:56 KST

JERUSALEM, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- An international team of researchers has discovered eruptions similar to solar storms near a giant black hole, the Israel Institute of Technology (Technion) said Sunday.
Published in the Astrophysical Journal Letters, the study provides the first evidence that the physical processes driving solar storms can also occur near supermassive black holes.
Solar storms occur when energy stored in magnetic fields is suddenly released, producing bursts of radiation and streams of charged particles that can disrupt satellites and communications on Earth.
The researchers analyzed X-ray emissions from the region around a black hole in the galaxy NGC 3783, using the XRISM and XMM-Newton space telescopes to track changes in radiation.
They identified a pattern known as the "Neupert effect," first discovered on the Sun in 1968 but never previously observed near a black hole.
The discovery suggests that powerful magnetic eruptions may occur across vastly different cosmic environments, from the Sun to black holes millions of times more massive, the researchers say. ■

China, Uzbekistan seek tangible gains from expanding cooperation during premier's visit
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
19:10:55 CST
20:10:55 KST

TASHKENT, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- During a productive day of high-level exchanges in Tashkent on Saturday, China and Uzbekistan pledged to deepen practical cooperation, from expanding trade and connectivity to exploring emerging fields such as artificial intelligence and the green economy.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang arrived in the Central Asian nation on Saturday for a two-day official visit, where he highlighted China's readiness to enhance bilateral practical cooperation and deepen the building of the China-Uzbekistan community with a shared future to deliver greater benefits to the people of both countries.
During his meeting with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, Li said China is ready to work with Uzbekistan to expand bilateral trade and optimize its structure.
China supports more capable Chinese enterprises in investing and doing business in Uzbekistan, he said, calling for continued provision of a favorable business environment for these enterprises.
China is also willing to import more high-quality and specialty products from Uzbekistan, and welcomes Uzbekistan to make full use of platforms such as the China International Import Expo to actively explore the Chinese market, he told Uzbek Prime Minister Abdulla Aripov in their talks.
China has been a major trading partner of Uzbekistan and its main source of imports. Two-way trade reached 16.1 billion U.S. dollars in 2025, marking a 17.9 percent increase year over year, Chinese official data showed.
In the first eight months of this year, China accounted for the largest share of Uzbekistan's foreign trade turnover, at 23 percent, according to the Uzbek official tally. More than 6,000 joint ventures involving Chinese participation are operating in Uzbekistan.
Building on a decade of flourishing cooperation under the China-Uzbekistan comprehensive strategic partnership, the two countries are exploring broader avenues for cooperation to inject fresh vitality into a golden age of bilateral ties.
In Tashkent, Li and Aripov jointly watched a video showcasing practical cooperation between China and Uzbekistan across various fields.
They also witnessed the signing of multiple cooperation documents covering trade and economy, education, customs, health and poverty reduction, among others. During the visit, the two sides also signed cooperation documents on such areas as e-commerce and climate.
In his diplomatic engagement with the Uzbek side, Li vowed China's readiness to strengthen the alignment of development strategies with Uzbekistan and further leverage the complementary strengths of the two economies.
China is ready to work with Uzbekistan to deepen cooperation in scientific and technological innovation in fields such as artificial intelligence, the green economy, and aerospace, so as to jointly seize future development opportunities, he said.
Eldor Tulyakov, executive director of the Development Strategy Center of Uzbekistan, told Xinhua that as bilateral engagement enters a broader and deeper stage, cooperation with China has worked to advance the Central Asian country's national development goals.
"Political trust creates favorable conditions, and practical work gives it substance," he said, highlighting tangible economic gains from electric vehicle manufacturing to green energy.
In recent years, Chinese-built solar plants and wind farms have been supplying electricity to grids across several regions in Uzbekistan, powering the country's green transition while bolstering its equipment manufacturing capabilities.
New projects are adding further momentum to this transition.
In August, a China-supported wind power project was completed in the Tashkent region's Bostanlyk district. Upon full operation, it is expected to save roughly 12 million cubic meters of natural gas, and cut carbon dioxide emissions by about 24,000 tons per year.
The Chinese premier and the Uzbek leaders also highlighted collaborations on regional connectivity initiatives, including the high-level construction of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, among other projects of Belt and Road cooperation.
Not long ago, Chinese President Xi Jinping called for efforts to ensure the high-quality construction of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, during his stay in Bishkek for a state visit to Kyrgyzstan and to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Summit 2026.
Xi described the railway as a major transportation artery that carries the development aspirations of the people across the region.
Officially launched in December 2024, the railway project, which is now under construction, is a manifestation of the practical side of multilateral collaboration for China and Central Asia.
The railway "links the interests of several countries around a common project," said Tulyakov, adding that it is expected to spur the development of trade and logistics infrastructure along the mainline and promote the use of digital solutions in trade and transport procedures.
"The tangible results of cooperation are most visible where enterprises are already operating, infrastructure has been built, and new professions have emerged," the expert added. ■

Russian drones hit western Ukraine as nationwide attacks kill 10, injure 73
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:10:49 UTC
20:10:49 KST

Russian attacks across Ukraine killed at least 10 civilians and injured 73 others over the past day, regional authorities reported on Oct. 18.
Russia launched an Iskander-M ballistic missile, 180 Shahed drones, including 26 jet-powered Shaheds, as well as S-8000 and Banderol loitering munitions, also known as Dan-T, and Gerbera and Parodiya decoy drones, Ukraine's Air Force reported.
Ukrainian forces intercepted 152 drones, including 16 jet-powered drones. Russian strikes hit 20 locations, while falling debris was reported at four other sites.
Three western Ukrainian oblasts came under Russian attack on the morning of Oct. 18, continuing Moscow's recent pattern of targeting critical infrastructure across multiple regions.
In Volyn Oblast, in northwestern Ukraine, Russian drones attacked an industrial facility in the town of Manevychi, sparking a large fire, acting regional Governor Roman Romaniuk said.
Warehouses and production facilities caught fire, with the blaze covering a large area and generating heavy smoke. No casualties or injuries had been reported as of the latest update.
The attack marked the second strike on an industrial facility in Manevychi in three days. An earlier Russian attack on the Agrofrukt LTD facility on Oct. 16 killed one person and injured eight others, Manevychi Mayor Oleksandr Havryliuk said.
In western Ternopil Oblast, Russian drones attacked an energy infrastructure facility near the settlement of Staryi Vyshnivets, Governor Taras Pastukh said. The strike left some consumers without electricity. No casualties had been reported at the time of his statement.
Russian forces also launched a large-scale drone attack on Rivne, in northwestern Ukraine, targeting civilian infrastructure, regional Governor Oleksandr Koval said. The strikes sparked fires at the impact sites. No casualties had been reported as of the latest update.
In Odesa, Russian forces struck the roof of a multistory residential building on the morning of Oct. 18, injuring two people, including a 14-year-old girl, regional Governor Oleh Kiper said.
In Donetsk Oblast, Russian attacks killed seven people and injured 14 others, Governor Vadym Filashkin said. Most of the casualties were reported in Sloviansk, where multiple houses were damaged.
Russian attacks in Kherson Oblast injured 32 people, including one child, regional Governor Oleksandr Prokudin said. Russian forces targeted critical infrastructure, social infrastructure, and residential areas across the region.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Russian attacks killed one person and injured four others, regional Governor Ivan Fedorov said. Russian forces launched 10 missiles at the city of Zaporizhzhia. Over the past 24 hours, they carried out 808 strikes on 53 settlements across the region.
In Sumy Oblast, Russian attacks killed two people and injured five over the past 24 hours, according to the regional military administration. Russian forces carried out nearly 50 attacks across the region, damaging or destroying civilian infrastructure.
In Kharkiv Oblast, 12 people were injured in Russian attacks, regional Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. Russian forces struck Kharkiv and nine other settlements using ballistic missiles, drones, glide bombs, known as KABs, and a multiple-launch rocket system.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, three people were injured in Russian attacks, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said. Russian forces attacked three districts more than 10 times using drones and artillery.
Russian forces again targeted critical infrastructure in the city of Dnipro on the morning of Oct. 18. Information about possible casualties was still being clarified, Hanzha said.
In Chernihiv Oblast, one person was injured when a Russian Geran drone struck a residential yard, regional Governor Viacheslav Chaus said.

Study explores airborne DNA to help solve burglaries
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
19:10:48 CST
20:10:48 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Forensic scientists are exploring environmental DNA (eDNA), including airborne traces left by intruders in residential burglaries, as a new tool to help solve criminal cases lacking biological evidence.
The study, led by Oslo University Hospital in Norway with collaborators at Flinders University in Australia, evaluated the possibility of finding viable evidence from 391 eDNA samples collected from air, dust and surfaces during simulated 15-minute residential burglaries, according to a statement released recently by Flinders University.
The research found evidence of human intruder eDNA from air samples collected under controlled conditions, although recovery varied depending on factors including air temperatures, humidity, dust and existing household DNA.
Researchers said the brief nature of burglaries, offenders' efforts to avoid detection and the difficulty of identifying where DNA traces were deposited may result in limited or absent biological evidence.
"Human eDNA can accumulate at a crime scene through passive shedding and dispersal throughout the environment, including in airborne particles and dust, where it may persist despite cleaning efforts," said Mariya Goray, a senior lecturer at Flinders University, co-author of the study published in Forensic Science International: Genetics.
The researchers said airborne DNA, combined with evidence from dust and surfaces, could help reconstruct recent and established occupancy patterns.
They added that standardized sampling, analytical and interpretation procedures, and further validation under longer post-event delays and wider environmental conditions could improve the reliability of results. ■

Egypt says ready to give Saudi Arabia necessary support

Breadcrumb
Egypt says ready to give Saudi Arabia necessary support amid Houthi conflict
Egypt is ready to provide Saudi Arabia with the support it needs to defend its security and stability, the presidency said on Sunday, as Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis intensify their attacks on the world's largest oil exporter.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi had requested an urgent parliament session to authorise the military, one of the region's largest and most powerful, to help defend Saudi Arabia if the kingdom requested its support.
The Houthis have in recent days attacked Riyadh's international airport and the state oil giant Saudi Aramco, amid renewed fighting with the Saudi-backed forces of the internationally recognised government following the collapse of a truce.
"Egypt will provide Saudi Arabia with all necessary and possible forms of support to defend its security and stability, protect its resources, territorial integrity and Islamic holy sites," the Egyptian presidency said in a statement.
The statement followed a meeting of Egypt's National Defence Council, chaired by Sisi and attended by the parliamentary speaker, the prime minister and the army chief.
Egypt's parliament postponed a vote on Sisi's request on Sunday, two lawmakers told AFP, extending deliberations to Monday.
One lawmaker said the session was extended "to give all lawmakers the opportunity to speak and express their views", while another said proceedings would continue on Monday "to allow all lawmakers to be heard".
Sisi said in a speech on Saturday that Egypt would act in accordance with guidance from Saudi King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who visited Sisi on 15 September, after fighting in Yemen reignited.
Egypt and Saudi Arabia are close strategic and economic partners. Saudi Arabia and other oil-rich Gulf states provided Egypt with billions of dollars in aid, central-bank deposits, and investments after the military ouster of President Mohamed Morsi in 2013.
Egypt had previously joined the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in Yemen in 2015 to support the government against the Houthis, but played a limited combat role.

New incident at Leipzig Airport: Fence rammed near Russian cargo aircraft

In Germany, unknown individuals rammed through the fence of Leipzig Airport near Russian cargo aircraft. The surveillance camera did not record the damage to the Leipzig Airport fence—it was switched off, reports UNN, citing Bild.
Details
As BILD has learned, at Leipzig/Halle Airport, unknown individuals, apparently in a vehicle, broke through the fence near the parking area for Russian An-124 cargo aircraft. The damage was discovered the previous evening at around 11:00 p.m. After the incident, the northern runway was closed and flights were redirected to the southern one.
Federal and state police officers arrived at the scene. The airport grounds were searched, but neither the vehicle nor any outsiders could be found.

In addition
At Leipzig/Halle Airport, the camera installed near the site where the fence was damaged did not record what happened because it was switched off. Late in the evening of October 17, an unidentified vehicle apparently rammed the airport fence; however, according to BILD, police have still found neither the vehicle nor any outsiders.
Airport representatives explained that the 360-degree camera installed in this area is intended not for continuous security surveillance, but to monitor aircraft movements. It is switched on manually only when necessary.
According to the administration, the airport complies with all aviation security requirements, but providing round-the-clock video surveillance along the entire 40-kilometre perimeter is difficult. At the same time, three Russian An-124 cargo aircraft are parked approximately 1.7 kilometres from the scene; they have been prohibited from taking off since 2022 because of EU sanctions.
Context

‘We are suffocating’: protests spread to Lisbon and Milan as housing and living cost tensions intensify
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:02:39 UTC
20:02:39 KST

The angry protests that have convulsed Spain and France in recent weeks have spilled over to Italy and Portugal, with rioters clashing with police and setting property on fire in Milan, and a tent encampment springing up in Lisbon over the weekend.
A march in central Milan on Saturday to protest against rising living costs began peacefully but ended with masked rioters throwing stones, paving blocks and other objects at riot police and setting fire to barricades made from bar tables.
Police used water cannon and teargas to disperse the crowds, and images of the aftermath showed a severely damaged carabinieri car.
At least two police officers were injured and about 50 demonstrators, including many minors, were detained, the LaPresse news agency reported.
Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, said that while demonstrating was a right, “setting our cities ablaze is not”. In a social media post, she said “hooligans” had exploited the protests “to sow chaos, attack those responsible for ensuring security and to hold entire cities hostage”.
Milan’s centre-left mayor, Giuseppe Sala, said that while “the reasons for the protests were understandable, the violence against law enforcement and serious damage to the city are not justifiable”.
In Lisbon, a tent camp reminiscent of the one established in Madrid three weeks ago was set up by protesters demanding action to tackle the housing crisis and living costs.
Hundreds of protesters rallied at night in Rossio Square – located in the bustling, touristic heart of the Portuguese capital – after a march that had drawn thousands of people nationwide.
The attenders vowed to stay overnight, with hundreds singing songs as they sat around the statue of King Pedro IV that dominates the square.
“The Portuguese social class that pays taxes, that which keeps this country going, is under attack and is losing its rights, notably its right to housing,” said Elena Costa, a 46-year-old social assistant. “So we are all here together to try to explain that we are suffocating.”
Antonio Margado, a 52-year-old engineer, criticised the centre-right government for “a total liberalisation of rents; owners are protected more and more, while tenants who need a house are those who are protected less and less”.
Portuguese housing prices rose by 124% between 2015 and 2024, roughly twice as fast as the EU average, according to official data. The impact is especially harsh on younger people and those in Lisbon – around a quarter of Portugal’s more than 11 million inhabitants live in the capital’s greater metropolitan area.
Saturday’s camp in Lisbon amplified a housing protest that started in the northern city of Porto, where dozens of tents had already been set up.
At the earlier protest in Lisbon called by the main CGTP union, demonstrators called for better public services, pensions and wages as well as measures against soaring housing costs.
Portugal’s prime minister, Luís Montenegro, has said his government understood that people wanted to “express their outrage at what, in their view, may be omissions in public policies”. But he has warned political rivals against “importing into Portugal climates of instability and protest that, in fact, have no support in Portuguese society”, in a likely reference to violent protests in France.
There have also been violent demonstrations in Albania this week, where demonstrators angry over university conditions and high tuition fees have demanded the resignation of the country’s prime minister, Edi Rama.
On Saturday, protesters threw rocks, molotov cocktails, metal objects and pyrotechnic devices at police, and torched cars and litter bins, using them as blazing barricades to stop police advancing.
In a sign of the escalating violence, police fired rubber bullets on the demonstrators for the first time since the protests began. The protests continued into the night, with buildings – including a court, banks and post office – set on fire or severely damaged.
The unrest follows months of anti-government protests in the Balkan nation, initially sparked by a controversial resort development linked to the family of the US president, Donald Trump.
Growing anger over soaring rents and social inequality boiled over in Spain last month after an 87-year-old woman was evicted from her home because she was unable to pay the 230% rent increase sought by the investment firm that had bought her flat.
The plight of the late María del Carmen Abascal – and the wider issue it embodied – led to street demonstrations and the creation of a protest camp in the middle of the Spanish capital, and spurred the socialist-led government to propose emergency measures to facilitate and protect access to housing. When rightwing and far-right parties voted down those measures in congress, the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, responded by announcing a snap general election for the end of November.
In France, fury over teacher absences and shabby facilities in schools in the poor northern suburbs of Paris has snowballed into a nationwide movement against inequality, weak public spending and falling standards.
More than 1,200 people were arrested in France on Saturday after protesters supporting high school students clashed with police, with some demonstrations later spiralling out of control as buildings were set ablaze and shops looted.
The Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

Britain yet to fill twenty-seven posts at Norfolk command
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:00:58 BST
20:00:58 KST

Britain has taken command of NATO’s Atlantic headquarters with twenty-seven of its own seventy-one posts there still unfilled, and the Ministry of Defence does not expect to complete them until the end of 2027, according to written evidence submitted to the Defence Committee.
The Ministry of Defence supplied the figures in answer to follow-up questions from the committee’s High North inquiry, after members asked for the percentage and actual numbers of British-allocated NATO posts at the headquarters that are currently filled.
The department said: “The UK holds over 1000 NATO posts, which are currently filled at around 90% – one of the highest fill rates in the Alliance. Fill rates naturally fluctuate as posts are created, filled and rotated. The UK holds 71 out of the 494 Joint Force Command Norfolk (JFC Norfolk) posts; 44 of these have already been filled, with the remaining 27 posts due to be filled by the end of 2027. The UK will assume command of JFC Norfolk from the United States in September 2026, when General Nick Perry will take up the 4* Commander (COM) role.”
Joint Force Command Norfolk is the NATO headquarters responsible for the North Atlantic, established in 2019 and declared fully operational in 2021 as the alliance reckoned with Russian submarine activity returning to Cold War levels. It is the only NATO command headquarters based in North America, co-located with the United States Second Fleet at Norfolk, Virginia, and its area of responsibility covers the sea lines of communication between North America and Europe that any reinforcement of the continent depends on.
General Nick Perry took up the four-star Commander role in September, putting a British officer in charge of the headquarters that would run the Atlantic in a crisis. The Royal Navy has long argued that anti-submarine warfare in the Greenland Iceland United Kingdom gap is where Britain contributes most distinctively to NATO, and the command appointment follows that logic.

====================================================================================================

Intelligence tests are a weaker predictor of job performance than long believed, large study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:00:18 UTC
20:00:18 KST

A large synthesis of recent workplace data reinforces evidence that general intelligence tests are a weaker predictor of overall job performance than long believed. By combining data from over 109,000 workers across more than 200 contemporary samples, researchers found that the predictive power of cognitive ability tests is less than half of the historical benchmark widely cited in textbooks. The findings, published in the Journal of Business and Psychology, suggest that employers should rely on a broader mix of hiring assessments rather than treating mental ability tests as a standalone measure of future success.
General mental ability refers to a person’s broad capacity to learn, reason, process information, and solve unfamiliar problems. Rather than representing a single narrow skill, it reflects the shared underlying capability that links specific talents like verbal comprehension, math skills, and spatial reasoning. In the workplace, standardized tests measuring this general ability are often used during hiring to estimate how well an applicant will learn job duties and perform once hired.
The traditional view in workplace psychology was that general mental ability stood out as the single best predictor of job performance across all types of occupations. This view was cemented by an influential 1998 review that synthesized decades of hiring data and estimated the correlation between mental ability and job performance to be just over .50. For a positive relationship like this one, a correlation of 0 indicates no relationship and 1 a perfect one, making .50 a strong link by the standards of behavioral research.
In recent years, that benchmark has come under scrutiny due to how earlier researchers handled a statistical issue known as range restriction. When a company hires only top-scoring applicants, the pool of hired workers has a much narrower range of test scores than the general pool of job seekers. Because looking only at hired workers can artificially shrink the apparent link between test scores and job performance, researchers apply mathematical adjustments to estimate how the test would perform across all applicants.
The authors of a 2022 meta-analysis, led by Paul Sackett, a co-author of the new study, argued that earlier workplace studies had applied overly aggressive statistical adjustments for range restriction, which inflated the apparent value of cognitive tests. When they recalculated those older datasets using more conservative adjustments, the estimated correlation dropped from .51 to .31, a conclusion other researchers have disputed. The foundational databases also relied mostly on studies conducted before the mid-1980s, many of them involving manufacturing jobs.
To see how these tests perform in modern workplaces, researchers recently conducted three separate meta-analyses looking at studies from 1990 through 2022, including a 2024 longitudinal meta-analysis that documented a sharp drop in the predictive power of cognitive tests over recent decades. Although all three modern reviews yielded lower correlations ranging from .16 to .23, they drew from partially overlapping time periods and shared several of the same underlying studies. The new research, led by Saron Demeke, a PhD candidate in industrial-organizational psychology at the University of Minnesota – Twin Cities, sought to merge these three datasets, remove all duplicate studies, and establish an accurate modern estimate of how well general mental ability predicts job performance.
“For decades, general mental ability (GMA), or cognitive ability, was described as the single best predictor of job performance, but that conclusion rested largely on studies conducted before 1980, and the nature of work has changed substantially since then,” Demeke told PsyPost. “Three recent meta-analyses, or comprehensive reviews of existing studies, reported much lower estimates. These papers, including work by members of our team, drew on partially overlapping sets of studies, so their results could not simply be averaged.”
Demeke and colleagues also wanted to re-evaluate the long-held assumption that intelligence tests become better predictors of performance as a job becomes more mentally demanding. The team gathered the full datasets from the three recent meta-analyses, which covered studies conducted between 1990 and 2022, and systematically cross-referenced the databases to strip out overlapping samples. To make the datasets comparable, they also dropped studies that used grade point averages instead of a test, relied on self-, peer-, or subordinate ratings, measured performance during training, or used data collected before 1990.
This filtering process left a combined dataset of 212 independent samples encompassing 109,396 workers. Job performance in these studies was primarily measured through supervisory ratings of overall performance or specific task proficiency, alongside a smaller number of objective performance metrics. To ensure their conclusions did not depend on one debated statistical choice, the researchers analyzed the data using multiple types of range restriction adjustments and different methods for weighting the three datasets.
Before applying any statistical adjustments for range restriction or measurement error, the average observed correlation between general mental ability and job performance across the 212 modern samples was .14, compared to .24 in older databases built mostly from studies conducted before the mid-1980s. After applying statistical corrections to account for restricted applicant pools and imperfect supervisor ratings, the contemporary correlation fell between .18 and .22 across all tested methods. The authors proposed .20 as the single best summary estimate for modern workplaces, a figure less than half the size of the historical .51 benchmark and noticeably lower than the .31 revised estimate for older data.
The authors favored the equally weighted figure of .20 partly because the largest of the three datasets, covering about 65,000 workers, came from studies of a single commercial test, the Wonderlic, and they did not want one test to dominate the estimate. They described the choice as a judgment call.
“As an illustration, if cognitive ability scores were used to make hiring decisions, someone scoring in the top 20% on a cognitive ability test would be roughly 1.6 times as likely to be rated as an above-average performer as someone scoring in the bottom 20%,” Demeke explained.
Demeke said two results stood out to the team. “First, the estimates barely moved (between .18 and .22) after we removed the overlapping studies and tried different statistical adjustments, which correct for things like measurement error and the limited range of scores among people who get hired.”
To investigate how job complexity affects these numbers, the researchers examined a subset of 137 single-occupation samples that could be matched to the Occupational Information Network, a comprehensive federal database of job characteristics. Each occupation was scored on three dimensions of complexity: cognitive demands involving information processing (“Data”), interpersonal demands involving teamwork and communication (“People”), and manual or technical demands involving equipment and physical processes (“Things”). The team then ran statistical models to see if these job ratings predicted how well cognitive tests worked in different roles.
Contrary to traditional expectations, cognitive complexity alone showed virtually no relationship with how well mental ability tests predicted job performance, yielding a correlation of -.04. Interpersonal complexity also showed no meaningful link to test validity. In contrast, manual and equipment-related complexity showed a positive relationship with test predictive power, with a correlation of .29.
When the researchers looked at how these job demands interacted with one another, they found that cognitive tests tended to be most predictive in jobs that combined high levels of both cognitive (“Data”) and manual (“Things”) demands. In the occupational database, high “Things” scores go beyond routine physical labor to include tasks like inspecting equipment, troubleshooting mechanical failures, and controlling complex machinery. The findings suggest that general mental ability remains particularly relevant in dynamic environments where workers must process complex information to solve hands-on, technical problems.
This pattern matched an earlier analysis by members of the research team but differed from the 2024 longitudinal meta-analysis, which had linked hands-on job demands to weaker predictive power. The authors suggest that the effect of hands-on demands may depend on whether a job also requires heavy information processing.
“Second, we expected the link to be strongest in the most mentally demanding jobs, but what we found was more nuanced,” Demeke said. “The relationship tended to be strongest in jobs that pair thinking with hands-on work, like troubleshooting, inspecting, and operating equipment. One possible explanation is that ‘hands-on’ work in many jobs today involves more than just routine physical tasks and often requires substantial information processing and problem solving.”
Emily A. Willoughby, a research assistant professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Minnesota and board member of the International Society for Intelligence Research, is in the same department as three of the study’s authors but was not involved in the research. She described the new paper as one that “mostly consolidates and confirms, rather than overturns” earlier work.
“The fact that intelligence test scores can predict job performance is very well-established, but the oft-repeated correlation of about .50 (which is pretty high, as psychological correlations go) is based almost entirely on studies done before 1980,” Willoughby told PsyPost. “There is reason to suspect that those old correlations were too generous, and Demeke et al. wanted to look only at newer data. The workforce today is clearly different than it was prior to 1980, and it’s reasonable to assume that older data doesn’t capture the modern association between cognitive ability and job performance. And when looking only at studies conducted after 1990 (and count each study once), the authors find the relationship to be closer to about .20, an estimate that seems to be remarkably resistant to correction method, weighting, and so on.”
To account for why cognitive ability tests appear less predictive of overall job performance today than half a century ago, the researchers point to two likely explanations, though the study did not directly test them. First, the nature of work has shifted away from individual manufacturing roles toward service and knowledge jobs that heavily emphasize teamwork, communication, and adaptability. If supervisors now factor these social and emotional skills into overall ratings, cognitive ability would represent a smaller piece of what they are judging.
Second, the pool of people applying for any given job appears to have become more similar in cognitive ability. The 2024 longitudinal meta-analysis found that the spread of test scores within job-specific applicant pools shrank by about 22 percent between data collected before 1973 and after 2004, which its authors attributed partly to better career information and growing degree requirements. When applicants already have similar levels of education and ability, test scores vary less, which limits a test’s ability to separate top performers from average ones. The authors stress that this is a real loss of predictive power for employers, not a statistical distortion to be corrected away.
“The most important takeaway is that general mental ability may not relate as strongly to job performance as the field has long assumed to be true,” said Erik Gonzalez-Mulé, a professor of organizational behavior and human resources, the Randall L. Tobias Chair in Leadership, and chair of the Kelley Direct Programs at Indiana University’s Kelley School of Business, who was not involved in the study. “The authors attribute that to a) the changing nature of work since the foundational studies on the validity of GMA were conducted, and b) overly generous range restriction corrections.”
He sees the findings as a challenge to what the field has long taught. “It definitely challenges the long-standing view in the literature that GMA is among the, or the, most important individual differences variable that predicts job performance,” Gonzalez-Mulé told PsyPost. “This is a big deal because one of the first things we would teach in our courses or tell practitioners about selection is to use GMA as a primary tool to have the highest likelihood of selecting good employees. Now, that guidance is tempered a bit (although the validities for GMA that the paper reports are still consequential in a personnel selection setting, just not nearly as strong as previously assumed).”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these results. The finding that general mental ability has a modest .20 correlation with overall job performance does not mean cognitive ability is irrelevant in the workplace. As the authors note, prior research indicates that intelligence tests remain strong predictors of how well workers perform in formal job training, with correlations ranging from .35 to .49, as well as how well they master hands-on technical proficiency.
“As we discuss in the paper, it’s important to consider the outcome that is being predicted,” Demeke noted. “Our results are about broad on-the-job performance. Our estimate is also an average across many settings, and the relationship varies between them. In most settings, we would expect the true relationship to fall roughly between .07 and .29, so it can be quite weak in some and moderate in others.”
Willoughby emphasized that general readers should not mistake a correlation of .20 for proof that intelligence no longer matters at work. “Readers might be tempted to conclude from the .50 -> .20 decline that intelligence matters little for job performance, or that intelligence stops mattering after a certain threshold,” Willoughby said. “This would be wrong: a pooled correlation of .20 is still a meaningful predictor of job performance, and a highly replicable correlation of that magnitude translates into significant material gains for a company with many employees.”
Most of the studies measured performance through supervisors’ ratings rather than objective records. In the authors’ reanalysis of one of the three datasets, studies that used objective performance measures showed a higher average correlation, about .35, while studies of managers showed the lowest, about .17.
Willoughby expressed fairly high confidence in the headline estimate but raised two cautions. “First, the criterion is mostly supervisor ratings, which are a notoriously noisy measure and are well known to be less reliable than more objective measures, such as performance, which correlates more strongly with IQ,” Willoughby said. “As such, some of the decline from .50 to .20 may reflect a change in how ‘performance’ is defined and doesn’t necessarily capture how much ability really matters.”
In addition, the job complexity analyses relied mostly on office, administrative, management, and sales occupations, with fewer samples representing industrial production, maintenance, or repair roles. Future research will need to examine a wider variety of hands-on occupations to see how well these complexity patterns hold up across the broader economy.
By convention, researchers usually require a p-value below .05 before treating a result as reliable. “Second, the key interaction (that validity increases with cognitive complexity only in jobs that require hands-on or technical work) is only marginally significant (p = .059) after accounting for occupations appearing more than once in the data,” Willoughby explained. “More research will be needed to replicate this interaction.”
Gonzalez-Mulé noted that the complexity findings are the part of the study most open to misinterpretation, and offered an example of how the two dimensions work together. “For example, a plumber would score high on ‘Things’ but relatively low on ‘Data’, whereas a trainer of plumbers who has to also educate new plumbers and keep up-to-date with best practices to effectively train new plumbers would also score high on ‘Things’ but higher on ‘Data’; the results would suggest that GMA would predict performance of the trainer to a greater degree than it would for the individual plumber,” he explained.
“As noted earlier, the amount of interaction with people (‘People’) has no effect on the validity of GMA which, combined with the increase in focus of 21st century jobs of interacting with people (either in service or teamwork contexts, etc), provides a theoretical explanation for the reduction in validity of GMA over time.”
Future research could also examine how the rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence alters workplace demands. As artificial intelligence takes over routine information processing, the relationship between human cognitive test scores and job performance may continue to shift.
“We encourage future research to examine why the relationship is weaker today,” Demeke added. “For example, one possibility is that ‘good performance’ now includes more teamwork and interpersonal skills, which cognitive ability predicts less well; examining how overall job performance changed over time could address this.”
Gonzalez-Mulé suggested that future studies should also examine other job characteristics, such as worker autonomy, and test whether alternative hiring assessments like interviews and personality tests have experienced similar declines over recent decades. “It could be that GMA has stronger validity in jobs with more autonomy, as higher GMA people might be better able to figure out priorities and determine where to spend their efforts,” Gonzalez-Mulé said.
“Many of those selection predictor validities are also based on older data (similar to the criticism the current paper levies against GMA), so it might be useful to see how the changing nature of work has changed those validities as well and compare them to GMA. Maybe all of these relationships have gotten weaker (as the foundational theories and measures are several decades old), and there are other things that better predict performance at work that we aren’t even studying or measuring yet!”
Because the predictive power of cognitive tests differs so noticeably between older and newer studies, the authors recommend that researchers report modern findings separately rather than pooling them with older data.
Willoughby also called for directly testing the competing explanations for the decline. “Whatever supervisor ratings are actually capturing could and should be empirically measured (or use objective output measures, where they exist), to see whether the decline shows up there as well,” she said, adding that researchers should also test whether occupations with the greatest narrowing in applicant test scores show the steepest drop in predictive power. “Both of these explanations are possible, and they are not mutually exclusive, but both have very different implications: either ability really does matter less for what employers are now looking for, or ability matters as much as ever but the sorting work now occurs before hiring, e.g. in educational attainment and job requirements.”
For employers and hiring managers, the findings indicate that general mental ability tests still provide useful information, even if they are not the standalone predictors once claimed. Relying less heavily on cognitive tests can also help organizations reduce adverse impact, a term for when a hiring test disproportionately screens out applicants from certain demographic groups. Combining cognitive assessments with other job-relevant tools, such as structured interviews or work sample tests, may help organizations build selection systems that capture both technical problem-solving and interpersonal skills and are seen as fairer.
“Our findings do not suggest that GMA is unrelated to job performance, or that being able to learn quickly and solve problems isn’t useful at work,” Demeke said. “For context, it is still a better predictor of job performance than the typical informal job interview.”
“Job performance is a product of many things, including the knowledge and skills someone built up, their personality and work habits, and how well they work with others,” Demeke concluded. “Cognitive ability tells us something about how someone is likely to perform, but it also leaves much of what drives performance unexplained. GMA could be best used as one part of a broader selection system alongside things like formal or structured interviews and work samples.”
The study, “Is general mental ability still the best predictor of job performance? Integrating contemporary meta-analytic evidence,” was authored by Saron Demeke, Paul R. Sackett, Christopher D. Nye, Yujia Li, and Nathan R. Kuncel.

Hong Kong excels at medical research. So what is holding it back?
Hong Kong’s biomedical ambitions face hurdles beyond research funding, experts say, pointing to limited industry investment, production capacity and specialist talent
In the first of a four-part Health Matters wellness series on frontier medicine in Hong Kong, Elizabeth Cheung looks into how the city can turn world-class research into real-world treatments and what it needs to become a global biomedical innovation hub.
Raymond Tong Kai-yu spent a decade overcoming challenges in cost and production to develop a device that could change lives: a robotic hand that helps stroke patients regain mobility and relearn everyday movements.
The Hong Kong biomedical engineer is best known for “Hand of Hope”, which he developed 15 years ago at the age of 39. The device is now used in hospitals across 15 countries, but getting there was far from smooth.
“It is challenging to turn scientific research products into real-life applications for others to use … breakthroughs in research and market access cannot happen at the same time,” said Tong, a professor at the Chinese University of Hong Kong’s department of biomedical engineering.

‘Damp squib’: Ed Davey can breathe easy as Lib Dem leadership challenge fails to materialise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:00:03 UTC
20:00:03 KST

As political showdowns go, this week’s gathering of Liberal Democrat MPs, billed by some as a crunch moment for Ed Davey, was a touch underwhelming. “I had expected a damp squib,” one attender put it. “It was damper than I thought.”
Far from generating a mass of opposition to Davey’s leadership, let alone a formal challenge to his position, the lengthy gathering in a Commons committee room on Tuesday evening brought a few minor grumbles, but little else.
“My main feeling was a sort of irritation that we were forced to sit through this very long meeting, one where in the main we all aggressively agreed with each other,” another MP put it.
This is not, however, the entire story. There is disquiet with Davey’s patient and sometimes cautious leadership style, as shown most dramatically by the sudden resignation a week ago of Charlie Maynard, the number two in the party’s Treasury team, over concerns the Lib Dems were failing to cut through with voters.
If Maynard hoped to spark a wider revolt, it did not happen. “It felt like he was trying to light the touchpaper, but it fizzled out instead of exploding,” one MP said. Another was more blunt: “Charlie really has fucked it up. He has zero political nous.”
The situation nonetheless remains tricky. Davey led the Lib Dems to a century-best performance in the 2024 election, winning 72 MPs, and is safe for the foreseeable future. That said, frustrations that were already bubbling up before September’s party conference have arguably become more acute since.
This is largely the result of the two policy decisions set out by Davey at the conference: a promise of £17bn in income tax cuts if the party is elected, and support for the pensions triple lock, just as Andy Burnham pledged to change it.
Both chimed explicitly with Lib Dem efforts to build momentum in the so-called blue wall of affluent home counties constituencies where the party made big gains from the Conservatives in 2024.
While just about every Lib Dem MP agrees that protecting these seats and potentially winning more is vital, some worry that Davey is being so careful to not alienate former Tory voters that any distinctively liberal message has been lost.
“Making us the party of tax cuts just jarred with activists,” one MP said. “It’s not that we don’t want taxes cut, it’s just that the overt positioning felt incredibly blue wall-y. It’s like we are aping the Conservatives, while they are aping Reform.”
They added: “There are levels of nuance here. Ed will be given time to make changes. But there are a lot of unhappy people in the party at the moment, and not just MPs.
“Charlie Maynard didn’t help. Now we have to rally around the leader, do all the Operation Big Dog stuff, and we haven’t addressed the issues about who we actually are.”
Supporters of Davey argue that he is listening, but also point to the lessons of the 2019 election, when the party had a very clear national message – stop Brexit – but won just 12 seats, with a vote total higher than 2024’s but spread too thinly.
“Ed was very clear in the meeting that he understands people’s frustrations,” an MP said. “There are some legitimate grievances. But he has enormous credit built up, and people are prepared to give him the time he needs to make the changes he needs to make.”
Thus far, public opposition has come from only a handful of people, also including another MP, Tom Gordon, who called Davey’s argument that the triple lock needed to be saved to protect the pensions of people currently in their 40s “downright insulting”.
Some MPs are privately unimpressed by what they view as performative complaints from, as one put it, a “small minority who feel the world fails to recognise their staggering genius”. Another said: “The plea, particularly among colleagues with small majorities, is: please think when you do these things, as it undermines us.”
Another factor protecting Davey is the absence of a plan for what would come next. There are ambitious and capable MPs in the 2024 intake, but they lack experience. If Davey was ousted, a leading contender would be Daisy Cooper, his deputy and Treasury spokesperson – who some Lib Dems feel shares the same cautious approach.
One MP said: “A lot of people are terrified of a Daisy leadership – it’s the main reason why Ed is still in place. It is politely phrased as a ‘lack of a viable alternative’.”
For now, it seems, the party will maintain its own version of Labour’s “Ming vase” tactic – trying to remain sufficiently benign and unobjectionable to hoover up enough tactical votes to gain more MPs, and then perhaps support a Labour government on the condition it introduces the Lib Dem holy grail of a proportional election system.
“That’s the big plan: win the seats to deliver PR and then we can be liberals,” one MP said. “But that relies on a lot of things going right.”
There is worry, and some disagreement. But as yet, no real rancour. “Some of this is just the usual mid-parliament blues, which the 2024 intake have never experienced,” one senior party figure said.
“We are still small enough that we can have individual conversations to sort things out. And we don’t do drama. So there will be no implosion. Just some soul searching.”

Dining across the divide: ‘He thought extra spending on defence would be wasted. He’s probably got a point’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:00:02 UTC
20:00:02 KST

Carey, 66, London
Occupation Logistics manager on a construction site
Voting record Tory until Thatcher, Labour until Blair, whom he viewed to be “another Thatcherite”; now votes between Labour and Green, and tactically “to keep Nigel Farage out of office”
Amuse bouche He was homeless as a teenager but later got BA and master’s degrees, and has since worked for charities, the oil industry and he was even a bingo caller for three years
Chris, 58, London
Occupation Works for a bank in a risk-and-control role
Voting record He’s flipped between Conservative and Lib Dem “for tactical reasons”
Amuse bouche He’s trying to visit all 92 professional football league grounds in the UK. He’s done just under 50
For starters
Carey I wasn’t nervous, I enjoy talking to people and, as my wife puts it, I’ve always got an opinion. Chris is a very amiable individual.
Chris I was a bit nervous. He’s had a radically different upbringing to me, so it was interesting to hear his life story.
Carey For starters I had monkfish skewers, then crab pasta with a glass of white wine, and for dessert I had an old fashioned with a nice cheesecake.
Chris I had tuna tartare to start, which was fantastic, then grilled monkfish and fries with a glass of white wine. For dessert I had panna cotta with an old fashioned.
The big beef
Carey Chris thinks we should increase defence spending, but there is currently waste within the military spend. Before I give somebody more money, I want to see they’re looking after the money they’ve already got.
Chris Given where we are geopolitically, increasing spending on defence is something we have to do. To me, it’s not a question of buying shiny new missiles, but defence against cyber-attacks.
Carey I would argue the value of big shiny toys like nuclear submarines is slightly degraded in the modern arena – and if you’re saving billions a year on not having big flashy toys, you don’t need an increase. But I also agree we should pick up the bill for cyberwarfare.
Chris I think he generally felt that more money would probably be wasted. He’s probably got a point, to be honest.
Sharing plate
Carey I think we should abolish the monarchy. For me, it’s about lack of transparency. There are more than 1,000 cases of the royals seeing acts of law before they were passed, with no information about what the act was like before it was given to them. We should remove the privilege of an individual to interfere in parliament. People argue that they bring in tourism, but France abolished their monarchy and the Palace of Versailles gets far more visitors than Buckingham Palace.
Chris I’m not a great lover of the monarchy, but what would you have instead? I look at the leaders of the current political parties and I’m not sure I necessarily want any of them as head of state.
For afters
Chris I think net zero as a target is completely the right thing to do, but I have no idea if the timing that we’ve set is achievable. I’m not against us using the oilfields in the North Sea – it would extend the timescale under which we could move to net zero, but that might seem more manageable for people.
Carey I agree with Chris that the likelihood of us achieving net zero as it stands is pretty low. But the big issue for me is: who pays? We have major players in this country, such as Amazon and Starbucks, that pay marginal or zero tax while paying low wages to a lot of people. Tax them and make them pay for it. Then it’s achievable.
Takeaways
Carey I always find it interesting to talk to people with opposing views, because it helps me build and question my own. The way that you learn is to say things to people who will challenge you.
Chris My takeaway is what a really interesting guy he was, how well-informed, and how he had turned his life around – I had absolute admiration for him. I do think mistrust of the government did underpin a lot of his views, and he’s probably right on that. He didn’t fundamentally change my opinions – but I would do it again in a heartbeat.
Additional reporting: Kitty Drake
Carey and Chris ate at Noisy Oyster in London, E1

Truck queue stretches 30 kilometers at Türkiye-Bulgaria border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:59:56 UTC
19:59:56 KST

A 30-kilometer queue of trucks has backed up at the Hamzabeyli Border Gate in northwestern Türkiye, leaving drivers carrying Turkish exports to Europe stuck for hours due to slow processing on the Bulgarian side.
Truck drivers said they had been stuck in the queue for up to two days, with limited access to food and sanitation facilities.
“We have been here since yesterday. We are currently around the 20th kilometer of the queue and have been stuck on the road for two days,” driver Sait Özkan told the Demirören News Agency on Oct. 17, adding that neither side was processing vehicles fast enough.
“We do not know how much longer we will have to wait. It could be another two or three days,” he said.
Özkan also raised concerns about irregular migrants allegedly entering parked trucks at night, warning that drivers could face penalties if their vehicle seals or tarpaulins were damaged.
Another driver, Ercan Ulus, said he had spent around 10 hours in the queue, which had moved from the 26th to the 23rd kilometer.
“The Bulgarian side is also operating very slowly. Only one person is handling passport checks,” Ulus said, calling for faster processing at the border.
Türkiye and Bulgaria are also discussing plans to open a new border crossing north of the existing Kapıkule facility to ease congestion and increase cross-border traffic capacity.
The proposed crossing, tentatively named “Kapıkule / Kapitan Andreevo – North,” is intended to provide an alternative to Kapıkule, one of the region’s busiest land border crossings and a major trade corridor connecting Asia and Europe.
