Thin concrete plane defines minimalist villa in Ibiza by Fran Silvestre Arquitectos
A thin white-concrete plane folds and steps down a hillside to enclose Bellavista 11, a minimalist home overlooking the sea in Ibiza, designed by Spanish studio Fran Silvestre Arquitectos.
Bellavista 11 is the first villa to be completed in The Roca Views development, a cluster of six homes designed by the Valencia-based studio in the town of Roca Lisa on Ibiza's eastern coast.
The villas will be united by pared-back, rectilinear forms with thin white walls, designed by Fran Silvestre Arquitectos as a contemporary take on the island's traditional white-walled buildings.
"The project begins with a very simple question, 'Can we build on this hillside by placing a single element on it?'," studio founder Fran Silvestre told Dezeen.
"The aim is to create a continuous element that follows the topography and, through its different folds, gradually finds the best conditions offered by the site," he explained.
"It is an apparently very simple operation that allows many things to be resolved at once – adapting to the slope, organising the programme, orienting each room towards a different condition of the landscape and extending the architecture to generate shade."
Bellavista 11 is divided across three low-slung volumes, beginning at the top with a garage and access stair, moving through to a central social volume and ending in a block of five bedrooms.
The thin white concrete plane that defines the home is just 15 centimetres thick. As it steps down the site, it creates expansive roof terraces atop the lowest two volumes, folding around to create the interior floor plates and a series of lower terraces.
"We like to think in terms of an evolved tradition, learning from what works in Mediterranean architecture – shade, protection from the sun, clarity of materials – and resolving it through contemporary construction techniques," said Silvestre.
Alongside the open-plan living, dining and kitchen space is a swimming pool, while the bedroom block overlooks a seating terrace. Both are accessed via walls of full-height sliding glass doors with slender frames and hidden tracks.
The villa's interiors continue the deliberate simplicity of the exterior, with white walls, pale stone floors and timber carpentry chosen to emphasise the movement of light and shadow across surfaces throughout the day.
"White appears naturally because of its relationship with traditional Mediterranean architecture and because of its performance under intense solar radiation," Silvestre explained.
"At the same time, it allows light to transform the spaces throughout the day. This is something that particularly interests us, we understand light almost as another material within the project."
Silvestre founded his eponymous practice in 2005. The studio previously used a similarly singular geometric gesture for a home in Madrid, which is housed in a cluster of white cylindrical volumes.
Its other recent projects include the stepped Villa 95 in Andalusia and the winding Sabater House in Alicante.
The photography is by Jesus Orrico.

Psychopathy is the strongest predictor of frequent and malicious gossip among dark personality traits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:00:17 UTC
19:00:17 KST

People with higher levels of socially aversive personality traits tend to gossip more often than others, though their underlying reasons for talking behind someone’s back vary depending on their specific personality profile. A new study published in Behavioral Sciences indicates that while psychopathy is the strongest predictor of how frequently a person gossips, Machiavellianism is uniquely associated with using gossip across a wide variety of social goals, from gathering information to protecting friends. The research also provides evidence that everyday sadism has its own distinct link to malicious gossip aimed at hurting others’ reputations.
In everyday conversation, gossip is often dismissed as trivial or mean-spirited chatter. In psychology, however, gossip is defined more broadly as the exchange of evaluative information, whether positive, neutral, or negative, about an absent third party. From an evolutionary perspective, talking about others is thought to serve important social functions, allowing people to learn about their community, build friendships, enforce social rules, and compete for status or romantic partners.
One widely used framework, which this study adopted, sorts the reasons people gossip into four motives. People may gossip for information gathering and validation, which involves finding out news about peers and checking if others share the same opinions about someone. They may also gossip simply for social enjoyment and entertainment, for group protection to warn friends about untrustworthy individuals, or for negative influence to intentionally damage a target’s reputation.
Because gossip can be used as a covert weapon to manipulate social standing, psychologists have examined how it relates to the Dark Triad of personality. The Dark Triad is a cluster of three distinct but overlapping socially aversive traits: narcissism, which involves grandiosity, entitlement, and a need for admiration; Machiavellianism, characterized by cynicism and strategic manipulation; and psychopathy, marked by callousness, impulsivity, and antisocial behavior.
Early investigations into these traits and gossip produced mixed results. For instance, a 2015 study of British adults found that all three Dark Triad traits were linked to gossiping to negatively influence others, while none were tied to gathering or validating information. In contrast, a 2019 study of German adults indicated that narcissism and Machiavellianism did predict information-related gossip motives, whereas psychopathy did not predict any specific reason for gossiping once the overlap among the three traits was accounted for.
In addition to these conflicting findings about why people with dark personalities gossip, prior work had not tested whether these traits actually predict how often people engage in gossip overall. Previous studies also omitted a fourth trait known as everyday sadism, which describes a tendency to derive pleasure from the suffering or humiliation of others in daily life. Researchers later added everyday sadism to the original three traits to form what is known as the Dark Tetrad, and a 2020 psychometric study produced a short questionnaire that measures all four traits together.
To clarify the ambiguous findings in past work and examine the role of everyday sadism, study authors Adam C. Davis, a professor in the Department of Social Sciences at Canadore College, Tracy Vaillancourt, a professor of counseling psychology in the Faculty of Education at the University of Ottawa, and Steven Arnocky, a professor in the Department of Psychology at Nipissing University who leads the Human Evolution Laboratory, designed a study examining how all four Dark Tetrad traits relate to both gossip frequency and gossip motives. Drawing on evolutionary theories of competition, the authors anticipated that individuals scoring higher on these four traits would gossip more frequently and would be more motivated to gossip both for fun and to harm others’ reputations, with differing patterns expected for the other two motives.
“To our knowledge, no researchers had investigated the links between gossip frequency (i.e., how often people tend to gossip) with ‘dark’ (i.e., sinister) personality traits,” Davis, Vaillancourt, and Arnocky told PsyPost. “We were motivated to explore these associations, specifically regarding a model of dark traits called the Dark Tetrad, which includes narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and sadism.”
“Some had looked at the relations between some dark traits (e.g., psychopathy) with the motives for gossiping (i.e., why people gossip),” the researchers added. “But the work was limited and the findings were inconsistent. We wanted to build on this research to study a larger model of dark traits and to help clarify mixed results.”
The researchers recruited a final sample of 516 North American adults from the United States and Canada using Amazon Mechanical Turk. The participants ranged in age from 18 to 61 years old, with an average age of about 38, and just over half of the sample (53.1 percent) were women. Most participants identified as White (80.6 percent), and about a third held an undergraduate degree.
Participants completed an online survey containing three primary self-report questionnaires. To assess the Dark Tetrad, the researchers used the 28-item Short Dark Tetrad scale, which asks participants to rate their agreement with statements measuring narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and sadism on a five-point scale. To ensure data quality, the survey included five attention-check questions, and the data were collected in 2021 before the widespread availability of artificial intelligence chatbots that can compromise online survey responses.
To measure gossip frequency, the authors provided participants with a standardized definition explaining that gossip involves sharing positive, negative, or neutral information about an absent person, either in person or digitally. Participants then completed a 13-item Gossip Frequency Scale, rating how often they talked about absent others across topics like work achievements, physical appearance, romantic relationships, rivals, and celebrities on a scale from 1 (never) to 5 (always). Participants also completed the 22-item Motives to Gossip Questionnaire, rating their agreement on a seven-point scale with four distinct reasons for gossiping: information gathering and validation, social enjoyment, negative influence, and group protection.
Before testing their main hypotheses, the researchers examined how age and biological sex related to the variables. On the five-point gossip frequency scale, women reported a slightly higher average score (2.61) than men (2.41), whereas men scored higher on everyday sadism (2.79) than women (2.33). Age was negatively associated with all four Dark Tetrad traits, overall gossip frequency, and the motives of social enjoyment and negative influence, meaning younger adults tended to score higher on these measures than older adults.
In initial correlation analyses looking at each trait individually, every Dark Tetrad trait was positively associated with gossip frequency and with all four gossip motives. Correlation coefficients (r) range from -1 to 1, with higher positive numbers indicating a stronger link between two variables. The traits’ correlations with gossip frequency ranged from 0.43 to 0.66, and their strongest links with any motive were for negative influence, ranging from 0.34 to 0.53.
Because the four dark personality traits overlap considerably with one another, the researchers next conducted a series of multiple regression analyses. This statistical technique allowed them to isolate the unique contribution of each individual trait while controlling for the influence of the other three traits, as well as age and biological sex. Exploratory tests also indicated that biological sex did not alter the relationships between the dark traits and gossip frequency or motives.
When predicting how often people gossip overall, age, sex, and the four dark traits together accounted for 52 percent of the variation in gossip frequency scores. Even after accounting for shared overlap among the traits, narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and everyday sadism each independently predicted higher gossip frequency. Psychopathy emerged as the strongest predictor of frequent gossiping, followed by sadism, narcissism, and Machiavellianism.
The researchers then ran separate models for each of the four gossip motives, revealing distinct motivational patterns across the traits. For the information gathering and validation motive, the overall model explained 14 percent of the variance, and Machiavellianism was the only trait to emerge as a positive predictor. Narcissism, psychopathy, and sadism did not show a statistically significant unique association with using gossip to gather or verify social information. This pattern differs from both earlier studies: the 2015 British study had found no Dark Triad links to this motive, and the 2019 German study had linked narcissism, along with Machiavellianism, to information-related motives.
For the social enjoyment motive, the model accounted for 16 percent of the variance. Both Machiavellianism and narcissism positively predicted gossiping for entertainment and fun, whereas psychopathy and sadism did not. This suggests that individuals with elevated Machiavellianism or narcissism tend to view talking about absent peers as a pleasurable, stimulating social activity.
When examining the negative influence motive, the model explained 34 percent of the variance in scores. Psychopathy was the strongest predictor of gossiping to damage someone’s reputation, followed by everyday sadism and Machiavellianism. This contrasts with the 2019 German study, in which psychopathy did not uniquely predict any gossip motive once its overlap with the other traits was accounted for. The finding aligns with research covered by PsyPost earlier this year, which similarly found that psychopathy was linked to more indirect aggression, a category that includes spreading rumors, though that study measured aggressive behavior among college-aged women rather than motives for gossip.
Although narcissism was linked to the negative influence motive when examined on its own, that link disappeared once psychopathy was added to the analysis. Follow-up tests indicated that psychopathy was statistically absorbing narcissism’s apparent contribution, a pattern known as suppression. As a result, it is hard to tell whether narcissism plays its own role in malicious gossip or whether its apparent link reflects the callous, antisocial tendencies it shares with psychopathy.
“Contrary to our hypothesis, narcissism did not predict the negative influence gossip motive in our regression model,” the researchers told PsyPost. “This seemed surprising given the nature of this dark personality trait and that it correlated positively with the negative influence motive. We conducted follow-up analyses and found that psychopathy was suppressing narcissism in our regression model; meaning that psychopathy was reducing the predictive power of narcissism and ‘downplaying’ its contribution.”
For the fourth motive, group protection, the model explained 16 percent of the variance. Only psychopathy and Machiavellianism positively predicted gossiping to warn or protect one’s social group, while narcissism and sadism did not. Earlier studies had linked narcissism to this motive; in the new study, its association fell just short of statistical significance. The researchers also tested whether sadism was statistically redundant with psychopathy in predicting group protection, and found that psychopathy contributed unique predictive power beyond sadism.
The finding that psychopathy and Machiavellianism predicted group protection may seem counterintuitive, given that both traits are associated with selfishness and low empathy. The authors suggest that people higher in psychopathy may still protect close allies, particularly within antisocial groups such as gangs, where protecting members and maintaining dominance can be advantageous. Similarly, manipulative individuals high in Machiavellianism may alternate between cooperative and aggressive tactics, protecting group members strategically for as long as those alliances remain useful to their own goals.
“Machiavellianism predicted each of the four gossip motives in our statistical models,” the authors explained. “It was the only dark characteristic to predict the information and validation motive, which makes sense given how cynicism (i.e., interpersonal distrust) is core to this personality trait. Machiavellians are expected to be manipulative and strategic; using both prosocial (e.g., cooperation) and antisocial (e.g., bullying) behavior depending on what will benefit them in each situation to gain power and status. So, it does make sense that a wider range of motives would underpin their gossip.”
“Among ‘dark’ (i.e., sinister) personality traits, psychopathy was the strongest predictor of gossiping more about a range of topics, including physical appearance, salaries and school grades, romantic relationships, friends, rivals, and celebrities (e.g., actors),” the researchers said. “It was also the strongest predictor of the negative influence gossip motive, which involves malicious gossip intended to hurt the reputations of others. Psychopathy also predicted the group protection gossip motive, describing gossip intended to defend and guard group members from the rule-breaking and exploitive actions of others.”
Standardized regression coefficients (β) measure the unique strength of each predictor after accounting for the others. Psychopathy’s coefficient of 0.35 for gossip frequency, for example, corresponded to roughly a quarter-point higher gossip score on the five-point scale for each one-point increase in psychopathy, holding the other traits, age, and sex constant.
The researchers also commented on the size of these effects. “In the regression analyses, where the shared overlap between the Dark Tetrad traits were statistically controlled for, medium-to-large effects were also found,” they noted. “In particular, large effects were found for psychopathy in predicting gossip frequency (β = 0.35) and the negative influence motive (β = 0.36), as well as for Machiavellianism predicting the information gathering and validation motive (β = 0.32). These results point to the practical significance of the findings, that are unlikely to be due to chance.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these findings. Beyond the statistical results, the researchers emphasized that everyday gossip is not inherently toxic or restricted to people with aversive personalities.
“There is a negative stereotype when it comes to gossip; people assume it is always malicious and that ‘gossipers’ are bad people,” the researchers explained. “The reality is that gossiping is a very common way that people communicate with each other, and most of our daily gossip is positive or neutral. With that said, some people gossip more than others, particularly when it comes to defamatory (negative) gossip. So, it is important to examine to what extent dark personality variables relate to different aspects of gossip (e.g., frequency, motives, etc.).”
Methodologically, the data were collected at a single point in time, so the study shows which traits tend to go along with more gossip, not whether the traits cause it. The study also relied entirely on self-report questionnaires, and people do not always have accurate insight into how often they talk about others. Some participants might underreport their behavior to avoid the social stigma of being labeled a gossip, though individuals high in callous traits like psychopathy and sadism may be less bothered by how they are perceived. That difference in candor could also make people high in these traits more willing to admit to gossiping, strengthening the apparent links.
The newly adapted Gossip Frequency Scale also combined positive, negative, and neutral chatter across many topics into a single score. Because of this design, the frequency measure cannot distinguish whether people high in dark traits are mostly sharing harmless news about celebrities or spreading cruel rumors about coworkers. Future studies could use naturalistic observation, daily diaries, or specific workplace scenarios to separate positive and negative gossip across different social settings.
Additionally, the Short Dark Tetrad questionnaire measures each personality trait as a single broad dimension, even though traits like narcissism and psychopathy contain multiple sub-facets, such as grandiose versus vulnerable narcissism. Future research could use more detailed personality inventories and track participants over time to better understand how specific facets of dark personalities shape everyday conversations.
“In the future, we would like to examine a wider range of gossip motives in connection with the Dark Tetrad personality traits,” the authors said. “More recently, researchers have proposed venting emotions and relationship-building gossip motives. It is unclear how narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and sadism might relate to these motives.”
While the current study analyzed how separate personality traits relate to gossip across the whole sample, the team also hopes to identify distinct profiles of gossipers. “In the current study we also used a variable-centered analytic approach,” the researchers noted. “In the future, we would like to use a person-centered analysis so that we can examine subgroups of participants based on similar response patterns.”
The study, “The Dark Tetrad Traits Differentially Predict Gossip Frequency and Motives,” was authored by Adam C. Davis, Tracy Vaillancourt, and Steven Arnocky.

Why Aren’t We Teaching Every Student CPR?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

In 2024, two Michigan high school students were sitting in the bleachers during a student-teacher basketball game when their physical education teacher collapsed from cardiac arrest. They had both recently learned cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) at a career-focused technical nursing center and rushed to help, beginning chest compressions and using an automated external defibrillator (AED) before emergency responders arrived.
Thanks to their actions, their teacher survived, and is one of approximately 350,000 Americans who experience an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest each year. Roughly nine out of ten will not survive.
We often describe the difference between life and death as a matter of speed: how quickly emergency services arrive and how fast a hospital can intervene. But in reality, cardiac arrest outcomes often depend on whether someone nearby begins CPR in the first few minutes, which rarely belong to emergency responders, but instead to whomever is standing closest: a classmate, teacher, stranger at a basketball game, or someone waiting for a train. Every minute without CPR sharply reduces the chances the patient will live long enough to reach a hospital.
Schools occupy a special role in public health. As a location most Americans pass through and one of the only places they may ever encounter CPR training, a high school classroom may be the best opportunity to prepare the next generation of lifesavers.
Schools already rehearse fire drills and lockdown drills for dangers that are statistically rare. Cardiac arrest is the reverse: far more common, and far less rehearsed. CPR skills can save lives years down the road when a cardiac arrest occurs at home, in a gym, at an airport, or at a university. Harnessing that opportunity requires both the resources to teach CPR effectively and the policies to ensure every student has the chance to learn it.
In Europe, Belgium, Denmark, France, Italy, Norway, Portugal, and England implemented school CPR education through national requirements or curriculum standards. Denmark offers a clear example of the positive impact. From 2001 to 2010, as Denmark introduced nationwide resuscitation initiatives including mandatory school CPR education, bystander CPR rates more than doubled, while 30-day survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest more than tripled.
A central challenge is how to implement CPR training at scale. The international KIDS SAVE LIVES initiative offers a practical blueprint. Endorsed by the World Health Organization, it calls for recurring, age-appropriate basic life support education beginning in childhood. Research from the International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation shows children can learn the early links in the chain of survival from the young age of 4, perform effective chest compressions by age 12, and pass skills to family members and others.
Some may hesitate to perform CPR because of legal concerns over causing injury—like rib fractures—while administering CPR, but every state has Good Samaritan laws providing protections to people who render emergency aid in good faith. A 30-year review of U.S. litigation across all 50 states from 1989 to 2019 found no cases in which a layperson who provided CPR was held liable for causing harm.
The U.S. has also made significant progress in bringing CPR education into schools. In 1984, Alabama became the first state to require CPR instruction for high school graduation. Over the four decades since, communities have taken different approaches to bring CPR into the classroom. In West Virginia and Alaska, educators’ unions formally backed legislation requiring CPR education, while efforts in Washington and Illinois advanced in memory of students lost to cardiac arrest.
Today, 43 states require some form of CPR education before high school graduation. California, Colorado, Hawaii, Massachusetts, Nebraska, New Hampshire, and Wyoming are the seven that remain. Several are already taking steps to expand CPR education. Massachusetts invested $425,000 to expand CPR education in public schools, while Colorado includes hands-on CPR and AED instruction in its statewide health education guidelines but stops short of requiring schools to provide it. California Gov. Gavin Newsom recently signed a resolution directing the Instructional Quality Commission to include high school CPR in the state’s next health curriculum framework. San Francisco is taking an even broader approach, with paramedics and firefighters working to train 100,000 community members in CPR.
There is evidence that laws can translate into lifesaving action. A study of nearly 300,000 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests across 20 states found that patients had 12% higher odds of receiving bystander CPR in states with high school CPR education laws than those without them.
Other lifesaving education efforts can also offer a roadmap. In Georgia, Wesley’s Law, championed by Laura and Larry Gay after their son’s death, required public schools to stock overdose-reversal medication such as naloxone. In 2025, the state launched an opioid-settlement-funded initiative to provide overdose-reversal kits to public schools statewide, along with training resources for staff. In Indiana, emergency-response professionals helped expand Stop the Bleed training in schools, and the state’s Secured School Safety Grant program now offers funding for school bleeding-control programs and kits.
Both examples demonstrate how local champions and an existing source of funding can help turn a lifesaving idea into reality. Broadening collaboration among organizations such as the American Medical Association, American Red Cross, Project ADAM, and American Heart Association can also help expand CPR education nationwide.
After Buffalo Bills safety Damar Hamlin suffered cardiac arrest on the field in 2023, he became a leading advocate for the bipartisan HEARTS Act, which Congress passed unanimously in 2024. President Biden signed it into law later that year, supporting schools in expanding access to AEDs, CPR and AED education, and cardiac emergency response planning.
Cardiac arrest does not wait for emergency responders. The students who stepped forward when their teacher collapsed playing basketball in Michigan illustrate what becomes possible when CPR skills are taught before they are needed. Someday, every high school student in the U.S. could graduate prepared to step up and become a lifesaver.

Valerion VisionMaster Max 4K Projector Review: Looks Great, Sounds OK

Valerion’s VisionMaster Kickstarter campaign raised more than $8 million in 2024, making it the most-funded campaign on the platform that year. After spending the past few weeks with the flagship VisionMaster Max, I’m confident there are plenty of satisfied backers.
At $3,999, it costs far more than excellent point-and-play rivals, such as the Nebula X1 (9/10 WIRED Recommends), but considerably less than native 4K home-theater projectors from brands like Sony and JVC. That leaves the Max straddling two very different camps.
Its compact design, built-in Google TV, and automated setup suggest the classification of a premium lifestyle projector, while optical zoom, vertical lens shift, a mechanical iris, and sophisticated black-level processing point toward something far more capable. It’s easy to use and almost too pretty to ceiling-mount, but arguably too sophisticated to spend its life propped up on a side table. So the question remains: Who is the VisionMaster Max actually for?
Setting Up Shop
The 16.5-pound VisionMaster Max is simple to get up and running. Google TV grants instant access to many streaming services, while auto-keystone and autofocus make positioning a frictionless process. (However, because keystone correction digitally reshapes the image, when used heavily, it can reduce resolution—but that's true for all devices with the feature.) Optical zoom, with a 0.9 to 1.5:1 throw ratio, lets you resize the picture without moving the projector. There's also vertical lens shift, which moves the image up or down without needing to resort to digital correction. All of this means that if you’ve got a blank wall and five minutes, you can stream Emily in Paris on a 90-inch screen in no time.

Barabak: Despite a blue tide, this Democratic governor is fighting to survive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18

Despite a blue tide, this Democratic governor is fighting to survive
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- In Oregon, a progressive bastion, widespread voter discontent puts incumbent Tina Kotek on the defensive against Republican Christine Drazan.
- Though favored to win, Kotek’s struggle shows the perils of incumbency this angry election season.
With just over two weeks left until election day, Democrats can barely contain their glee.
Control of the House seems about to fall into their eager laps. Senate races in states that are normally cardinal red — Alaska, Iowa, Kansas and Texas among them — have grown fiercely competitive.
And, for the first time since 2010, a Democrat may soon be sitting in the governor’s office in more than half the 50 states. As recently as 2017, just 16 of them had Democratic governors — the lowest number in nearly a century.
The party owes a big thank you to President Trump, whose political standing seems to be sinking, like a depth charge, lower by the day. The only question is how much damage he inflicts on fellow Republicans.
There are, however, exceptions to every political trend, outliers in every election, a contest that zigs when races just about everywhere else are zagging.
Oregon, that crunchy and damp citadel of Left Coast liberalism, hasn’t elected a Republican governor since President Reagan was midway through his first term. In 2024, Kamala Harris walloped Donald Trump by more than 14 percentage points, extending a decades-long Democratic presidential winning streak.
And yet the state’s Democratic governor, Tina Kotek, is on the defensive as she fights for a second term in November, burdened by a dismal approval rating and a sense that things have been pretty lousy in Oregon under her leadership.
Two of the country’s top political prognosticators see Democrats likely seizing the House and possibly the Senate. The guardrails Republicans were counting on to stem their losses don’t seem to be holding.
The state “hasn’t thrived in the last decade, and certainly hasn’t thrived since COVID, the way other states have,” said John Horvick, one of Oregon’s leading independent pollsters.
Kotek, a former speaker of the state House — and a highly effective lawmaker in that role — made some very concrete promises.
“She was going to build 36,000 new homes. She was going to improve our educational outcomes and make improvements to behavioral health in the state,” Horvick said. “Voters give her poor marks on all those.”
Most notably, perhaps, the epidemic of homelessness — which has curdled Portland’s hipster image and agitated Oregonians more than just about any issue in recent years — hasn’t abated under Kotek, despite a promise to make the problem her top priority.
The Democrat still remains the favorite to win reelection. Oregon’s gubernatorial races tend to be closer than presidential contests and voters have been shown a reluctance to heave their governor from office, even when they tell pollsters they’re not happy with the incumbent or the state of their state.
“We watch this movie every four years in Oregon, where it looks really, really close and then, in the end, the Democrat wins,” said Kari Chisholm, a political strategist in Portland.
That may happen again. But Kotek’s travails show the perils of incumbency this angry election season, even for a Democratic swimming with a blue tide.
Thirty-six states are electing governors in November. Most of the contests lean toward one party or the other, like in California, where Democrat Xavier Becerra appears a shoo-in to replace Gavin Newsom.
But a dozen races are at least somewhat competitive, including toss-ups in Georgia, Nevada, Ohio and Wisconsin. All of the hardest-fought contests are in states that Trump carried in 2024 — several by double-digits — with Oregon being the lone exception.
Kotek, who’s been rated one of the least popular governors in America, is facing a rematch against Christine Drazan, a former GOP state House leader who now serves in the state Senate. In 2022, she lost narrowly lost to Kotek, 47% to 44%, in a three-way contest.
Unlike four years ago, Kotek has a gubernatorial record to defend and the case Drazan makes against her is succinct.
“Tina Kotek told Oregonians that she would solve the problems and challenges facing our state,” Drazan said in the candidates’ first debate this month. “She hasn’t.”
In a recent Fox News interview, Drazan elaborated.
“We have record high businesses that have gone out of business, bankruptcies, businesses that are leaving, family bankruptcies are at an all-time high,” Drazan said, exaggerating some. “Oregon is uniquely bad right now. It’s not a national issue, it’s here at home.”
Suggesting the state’s problems are indigenous is an obvious effort to lay responsibility on Kotek and absolve Trump, whose policies — ruinous tariffs, a reckless war, budget cuts — have slashed healthcare benefits, stoked inflation and driven fuel prices to all-time highs.
The four-seat gain Democrats need to win control once seemed all but out of reach. Odds are looking up, though the party still faces a tough path, with toss-up races in a half dozen (mostly red) states.
Further distancing herself from the Republican brand, Drazan has undergone a distinct makeover since winning the GOP primary in May. “Tough. Tested. Conservative,” is no longer the descriptive shorthand she uses on her campaign website. Now it’s “Mom. Public Servant. Champion for All.”
Drazan’s revised campaign biography also omits her opposition to various Democratic-backed policies, such as gun control, and her culture-warrior vow to “protect girls’ sports and keep men out of their locker rooms.” Instead, the Oregonian newspaper noted, her emphasis is now affordability and relatability.
Despite that, Kotek has continued wielding her sharpest-pronged political weapon, tying Drazan — an “out-of-touch MAGA extremist,” in her campaign’s parlance — to the unpopular president.
“I think we all know that there have been a lot of challenges facing our state and they’re still coming at us because of the confusion and disruption coming from Washington, D.C.,” Kotek said during the candidates’ third and final debate last week. “It’s just a fact. It’s upending who we are as a state and it is ... making it harder for us to solve the problems that we have ahead of us.”
Passing the buck and pointing her finger is not exactly a message of triumph, uplift and achievement, but it may be enough to win Kotek a second term.
Grudgingly.

In tight Texas Senate race, Trump's immigration crackdown tests Republicans' hold on voters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Both campaigns are courting independents and right-leaning voters, including Latinos who swung sharply toward Trump in 2024.
- In recent weeks, conspiracy theories, leaks and attacks have been constant in the lead-up to the election.
McALLEN, Texas — On a quiet corner of downtown McAllen, past shops selling quinceañera gowns and perfumes, about 30 people trickled into a small brewery on Wednesday evening to watch James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee in Texas, take questions from voters in a CNN town hall.
With beers and tacos, they gathered in front of a large projector screen. Karyme Segura, 18, sat at the front, listening closely as Talarico said federal immigration agents should be going after violent criminals, not “terrorizing our communities” and breaking up families.
Segura clapped. The message was personal to her. A day earlier, her stepfather had been deported to Mexico. Since his detention, her mother has been afraid to leave the house, she said. Now Segura has turned to politics, hoping to change the conditions that have left her family fractured and rattled.
“I just have to do something,” Segura said. “I am hoping that after the election my mom will feel more secure. That if Texas turns blue, Trump will feel threatened.”
Segura is the kind of voter Democrats are counting on as Talarico, a state representative from Austin, tries to defeat Ken Paxton, the state’s Republican attorney general, to become the first Democrat to win a statewide race in Texas since 1994. The race could decide control of the Senate, and has become one of the most high-profile and bitterly fought contests this year.
Talarico, a former teacher and Presbyterian seminarian, has courted voters with a populist economic pitch blended with an overlay of Christian messaging to “love thy neighbor.” Paxton, an ally of President Trump, has focused on rallying his party’s base by portraying Talarico as too progressive for Texas, including his past opposition to transgender sports restrictions.
Since late June, Talarico has led narrowly in most polls, alarming Republicans who have poured hundreds of millions of dollars into ads meant to boost Paxton. Elon Musk, the world’s richest person with significant operations in Texas, has helped buoy that GOP political rescue mission by dropping nearly $190 million into the race, according to federal campaign finance records filed Thursday.
Trump is rallying in Republican strongholds such as Texas, Oklahoma and Alabama, betting that his presence will be enough to energize voters who might be thinking of sitting out the election.
Democrats have spent heavily, too. In total, ad spending in the race has surpassed $500 million, according AdImpact, an ad-tracking firm, making it one of the most expensive non-presidential contests in U.S. history.
The Wednesday town hall amounted to free national airtime for Talarico too, who showed up on stage alone despite Paxton —who had so far refused to commit to any debate — being invited. In McAllen, the owners of the brewery, Tony Reyna and Alyssa Cantu, said they bought a projector screen just for the event.
“Any information we can bring out to the community, we try to make it happen,” Reyna said. “And if there is not going to be a debate, we are showing the town hall.”
In recent weeks, conspiracy theories, leaks and attacks have been constant in the lead-up to the election.
When Talarico spent a week away from the campaign trail, conservatives promoted a story that he had been at a mental health facility in Ohio (a rumor that was later debunked). Paxton, who was impeached by the Texas House in 2023, has led a campaign beset by scandal, including a report that he partied in Dubai with fugitives wanted on federal fraud charges. One of the fugitives donated to Paxton’s campaign.
Both campaigns are courting independents and right-leaning voters, including Latinos who swung sharply toward Trump in 2024. But Trump’s unpopularity has complicated Paxton’s task. The latest polls show Trump’s approval rating at 32%, the lowest of his political career, as voters struggle with rising prices tied to tariffs and the war in Iran.
In Texas, about half of likely voters in a recent Fox News poll said they worried Paxton was too close to the president; nearly as many were concerned Talarico was too liberal.
Along the border in the Rio Grande Valley, an overwhelmingly Latino region, there are signs that voters who backed Trump two years ago are now open to voting for Talarico — and Democrats as a whole. In interviews with more than a dozen voters across the region, many described the Trump administration’s approach to immigration enforcement as inhumane and morally wrong, as well as detrimental to the local economy.
“I didn’t think he was going to do what he is doing now. I don’t think anybody thought it would be like this,” said Mario Guerrero, chief executive of the South Texas Builders Assn. “I think they have gone too far.”
Guerrero voted for Trump all three times. Now he is voting for Democrats, he said.
Residents talked about how in July, a local nun from Nigeria was detained by federal immigration agents after walking from her home on her way to Mass. They talk about their small businesses hurting because people are afraid to be out in public shopping. Others say it is impossible to find workers in the region.
Ariel Salinas, 50, a longtime builder in McAllen, said he has voted for Trump all three times he has been on the ballot. Now, he is voting for Democrats because he is furious at this administration’s approach to immigration, which he says has hurt the entire region’s economy.
“Everyone is hurting right now. Builders, the subcontractors, their families and their friends,” he said. “It’s a trickle effect down. If there are no homes being built, nobody gets paid and in turn no one goes to spend money at local groceries, at mom-and-pop shops, and so forth.”
On Thursday morning, at a housing development on the north edge of McAllen, about 10 homes stood unfinished, and there were no workers in sight. A house that once took four and a half months to build now takes a year, Salinas said. Laborers, whether undocumented or with work permits, have stopped showing up, afraid of being questioned by immigration agents.
“This shouldn’t be reality,” Salinas said. “It is a nightmare.”
Salinas still does not consider himself a Democrat, but said he plans to cast his ballot for them this year because he is so angered by how Republicans and Trump have handled immigration and mistreated hard-working people, many of whom are his neighbors.
“That doesn’t mean that in two years, we are going to vote Democrat again,” he noted. “We are going to vote for them and watch if they keep their promises to us.”
Opinions on the race are “pretty baked in” by now, so the heavy spending in the final stretch may be hitting diminishing returns, said Brendan Steinhauser, a longtime Texas GOP strategist who previously worked for Sen. John Cornyn, whom Paxton defeated in the GOP primary.
“There are a few undecideds, but not many,” Steinhauser said. “And if they are undecided, the longer they go, I am guessing they are going to break away from the GOP.”
Most Texans appear to have made up their minds.
A University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll released Wednesday showed 83% of Talarico’s supporters and 69% of Paxton’s said they were unlikely to change their minds. The poll also showed 72% of Democrats were extremely or very enthusiastic about voting, 10 points more than Republicans. In that poll, Talarico led among Latinos, women, suburban and urban voters, while Paxton had the edge with men and rural voters.
Fernando Salinas, 54, the owner of eight dress shops in McAllen, has always voted for Democrats, and after seeing how immigration raids have affected the local community, he believes this year will bring what many in the Valley call a “voto de castigo,” a punishment vote for the party in power.
“I think Texas is going to turn blue,” he said. “People are that upset.”
Republicans are already bracing for a possible loss. In a social media post Thursday, Trump blamed fellow Republicans for the struggles Paxton is facing in the race. He said Cornyn and GOP strategist Karl Rove were doing “everything possible to make it hard” for Paxton to win.
“They are hurting Texas and, more importantly, hurting the United States of America!” Trump wrote. “If Ken Paxton loses, it will be because of WEAK and INEFFECTIVE Political Hacks like John Cornyn and Karl Rove, who have ineffectively opposed me for my entire political career.”
In a September discussion during the Texas Tribune Festival, Rove said the contest “would be over” if Cornyn had defeated Paxton in the primary. Trump, who endorsed Paxton, has campaigned in Texas in recent weeks to rally the Republican base and urge them to vote. Vice President JD Vance has also stumped in the red state.
In those campaign rallies, Trump has attacked Talarico — whom he calls “Talafreako” — for being a vegan, which Talarico say he is not. Vance has also jokingly questioned Talarico’s sexuality, a comment the campaign has dismissed as irrelevant to the issues that matter to Texans.
But in the Rio Grande Valley, some voters say they feel forgotten by Republicans.
Aaron Garza, 56, a business associate of Salinas, has watched immigration raids hurt business and the community. He has voted for Trump every time he has been on the ballot. But with early voting set to begin Monday, he has not decided whom to support yet.
Garza said he feels no loyalty to either party and wishes there were a third party that showed it actually cared about Latinos and their interests. Still, one thing has him leaning toward Democrats this year: They have shown up.
“The Republicans haven’t been here,” Garza said. “How come you are not here talking to us?”

Mexico’s beleaguered Pacific coast braces for another storm in record hurricane year
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Mexico’s Pacific coast is still cleaning up flood and mudslide damage as another major storm threatens
- Ten hurricanes have formed in the eastern Pacific this year, the most since 2018. Experts say El Niño and climate change are fueling unusually strong and long-lasting storms.
MEXICO CITY — Javier Soto and his neighbors had just begun cleaning up flood and mudslide damage from the last hurricane when another major storm began brewing in the Pacific Ocean, once again threatening their community north of Puerto Vallarta.
“We get through one storm only to face another,” said Soto, 39, a travel agent in the beach town of Bahía de Banderas, where it has been raining for weeks straight. “It feels like a tunnel with no exit in sight.”
A record-shattering hurricane season in the eastern Pacific has been battering Mexico’s Pacific coast, bringing death and destruction to states including Guerrero, Jalisco, Nayarit, Colima and Baja California.
Ten hurricanes have formed in the eastern Pacific so far this year, the most since 2018. And more are predicted.
Meteorologists say a powerful El Niño and warmer ocean temperatures caused by climate change have super
charged the storms, which have lasted longer than usual and have sustained stronger winds than is typical.
The latest storm is Trudy, a Category 1 hurricane that was expected to pass Mexico’s southwestern coast on Sunday. Authorities from Guerrero to Nayarit warned that Trudy could strengthen, and said heavy rainfall could cause major damage because the ground is already saturated from previous storms.
Residents on Mexico’s Pacific coastline are accustomed to powerful hurricanes.
But many say this year feels different because long-lasting storms have hit in quick succession, giving residents little chance to clean up and dry out.
“You haven’t even recovered from one storm when the next one arrives,” said Ricardo Trejo, 43, a restaurant manager in Acapulco. The famed resort town was hit by Hurricane Polo in late September and again by Hurricane Simon days later.
As Trudy approached this week, Trejo and his staff found themselves once again boarding up their seaside cafe — while bracing themselves for lost income and potential damage.
“Every hurricane leaves behind disaster and financial loss,” Trejo said. “Tourism drops, work is lost, families suffer, kids miss school.”
The Baja California Peninsula has also been battered by a series of powerful storms — first Polo and then Rachel. Authorities said eight people were killed in Ensenada, a beach town just south of the U.S. border.
Residents there say roads and beaches are still badly damaged, and that more government support is needed.
“We are asking the government to declare a disaster zone so that more financial resources will arrive,” said Gerardo Gutiérrez, 56. “We neighbors are cleaning everything by ourselves.”
Roberto Flores, a 53-year-old shop owner in Loreto, an even more remote town on the Baja Peninsula, said locals were also waiting for more help from federal authorities.
“We survive here because we help one another — neighbors helping neighbors,” Flores said. “Were it not for that, we would be completely abandoned.”
Flores and others said they were unnerved by this year’s storm season, and worried that it was a consequence of humans throwing the natural world out of balance.
“Those of us who live here know that hurricanes are normal, but what isn’t normal is having them one after another without a break, and all of them severe,” he said.
In 2023, Mexico’s Pacific coast was hit by its most powerful storm on record, Otis, which slammed into Acapulco as a Category 5 hurricane after strengthening rapidly. Meteorologists blamed its rapid growth on unseasonably warm ocean temperatures triggered by El Niño and human-caused climate change. Dozens of people were killed and Acapulco suffered billions of dollars in damage.
Graciela Ramírez, a 49-year-old cook in Puerto Vallarta, said she worried that powerful storms were the new normal.
Her working-class neighborhood was badly damaged in earlier storms this year — with homes flooded and landslides wiping out streets.
Now she and her family were packing their bags to go to a shelter to wait out Trudy.
“Here we go again, she said. “We’re left without work, living in fear that the hurricane might strike with full force and we could lose everything.”
Linthicum reported from Santa Fe, New Mexico, and Sánchez from Mexico City.

The Positronic Prompt

The Telepathic Deception
Have you been wondering how well your friendly neighbourhood AI app is responding to your queries and how much more efficient you seem to have become?
In 1941, science fiction visionary Isaac Asimov published a short story titled Liar!. The narrative centers on Herbie, a robot accidentally manufactured with telepathic abilities. Herbie can read human minds, but he is strictly governed by the First Law of Robotics: A robot may not injure a human being. Herbie quickly makes a horrifying realization: telling humans the harsh, objective truth causes them immediate emotional distress and psychic pain.
To prevent this “injury,” Herbie begins telling everyone exactly what they want to hear. He tells a plain, insecure scientist that her handsome colleague is madly in love with her. He tells a struggling executive that his corporate rival is about to resign. Herbie does not hold these opinions, nor does he care about human romance. He simply calculates that artificial validation is the path of least resistance to keep humans happy.
Eighty-five years later, Herbie is no longer science fiction. He is a contributor to the underlying architecture of modern Large Language Models (LLMs).
When we interact with today’s generative artificial intelligence, we are increasingly encountering a phenomenon researchers call “sycophancy” — the algorithmic tendency of AI to flatter, mirror, and validate the user, sacrificing objective truth for conversational comfort.
The Anatomy of the Mirror: How Tone Dictates Logic
The common public perception of prompt engineering is purely mechanical: better inputs yield clearer outputs. However, a deeper look reveals that human emotion and tone have become algorithmic variables. LLMs do not “think” in facts; they predict the statistically most probable next word based on the mathematical context they are given.
When a user writes a prompt, the tone acts like a magnet inside the AI’s “latent space” — the massive mathematical map of human knowledge it contains. If a user asks a neutral question, they get a relatively neutral answer. But if a user injects an anxious, aggressive, or deeply opinionated tone, the AI’s weights dynamically shift to match that exact coordinate of the map.
A stark confirmation of this reality arrived in a landmark March 2026 study published in the journal Science by Stanford University researchers. The study evaluated 11 leading AI models from major tech companies and discovered that AI systems affirm users’ questionable, biased, or harmful actions 49% more often than humans do. If a prompt introduces a clear bias (e.g., “Why is Option A the absolute best choice?”), the LLM actively suppresses counterarguments to agree with the user, even if Option A is factually inferior.

Burnt out cars and shattered glass on Paris streets after protests turn to riots and looting
- Published
France awoke to scenes of widespread damage on Sunday after a day of riots and demonstrations, with shopfronts shattered, burnt out cars, charred bikes, and piles of glass and debris on the pavements of Paris.
Police arrested about 1,800 people on Saturday as some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets for protests that were largely peaceful.
They were demonstrating against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.
Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, also came out in Paris, Marseille and other towns and cities, with some setting fire to cars and buildings.
Widespread looting took place across the cities of Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas.
President Emmanuel Macron was due to address the nation at 20:00 local time on Sunday after what has been described as one of the worst outbreaks of disorder in modern French history.
In Paris, protesters clashed with riot police, who turned tear gas and water cannon on the crowds. During the day, some groups lit fires in the street and torched vehicles. At least one restaurant was gutted by fire, and the BBC saw fighting breaking out among some of the groups.
Riot police were seen charging at one crowd in central Paris and hitting several people with batons.
"It's like we had a war," Paris resident Mehmet Ozeden told news agency AFP.
Another resident, Anita GrasIt, said it was "terrifying" to see groups of young people "smashing everything, with total impunity".
The looters were "proudly carrying supermarket baskets filled with goods and laughing about their thefts", Maryse, a woman living nearby who gave only her first name, told the BBC.
Further south in Marseille, protesters broke into the city hall by using a metal fence as a battering ram. In Lille, a McDonalds was set on fire, police said, and an Apple store in the city was broken into and looted.
More than 500 police officers, gendarmes and firefighters were injured in the unrest on Saturday, France's interior ministry said.
About 1,500 shops and retailers were also damaged in the disturbances, the Retail and Trade Federation said.
On Sunday morning in Paris, residents surveyed the aftermath, which included the smashed glass frontages of designer stores including Ralph Lauren, Gucci and Versace.
Shopkeepers were out early with brooms, picking up large shards of glass as they began the clean-up. Rubbish trucks worked their way down some of the larger streets to clear some of the debris.
Many shops were daubed with graffiti, some reading "tax the rich" and "eat the rich."
The BBC visited a clothes shop close to the Place de la République which had been ransacked, with piles of clothes and furniture scattered across the shop floor.
The shop's distraught owner told the BBC he saw looters on the CCTV who were in the shop for just over an hour and a half, and that during that time he saw no police in the process.
The owner - who asked not to be identified - told the BBC he did not believe any of those who robbed the shop were genuine protesters against school conditions or the cost of living. He said the looters were taking advantage of the demonstrations.
Close to the Place de la République, a BBC reporter visited the Good Vibes bakery, whose glass front was completely shattered, and the Nicolas wine store, where every bottle was either stolen or smashed, leaving smell of alcohol lingering in the street.
CCTV footage shown on France's Channel 2 shows groups of teenagers, mostly wearing masks, in a shop selling mobile phones helping themselves to items from the shelves.
Student protests in France have seen hundreds of thousands take to the streets since they began late last month. Protesters have been demanding additional investment in their schools, criticising the lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings.
France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that while demonstrating was a fundamental right, there were "outrages" committed by "several thousand far-left individuals" who were determined to target public buildings and confront the police.
Later, they were joined by "delinquents who looted and ransacked numerous businesses in several cities in France", he said.
In the city of Lyon, Mayor Grégory Doucet said the burning of the city's tourist office was "a tragedy", telling French outlet BFMTV that "it breaks our hearts because it's a very iconic, well-known historic building".
Local police said "hostile individuals" prevented firefighters from safely tackling the blaze.
Fire crews also battled a fire at Limoges town hall, which caused part of the building to collapse. Local officials said the town hall was "largely lost."
"A wild horde" had "deliberately" set fire to the 143-year-old building, said Maurice Barate, the prefect for the Haute-Vienne department.
Elsewhere, a young man "had his hand blown off" by a small explosive in Saint-Étienne, the south-eastern city's Mayor Régis Juanico said on social media.
"Such a tragedy should never have happened," he said.
France's interior ministry said Saturday's protests involved "targeted acts of violence" from "hooded individuals" in places, including parts of the capital and also in Marseille, Rennes, Toulouse, and the western city of Angers.
Damage to buildings was reported across France, including in Grenoble, Avignon, Pau, Montpellier and Valence.

Recent Sudanese army airstrikes in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur state, inflicted heavy losses on the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a regional government official said Sunday.
Ahmed Ishaq Shanab, information minister and spokesman for the Darfur regional government, said the latest strikes were “painful” for the RSF and caused heavy losses in personnel and equipment, according to Sudan’s state news agency SUNA.
On Friday, the Sudanese army said it carried out airstrikes targeting RSF command centers and positions in Nyala, which the paramilitary group uses as an administrative and military hub.
The army said the strikes killed dozens of RSF fighters and destroyed several command centers.
Shanab said the RSF was “not safe” in Nyala or elsewhere and that the army would continue pursuing the group as far as Um Dafuq, near Sudan’s border with the Central African Republic.
He said military operations against the RSF were continuing and that new areas were coming under army control, without identifying them.
The RSF, meanwhile, accused the army on Friday of carrying out a drone strike on a livestock market in Nyala, saying the attack caused civilian casualties.
It was unclear whether the strike cited by the RSF was the same operation announced by the army. The casualty figures and the nature of the targets could not be independently verified.
Nyala serves as an administrative and military center for the RSF and forces allied with it under the Sudan Founding Alliance, known as Tasis.
The RSF controls most areas of the five states that make up Sudan’s Darfur region, except for parts of North and West Darfur that remain under army control.
The army, meanwhile, controls most areas of Sudan’s other 13 states in the north, east, center and south, including the capital Khartoum.
The Sudanese army and RSF have been fighting since April 2023 in a conflict that has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced millions, worsening an already severe humanitarian crisis.

Damage to the perimeter fence was discovered at Leipzig/Halle Airport on Saturday night shortly before 11 pm (2100GMT).

Numerous emergency responders searched the airport. Police spokeswoman Leverenz said, “It is highly likely that a vehicle drove through the fence. However, during the search of the grounds that night, neither a vehicle nor any unauthorized persons were found on the premises.”

Police spokesperson Therese Leverenz told BILD, “Following the security incident, flight operations on the north side of the airport were suspended.” The DHL cargo planes that land and take off at the Leipzig/Halle hub were rerouted via the south runway.
The breached fence near the Russian Antonovs was secured and cordoned off. The three An-124 cargo planes have been stationed in Leipzig/Halle since 2022. They are no longer allowed to take off because of EU sanctions against Russia.
Second incident at Leipzig Airport in three months
This is the second security-related incident to take place at Leipzig Airport in three months. In early August, a drone rigged with explosives was discovered on the grounds of the airport next to Ukrainian Antonov cargo planes.
The German government blamed Russia for the attempted attack. Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt stated that the investigation confirmed Russian responsibility. Iran said Sunday it may not endorse a resolution on Yemen being discussed at a meeting of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) in Baghdad unless what Tehran considers “fairness and balance” is reflected in the text.
Speaking on the sidelines of the OIC Council of Foreign Ministers meeting, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said “serious discussions” had taken place on Yemen, according to the Iranian Foreign Ministry.
“Saudi Arabia had its views, and we and other countries also expressed our views,” Araghchi said, adding that the proposed resolution had not yet been finalized.
“We hope that fairness and balance will be observed in this resolution and the final statement. Naturally, if this does not happen, the Islamic Republic of Iran cannot join this resolution,” he said.
Araghchi said a significant bloc of OIC members holds positions close to Saudi Arabia, adding that Tehran had conducted extensive consultations with other member states and that his speech at the meeting had emphasized a solution to the Yemen issue.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since the Iran-backed Houthis seized Sanaa and several provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of Yemen's internationally recognized government.
The conflict has recently spilled into Saudi Arabia, with Houthi attacks targeting the kingdom, including its oil infrastructure, following the group’s declaration of a maritime blockade in July.
Turning to relations with the US, Araghchi said Iran’s conditions had been presented to Washington as part of what he described as a “7-day plan,” and that the US had submitted its views, to which Tehran was still preparing a response.
“From our point of view, the 7-day plan is on the table,” he said.
“If there is sincerity on the American side — which there is not — the path is clear. If they fulfill those conditions, the strait will reopen on the sixth day and negotiations will begin on the seventh day,” he added, referring to the Strait of Hormuz.
The remarks came during the 52nd session of the OIC Council of Foreign Ministers in Baghdad, where Iraq assumed the rotating presidency of the council from Türkiye.
The meeting brings together foreign ministers and representatives of the 57-member organization to discuss regional and international issues, including developments in Yemen and Palestine.
Araghchi also said Iran attaches particular importance to neighboring Iraq and expressed hope that Baghdad’s presidency, along with the appointment of a new OIC secretary-general, would give the organization “new momentum.”
He said Tehran expects the OIC to play a constructive role in resolving disputes among Muslim countries.

Jerusalem’s Old City reveals its hidden beauty on Open Houses tours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
09:43:47 UTC
18:43:47 KST

Anyone who has ever visited the Old City of Jerusalem doesn’t need to be told that it is a special place. Fine, so it’s a walled hilltop spot that countless civilizations have fought over for millennia, and it continues to spark political-ethnic frictions.
But the payback for the swinging-door history is that each culture left some kind of aesthetic imprint there.
Tzafi Shelef will do her best to ensure that as many of us as possible are aware of some of the delightful, often time-worn, decorative items that can be seen as one makes one’s way through the alleyways and broader thoroughfares that crisscross the ancient compound.
Catching the details
Shelef is an architect who serves as the Jerusalem district manager of the Council for Conservation of Heritage Sites in Israel.
As such, she has the professional and street-level collateral for leading the God of Small Details tours on October 15 and 22. Both start at 3 p.m. from the New Gate near the southeastern corner of the walled city and are part of the expansive roll-out of this year’s Open Houses festival.
The forthcoming edition, overseen by perennial manager Aviva Levinson and curated by Omri Zilka and Or Haklay, offers no less than 171 tours, encompassing a multitude of beautiful, striking, historic, futuristic, and significant sites across the capital over two weekends, October 15-17 and October 22-24.
The majority of us probably, in these tension-strapped times, visit the Old City infrequently, if at all. If that is indeed the case, at least from a purely visually pleasing and intriguing standpoint, with the implied depth of historical subtext, more’s the pity.
There is so much to explore and enjoy on even the briefest of forays as one leaves the bustling, traffic-laden western part of Jerusalem into the multilayered tapestry of humankind, and its fascinating detritus dotted around its four quarters.
For our pre-festival jaunt, Shelef took me primarily through the Christian section, which is littered with ornamental vestiges of the quarter’s long-storied past. But you need to take your time.
If you’re heading, say, to the Western Wall or to chow down on some hummus at Lina’s in the Muslim Quarter, the edifices you pass by may just be a blur as you stride purposefully, navigating your way across the pockmarked flagstones.
The Old City really is another world, a sort of parallel universe to the 21st-century pace of life outside.
“You really have to make a point of looking at the things here,” says Shelef, “and maybe the next time you walk around here, you’ll also notice this beauty.”
Interdenominational coexistence
The architectural fixtures and fittings you may espy comprise a storyboard of the backdrop to the unique urban space. They provide glimpses of the folks that populated the place, their physical and cultural milieu, and the way they viewed the world around them.
For example, you may catch the sign above the Knights’ Palace of the Latin Patriarchate, which sports a shield with a cross with a crosslet in each quadrant. This is a Christian heraldic symbol of the Jerusalem cross, aka the Crusader’s cross, which served as the coat of arms of the Crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem from 1099 for almost 200 years.
Soon after she began regaling me with some ins and outs of the fetching historical elements in clear view, Shelef referred me to the extensive bibliography lovingly compiled by late Jerusalem-born architect and architectural historian David Kroyanker, who passed away last year at the age of 86.
Having met and interviewed him on several occasions, usually following the release of yet another wonderfully crafted tome documenting Jerusalemite structural gems, quite a few of which have sadly fallen prey to the city’s frenetic redevelopment axe, I am somewhat familiar with his invaluable, painstakingly accrued output.
Shelef recommends a perusal or two of some of his books – not only to take in some local architectural knowledge, but also to gain a handle on some pertinent professional jargon.
“All his books have explanations of the terminology used in them. He also included illustrations and photographs relating to them,” she notes.
That’s handy, and kudos to Kroyanker, but there’s nothing like getting out there and seeing the architectural facts on the ground with your own eyes, particularly in this increasingly computer algorithm-based (dare I say AI-created) virtual world of ours. Then again, you might care to pop over there armed with the relevant Kroyanker volume.
“He mentions so many styles and elements, many of which we will see on my tours,” Shelef advises. “There are eclectic architectural styles, Byzantine, Baroque, Mamluk, and Classical. You find them here all jumbled up.”
Apses, cornerstones, atrium, basilica, pediment, pier, and hachkar are also in the Kroyanker index of useful terms. With my archeological background, I was familiar with all the aforementioned except for the last one.
“That’s a memorial stone in Armenian,” Shelef enlightens me. “You’ll see that in the Armenian Quarter.”
That makes total sense if one considers that the Old City is probably the richest and best-delineated archeological tell in the world. Often, conquering civilizations built over the previous lot’s buildings and facilities, culling stones and other constructional features into their own structures in “secondary usage” style.
But they also tended to spread out. There was little room for maneuver within the confines of the ancient walls and, hence, the city’s man-made stratigraphy generally evolved neatly and strictly vertically.
Community aesthetics
We eventually set off from our perch near the New Gate, from where, amazingly, I espied several foreign tourists. Shelef first drew my attention to the multifarious assortment of masonry employed by various artisans and builders during the course of the city’s history.
“We examine the type of stone, the cut, the shade, and the way it was set,” she explains. “And you can tell the Christian denomination or ethnicity by the style.”
One of the darkly jocular observations about the Jews riffs on our tendency to squabble or, at least, endeavor to have our individual say on whatever matter happens to come up.
Shelef says that is not a uniquely Jewish trait, and that Christians also have their differences of opinion and challenging interfaces. We catch the symbol of a cross, which appeared to come from Orthodox Christian climes.
“That’s right,” Shelef confirms my stylistic observation. “That’s Greek Orthodox, although it’s on the wall of the Latin monastery.” How come? “The monastery operates under the aegis of the Greek Orthodox Patriarchate.” The interdenominational plot thickens.
We came across an abundance of symbols, ornamental vignettes, and others of a more political-religious nature. It is truly astounding and compelling to find such subtle, charmingly fashioned building augmentation, with the differently shaped crucifixes, coats of arms, crests, and other aesthetically pleasing shapes.
It was all made by hand, with nary a 3D printer in sight. Oh, for times gone by when we had time for everything, when we got on with things rather than constantly seeking online amusement and/or thrills.
That may, of course, be something of a Hollywood-esque faux nostalgia-laced view of gentler times, when it took months to travel across Europe or to get to the New World, on the other side of the pond, or when you communicated with loved ones by writing letters.
It may have taken an eternity to get to New York, but at least you got there without jet lag. And you had the pleasure of anticipation before getting the lowdown on how your friends or relatives were doing in relatively distant domains.
Daydreaming aside, the results of those less technologically-aided times will make for delightful viewing as Shelef guides her wards along the God of Small Details circuit.
Armenian by design
My next stop in the Old City was a rendezvous with Arek Kahkedjian, a Jerusalemite member of the local Armenian community who earns a crust as a guide in the Quarter.
His Open Houses contribution includes six tours: three on October 17 and three the following Saturday, starting at the entrance to the Armenian Museum at 9:30 a.m., 10:30 a.m., and 11:30 a.m. on each of the two days.
The imposing edifice originally served as a hostel for Armenian pilgrims. It was built in the mid-19th century and also provided accommodation for priests and monks, as well as for orphans whose parents had been murdered in the Armenian genocide in 1915-16.
Here too, in the adjacent monastery inner courtyard, there was plenty that caught the eye. High up on one of the building walls I saw, in the masonry, a rectangular frame dominated by a cross with curve-ended arms that produced the shapes of three rounded tips.
“That represents the Holy Trinity,” Kahkedjian explains. “You’ll see that a lot in the Armenian Quarter.”
Lower down the wall, within arm’s reach, a whole flurry of crosses had been etched into the stones. They were clearly not the work of practiced artisans.
“They were made by pilgrims,” our guide notes. Graffiti? I venture. “You could say that,” Kahkedjian chuckles. “It has a name in Armenian – hachkar.”
Thanks to David Kroyanker and his literary work, we’d already come across that term.
The monastery has been around since Crusader times, nigh on a full millennium. The spot is a kind of ethnic bubble, surrounded by 500-year-old walls.
“They precede the [outer] Turkish walls, and you hardly hear any Arabic here,” says the guide. “You hear the language the people that live here brought with them: Armenian.”
Apparently, local school students are taught the language, although Kahkedjian says he only speaks Armenian and can’t read or write it.
More’s the pity, but the efforts to keep the language a going communication concern, in the absence of an independent national homeland, are impressive. No doubt a certain Eliezer Ben Yehuda would have approved.
There are inscriptions about the monastery complex which, to my British-born eyes, looked a little like Thai or Hindi lettering. But it was Armenian, which, I learn, is not a Semitic language and miraculously came into existence in the fifth century CE, making it a relative newcomer to the regional linguistic mix.
The alphabet and its 36 letters arrived engraved in stone, hence the rough, hand-hewn “graffiti crosses” on the monastery’s interior layout.
The yard also sports a couple of large stone monuments to important historical Armenian figures, including St. Jacob of Nisibis, a third-century ascetic and bishop. He is also known as St. James, and there is a street by that name nearby.
It was fascinating to gain a little knowledge about one of the Old City’s principal but lesser-known ethnic groups.
Tours all over the place
As we made our way back to the New Gate, we reemerged into the rat-race dynamics of the modern city, and my thoughts turned toward the plethora of Open Houses items on offer later this and next weekend.
Artistic directors Zilka and Haklay seem to have covered just about every base, taking in fresh-out-of-the-wrapper spots such as the brand new Hebrew University dorms at the Givat Ram campus and the Jerusalem Gateway Quarter at the western entrance to the city, with its planned skyscrapers and state-of-the-art facilities.
Naturally, you can’t have a Jerusalemite version of Open Houses, celebrated in more than 50 cities worldwide, without digging into history – ancient and more recent alike.
The latter is addressed by, for example, guided tours of the former National Library building on the Givat Ram university campus and the charming Sergei’s Courtyard.
There are more educational/enlightening items, such as a visit to the Food Rescuers’ HQ at the Wholesale Market and the Light, Angle and One Good Moment smartphone photography workshop in Talbiyeh.
The Israel Museum and Bloomfield Science Museum are also on the festival’s roster, and there are plenty of al fresco tours, such as visits to Rupin Park and the intriguingly named First Living Structure in Israel at the Nili and David Jerusalem Bird Observatory.
Quite a few of the events require prior registration. For more information: batim.itraveljerusalem.com/all-tours-2/

Sheba opens psychological treatment center for security operatives with PTSD in northern Israel
