Sheba Medical Center opened a new psychological treatment center in northern Israel on Wednesday, intended for security operatives and their families who may be suffering from trauma.
The center, called the Mevo’ot HaHermon - Sheba Clinic, UJA NY Home, is located at the Mevo’ot HaHermon Rehabilitation Campus at Koach Junction and was founded in partnership with the US-based Cohen Veterans Network (CVN), with support from UJA-Federation of New York and Friends of the IDF (FIDF).
The treatment center is also the first of its kind to be established in northern Israel, providing a wider range of coverage and opening new opportunities for residents of the area.
In addition to individual and group therapy for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), the center provides treatment for anxiety, depression, adjustment difficulties, grief and loss, sleep disturbances and nightmares, and relationship and family challenges.
It also offers a dedicated support group for spouses of combat soldiers.
After October 7, Israeli healthcare system must address both body and mind
“The war has presented Israel’s healthcare system with an unprecedented rehabilitation challenge, affecting not only the body but also the mind," Prof. Amitai Ziv, Director of Sheba’s Integrated Rehabilitation Hospital, said.
"At Sheba, we have supported security personnel for many years, and our experience has taught us that trauma care must be professional, continuous, and accessible. It must address not only the individual service member but also the family around them."
Ziv also said that since October 7, Sheba has taken on the responsibility of building a nationwide support network with its partners.
"The opening of the center in northern Israel is another important step in this effort, allowing us to bring Sheba’s accumulated knowledge and expertise closer to those who need it.”
New York community's mobilization allowed for support to northern Israelis
Director General of UJA-Federation of New York in Israel, Itzik Shmuli, said, “The extraordinary mobilization of the New York community enabled us to begin supporting northern Israel from the very start of the war, reaching an unprecedented scale across more than 100 communities throughout the region."
He added that, since October 7, "UJA has allocated more than $366 million to provide essential support to the people of Israel, a tangible expression of our love for Israel and the mutual responsibility that guide our community.”
Brig.-Gen. (Res.) Liron Donnell, CEO of FIDF Israel, emphasized the importance of the center after the October 7 massacre and ensuing war. “Since October 7, we have seen just how much the psychological impact of trauma continues long after service members return home, and how deeply it affects their families as well. Our contribution to establishing the center in northern Israel is intended to help security personnel and their families access high-quality, professional care closer to home. Together with Sheba and CVN, we will continue expanding mental health services and supporting service members and their families throughout their recovery.”

Kfar Blum’s Voice of Music Festival offers five days of musical discovery in Israel's North
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
09:43:34 UTC
18:43:34 KST

Best-selling late 17th-early 18th-century English playwright William Congreve hit the curative psychological nail on the head when he observed: “Music hath charms to soothe a savage breast.”
Indeed, it undoubtedly does, but there are plenty more benefits to be had from quality, adventurous, and alluring sonic wares.
All that and class entertainment are on offer at this year’s Voice of Music Festival, the 41st edition, taking place at the Pastoral Hotel at Kfar Blum, in the far northern reaches of this battered and beautiful country, October 28-November 1.
As anyone who has attended the annual classical music event there in the past surely knows, holding a festival in such pleasant surroundings enhances the aural experience, complementing the onstage mix with other sensory pleasures.
There is more of that in the offing. The folks over at the hotel have been hosting the festivalgoers and artists in style for some time now and, more recently, have been expanding the facilities and upgrading the aesthetic backdrop so that the event is now a fully in-house spread that is just as pleasing on the eye as on the ear.
They have added an all-purpose concert auditorium building and are now investing in beautifying the commodious grounds, betwixt the sprawling lawns dotted with shade-giving trees.
And that’s even without noting the peerless majesty of the Golan Heights and steepling Mount Hermon seemingly – even without pre-winter whitecap – but a stone’s throw away to the east.
Hotel deputy CEO Michal Moraly took me for a guided tour of a place I have come to know well over the past two-plus decades of popping up North for the music-based cultural weekends and the music festival.
They do say that familiarity can breed contempt, suggesting that one can become inured to charms encountered too often; but in all this time, my enjoyment of the accommodation and facilities offered by the Pastoral Hotel has dimmed nary a jot. There is nothing formulaic about the rooms and suites, housed in Italian-style, two-story buildings around the grounds.
Now the hotel plans to up the Tuscany ambiance ante by some deft design reimagining, such as the installation of ponds complete with goldfish and lilies, and an aqueduct to add the sound of gurgling water to the twittering of birds, and a soundtrack of pop and folk favorites gently piped through speakers at various vantage points.
The renovation and refurbishment program also includes constructing a large swimming pool, shaped to follow the contours of a grand piano, and relocating the gym from the basement of the spa wing of the main building to an upper floor overlooking the pool.
The current gym will be turned into an activity space for kids, as the hotel aims to bring more families and younger folk into its consumer catchment reach.
Keeping cool in Kfar Blum
The Voice of Music Festival traditionally takes place in the summer, when the thermometer mercury level is high and even short walks between the comfortable air-conditioned concert halls and your accommodation or the dining room can get the sweat glands working overtime.
The forthcoming edition was shifted down the calendar due to yet another round of regional altercation, which means that the festivalgoers get to bask in gentler meteorological conditions betwixt the musical entertainment.
But even when the festival reverts to its regular July slot, the new pergolas, complete with climbing vegetation, fountains, and shaded benches should provide some respite from the summer heat.
Once again, veteran pianist-educator Dr. Ofra Yitzhaki serves as artistic director, and has put together a varied program that arches across manifold genres, eras, mindsets, and formats.
Over the years, open rehearsals have become a popular addition to the program, offering fascinating behind-the-scenes glimpses of what goes into the elbow-grease preliminaries for the staged end product.
Each of the first four days features a bunch of Open Rehearsal spots, both at the hotel Opera Hall and at the nearby Charles Clore Center, as ensemble players go through their paces while toiling on scores by the likes of Bach, Beethoven, Mozart, and Ravel.
But Yitzhaki does not focus exclusively on the usual suspects. There are more contemporary works in the five-day agenda, such as by 20th-century American composer Samuel Barber, compatriot Florence Beatrice Price, Jewish Austrian-American modernist Arnold Schoenberg, and, coming bang up to date, contributions from 89-year-old Ukrainian composer Valentin Silvestrov and 68-year-old Danish counterpart Bent Sorensen.
Yitzhaki says she tends to keep an open mind, ear, and heart when crafting her curatorial offerings.
“When I put together the festival program, I feel a threefold obligation: towards the audience, the musicians, and towards that abstract entity that is music,” she declares. “I want to provide the audience with a heart-lifting experience and give the musicians a repertoire that brings them joy and interest. But I feel it is also my job to care for culture.”
For Yitzhaki there is far more on the line than just giving the patrons a decent return for their hard-earned shekels.
“[I am duty bound] to preserve the gems through superb performances, generating cultural contexts that make it possible to gain a new and refreshing perspective, linking the music of the past and the music of the present, and to safeguard a place for local classical music so that art from here, from Israel, can progress and grow.”
Trumpeting homegrown composers
That is, indeed, a lofty, commendable aim, with the artistic director putting her money where her mouth is – for example, with the inclusion of the first airing of Piano Concerto No. 5 by Israeli composer Naama Perel-Tzadok, and the premiere of a definitively cross-cultural work by 28-year-old oud player-composer Onn Yosef Kadosh, Homage to Scarlatti for Flute, Harp and String Trio. The latter was commissioned by the festival with the support of the Israel Music Institute.
There is also a multidisciplinary aspect to the rollout, with Yitzhaki flexing her curatorial muscle to include a multifariously crafted production of Prokofiev’s perennially popular Peter and the Wolf.
The rendition at Kfar Blum will be spearheaded by the Tel Aviv Wind Quintet, with the polychromic performance taking in acting and movement under the directorial aegis of theater and opera performer, dancer, and sound and video artist Ari Teperberg.
Any onstage object is fair game for the artistic process, as junior audience members get a close earful and eyeful of the instruments doing their melodious thing.
With the classical world as a whole grappling with the ongoing challenge of aging audiences, the Culture and Sport Ministry-aided fivesome might just spark some youngster’s imagination and even inspire them to consider getting hands-on instrumental knowledge of their own.
At the very least, catching a live rendition of the Prokofiev work may induce a lasting interest in the classical music world, thereby nurturing future musical consumership.
Literature gets a vicarious look in, with Schoenberg’s Verklärte Nacht (Transfigured Night), string sextet with Israel Philharmonic Orchestra violinist and concertmaster Nitzan Bartana and fellow IPO member cellist Linor Katz in the lineup.
Verklärte Nacht feeds off a poem of the same name by German poet-author Richard Dehmel. It is a romantically inclined chart in which the composer expresses his ardor for his then-future wife Mathilde Zemlinsky, who happened to be his teacher’s sister.
The Schoenberg work appears in a concert that goes by the tantalizing name of Kee Saarta Alai (For You Stormed Me), with the epexegetical addendum of “Love and Passion in Songs, Music and Texts.”
The title hails from a poem by feted Israel Prize laureate poet Natan Alterman, which some may recognize from pop-folk readings by Arik Einstein and Chava Alberstein put to music by iconic songstress Naomi Shemer.
The eponymous number features in the Hebrew Love Song Selection concert opener, with Yitzhaki accompanying vocalist-actress Ola Schur Selektar.
The October 31 (10:30 a.m.) performance concludes with Rachmaninoff’s Trio elégiaque No. 1 in G minor, with Katz in the thick of things here, too, along with violinist Natasha Sher and pianist Renana Gutman.
The overarching sensibility also comes through loud and strong in the October 31 (5 p.m.) concert by the Cecilia Octet vocal troupe, one of the few extramural events, at Domus Galilaeae.
The Christian meeting place, used primarily for seminars and conventions, sits atop the Mount of Beatitudes and commands a spectacular view of the Sea of Galilee from the north.
Another off-campus vignette, the Family Picnic vignette, takes place on the banks of the River Jordan with the high-spirited Jerusalem Street Orchestra, under baton-wielding founder Ido Shpitalnik, doing the sonorous honors.
The thinking behind the creation
As usual, Yitzhaki puts in an extra couple of dozen shifts over the five days, giving festivalgoers insights into the machinations behind the lives and scores of a broad sweep of creators.
She opens the Work in Focus three-parter on the second day of the festival, at 4 p.m., with a talk about 20th-century Japanese composer Toru Takemitsu and his 1992 work And Then I Knew ‘Twas The Wind.
That is followed, at the same time on the morrow, with a talk about Hungarian composer Gyorgy Kurtag, who turned 100 in February.
The program includes renditions of excerpts of Kurtag charts by Yitzhaki, along with Jerusalem Symphony Orchestra flutist Rotem Bartan.
The series closer, on October 30 (5 p.m.), called Secrets from the Safe, sees Yitzhaki once again behind the piano keyboard, playing a broad selection of works, with some in-between verbal enlightenment about the featured music.
There is some local stuff-strutting in the Café Concert section, which has the Upper Galilee-based Classis Trio of cellist Oshri Shatil, French horn player Shir Farkash, and pianist Liri Dubin playing a selection of light classical works and Israeli songs.
The October 29 (5 p.m.) date also features some original material.
The previous day, Bartan joins the other members of the Rosemarin Ensemble, US-born violist Itamar Ringel and harpist Marina Fradin, in an adventurous program that takes in scores by 20th-century Israeli composer Marc Lavry, Bartok, Mozart, and genre boundary-leaping Israeli composer Gilad Cohen.
There will also be some intriguing arrangements of Israeli songs in the first Café Concert showing.
Other than the single-item final day, which brings the curtain down on the festival program with the Nahal Sheli (My Stream) concert at 11 a.m., the daily agenda ends in suitably more laid-back fashion with The End of Day 10:30 p.m. slots in the Pastoral Hotel lobby.
The quartet-based fixtures feature various musicians from the festival roster playing chestnuts from the chamber music repertoire. Audience members, ensconced in comfortable armchairs and sofas in the inviting lobby layout, will no doubt enhance their relaxing listening pleasure with a nightcap and possibly a nibble of something tasty.
And if you take the all-embracing, nonjudgmental view that music is just music, and don’t attach too much importance to genre pigeonholing, you should enjoy the headlining act on opening day, as celebrated pop-rock pianist-vocalist Shlomo Shaban takes the stage of the Beit Ha’am auditorium on Kibbutz Kfar Blum. His 8:30 p.m. solo date is described as “an intimate journey between his songs and the works and songs that paved his artistic road.”
Over the past three decades or so, the classically trained ivory tickler has cemented his place in the uppermost reaches of the national showbiz scene, with his singular vocals, eclectic musicianship, compelling songwriting, and tongue-in-cheek asides. Yitzhaki is surely on a winner with that one.
Veteran rock singer Nurit Galron bookends the nonclassical festival fare on October 31 (9 p.m.).
The Galron slot will be preceded by a rendition of Mozart’s Flute Quartet in D Major, after which the members of the foursome that performs the Mozart quartet will join Fradin, clarinetist Danny Ardman, and guitarist Adam Ben Amitai to back Galron, as the evergreen 75-year-old vocalist rolls out some of her yesteryear hits, including “Ani Eshtagea” and “Ze Hageshem.”
The Voice of Music Festival clearly keeps its programmatic options open, and the 2026 spread offers quality and varied sounds, as well as enlightening and fun events, all in one of the country’s most beautiful pastoral spots. Sounds delightful.
For tickets and more information:
www.kol-hamusica.org.il

Rubio says Ukraine without access to Starshield, future ‘under discussion’

Rubio says Ukraine without access to Starshield, future ‘under discussion’
US secretary of state says Ukraine has requested access to military-grade version of Starlink for strikes deep inside Russia.
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite service, is currently unavailable to Ukraine, but a request from Kyiv to access the system for attacks deep inside Russia is “under discussion”.
Speaking to reporters on Saturday, Rubio stressed Starshield’s distinction with Starlink, the internet service provided by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.
“Starlink is a commercial product, okay? And so it’s regulated and handled as a commercial product. Starshield is a defence product, a military product,” said Rubio, in comments released by the Department of State.
“They’ve asked for access to it in order to conduct deep strikes inside of Russia. They do not have access to it at this moment,” he added. “That’s under conversation.”
Launched in 2022 and provided to the US government, Starshield is designed for military use as it allows for deeper encryption to process sensitive information. SpaceX says it is primarily used by US defence agencies and other “government partners”.
Last week, Ukrainian officials said restrictions on Starlink terminals had slowed some drones on the battlefield, as Ukraine tries to hold back Russian forces in their nearly five-year war.
In his comments at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, Rubio also rejected Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s suggestion that the reported disruption to Starlink services in Ukraine on Wednesday was deliberate.
“Well, I don’t know what Zelenskyy said. I’m not sure Zelenskyy knows what he’s talking about, but it wasn’t deliberate. We have nothing to do with that,” Rubio said.
Zelenskyy said on Saturday that the satellites are not tracking antennas on flying objects travelling faster than 161 kilometres per hour (100 miles per hour). This is affecting Ukrainian drones in their defence against Russian jet-powered drones and in their own medium-range attacks, he added.
Rubio said the US had not ordered Starlink speeds to be reduced and that the service had reportedly been restored to its previous level.
“No one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet or slow down speed so that certain drones couldn’t use it,” he said, calling the reports “categorically false”.
The remarks came as US President Donald Trump drew criticism from Democrats and Republicans after waiving sanctions on Russia and countries that buy its oil and gas, days before the restrictions were due to take effect under a law he signed last month.
Zelenskyy also criticised the sanctions waiver on Saturday, saying easing pressure on Russia would encourage further attacks.
“Financial rewards for [President Vladimir] Putin – all of this only encourages him to keep attacking,” Zelenskyy posted on social media, urging the US to maintain pressure on Moscow.

Ancient fountain to regain former glory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
09:41:54 UTC
18:41:54 KST

AA Photo
Archaeologists are restoring an 1,800-year-old monumental fountain in the western province of Denizli’s Tripolis, meticulously piecing together 400 stone blocks to bring it back to its original glory.
Excavations and restoration work at the ancient city in the Buldan district are being carried out under the direction of Bahadır Duman, a faculty member in the Department of Classical Archaeology at Pamukkale University.
The monumental fountain, measuring 31 meters long, seven meters wide and approximately 15 meters high, was identified in the city center in 2018. Excavations were followed by restoration work to reconstruct the structure.
A team of specialists, including two Italian archaeologists, has been examining the architectural blocks and layers of the structure to determine how the fountain originally looked.
The restoration project for the fountain’s first level has been completed, while work continues to reassemble 400 stone blocks belonging to its second and third levels. Returning the blocks to their original positions is expected to help restore the monument’s historic appearance.
An international research process
Tommaso Ismaelli, an archaeologist from Italy’s National Research Council who is taking part in the project, told Anadolu Agency that the work at Tripolis goes beyond restoration, bringing together different scientific methods and technologies as part of an international research effort.
Turkish and Italian archaeologists live and work together at the excavation house, Ismaelli said, describing the team as a family.
“We are the same team; we live together and work together. We live at the Turkish excavation house and are like a family,” he said.
Ismaelli noted that Tripolis was particularly important during the Byzantine period, adding to the significance of the research. He also highlighted the remarkable state of preservation of structures, sculptures and other artifacts uncovered at the ancient city.
A new project will be prepared after the fountain’s restoration is completed, he said.
Reassembling the 400 blocks will allow researchers to better understand the monument’s architectural features, Ismaelli said, adding that the aim is to make the structure accessible to visitors.
He also said the team hopes to establish an open-air museum at the site to introduce visitors to Roman and Byzantine architecture.
Duman said the restoration work on the fountain is scheduled to be completed by the end of the year.

Scientists who discovered a third form of magnetism win major physics prize
Physicists have discovered a third form of magnetism hidden for over a century, potentially rewriting physics textbooks and transforming future technology.
- Date:
- October 18, 2026
- Source:
- Johannes Gutenberg Universitaet Mainz
- Summary:
- Physicists have uncovered a hidden third form of magnetism that challenges more than 100 years of established physics. Called altermagnetism, the discovery could transform future computing and electronics while opening an entirely new frontier in quantum research.
- Share:
Scientists have uncovered a previously unknown form of magnetism, overturning an understanding of magnetic behavior that had stood for more than a century. The discovery, known as altermagnetism, has revealed a third fundamental category of collinear magnetism and opened new possibilities for quantum materials, advanced electronics, and future computing technologies.
Three physicists responsible for the breakthrough have been named recipients of the 2026 Europhysics Prize, one of Europe's most prestigious honors in condensed matter physics. The European Physical Society (EPS) Condensed Matter Division selected Professor Jairo Sinova of Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU), Dr. Libor Šmejkal, and Professor Tomas Jungwirth for their work establishing altermagnetism as a distinct form of magnetic order alongside ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism.
"This award recognizes a fundamental discovery that challenged one of the most established paradigms in condensed matter physics," said Professor Jairo Sinova, Director of the Spin Phenomena Interdisciplinary Center (SPICE) at Mainz University. "Discovering that an entirely new magnetic phase had remained hidden for more than one hundred years demonstrates that even the most mature scientific fields can still hold fundamental surprises."
The breakthrough emerged from years of collaboration between Sinova's research group at Mainz University and Jungwirth's team at the Institute of Physics of the Czech Academy of Sciences in Prague. Šmejkal, who also maintained an affiliation in Prague, spent eight years at Mainz between 2016 and 2024, first pursuing doctoral research and later working as a postdoctoral scientist in Sinova's group.
During that period, Šmejkal played a leading role in developing the theoretical framework behind altermagnetism. By combining advanced mathematical approaches to symmetry with spintronics, which studies how electron spin can be used in electronic devices, the researchers identified a previously unrecognized pattern of magnetic behavior.
Their predictions soon attracted experimental teams around the world. Measurements of electronic properties and electrical transport in multiple materials provided evidence supporting the new magnetic classification. Altermagnetism has since grown into one of the most active areas of condensed matter physics, with research efforts expanding across Europe, North America, and Asia.
A Third Form of Magnetism Rewrites Physics
For more than 100 years, physicists generally divided collinear magnets into two fundamental categories: ferromagnets and antiferromagnets.
Ferromagnets have an overall magnetic alignment that produces a net magnetization. These materials are essential to many magnetic memory technologies used today. In conventional antiferromagnets, opposing magnetic moments cancel one another, leaving no overall magnetization and producing electronic behavior very different from that of ferromagnets.
Altermagnetism introduces a surprising third possibility.
Like antiferromagnets, altermagnets have magnetic moments that cancel out, resulting in no net magnetization. However, their electrons can exhibit properties previously associated with ferromagnets.
This unusual combination allows altermagnets to support electrical currents with strongly polarized electron spins while also displaying extremely rapid magnetic dynamics. Those characteristics could make them valuable for a new generation of spintronic devices, potentially advancing the speed and capabilities of future information technologies.
The significance extends well beyond electronics. Altermagnetism represents a previously unrecognized symmetry class of matter and has revealed unexpected connections to several major areas of modern physics, including topological phenomena, unconventional superconductivity, and quantum materials with strong interactions between electrons.
How Scientists Discovered Altermagnetism
The path toward this discovery began with theoretical investigations into unusual ways that electricity moves through magnetic materials. Among the early advances was the prediction of the crystal anomalous Hall effect, a phenomenon involving electrical transport in certain crystal structures.
Initially, these unexpected behaviors might have appeared to be unusual features of individual materials. However, the researchers eventually recognized that they were connected by a broader principle involving symmetries of electron spins.
Rather than representing isolated exceptions to established magnetic behavior, these materials belonged to an entirely different magnetic category.
A major milestone came in 2022, when the team published a comprehensive symmetry classification of altermagnetism and identified hundreds of materials that could potentially exhibit it.
Experimental physicists subsequently tested these predictions using several complementary methods. These included angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), which reveals how electrons behave inside materials, along with measurements of electrical transport.
The results confirmed altermagnetic behavior in several materials, helping establish the new classification experimentally.
Interest in the discovery has expanded rapidly. Hundreds of scientific papers have appeared within just a few years, and altermagnetism has become a prominent subject at international physics conferences. The growing research community is now investigating both its fundamental properties and its potential technological applications.
Discovery Earns Prestigious 2026 Europhysics Prize
The Europhysics Prize recognizes major advances in condensed matter physics, a field concerned with the physical properties and behavior of materials. Established in 1975, the award honors discoveries that have significantly advanced scientific understanding, with a substantial share of the recognized research conducted in Europe.
The 2026 prize recognizes the theoretical and experimental advances that established altermagnetism as a new fundamental form of collinear magnetic order.
The award ceremony was scheduled for September 2026 at the 32nd General Conference of the European Physical Society Condensed Matter Division (CMD32) in Graz, Austria.
The Scientists Behind the Breakthrough
Professor Jairo Sinova is a physics professor at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz in Germany and director of the university's Spin Phenomena Interdisciplinary Center. His research investigates magnetism, spintronics, and quantum materials.
Dr. Libor Šmejkal conducted much of the crucial theoretical work that led to the identification of altermagnetism while working at Mainz University from 2016 to 2024. His current affiliations include the Max Planck Institute for the Physics of Complex Systems, the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Physics of Solids, and the Institute of Physics of the Czech Academy of Sciences.
Professor Tomas Jungwirth is affiliated with the Institute of Physics of the Czech Academy of Sciences and the University of Nottingham. He has collaborated extensively with Sinova's Mainz research team and played a central role in establishing the theoretical foundations of altermagnetism.
Together, their work has revealed a fundamental property of magnetic matter that escaped recognition for more than a century, opening an entirely new direction for research into quantum physics and future electronic technologies.

Deaths reported when 'significant' blaze hits Canada military base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
09:41:00 UTC
18:41:00 KST

People were killed and injured in an incident that sparked a major fire at a military base in Alberta, Canada’s defense minister said Saturday, as reports indicated that large numbers of wounded were being taken to hospitals.
Fire crews scrambled late into the night as fierce winds whipped flames beyond Canadian Forces Base Wainwright and into the surrounding rural area.
It was not immediately clear how many people were killed or injured, but a doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, 180 kilometers (120 miles) northwest, told Canada’s national broadcaster that patients were being brought to hospitals across the city as health-care facilities around the base became "completely overwhelmed" by the number of people needing care.
"This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton," Dr. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told CBC News. "It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It’s a disaster. It’s a one in every 15- to 25-year disaster."
The town of Wainwright, near the base, has about 7,000 residents.
Defense Minister David McGuinty said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were involved in investigating the incident and described the situation as "very, very active and delicate." He said authorities were still working to determine what happened and expected to provide further information.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police said officers were called shortly after 4 p.m. Saturday following reports of a fire in a training area at the base.
Firefighters faced a volatile situation. Large areas of the province were hit during the day by a windstorm with gusts up to 100 kph (62.14 mph). The wind toppled some trees and sent signs flying and garbage cans rolling down streets.
By 11 p.m., the Municipal District of Wainwright said on social media the fire was being held and that property and critical infrastructure were protected. There was no evacuation order for residents.
McGuinty, speaking to reporters in Ottawa, confirmed the casualties but had no other details to share.
"I cannot recall such an incident in my short time for sure as a minister, but I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory," McGuinty said.
"We will have more to say in the coming hours and days," he added.
He said Armed Forces members were at the scene and that RCMP were also involved. "This is an active and delicate situation and soon to be an active and delicate investigation."
Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said his province was sending assistance to Alberta but did not specify what resources were being deployed.
"Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected," Prime Minister Mark Carney said earlier in a social media post.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith described the fire as "significant and tragic" and said it was affecting many military personnel.
CFB Wainwright is one of Canada’s busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations. It is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which conducts realistic battlefield exercises, and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, which provides military training.
Canadian Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre said he had spoken with Carney and the defense minister to offer support to those affected by the fire.
"Pray for Wainwright, everyone," Poilievre said in a social media post. He urged people in the area to follow emergency instructions and keep roads clear for first responders.
The fire also disrupted advance voting ahead of Monday’s referendum on whether Alberta should begin a process that could lead to independence from Canada.
Elections Alberta said two polling locations, in Lloydminster and Vermilion, closed early Saturday and the ballots were transported securely.

NHS staff who inappropriately accessed the medical records of a man mauled to death by a tiger should be sacked, Yvette Cooper said.
The health secretary said the incident – which followed reports earlier this year that staff had unnecessarily viewed details about the Southport attack victims and those murdered by Valdo Calocane in Nottingham in 2023 – was a “total disgrace”.
On Friday, Yorkshire ambulance service said it was investigating two staff who had inappropriately accessed information about William Chapman, who was mauled to death by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park last Saturday.
Cooper told Sky News on Sunday: “I take this extremely seriously. I know there’s a specific investigation going into that case, but we just need to be absolutely clear.
“No member of NHS staff should be accessing records that they do not need to see for medical care, and reasons simply for something to do with voyeurism, or what is in the news, or any of that kind of reason.
“Not only is it a total disgrace, but I’ve spoken to the NHS chief executive about this. We agree that if there are cases here of people inappropriately accessing medical records, then they should be suspended while the investigation takes place and we need a much swifter line on this because these are basic standards, and everybody across the NHS knows that these are the basic standards.”
Asked if people should be sacked, she added: “If there are breaches then people actually need to be sacked.”
A total of 15 NHS staff have now been sacked after accessing medical records belonging to the victims of a 2023 Nottingham attack, it emerged on Saturday. Calocane killed two 19-year-old students, Barnaby Webber and Grace O’Malley-Kumar, and Ian Coates, a 65-year-old caretaker, and attempted to kill three other people in the city in June 2023.
During its investigation, Nottingham university hospitals NHS trust has so far dismissed 15 staff, issued 15 final written warnings and two first written warnings. Doctors, nurses, registered healthcare professionals and other staff have been included in the investigation. The victims’ families were told about the latest update this week.
In May, the NHS trust that runs Aintree hospital in Liverpool admitted that nearly 50 staff members had looked inappropriately at the medical records of victims of the Southport knife attack. Nicola Ryan-Donnelly from Fletcher’s Solicitors, which represents many of the injured children, condemned the “deeply disturbing abuse of power and a shocking breach of privacy”.

Gaza buries remains of 75 Palestinians recovered from rubble of Israeli-bombed homes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
09:37:14 UTC
18:37:14 KST

Hundreds of Palestinians on Sunday attended the funeral of 75 people, including women and children, whose remains were recently recovered from beneath the rubble of homes destroyed by Israeli forces in Gaza during the early months of Israel’s genocidal war.
The funeral procession began outside the Daraj Sports Club before the remains were buried at Sheikh Radwan Cemetery in Gaza.
The remains, wrapped in Palestinian flags, had been laid out at the site on Saturday evening to allow relatives to bid farewell.
Abdullah al-Majdalawi, director of public relations and media for Gaza’s Civil Defence, told Anadolu that the remains had been recovered over recent weeks from several destroyed homes in the Daraj neighbourhood in northeastern Gaza.
He said the buildings were bombed while residents were inside during the early months of the war and that the victims belonged to around 20 Palestinian families, including people who had been displaced to the homes.
Majdalawi said efforts to recover bodies from beneath the rubble continue to face severe difficulties due to a lack of equipment and heavy machinery.
The recovery operations are part of the second phase of the Civil Defence’s project to retrieve the bodies of Palestinians trapped under rubble, launched on July 19.
Civil Defence spokesman Mahmoud Basal said at the time that the phase would involve searching 147 destroyed homes across Gaza and the northern and central parts of the enclave, where an estimated 1,072 bodies were believed to be trapped.
The first phase, launched in November 2025, recovered 333 bodies and remains out of 559 people believed to be buried beneath 54 destroyed homes and buildings. Limited resources prevented teams from reaching around 226 others.
Basal told Anadolu on October 7 that more than 8,000 missing Palestinians were still believed to be under the rubble and warned that recovering them with currently available resources could take around eight years.
Under the first phase of a ceasefire agreement in effect in Gaza since October 10 2025, Israel was expected to allow heavy equipment and machinery into the enclave, but Palestinian authorities and factions have accused it of failing to meet that and other commitments.
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 injured since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, while around 90 percent of the enclave’s civilian infrastructure has been destroyed.

When shoppers step into Rokid’s brand new flagship store in Hong Kong, they are greeted not by eager sales associates, but by glowing monitor screens and a robotic system waiting at the exit.

A drone entered Lithuania from Poland on Sunday morning before crashing in the north of the country.
“The object is preliminarily believed to have entered Lithuanian airspace from Poland. I have already contacted the Polish defence minister and asked Poland to join the investigation so that we can look into this incident together,” Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas told reporters.
“The latest information from the police is that the debris may have damaged a civilian car,” Kaunas said. “The debris has been found, the area has been cordoned off, and the police are working to gather all the information.”
National Crisis Management Centre (NKVC) head Vilmantas Vitkauskas confirmed to LRT RADIO that the object was most likely a Ukrainian drone, which could have entered the country as Kyiv carried out strikes in the St Petersburg region.
The authorities later confirmed that drone debris hit and damaged a moving car in northern Lithuania, but no one was injured.
“A person travelling from Biržai towards Pasvalys heard an explosion. Debris damaged their private car, denting the door. Clearly, some kind of explosion occurred. That is at least the preliminary information we have from the person who was at the scene,” Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius told reporters.
NATO jets scrambled
Defence Minister Kaunas said fighter jets were scrambled after the object was detected, but pilots couldn't see it visually because of poor weather.
In response to the suspected drone threat, an air alert was issued only in northern Lithuania. Kaunas said he found the situation “strange and unacceptable”.
“The military has already been tasked with gathering all the information and providing me with a detailed report. We will also look into the matter with the Fire and Rescue Department to establish why alerts were not sent out in time, if that is indeed what happened. We will analyse this, because it is absolutely unacceptable.
“If the object had already been detected in one part of Lithuania, everyone should have been informed in time. This issue has therefore already been raised,” Kaunas said.
War is ‘spilling over’
Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said Russia’s war against Ukraine “is spilling over onto the Eastern flank of NATO and EU”.
“What appears to be a drone exploded over the northern part of the country, posing a danger to the civilian population,” he posted on X.

Police arrest 1,800 after worst rioting in years shakes France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
09:31:00 UTC
18:31:00 KST

France grappled Sunday with widespread damage from violent protests that had led to 1,800 arrests, a torched historic town hall and looted shops.
The unrest, which officials described as extraordinarily intense, raised the stakes for President Emmanuel Macron. He is in his final months in power before elections in six months. The unrest followed weeks of student protests that also turned violent.
"About 1,800 people have been arrested, and investigations are underway to identify and prosecute perpetrators," Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on X Sunday.
In Paris, where police said a record 855 people had been arrested, streets were littered with burnt-out barricades made of bikes, bins and other materials. Shop windows were smashed and cars torched on several streets.
The capital experienced "a level of violence that we have never, I believe, seen before," said Paris Deputy Mayor Lamia El Aaraje.
Masked youths pillaged scores of shops in Paris and many other cities, including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Strasbourg, during the protests, which were called against high inflation and rising living costs.
Limoges' 19th-century town hall was destroyed by a fire that local prefect Maurice Barate told LCI television had been deliberately set by a "wild horde." Firefighters brought the blaze under control early Sunday.
Political recriminations followed the scenes of destruction.
Macron's centrist government and far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen both blamed "ultra-left" groups for the violence.
Far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon, who had strongly backed the demonstrations, urged protesters late Saturday to avoid looting, describing it as "contrary to our methods."
Paris' Socialist Deputy Mayor Lamia El Aaraje accused Le Pen's party of fueling tensions related to the protests to further her ambition of becoming president next year.
The far-right National Rally party was "acting like a pyromaniac firefighter," El Aaraje said.
U.S. Vice President JD Vance also commented, implying that the unrest stemmed from immigration.
"Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion. They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility," Vance said on X.
In Paris, where startled tourists ran with suitcases Saturday on streets filled with tear gas and protesters, the prosecutor's office said more than 500 people were in custody.
It said officials made arrests overnight into Sunday, with most held on suspicion of receiving stolen goods, association with intent to commit violence and vandalism.
Officials in Lyon said 160 people were in custody.
About 500 police officers, firefighters and paramedics were injured in the protests, Interior Minister Nunez said, adding the figure was provisional.
The violence occurred alongside nationwide cost-of-living protests, attended by 550,000 people according to the Interior Ministry, while the CGT union reported 800,000 participants.
Police used tear gas and water cannons against protesters who threw projectiles and aimed fireworks.
A crowd-control grenade blew off a 17-year-old boy's right hand in the southern city of Saint-Etienne.
Analyst Mujtaba Rahman of the Eurasia Group think tank said on X that Saturday's "terrible scenes were not political protest in any true sense. Most of the real demonstrations against high oil prices and failing schools were peaceful."
He added, "The violence came from a fringe of the ultra left. The looting by opportunistic gangs from the poor suburbs. All good news for Marine Le Pen."
During and after the demonstrations, gangs of youths roamed city streets, sporadically confronting police, setting fires and attacking shuttered stores to break in and empty shelves.
France's Yellow Vest movement, which staged protests eight years ago against planned fuel-tax hikes by Macron's government, called for Saturday's "yellow and youth" demonstrations.
The primary grievance was the cost of living, which the war in the Middle East partly drove up, contributing to soaring inflation in Europe and elsewhere.

Feature: How Zhengzhou Marathon turns race into journey through Chinese civilization
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
17:27:10 CST
18:27:10 KST

ZHENGZHOU, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- For most marathon runners, 42.195 kilometers is a test of endurance, discipline and will. In Zhengzhou, central China's Henan Province, the distance can also become a journey through thousands of years of Chinese civilization.
Held on October 18, the 2026 Zhengzhou Marathon offered a distinctive fusion of city running and cultural heritage.
"What surprised me most this year was the encounter between poetry and the marathon," said Tang Tao, a 35-year-old runner from Zhengzhou who has taken part in six consecutive editions of the event.
"Whether it was the ambience of the event or the on-site interactive activities, I felt surrounded by poetry," Tang said.
At the pre-race carnival, a specially designed "poetry corridor" drew visitors eager to photograph banners bearing famous Chinese verses. Lines such as "A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step" and "Wildfires cannot burn it all away; the spring breeze brings it back to life" prompted spontaneous recitations, creating a fitting prelude to a race defined by perseverance and determination.
Together, these poems offered a fitting prelude to the marathon, where perseverance, uncertainty and the determination to keep moving forward are part of every runner's experience.
For Jong-May Urbonya, an American cultural influencer with nearly half a million followers who promotes Hanfu and Chinese traditions online, the poems struck a chord.
"The indomitable and forward-looking spirit depicted in the verses is precisely what marathon runners must possess," Urbonya said.
Poetry is only part of the story. As one of the cradles of Chinese civilization, Zhengzhou bears a long, continuous cultural thread beneath its layers of history. The 3,600-year-old Shang Dynasty city wall still stands in the city center , a reminder of the meeting of ancient and modern.
Zhao Hengkang, director of the Zhengzhou Sports Bureau, said the 2026 event wove four major local cultural elements - poetry, surnames, Henan Opera and kung fu - throughout the program.
Since its inaugural edition in 2018, the Zhengzhou Marathon has promoted a "Surname Marathon" concept rooted in Henan's kinship culture - the province is regarded as the ancestral home for many Chinese families and the origin of numerous surnames.
"For Chinese participants, a surname can evoke family history, ancestral origins and a sense of belonging. For international runners, the experience offers an accessible introduction to a cultural tradition in which a single family name may carry centuries of historical memory," said Ge Xiangyu, a runner who crossed the finish line carrying a flag bearing his surname.
Showing his medal, Ge added, "The symbolism goes beyond that of a souvenir," he said, noting that runners can personalize the design with magnetic stickers bearing their own surnames, making each medal uniquely their own.
Amid the hundreds of marathons held across China each year, culture is what sets Zhengzhou apart.
"We hope to make the Zhengzhou Marathon not only a competitive event for 25,000 runners, but also an immersive journey into the charm of traditional Chinese culture," Zhao said. ■

Interview: IMF official says China makes proactive efforts for maintaining multilateral, rules-based trading system
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
17:27:02 CST
18:27:02 KST

Thomas Helbling, deputy director in the International Monetary Fund (IMF)'s Asia and Pacific Department, speaks in an interview with Xinhua in Bangkok, Thailand on Oct. 12, 2026. (Photo by Rachen Sageamsak/Xinhua)
by Geng Lingnan, Liu Yang
BANGKOK, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- China makes proactive efforts for maintaining a multilateral and rules-based trading system, and Chinese companies can play an important role in the diffusion of new technologies and in supporting their application through outbound investment, an International Monetary Fund (IMF) official has said.
The IMF has welcomed China's proactive efforts for maintaining a multilateral and rules-based trading system, Thomas Helbling, deputy director in the IMF's Asia and Pacific Department, told Xinhua in an interview on the sidelines of the 2026 Annual Meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group held in Bangkok, Thailand.
"Ultimately, it will be important that countries resolve underlying tensions and differences behind trade disputes. For a large economy like China, it will be important for it to take on a leadership role in resolving some of these differences," he said.
Helbling also expects China to help deliver the benefits from new technologies to other countries through investment. Foreign direct investment by Chinese companies can play an important role in the diffusion of new technologies and in supporting their application in other countries, including in the digital and green energy sectors, he explained.
Helbling said the IMF remains concerned about risks from greater geoeconomic fragmentation and geopolitical tensions, which could obstruct trade and lead to greater trade frictions and more inefficiencies in the global and regional economy, as well as lower growth.
He stressed the IMF has long advocated that countries work toward resolution of the underlying issues behind trade tensions and toward an open, ideally multilateral trading system.
Speaking of economic resilience in China, and in Asia overall, Helbling noted that the impact of the energy shock has been more muted than expected earlier in the year, adding that in China's case, the government has mitigated the impact on end-user prices and mobilized other energy sources to partly compensate for the negative fossil fuel supply shock.
In addition, the AI boom is broadening and has broader positive spillover effects on the region, including China, he said.
In its latest Regional Economic Outlook for Asia and Pacific released on Thursday, the IMF raised Asia's 2026 economic growth forecast to 4.8 percent, up 0.4 percentage points from its April projection.
On the Asia-Pacific economic outlook, Helbling noted that while inventory buffers and measures such as energy subsidies or tax reductions have limited the impact of the energy supply shock, such measures are difficult to sustain over time.
He explained that if the energy shock lasts longer or intensifies, countries will at some point deplete their inventories, and the full price impact will affect the economy more severely. He recommended that countries rebuild buffers to ensure that they are in a position to effectively respond to another energy supply shock. ■
Thomas Helbling, deputy director in the International Monetary Fund (IMF)'s Asia and Pacific Department, speaks in an interview with Xinhua in Bangkok, Thailand on Oct. 12, 2026. (Photo by Rachen Sageamsak/Xinhua)

Food or medicine? The impossible choices facing Sudan’s chronically ill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
09:22:44 UTC
18:22:44 KST

Food or medicine? The impossible choices facing Sudan’s chronically ill
Sudanese are facing growing costs of medicine caused by the country’s civil war.
Hasanat al-Rashid, 48, has lived with diabetes for 15 years, and the three-and-a-half-year civil war between Sudan’s military and the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary group has worsened her situation. Finding the treatment she needs has become a daily struggle.
When the war broke out in April 2023, she was forced to flee south from her home in Haj Yousif in Khartoum North to Umm Daw Ban in Khartoum State.
During her displacement, she went for days without medication and was forced to eat foods unsuitable for her condition, such as asida, a traditional Sudanese porridge.
She underwent operations on her foot twice when she developed complications of diabetes, including a severe infection.
She moved between hospitals in Gezira State south of Khartoum, seeking treatment in Rufaa, Wad Madani and Al-Hasahisa. When fighting spread to these areas in December 2023, she fled again, arriving in Port Sudan, a city on the Red Sea that was less affected by the war.
Her condition has worsened to the point that she now has to use insulin every day and with this comes added costs, something that forces diabetes sufferers in Sudan to choose between medicine and other essentials, such as food.
“The doses vary depending on whether my blood sugar is high or low,” she told Al Jazeera.
The war has pushed income levels in Sudan back to those last seen in the 1990s, according to the United Nations Development Programme. This means Hasanat and other diabetes sufferers are struggling to afford the medicine they need to treat the condition.
Hasanat’s doctor recommended she use an insulin pen, a device used to inject insulin under the skin. She would need one or two of the devices a month, but the cost at 70,000 Sudanese pounds ($8) is more than she can afford up front, so she opts for a vial of insulin.
This is cheaper at 17,000 Sudanese pounds ($1.80), but there is the additional cost of buying ice every day to keep the insulin cool. She spends 180,000 pounds ($20) a month on ice to preserve the medicine. But she is able to spread these costs out through the month, making the vials her only viable option even if the overall costs are higher than an insulin pen.
“It may last a month or less, but the challenge is that I don’t have a refrigerator, so I struggle to store the insulin properly,” she said.
She also needs painkillers and vitamins on a regular basis to manage complications caused by the diabetes.
The rising cost of treatment
Fatima Adam, 75, is among the patients at Port Sudan Hospital struggling to afford the medicines she needs to manage her hypertension and a thyroid condition.
She was admitted to the hospital with complications caused by high blood pressure, which has started to impact her heart. Too unwell to speak to Al Jazeera herself, her daughter, Aisha, described how the rising cost of treatment has affected her whole family.
Before the war, Fatima received medicine through the National Health Insurance Fund. She paid a quarter of the cost while the fund covered the rest. But when the war started and the economy collapsed, the medicines she needed were no longer covered by the scheme.
“My mother takes six different medicines because hypertension has affected her heart in addition to her thyroid medication. The war has made things harder because the prices of these medicines have gone up,” Aisha told Al Jazeera.
The responsibility for paying for Fatima’s treatment and supporting her and her daughter falls on her son, who works as a casual worker. With no fixed income, he goes to the market every day in search of work but sometimes returns home empty without any luck.
“Sometimes, when my brother finds work, we buy enough medicine to last a month. Other times, we have to buy smaller quantities and take the medicines intermittently,” Aisha said.
She bought a month’s supply of her mother’s medication a few days ago for 160,000 Sudanese pounds ($17.80), a substantial expense for a family whose income depends on day labour but essential to treating Fatima’s condition.
War damage
The war has caused an estimated $500m in losses to medicine stocks, infrastructure and transport fleets, dealing a major blow to Sudan’s pharmaceutical supply system, the National Medical Supplies Fund told Al Jazeera.
The National Medicines and Poisons Board estimated that only eight of the 30 pharmaceutical factories in Khartoum that shut down during the conflict have resumed operations despite the security situation in the capital recently improving.
This has increased Sudan’s reliance on imported medicines, but the subsequent depreciation of the Sudanese pound has driven up the costs of pharmaceutical procurement and production.
Hossam al-Naeem, who works as a pharmacist in Port Sudan, said customers with diabetes and hypertension require regular painkillers and vitamins to help their overall condition.
“I feel deeply saddened when I see the expressions on some patients’ faces as they ask about the prices of medicines and discover how much they have increased because of the depreciation of the Sudanese pound,” Hossam told Al Jazeera.
The currency’s collapse has created added challenges for pharmacists. Before the war, a dollar traded for roughly 600 Sudanese pounds. Now black-market currency traders are quoting rates of 9,300 pounds to the dollar, meaning higher costs for most goods in Sudan.
Sometimes Hossam incurs losses himself when he finds that the prices of drugs have risen sharply, and keeping essential medicines stocked is becoming difficult.
“I used to sell a strip of cold and flu tablets for 6,000 Sudanese pounds [70 cents]. But when I went to buy new stock, I found that the supplier’s price was also 6,000 pounds per strip. That means I made no profit, not even enough to cover the pharmacy’s operating costs,” he said.
The struggle to afford heart medication
Huda Mahmoud, 58, lives in el-Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan state in south-central Sudan, where drone attacks and other violence remain a problem while the military is making advances towards the city.
Huda has lived with heart problems for more than 12 years and described the impacts of the war as being physical, financial and emotional.
“I take five different medicines. There was a time when they weren’t available, and I suffered a lot. Sometimes, I had to ask people in Wad Madani, Sennar or Port Sudan to send them to me,” she told Al Jazeera. “The medicines were extremely expensive, costing me 300,000 Sudanese pounds [$33.30] a month.”
Taking medication has become a carefully managed routine with each pill tied to a specific time of day.
“I’ve become tied to my pills: this one before eating, that one afterwards. If I forget one, my heart starts beating very fast,” she added.
In March, Huda was forced to travel from el-Obeid to Omdurman. Following her strict treatment regimen has become increasingly difficult during repeated periods of upheaval.
She has now returned home to el-Obeid, where her regular medicine is priced at 151,000 Sudanese pounds ($16.80) a month, something she can barely afford.
Her greatest fear is running out of medicine or being unable to afford her next supply, which would put her at risk of a blood clot.
“I’m afraid of becoming incapacitated. I used to be responsible for the whole household, but now I need help. I feel like I’ve become a burden on my family,” she said.

Footage released by Yemen’s Houthis appears to show a Saudi National Guard AH-6i helicopter being struck by a loitering munition over Saudi Arabia’s Najran province, after the Saudi-led coalition said the aircraft crashed because of a technical malfunction, killing its two crew members.
Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki said on Oct. 18 that the AH-6i reconnaissance helicopter, which belonged to Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of National Guard, crashed and was destroyed inside Saudi territory in the Najran area, near the border with Yemen. Both officers on board were killed. The coalition did not identify them or give further details.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree had said a day earlier that the group shot down a Saudi helicopter, which he described as an Apache, near Najran while it was attacking Houthi positions along the border. Al-Maliki responded on social media with a photo of a row of Apache helicopters, writing that the Houthis claimed to have shot one down but that it would enter the battlefield soon.
The video the Houthis later published appears to show a small helicopter consistent with the AH-6i being hit in flight. The weapon in the footage appears to be an Iranian-designed loitering munition from the 358 family, which the Houthis field under the name Saqr.
The 358 is a small, jet-powered surface-to-air loitering munition. Launched from a rail, it can circle over an area, search for low, slow targets such as helicopters and drones, and detonate near them. Iranian-made 358 components have been found in weapons shipments to the Houthis intercepted at sea, and the group has used the munition against drones over Yemen.
The AH-6i is a light attack and reconnaissance helicopter built by Boeing and based on the MH-6 Little Bird used by U.S. special operations forces. It carries a crew of two and can be armed with machine guns, rockets and guided missiles. The Saudi Arabian National Guard ordered about two dozen of the helicopters from the United States in the mid-2010s and uses them for reconnaissance and close air support.
Najran has come under repeated Houthi drone and missile attacks in recent weeks as fighting between the coalition and the Yemen-based group escalated. A week before the crash, Houthi strikes killed 13 people at Riyadh’s international airport, the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.

Vietnam signs free trade deal with four European countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

09:19:00 UTC

Vietnam signs free trade deal with four European countries
October 18, 2026
Vietnam and four European countries signed a free trade agreement in Hanoi on Sunday.
The deal was announced by the governments of Vietnam and Norway.
Vietnam's Trade Ministry said it signed the deal with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), which is made up Norway, Switzerland, Iceland and Liechtenstein.
The four European countries are not part of the European Union (EU).
The official talks between Vietnam and the EFTA began in 2012. The talks were interrupted in 2018 and only resumed last year.
How does the deal benefit Vietnam?
The agreement between Vietnam, which is Southeast Asia's fastest-growing economy, and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) waives or reduces customs duties, including on imports of industrial, fish and agricultural products.
Under the deal, around half of Norway's exports to Vietnam will be tariff-free, with more than 98% to be tariff-free within seven years, the Norwegian government said in a statement.
According to the signing parties, the deal covers trade in goods and services, intellectual property rights, trade remedies and sustainable development, among other areas, both parties say.
Last year, the trade value between the EFTA and Vietnam stood at €4.8 billion ($5.4 billion), according to the association.
Vietnam said the agreement showed the parties' resolve to "reinforce the rules-based trading system amid continued volatility in the global economy," according to a government statement.
It was also expected to help Vietnam "diversify its import and export markets" and "integrate more deeply into global value chains," the government said.

How Often Do Car Parts Need to Be Replaced?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
09:18:40 UTC
18:18:40 KST

There is no single interval for every part. Brake pads may be replaced according to wear, while timing belts usually follow a specific mileage or time interval.
Owners searching for kia spare parts sharjah, hyundai spare parts sharjah, or infiniti spare parts sharjah should match parts with the exact model, engine specification, and manufacturer requirements. Al-Miyar offers replacement parts matched to different vehicle specifications.
How Often Do Car Parts Need to Be Replaced?
Every component experiences different stress. Some parts wear through friction, while others deteriorate because of heat, vibration, contamination, or age. As a result, car parts replacement intervals vary significantly.
Driving conditions also affect car parts replacement schedule. Heavy traffic, short trips, dusty roads, extreme temperatures, towing, and heavy loads can increase wear.
A practical plan should consider:
· Mileage and vehicle age
· Manufacturer recommendations
· Driving and road conditions
· Climate
· Visible wear or damage
· Changes in performance
· Maintenance history
This provides a more realistic way to determine how often to replace car parts.
Which Car Parts Usually Need More Attention?
Some components need regular inspection because they experience continuous wear or affect vehicle control. Understanding when to replace car parts is particularly important for brakes and tires.
Brake Pads and Brake Rotors
Brake components directly affect stopping performance. Brake pads become thinner through friction, but their service life varies with driving habits, traffic, vehicle weight, road conditions, and brake-system design.
Warning signs include:
· Squealing or grinding
· Vibration during braking
· Changes in pedal feel
· Longer stopping distances
· Reduced pad material
Brake rotors may also require replacement when excessively worn, damaged, or below the manufacturer's specified thickness. Inspection is more useful than relying only on mileage.
 
Tires
 
Tire replacement cannot be determined by mileage alone. Tread depth, uneven wear, cracks, age, damage, and handling changes can indicate that a tire needs attention.
 
Incorrect pressure and poor wheel alignment can accelerate uneven wear. Regular inspection helps maintain traction and handling.
 
Engine Oil and Filters
 
Engine oil becomes contaminated and may lose protective properties. Oil-change intervals depend on the vehicle, engine, oil specification, driving conditions, and manufacturer recommendations.
 
Oil filters are commonly replaced during an oil service. Al-Miyar offers parts for different vehicle models.
 
Parts With Longer but More Important Replacement Intervals
 
Some components remain in service longer, but their specified intervals are important.
 
Timing Belts
A timing belt synchronizes important engine components and may fail without an obvious warning. Replacement is generally based on the manufacturer's mileage or time interval.
 
On some engines, failure can cause significant engine damage. The car parts replacement schedule should account for both mileage and age when specified.
 
Batteries
 
A battery gradually loses its ability to hold a charge. Climate, driving patterns, electrical demand, battery type, and vehicle usage affect its useful life.
 
Slow cranking, dimming electrical systems, or starting difficulties may indicate that testing is needed. Unlike a timing belt, a battery does not have one universal replacement point.
 
Spark Plugs
 
Spark plugs are essential to petrol-engine combustion, but service intervals vary by engine and plug type.
 
Worn plugs can contribute to rough running, difficult starting, reduced fuel efficiency, or misfires. The vehicle-specific maintenance schedule is more reliable than a generic mileage figure.
How Driving Conditions Change Replacement Timing
 
Two vehicles with identical mileage can have different maintenance requirements. A vehicle driven on open roads may experience different wear from one driven the same distance in congested traffic.
 
Severe conditions include:
 
1.     Frequent short journeys
 
2.     Heavy stop-and-go traffic
 
3.     Extreme temperatures
 
4.     Dusty or poorly surfaced roads
 
5.     Heavy towing or loads
 
6.     Long periods of inactivity
 
Therefore, how often to replace car parts should be considered alongside actual vehicle use. Urban braking can increase brake wear, while dusty roads may require more frequent air-filter inspections.
 
A Practical Replacement Schedule
 
There is no universal schedule, but this framework identifies key items to monitor.
This table is a general framework, not a substitute for the maintenance schedule for a specific vehicle.
 
When Should You Replace a Part Before It Fails?
 
Waiting for complete failure is not always appropriate, particularly for braking, steering, suspension, tires, and engine timing components.
 
The useful question is whether the part still operates within its required limits. Replacing a brake pad at its specified wear limit is different from waiting until all friction material disappears.
 
Similarly, replacing a timing belt at its scheduled interval is different from waiting for failure. Understanding how often should car parts be replaced can help address wear before it becomes a larger mechanical problem.
 
The Maintenance Schedule Is a Starting Point, Not the Whole Story
 
A manufacturer's schedule provides a baseline for a specific vehicle and powertrain, but actual component condition also matters.
 
Drivers should notice unusual sounds, vibrations, warning lights, fluid leaks, braking changes, starting difficulties, or handling changes. Regular inspections can identify developing problems before they result in expensive repairs.
 
A vehicle-specific maintenance plan is the clearest reference for "how often do car parts need to be replaced", while inspections help account for actual wear and changing driving conditions.
 
Maintenance records are also useful for tracking time- and mileage-based services. For owners asking how often do car parts need to be replaced, the most reliable approach combines manufacturer recommendations, mileage and age, and the actual condition of each component.
 
Not sure whether a part is due for replacement or simply needs inspection? Start with the vehicle's maintenance schedule, then have the component's actual condition checked before deciding to replace it.
 
Conclusion
 
There is no universal answer to how often do car parts need to be replaced because components have different service requirements. Brake pads and tires depend heavily on wear and driving conditions, while timing belts and spark plugs generally follow vehicle-specific intervals.
 
The practical approach is to combine the manufacturer's schedule with regular inspections and attention to warning signs. This helps owners address worn components before complete failure.

Fighting intensifies across Yemen as humanitarian crisis deepens
Clashes between Yemeni forces and Houthis cause casualties on both sides as aid agencies warn of a deepening human crisis.
Fighting between government forces and Houthi fighters has intensified across multiple fronts in Yemen amid a spiralling humanitarian crisis.
Eight soldiers loyal to the internationally recognised Yemeni government were killed during heavy clashes on the al-Maqatirah front in Lahij governorate, the government-affiliated Tur al-Bahah military axis said in a statement on Saturday.
In Taiz governorate, government troops said they killed 12 Houthi fighters in al-Aqroud, following days of fighting on the outskirts of Taiz city, where Saudi Arabia-backed government forces reported repelling Houthi advances and inflicting heavy losses on the group.
Elsewhere in Taiz, government forces said they broke a Houthi attack on the al-Shaqab front, while government-aligned Homeland Shield Forces reported destroying a Houthi supply vehicle with a drone in al-Wazziyah. The Southern Giants Brigades also said they targeted Houthi positions with precision strikes in al-Madaribah, near the Lahij border.
Meanwhile, government troops and allied Popular Resistance fighters pressed ahead with their offensive in al-Jawf and Marib.
Military officials reported using artillery barrages and drone strikes against Houthi military positions, barracks and troop assemblies in al-Jawf, while coalition aircraft bombed Houthi command hubs and supply depots.
Government artillery and missile units also targeted Houthi lines in Marib.
Yemen’s war has escalated sharply since the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), seized strategic territory from forces loyal to the country’s internationally recognised government along the Red Sea coast last month.
Government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, responded to the losses with a counteroffensive, and then launched the “Dawn of Yemen” operation, which aims to recapture Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, seized by the Iran-aligned group in 2014.
Saudi helicopter crashes
On the aerial front, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed that the group’s air defence forces brought down a Saudi reconnaissance drone over the governorate of Hajjah. He identified the aircraft as a Turkish-manufactured Lentatek Karayel drone, saying it was the fourth of its kind downed since the latest escalation began.
The Houthis also claimed they shot down a Saudi Apache helicopter in the kingdom’s border province of Najran.
Saudi-led coalition spokesman Colonel Turki al-Maliki said an AH-6i reconnaissance helicopter had crashed in Najran due to a technical malfunction, killing two crew members.
Houthi media also reported 10 Saudi air strikes targeting sites in Saada governorate.
Off the coast of al-Mukalla, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency reported that at least seven armed men on board a skiff attacked a liquefied natural gas (LNG) tanker. They fired two shots at the tanker before the vessel’s onboard security detail returned two warning shots, forcing the attackers to change course and disengage.
Worsening humanitarian crisis
Meanwhile, the human cost of the conflict continues to rise, with humanitarian agencies warning of worsening conditions for civilians.
According to the International Organization for Migration, more than 233,000 people have been displaced since fighting escalated in Yemen, including about 121,000 in Taiz governorate alone.
The World Health Organization has also warned that Taiz city has become functionally isolated, with its 12 hospitals holding fuel for only four days, no surgical supplies, and facing critical shortages of oxygen and medicine amid a growing cholera outbreak.
The displacement crisis has spread to East Africa, with the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) confirming that more than 4,000 refugees have reached the region — 3,800 in Djibouti and roughly 200 in Somalia. The UNHCR also reported that health workers are treating a cholera outbreak at Djibouti’s Markazi camp, where 31 cases and one death have been recorded.

Summer drought drives up truffle prices in Switzerland

Summer drought drives up truffle prices in Switzerland
This summer’s drought has severely impacted the truffle season. The truffles are smaller than usual and scarce in the forests of canton Vaud, which has driven up prices. At the truffle market in the region La Côte, for example, the price per kilogram of truffles has risen by 30%, from CHF700 to CHF1,000 ($847-$1,210).
In the forests of Vaud, Joachim Fivaz and his dog Cita are searching for the prized mushroom. The dog’s nose is spot-on, but the haul is disappointing: the truffles are significantly smaller than usual. The reason? These mushrooms need moisture during their seven-month growth cycle, and the summer heatwave proved fatal for them.
+ Drought in Switzerland: Europe’s ‘water tower’ runs dry
At La Côte truffle market, the effects are being felt. This Saturday, there were only three vendors – half as many as last year. This scarcity is driving up prices: CHF1,000 per kilo this year, compared to CHF700 last year. A 30% increase that hasn’t deterred enthusiasts, however. “Chocolate is expensive, but we don’t deprive ourselves of it – and neither do we with truffles,” says one customer. “We can treat ourselves with just a few grams – no need to buy kilos,” adds another.
Rahman Dedic, president of the French-Speaking Switzerland Truffle Association, explains the price increase. “Given that there are fewer truffles and we have to travel farther to find them, it’s normal for prices to be higher than last year.” For those who make their living from truffles, he acknowledges that “it’s been a very difficult year”.
Several other truffle markets are scheduled for the coming weeks in French-speaking Switzerland.
