Japan to launch world-first mission to collect samples from Martian moon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
08:11:55 UTC
17:11:55 KST

Japan is to launch a spacecraft on the world’s first mission to bring back samples from Phobos, one of the two small, potato-shaped moons orbiting Mars.
Scientists hope the mission, which is expected to take five years, will provide clues to how Phobos and its smaller sibling Deimos formed, and hopefully even shed light on the origins of life in the solar system.
The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (Jaxa) is aiming to launch the spacecraft on Tuesday on a new Japanese mainstay H3 rocket.
Yasuhiro Kawakatsu, the project manager for the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission, said samples from Phobos would provide useful data for scientists to consider using a Martian moon as a base for a future manned mission to the planet. The US, China and others are hoping to send astronauts to Mars.
“Despite their potential importance, Martian moons have never been fully investigated,” Kawakatsu said. “They are known as the most important unclimbed mountains in the solar system.”
Japan is leading an international mission, which includes equipment and communications support from Nasa and other national space agencies.
Since the 1960s, dozens of missions have been sent to Mars, but its moons largely remain a mystery. Multiple Russian attempts to land on Phobos, including one launched in 2011, have failed.
Phobos and Deimos take their names from the Greek mythological personifications of fear and terror, sons of the war god Ares, whose Roman counterpart is Mars.
A key question is how they formed and what they are made of. Some scientists think the two irregular crater-pocked bodies could be remnants of debris formed after a large celestial object crashed into Mars. Others say the moons could be asteroids that have come from elsewhere.
Jaxa officials think samples from Phobos will provide answers. “We can almost certainly come to a conclusion by analysing soil samples,” said Kiyoshi Kuramoto, the principal investigator on the mission.
Scientists chose to collect samples from Phobos mainly because the moon is closer to Mars than Deimos, and therefore may have more information about the planet. Material from Mars is expected to make up about 0.1% of the material collected from Phobos, Jaxa officials say.
Phobos is about 27km (17 miles) in diameter at its widest point, and orbits Mars at a distance of about 6,000km (3,700 miles) three times a day.
Samples from Phobos could also shed light on the origin of Deimos as the two moons were believed to have similar roots, Kuramoto said. The mission includes plans to fly by Deimos and collect observations.
It will be a long journey to reach the red planet, which is 55m km away from Earth at its closest point. The actual flight distance would be 500-600m km, Kawakatsu said.
After launching on the H3 rocket, the spacecraft will arrive at the Mars region around August 2027. It will then fly near and around Phobos for three years to collect data and samples from the moon, before returning home in 2031.
MMX is made up of three modules, for propulsion, exploration and return. Only the third module will return home with the samples.
The spacecraft will carry 13 instruments, including a rover jointly developed by France and Germany that will land on the moon, as well as a Nasa sampling device and instrument to measure gamma rays, and the European Space Agency’s deep space communication device. A Japanese radiation monitor will collect data that can help a future manned Mars exploration.
The French-German rover Idefix is due to land on Phobos first. During a 100-day mission in around 2029, it will explore the surface to help the subsequent Japanese soil-sampling. The spacecraft will choose a relatively smooth and level site for its landing based on topographical data provided by the rover.
Once the MMX mission lands, Jaxa scientists aim to collect at least 10g (0.35oz) of soil from the moon from two sampling attempts using US and Japanese methods.
Nasa’s sampling device uses pressurised gas to lift surface dust into a container, and Jaxa’s coring method will collect samples from a depth of about 2cm (0.8in). In the first attempt, the MMX will collect surface and underground samples using both devices, and take additional underground samples in the second landing.
Scientists say collecting samples from multiple locations increases the chances of obtaining any potential traces of past microbial life from Mars.
Landing on the pockmarked moon, which has just one two-thousandths of Earth’s gravity, is a challenge. To minimise bouncing at touchdown, the MMX’s exploration module is equipped with four-legged landing gear with shock absorption features.
The rover has wheels that can get traction in low gravity, right itself if it tips over, and move “at a snail’s pace”, according to Jaxa.
The samples will be stored in a heat-protected capsule designed to survive reentry into Earth’s atmosphere. The module is expected to land in Australia before being sent back to Japan.

Latvia’s combat-tested ground drone shows off in Finland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
08:11:25 UTC
17:11:25 KST

- Latvian company NATRIX demonstrated its combat-tested unmanned ground vehicle at Millog’s UGV Demo 2026 in Mikkeli, Finland, on Oct. 8.
- The vehicle showed forest mobility, obstacle crossing, cargo transport and remote control before Finnish military, border guard and police officials.
Latvian company NATRIX, already a supplier of ground drones to Latvia’s armed forces, showed its battle-tested unmanned ground vehicle to Finnish military and security officials on Oct. 8, driving it through forest terrain and hauling cargo at an unmanned ground systems demonstration in Mikkeli, Finland.
The event was organized by Millog, the Finnish defense maintenance company that services much of the Finnish Defence Forces’ equipment, and brought together several manufacturers of ground drones. NATRIX attended with its Finnish partner Armatech Finland, the company said in a LinkedIn post, and showed the vehicle to representatives from several branches of the Finnish Defence Forces, the Finnish Ministry of Defence, the Finnish Border Guard, the Police of Finland and international military delegations.
In its live demonstration, NATRIX said the vehicle showed its mobility and ability to cross obstacles in rough forest terrain, carried cargo, and was driven remotely by an operator. The company also briefed visitors on lessons from the platform’s use in combat.
The NATRIX UGV is a compact, battery-powered vehicle built for front-line resupply, casualty evacuation and reconnaissance support. The company says it can carry more than 200 kg (440 pounds) of cargo and can be fitted with a NATO-standard stretcher to bring out wounded troops, and that its communications use several backup channels to stay connected in jammed environments.
The platform began combat testing in Ukraine’s Donbas region in early 2025, after the first vehicles were funded through a donation campaign run by Latvian public media and the Ziedot.lv charity platform. Co-founder Gatis Vectirāns said at the time that a fully charged vehicle could travel about 20 km (12 miles), and that Ukrainian operators had praised its power and build quality, Latvian public broadcaster LSM reported.
In April 2026, Latvia’s Ministry of Defence signed contracts with NATRIX and two other Latvian companies, Brasa Defence Systems and LV-Teh, to supply domestically made ground drones and gradually introduce them into regular units of the National Armed Forces, The Defence Blog reported. The deals followed live demonstrations on military training ranges in 2025 and include support, repair and modernization, as well as the right for Latvia to order more systems quickly under the same framework.
Ukraine now relies heavily on ground drones to move ammunition, food and water to positions where Russian surveillance drones make vehicle and foot traffic dangerous, and to evacuate wounded soldiers under fire. Finland, which shares a 1,340 km (830-mile) border with Russia, has been studying those lessons as it expands its own forces.
NATRIX is developing autonomous features such as “follow me” and automatic return modes and plans to add mine-clearing equipment and weapon integration. Last month the company also unveiled a separate ground drone designed to patrol critical infrastructure such as energy sites, ports and airports, and it said the Mikkeli demonstration opened talks with Finnish defense and security officials on possible future cooperation.

Ng Hon-mun, an influential pro-Beijing educator and long-serving Hong Kong deputy to the National People’s Congress who at one point called for its reform, has died at the age of 100.
City leader John Lee Ka-chiu offered his deepest sympathies to Ng’s family on Sunday, praising him for his lifelong devotion to the nation and his significant contributions to Hong Kong’s smooth return to the motherland.

Earthquake of magnitude 4.0 recorded in Switzerland
The earth shook during the night in Linthal in canton Glarus leading into Sunday with a magnitude of around 4.0 on the Richter scale. This earthquake is likely to have been felt throughout Switzerland, according to the Swiss Seismological Service at the Federal Institute of Technology ETH Zurich (SED).
The earthquake occurred at 4:37 am, approximately six kilometres west of Linthal, the SED stated in an automated message.
Minor damage is possible in isolated cases near the epicentre following an earthquake of this magnitude. A few hours after the earthquake, the Glarus cantonal police had no reports of damage, a spokesperson told the Keystone-SDA news agency when asked.
+ Earthquakes in Venezuela were detectable in Switzerland
Barely ten minutes after the earthquake, which measured around 4.0 on the Richter scale, another tremor struck Linthal. However, this one had a magnitude of just over 1.0, according to the SED’s website.
The SED records an average of three to four earthquakes per day in Switzerland and neighbouring countries, or 1,000 to 1,500 earthquakes per year. Around 10 to 20 tremors per year, with magnitudes of 2.5 or higher, are actually felt by the public.

Ukraine Strikes Russia’s Newest TOS-3 Dragon Thermobaric Rocket Launcher for First Time, Video
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
08:07:27 UTC
17:07:27 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Strikes Russia’s Newest TOS-3 Dragon Thermobaric Rocket Launcher for First Time, Video
Ukrainian forces have struck Russia’s newest TOS-3 “Dragon” heavy flamethrower system for the first time, using a drone to target the tracked thermobaric rocket launcher approximately 12 kilometers (7.5 miles) behind the front line.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s Third Army Corps on October 17, the strike was carried out by operators of the Muramasa unit, part of the Kraken Unmanned Systems Regiment, during the ongoing offensive operation known as “Vivaldi.”
The Ukrainian military said the Russian launcher was identified after it had conducted a firing mission. Drone operators subsequently located and struck the system, with footage of the engagement released through the corps’ official channels.
The Third Army Corps described the attack as the first reported successful strike against the TOS-3, a recently developed Russian weapon designed to deliver thermobaric rockets against fortified positions and concentrations of troops.
The TOS-3 “Dragon” is the latest addition to Russia’s family of heavy flamethrower systems, following the TOS-1A “Solntsepyok” and TOS-2 “Tosochka.”
Unlike the wheeled TOS-2, the TOS-3 uses a tracked, tank-type chassis intended to improve mobility across difficult terrain while providing greater protection for its crew.
According to specifications shared by the Third Army Corps, the launcher carries 15 tubes for unguided thermobaric rockets and has an estimated firing range of up to 15 kilometers (9.3 miles).
The system is operated by a three-person crew and incorporates additional protective measures, including slat armor and explosive reactive armor intended to improve its survivability against incoming attacks.
Thermobaric weapons use explosive mixtures that generate intense heat and prolonged blast pressure, making them particularly destructive against enclosed positions, trenches, and fortified structures.
The reported strike took place during Operation Vivaldi, an offensive campaign conducted by Ukraine’s Third Army Corps in the northern part of the Donetsk region.
During the same operation, Ukrainian forces deployed unmanned ground vehicles behind Russian positions, contributing to the liberation of two villages and the clearing of another settlement.
Ukrainian units also adapted ground-based attack drones with grenade launchers to engage Russian positions, demonstrating the expanding use of unmanned systems in offensive operations.

Ukraine Repels Russia’s Largest Motorcycle Assault of 2026 Near Pokrovsk, Video
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
08:07:10 UTC
17:07:10 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Repels Russia’s Largest Motorcycle Assault of 2026 Near Pokrovsk, Video
Ukrainian forces repelled what they described as the largest Russian motorcycle assault of 2026 in their area of responsibility near Pokrovsk, killing 43 Russian soldiers, wounding 12 others, and destroying nine motorcycles and a passenger vehicle.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s 155th Separate Mechanized Brigade on October 17, the Russian troops attempted to exploit weather conditions to advance toward Ukrainian positions on motorcycles. The attack was stopped by the brigade in coordination with neighboring Ukrainian units.
The brigade reported that Russian forces suffered 55 casualties during the engagement, including 43 killed and 12 wounded. Ukrainian troops also destroyed nine motorcycles and one civilian-type passenger vehicle used during the assault.
Following the failed attack, surviving Russian soldiers attempted to take cover in nearby shelters and defensive positions. Ukrainian forces subsequently struck 36 locations where Russian troops had reportedly sought refuge.
Russian units also deployed several types of drones to support the ground assault. Ukrainian defenders reported destroying 19 FPV drones, two FPV drones positioned to wait for targets, and five Russian Molniya strike drones.
Footage published by the 155th Brigade shows Ukrainian drones targeting Russian personnel and motorcycles during the engagement. The video documents several strikes against Russian assault units, although the full casualty figures could not be independently verified.
The brigade described the engagement as the largest motorcycle assault it had encountered since the beginning of 2026 within its assigned sector of the front.
Motorcycles have become one of the vehicles used by Russian assault units attempting to cross exposed terrain and approach Ukrainian defensive positions. Their mobility allows troops to move quickly across certain sections of the battlefield, although riders remain vulnerable to drone surveillance and precision strikes.
Earlier, Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps reported killing more than 250 Russian troops at a single location during Operation Vivaldi. Ukrainian commanders said they exploited a narrow, 100-meter-wide area to repeatedly target Russian infantry reinforcements, disrupting troop movements and preventing Russian forces from establishing defensive positions.

British startup develos modular ground drone for front line
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
08:04:50 UTC
17:04:50 KST

- UK-based Stratonex Defence Technologies unveiled VARAN, a modular unmanned ground vehicle concept for ISR, logistics, force protection, electronic warfare and counter-drone missions.
- The company says VARAN can navigate without GPS, uses passive 3D sensing and is designed for low visual, thermal and acoustic signatures.
British defense technology company Stratonex Defence Technologies has unveiled VARAN, a modular unmanned ground vehicle concept designed to accompany and support forward units on the battlefield, with swappable mission equipment and the ability to navigate without satellite positioning.
The company introduced the vehicle on social media and on its website, describing VARAN as a payload-agnostic platform that can be configured for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, logistics, force protection, electronic warfare and counter-drone missions.
Stratonex says VARAN uses autonomous navigation and passive 3D sensing to move across rough terrain, including in areas where GPS and other satellite navigation signals are jammed or unavailable. Passive sensing means the vehicle builds a picture of its surroundings without emitting signals such as radar or lidar pulses that an enemy could detect, and the company says the platform is designed to keep a low visual, thermal and acoustic signature.
The vehicle is built on an open systems architecture, which Stratonex says allows mission-specific payloads and future technologies to be integrated as requirements change. The company pitches VARAN as a way for troops to move farther and carry more in expeditionary operations, from reconnaissance support to counter-drone and rapid deployment tasks.
Stratonex framed the platform around configuration and integration, asking what capabilities potential users would want added to an unmanned ground vehicle.
Stratonex is a UK-based company co-founded by Ben Everitt, a former Conservative member of Parliament for Milton Keynes North, and describes itself as a developer of autonomous systems and mission software focused on sovereign capability for Britain and its allies. In July 2026, Nasdaq-listed VisionWave Holdings appointed Stratonex as its commercialization and integration partner for the UK and Europe under a non-exclusive distributor agreement covering VisionWave’s autonomous systems, sensing and counter-drone technologies.
Uncrewed ground vehicles have become a growing focus for European armies after their wide use in the war in Ukraine, where both sides rely on them to haul supplies, evacuate wounded troops and carry weapons along front lines exposed to constant drone surveillance. Britain’s Ministry of Defence has also been funding and trialing uncrewed ground platforms for logistics and combat support roles.
Stratonex presents VARAN as a concept platform, and the company is inviting feedback from potential users on which capabilities to integrate as development continues.

The American creative who devoted his career to an imaginary Swiss art school
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

The American creative who devoted his career to an imaginary Swiss art school
Dan Levenson is an artist based in Los Angeles. He has invented a Swiss art academy that never existed, complete with a curriculum, furniture and tens of thousands of students. What drives him?
“It really appeals to me to make art in a language that is foreign to me,” Dan Levenson says. He works as an artist in Los Angeles, as far as one gets from Switzerland in terms of time zones. Yet for many years, his work has revolved around the Staatliche Kunstakademie Zürich (SKZ), or Zurich State Academy of Art. But the SKZ never existed. Levenson invented it. He has never made a secret of that.
In his exhibitions, he shows exercises exploring colour scales and paintings built around basic geometric forms. Many of the works appear heavily aged. His performances recreate classes from the art school, and he sometimes exhibits painting aprons that look as though they have been used for years.
The artists whose names appear beneath the paintings – Hanneli Frick, Ramona Gutknecht and Christoph Randegger – never existed. In 2004, a computer programme generated their names from surnames in Zurich’s telephone directory and common Swiss first names. Levenson compiled 135,000 of these names into a book and published it. Ever since, he has drawn on this pool of names for his painting titles, in random order. No name is ever repeated.
Some of the furniture bears traces of genuine studio work. Other objects and paintings are subjected to processes that accelerate their deterioration: Levenson sands them down, soaks them in water and sometimes leaves them exposed to the elements for years. What remains are hairline cracks, scuff marks and stains – as if the objects had spent half a century in storage.
The SKZ is the centre of an entire parallel universe that Levenson has created over the past few years. Its fictional graduates sell their work through the “Little Switzerland” gallery, supposedly founded in the mid-1990s, according to Levenson’s account, by an idealistic group of newly graduated SKZ students.
They ship their art in sturdy wooden crates made by the fictional company Tsüri Logistik. While waiting for their paint to dry, they smoke the fabricated “Letzte” brand of tobacco or hang out at the equally fictitious “Rösti-Wirt” restaurant.
Why Zurich?
Levenson spent a long time thinking about where his fictional art academy should be based. New York was not an option: he was living there himself in the early 2000s, and it would have made the project too autobiographical. “With Berlin and Paris, the associations were too strong for me,” he says. He settled on Zurich.
Language was one factor. Swiss German, which Levenson neither speaks nor understands, crops up repeatedly in his work. His Social History of the SKZExternal link, for example, features fictional first-hand accounts by female students written entirely in Swiss German. For the recordings, he hired professional dialect speakers and translators.
“Even speakers of standard German often don’t understand this language, and I like that it doesn’t have a standardised orthography,” Levenson says. Just as he situated his project geographically at a distance from himself, he put it in a language foreign to him. “It’s twice removed from me,” he says.
Another factor in choosing Zurich was Switzerland’s reputation for being “somewhat harmless”. At the same time, the country plays a surprisingly significant role in the art world and is closely associated with the history of the 20th-century avant-garde.
In Zuefallsoperatione (Chance Operations), an art game for children in which shapes can be rearranged endlessly in different combinations, Levenson makes a clear reference to the chance-based games of the Dadaists, who repeatedly recombined words and forms through collage. The Dadaists came together in Zurich in 1916.
Modernism as a haunted house
The formal exercises Levenson paints under the names of fictitious Swiss artists are rendered in the style of classical modernism from the first half of the 20th century. In this tradition, good form was not merely a question of beauty; it was also bound up with the hope of creating a better world.
Yet the modernism that Levenson repeatedly revisits through formal exercises also resembles a haunted house. “Since the 1960s or 1970s, fine art education has moved away from this idea of fundamentals, of formalism, of composition, of colour theory,” Levenson says. “But the older generation remained a kind of antagonist, and that kind of painting and modernism and tradition haunted my generation of artists.”
Many of his exhibition pieces, with their dusty, museum-like appearance, seem like relics of a fallen regime. Levenson’s early works that explored Switzerland were interested in the aesthetics of bureaucracy: files and collective standards such as the A4 paper format, which is uncommon in American usage.
Given the strong connection to Zurich, it is tempting to see the strict geometries of his paintings as an echo of the Zurich Concretists. This movement, whose artists included Max Bill, set out to shape the entire environment for the better, “from the spoon to the city”. They later achieved international success, particularly with their meticulous typography and sophisticated corporate designs for major companies.
In the 1960s, modernism’s enthusiasm for form came under fierce attack, as young artists mocked it. Despite what his paintings might suggest, if nostalgia surfaces in Levenson’s work, it is directed less at early modernism than at the creative force of the 1960s.
He sees himself as part of the tradition of artistic institutional critique practised by Marcel Broodthaers. In 1968, the Belgian artist appointed himself director of his own Musée d’Art Moderne, Département des Aigles (Museum of Modern Art, Department of Eagles). He opened its first department in his Brussels apartment.
“As an 80s kid, with parents who lived through the 1960s, they were always talking about this magical but also disorienting time that happened just before I was born. I think I grew up with the feeling that I had somehow been born post-festum, after the party,” Levenson says.
While studying at the Royal College of Art in London in the 1990s, he was “constantly angry”. After the Cold War, art schools, too, began orienting themselves more towards the market. But Levenson had no desire to paint portraits for patrons, and he also struggled with the demand to specialise. He wanted to move between styles and work across painting, installation and performance.
“There’s something about being an art student that is more pure or authentic than being a professional artist. Art school should be years where you’re protected from the market. It should really just be about creativity, growth, exploration and community,” Levenson says.
That is why his fictional Swiss artists have no biographies. He used to invent them, he says, but found the exercise unsatisfying: “I really downplay their individuality. The important thing is that they are working together to try to solve a problem.”His imagined Switzerland also embodies this idea: it is an “idealised image of a true community, where people are bound together by a language, by a programme of research and by creative exploration.”
For Levenson, the SKZ is also a kind of second youth: “The point of my work is to send myself back to school.”

====================================================================================================

Iranian nation: The factor behind failure of US calculations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
07:49:36 UTC
16:49:36 KST

A war that was supposed to weaken Iran and place Iranian society against the country's political system has become a factor in strengthening national solidarity and changing Washington's calculations.
The Iranian nation, contrary to the assumption of the architects of maximum pressure, has distinguished between criticism of certain domestic issues and defending the country against foreign aggression; a distinction whose neglect can lead to the failure of strategies that have bet on the erosion of Iran's internal cohesion.
The American publication Foreign Affairs, in an analysis titled "The Theory of Iran's Victory," addresses this very issue and explains that military attacks and economic pressures, contrary to initial expectations, have not been able to realize the strategic objectives of America and the Zionist regime. This analysis states that the Iranian people do not see the war of America and Israel as liberating. Instead, they consider it an unjustified aggression, and the nationalism resulting from it has blurred the boundaries of political factions and reduced the possibility of another political uprising taking shape. This war has strengthened the Islamic Republic.
The importance of this assessment lies in the fact that the outcome of a confrontation cannot be measured solely on the basis of the extent of military damage, the destruction of infrastructure, or economic pressures. In strategic calculations, society and the people's reaction to the crisis also play a determining role. A country may face serious economic difficulties and parts of its infrastructure may be damaged, but this situation does not necessarily mean political defeat or the collapse of its national cohesion. Especially when the people consider the main cause of the crisis to be not internal disputes, but foreign attack and the threat to their country's existence.
The Gap Between Domestic Dissatisfaction and Reaction to Foreign Aggression
One of Washington's miscalculations is ignoring the difference between social and economic dissatisfactions in Iran and society's reaction to a foreign military attack. Dissatisfaction with living conditions, political demands, and criticism of officials' performance are realities that cannot be denied; but from the existence of these demands, one cannot conclude that Iranian society will move in the very direction that the architects of pressure expect in the face of any foreign pressure.
In fact, foreign pressure can change society's priorities. When people feel that their security, independence, or territorial integrity is under threat, they may temporarily marginalize internal disputes and make the defense of the country their common priority. This reaction does not necessarily mean the disappearance of all disputes or the end of criticisms; rather, it shows that national identity and sensitivity toward the country's independence have a capacity independent of political disputes.
From this perspective, the expectation that bombardments and economic pressure will automatically lead to protests against Iran's political structure is based on an incomplete understanding of Iranian society. Such an expectation reduces the people to a variable subordinate to military pressure, as if the more economic and human costs increase, the more likely society is to align with the objectives of the aggressor side. Whereas in many situations, a foreign attack can lead to strengthening the sense of a common threat and increasing the distance between the target society and the aggressors.
Why Does Foreign Pressure Produce the Opposite Result?
Economic and military pressure can lead to the political changes desired by its architects only when there is a reliable relationship between the pressure exerted and the expected political result. But this relationship is neither certain nor does it operate in the same way in all societies. Sanctions may increase people's living costs, disrupt economic activity, and exert pressure on various segments of society; however, whether these pressures lead to the weakening of the government, the strengthening of opponents, or an increase in national solidarity depends on numerous factors.
One of these factors is society's perception of the purpose of the pressures. If people imagine that foreign actions are being carried out with the aim of improving their living conditions, they may show a different reaction than when they consider these actions an attempt to impose political will or weaken their country. When a military attack is accompanied by widespread threats against infrastructure and national capacities, this perception is strengthened that the issue is not merely a dispute with a government, but that the matter is related to the country's security and future.
The Foreign Affairs analysis also emphasizes this same change in the social atmosphere. According to this assessment, foreign attacks, instead of turning existing political fissures into a factor for widespread instability, have at times paved the way for strengthening nationalism and removing factional boundaries. This process shows that external pressure, contrary to the assumption of some American policymakers, does not lead to the weakening of national will and may even increase the motivation to defend the country among groups that had serious disagreements with one another before the crisis.
The Nation: A Determining Variable in the Outcome of the Confrontation
National power is not limited to weapons capability, economic capacities, or the extent of access to advanced technologies. A society's ability to maintain cohesion under crisis conditions is also considered part of a country's power. A country that can preserve social bonds and a sense of national responsibility against external pressure possesses a capacity that purely military calculations are unable to fully explain.
In this context, the role of the Iranian nation must also be examined within the framework of this country's historical experience. Sensitivity toward independence, foreign interference, and attempts to impose the will of great powers has been among the important issues in shaping Iranians' political memory. This background does not mean that all people have the same view on domestic issues or foreign policy; rather, it shows that under conditions in which an external threat becomes prominent, national belonging can become a point of common ground for groups that have many disagreements under normal conditions.
Of course, the strengthening of national solidarity during a crisis should not be taken to mean the permanent elimination of social demands or the resolution of economic problems. Livelihood pressures can still affect people's lives, and after the external threat subsides, domestic demands will again become prominent. However, this very distinction shows that domestic dissatisfactions cannot be used as a definitive tool for advancing foreign military and political objectives. A society that is critical of its officials' performance does not necessarily want foreign military intervention or the weakening of its country.
For American policymakers, the message of this reality is clear: understanding Iranian society without paying attention to national identity, historical experience, and its sensitivity toward independence will lead to incomplete assessments. Relying on the assumption that increased pressure will automatically change the people's political will in the direction desired by Washington can make that very policymaker heedless of the real consequences of his decisions.
Ultimately, assessing the success or failure of a strategy against Iran is not possible merely through the number of attacks, the extent of damages, or the severity of sanctions. One must see what political and social results these measures have produced and whether they have been able to steer society toward the objectives declared by their designers or not. What the Foreign Affairs analysis highlights is the gap between America's expectation and the reaction of Iranian society. Ignoring the role of the nation is considered one of the most important weaknesses of these calculations, because external pressure is not only not a guarantee for the collapse of internal cohesion, but under certain conditions can lead to the opposite result and strengthen the national will to defend the country.
MNA

Speaking to Axios, White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers defended US President Donald Trump’s decision to indefinitely suspend mandatory sanctions and import tariffs enacted under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Rogers stated that the statute equips the president with critical leverage in ongoing diplomatic consultations rather than serving as an immediate punitive instrument.
“President Trump has been clear that he wants to see this brutal war come to an end. As talks continue, this Act provides the president with additional authorities to pursue a peaceful resolution,” Rogers said in an official statement.
“Enforcing the sanctions provisions now would impede ongoing US efforts to negotiate a durable and comprehensive peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia.”
Rogers stressed that the executive waiver does not permanently dismantle the statutory penalties, emphasizing that the administration retains the authority to invoke them whenever national security considerations warrant.
“The president retains the ability to exercise these authorities at any time if he determines that doing so would advance national interests,” Rogers added.
Rubio: Ukraine Does Not Have Access to Starshield
Diplomatic leverage and the Section 115 waiver
The administration’s defense provides public justification for an executive order signed by Trump on Friday, Oct. 16, which waived sweeping statutory trade duties and secondary penalties just 48 hours before mandatory implementation was scheduled to begin on Sunday, Oct. 18.
In issuing the suspension, Trump invoked Section 115 of the Graham Act, which authorizes presidential waivers upon submitting formal certification to Congress that such actions align with US national interests.
While the formal certification was delivered to Capitol Hill on Friday, the White House had initially withheld specific details regarding the strategic rationale behind the determination.
The waived mechanisms represent some of the most punitive economic measures approved by Congress to date, including a mandatory 500 percent tariff on all Russian imports and 100 percent duties targeting the five largest global purchasers of Russian crude oil and natural gas, such as China and India.
The statute also required retaliatory duties on third countries facilitating petroleum sanctions evasion and established trade actions against Moscow’s maritime “shadow fleet” of oil tankers.
Pushback from Kyiv
The White House statement follows condemnation from President Volodymyr Zelensky, who characterized the executive waiver on Saturday as a grave policy miscalculation that directly aids the Russian military.
“Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue. I consider the diesel deal to be the first step,” Zelensky told reporters.
“It seems to me that it is impossible to stop [Russian President Vladimir] Putin in this way. On the contrary, he feels joy, happiness that he has such support... It definitely helps only the Russians. It definitely does not stop the war.”
Zelensky warned that pairing demands for Ukrainian military restraint with unilateral economic accommodations to Moscow only encourages the Kremlin to sustain long-range bombardments against Ukraine’s civilian power grid ahead of winter.
The waiver also drew bipartisan criticism on Capitol Hill, where the Graham Act passed with veto-proof margins, including an 86-11 vote in the Senate.
Republican Senator Thom Tillis called the executive order “more than irresponsible,” while Democratic leaders Chuck Schumer and Elizabeth Warren accused the White House of bypassing the statutory will of Congress to offer unwarranted concessions to Putin.

sardinian school wraps in perforated aluminum facade to enclose flexible agorà
wrapped in a textured skin of micro-perforated corrugated panels, the building presents a light-reactive metallic shell that softens along curved edges, concealing a permeable two-story layout.
prefer designboom on google
CORRUGATED ALUMINUM SKIN ESTABLISHES A CIVIC LANDMARK IN SARDINIA
Designed by Leicho architettura, the new Via Caravaggio school in Sinnai, Sardinia, replaces an obsolete structure with a civic facility that redefines the relationship between public architecture, pedagogy, and urban identity. The building presents a dual spatial character: a compact, highly recognizable exterior volume contrasts with a permeable, porous interior layout.
The exterior building envelope is wrapped in micro-perforated corrugated aluminum panels that soften straight edges along curved margins. The textured metal skin shifts in response to daylight, establishing the school as a distinct visual landmark within the neighborhood. A deep, carved recessed entryway marks the transition from the public plaza into the building.
FLEXIBLE CLASSROOM GEOMETRIES CREATE POROUS LEARNING SPACE
Inside the building by Leicho architettura studio, the rigid geometry of the shell dissolves into a continuous learning landscape. At the center of the two-story structure is an agorà, a double-height, non-specialized communal hall equipped with stepped seating (koilon) that faces an adjacent music room (skené) separated by a movable wall. The space functions interchangeably as an auditorium, media library, or gathering area. Around this central atrium, flexible classrooms and laboratories vary in geometry, wall concavity, and window placement to prevent repetitive layouts. Broad circulation corridors, seating niches, and integrated green courtyards function as informal learning zones, transforming traditional hallways into usable public space.

name: Nuova scuola di Via Caravaggio

China railway passenger trips hit record high in first three quarters
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
15:42:02 CST
16:42:02 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- China's railway network handled 3.71 billion passenger trips in the first three quarters of 2026, up 4.8 percent year on year, the highest for the period, according to the China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. (China Railway).
During the period, the railway network operated an average of 11,511 passenger trains daily, up 5.3 percent from a year earlier.
Railway departments have actively responded to demand for sightseeing, wellness tours and red-themed study tours, according to China Railway. In the first nine months, a total of 2,860 tourist trains were operated across the country, up 25.5 percent year on year.
The railway network also operated 947 special trains for concertgoers and sports fans during the period, effectively boosting the catering, hotel and cultural tourism sectors.
Cross-border rail travel also continued to grow. The China-Laos Railway carried 265,000 cross-border trips, up 37.8 percent, while the Guangzhou-Shenzhen-Hong Kong high-speed railway handled over 25.8 million cross-border trips, up 11.8 percent, China Railway said.
China Railway also adapted to the inbound travel boom created by the country's visa-free transit policy. The railway network carried over 19 million foreign passenger trips in the first three quarters, up 33.4 percent year on year, the company said.
Behind the steady growth in passenger traffic is China's increasingly dense high-speed rail network.
By the end of 2025, the country's total operating railway mileage had reached 165,000 km, which included more than 50,000 km of high-speed rail.
On Sept. 28, China opened four high-speed rail sections, connecting Xiongan in north China's Hebei Province with Shangqiu in Henan Province in central China, Xi'an with Ankang in Shaanxi Province in northwest China, Yichang with Xingshan in central China's Hubei Province, and Harbin with Yichun in Heilongjiang Province in the country's northeast.
China's high-speed rail network is projected to hit 70,000 km by 2035, featuring eight north-south vertical lines and eight east-west horizontal lines. Once complete, the network will connect major cities, city clusters and key economic zones across the country. ■

YEREVAN, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- The UN chief and government officials called for accelerated global action to protect biodiversity at a summit held here on Friday, urging countries to turn international commitments into concrete measures and strengthen cooperation to address biodiversity loss.
The Leaders' Summit on Biodiversity, themed "Leaders for Nature," brought together heads of state and government and representatives of international organizations ahead of the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17), scheduled for Oct. 19 to 30.
Representatives of governments, non-governmental organizations, experts and other stakeholders also attended the summit.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urged countries to show "more action, more speed, and more will" to protect biodiversity.
"Halfway to 2030, Yerevan is our moment of accountability," Guterres said at the summit, calling for assessing progress toward global conservation targets laid out in the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework adopted in 2022.
He warned that progress to halt biodiversity loss remained uneven and too slow, with financing and other support still falling short of what was needed.
Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan highlighted the links between peace and biodiversity conservation.
"Peace and biodiversity are of great significance, both domestically and across borders," Pashinyan said during a roundtable discussion held as part of the summit. He stressed that environmental challenges could not be addressed by any country alone, calling for greater international cooperation.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian also noted the importance of biodiversity conservation in the context of peace, security and sustainable development. He highlighted the environmental damage caused by armed conflicts and called for stronger international support for conservation efforts.
Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev called for broad international cooperation to safeguard the world's natural heritage, stressing that "biodiversity sustains human well-being, economic resilience and long-term security."
Chinese Minister of Ecology and Environment Huang Runqiu said China had consistently participated in global biodiversity governance with strong political commitment and concrete action, helping promote the adoption of the landmark Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
Huang called for greater financial, technological and capacity-building support for developing countries to ensure the framework's comprehensive, balanced and effective implementation.
The summit adopted the Yerevan Declaration, entitled "Taking Action for Nature," which reaffirmed commitments to the Convention on Biological Diversity and to the effective implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, with its mission of halting and reversing biodiversity loss by 2030 and its vision of living in harmony with nature by 2050. ■

Interview: China plays significant role in global poverty reduction -- Kyrgyz economist

16:41:09 KST

BISHKEK, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- The eradication of absolute poverty stands as one of China's most significant socio-economic achievements in recent decades, highlighting its important contribution to international poverty reduction efforts, a Kyrgyz economist said ahead of the International Day for the Eradication of Poverty.
China's success in lifting hundreds of millions of people out of poverty within a relatively short period was driven not only by government social support programs but also by large-scale industrialization, improved employment opportunities, and the development of infrastructure, education, and rural areas across the country, said Tolonbek Abdyrov, a professor of economics and vice rector of the International Higher School of Medicine in Kyrgyzstan.
"China's experience demonstrates that poverty cannot be overcome solely through the provision of welfare payments. Rather, it is necessary to create conditions in which people can earn a living on their own and improve their quality of life," he said, adding that this experience holds immense global significance.
"It proves that even in a nation with a vast population and significant regional disparities, a consistent economic policy can substantially transform people's standard of living," the expert noted.
Regarding China's remarkable role in international poverty reduction efforts, he said, "Through the Belt and Road Initiative, the Global Development Initiative, and cooperation with countries in Africa, Asia and other regions, China is involved in the construction of roads, energy facilities, and industrial plants, as well as the development of agriculture."
According to Abdyrov, China's contribution to global poverty reduction should be measured not simply by the scale of its investments or the number of facilities built, but by how effectively such cooperation enables other countries to develop their own drivers of economic growth, create jobs, and improve living standards.
"For Kyrgyzstan, this is particularly relevant. Cooperation with China can help us develop transport corridors, the energy sector, processing industries, and agriculture," he said. ■

After a year in turmoil, the Louvre faces uncertain future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
07:40:00 UTC
16:40:00 KST

After a year in turmoil, the Louvre faces uncertain future
PARIS – The Louvre is gradually plugging the security gaps exposed by the spectacular burglary of Oct 19, 2025, but its reputation has taken a battering and its creaking infrastructure is a growing source of concern.
The beloved Parisian museum, one of the most visited in the world, has spent a year as the subject of police investigations, government reports and parliamentary inquiries following the theft of eight crown jewels in broad daylight a year ago.
The heist exposed a string of failures, from old or non-existent CCTV cameras and a chronic shortage of equipment to the lack of a modern security control room and a security director.
“We still feel the trauma of the burglary,” Valerie Baud, a workers’ representative from the CFDT trade union, told AFP.
Parliament has heard how, in the run-up to the burglary, the institution had spent just €3 million (S$4.3 million) out of €83 million earmarked for a security masterplan because of administrative delays, management decisions and red tape.
The museum had “prioritised projects that were visible and attractive”, the French Court of Auditors found in one of many damning judgements.
That report and others, compounded by a staff strike and a spate of other incidents – including a water leak and a major ticket-fraud scandal – hastened the downfall of Louvre president Laurence des Cars, who resigned in February.
“The Louvre needs a change in security culture, which has yet to happen and will take several years,” said Laurent Lafon, who is monitoring the museum as chairman of the Senate’s culture committee.
“The Louvre’s leaders must embrace the idea that security is a priority, which wasn’t the case,” he told AFP.
‘Rapid progress’
New museum chief Christophe Leribault, who replaced des Cars in February, argues that change is taking place.
“The security masterplan is making rapid progress,” he told AFP in a written statement, while stressing the “complexity” of carrying out the work while keeping the museum open to the public.
The museum has pledged to invest around €20 million a year until 2032 and, since July, has a new dedicated security director.
Short-term worries about security are also giving way to longer-term questions about how to finance a palace-wide modernisation programme.
Every year, nearly nine million visitors walk the Louvre’s galleries, many unaware of the decrepit state of some of the rooms, the ageing plumbing and wiring, as well as poor ventilation in summer and non-existent heating in winter.
Leribault issued his most alarming warning yet earlier this week, telling Le Figaro newspaper “that if the Louvre is not repaired, updated, and transformed, it will very quickly fall behind and will eventually have to close its doors to the public”.
Money worries
French President Emmanuel Macron unveiled his vision – called “Louvre – Nouvelle Renaissance” – in January 2025 which included a new entrance and gallery for the Mona Lisa among other changes.
It came with an eye-watering proposed price tag of a billion euros – which now looks unrealistic for a country facing a severe budget crunch.
Unions accused him and Louvre management of prioritising grandiose plans for an architectural overhaul instead of more modest changes that would improve the visitor experience.
“We can step up security without going through with this project, which does not address the priorities and states as its goal an unsustainable increase in visitor numbers,” said Christian Galani, a representative of the hard-left CGT union.
Leribault remains committed to it, however.
Part of his task as Louvre head is finding new private sources of income from donors who will be invited to sponsor work – and earn public recognition and perhaps naming rights in return.
Other sources of income could come from further ticket price hikes.
The target is €360 million.
“It’s a huge challenge, and I don’t know whether I’ll succeed,” he said in June. AFP

The participating countries are also expected to review ongoing cooperation initiatives and consider decisions related to the organisation’s financial and institutional functioning.

It called for greater use of digital and cross-border payments and improved access to trade finance for micro, small and medium enterprises and start-ups.The October meeting will provide India an opportunity to exchange views with other SCO member states on advancing practical and mutually beneficial cooperation. India remains actively engaged in SCO mechanisms and contributes to regional cooperation through initiatives in start-ups and innovation, digital public infrastructure and people-to-people exchanges, the Ministry of Defence said.
The Council of Heads of Government adopts the SCO’s budget and addresses key issues related to cooperation within the organisation, particularly in the economic sphere. The body meets annually and is distinct from the Council of Heads of State, which serves as the organisation’s highest decision-making forum.The previous meeting of the Council of Heads of Government was held in Moscow on November 18, 2025, where India was represented by external affairs minister S Jaishankar, according to ANI.

Why Iran-US negotiations keep failing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
07:32:59 UTC
16:32:59 KST

Why Iran-US negotiations keep failing
Relations between the two countries are dominated by policy complexes shaped by a history of hostility.
Since the start of the war, there have been several negotiation initiatives between the United States and Iran. Only one – the memorandum of understanding signed in Islamabad on June 18 – was concluded, but it collapsed within days.
While prevailing analyses tend to explain this failure through the details of the provisions, this article proceeds from a different premise: that the diplomatic stalemate between the two sides is shaped by a syndrome that has governed US-Iranian relations for years.
In international relations, psychological syndromes can arise as a result of deep crises that leave their mark on political consciousness and memory, potentially obstructing efforts at rapprochement and negotiation between countries.
In the case of Iran and the US, the syndrome is comprised of two complexes: the complex Washington developed as a result of the 1979 siege of the US embassy in Tehran and the complex Tehran developed as a result of historical US hostility and its withdrawal from the Iran nuclear deal in 2018.
The roots of the rupture between the two countries go as far back as August 1953 when US and British intelligence agencies helped overthrow the nationalist government of Mohammad Mosaddegh after it nationalised the oil industry in 1951. Since then, a perception has become entrenched in Iranian consciousness: that Washington does not accept an independent government in Tehran and it is prepared to sabotage it if it goes against its interests.
From this perspective, Washington’s decision to host Shah Reza Pahlavi, who had just been overthrown by his people, for medical treatment in October 1979 was read in revolutionary Tehran as a prelude to a second coup.
Iranian students stormed the US embassy on November 4 that year and held 52 Americans for 444 days. Diplomatic relations between the two countries were severed and have not been restored to this day.
While the incident is portrayed in the Iranian narrative as a defence of the revolution, in American consciousness, it established the image of Iran as a state that does not respect international norms, whose word cannot be relied upon and whose behaviour should not be rewarded.
That is the embassy siege complex. It is not about the incident itself so much as the informal rule it produced in US decision-making: that Iran must concede first and its concession must be verified before it receives anything in return.
The Iranian complex was shaped by this history as well, but it reached its peak in May 2018 when US President Donald Trump withdrew from the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) despite the International Atomic Energy Agency’s (IAEA’s) confirmation that Tehran was complying with it.
Just two weeks later, US Secretary of State Mike Pompeo announced 12 demands for a new deal, only four of which were related to the nuclear file. Seven of them were related to Iran’s regional behaviour in Lebanon, Palestine, Iraq, Yemen, Syria, Afghanistan and the Gulf. In other words, Washington did not merely revoke an existing agreement; it also raised the ceiling of its conditions for any future agreement.
The knot then deepened in June 2025 when the US took part in the Twelve-Day War and struck the nuclear facilities at Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan at a time when a new round of indirect negotiations was scheduled in Muscat. It then reached its furthest point with Washington’s participation alongside Israel in the current war.
Accordingly, a conviction became entrenched in the Iranian consciousness that an American signature guarantees nothing, that any agreement can be overturned with a change of administration and indeed that negotiation itself may be a cover for war rather than an alternative to it.
The informal rule this has produced in Iranian decision-making is that there will be no step taken before binding guarantees and no concession before pressure is lifted.
Thus, the two complexes stand at opposite ends: The first requires Iranian action before an American quid pro quo while the second requires an American guarantee before Iranian action.
A reading of the recent negotiation initiatives shows that every US initiative bears the imprint of the embassy siege complex. The 15-point plan put forward in March demanded the dismantling of the Natanz, Isfahan and Fordow facilities; an end to uranium enrichment; the suspension of Iran’s missile programme; and the abandonment of its allies in exchange for promises to lift sanctions later.
The May draft by White House envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner linked the release of Iran’s frozen funds to the suspension of enrichment first. The American response in September also stipulated the freezing of enrichment and the entry of inspectors throughout the negotiation period.
What remains constant in the American initiatives is that Iranian action precedes the quid pro quo and verification precedes trust.
The imprint of the JCPOA withdrawal complex in the Iranian initiatives is also a constant. The five-point response in late March demanded guarantees that war would not be repeated. The 10 points put forward in April demanded a binding UN Security Council resolution shielding any agreement from being overturned. And the 14 points in May demanded a nonaggression pledge that includes Israel.
Meanwhile, the seven-day plan proposed by Tehran last month stipulated the lifting of sanctions and the US naval blockade on Iran before the opening of the Strait of Hormuz on the sixth day and the start of nuclear negotiations on the seventh. What remains constant in the Iranian initiatives is that guarantees precede action and the lifting of pressure precedes Iranian concessions.
All these initiatives were dialogue between two complexes with each side drafting its text to protect itself from a repetition of its historical experience with the other, rather than to meet the other halfway. This may explain why the gap in substance has narrowed, but the gap in trust has not.
The Islamabad memorandum represents the exception that proves the rule as it was the closest moment to a settlement because it was formulated to reassure both sides over their core concerns. To reassure Washington, it stipulated the dilution of Iran’s stockpile of enriched uranium and made the lifting of sanctions and unfreezing of funds conditional on Iranian implementation.
To reassure Tehran, it provided for an end to hostilities, respect for mutual sovereignty, a mechanism to monitor implementation and UN Security Council approval of the final agreement. Ballistic missiles were also entirely absent from the text.
But this agreement did not hold. Tehran suspended its participation in the Geneva round of talks because of the absence of a ceasefire in Lebanon, which had been a consistent demand in every Iranian initiative since March. In the Iranian reading, Washington’s inability to rein in Israel confirmed that an American signature was not enough. The JCPOA withdrawal complex immediately kicked in, and the two sides returned to square one.
By late September, the dispute appeared to have shifted definitively from substance to sequencing. Informed sources indicated that it now revolves around the order of steps rather than their content and the stated goal has become a return to an enhanced version of the June memorandum.
Here the two complexes appear in their clearest form: Washington wants the Strait of Hormuz opened and enrichment frozen first because it does not trust Iran while Tehran wants the naval blockade lifted first because it does not trust the US.
A comparison between Pompeo’s 2018 conditions and the June 2026 memorandum shows that US demands have retreated from redefining Iran’s regional role to focusing on the nuclear file and the Strait of Hormuz while Iranian demands have shifted from compensation to be paid by Washington to a conditional investment fund financed by other parties.
In other words, the substantive gap between the two sides has narrowed considerably – something that would have been unimaginable eight years ago.
However, the two complexes have not diminished; indeed, they may have deepened because of the war. Each complex feeds the other until together they have become a single syndrome, and diplomatic deadlock has turned from a passing condition into a stable structure.
Accordingly, any new formula for sequencing the steps, however precise, will remain unable to break this deadlock unless it addresses both complexes at once – something that requires a third party capable of guaranteeing both the action and the reciprocal action simultaneously.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

CURE Art Gallery opens in Bursa with works by Oran, Yalçındağ
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
07:32:18 UTC
16:32:18 KST

AA Photo
CURE Art Gallery opened in the northwestern province of Bursa’s Balat district on Oct. 15 with an inaugural exhibition featuring recent works and previously unseen pieces by Turkish artists Ahmet Oran and Ekrem Yalçındağ.
Running through Nov. 12, the exhibition brings together two distinct approaches to contemporary painting, exploring color, texture, repetition and abstraction.
Oran builds layered surfaces by applying paint in different colors onto canvas and selectively scraping away sections with spatulas and scrapers. The technique reveals underlying layers, creating lines and bands of color across the surface.
Yalçındağ incorporates recurring botanical motifs and circular compositions into his paintings. His dense application of paint through small brushstrokes creates a raised, textured surface. Both artists have exhibited in Türkiye and abroad.
The gallery’s founders said the initiative establishes a dedicated space in Bursa where audiences can regularly engage with contemporary art and interact directly with artists.
Beyond its exhibition program, CURE Art Gallery plans to develop long-term relationships with artists, collectors, art writers and other professionals in the art world.
The opening exhibition was held with the participation of Oran and Yalçındağ, in collaboration with Lexus Nilüfer. The works remain on display at the gallery until Nov. 12.

Drones Hit St. Petersburg Oil Terminals, VK Data Center, and Bridge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
07:22:00 UTC
16:22:00 KST

A Ukrainian drone attack early Sunday morning, Oct. 18, struck fuel transshipment infrastructure, a major enterprise data center, a logistics warehouse, and a highway bridge across St. Petersburg and the surrounding Leningrad region, sparking multiple fires and knocking out power to 20,000 residents.
St. Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov confirmed that the municipality came under attack by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) overnight, resulting in blazes across four city districts.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Beglov acknowledged impacts at the Petersburg Oil Terminal (PNT) alongside damage to additional infrastructure sites, while claiming that emergency responders had been dispatched to contain localized fires.
According to independent Russian outlet Astra, municipal emergency warning systems failed to notify residents ahead of the strikes, with alerts transmitted either after impacts had occurred or with substantial operational delays.
Open-source intelligence (OSINT) analysis conducted by Astra verified that fires erupted at the Petersburg Oil Terminal, the Baltic region’s primary petroleum transshipment hub.
Concurrently in the city’s Krasnogvardeisky district, drone debris ignited a blaze at the “Ruchyi” oil depot. The Ruchyi fuel depot maintains an operational capacity of 3,900 cubic meters, functioning as a bulk storage and loading facility for AI-92 and AI-95 gasoline alongside commercial diesel.
Mushrooms and the Autumn Moon
Hits on VK data center, substation, and Ozon logistics depot
The overnight assault extended across the administrative boundary into the Leningrad region, targeting corporate digital backbones and electrical distribution facilities.
In the village of Novosergievka in the Vsevolozhsk district, strike drones hit a large server data center owned by Russian technology giant VK (VKontakte).
Although VK company representatives claimed corporate services continued operating normally, users across Russia reported widespread connection dropouts and outages affecting the VKontakte social media platform and its integrated ecosystem.
Astra’s OSINT analysts established that an electrical substation located adjacent to the VK data center was also damaged during the strike.
Leningrad Region Governor Alexander Drozdenko confirmed that damage to electrical distribution installations triggered emergency power cuts, leaving approximately 20,000 residents in the area without electricity.
Separately, Russian e-commerce company Ozon confirmed that an aerial impact sparked a fire at its fulfillment center in St. Petersburg’s Kolpino district on Sofiyskaya Street.
Operating as one of Ozon’s busiest logistics facilities in northwestern Russia, the hub spans up to 79,000 square meters.
The company reported that emergency brigades contained the blaze and confirmed no personnel were injured.
Strike on Western High-Speed Diameter bridge
Drone impacts were also recorded on municipal transport arteries. According to Astra, a drone struck the cable-stayed bridge spanning the Korabelny fairway in St. Petersburg, located roughly 4.5 kilometers from the Petersburg Oil Terminal.
The bridge forms a critical section of the southern viaduct of the Western High-Speed Diameter (WHSD), a multi-lane toll expressway connecting northern and southern sectors of the metropolis.
Municipal engineering teams were deployed to evaluate structural damage to the suspension cables and road deck.
The multi-site strikes in St. Petersburg and Leningrad region reflect an expanding Ukrainian asymmetric campaign to degrade Russian rear logistics, petroleum transshipment, and corporate digital logistics.
The incident follows consecutive strikes on Russian technology hubs earlier in the month, including attacks that disabled Yandex data centers in Vladimir, Ryazan, and Kaluga regions, alongside reported strikes on a Sberbank data center facility in Saratov region.

With just nine days left until the election, Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party has maintained a consistent lead over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud in four recent election polls, but neither political bloc comes close to securing the 61 seats needed for a Knesset majority, according to surveys published by Maariv, Channel 13, Kan News, and Channel 12.
The four surveys paint an almost identical picture: the Zionist opposition averages 51.25 seats, compared with 51 for Netanyahu's bloc, a virtual tie that leaves the Arab parties and smaller factions hovering around the electoral threshold in key positions ahead of election day.
Maariv poll: Winter below electoral threshold, Eisenkot leads
The Maariv poll shows the Arab parties each gained one seat over the past week, bringing their combined total to 14 seats. By contrast, Likud has lost two seats, falling to just 18.
Despite Likud's two-seat decline, the coalition bloc loses only one seat, dropping to 51. This follows United Torah Judaism's gain of one seat, bringing it to eight, and People of Israel’s success in crossing the electoral threshold with four seats.
However, Yisrael Beytenu also lost one seat, falling to eight, which reduced the Zionist opposition bloc to 51 and tied the two blocs.
Channel 13 poll: Netanyahu bloc loses four seats
Channel 13's election poll gives Netanyahu's bloc just 51 seats, compared with 55 in the previous survey. Likud dropped two seats to 18, while Eisenkot's Yashar party maintained its lead with 20 seats.
Eisenkot's bloc remains unchanged at 50 seats. The Arab parties, which are not affiliated with either bloc, receive a combined 15 seats.
KAN News poll: Winter fails to cross electoral threshold, Bennett gains a seat
A poll published by KAN News showed that Eisenkot's Yashar party continued to lead Netanyahu's Likud, although the distribution of seats between the political blocs gives Netanyahu the advantage.
At the bottom of the list of parties crossing the electoral threshold are People of Israel, which receives four seats, and the joint Reservists/Economic Party led by Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha, which also received four seats.
The key finding in the survey concerns the balance between the blocs. Netanyahu's bloc receives 53 seats, compared with 50 for Eisenkot's bloc, giving the political camp aligned with the prime minister a three-seat advantage.
Channel 12 poll: Eisenkot leads Netanyahu, People of Israel remains out
Channel 12's poll placed Eisenkot's Yashar party in first place with 23 seats, compared with 20 for Likud under Netanyahu.
Winter's People of Israel fell below the electoral threshold, receiving 1.8% of the vote.
Meanwhile, the balance between the blocs remained unchanged, with 54 seats for the opposition parties, 49 for the coalition, and 13 for the Arab parties. Hendel and Zelekha's party received four seats.
Polling average: Eisenkot holds narrow lead, blocs remain virtually tied
The average of the four polls presented an almost symmetrical picture of the two political blocs. The opposition averages 51.25 seats, compared with 51 for Netanyahu's bloc.
In other words, among the Zionist parties, neither side has a decisive advantage.
The gap widens when the Arab parties are included. They average 13.75 seats, while the Hendel-Zelekha party stood at four seats and remained outside the two-bloc division.
Together, the Zionist opposition and the Arab parties average 65 seats.
Eisenkot also holds an advantage among the largest parties. Yashar averages 21.5 seats, compared with Likud's 19, while Bennett trails significantly with 12.5.
The overall picture is of an extremely close election within the Zionist political camps, in which the Arab parties and smaller factions could become decisive factors.
The average is based on the distribution of Knesset seats in four separate polls and does not constitute a new survey or a forecast of the election results.

The day after waiving sanctions and tariffs related to Russian exports, US President Donald Trump said on Saturday he has yet to announce a final decision on the matter, as Secretary of State Marco Rubio said officials want more time to evaluate the situation.
Rubio said on Saturday that the president will use up to 60 days to assess the economic impact of Russia-related sanctions and tariffs that he waived a day earlier.
"A lot of you don't know what my decision is yet, but we'll figure it out, and you'll figure it out," Trump told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida.
The waiver comes just weeks before November's midterm elections, with Trump under pressure over high energy prices as war with Iran disrupts global oil supplies.
Trump signed an executive order on Friday waiving key sanctions and tariffs under the law known as the Graham Act, which he signed last month at the urging of lawmakers who want to pressure Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
The measures, including tariffs on Russian goods and penalties on countries buying Russian oil and gas, were due to take effect next week. Friday's order didn't specify how long the waiver would last, but Rubio said Trump chose a 60-day review.
"I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy," Rubio told reporters before boarding a plane for a trip to Uzbekistan.
Complicating matters is the Graham Act's call not only for sanctions on Russia but also for tariffs on goods from countries that import Russian energy supplies. Rubio pointed to India, an important US partner that has diversified its energy supplies but remains heavily dependent on Russian oil.
Trump's decision draws criticism from Zelensky, Republican senator
Friday's executive order drew criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who warned it would embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin and prolong the war.
Senator Darline Graham, a South Carolina Republican whose late brother Lindsey Graham championed the legislation that bears his name, said she disagreed with Trump's decision and planned to discuss it with him when he campaigns for her next week.
"Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia," she told reporters on Saturday. "Because I don't trust Putin and I don't trust Russia."
Rubio also defended a separate US agreement with Russia to increase diesel supplies to global markets, aimed at easing fuel prices that have climbed amid the war with Iran and disruptions to energy supplies.
Under the agreement, Trump said Russia initially would supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to the United States, followed by shipments in November and beyond.
"That diesel is going to be sold one way or the other," Rubio said. "The only difference is how much of it the United States was going to get."
Rubio said the diesel deal and sanctions waiver reflected the challenge of managing conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine that have disrupted global energy supplies.
"These conflicts around the world are starting to crash into each other," he said.
