General Staff: Russia has lost 1,565,060 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
06:37:19 UTC
15:37:19 KST

Russia has lost 1,565,060 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 18.
The number includes 2,090 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,416 tanks, 25,561 armored combat vehicles, 164,246 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,293 artillery systems, 2,224 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,711 air defense systems, 449 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,968 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

====================================================================================================

No arrests after West Bank settler attack; police accuse European diplomats of not cooperating
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
06:31:27 UTC
15:31:27 KST

No suspects have been arrested in the attacks on European diplomats and an American photojournalist in the West Bank over the weekend, and Israeli police officials are now accusing European diplomatic missions of failing to cooperate with the investigation into Saturday's assault near the Palestinian village of Taybeh, northeast of Ramallah.
According to police sources, investigators have sought detailed witness statements and photographic evidence from the European diplomats who were attacked by Jewish rioters while attending an olive harvest. However, the officials claim that the diplomatic missions involved have so far failed to cooperate with those requests.
Police said investigators from the West Bank District had contacted Israel's Foreign Ministry to approach the diplomatic missions and arrange the collection of evidence. As of Saturday evening, according to the sources, the missions had not provided the requested cooperation.
Investigators are seeking detailed testimony, video and photographic material, access to the vehicles involved in the attack and permission to collect forensic evidence. Police officials said the requests were intended to help identify the attackers, arrest them and ensure that everyone involved is brought to justice.
The investigation is continuing, but no arrests have been made in connection with either Saturday's attack on European diplomats in Taybeh or Friday's assault on American photojournalist Heidi Levine, who works for The Washington Post, in the Palestinian village of Abu Falah.
Police said their investigators and the Shin Bet domestic security agency were continuing efforts to identify those responsible for the attack on Levine, who underwent surgery on her hand Saturday.
Her daughter, Ashley Milner, said one of the fingers on her mother's left hand had been cut so deeply that the bone and tendon were exposed. Levine also suffered a broken rib, fractures in several vertebrae and cuts across her body.
According to police sources, West Bank District commander Maj. Gen. Moshe Pinchi is personally overseeing the investigations into the weekend's violence. He has assigned both cases to the district's central investigative unit, which is working alongside the Shin Bet.
Additional investigators have been assigned to the cases, and Pinchi has emphasized the importance of intelligence sharing and investigative cooperation between police and the Shin Bet to identify the attackers and bring them to justice.
Saturday's assault on the European diplomatic delegation took place during an olive harvest in Taybeh, the last entirely Christian Palestinian village in the West Bank. The delegation included representatives from France, Belgium and Poland, as well as French Mayor Bernard Baudoux of Aulnoye-Aymeries, whose municipality has a sister-city relationship with Taybeh.
"They were attacked by seven adult men, ages 20 and older, who apparently did not come from a nearby outpost but from farther away, meaning they had been specifically summoned," one of the diplomats present at the scene told ynet. "They kicked the French mayor, and he was injured."
A European diplomat traveling in one of the vehicles described how the delegation was forced to flee when masked settlers approached carrying sticks and metal crowbars.
"The residents of Taybeh invited diplomats and peace activists to the olive harvest to protect them. At one point, we heard that settlers were approaching, so we immediately got into the car and started driving. Then I saw masked settlers carrying sticks and metal crowbars running toward us. It was clear they had no good intentions. It was frightening. They hadn't come to pick olives," the diplomat said.
"They kicked the French mayor, and after beating him, they shouted 'Viva la France.' They had recognized the French flag," he continued. "They also attacked the Belgian vehicle. When you see something like that, you say to yourself, 'My God, how can something like this happen?'"
The diplomat said the delegation had arrived with security personnel and found it particularly troubling that the violence occurred in an area under Israeli control.
"We knew settler violence was serious, but when you witness it firsthand, you understand just how terrible it is, especially for the residents who depend on the olive harvest for their livelihoods," he said.
Although the reported assault on Baudoux was not captured on camera, footage subsequently showed him on the ground, while photographs documented a shattered window in a vehicle belonging to the Belgian Consulate.
The attacks have provoked an international outcry and exposed conflicting responses among senior Israeli officials. Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar, the IDF and Israeli police condemned the violence, while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office issued an English-language statement questioning whether the available evidence established the full sequence of events and the identity of those responsible.
The Prime Minister's Office also noted that the delegation had entered a sensitive area without prior coordination with the IDF and raised concerns about what it described as a coordinated campaign to discredit Israel and Jewish residents of the West Bank during the olive harvest.
Members of the European delegation rejected the suggestion that they should have coordinated the visit with the military.
"That is a misleading claim," delegation members said. "Taybeh is in Area B, and visits there do not require coordination. Diplomats visit frequently, and the military has never escorted them or required prior coordination."
One of the diplomats also criticized Netanyahu's response, saying the prime minister had failed to acknowledge the significance of the attack on a delegation visiting a Christian community.
"The mayor's political background is irrelevant to the question of who attacked him. Netanyahu's statement completely ignores the fact that this is a Christian village and that the delegation came from Catholic countries that consider themselves committed to protecting Christians in the West Bank. In Europe, Netanyahu's statement is seen as shocking," the diplomat said.
The incident has also prompted warnings of diplomatic consequences for Israel. Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot said his country would continue pushing for European Union sanctions against those responsible for settler violence and those supporting it.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot demanded that Israeli authorities arrest and prosecute those responsible for the attack and take urgent steps to protect civilians from further violence. Poland's Foreign Ministry also condemned the incident.
The assault on Levine the previous day drew sharp criticism from Washington. U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee described the attack on the unarmed photographer as a despicable act of violence and called for a full investigation, arrests and prosecutions.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio also expressed concern over the incidents and called on Israel to take stronger action against settler violence.
"We're very disturbed by those images and what we're seeing. We've asked the Israelis and continue to ask them to crack down on that stuff," Rubio told reporters.
The violence has renewed attention on the situation in Taybeh, where residents have reported repeated attacks on homes, vehicles and agricultural land. The village, which holds particular religious significance for Christians, has seen families leave amid growing fears over their safety.
In July 2025, following an attack in which rioters set fire to a cemetery and desecrated a church, Huckabee visited Taybeh and described the incident as an act of terrorism.
Despite the repeated condemnations from Israeli and foreign officials, no suspects had been arrested in either of the two latest attacks as of Sunday morning. Police say they are continuing their efforts to identify those involved and bring them to justice.

Months-long Indonesia wildfires spew toxic haze across Southeast Asia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
06:30:35 UTC
15:30:35 KST

Months-long Indonesia wildfires spew toxic haze across Southeast Asia
Parts of southern Southeast Asia have been put under the highest-level haze alert as wildfires that have swept Indonesia for months continue to belch toxic smoke across the region. The seasonal wildfires are worse this year due to the drought conditions caused by a severe "super-El Nino" effect.
Fires in Indonesia that have sent toxic smoke sweeping across Southeast Asia have triggered the highest-level alert by the regional bloc's meteorological monitor.
The months-long pollution spell has closed schools, fuelled a surge in respiratory conditions and restricted outdoor activities in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and East Timor.
The haze is made up of fumes the forest and peatland fires that have ravaged parts of Indonesia, most notably on the islands of Borneo and Sumatra.
These areas are covered in dense forests and vast stretches of peatland that are especially prone to fire during the dry season, which usually runs from April to October.
The region is also currently under the influence of severe "super-El Nino" weather conditions, which brought additional heat and dryness and caused wildfires to spread more quickly.
While the extent of the damage remains unknown, environmental group Auriga reported that more than 637,000 hectares were burned from January to August this year, nine times the area of Singapore.
Deforestation monitor Nusantara Atlas put the figure even higher at nearly 900,000 hectares.
'High risk'
"This thing needs to stop," Zul Hafiz, a 39-year-old teacher cycling from the Malaysian city of Shah Alam to the capital, told AFP on Saturday, calling on the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to take action.
The 11-country organisation's ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre (ASMC) said in a notice on its website on Friday that it had activated "Alert Level 3 for the Southern ASEAN region" – the highest rung of a four-tiered alert system.
The alert level is triggered when there is a "high risk of severe transboundary haze in the region" and is reserved for widespread moderate to dense smoke haze, observed over two or more consecutive days.
The ASMC has already issued two Level 3 alerts this year, according to its website.
Singapore ranked second on IQAir's live ranking of the world's most polluted major cities behind Baghdad on Saturday, with Kuala Lumpur third. All readings showed "very hazardous" levels."
'Irresponsible behaviour'
Indonesia said Saturday it had been using dry ice at one of South Sumatra province's main airports in an attempt to disperse the haze.
The country's national disaster mitigation agency said that 2.4 tonnes of dry ice were dispersed by plane.
"The smoke not only reduces visibility and disrupts aircraft operations, but also affects residents' health," the agency warned.
The haze has disrupted life across Southeast Asia, sparking fresh calls for action from those affected.
"It's a bit unfair on Malaysia because of the irresponsible behaviour of our neighbouring country," Khairul Azhar, a 33-year-old bank officer told AFP in Kuala Lumpur.
"This is affecting our weekend routine – not just for us but many Malaysians," he said.
In Indonesia's Palangkaraya – part of the epicentre of the fires where thick haze turned the skies into apocalyptic shades of yellow and orange – residents said they were suffering from its effects on Saturday.
"The haze has a big impact on us, especially on health and the economy, with our income decreasing," said Marzuki, a 38-year-old mechanic who like many in Indonesia, goes by only one name.
"Right now the economy is already very difficult, and the haze just makes it worse," he told AFP, adding that this year's situation was worse than even previous major bouts of haze in 2015.
"Hopefully it rains soon, the fires go out, and the smoke disappears so that activities can return to normal and it's easier to earn a living again," he said.
'What else to do?'
Joko, 51, a construction worker, said he had no choice but to keep on working or he would lose out on income.
"The thick smoke, when inhaled, makes it hard to breathe and stings the eyes, but what else can you do? This is how we earn a living," Joko said, explaining he had no fixed income and relied on daily wage jobs.
In East Timor, unhealthy air pollution persisted on Saturday, including in the capital Dili, according to IQAir.
Authorities warned that the situation may worsen on Saturday and schools were closed.
Singapore said Friday it would issue warnings to seven companies in Indonesia it identified as responsible for the fires.
Philippines foreign department spokesman for ASEAN issues, Dominic Xavier Imperial, said Friday that the haze would be discussed at upcoming meetings ahead of a November ASEAN summit in Manila.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP and Reuters)

India: CJP leader Abhijeet Dipke released after detention

India: 'Cockroach' leader Abhijeet Dipke released after detention
October 18, 2026
Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), was released on Saturday, a day after he was detained by the Delhi police during protests against the election authority in India.
The 31-year-old youth leader was detained while he was trying to join the protest rally which the CJP movement had called in the capital's central Connaught Place district.
The movement published a photo of him on X in which it referred to Dipke as "a free man."
"Abhijeet Dipke released," CJP legal affairs chief Ratna Singh said on social media.
Singh said Dipke was released after agreeing to certain conditions. She did not provide details about the terms.
In a post on Instagram, Dipke said he "knew going to jail was inevitable" and that he was ready to face "whatever comes my way."
"Because the day I decided to come back to India, I placed my fate in the hands of the people of India and the Constitution of this country."
What are the protests about?
All India Students' Association (AISA) President Neha Bora, who was also detained during a protest in New Delhi on Friday, was released later on Friday evening.
Bora has emerged as a prominent face in the protests against India's Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over alleged manipulation of voter lists.
A widespread review exercise — called Special Intensive Revision (SIR) — has struck off over 130 million names from India's electoral rolls since it began last year.
Opposition leaders and critics say that those removed from the voter lists include a large proportion of minority voters. They accuse Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist BJP of using the exercise as a tool to secure future electoral gains.
The neutrality of the Election Commission of India (ECI) is also being questioned.
The ECI denies favoring any party. It says the SIR removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and also helps in preventing the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."
Youth being made 'pawns' — BJP
Modi's party has slammed its opponents for undermining democracy and has denounced the protests as attempts to create "anarchy". 
BJP's Rajnath Singh — who is also India's defense minister — addressed the protests at a press conference on Friday.
Singh accused the opposition, led by the Congress party, of wanting to bring a "regime change along the lines of Bangladesh" and using Indian youth as "pawns in the politics of disorder."
"It appears that the Congress and its political allies, both directly and through their affiliated organisations, are attempting to channel the energy of young people not into constructive activities and nation-building, but into instruments of political confrontation and the spread of chaos," he said.
Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka's custody ends Sunday
Two other senior CJP leaders, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, were arrested on October 14 for entering Jantar Mantar.
Jantar Mantar had been a prominent protest site in the heart of Delhi for decades. However, Delhi police blocked it amid heavy barricading and deployment.
The two leaders were sent to five days of judicial custody, which ends Sunday. The CJP has warned of legal action if Das and Ranka are not released.
"Now just waiting for my brothers to be free", Dipke said in a post on X that included a photo of Ranka and Das.

Rubio: Ukraine Does Not Have Access to Starshield
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
06:28:00 UTC
15:28:00 KST

Ukraine currently lacks access to the specialized military-grade Starshield satellite network and has requested the technology to conduct deep-interdiction strikes inside Russia, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said.
Speaking to journalists in comments released by the US Department of State, Rubio clarified the distinction between SpaceX’s standard commercial Starlink communications framework and the dedicated Starshield architecture operated under contract with the US Department of Defense.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Starlink is a commercial product, okay? And so it’s regulated and handled as a commercial product. Starshield is a defense product, a military product,” Rubio stated.
“That is something that the United States military uses. It’s not at this moment available to Ukraine, and that’s under conversation. It’s under discussion right now how they would want to use it.”
Responding to questions regarding reports of technological throttling, Rubio directly refuted claims that the Trump administration had mandated bandwidth or velocity caps on terminals operating in Ukrainian combat sectors.
“I know Ukraine wants access to Starshield. They do not have Starshield now. They’ve asked for access to it in order to conduct deep strikes inside of Russia. They do not have access to it at this moment,” Rubio emphasized.
“Those are two different products.”
Zelensky Calls Trump’s Sanctions Waiver a Mistake
White House denies intentional velocity caps
Rubio pushed back against assertions by President Volodymyr Zelensky that artificial operational constraints imposed on Starlink terminals inside Ukraine were deliberate administrative measures.
“I don’t know what Zelensky said. I’m not sure Zelensky knows what he’s talking about, but it wasn’t deliberate. We have nothing to do with that,” Rubio said.
“Nobody ordered that Starlink speed to be slowed down. It sort of happened, but my understanding is it’s been restored. It’s back to where it was before. That’s Starlink, though. They were using Starlink for their drones.”
Addressing media reports suggesting executive coordination to limit unmanned systems, the secretary of state characterized the allegations as completely unfounded.
“Nothing to do with the White House. I saw a report on that the other day. It’s just categorically false,” Rubio told reporters.
“No one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet or slow down speed so that certain drones couldn’t use it. But my understanding is it’s back up and running. That’s what I read – that’s what we heard two days ago.”
Zelensky’s 161 km/h disclosure
Rubio’s comments follow detailed disclosures delivered on Saturday, Oct. 17, by President Zelensky, who revealed that Starlink terminals operating inside Ukrainian territory had been subjected to a strict velocity limitation of 161 km/h (100 mph).
According to Zelensky, whenever equipped domestic platforms exceeded the 161 km/h threshold, satellite connections automatically severed, causing operators to lose control of unmanned interceptors in mid-flight.
The velocity cap effectively disabled domestic drone interceptors tasked with neutralizing high-speed, turbojet-powered Russian Shahed loitering munitions, which penetrate sovereign airspace at speeds exceeding 400 km/h (250 mph).
Zelensky highlighted that Ukrainian technical teams conducted cross-border comparative evaluations, sending Starlink-equipped vehicles into EU territory, where the devices operated uninterrupted at velocities of 180 km/h (112 mph). The Ukrainian leader argued that the trials confirmed the restrictions were geographically targeted at Ukrainian airspace rather than stemming from global software glitches.
The Starshield controversy
The technological dispute underscores widening geopolitical friction between Washington and Kyiv over long-range interdiction limits and commercial communications dependencies.
Rubio’s denials echo statements by US President Donald Trump, who told that neither he nor SpaceX founder Elon Musk ordered operational caps on Ukraine’s military communications, asserting that “everything is the same as it’s always been.”
However, both official denials contradict reporting by The Telegraph, which cited four sources familiar with the matter stating that Musk directly proposed satellite service limitations to Trump, who approved the measure, clearing the way for the Pentagon to restrict Starshield functionality.
Sources cited in the report claimed Musk sought to shift public accountability onto the White House amid concerns over potential consumer boycotts across European markets following civilian casualties in Kyiv.

A 140-year-old town hall in France was largely destroyed as a fierce fire took hold on Saturday after masked protesters set the building alight, authorities said.
Dramatic footage showed the spire of the Limoges town hall collapse as flames engulfed the roof overnight amid mass cost-of-living protests across the country.
According to the Haute-Vienne prefecture, rioters broke into the town hall at around 6 pm on Saturday before setting it ablaze.
"Firefighters from Haute-Vienne were immediately mobilised in large numbers to tackle the fire," it said in a press release. "Limoges town hall, a heritage site and iconic landmark for everyone, was largely destroyed."

Maurice Barate, the prefect of Haute-Vienne, has strongly condemned the "arson attack" on the town hall as well as other incidents in the city on Saturday.

Four police officers sustained "more serious" injuries, and four police vehicles were destroyed, it said. The protesters then moved to block the A20 motorway before heading for the city centre.
Nineteen people have been detained by police in the region in relation to the protests, and investigations are continuing.
Construction on the Limoges town hall began in 1879, and the building was inaugurated on 14 July 1883.
"Protesting is a right, and anger deserves to be heard. Yet, no disagreement or grievance can ever justify the destruction of public property," Guillaume Guérin, the mayor of Limoges, said, calling the violence "unacceptable."
Violence sweeps France
Major cost-of-living protests taking place across France on Saturday turned violent in a number of parts of the country as demonstrators clashed with police.
The French Interior Ministry said around 550,000 people took part in the protests - which joined up with ongoing student demonstrations - nationwide, including roughly 110,000 in Paris.
In the capital, chaotic scenes saw widespread looting as officers fired tear gas and water cannons to disperse crowds. A Euronews crew were also assaulted by looters and rioters in Paris on Saturday, near the Place de la Republique, as they covered the ongoing demonstrations.
However, in other parts of the city, such as around the Boulevard de Clichy and Place de Clichy in the 18th arrondissement, the situation remained peaceful, another Euronews journalist reporting from the scene said.
Addressing the protests in a post on social media on Saturday evening, French President Emmanuel Macron said there was "no place for violence" in France.
"Those who have vandalised and attacked prefectures and shops alike, and even looted our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished," he said.

Expert: Trump's recent decisions have nothing to do with midterms
Analyzing U.S. President Donald Trump's latest moves that have harmed Ukraine and favored Russia, U.S. politics expert Andreas Kaju admitted he could not explain why the president was making such decisions.
Fuel retailer Alexela's head of energy sales, Tarmo Kärsna, does not believe Russian diesel will help U.S. President Donald Trump achieve his goals of lowering fuel prices and saving American farmers.
"If Russian diesel were brought to the U.S. market, we would be talking about less than a day's consumption. It's a drop in the ocean. Markets are also skeptical today, questioning whether Russia even has the capacity to increase its diesel exports from their current level. After all, exports have fallen sevenfold since January of this year," Kärsna said.
The curtailment of Ukraine's satellite capabilities for striking Russia and defending itself, followed by the decision to abandon planned sanctions, are the latest surprises.
"It is clear that President Trump has taken Russia's side in the war and is clearly acting against Ukraine's interests. This is a very bad development," said European Parliament member Riho Terras (Isamaa).
Why? U.S. politics expert Andreas Kaju said he did not know. The midterm elections have nothing to do with it.
"If he wanted to win elections, he would have acted very differently long ago. What he has been doing consistently over the past year is endorsing extremely unpopular candidates within the Republican Party in various states. As a result, it is entirely possible that Republicans will lose states in the midterm elections that previously would have been unthinkable," Kaju said.
Kaju pointed to an article in the U.S. conservative publication National Review.
"The article argued that it is time for Republicans and Democrats to jointly launch a major congressional investigation into the reasons behind President Trump's Russia policy," Kaju said.
Kaju speculated that such investigations might indeed begin in Congress, including the Senate, after the midterm elections.

Mandolin orchestras: A 120-year cultural tradition in Bulgaria’s capital
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
06:15:50 UTC
15:15:50 KST

Author
Tsvetana Toncheva
News
Mandolin orchestras: A 120-year cultural tradition in Bulgaria’s capital
Sunday 18 October 2026 09:00
Sunday, 18 October 2026, 09:00
PHOTO Facebook/ Mandolin ensembles conducted by Plamen Maslev
Font size
The mandolin- an almond shaped music instrument that replaces the bow’s warm tones with the sparkling plucks of a plectrum- originated in Renaissance Italy, where it was already the most beloved folk instrument in the 16th century. By the late 19th and early 20th centuries, it had gained enormous popularity worldwide.
In Bulgaria, the tradition of mandolin orchestras dates back more than a century. The instrument was introduced to Bulgarian lands as early as the mid-19th century, and the first ensembles emerged towards the end of that century. The first mandolin orchestra in the capital city was founded in 1906, and the first mandolin textbook was published in 1907.
PHOTO Facebook/ Golden Strings Quartet
In October 2026, Culture Centre Struni is organizing a series of events to mark the 120th anniversary of Sofia’s first mandolin ensemble. The project includes the publication of a monograph by Lora Nedyalkova, a lecture by conductor, mandolinist and luthier Plamen Maslev, and a series of concerts.
The celebrations will culminate in a concert by the Prima Visione Orchestra at Sofia’s Central Military Club on 24 October.
Prima Visione Orchestra
PHOTO Facebook/ Iskra – 1964 Community Cultural Centre in Sofia
In an interview with Radio Bulgaria, Lora Nedyalkova, author of the monograph 120 Years of Mandolin Orchestras in Sofia, said that preparations for the anniversary and research into the history of the ensembles began as early as 2020. Information available in periodicals and books is scarce, so she has also conducted interviews with people who were directly involved in the ensembles.
“Many members of our Prima Visione Orchestra are quite elderly. As children, they began playing in some of the earlier mandolin orchestras. Thanks to them, we were able to gather a wealth of material. I continued collecting information over the years. Interestingly, some orchestras are known to us only through the people who took part in them. For instance, the father of the renowned tenor Boyko Tsvetanov played in a mandolin orchestra affiliated with TABSO. (TABSO was a Bulgarian airline that operated from 1948 to 1968 and was the predecessor of Balkan Airlines — author’s note.)
There were other orchestras that we learned about exclusively through these interviews. When I began compiling and organising the material, I suddenly realized how much information I had accumulated. As I started putting it all together, it grew into a book. We will publish the full version, because there is no time to lose — this information is being lost.”
PHOTO National Polytechnic Museum
Lora Nedyalkova recounts how Atanas Kovachev, born in Plovdiv in 1882, moved to Sofia at the beginning of the 20th century to study. Unable to finish secondary school due to financial difficulties, he began working as a printer. However, when the Sofia School of Music officially opened in 1905, he enrolled there.
Several sources now cite 1906 as the year the first mandolin orchestra was founded, with Kovachev as its conductor. In 1908, he left for Odesa to continue his musical education. After graduating and qualifying as a bandmaster, he returned to Sofia and spent several months conducting the local tambura orchestra in 1911. The Balkan Wars then broke out, and he left for the front.
PHOTO archive
The mandolin ensembles established in Sofia in later years were short-lived. In the 1930s and 1940s, the Sofia Mandolin Quartet regularly delighted listeners with live performances broadcast on Radio Sofia.
PHOTO Facebook/ Iskra – 1964 Community Cultural Centre in Sofia
The largest mandolin orchestra in the capital was based at the Trade Union House of Culture, whose membership grew to more than 70 over the years. It was founded in 1940 by Assen Arsov, who conducted it until 1985. The orchestra played an active role in Bulgaria’s cultural life, performing at national festivals and competitions and touring abroad. In the 1970s, it won gold medals at competitions in the Netherlands and West Germany.
Several other successful amateur mandolin orchestras also existed in Sofia during the 20th century.
Ivan Maslev played an important role in raising these ensembles to a professional standard. He began playing the guitar and mandolin as a child. After graduating from the Music Academy with a degree in oboe, he joined the Sofia Opera Orchestra. In the 1960s, he founded the Sofia Mandolinists to provide professional accompaniment for singers recording for Balkanton and the Bulgarian National Radio.
Speaking to Radio Bulgaria, Ivan Maslev’s son, Plamen Maslev, recalls:
Plamen Maslev
PHOTO Facebook/ Mandolin ensembles conducted by Plamen Maslev
“I was still a child when, in the 1970s, he made recordings with Nicolai Ghiaurov in Vienna for the British record label Decca Records. Later, in the early 1980s, he released a double album with tenor Rumen Doykov entitled Italian Canzonettas. We also had a very interesting project with Boris Christoff. Unfortunately, he fell ill in the final years of his life, and we eventually completed the project with baritone Sabin Markov instead. There has always been interest among leading singers in Bulgaria and around the world in this type of instrument, because it offers something different.”
Translated by Kostadin Atanasov

The operations at Australian oil and gas giant, Woodside's $12.5 billion Scarborough project in Western Australia have stopped after Greenpeace staged a protest at a floating platform.
On Sunday, the company said it had to pause work at a Scarborough floating production unit off the coast of WA. Two activists from the environmental advocacy group slept overnight on the semi-submersible unit, located about 375 km off the state's northwest coast, in a protest that started on Saturday.
"Temporary hanging tents" were set up on the unit and the activists would "occupy the platform for as long as possible", Greenpeace had said.
The group staged the protest over concerns that Woodside's proposed Browse project's could inflict potential damage to Scott Reef, a remote coral system and foraging area for the endangered pygmy blue whale. Browse and Scarborough are in the same northwest location but more than 1,000 kilometres apart.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Browse is Australia's biggest undeveloped offshore gas resource and worth about $37 billion. Woodside had said it the project would make no physical contact with the reef above the 75-metre water depth.
Greenpeace is not the only group concerned about Browse's impact on Australia's natural surroundings. The Australian Conservation Foundation launched a legal intervention to the project in June, which is now before the courts.
ACF says the Browse gas project's carbon emissions fuel climate change, which could destroy nature in WA and other areas in Australia such as the Great Barrier Reef.
In June, the Great Barrier Reef avoided being listed as an endangered world heritage site by UNESCO, despite concerns about climate change-fuelled damage to the ecosystem's corals. The decision was driven by Australia's promise to clean up the reef but UNESCO remained concerned over mass coral bleaching events.
Meanwhile at Scarborough, a Woodside spokesperson said "operations at the Scarborough floating production unit remain safely paused" after temporarily halting pre-commissioning activities as a result of the "unauthorised access" by Greenpeace.
Four activists scaled the 70,000 metric ton unit, part of the 98% completed Scarborough project, and displayed banners with the message "Stop Woodside’s Dirty Gas. Save Scott Reef".

Occupied Oleshky Turned Into ‘Death Trap’, Sybiha Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
06:01:00 UTC
15:01:00 KST

Russian forces have turned the occupied city of Oleshky in the southern Kherson region into a “death trap,” leaving approximately 1,700 remaining residents trapped under acute starvation, pervasive mining, and relentless drone surveillance, Ukrainia Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha warned.
In an official public appeal, Sybiha disclosed that the sole overland exit route from the ruined municipality has been heavily mined and placed under continuous Russian drone targeting, rendering escape attempts potentially lethal for trapped non-combatants.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Those who try to flee risk their lives. The adjacent river is also mined. Residents doubt they will survive this winter. The hospital has run out of medicine. Dozens of bodies lie in the streets or in houses, as the Russians forbid residents from burying them,” Sybiha stated.
The foreign minister described extreme shortages of basic sustenance, noting that isolated civilians are struggling to endure on minimal rations while confronting harassment from occupation troops.
“Families are starving, surviving on leftover garden vegetables, canned goods, and even snails. Residents say that Russian soldiers have threatened them at gunpoint to seize their food,” Sybiha added.
Reiterating that Kyiv has repeatedly pressed for safe civilian evacuations and unhindered humanitarian access, Sybiha issued an urgent appeal to the United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), and international partners to mobilize every diplomatic and operational conduit to deliver emergency supplies and evacuate those seeking to depart.
Mushrooms and the Autumn Moon
“People cannot survive on statements of concern. They need action. They need a way out. And they need it now,” Sybiha emphasized.
Encirclement and isolation on the Dnipro left bank
Oleshky, situated on the east (left) bank of the Dnipro River approximately five kilometers southeast of the regional capital of Kherson, has been under Russian military occupation since the initial weeks of the full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The city has been completely cut off from authorized commercial freight convoys and organized institutional aid since late May.
While earlier demographic assessments by Ukrainian authorities indicated several thousand residents remained scattered across the wider river basin, civilian numbers within the municipal core have contracted to roughly 1,700 as conditions have deteriorated ahead of sub-zero winter temperatures.
Local municipal officials have confirmed that central utility grids – including drinking water supply, electrical networks, and municipal gas heating – have suffered significant damage.
With ground logistics paralyzed by dense minefields, destroyed bridge spans, and persistent Russian first-person view (FPV) drone patrols along the riverfront, Ukrainian defense units have intermittently deployed heavy multi-rotor transport drones to air-drop food and medical packages directly into residential yards.
Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets previously reported that his office had documented hundreds of verified appeals from civilians trapped in the enclave, noting that residents desperate to flee have attempted to navigate active minefields on foot due to the absence of negotiated humanitarian corridors.
Vatican diplomatic outreach
The escalating emergency in Oleshky has attracted top-level international diplomatic intervention.
On Friday, Oct. 16, Pope Leo XIV held a telephone consultation with Russian President Vladimir Putin to urge an immediate localized ceasefire in Oleshky, calling for verified arrangements to permit emergency food and medical deliveries alongside the safe, voluntary evacuation of non-combatants.
The Vatican confirmed that the pope expressed deep concern over the grave humanitarian collapse in the municipality and pressed Moscow to facilitate unhindered relief operations.
In its official readout of the discussion, the Kremlin claimed that Putin offered what it described as a “detailed explanation” attributing responsibility for the municipal situation to Ukrainian authorities, while expressing general willingness to coordinate with Vatican initiatives.
UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk has similarly characterized the humanitarian situation in Oleshky as desperate, appealing directly to the Russian Federation to fulfill its legal obligations under international humanitarian law as an occupying power by permitting the immediate evacuation of civilians and allowing international aid agencies unfettered access.

Look, no hands: Euronews rode driverless in Europe's first robotaxi in Zagreb
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
06:00:55 UTC
15:00:55 KST

The US firm’s robotaxi service is up and running in Zagreb in partnership with local company Verne and Chinese AI firm Pony.ai, a partnership that plans to expand across Europe. Euronews got to see how it works firsthand in Croatia.
Uber launched a driverless taxi service in Zagreb, Croatia, earlier this year and has now unveiled plans to roll out a fully autonomous vehicle service in a host of European cities with partners across the continent, starting with Manchester.
The US tech company deployed driverless robotaxis on the streets of Zagreb in April in partnership with local service operator Verne and Chinese AI firm Pony.ai in a business model they want to scale up across the continent.
It is an odd partnership given the divergent philosophies at play in Europe, the US and China, with Europe being particularly cautious compared with the latter two. But the companies believe the partnership works thanks to their shared ambition to deploy autonomous vehicle taxi rides around the world.
The partnership is one of more than 30 Uber runs across Europe. Together with Verne and Pony.ai, Uber has begun tests in Manchester, and Pony.ai and Uber plan to launch in London, with many more cities in the pipeline.
The Zagreb partnership is the most advanced and was announced in March, in a move that aimed to bring driverless taxis out of testing grounds and onto the market in Europe for the first time.
Zagreb was a particularly appealing candidate city for Uber, as it is home to electric hypercar maker Rimac, whose founder Mate Rimac had already branched out into robotaxis through Verne. Verne has its own plans to roll out a “business class” form of autonomous vehicle mobility service.
In April, the partnership launched its robotaxi service, giving users in Zagreb the chance to order a driverless vehicle for their journey. These cars still have a human in the driving seat, known as a safety operator, who oversees the trip as a security measure. Safety operators are usually former taxi drivers.
The service’s vehicles have since clocked up 200,000 kilometres on Zagreb’s roads.
Now the partnership feels confident enough to take the next step and remove the operator from the car, leaving just you, the passenger, alone in the vehicle.
Europe’s first fully driverless trips began on 10 September, open to a limited number of invited users on a 22-kilometre route linking Verne’s headquarters with Zagreb’s Franjo Tuđman Airport.
‘Look, no hands’
Ordering an Uber with the currently available driverless ride service is just as simple as booking any other trip with the platform. Users can choose between human-driven and AI-driven robotaxi rides when requesting UberX or Comfort journeys.
Riders can unlock the car with their phone, get in and get comfortable, or as comfortable as possible in a car with no one driving, but with full access to Uber support should anything happen.
In Zagreb, riders travel in the BAIC Arcfox Alpha T5, a Chinese electric SUV. A human safety operator sits in the driving seat, and the front passenger seat has been removed to make more space for luggage.
Uber and Verne currently run about 30 autonomous vehicles in Zagreb, which return each night to a central hub called a “mothership” for cleaning and maintenance by the Croatian startup.
The current setup is what is known as a level 4 driverless car programme, which means the car can drive itself without human interference, but only in strictly controlled areas. Nowhere in the world runs a level 5 programme, which means unrestricted road access.
It is a strange feeling seeing a car drive itself for the first time. From the rear passenger seat, you can see the steering wheel spinning as the car makes a turn calmly and methodically, even while negotiating oncoming traffic.
The smooth ride puts you at ease, and after a while you forget that it is not a person but an AI driving you to your destination.
“We call it a little bit magically boring, meaning, you get in and first you’re like ‘oh, no one’s hands are on the wheel’ and then all of sudden you’re in a car like you normally would be,” said Annie Duvnjak, global head of autonomous mobility operations at Uber.
That is not to say the ride is free of interruptions. The car comes to a complete stop at every stop sign, even when the road is empty, and it pulls over to avoid overly aggressive human drivers trying to overtake.
It is a learning process for the partnership, which is testing fully driverless vehicles, its end goal, in a limited area of Zagreb.
A unique partnership
The partnership, launched in April, is a unique combination of an American mobility firm, a European startup and a Chinese AI company, with each organisation coming from regions with wildly differing approaches to mobility and AI.
Given these divergent approaches and the current geopolitical friction on issues ranging from trade and consumer rules to technological sovereignty and supply chains, it may seem surprising that these companies have joined forces.
But Uber says the model works because the three companies share a common goal of bringing autonomous taxis to more markets.
“You have Verne, which is an incredible local company in Zagreb, with fleet expertise and vehicle operations and then you Pony.ai, which has world-class AV technology, and you have Uber which helps bring that all together in terms of the mobility platform, rider experience,” said Duvnjak.
“So, it’s really everyone’s bringing the best of what they do coming together.”
Verne, the European partner in this venture, was co-founded by Mate Rimac and is named after the sci-fi writer Jules Verne. It has been working on robotaxis since 2019 and launched its own service in April.
Verne acts as the local service operator and fleet owner, managing the day-to-day operations of the robotaxi service. It also serves as the regulatory lead, talking to local, regional and national authorities to secure legal approval for autonomous vehicles on the road in these areas.
This is perhaps the biggest obstacle facing the partnership. Europe’s patchwork legal framework governing driverless cars has left the continent lagging far behind the US and China, where robotaxis have operated commercially for several years.
The partnership with Uber gives Verne the opportunity to scale up its operation by offering its services through the app and bring them to other cities across Europe as the roll-out expands.
“This is an important milestone not only for Verne, but also for Croatia. A service pioneered here in Zagreb is now available through the world’s largest mobility platform. The experience we are gaining every day in Zagreb will help us bring Verne to other European cities,” said Marko Pejković, the CEO of Verne.
In June 2024, the Croatian company unveiled its own autonomous two-seater concept car aimed at business travellers.
“We want people to be impressed when you arrive in one of these vehicles,” said Pejković.
It is a long, sleek vehicle with enough room for the seats to recline fully while driving. A huge dashboard screen entertains and informs passengers during their ride.
Despite its more luxurious appearance, the company says rides will not come at a premium, because removing the driver cuts costs significantly.
“We are introducing a completely new vision for the vehicle interior, one designed not as a concept for the distant future, but as something that can work in real service. It will help people use their time in a way that is more productive, more enjoyable, and more relaxing,” said Pejković.
The company plans to roll out the vehicle in future but, for now, uses the BAIC Arcfox.
A driving school for AI agents
The third partner in this venture is Chinese AI firm Pony.ai, which provides the artificial intelligence technology that drives the vehicles.
The company also brings a lot of experience in the sector. Pony.ai says it was the first autonomous vehicle company to secure a taxi licence in China, and it is one of the few companies globally operating fully driverless commercial vehicles.
In Zagreb, the Arcfox vehicles are equipped with Pony.ai’s Gen-7 autonomous driving system, its latest level 4 autonomous driving kit.
The kit includes 34 individual sensors. Among them are nine LiDAR sensors, 14 cameras and four millimetre-wave radars, as well as four microphones, two water sensors and one collision sensor. Together they give the vehicle considerable awareness of its surroundings and enough redundancy to reduce the chance of accidents.
Driving the car is the Pony.ai Virtual Driver, which treats the vehicle like a physical AI agent. But before an AI agent can hit the road, it must first drive in a virtual environment.
“It’s like a virtual training ground, that shows the AI how to drive. It’s like how humans learn to drive is how the AI drivers learn to drive in that environment. Then, after it graduates the ‘virtual driving school’, the AI drivers take control, so we don’t rely on any remote control,” said Dr Ludi Wang, director of global communications at Pony.ai.
Next steps
Uber announced this week that the partnership’s next city will be Manchester, in the UK. Tests are already under way in the city, and Uber says a service like the one in Zagreb will follow in the coming months.
In total, Uber is considering more than 30 cities and has schemes at various stages in London, Madrid, Munich and Zurich.
“And we hope to expand this model to other cities as well. So we’ve announced Manchester, where we’ll be coming next with this partnership, and so, more to come from there,” said Duvnjak.
But could Brussels be next?
“We’re actually talking to Brussels, we’re talking to 30 cities and Brussels is one of those cities. But we don’t want to roll out tests in a city if we don’t see it as an option in the future to fully roll out a driverless service as the end goal. But Brussels is definitely on the map,” said Pejković.

Heat pumps and insulation would cut UK living costs more than new oilfields, study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
06:00:52 UTC
15:00:52 KST

Insulating Britain’s homes and investing in heat pumps would do more to cut the cost of living, create jobs and boost the UK’s economy than drilling for new oil, research suggests.
The government’s £15bn warm homes plan, currently under threat of cuts as ministers seek budget savings, would slash £1bn a year from household energy bills across the UK, concentrated on those on low incomes, according to research by the thinktank E3G. It would also provide a £1.6bn yearly boost to the economy, and about 50,000 new jobs spread across thousands of small businesses.
The Rosebank oilfield, west of Shetland, would create about 1,100 direct and indirect jobs, the analysis found. The jobs would be concentrated in the North Sea and in two companies, one of them – Equinor – an overseas investor.
A decision on whether to give the green light to the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea was “imminent”, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said on Wednesday. A decision on Rosebank would take a little longer, she said.
Labour promised in its 2024 election manifesto to halt new licensing for oil and gas, but Jackdaw and Rosebank could be exceptions because they were already in the licensing system.
Equinor previously estimated 3,500 jobs would be created at peak for Jackdaw and Rosebank combined.
Experts have repeatedly pointed out that new North Sea oil and gas would not bring down fuel prices or ease any supply constraints on the UK arising from the Iran war, because oil and gas are sold on international markets.
Some proponents of drilling argue that the economic boost to the UK and tax revenues for the government are reasons to grant licences. But related research by WWF and the campaigning group Uplift shows that tax revenues are likely to be limited, given the concessions that drillers can expect. While the total profits from Rosebank for its backers, Equinor, Shell and Ithaca Energy, could be £1.5bn over its 25-year lifespan, the UK government faces a potential loss of £258m through tax breaks and incentives.
Tax revenues from the North Sea were about £4bn in 2025-26, but upstream tax relief and support measures amounted to an estimated £3.26bn.
As the North Sea is a basin in steep decline, tax revenues from drilling are projected to fall to about £100m by 2030. Decommissioning costs for drilling platforms are also a major factor: taxpayers are likely to be asked for £12bn as the North Sea’s infrastructure is dismantled.
The warm homes plan, under which up to 5m homes would be insulated, would draw in a further £15bn in private investment, according to E3G, which would be spread across the country rather than concentrated in one area, in line with Andy Burnham’s pledge for economic growth “in every postcode”.
E3G also estimates that delivering the warm homes plan in full would boost GDP by 0.08%, while AI modelling suggests Rosebank would add about 0.025% on average through its lifetime, assuming the average oil price returning to $70 a barrel from recent highs. If the UK taxpayer paid for decommissioning, this would outweigh any positive impact.
James Huw Dyson, a senior researcher at E3G, said: “When the first cold snap rolls in, the public aren’t going to thank the government for cutting home insulation while giving big oil tax breaks to drill for polluting energy that keeps our bills high. If the government is serious about tackling the cost of living, and investing across the country, it should focus its attention on insulating homes and rolling out clean energy, which will cut bills and create good jobs across Britain at the same time.”
Ten major unions wrote to the government on Thursday to oppose granting a licence to the Rosebank oilfield. Scores of Labour MPs also oppose the move, and 600 scientists wrote to ministers over the summer urging a rethink.
Dhara Vyas, the chief executive of Energy UK, which represents the energy industry, said: “We need government to stick to its ambitions on electrification. Watering down the warm homes plan or making further changes to the zero emissions vehicle mandate sends mixed signals to a market that has been in a state of flux for far too long – these businesses cannot easily ramp up production again, and sadly for too many have already had to close.”
The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero declined to comment on E3G’s findings or the future of the warm homes plan.
A spokesperson for Adura, the joint venture between Equinor and Shell that owns Jackdaw and Rosebank, said: “Analysis has shown that approving Rosebank and other planned North Sea oil developments would support £35.3bn in UK economic value between 2026 and 2035. Rosebank alone represents private sector investment of £8.7bn, three quarters of which will be spent in the UK, and together with Jackdaw will contribute £4.1bn in additional tax revenue over the next decade.”
These figures take in the company’s wider operations beyond Rosebank and Jackdaw, and also make assumptions about the wider supply chain and the spending of employees as economic benefits, which are uncertain. On the tax take, they do not take account of the large tax reliefs available, estimated at more than £2.4bn. Contrary to standard HM Treasury practice, Adura’s estimates do not appear to factor in a discount rate for future income.

‘We hang on to summer a little longer here’: five of the best places for autumn sun in Europe and Turkey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
06:00:52 UTC
15:00:52 KST

Kalkan, Turkey
A Kalkan sunset is always a beautiful thing – the horseshoe-shaped bay deepening to azure blue against an apricot-rose sky – but, in October, when the light is low and the sun drops early, it’s almost transcendentally lovely. In some Turkish resorts, you’d be sitting watching it surrounded by quiet streets, half-empty bars and that melancholic sense that another season is over. In Kalkan, it still feels like summer; the harbourfront restaurants throng with visitors, the day gulets (wooden boats) still putter in and out of the bay and you don’t have to wait an hour to get a taxi back to your villa.
For me, the best thing about an autumn break – besides the sunsets – is that I can visit some of my favourite places that just get overrun in summer. The glittering beach at Kaputas, sandwiched into a triangular gap on the mountainous Kalkan-Kas road, has become a victim of Instagram; from May to September, it’s impossible to get near. In October, the waters are still warm and the beach – although still busy – has plenty of space for a dip and a laze.
About 20 minutes’ drive inland, the mountain village of Bezirgan, which used to serve as a summer retreat for wealthier Kalkan residents, settles back into complete peace in autumn, save for the woodpeckers battering away at the bark of the almond trees and the squirrels skittering through the leaves. The Lycian Way weaves through the village, past Ottoman-era grain stores, with the lush gardens of the Pirha Köy Sofrası restaurant a great bet for a plate of traditional manti (dumplings in yoghurt) or kofte (meatballs), before setting off for a hike (they do fantastic breakfasts too).
Back in Kalkan, it’s always cocktail hour somewhere; often on a roof terrace, with a jazz soundtrack floating out above the streets of the Old Town. This year, the Fountain Terrace Cocktail Bar has been popular, but I still love sitting in the Merkez Cafe, a Kalkan institution since the early 1990s, smack-bang in the heart of the village and a prime spot for people-watching when the evening begins.
And because the season’s end is in sight, all the restaurant owners and waiters are cheerfully giddy, and the whole place swings with an end-of-term vibe. Sitting at the Blue Marlin (tucked away beneath the Pirat hotel) with a cold Efes beer and a selection of the town’s best meze, the only thing that makes me rueful is that it will be several months before I’ll be back here again.
 
White House has doubles from £120 B&B
 
Annabelle Thorpe
Agua Amarga, Spain
Along Spain’s wild Costa de Almería are a handful of exquisite little towns and villages. San José is probably the best known, put on the map by its most famous inhabitant, the late Joe Strummer, but 25 miles east is the real jewel of the Almería coast. Agua Amarga is a typical Andalucían fishing village moonlighting as a stylish low-key holiday destination, perfect for late-season sun-seekers.
Its location, on a crescent bay, makes for spectacular sunrises and sunsets over the arid headlands that bookend the 500-metre-long beach. In the narrow, whitewashed streets, a lush palm grove and splashes of pink bougainvillaea remind you that north Africa is just a short hop across the Mediterranean. In the summer, Agua Amarga’s unspoilt sands and turquoise waters attract plenty of visitors, but the vibe remains relaxed. There are a handful of restaurants and bars around the main plaza, and a few eateries on the beach, including Los Tarahis, a traditional chiringuito (beach bar) where you can enjoy dishes such as arroz negro con bogavante (black rice with lobster) with your toes in the sand. In winter, the town goes into hibernation, but in autumn the sun and sea are still warm and the bars and restaurants are still open for business.
Agua Amarga is not the place to go to party. It’s a world away from the overdeveloped costas to the west and north, but it is the perfect base to immerse yourself in nature. Hiking trails lead from the village over the cliffs to a string of isolated coves and the ruins of 18th-century forts dotted along the headlands. And if you tire of following the shimmering sea, you can strike out inland to explore the Cabo de Gata nature reserve, with its winding ramblas (dry riverbeds), prickly pears and eerie abandoned goldmines.
This corner of Spain is famous for its movie locations, notably Sergio Leone’s spaghetti westerns and Hollywood blockbusters including Lawrence of Arabia and Conan the Barbarian. For UK cinephiles, British gangster classic Sexy Beast was filmed in Agua Amarga, and Ray Winstone’s swanky villa is available as a holiday rental (minus the boulder in the swimming pool).
The name Agua Amarga translates as “bitter water”, dating back to the 19th century and the contamination caused by mining iron ore. Those days are gone, and now Agua Amarga couldn’t be sweeter.
 
Hotel Las Calas has doubles from £80 
 
Lois Pryce
Cascais, Portugal
As many of Portugal’s southern resorts prepare to hibernate for winter, Cascais’s green-fingered municipal workers set to work on the town’s well-manicured flower beds, ensuring a seamless seasonal rotation. Violas, primroses and cyclamen furnish pops of purple, magenta and orange below tall palms lining a promenade punctuated with palatial homes and pockets of golden sand. Even in late autumn, the semi-tropical scene banishes the blues.
My happy place when the off-season rolls around, Cascais has enough energy and atmosphere to entertain, and is arguably at its finest after summer’s beach throngs and Lisbon day trippers (Cascais lies 20 miles west of the city, a 30- to 40-minute train ride from Cais do Sodré station) have receded.
Once the summer retreat of Europe’s nobility, Cascais is now Portugal’s year-round crowd-pleaser – and come autumn, accommodation prices are far less aristocratic. There are stately manors and spa hotels aplenty, but my pick is Casa Vela, a surprisingly spacious sidestreet bolthole. Its sauna, shrouded in tropical gardens imported by the owner and his grandfather, brings joy even on the chilliest days. And if rains do come, there are a clutch of cultural attractions in the town, including the pyramid-shaped, terracotta-hued Casa das Histórias Paula Rego, featuring works by the acclaimed Portuguese-British artist.
Still, with about 300 sunny days a year, Cascais’s main off-season pull is for those who like to be active outdoors. Blue-sky mornings see waterfront joggers pass pretty squares carpeted in black-and-white calçada portuguesa (the distinctive patterned pavement mosaics), the hulking 15th-century citadel, and a mustard-hued palace overlooking a cove. Swimming is bracing, but kayaking on the calmer waters where the Tagus River meets the Atlantic more than compensates.
Better still, hire a bicycle and trace the craggy coastline, which grows wilder as it arches north-west, with sheer cliffs appearing in the distant haze. Praia do Guincho is the star, a glorious dune-backed beach battered by winds that keep surfers of all stripes well sated.
A half-hour bus ride from Cascais, Sintra’s iconic palaces and quintas unfurl across the forest-clad mountains. Summer in the town will test your patience. But with fewer crowds in the off-season, the essence of this former elite enclave and trove of European Romantic architecture returns. Hiking the hewn stairs to the Moorish Castle in thick fog is magical, while the vibrant burgundy-and-yellow facade of the fairytale National Palace of Pena brightens the greyest of days.
As the nights start to draw in, you can chase the dwindling sunlight by heading to windswept Cabo da Roca at Portugal’s far western tip. Not only are the sunsets here spectacular, for much of autumn and winter they are the latest in mainland Europe – a sweetener for the shorter days.
 
Casa Vela has doubles from €79 room-only
 
Daniel James Clarke
Senigallia, Italy
Velvet Beach (Spiaggia di Velluto) is the alluring name for the miles of fine sand that fringe the town of Senigallia, in Italy’s Marche region. But from May to September, that golden loveliness all but disappears under the umbrellas and sunbeds of beach clubs.
Italians love the place, some returning every summer for decades, but in high season it is probably best left to them. However, Senigallia has an allure beyond the beach that can be enjoyed year-round – and autumn is particularly rewarding.
It’s known in Italy as the “five-star town” for the number of Michelin stars its top two restaurants hold between them. At Uliassi (three stars) and Madonnina del Pescatore (two), ambitious locally born chefs have kept one another on their toes for decades, and their fame has encouraged other restaurateurs to up their game.
If Uliassi’s famous €280 tasting menu is beyond your budget, Senigallia has plenty of innovative, quality places that are more affordable. It’s hard to eat badly here, but fish fans will relish the exquisitely prepared raw stuff at Cuoco di Bordo (two courses from €34) on the seafront. The more rustic Rimante (two courses from €27), in the cobbled centre, offers super-friendly service, great pasta and a roast goose speciality. For pizza nights, nearby O’sarracin has superlative margheritas (€8.50) and tasty ragù-filled arancini to start.
Pizza al formaggio, by contrast, isn’t pizza at all, but a sort of savoury panettone, flavoured with parmesan and pecorino cheese, maybe with chunks oozing out of a warm slice. It’s usually an Easter treat, but bakery Pandefrà makes it from October until May. Autumn in Senigallia also brings amazing fresh produce (chestnuts, persimmons, grapes and pomegranates; pumpkins, greens and radicchio) to chefs and market stalls.
And, of course, it brings the olive harvest, with new oil to taste in local delis and at the Festa dell’Olio Nuovo (6-10 November) in Scapezzano, three miles inland, reached by a pleasant hour’s walk up the quiet Strada di Fontenuovo (there’s a bus back).
With so much eating, you do need to work up an appetite. Hiking the Heron Trail along the Misa River will help, and offers downy oaks in their autumn finery, but the best walk for me starts at the splendid Rotonda a Mare gallery on its 1930s pier, heads inland on quiet lanes to Gabriella and Montignano villages, then descends to the coast for a sunset stroll back along that – now peaceful – Velvet Beach.
 
Al Foro Annonario has doubles from €80 B&B
 
Liz Boulter
Saint-Jean-de-Luz, France
Tucked away in the corner of France just before the Basque coast runs into Spain, Saint-Jean-de-Luz hangs on to the warmth of summer a little longer than the rest of the west coast. Its enticing crescent beach is sheltered by two headlands and so, as the Atlantic crashes against the rest of the coast, you can dig your toes into the golden sand as the sea gently laps the shore and truly feel as if you’ve escaped the world.
The town makes for a great introduction to the French Basque Country, with its traditional red or green timber-framed architecture, adorned in many cases with strings of the local espelette chilli pepper – its gentle heat infuses many of the local dishes. Pick up a pot at the local market hall, which is a good place to find other hero products of the local cuisine, such as Ossau-Iraty cheese and black cherry jam.
Elsewhere, the patisserie Maison Adam is the place to find the local almond macaron called the pare gabea (it means incomparable in Basque), which was first made in 1660 to celebrate the marriage of King Louis XIV and Marie-Thérèse of Spain. Their nuptials took place just round the corner at the Saint-Jean-de-Baptiste church – half-built at the time – which has an extraordinarily detailed gilt altarpiece that was installed in 1669, as well as a three-tiered gallery for the congregation. Meanwhile, a votive ship hanging from the ceiling is a nod to the town’s close relationship to the sea, with small fishing boats departing the neat harbour to fish for hake, a local speciality.
You can venture out on to the seas too, with a boat trip on the small cruiser Nivelle V (€20), which goes along the coast towards Spain, first passing the 17th-century cylindrical fort at Socoa and its sea wall that juts across the bay. As you cruise past the Flysch cliffs, which look like layers of diagonally stacked cardboard, you might spot a few silver flying fish jumping out of the steely blue Atlantic.
On arrival back at port, take the short walk across the bridge that spans the River Nivelle to the neighbouring village of Ciboure. It’s a warren of red and green Basque townhouses that overlook narrow streets winding up the hill. Between them sits the restaurant Chez Mattin (mains from €28), a local institution, where chef Michel Niquet serves his signature dish, ttorro, a fish stew that was invented by his grandfather.

MYB Textiles Ltd is the last mill in the world weaving patterned Nottingham lace on traditional looms. Once there were 20 lace mills in the Irvine Valley towns of Newmilns and Darvel alone. The lace industry became the largest employer in the area for a time and flourished until the late 1970s when competition emerged from other European countries and Asia. Now the majority of their trade comes from the film, theatre, TV and entertainment industry

£3,500 and no work done: the offer to help that’s really a roofing scam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
06:00:51 UTC
15:00:51 KST

The builder who calls at your door says they are doing some work in the area and has spotted a loose tile on your roof. They offer to fix it for a good price that you agree to.
But when they go up on their ladder to inspect the problem, they see another problem. Rain has been splashing out of the gutters and the wood around them is getting damaged. The only solution, the builder says, is to have rigid PVC trays installed to divert the water.
More rain is forecast and you are worried about what damage could be done so you pay the builder via bank transfer to get the job done there and then. They are gone within an hour, having apparently completed the work.
But nothing was done because there was no problem with your guttering. Instead you were one of a growing number of people who have been targeted by criminals posing as roofers, only to make off with payment after doing unnecessary or no work.
The charity Citizens Advice says suspected roofing frauds were the top scam it heard from consumers about in the last year. It received more than 2,200 complaints of suspected roofing scams in the year to August in England and Wales, about 10% more than the previous year.
“The vast majority of cases is … somebody just knocking on your door saying that they’ve noticed that there’s something wrong with your roof and they’re in a position to help you,” says Ruwani Purcell, the director of external affairs at Citizens Advice.
“The difficulty is [that] your roof is out of sight and out of reach. You can’t fully see what’s going on.”
Purcell says the fraudsters use really persuasive tactics to offer you confidence and reassurance that they know what they’re talking about. “And you might not be familiar with [the] terms,” she says. “In the worst case scenarios, they’ve been quite intimidating to compel people to hand over money there and then.”
What it looks like
While more than three-quarters of the roofing scams reported to Citizens Advice start with someone knocking at the door, some criminals look online for potential victims.
In one case dealt with by Citizens Advice, a 65-year-old woman posted on an online platform that she needed someone to fix a dripping sound in her gutters. A builder phoned her to say that it would cost £250 but when he and another man came and examined her roof they said they had discovered more problems and the price quickly grew. At one point they showed her a bucket of cement and said it was crumbling from under the tiles.
The woman said the man and his accomplice said the work needed to be done immediately and once they claimed to have finished they wanted the payment straightaway.
“I was afraid, two men in front of me in the dark, demanding money and making it clear they weren’t moving,” the victim told Citizens Advice. “They knew I was alone, I didn’t feel like I could deal with anything that might happen after, so I paid £3,500.”
She paid it using bank transfer. “The next day there was no trace that any work was done,” she said. “I felt stupid, and tried to contact them, but couldn’t get through.”
What to do
Be wary of anyone offering unsolicited work by cold calling and demanding confirmation of a job and payment there and then. No reputable builder will do that, says Purcell.
To check the roofer’s authenticity, ask for references and for all proposed work to be confirmed in writing. Treat it as a red flag if they refuse this or if they insist on being paid in cash.
To see if a trader is reputable, you can check your local council’s website as it often lists trusted traders. The government runs the TrustMark scheme which lists approved tradespeople.
Citizens Advice says that if a trader has done a poor job without reasonable care and skill, the victim is entitled to ask for the problem to be fixed or get a refund under the Consumer Rights Act 2015. Keep any paperwork and receipts, take photos and document what happened to make your case.

Ever since, Washington and Delhi have been locked in negotiations.
Relations were rattled when Trump imposed 25% tariffs on Indian goods in retaliation for Delhi’s purchases of Russian oil, but those duties have since been lifted.
In Mumbai and Jamnagar, Rubio will offer the new US brand of so-called “commercial diplomacy” in his meetings with Indian business leaders.

====================================================================================================

Leisure out of reach for one in eight people in the EU: Where is the problem biggest?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
05:54:13 UTC
14:54:13 KST

From sport to cinema trips, regular leisure activities are out of reach for around 46 million people in the EU. Income helps explain the gap between countries, but it does not tell the whole story.
About 46 million people in the EU miss out on regular leisure activities because they cannot afford them, according to Eurostat. In Greece, more than one in four people face this barrier — the highest share in the bloc.
The figures reveal wide differences across Europe, even between countries with similar income levels.
Several studies link social and leisure participation to better mental well-being and fewer symptoms of depression and anxiety. Eurostat also highlights the role leisure and social interactions can play in improving quality of life.
So, where are costs most likely to prevent people from taking part, and how much does income explain the gap?
In 2025, the share of people who couldn't afford to participate regularly in a leisure activity ranged from 3.9% in Croatia to 27.3% in Greece, compared with an EU average of 12.1%, according to Eurostat.
Figures cover people aged 16 and over. With about 381 million people in this age group in 2025, this means around 46 million people in the EU faced this financial barrier.
This share was also above 15% in Romania (23.3%), Lithuania (17.9%), Latvia (16.2%), North Macedonia (15.9%) and Hungary (15.8%).
France and Spain are above the EU average
More than 13% of people in France (13.9%) and Spain (13.4%) also reported that cost prevented them from taking part regularly in leisure activities. Switzerland (13%) was also above the EU average.
Germany (11.7%) was just below the EU average. In Italy, regular leisure activities were out of reach for 10.7% of people because of the cost.
Czechia (4.1%), Luxembourg (5.4%), Norway (5.7%) and Slovakia (5.7%) were also close to Croatia (3.9%) at the lower end.
The share was also higher than in Croatia in the Nordic EU countries: Denmark (10.4%), Sweden (9.7%) and Finland (7.9%).
Elsewhere, it stood at 6.7% in the Netherlands, 8.7% in Turkey and Portugal, 9.2% in Ireland and 9.7% in Belgium.
Leisure activities are less affordable for women
Except for Malta, where the difference was slight at 0.1 percentage point, leisure activities were less affordable for women than men. In the EU, the share was 13% among women, compared with 11.1% among men.
The gender gap was particularly large in several countries: 5.1 percentage points (pp) in Lithuania, 4.7 pp in Romania, 3.9 pp in Denmark and 3.7 pp in France.
Is income linked to leisure affordability?
Analysis by Euronews Business covering 33 European countries shows that income plays a role, but it does not tell the whole story. There is a moderate link between median income and the share of people who miss out on regular leisure activities because of the cost. Income data come from Eurostat and show median equivalised income in purchasing power standards (PPS).
Income accounts for less than a fifth of the variation between countries. Czechia, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania had almost identical median incomes, all between 17,097 and 17,190 PPS. Yet only 4.1% of people in Czechia couldn't afford to take part regularly in a leisure activity, compared with 10.7% in Estonia, 16.2% in Latvia and 17.9% in Lithuania.
The same pattern appeared among wealthier countries. France and Cyprus had virtually the same median income, at 23,792 and 23,782 PPS, respectively. But the share of people facing this financial barrier was more than twice as high in France (13.9%) as in Cyprus (6.3%).
Greece had the highest rate at 27.3%, with a median income of 13,612 PPS. Turkey (8.7%) and Serbia (9.9%) had lower incomes but much lower rates. Croatia, Czechia and Slovakia had some of the lowest rates despite incomes below the EU median of 22,638 PPS.
The role of inequality within countries
Across the EU, people below the poverty line were more than three times as likely to miss out on regular leisure activities as those above it, with 29% unable to afford them.
While inequality within countries may play a role, Euronews Business analysis finds only a weak link between income inequality and leisure affordability, which is not statistically significant.
The analysis uses Eurostat’s Gini coefficient, a measure of how unevenly income is distributed.
How people answer the survey may affect the results
How people answer the survey matters. A Eurostat working paper by Anne-Catherine Guio and colleagues found that “poor people may report that they do not want things, simply because they cannot afford them”. They found that leisure was the item most often not seen as a necessity.
What is a leisure activity?
According to Eurostat, leisure activities include sport, cinema and concerts, among others, and should take place outside the home. These activities involve spending money on entrance fees or travel, such as for swimming; on equipment, such as a bicycle; or on participation in organised activities, such as football club fees.
