The coalition also said two ballistic missiles were intercepted in the kingdom’s south. Threat alerts for Najran city and As Sulayyil governorate in Riyadh province were issued but quickly cancelled on Oct 18.
The Houthis have declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia and captured territory around the Bab al-Mandab strait, the Red Sea chokepoint and vital export route for Saudi oil since Iran blockaded the Gulf’s Strait of Hormuz.
The Houthis badly disrupted the Red Sea, a key route connecting Asia with Europe via Egypt’s Suez Canal, with attacks on ships during the Israel-Hamas war.
On Oct 18, Egypt’s Parliament held an emergency session after President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi asked lawmakers to authorise support to defend Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks.
The session was extended into Oct 19 “to give all lawmakers the opportunity to speak and express their views”, one of them told AFP.

“I’m not talking about fighting anyone or attacking anyone,” he said on Oct 17. “We are speaking only about defence.” AFP

Rubio rebukes Zelensky over Starlink claims
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has rejected Vladimir Zelensky’s claim that Washington ordered restrictions on satellite services used by Ukraine to carry out drone strikes deep inside Russia. The dispute comes amid a public spat between the Ukrainian leader and US President Donald Trump over sanctions and strikes on Russian energy facilities.
Earlier this week, Ukrainian officials said SpaceX’s Starlink terminals had suddenly stopped working on drones traveling faster than 160 km/h (100 mph). Zelensky told journalists on Saturday that tests on Starlink equipment in EU countries indicated that the restrictions imposed in Ukraine were “a planned operation.”
When asked to comment on Zelensky’s remarks later that day, Rubio offered a different account.
“I don’t know what Zelensky said. I’m not sure Zelensky knows what he’s talking about, but it wasn’t deliberate,” he told reporters at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland.
“We had nothing to do with it. Nobody in the United States ordered that Starlink speed be slowed down. It sort of happened, but my understanding is it’s been restored. It’s back to where it was before,” the US diplomat said.
Rubio confirmed that Ukraine currently had no access to Starshield, Starlink’s military-grade sister service, but had requested it.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk similarly denied restricting Starlink in Ukraine but clarified that the service must be used for civilian and defensive purposes only, not offensive operations.
The Telegraph, however, reported on Friday that Musk had personally asked Trump to cap Starlink speeds for Ukraine, while Reuters reported that the White House had instructed the Pentagon to slow down Starshield. Trump has denied any involvement and said he did not believe Musk was responsible either.
Zelensky said on Saturday that the Starlink restrictions remained in place. A Ukrainian official told Axios that SpaceX had blamed the cap on “a technical problem.”
Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports earlier this month in an effort to curb rising energy prices ahead of the US midterm elections. On Friday, he went further, suspending new sanctions on Russian oil and gas trade on national security grounds. Trump also sought to pressure Ukraine to stop attacking Russian refineries, which he blamed for contributing to high energy prices.
Zelensky said he felt betrayed by Trump, who, in turn, argued that the Ukrainian leader was “not a good guy for us to deal with” and should be replaced.

12:52:45 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Army’s Lu Sheng 2 force-on-force exercise began Wednesday, pitting the 269th Combined Arms Brigade against the 564th Combined Arms Brigade in round-the-clock combat drills.
During the 10-day exercise, artillery units have rehearsed providing fire support, from target acquisition and fire-support requests to firing-data calculations and gun-crew preparations, the Military News Agency reported.
Tank crews also simulated repairing a CM11 tank immobilized after its track was damaged by enemy obstacles. Soldiers used tools including track clamps to release tension and remove damaged track links.
They then used a rope and the tank’s own power to guide the track back onto the drive sprocket, per the Military News Agency. The drill aimed to improve troops’ ability to make field repairs and rapidly return damaged equipment to service.
Reconnaissance platoons used drones for aerial surveillance and to provide information for operations. Engineers deployed steel hedgehogs, concertina wire, Jersey barriers, and HESCO blast walls to restrict enemy movement and strengthen defensive positions.
The Army said the force-on-force training would help it assess command and control, responses to unexpected situations, and coordination among units. It said it would use the results to refine training for defensive operations.

MOSCOW, October 18. /TASS/. Ukrainian forces launched a massive drone attack on St. Petersburg and the Leningrad Region, with Russian air defense forces downing 126 UAVs over the region, Governor Alexander Drozdenko reported on his Telegram channel.
Russia's Federal Air Transport Agency, Rosaviatsia, said Pulkovo Airport imposed temporary operational restrictions. Airport officials added that they moved passengers and staff to safe locations.
In St. Petersburg, drones targeted the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal and civilian infrastructure across four city districts, causing no casualties, Governor Alexander Beglov confirmed.
Debris hit a private house near the town of Kirovsk and an apartment building in Vsevolozhsk, in the Leningrad Region.
In the meantime, Russian tech giant VK confirmed a drone attack on its data center, noting that all services continue to operate normally.
TASS has compiled the key details regarding the aftermath.
Scale
- Air defenses shot down 126 drones over the Leningrad Region, Drozdenko reported.
- In the region, the attack targeted Nizino in the Lomonosovsky District, the area near the town of Kirovsk, and Vsevolozhsk.
- St. Petersburg faced an overnight attack by military-grade drones, Beglov stated.
- Impact and debris fallout were recorded across the Nevsky, Krasnoselsky, Krasnogvardeysky, and Moskovsky districts of St. Petersburg.
Consequences
- Pulkovo Airport suspended all arrivals and departures, according to Rosaviatsia.
- Airport authorities moved passengers and staff to safe locations.
- Drone debris damaged a private house near Kirovsk and an apartment building in Vsevolozhsk, Drozdenko stated.
- In Nizino, falling debris damaged four parked vehicles and ignited a fire.
- Drone debris striking power lines caused localized power outages.
- Drones targeted a VK data center, though the company stated all services remain fully operational.
- A fire broke out at the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal, Beglov reported.
- Emergency services (EMERCOM) are extinguishing fires at civilian infrastructure sites across four St. Petersburg districts.
- The attacks caused no casualties.
- Mobile internet services in St. Petersburg may experience disruptions.
- An operational headquarters led by Beglov is coordinating the emergency response and interagency efforts.

Tim Winton's Cloudstreet wins Top 100 Australian Books countdown — as it happened
Tim Winton’s 1991 classic, Cloudstreet, has placed first in ABC Radio National’s Top 100 Australian Books.
The West Australian author had four books feature in the top 100, with Breath (2008) coming in at 33, Dirt Music (2001) at 41 and Juice (2024) at 88.
Winton, in the Perth studio, said he was honoured and slightly "bewildered" by the news.
"It's something I wrote when I was in my 20s. I'm not ashamed to have written it, but I can't quite make out what the fuss is about. I don't go back and read it but I'm quite aware of the place it has in some people's hearts because they write to me about it still.
"It's a mystery, but it's a great mystery. Somehow stories touch people."
Rounding out the top five were The Book Thief by Markus Zusak, Boy Swallows Universe by Trent Dalton, Burial Rites by Hannah Kent and A Fortunate Life by AB Facey.

Another childhood favourite
John Marsden was a titan of young adult literature in Australia, publishing more than 40 books in his career.
When he died in 2024, aged 74, the ABC Arts team cherrypicked a handful of Marsden titles that moved them most as young readers.
Tomorrow When the War Began was my pick — and one of my votes for the Top 100 Australian Books.
When Marsden set out to write Tomorrow, When the War Began — the first instalment of what would become his seven-part Tomorrow series — he reportedly wanted to show that young people had the same capacity for grit and resilience that previous generations showed when they were called up to war.
In this, he was successful. The first Tomorrow book, published in 1993, is an adventure story that presents teenagers as independent, courageous and capable in the face of crisis.

Tents spring up in Lisbon as Portugal housing protests spread
- Dozens of tents were pitched in Lisbon as protesters demanded action on housing and living costs, echoing similar unrest in Spain.
- Protesters said rents and prices are crushing workers and young people, with housing prices up 124% from 2015 to 2024, official data shows.
- Prime Minister Luis Montenegro said the government understands public anger, but warned against importing foreign unrest into Portugal.
AI generated
LISBON – Protesters pitched dozens of tents in Lisbon on Oct 17, demanding action to stem housing and living costs in Portugal, mirroring demonstrations that have gripped neighbouring Spain for weeks.
Hundreds of protesters rallied at night in Rossio Square – in the bustling, tourist heart of the Portuguese capital – following a march that had drawn thousands of people nationwide.
The mostly young attendees vowed to stay overnight, with hundreds singing songs as they sat around the statue of King Pedro IV that dominates the square, according to AFP journalists.
“The Portuguese social class that pays taxes, that which keeps this country going, is under attack and is losing its rights, notably its right to housing,” said Elena Costa, a 46-year-old social assistant.
“So we are all here together to try to explain that we are suffocating,” she said.
Engineer Antonio Margado, 52, criticised the centre-right government for “a total liberalisation of rents; owners are protected more and more, while tenants who need a house are those who are protected less and less”.
Portuguese housing prices rose by 124% between 2015 and 2024, roughly twice as fast as the European Union average, according to official data.
The impact is especially harsh on young people and in Lisbon, which concentrates around one-quarter of Portugal’s more than 11 million inhabitants, including the capital’s greater metropolitan area.
Another protester, Isabel Guerreiro, told public broadcaster RTP: “As a self-employed professional, I obviously don’t have the means to pay Lisbon’s exorbitant rents – and I’m a daughter of Lisbon.”
The Oct 17 camp in Lisbon amplified a housing protest that began in the northern city of Porto, where dozens of tents were set up.
‘Matter of survival’
At the earlier protest in Lisbon called by the main CGTP union, demonstrators called for better public services, pensions and wages as well as measures to tackle soaring housing costs.
Marching to the roar of drums, they held placards with slogans, including “Their greed, our misery” and “the cost of living increases, the people can’t take it any more”.
“There are many problems. Wages, housing, the cost of living: it’s a matter of survival,” said Yolanda Silva, a 43-year-old civil servant.
Earlier this week, Prime Minister Luis Montenegro said “we fully understand that people want answers” and to “express their outrage at what, in their view, may be omissions in public policies”.
But he warned political rivals against “importing into Portugal climates of instability and protest that, in fact, have no support in Portuguese society”, in a likely reference to violent protests that have rocked France.
The expanding Portuguese movement comes as Spain is gripped by housing protest camps and demonstrations now in their fourth week, which have culminated in the calling of an early general election for Nov 29. AFP

Moon rocks offer clues to its two faces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18

12:30:17 KST

Moon rocks offer clues to its two faces
Samples returned from the Moon’s far side suggest that uneven heating caused by Earth’s gravity helped shape its contrasting hemispheres billions of years ago, reports a Qazinform News Agency correspondent, citing a study published in National Science Review.
A team led by Professor Hejiu Hui of Nanjing University examined rocks collected by China’s Chang’e-6 mission, which returned the first samples from the lunar far side in 2024. Researchers compared their chemistry with material brought back by Apollo and Chang’e-5 missions.
The Moon’s Earth-facing side contains extensive dark volcanic plains, while its far side has a thicker crust dominated by ancient, heavily cratered highlands.
The analysis found that rocks originating from the mantle beneath both hemispheres had broadly similar chemical characteristics. Far-side crustal rocks, however, were richer in magnesium, while other samples contained less material enriched in potassium, rare earth elements and phosphorus.
The researchers propose that these differences developed as the Moon’s ancient ocean of molten rock cooled and solidified.
After the Moon became tidally locked, keeping the same hemisphere facing Earth, stronger tidal heating on the near side may have driven vast currents beneath the developing crust. These flows could have carried early magnesium-rich crust toward the far side, thickening it while concentrating remaining molten material on the near side.
“This systematic geochemical comparison … indicates that the mantle displays no clear compositional dichotomy,” the authors wrote.
The proposed mechanism offers an explanation for how similar underlying mantle materials produced such different lunar landscapes. However, the researchers acknowledge that the samples may not represent the entire far side and that their model is not the only possible explanation. Further geochemical evidence will be needed to test the findings.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that October’s skywatching highlights include Saturn at opposition, the Orionid meteor shower and the Moon appearing near the Pleiades star cluster.

Scientists find a youth protein that helps aging brain cells act young again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
03:27:40 UTC
12:27:40 KST

Scientists find a youth protein that helps aging brain cells act young again
- Date:
- October 17, 2026
- Source:
- The Mount Sinai Hospital / Mount Sinai School of Medicine
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered that a protein linked to youth helps protect the brain’s immune cells from age-related decline. Restoring the protein in older mice improved the cells’ ability to clear debris and reduced signs of inflammation, raising hopes for future treatments targeting brain aging and Alzheimer’s disease.
- Share:
A protein associated with youth may help aging brain cells regain some of their lost abilities. Scientists at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai have discovered that TIMP2 plays an important role in keeping the brain's immune cells healthy, offering new clues about how the brain changes with age.
In a study published in Nature Communications, researchers found that removing TIMP2 caused brain immune cells, known as microglia, to develop characteristics linked to aging and neurodegenerative disease. When the scientists restored TIMP2 in the bloodstream of older mice, these cells became better at removing cellular debris and showed fewer molecular signs of inflammation and other potentially harmful changes.
The discovery suggests that proteins associated with youth may help preserve the brain's natural defenses as it ages. It also identifies TIMP2 as a potentially important factor in maintaining healthy immune activity in the brain.
Why the Brain's Immune Cells Become Less Effective With Age
Getting older is the greatest known risk factor for Alzheimer's disease and other neurodegenerative disorders. However, scientists still do not fully understand the biological processes that make the aging brain increasingly vulnerable to these conditions.
One important piece of the puzzle involves microglia, specialized immune cells that serve as the brain's maintenance and defense system. They remove cellular waste, help maintain the networks through which neurons communicate, and respond when brain tissue is injured.
As the brain ages, these cells can lose some of their ability to perform these essential tasks. They may also shift into states that promote inflammation and interfere with normal brain function.
"TIMP2 facilitates healthy function for the brain's immune cells," said Joseph M. Castellano, PhD, Associate Professor of Neuroscience at the Ronald M. Loeb Center for Alzheimer's Disease and The Friedman Brain Institute at The Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, and corresponding author of the study. "By supporting the ability of microglia to clear debris and limit maladaptive responses, TIMP2 may help restore aspects of microglial function that become compromised with age. Since our previous work identified TIMP2 as a regulator of synaptic plasticity through the extracellular matrix, these findings suggest that this factor sits at the intersection of several processes that are critical for normal brain function."
Synaptic plasticity refers to the brain's ability to strengthen or weaken connections between neurons, a process essential for learning and memory. The extracellular matrix is a network of molecules surrounding cells that helps support and regulate their activity.
What Happens When the Brain Loses TIMP2?
To investigate how TIMP2 affects brain immune cells, the research team studied several groups of mice representing different biological conditions.
The study included Brittany Hemmer, PhD, the first author, who was a graduate student in Castellano's laboratory during the research.
Some of the mice were genetically modified to lack TIMP2 throughout their bodies. In others, the researchers removed the protein specifically from either microglia or neurons. Comparing these models allowed the team to examine how TIMP2 influences immune cell behavior in both healthy and aging brains.
The scientists used several advanced techniques to study the changes. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing allowed them to examine patterns of gene activity in individual cell nuclei. They also used detailed imaging, functional tests, and a technique called in vivo microdialysis, which collects and measures substances from the fluid surrounding cells in living brain tissue.
The results revealed striking changes when TIMP2 was absent.
Microglia developed several features typically associated with aging and brain injury. Their cellular activation markers changed, their ability to remove debris declined, and they showed molecular signatures linked to cellular senescence, a biological state associated with aging and cellular stress.
The effects extended beyond the immune cells themselves. Using in vivo microdialysis, the researchers also detected higher levels of proteins associated with inflammation and stress in the extracellular environment surrounding brain cells.
Together, these findings indicated that TIMP2 helps prevent microglia from shifting toward potentially damaging states.
Restoring a Youth-Associated Protein Improves Aging Brain Cells
The researchers next explored whether supplying TIMP2 could counteract some of the changes observed with age.
They administered TIMP2 through injections to older mice, allowing the protein to circulate throughout the body. The treatment produced encouraging results.
Microglia became more effective at clearing cellular debris and showed a reduction in molecular markers associated with inflammatory states. In other words, restoring the youth-associated protein helped the aging immune cells recover some of the functions that normally deteriorate over time.
These improvements suggest that TIMP2 influences how microglia respond to conditions within the brain. By supporting their protective activities and limiting potentially harmful responses, the protein may help maintain a healthier environment for neurons.
The results also point to a possible biological connection between factors circulating in the body that are associated with youth and the activity of the brain's innate immune system. This system provides a first line of defense against injury and other threats.
A Potential New Direction for Brain Aging and Alzheimer's Research
The discovery adds to growing scientific interest in whether biological factors associated with youth can influence the aging process.
Because microglia help maintain brain health and can contribute to harmful inflammation when their behavior changes, finding ways to preserve their normal function could have important implications for understanding age-related neurological disorders.
"While additional studies are needed, this work provides new insight into how youth-associated factors influence pathways involved in brain aging and age-related neurological disorders that may ultimately inform therapeutic strategies," Dr. Castellano added.
However, the researchers caution that these findings come from experiments in mice. It remains unknown whether TIMP2 produces similar effects in humans or whether manipulating the protein could eventually become an effective treatment.
Additional studies will be necessary to determine whether TIMP2 itself, or the biological pathways it controls, can be targeted to reduce harmful changes associated with brain aging.
For now, the findings provide a promising new explanation for how a protein linked to youth helps maintain the brain's immune defenses, and how restoring it may recover some functions that weaken with age.
This work was supported by the National Institute on Aging (R01AG061382 (JMC), RF1AG072300 (JMC), 1F31AG079604-01A1 (BMH), T32AG049688 (BMH, SMP), R01AG061382-02S1 (JMC, SMP), and Cure Alzheimer's Fund (JMC).
Story Source:
Materials provided by The Mount Sinai Hospital / Mount Sinai School of Medicine. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Brittany M. Hemmer, Sarah M. Philippi, Ana Catarina Ferreira, Samuele F. Petridis, Annie Phan, Joseph M. Castellano. Youth-associated protein TIMP2 regulates microglial state and function in healthy and aged mice. Nature Communications, 2026; 17 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-74906-z

JNF allocates NIS 33 million to rebuild border-adjacent northern towns 2-5 km from Lebanon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
03:24:59 UTC
12:24:59 KST

The Board of Directors of the Jewish National Fund (JNF) approved on Tuesday a NIS 33 million budget to support 22 communities along the northern border, 2 to 5 kilometers from the Lebanese border.
Under the decision, each community evacuated during the fighting that has not yet received JNF support will receive 1.5 million NIS for infrastructure rehabilitation and development.
Among the benefiting communities are Kibbutz Ma'ayan Baruch and Kibbutz Dan in the Upper Galilee Regional Council, Beit Hillel, and Ramot Naftali. The plan also includes the remaining communities in the Mevo'ot HaHermon Regional Council, Liman in Mateh Asher, Ibn Menachem, Elkosh, Goren, Manot, and Avdon in Ma'ale Yosef, as well as Kerem Ben Zimra and Alma in the Merom HaGalil Regional Council.
Unlike the government's uniform funding model, JNF adopted a graduated support model based on distance from the Lebanese border and the severity of damage to the communities. Under this framework, front-line communities, including Kibbutz Manara and Moshav Dovev, are eligible for NIS 2.5 to 3 million per community. The current phase approves support for communities 2 to 5 km from the border, while the next phase plans to fund approximately 1 million NIS for each community 5 to 9 km away.
The funds are earmarked for infrastructure development, upgrading and fortifying public buildings (such as kindergartens, community centers, and dining halls), and enhancing open public spaces. Residents and local leadership will decide on specific projects independently.
Communities to be visited, plan to begin soon
JNF professional teams are scheduled to visit the communities in the coming days to formulate the project list, aiming to begin execution within roughly a month and a half. This step joins additional JNF investments in northern cities and regional hubs, including Tiberias (allocated approximately NIS 35 million), Karmiel, Afula, and Beit She'an.
JNF Chairman Eyal Ostrinsky commented on the expanded support plan: "We decided that JNF's northern rehabilitation efforts will not stop at the 2-kilometer border line. Adjacent communities within up to 5 km also paid a heavy price during the war and continue to pay."
Ostrinsky added: "JNF stands with the women and men of the North, and I promise we will remain shoulder-to-shoulder with them. In our view, national responsibility means looking at the broad picture, not leaving communities behind, listening, and helping. JNF acts to make rehabilitation a reality on the ground."
The Moshavim Movement welcomed the decision. Amit Yifrach, the Movement's general secretary and chairman of the Israel Farmers Association, said JNF is a true partner to the moshavim and the entire rural sector. He said this cooperation will strengthen border-adjacent moshavim and rural settlements as a whole, emphasizing that the resilience of border communities is integral to the resilience of the State of Israel.

Israel launches NIS 25 million initiative to close high-tech gender gap
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
03:24:01 UTC
12:24:01 KST

The Israel Innovation Authority and the Labor and Social Affairs Ministry announced in mid-October that they will jointly invest NIS 25 million in training senior female high-tech executives, integrating women into the tech industry, helping women return to work after a long break, and reducing the gender wage gap in the high-tech sector.
This initiative is a response to persistent gender gaps in the high-tech industry, both in representation across technical and managerial positions and in salary levels.
The funding will support programs targeting five challenges identified by the IIA and the Labor and Social Affairs Ministry: advancing women into senior high-tech management roles, integrating highly educated women into deep-tech industries, helping experienced women return to the sector, supporting career advancement after maternity leave, and promoting gender equality within high-tech companies.
This budget, which includes matching funds from private organizations, will be allocated to 15 programs designed to address the barriers facing women in high-tech in Israel.
Orgs identify significant wage and representation gaps in the high-tech sector
Women in high-tech earn an average of approximately NIS 23,000 per month compared with approximately NIS 33,000 among men, according to the IIA and the Labor and Social Affairs Ministry. This represents a gap of approximately NIS 10,200 per month, with men's salaries about 44% higher than women's. Significant gaps also exist within different occupational categories, including research and development, corporate staff, and management positions.
"The increase in life expectancy and changes in the labor market require us to prepare for a diverse, inclusive employment market adapted to all age groups," Labor and Social Affairs Ministry Director-General Robi Shemesh said. "Employment rates among both women and men begin to decline as early as age 50, and ageist perceptions, including internalized ageism, constitute a significant barrier to continued participation in quality employment.
"The new programs are part of this approach, which seeks to enable women to make use of their experience, skills, and professional abilities, reintegrate into the labor market, and advance to meaningful positions in knowledge-intensive industries," Shemesh added.

U.S. measles cases top 4,400 as Pennsylvania outbreak worsens
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:23:53 CST
12:23:53 KST

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- The United States reported 4,410 confirmed measles cases in 2026 as of Thursday, nearly double the 2,289 cases reported for all of 2025, putting the country on track for its highest annual total since 1991, according to the latest data from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
Of the confirmed cases, 4,392 were reported by 47 jurisdictions, while 18 cases were reported among international visitors to the United States, the CDC said.
Children and adolescents aged 5 to 19 accounted for the largest share of cases, with 1,856 infections, or 42 percent of the total.
A total of 451 patients, or about 10 percent of all confirmed cases, have been hospitalized. About 96 percent of cases were among people who were unvaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown, according to CDC data.
Meanwhile, the outbreak in the U.S. state of Pennsylvania continues to grow. The Pennsylvania Department of Health said on Friday that 1,260 measles cases have been confirmed across 43 counties in the state so far this year, including 238 hospitalizations and five confirmed measles-associated deaths.
The state reported 38 new cases since Wednesday. It is also investigating a recently reported death in Franklin County, the department said.
The CDC plans to send one of its scientists to Pennsylvania to help respond to the outbreak, NBC News reported Thursday, citing a CDC spokesperson. The scientist, an officer with the agency's Epidemic Intelligence Service (EIS), is expected to arrive later this week. EIS officers are often referred to as "disease detectives" because of their work investigating disease outbreaks.
"CDC will continue working closely with Pennsylvania health officials to provide the expertise and support needed to respond to the outbreak and protect public health," the CDC spokesperson was quoted as saying.
The CDC recommends two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine as the best protection against measles.
The agency says that when more than 95 percent of people in a community are vaccinated, community immunity, also known as herd immunity, helps protect more people from the disease. ■

Cross-sea bridge protected by graphene anti-corrosion coatings in east China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:23:25 CST
12:23:25 KST

HANGZHOU, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- A graphene anti-corrosion coating technology has been deployed at scale on the cross-sea bridge of Xiangshan Port in east China's Zhejiang Province.
Stretching about 8.28 kilometers across the port, it is a bridge on China's first cross-sea suburban railway and currently the world's largest-span ballastless track cable-stayed railway bridge.
Cross-sea bridges are exposed to high salinity, high humidity and strong ultraviolet radiation. These harsh marine atmospheric conditions pose serious challenges to the structures' weather and corrosion resistance, and service life of protective materials used.
The graphene-modified heavy-duty anti-corrosion coatings applied to the Xiangshan Port cross-sea bridge were developed by the Ningbo Institute of Materials Technology and Engineering (NIMTE) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and its incubated enterprise.
The coatings offer sound barrier performance, strong adhesion and high salt-spray resistance, helping mitigate corrosion of the bridge's main steel structures in the harsh marine atmospheric environment.
By doubling the service life of conventional anti-corrosion coatings, the new coatings can substantially cut maintenance costs and safety risks, according to the developer.
The large-scale application is expected to enhance the safety and durability of cross-sea rail infrastructure.
This coating technology has also been used in the Jakarta-Bandung High-Speed Railway in Indonesia and a dual-fuel power station in Cambodia. It also holds promise for wider use in marine engineering, high-end equipment and aerospace, according to the NIMTE.
The bridge is part of the Ningbo-Xiangshan suburban railway which opens up a rapid commuting corridor between downtown Ningbo and its southern coastal area. ■

Israel must explain why it failed to prevent attacks on diplomats in West Bank - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
03:05:14 UTC
12:05:14 KST

Attacks on Palestinians, Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, and European visitors during the West Bank olive harvest expose a failure of protection. Israeli authorities anticipated unrest. They must now explain why preparations failed to prevent these assaults.
On Friday, masked Israeli extremists attacked Palestinian olive harvesters near Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah. Levine, wearing clearly marked press gear, was beaten and hospitalized.
She underwent surgery for a severe hand injury. A journalist documenting violence became its victim, while Palestinians gathering their crops were terrorized.
On Saturday, masked Israelis reportedly attacked a delegation visiting olive groves near the Palestinian Christian village of Taiba. Diplomats from Belgium, France, and Poland were present.
A Belgian consular vehicle was damaged, and visiting French Mayor Bernard Baudoux was reportedly assaulted. Police opened an investigation, and the IDF condemned the attack.
Katz orders removal of threats to public order during olive harvest
On October 8, Defense Minister Israel Katz instructed officials to pursue administrative removal orders against activists deemed threats to public order during the harvest.
The Yesha Council, which represents Israeli settlements, had requested action, citing concerns about provocations and confrontations. The directive focused on left-wing and foreign activists accompanying Palestinian farmers.
Katz’s instructions demonstrate that the government expected confrontation. The IDF had also prepared for nationalist violence, clashes, and terrorist attacks. Officials could not have predicted either assault’s exact location. They must establish where protection and the response fell short.
The IDF is reportedly preparing to reinforce its West Bank presence. Reinforcements may be necessary, but authorities should explain what forces were available, when warnings arrived, and how units responded.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office responded to Saturday’s incident on X/Twitter by declaring: “Any violence against diplomats is unacceptable.” It also stated: “The more serious the accusation, the greater the demand for compelling evidence.” The statement noted an ongoing police investigation and argued that video footage did not establish the complete sequence of events.
Yet the PMO also singled out Baudoux as “a French Communist Party mayor who previously raised the Palestinian flag over his municipal building, prompting French authorities to order its removal.”
His politics provide no justification for an assault. Introducing them without establishing their relevance weakens the office’s appeal for objectivity.
The PMO also suggested the reports reflected a campaign to smear Israel and Jewish residents of the West Bank.
Israel must protect all, regardless of political views
Investigators must establish individual responsibility. Authorities must protect farmers, journalists, and visitors regardless of their political views.
President Isaac Herzog struck a different tone on Saturday, calling Levine to apologize.
“I was morally tormented during Shabbat when I thought about it, and I express deep sorrow and apologize for what you went through,” he told her, according to his office. Herzog urged law enforcement to investigate and prosecute those responsible.
US Ambassador Mike Huckabee, an outspoken supporter of Israel and its settlements, has previously been just as clear. Condemning a separate West Bank incident in August, he called violent intruders “Israeli terrorists” and said there was “no excuse for such thuggish behavior.”
Condemnation by Israel’s allies should reinforce the urgency of action.
Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar condemned Saturday’s assault but suggested advance coordination with the IDF could have helped protect the delegation. Coordination can materially improve protection. Its absence leaves authorities responsible for intervening when an assault occurs.
The IDF said an alert during the Taiba incident reached a brigade operations room intended for security personnel rather than civilians. If reporting channels fail to get urgent warnings to those able to intervene, they must be fixed.
This past week’s reported warning of a planned Hamas attack underscores the continuing threat of Palestinian terrorism.
The extremists attacking Palestinians do not represent the vast majority of Jewish residents in Judea and Samaria, whose safety must remain a priority for Israel’s security forces.
Israel faces real West Bank security threats, including Palestinian terrorism. Commanders must protect Israeli communities while ensuring Palestinian farmers can harvest safely.
Violence by Israelis undermines state authority and complicates soldiers’ work. Prevention requires patrols in known hot spots, prompt intervention, arrests, and credible prosecutions.
Officials must account publicly for any failures identified and explain how they will protect the remaining harvest. Farmers should be able to gather their crops, and journalists to document events, in safety.

NASA’s SpaceX launch lights up the sky with a giant glowing jellyfish
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
03:02:35 UTC
12:02:35 KST

NASA’s SpaceX launch lights up the sky with a giant glowing jellyfish
- Date:
- October 17, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket created a dazzling, jellyfish-shaped glow across the eastern United States as sunlight illuminated its exhaust during an early morning launch. The mission delivered equipment and scientific experiments to the International Space Station, including research that could advance treatments for blindness, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and other diseases.
- Share:
A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket transformed the early morning sky into a spectacular display of light on October 13, 2026. As the rocket climbed above Earth carrying a Dragon spacecraft, sunlight illuminated its expanding exhaust plumes, creating an enormous glowing shape that resembled a jellyfish.
This striking phenomenon, known as a "jellyfish," occurs when a rocket launches near sunrise or sunset. Sunlight reaches the exhaust high in the atmosphere, making the spreading plume shine brightly against the darker sky below.
See a wider view of the "jellyfish."
SpaceX Launch Creates a Spectacular Sky Display
The mission lifted off at 6:33 a.m. EDT from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. The illuminated exhaust plumes were visible across the eastern United States, giving observers a remarkable view of the rocket's journey into space.
The launch marked SpaceX's 35th commercial resupply mission for NASA, delivering scientific experiments, essential supplies, and equipment to the International Space Station.
New Space Station Upgrades and Medical Experiments
Among the cargo aboard Dragon is the final set of International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Arrays, known as IROSAs. These additional solar panels are scheduled for installation later this fall and will help provide electricity for the orbiting laboratory.
The spacecraft is also transporting equipment for several scientific investigations that could lead to important advances in medicine and materials science.
One experiment will explore manufacturing artificial retinas in microgravity, where the near absence of gravity creates conditions that cannot easily be reproduced on Earth. The research could help develop technologies to restore vision in people with certain forms of vision loss.
Another investigation will use 3D heart tissue models to support the development of more efficient drug testing methods during future space missions.
Additional experiments will examine how a new type of glass forms in microgravity and investigate brain organoids, miniature models of brain tissue grown from cells. These models could help researchers identify new targets for treating neurological conditions, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and multiple sclerosis.

Carney said he'd requested a detailed account and formal briefing on the incident at Canadian Forces Base (CFB) Wainwright, which senior officials on the ground at the site were expected to deliver later on Sunday.
After the incident happened on Saturday, a doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, 120 miles northwest of the military base, told Canada's national broadcaster that patients were being brought to hospitals across the city as health care facilities around the base became "completely overwhelmed" by the number of people needing care.
"This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton," Dr. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told CBC News. "It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It's a disaster. It's a one in every 15 to 25-year disaster."
"I'm saddened to share that there have been both fatalities and injuries as a result of an incident on the base," Defense Minister David McGuinty said.
The incident occurred at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, located about 112 miles southeast of Edmonton.
"We are dealing with a serious incident at CFB Wainwright, and are fully engaged with federal, provincial and local authorities," said Gen. Jennie Carignan, chief of the defense staff for the Canadian Armed Forces, in a social media post. "Our priority remains the welfare of our members, their families and their community, and my thoughts are with all those affected by this incident."

McGuinty said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were involved in the investigation and described the situation as "very, very active and delicate."
"I cannot recall such an incident in my short time for sure as a minister, but I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory," McGuinty said.

"Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected," Carney said earlier in a social media post.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith described the fire as "significant and tragic" and said it was affecting many military personnel.
Canadian Forces Base Wainwright is one of Canada's busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations. "We will have more to say in the coming hours and days," he added.
Carney said the federal government was working closely with Alberta officials and local authorities. He said he and Smith were in close contact, as were their ministers and officials.

A 6-year-old boy and a 35-year-old man were killed Saturday, and 11 others were taken to hospitals after a pickup truck drove onto a soccer field during a children's game in Wichita, Kansas. The female driver was arrested, and local police said two minors were in the vehicle with her. The circumstances remain under investigation, and authorities have not determined whether the incident was accidental or intentional.
The incident occurred around 3:25 p.m. local time at Stryker Sports Complex, which hosts soccer games for children and teenagers. According to police, emergency dispatchers received several calls reporting that a vehicle had entered the soccer fields and struck people. Large numbers of police officers, firefighters and medical personnel were dispatched to the scene, where they provided initial treatment before transporting the victims to area hospitals.
At a subsequent briefing, police identified the two people killed as a 6-year-old boy and a 35-year-old man, both residents of McPherson, Kansas. Authorities emphasized that the two were not related.
Police said 11 people were taken to hospitals, 10 of them with physical injuries. Among the injured were five children: a 5-year-old girl and a 5-year-old boy, two 8-year-olds and a 9-year-old girl. Five adults were also injured, while another woman, 61, was taken for medical treatment unrelated to a direct physical injury. Police said none of the injuries were life-threatening.
A witness who spoke to local television station KWCH said a black pickup truck drove onto the children's soccer fields, struck several people and continued for approximately 90 to 180 meters (300 to 600 feet) before stopping. The witness said dozens of emergency responders arrived at the scene and performed resuscitation efforts on victims.
Vanessa Trammell, who had come to watch her 13-year-old son's soccer game on a nearby field, told CNN she saw the truck drive across the field and strike several people. Her son's game had ended shortly before the incident, and the players were gathered along the sidelines when the pickup passed close to them.
"We thought it was going to stop but then it like kept going. It was pure panic. I didn’t know what was going on – just that people were being hit. I’m pretty sure I probably screamed," she recalled.
Trammell said her first instinct was to find her son amid the chaos, while his team's coach ran toward the victims to help before emergency responders arrived.
Wichita Fire Chief Michael Mire said that when firefighters arrived, bystanders had already begun providing medical assistance to the injured.
"The community was very impressive when our firefighters arrived," he said. "They didn’t begin patient care, they continued patient care, taking charge of what the community had already begun providing to those who were injured."
Footage from the scene showed children wearing red sports uniforms near emergency vehicles and police tape.
"This is a tragedy," police officer Aaron Moses said. He said the driver was in custody and no longer posed a threat to the public. Moses confirmed that two minors were inside the vehicle at the time of the incident.
According to police, when officers and emergency personnel arrived, the driver and the two minors who had been with her were still near the pickup truck. The woman, 34, whose child was participating in a soccer game on another field at the complex, is cooperating with investigators. Police are still examining whether she intended to harm those present, and no decision has been made on whether charges will be filed against her.
Investigators are now trying to determine how the pickup reached the field, which is separated from the parking area by fences and gates, and how fast it was traveling. The complex has 11 outdoor soccer fields. Authorities have also not established whether the driver entered the field deliberately or lost control of the vehicle. Police have asked the public to submit videos and other footage recorded in the area during the incident to help reconstruct what happened.
At the same time as the soccer games, the complex was hosting games as part of the Kansas high school girls' flag football championship. Four teams from the Kansas City area were participating in the competition on a nearby field. Following the incident, the games were suspended, and participants and spectators were asked to leave the complex.
The Shawnee Mission School District announced that all its students and staff members had been accounted for and were safe.
Following the tragedy, Stryker Sports Complex management announced that all events at the venue had been canceled until further notice.
"Families came to Stryker Sports Complex to enjoy a Saturday afternoon watching their children play soccer. No one could have imagined the tragedy that would unfold," Wichita Mayor Lily Wu said at a news conference.
"My heart breaks for the families who have lost loved ones, especially the family grieving the loss of a child," she added.

Animal welfare group calls for accountability after latest racing death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
02:48:12 UTC
11:48:12 KST

Caulfield Cup death of Ohope Wins leads to calls for accountability from racing industry
In short:
Animal rights group the Coalition for the Protection of Horses says the death of Ohope Wins in the Caulfield Cup was one of 160 in Australia this year.
Last year's Cup winner, Half Yours, received minor injuries when it fell, bringing down Ohope Wins, who was euthanased by vets at the track.
What's next?
Racing Victoria stewards will hold an inquiry into the incident at a time yet to be announced.
Animal welfare campaigners have called for the racing industry to be made more accountable for racehorse deaths after Ohope Wins was put down following a fall in the Caulfield Cup.
The Chris Waller-trained Ohope Wins was in the finishing straight of the 2,400m Group One race when it was brought down by last year's winner, Half Yours, which had fallen at the 300m mark.
Half Yours got up and ran riderless down the straight, while Ohope Wins was assessed by vets as it lay on the track and was euthanased.
Half Yours's rider Mark Zahra and Ohope Wins's jockey Jye McNeil were taken to hospital for observation.
Racing Victoria confirmed Zahra was released on Saturday night, and McNeil would be released on Sunday, with both jockeys escaping serious injury.
Racing Victoria stewards will hold an inquiry into the incident, although a time has not been set for this to happen.
The Coalition for the Protection of Horses campaign director Elio Celotto said at least 160 horses have been killed as a result of injuries sustained in racing across Australia this year.
"When a horse falls their legs are very delicately poised when they hit the turf," Mr Celotto said speaking to ABC's News Breakfast.
"They're a half a tonne horse and all they need to do is fall slightly off and it can result in damage to their bones and that is why we see so many horses killed on our race tracks."
He said the racing industry was responsible for deaths on race tracks.
"The racing industry has got a lot to answer for. They say they are open and transparent, they are anything but," he said.
"They really need to be made accountable for the thousands [over the years], not just the horse that was killed yesterday, but all the horses that are killed around Australia simply to make money and for the pleasure of punters. It's simply not acceptable."
Top racing trainer Peter Moody defended the industry, saying that safety improvements had been brought in since a series of deaths in the Melbourne Cup beginning more than a decade ago.
Moody told ABC Radio Brisbane there were less incidents in major races following the changes, including what he called "stringent protocols" horses go through before they are allowed to race by authorities.
Most of the deaths in the Melbourne Cup were standalone incidents, where horses broke down while running rather than colliding with or falling over other horses.
Racing Victoria requires all international horses coming for major races to have one CT scan of the distal (lower) limbs to identify possible bone damage before travel. They then must have a standing CT scan before every start in the Spring Racing Carnival.
There have been no further deaths in the Melbourne Cup since the introduction of scanning requirements.
Moody described the incident at Caulfield as "very sad and very disappointing".
Moody was asked if there was any way such incidents could be avoided when big fields of horses were running around.
"Whether there were some misjudgements, some horses rolled around in the race, it got tight, one horse (Half Yours) stumbled and dislodged the rider, and then the second horse unfortunately got tangled in that horse and fell also," he said.
"It's just one of those unfortunate accidents. No-one sets out for that to happen. Everyone wants to see the horses and the riders come home safely.
"The love and care and attention [given] to these animals is second to none.
"Unfortunately in all walks of life, whether it's horse racing, a football match, walking across the road to catch a bus and accidents do happen."

- Elon Musk is back in the spotlight for SpaceX, X and Tesla, but his politics have reduced the awe around his work.
- His support for Trump and hard-right views have damaged his image, while DOGE cuts helped dismantle USAID and cost hundreds of thousands of jobs.
- Musk has given at least US$276 million to Republican campaigns, which may be an investment to protect SpaceX and Tesla’s ties to the federal government.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – With a sports car that somersaults through the air, Elon Musk is back in the headlines for technological daring, but his plunge into politics and his return to US President Donald Trump’s side mean the world’s richest man no longer enjoys the unqualified praise of years past.
“All the things that we were promised since the 1950s, of space travel and flying cars... he’s doing all of those things,” said Andrew Selepak, a social media professor at the University of Florida.
“And yet we’re not giving it the attention, we’re not giving it the awe that it probably truly deserves,” he added.
In recent weeks, Musk has seemed to be everywhere at once.
On Sept 28, SpaceX’s Starship megarocket reached orbit for the first time and deployed 26 Starlink satellites before splashing down in the Pacific – a milestone for the rocket central to Musk’s Mars ambitions.
His central role in geopolitics has also been on display, with Ukraine complaining of disruptions to the Starshield satellite communications system its military relies on.
Even the platform formerly known as Twitter is enjoying something of a renaissance, with Musk’s X now the go-to social media app for Silicon Valley insiders and the main marketplace for talk about artificial intelligence.
But despite his continued success, Musk’s unrelenting commitment to right-wing politics has taken a toll.
No image captured that shift more than Musk brandishing a chainsaw on stage in February 2025 – a gift from Argentine President Javier Milei – as a symbol of his drive to slash the US government as head of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) in the early months of Trump’s second term.
Through DOGE, Musk’s allies fanned out across federal agencies, driving cuts that effectively dismantled the US Agency for International Development (USAID) and contributed to a net loss of hundreds of thousands of jobs.
‘National treasure’
That combative imagery has been matched by Musk’s posts on X, where hardline anti-immigration views and right-wing conspiracy theories sit alongside posts about rocket launches and Tesla robotaxis.
Now he is back in Trump’s good graces, after a spectacular falling-out that followed his exit from DOGE in May 2025.
Last week, Trump presented him with the nation’s top science medal, calling him a “national treasure” and “our modern-day Thomas Edison”.
The renewed relationship comes as Musk has spent at least US$276 million (S$353.2 million) on Republican political campaigns ahead of the midterm elections, in which the president’s party is expected to struggle.
Of that, US$158 million is funding a massive advertising campaign in Texas, Musk’s home state, where the Republican candidate is trailing in the polls.
For left-leaning pundits, he is now increasingly seen as an agent of Trump and the tech billionaires, rather than a technology savant working for the good of humanity.
That opposition plays out in Musk, a four-hour documentary by Oscar-winning film-maker Alex Gibney now in US theatres, which traces the life and career of the South Africa-born billionaire.
“I once described him as somebody who can jump off the edge of a cliff and invent a parachute on the way down. I think he thrives on chaos,” Musk’s first wife Justine, who features prominently in the film, told podcaster Kara Swisher.
She added: “I always assume that there’s a method to his madness” and many of his loudest actions may in fact be deflections and “sleight of hand”.
The same may be true of Musk’s dealings with Washington.
Few entrepreneurs depend as heavily on the federal government as he does.
SpaceX – which went public in June in the largest initial public offering in history – earns billions of dollars a year from NASA and Pentagon contracts, while Tesla’s bet on robotaxis hinges on how quickly regulators allow driverless cars onto US roads.
Seen in that light, Musk’s millions for Republicans may be less a political conversion than an investment. AFP

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has defended President Donald Trump's waiver of sweeping sanctions and tariffs on Russia, confirming that the measure represents a 60-day pause designed to assess its broader economic consequences.
"The president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy," Rubio said, noting that the restrictions affect several nations.
Rubio attributed soaring global energy prices to colliding international conflicts, citing the US war on Iran and Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia: "These conflicts around the world are starting to crash into each other, and they're having an impact not just on global oil and diesel prices but on economies as well."
Trump described the decision late on Saturday as beneficial to the United States: "It's a very good decision, and it's going to be a decision that's good for the country, and I think good for the world."
Bipartisan criticism
The executive order, signed on Friday, triggered immediate condemnation from lawmakers across both political parties.
The legislation passed by Congress in September had mandated sanctions against Russian officials, oligarchs, and financial entities, whilst giving the president authority to penalise major buyers of Russian energy to curb Kremlin revenues.
Republican Senator Thom Tillis called the waiver "beyond irresponsible" on X, adding: "If the President wants to actually bring down energy prices, he can do it by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid for Vladimir Putin."
Republican Senator Ted Cruz described the move as "a mistake" on Fox News.
The waiver follows an agreement between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin to permit Russian diesel exports in exchange for eased economic measures.
Steep fuel costs are impacting US road haulage, agriculture, and construction ahead of key midterm elections next month, where polls indicate Republicans face substantial electoral headwinds.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that the move directly rewards Moscow.

====================================================================================================

China Focus: Decades of restoration work breathes new life into once-vanished lake
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:34:38 CST
11:34:38 KST

HOHHOT, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- In the core zone of a wetland in Ulanqab, north China's Inner Mongolia, a smart ecological supervision center deploys drone patrols and AI-powered wildlife tracking technology to help restore a lake that had once dried up.
Autumn envelops the Huangqihai Lake with quiet vibrancy. Birds such as white-naped cranes wade across the muddy shallows in search of food.
The lake spans 85.22 square km, according to the center's September figures. This vibrant landscape is almost unrecognizable from 2006, when the water dried up, and most of the lakebed was exposed.
Even after water partially returned in 2012, the lake's size rarely exceeded 25 square km in the wettest months, and it shrank to less than 5 square km in dry seasons.
The lake once ranked among eight major lakes in the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, forming a critical wetland in northern China.
Back in the 1950s, it stretched across some 130 square km and sustained a thriving fishery. Its local specialty, Guancun crucian carp, once graced state banquets. But rising human activity and persistent drought reduced its size.
"Huangqihai is coming back to life. Fish have returned, giving migratory birds a safe haven on their migrating journeys," said Wang Shaojun, with the administrative office of the Huangqihai Wetland Nature Reserve. He attributes the recovery to decades of targeted restoration efforts.
The smart ecological supervision center launched in 2024 as the first of its kind in Inner Mongolia has transformed conservation work that once depended solely on human rangers. The system now generates over 100,000 monitoring data points each month, supplying scientific evidence to guide restoration decisions.
Wildlife offers the most telling barometer of the lake's ecological recovery. In May 2025, schools of fish reappeared in the lake. The scene had not been seen for 27 years. Wang said this milestone signals the restoration of the lake's natural self-purification capacity and a functional aquatic food web.
The center's AI-driven biodiversity system automatically identifies bird species from camera footage. This spring, the system captured images of a relict gull, a rare national Class-I protected species. The valuable footage provides conservation teams with important evidence to support field surveys and protection planning. So far, researchers have recorded 168 bird species within the reserve.
Sensors linked to the smart system also track water levels, stream flow and pest density. Conservation staff use this data to run targeted pest control, keeping migratory birds safe.
"The data-driven approach provides solid scientific grounding for targeted ecological management of the lake," Wang said.
Inner Mongolia, home to four major deserts and four extensive sandy lands, is among the most severely desertified areas in China. The region has taken a leading role in the country's push to restore damaged ecosystems.
Local farmer Lian Sixiong saw his irrigation practices shift in 2024. That year, local water authorities introduced irrigation water quotas for every village and household in the lake basin. Smart meters installed on irrigation wells track water use round the clock.
"In the old days, all farmers here used flood irrigation to get the soil completely soaked," Lian recalled. "With new regulations on the water use, farmers are far more conscious about saving water," he said.
Since 2021, local authorities have launched 44 restoration projects across the lake reserve, including riverway dredging, wildlife habitat rehabilitation, agricultural pollution mitigation, waste treatment and sewage-treatment infrastructure upgrades.
As a result, the lake receives no industrial or domestic wastewater. Residential waste and sewage are fully treated on a daily basis.
"Though the lake has not recovered to its 1950s scale, above-normal precipitation in recent years has improved regional water recharge conditions. Coupled with effective conservation efforts, this will accelerate the lake's recovery," Wang said. ■

Diaz hat-trick powers Bayern past Leipzig to reclaim Bundesliga lead
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:34:17 CST
11:34:17 KST

Luis Diaz (1st R) of Bayern Munich celebrates his goal during the German first division Bundesliga football match between FC Bayern Munich and RB Leipzig in Munich, Germany, Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Philippe Ruiz/Xinhua)
BERLIN, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Luis Diaz scored a hat-trick as Bayern Munich crushed RB Leipzig 6-1 on Saturday to return to the top of the Bundesliga and end a run of two consecutive draws.
Vincent Kompany's side dominated from the outset, overwhelming Leipzig with relentless pressing and attacking intensity after disappointing draws against Augsburg and Viking Stavanger.
Diaz opened the scoring in the 12th minute, racing onto Joshua Kimmich's pass before beating goalkeeper Maarten Vandevoordt.
Aleksandar Pavlovic doubled the advantage in the 26th minute after Diaz had created the opportunity, while Michael Olise added a third eight minutes later with a precise strike from 18 meters.
Leipzig struggled to contain Bayern's movement and repeatedly surrendered possession. Only several saves from Vandevoordt prevented the hosts from establishing an even greater halftime lead.
Bayern maintained its dominance after the restart. Diaz curled home his second goal in the 47th minute before Harry Kane converted Nathaniel Brown's delivery from close range six minutes later.
Kompany made four substitutions shortly after the hour mark, resting key players ahead of Wednesday's Champions League encounter at Arsenal.
Diaz completed his hat-trick in the 69th minute with a powerful long-range finish. Vandevoordt then tipped an Olise close-range effort onto the crossbar. Leipzig grabbed a late consolation through Maksimovic in stoppage time.
"Today we were a completely different team. We were far too passive without the ball and offered very little going forward. We have to congratulate Bayern. You can lose here, but not the way we did today," Leipzig coach Martin Demichelis said.
The victory sent Bayern back to the top of the Bundesliga with 14 points from six matches, ahead of Borussia Dortmund on goal difference. Leipzig slipped to seventh with nine points, while third-placed Freiburg remains one point behind with a game in hand.
Elsewhere, Borussia Dortmund surrendered top spot after being held to a goalless draw at Union Berlin, while Mainz climbed to fifth with a 1-0 victory at Schalke. Elversberg edged Augsburg 4-3 to move into sixth, Hamburg defeated Stuttgart 1-0, and Werder Bremen fought back from two goals down to draw 2-2 with Paderborn. ■

Interview: Confidence, resilience, courage: China's Asian Para Games flagbearers aim to inspire
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:34:09 CST
11:34:09 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- When para taekwondo athlete Li Yujie and para powerlifter Yan Panpan learned they had been chosen as flagbearers for China at the opening ceremony of the 2026 Asian Para Games in Nagoya on Sunday, they were thrilled but keenly aware of the responsibility that come with the honor.
"It feels like a big vote of confidence in me," Li said. "This time I'm not just representing myself, but the whole Chinese delegation. It's not just an honor, it's a responsibility."
Yan said he felt humbled by the appointment. "There are people on the delegation who have achieved more than I have," he said. "I still have room to improve."
Both athletes bring impressive resumes to Nagoya. Li won China's first-ever Paralympic taekwondo medal in Tokyo and went on to claim the country's first Paralympic taekwondo gold in Paris. She was named 2025 World Para Taekwondo Female Athlete of the Year, becoming the first Team China athlete to receive the honor.
Yan has established himself as a leading force in para powerlifting, winning gold at the World Cup, the Tokyo Paralympics, the World Championships, the Hangzhou Asian Para Games and the Paris Paralympics.
Serving as flagbearer, Yan said, brings both pressure and motivation; for Li, the role has given her a renewed sense of purpose.
"Before, when I stepped onto the mat, I was mostly focused on each round and each technique," she said. "But walking out as a flagbearer, I feel a mission. Beyond giving everything in competition, I want to show the confidence and positive spirit of athletes with disabilities."
Both athletes have ties to Beijing Sport University: Li is studying sports training there, and Yan is a recent graduate.
"I had a really fulfilling time at university," Yan said. "I didn't just learn from textbooks. I made a lot of friends, and group activities taught me how to work with others."
Those teamwork lessons could prove useful in Nagoya, where Yan will compete in the mixed-team powerlifting event, making its debut at the Asian Para Games.
"In the lead-up to the competition, I need to communicate more with my teammates and keep myself in top form for longer," he said.
He will also compete in an individual powerlifting event: "My goal is to show everything I've put into training and to remain calm. If I get a good result, that will be great."
"I want to show the self-confidence, independence, resilience and courage of athletes with disabilities," Yan added. "No matter who we face, we'll keep fighting and never give up. I hope people can see the power of perseverance and find the courage to chase their own dreams."
Li will compete in the women's K44-57kg para taekwondo category. "My goal is simply to fight every bout well and go all out for gold," she said. "I want to show that athletes with disabilities are not afraid of challenges, and that we, too, can compete on the big stage and enjoy it."
"I hope more people will see that sport has no boundaries," she added. "Whatever our physical condition, we can all gain confidence through sport. Through my own story, I want to encourage more people with disabilities to step out of their homes, take up exercise, and feel the power sport can bring." ■

The coastguard and US Navy used multiple aircraft and boats, along with assistance from the Mexican Navy, to search the area for the remaining passengers. An additional helicopter will be deployed later on Saturday, according to the coastguard.
A Mayday call was transmitted from someone on the boat at about 1am on Friday, coastguard Lieutenant Santiago Tamburini said on the day.
A rescue helicopter reached the site about two hours later. It took about 90 minutes for the crew, which included a rescue swimmer, to pull the 16 people from the water, he added.
The boat went down about 225km (140 miles) west of Ensenada, Mexico, an area popular with fishing and leisure boats, but that is also frequented by smugglers.
Although the incident did not happen in US waters, coastguard official Charlie Valor said on Saturday they “were able to help, and that’s why we launched our assets”.
Fatal attempts to transport refugees and migrants from Mexico to the US have occurred in the past.
In May 2025, at least three people died when a boat flipped off the coast about 56km (35 miles) north of the US-Mexico border.
In 2023, eight people were killed in one of the deadliest maritime smuggling accidents off the US coast, when two boats approached a San Diego beach in heavy fog, and one capsized in the surf.
