Archaeologists discover 1,200-year-old mummified hairless dog in Peru
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
02:32:58 UTC
11:32:58 KST

Archaeologists discover 1,200-year-old mummified hairless dog in Peru
Remarkably preserved 1,200-year-old hairless dogs found in Peru reveal surprising clues about the bond between humans and their canine companions long before the Inca Empire.
- Date:
- October 17, 2026
- Source:
- Dartmouth College
- Summary:
- Archaeologists have discovered 1,200-year-old remains of Peru’s famous hairless dogs at an ancient Wari Empire burial site, including remarkably preserved mummies and puppies buried alongside humans. Their unusual teeth, diets, and burial arrangements reveal surprising clues about how ancient Peruvians cared for, bred, and sometimes discarded their dogs.
- Share:
Archaeologists working at an ancient burial complex in Peru have uncovered remarkable evidence of hairless dogs that lived more than 1,200 years ago, long before the rise of the Inca Empire. The discoveries include naturally mummified remains, unusual skeletal features, and clues about what the animals ate and how they were treated by the people around them.
Peruvian hairless dogs are a distinctive Indigenous breed known for their slender bodies, pointed ears, and lack of fur. They frequently appear in pottery created by ancient societies along the Andean coast. Today, a variation of the breed is recognized by the American Kennel Club as the Peruvian Inca Orchid. The dogs are also an important national symbol, having been officially designated part of Peru's cultural heritage in 2000.
A study published in the Journal of Anthropological Archaeology reports the first physical evidence of Peruvian hairless dogs at Castillo de Huarmey, the only known Wari Empire site discovered so far on Peru's northern coast.
Ancient Dog Remains Discovered at a Wari Empire Site
Located approximately 190 miles north of Lima, Castillo de Huarmey covers 110 acres and once served as an administrative and burial center for the Wari Empire. The complex was occupied between 600 and 1050 CE, roughly 400 years before the Inca rose to power.
The site has already produced several extraordinary archaeological discoveries. In 2012, researchers uncovered the first undisturbed elite Wari tomb, containing the remains of 58 high-status women, six human sacrifices, and approximately 1,300 artifacts. Another important discovery followed in 2022, when archaeologists identified nearby burials of elite craftspeople accompanied by gold, silver, and bronze tools. Together, these findings have helped researchers understand how the Wari Empire governed its territories.
The newly examined dog remains offer a different perspective on daily life at the site, particularly the complicated relationships between people and animals.
"Our findings indicate that humans and dogs coexisted at this Wari site, but reconstructing their bond is challenging, as past emotions are difficult to capture through archaeological methods," says first author Weronika Tomczyk, a research associate in Dartmouth's Department of Anthropology and a postdoctoral fellow in its Ecology, Evolution, Environment and Society Program.
"The goal of our study was to not only present data on Castillo de Huarmey's dog burials, but also emphasize that people in the past had often contradictory relationships with the animals, just as they do today: a pet for one group of people could at the same time be considered a pest by their closest neighbors."
Remarkably Preserved Dog Mummies Found in the Peruvian Desert
Castillo de Huarmey lies in an extremely dry region of Peru's Pacific coast. The desert's exceptionally arid conditions have helped preserve materials that would normally deteriorate over time, including hair, bones, clothing, leather, pigments, and decorated pottery.
Among the artifacts recovered from the site is an unusual ceramic vessel depicting a seated Peruvian hairless dog with humanlike features. The animal appears to be holding an object resembling a musical instrument.
Between 2010 and 2025, excavations also uncovered numerous remains of South American camelids, probably domesticated llamas and alpacas. Some may have been deposited as offerings during funerary ceremonies, while others appear to have been discarded as waste. Archaeologists also recovered the skeletal remains of dogs.
However, interpreting these discoveries has been complicated by extensive damage and looting. A powerful earthquake in 1970 caused part of Castillo de Huarmey to collapse, exposing burial chambers containing pottery and other valuable objects. Looters subsequently disturbed large sections of the complex.
The deeper archaeological layers remained untouched and retained their original Wari context. In contrast, the upper layers, where most of the animal remains were discovered, contained materials that had become mixed together.
During excavations in the northern section of the main ceremonial area, three sets of dog remains stood out.
One was a naturally mummified skull that still retained visible hairless skin and attached ears. The skull had also been colored with cinnabar, a bright red pigment commonly used in ancient Peruvian funerary traditions.
Researchers discovered a second, larger dog skull, along with the naturally mummified skeleton of a male dog buried in a shallow pit. The male skeleton was almost complete, missing only the lower portions of its front limbs.
At first, the researchers suspected that the mummified dog might have been buried relatively recently, perhaps around 50 years earlier during the period of looting. But Tomczyk noticed two important details: the animal was hairless, and all three dogs lacked their first premolars.
Missing Teeth Reveal the Dogs' Ancient Identity
The missing teeth provided an unexpected clue that helped researchers identify the animals.
"What I noticed is that some of the dog skeletons were missing teeth, and not that they lost them during their lifespan; some teeth, especially first premolars and sometimes last molars, had just never erupted," said Tomczyk. "And then I found in the literature that the same gene which is responsible for hairlessness in dogs is responsible for a reduced number of teeth, indicating that these were Peruvian hairless dogs."
In other words, the animals were not necessarily missing teeth because of injury, disease, or old age. Their reduced number of teeth was linked to the same genetic trait responsible for their hairlessness.
This distinctive biological connection offered evidence that the remains belonged to Peruvian hairless dogs rather than other ancient dog populations.
To investigate further, the researchers applied standard zooarchaeological techniques, which involve studying animal remains recovered from archaeological sites. These methods helped them estimate the ages of the dogs and examine their physical characteristics.
The team also analyzed chemical signatures preserved in the animals' bones and teeth. Known as isotopic analysis, this technique can reveal information about what an animal ate and drank, as well as where it may have lived.
The researchers examined isotopes of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and strontium. These are different forms of chemical elements that can preserve clues about diet and environmental conditions. Strontium is particularly useful because its composition varies with local geology and can help scientists trace an animal's geographic origins or movements.
The results were compared with similar measurements from human and camelid remains recovered at Castillo de Huarmey.
"Isotopic analyses of a dog's tooth give a signal of its life as a puppy because dog teeth erupt so fast, and the bone gives a signal of more or less the last year of its life," said Tomczyk. "Such sampling strategy aimed to provide signals from distinct stages of a dog's life."
Ancient Puppies Buried Alongside Elite Members of Society
Altogether, the excavations produced 341 dog bone specimens representing at least 19 individual dogs, in addition to the complete mummified male dog.
Some of the remains were found in particularly intriguing burial contexts.
For example, the bones of a puppy estimated to have been just 6 to 8 weeks old were discovered alongside an elite craftsperson nicknamed the "Master Basketmaker." Other finds included the bones of an adult dog buried within the site's palace and part of a puppy skeleton buried with a male individual identified as XY, who was probably sacrificed to serve as a tomb guardian.
Most of the dogs were adults at the time of burial. However, their remains suggest that the animals did not all receive the same treatment.
Some appear to have been deliberately buried, potentially reflecting a special role in Wari society. Others were found among discarded materials. Only a small number of bones displayed butchery marks, suggesting that dogs were not commonly consumed as food.
Radiocarbon dating provided another important discovery. The complete mummified male dog was determined to be at least 1,200 years old, making it the oldest radiocarbon-dated specimen recovered from Castillo de Huarmey so far.
This result has important implications for understanding the site's chronology because it provides an additional dating reference for the ancient complex.
Ancient Hairless Dogs May Have Eaten Like Humans
The isotopic evidence also revealed surprising similarities between the diets of dogs and people living at Castillo de Huarmey.
Most of the dogs had consumed at least some maize, or corn, which was a major food source throughout the pre-Hispanic Andes. Their diets therefore overlapped with those of the human population.
An especially interesting pattern emerged among the dogs believed to have been hairless.
When these animals were puppies, their diets appeared more similar to those of human children. As they grew older, however, their food sources became more varied.
The findings raise the possibility that some puppies received particular attention or were raised under controlled conditions, potentially as part of an organized breeding practice.
"We do not know if the dogs were intentionally fed maize or if perhaps, they were just eating leftovers or trash," said Tomczyk. "Yet, the distinct dietary patterns of hairless puppies provide insights into what may have been organized breeding."
The researchers emphasize that the archaeological evidence cannot establish whether these dogs were cherished pets, working animals, or animals with other roles in Wari society.
Nevertheless, the differences in burial practices, physical characteristics, and dietary patterns suggest that the hairless dogs held a distinctive place within the community.
"While we will never know if any of the three dogs were pets or how people treated them, it is evident they received different treatment than other dogs," said Tomczyk.
The discoveries provide a rare glimpse into the lives of dogs and humans more than a millennium ago, showing that relationships with animals could be just as varied and complicated in ancient societies as they are today.
The study's co-authors include Miłosz Giersz, Wiesław Więckowski, and Roberto Pimentel Nita of the University of Warsaw, along with Claire Ebert of the University of Pittsburgh.

Journal of Anthropological Archaeology, 2026; 82: 101767 DOI: 10.1016/j.jaa.2026.101767

Keen for change, Israel’s Arab minority sees election as existential
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
02:30:00 UTC
11:30:00 KST

Keen for change, Israel’s Arab minority sees election as existential
Majd al-Krum, Israel – After boycotting Israeli parliamentary elections his entire life, 55-year-old Said Kabat will head to the polls for the first time on Oct 27.
For him, the vote is existential – if a right-wing government is returned to power, he fears for the future of Israel’s Arab minority, to which he belongs.
The pharmacist from the Arab village of Majd al-Krum in northern Israel told AFP he used to boycott elections “all the time”.
“But now, I will go out and vote,” he said, concerned that a low turnout among the Arab population would embolden the far-right elements of the current ruling coalition.
Arab Israelis, also known as Palestinian citizens of Israel, account for about 21% of the country’s population.
They are descendants of Palestinians who remained within Israel’s borders after the state’s creation in 1948, and have long complained of discrimination compared with Israel’s Jewish majority.
The close-fought election is sparking calls for a mobilisation push among Israel’s Arab population, after their situation worsened under the outgoing government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – one of the most right-wing in the country’s history.
Driven by far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, settlement construction in the occupied West Bank has soared, and their attention is now turning to predominantly Arab areas inside Israel.
In September, land belonging to Kabat’s family in Majd al-Krum was the site of a confrontation between residents and Jewish Israelis who came to establish an outpost – a tactic used by West Bank settlers to take control of land.
Israeli police eventually removed the outpost, which had garnered the backing of Smotrich, who held a rally at the site and in August unveiled a plan to “Judaise” Israel’s predominantly Arab regions.
“In the light of the events, whether in Majd al-Krum or other villages, I urge every young person and everyone with a vote to cast it,” Kabat said.
‘Battle for existence’
Turnout among the Arab minority has traditionally been lower than that for Israel as a whole.
In the last election in November 2022, turnout among Arab and Druze voters was around 53%, while the country’s overall figure stood at around 70%.
In Majd al-Krum, activists like 31-year-old Dana Salameh were touring the village to explain the importance of voting.
“Everyone, even those boycotting and those unconvinced about voting, has begun to see the danger very close to them if this government remains in power,” Salameh said.
“They don’t want Arabs in this state at all... whether here or in Gaza or the West Bank,” she added.
On Oct 27, the Arab vote is expected to be split among four parties running on two lists.
The far-left Joint List brings together three parties, while Raam, or the United Arab List, is more open to negotiating with the right.
Raam became the first Arab party to join an Israeli government in a 2021-2022 coalition, and it could again play a kingmaker role this year.
A recent poll by Israel’s Channel 12 projected that the two lists would garner 13 seats in the next Israeli Parliament. They currently have 10 between them.
For Salameh, the poll is evidence of a growing conviction among Israel’s Arab citizens that they are facing “a battle for existence”.
Surging crime levels within the community could also push people towards the ballot box.
Since the start of 2026, at least 175 Arab citizens have been killed in violent crime incidents, according to the Abraham Initiatives coexistence organisation.
The violence is predominantly driven by criminal gangs, with Arab Israelis accusing the police – under the ministerial responsibility of Ben-Gvir – of lax enforcement. “The state has completely withdrawn from the scene,” said criminologist Walid Haddad.
‘Change is in our hands’
In Majd al-Krum, home to about 17,000 people, campaign billboards for the Joint List have popped up bearing the slogan “The change is in our hands”.
Several homes in the village face the threat of demolition, reflecting the reality for Arab localities across the country.
The Israeli authorities say the houses were built without permits or on state-owned land, but Palestinians say permits are near impossible to obtain.
In the city of Tayibe in central Israel, around 40 members of the Abu Mtair family face the looming threat of displacement, waiting for a decision on demolition orders that have been temporarily frozen.
“I cannot imagine this right-wing government returning,” said Akram Abu Mtair, 47, urging the city’s residents to vote.
Farther south, in the Negev desert, Israeli bulldozers recently demolished around 80 structures housing about 400 people in the Bedouin village of Al-Dahiya.
For Adnan Abu Wadi, who was left homeless with his four children, the demolitions were nothing more than an election stunt.
“People will turn out to vote in large numbers. We will vote as Arabs to change the government and remove the extremists.” AFP

Fears grow in DRC as former President Joseph Kabila joins rebellion

Fears grow in DRC as former President Joseph Kabila joins rebellion
Kabila’s move raises fresh questions about the war in eastern Congo and prospects for peace.
Goma, DR Congo – Hopes for peace in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have suffered another setback after former President Joseph Kabila joined a new political-military coalition challenging President Felix Tshisekedi.
Announced in Goma on Monday evening, the Front pour la Refondation de la Nation (FRN), or Front for the Refoundation of the Nation, is led by Kabila and replaces the existing alliance between the Alliance Fleuve Congo (AFC) and the March 23 Movement (M23). The new coalition brings together figures and forces associated with the two movements, accuses Tshisekedi of tyranny and calls for resistance by all means, including force.
Goma, the main city in eastern Congo’s North Kivu province, has been under M23-AFC control since January last year. Kabila’s move brings a former head of state directly into the leadership of the rebellion.
The conflict has displaced millions and drawn in neighbouring countries. Its roots stretch back decades, shaped by regional rivalries, unresolved security concerns and competition for territory and mineral resources. The aftermath of Rwanda’s 1994 genocide helped fuel wars across the region, while tensions between Kinshasa and Kigali continue to shape the fighting.
M23 says it took up arms because the Congolese government failed to honour earlier commitments. The Congolese government and international actors have accused Rwanda of supporting the group, an allegation Kigali denies, citing security threats from armed groups operating in eastern Congo.
Whether Kabila’s leadership will reshape the rebellion or further complicate efforts to end the war remains unclear. In Goma, residents fear the latest realignment will push peace further out of reach.
Why do residents fear the war is far from over?
For Basa Juhudi, Kabila’s decision has revived fears that the conflict will drag on.
“As a resident of Goma, I believed the war might end in the very near future, hoping that the Congolese government would liberate us. And we are greatly surprised that even our former president has joined the fray,” he told Al Jazeera.
Juhudi said Kabila’s political experience makes his involvement particularly troubling.
“The fact that Joseph Kabila has joined the rebellion, bearing in mind that he is our former president and knows this country inside out, means the war is far from over. I am not happy about this frightening situation.”
He also fears for the country’s democratic future, recalling the peaceful transfer of power in 2019, when Tshisekedi succeeded Kabila.
“Today, I am very afraid. I don’t know if I will be lucky enough to experience a proper democracy in the DRC. I was delighted by the country’s very first peaceful transfer of power,” Juhudi said.
How does Kabila’s past shape his return to the conflict?
Kabila came to power in 2001 following the assassination of his father, Laurent-Desire Kabila. He was elected president in 2006 and re-elected in 2011.
His second constitutional term was due to end in 2016, but elections were delayed. Critics accused him of seeking to remain in power beyond the constitutionally permitted two terms. Protests against the delays were met with deadly violence before a political compromise paved the way for elections in December 2018.
Tshisekedi was declared the winner and took office in January 2019, marking the DRC’s first peaceful transfer of presidential power through elections. Kabila defended the election delays, arguing that the Congolese people had ultimately resolved their problems through dialogue.
His alignment with the FRN marks a new phase in his confrontation with Tshisekedi. The coalition presents itself as a political alternative to the government while maintaining an armed challenge to its authority. Whether Kabila can translate his political experience and networks into wider support remains uncertain.
Can dialogue still avert a wider confrontation?
Kabila’s move has drawn criticism from within the Congolese political establishment.
Vital Kamerhe, a former speaker of the National Assembly and leader of the Union for the Congolese Nation (UNC), urged the movement to abandon armed struggle.
“You cannot erase your own record by accusing your successor,” Kamerhe declared in a speech on Wednesday.
“I call on the leaders of this movement to abandon their plans and prioritise the path of dialogue. Whatever our frustrations, our differences or our ambitions, nothing, absolutely nothing, can justify us taking up weapons against our own country, at the risk of sacrificing our own Congolese lives,” he said.
His appeal highlights the central challenge facing peace efforts: political grievances remain unresolved, while renewed fighting threatens a population already battered by conflict.
What does Kabila’s move mean for peace initiatives?
The United States and Qatar have pursued separate diplomatic initiatives aimed at ending the conflict.
In Doha, representatives of the Congolese government and AFC-M23 have discussed a ceasefire, the return of refugees, the release of detainees and measures to counter rhetoric that stigmatises ethnic minorities.
Washington has pursued an agreement between the DRC and Rwanda, including commitments relating to the neutralisation of the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) and the withdrawal of Rwandan troops from Congolese territory.
The initiatives address different but connected dimensions of the crisis. Kabila’s emergence as leader of the FRN raises questions about who will represent the armed opposition and whether existing commitments will be respected.
However, the new coalition has said it intends to honour commitments made during the Doha negotiations.
In a communique released on Wednesday, Freddy Kaniki, one of the FRN’s leaders, said the signing of the coalition’s memorandum of association and its official launch marked the dissolution of the Alliance Fleuve Congo (AFC), which the FRN succeeds by right.
The communique said the FRN would assume the AFC’s “rights, obligations and commitments, in particular those entered into as part of the Doha negotiations”.
The statement suggests that the coalition intends to maintain the commitments made by its predecessor. It remains to be seen, however, how this pledge will translate into progress towards a ceasefire and a lasting settlement.
For Josue Akuzwe Walayi, a Congolese human rights activist, the development threatens to undermine hopes raised by the negotiations.
“My greatest fear is for the future of the Doha and Washington peace initiatives; it is not just that they will be a diplomatic failure, but that they will become yet more agreements without any real peace for the Congolese people,” he tells Al Jazeera.
Walayi argues that agreements without effective accountability mechanisms risk becoming empty promises. Lasting peace, he says, requires parties to honour their commitments and violations to be documented, investigated and punished in accordance with the law.
“What would the Doha and Washington agreements be worth if, despite the negotiations, Congolese people continue to die, families remain forced into exile and communities live in fear? The danger would be to normalise the war whilst the people pay the price,” he warns.
Could Kabila’s return pose a broader challenge to Kinshasa?
Kabila’s return to the centre of the conflict comes amid his legal confrontation with the Congolese state. Last year, a Congolese military court sentenced him to death in his absence on charges, including treason and war crimes, linking him to the M23 rebellion. His relatives described the conviction as “unjust” and “politically motivated”.
Goma resident Willo Riziki says Kabila’s involvement should prompt the government to reassess the challenge it faces.
“The Congolese authorities must now take this war very seriously. If Kinshasa thought it was dealing with puppets, that is no longer the case. There are people all over the country who remain loyal to Kabila,” Riziki told Al Jazeera.
How far that loyalty extends, and whether it can translate into organised political or military support, remains uncertain.
There has been no official government reaction to the coalition’s announcement. Last week, after Kabila warned that the country was in peril and needed to be saved, government spokesman Patrick Muyaya said the former president had “nothing to offer but chaos”. In a post on X, Muyaya described Kabila as a “man of the past, nostalgic for anti-democratic methods”.
The confrontation between Kabila and Tshisekedi reflects a wider struggle over the country’s political future. But for civilians in the east, the immediate question is whether the latest realignment will bring more fighting and further delay a negotiated settlement.
“We don’t know if the war will end here,” said Juhudi.

‘They kicked the French mayor, shouted Viva la France’: Diplomat recounts West Bank settler attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

02:17:57 UTC
11:17:57 KST

Israel's diplomatic standing in Europe is at a historic low, and as if that were not enough, Saturday afternoon brought an attack on European diplomats by Jewish rioters. Once again, security forces failed to arrive at the scene in time, and the suspects fled without being arrested. "They were attacked by seven adult men, ages 20 and older, who apparently did not come from a nearby outpost but from farther away, meaning they had been specifically summoned," one of the diplomats present at the scene said. "They kicked the French mayor, and he was injured."
A European diplomat who was in one of the vehicles targeted in the attack described the terrifying moments to ynet. "The residents of Taybeh invited diplomats and peace activists to the olive harvest to protect them. At one point, we heard that settlers were approaching, so we immediately got into the car and started driving. Then I saw masked settlers carrying sticks and metal crowbars running toward us. It was clear they had no good intentions. It was frightening. They hadn't come to pick olives."
"They kicked the French mayor, and after beating him, they shouted 'Viva la France.' They had recognized the French flag," the diplomat continued. "They also attacked the Belgian vehicle. When you see something like that, you say to yourself, 'My God, how can something like this happen?' We came with security personnel, and it's absurd because this is an area under Israeli control. We knew settler violence was serious, but when you witness it firsthand, you understand just how terrible it is, especially for the residents who depend on the olive harvest for their livelihoods."
The mayor is Bernard Baudoux of Aulnoye-Aymeries, France, a member of the French Communist Party. The attack itself, which took place in the Christian village of Taybeh in the Binyamin region of the West Bank, was not captured on camera. However, Baudoux was subsequently filmed lying on the ground, and a vehicle belonging to the Belgian Consulate was photographed with a smashed window.
"This was professional-style violence, far more severe than anything we have seen in previous incidents," the diplomat said, emphasizing that all members of the delegation were "convinced" it was "an organized operation intended to send a message to Europeans, rather than to local residents."
The diplomat said members of the delegation were deeply angered by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's response to the incident. Netanyahu has so far refrained from explicitly addressing the attack, as have the leaders of other parties in his political camp. However, the Prime Minister's Office issued a statement in English casting doubt on the European account, even after Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar and the IDF said "Israeli rioters" were responsible for the incident.
Beyond the fact that Israel is once again presenting conflicting messages to the international community, with its own officials contradicting one another, the diplomat said, "The mayor's political background is irrelevant to the question of who attacked him. Netanyahu's statement completely ignores the fact that this is a Christian village and that the delegation came from Catholic countries that consider themselves committed to protecting Christians in the West Bank. In Europe, Netanyahu's statement is seen as shocking."
'This was an attack with clubs'
Members of the European delegation also responded to claims made in Israel that the visit should have been coordinated with security forces so they could provide protection for participants.
"That is a misleading claim," delegation members said. "Taybeh is in Area B, and visits there do not require coordination. Diplomats visit frequently, and the military has never escorted them or required prior coordination."
The Prime Minister's Office, for its part, issued the following statement:
"The diplomatic delegation entered a sensitive area with a history of confrontations without prior coordination with the IDF, as officially confirmed by the military. Such coordination is essential to protecting visiting diplomats and preventing violence. The visit included Bernard Baudoux, a French Communist Party mayor who previously raised the Palestinian flag over his municipal building, prompting French authorities to order its removal.
"Published footage shows masked individuals confronting a diplomatic vehicle. Separate images show a smashed window and a person lying on the ground. These images alone do not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility. Those circumstances remain under investigation. Israeli police and forensic investigators have launched an investigation to establish the facts and identify those responsible.
"These reports come amid concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest, relying on sensational headlines before the full facts emerge."
The European delegation included representatives from Belgium, Poland and France, along with the French mayor, whose municipality has a sister-city relationship with Taybeh. They arrived a day after an attack on photojournalist Heidi Levine, who was moderately injured and underwent surgery in Israel.
"They came to the only remaining entirely Christian village in the West Bank to show solidarity during the olive harvest," the diplomat said. "An 'alleged attack' or a 'confrontation with a vehicle' does not describe what happened. This was an attack with clubs, and a French elected official was injured."
Unlike the leaders of parties in Netanyahu's political camp, Ofer Winter's Amcha Yisrael party condemned the attack. "The violence displayed by a handful of extremists in Judea and Samaria against diplomats is serious and deserves unequivocal condemnation," the party said. "This violent minority does not represent the residents of Judea and Samaria. It tarnishes the reputation of the great Zionist settlement enterprise in Judea and Samaria and harms the settlements themselves. Anyone who supports the settlement enterprise must condemn this violent minority and take firm action against it."
In Israel, meanwhile, there are concerns that the growing frequency of violent incidents in the West Bank, coupled with the failure of police and the IDF to contain them, could lead to tougher sanctions against Israel, potentially extending beyond the settlements. Following the incident, Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot said his country "will continue to push for European Union sanctions against those responsible for this violence and those who support them."
On Saturday evening, hours after the incident, which occurred amid turmoil in France itself, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said, "The Israeli authorities must arrest those responsible for these despicable acts and bring them to justice. They must, with the utmost urgency, put an end to these criminal acts of violence and ensure the safety of civilian populations, as they are required to do under international law."
Poland's Foreign Ministry also expressed outrage over the attack, as did several other European countries whose representatives had not participated in the delegation.
Meanwhile, U.S. Ambassador Mike Huckabee addressed the attack on Levine, saying, "Heidi is US Citizen, clear ID as journalist. Details of who under investigation, but those who attacked unarmed reporter should spend YRS in prison. We have called for a full investigation, arrest, and prosecution to the fullest extent of the law to whoever participated in this.  Attacking a female photographer is despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards. Dishonorable act of senseless violence."
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio also commented overnight on the attacks in the West Bank, calling on Israel to take strong action against settler violence.
"We’re very disturbed by those images and what we’re seeing. We’ve asked the Israelis and continue to ask them to crack down on that stuff," Rubio told reporters.
His remarks followed the release of footage showing the attack on American photojournalist Heidi Levine, who works for The Washington Post. Levine was injured Friday during an assault by settlers on Palestinians. Rubio said the State Department had sought to establish the circumstances of the incident and that he expected to receive answers from the U.S. Embassy in Jerusalem by Sunday. He made the remarks before departing for Uzbekistan.
The village that is disappearing
Taybeh is the last village in the West Bank whose entire population is Christian, without exception. In ynet's "No Man's Land" series, Rabbi Benny Lau noted that the Christian population between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea has been steadily declining and now accounts for less than 1% of the Palestinian population in the area. Signs of this exodus are visible in the village's empty homes. Since October 7, 15 families have left Taybeh and the country, relocating to places where substantial communities of Taybeh expatriates have already established themselves.
Father Jacques, one of the local church leaders, described to Lau how despair has been taking hold among residents. He spoke nostalgically about the years before the Second Intifada and the Oslo Accords, when, he recalled, he could get into his car and drive to Jaffa, while settlers would stop in the village to buy popsicles and ice cream for their children.
The settlement of Ofra lies west of Taybeh, and numerous settler farms have been established around the village in recent years. Christian tradition identifies Taybeh with the ancient town of Ephraim, where Jesus stayed with his disciples before traveling to Jerusalem. The village is therefore considered a holy site and is home to historic churches and Christian institutions.
Taybeh is also home to the brewery that has produced Taybeh Beer, the first Palestinian beer, since 1995. The village hosts an Oktoberfest-style beer festival that typically attracts Europeans visiting the region.
Since 2025, Taybeh has been subjected to several attacks by Jewish rioters, including incidents in which vehicles and homes were set on fire. Several Palestinians have also been killed by live gunfire.
In one incident in July 2025, rioters set fire to a cemetery and desecrated a church, prompting Huckabee to visit the village and describe the incident as an act of terrorism.
But even after that visit, settlers continued their attacks, setting Palestinian vehicles on fire and spray-painting graffiti that read, "You will regret this."

Man fishing near a Florida lake killed by alligator

- Police said the nearly 3.6m alligator was “removed as a danger to the public” after the attack. Fish and Wildlife is investigating.
- Officials said alligators are common in the area and Florida has more than 1 million alligators, but attacks on people are rare. They warned: “respect it, keep your distance”.
AI generated
FLORIDA – A man who was fishing on the shore of a Florida lake was bitten and killed by an alligator on Oct 16, according to US police and wildlife authorities.
Steven Hamilton, 71, was fishing at Dr Bradford Memorial Park on the south side of Lake Apopka, a spokesperson for the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission said in a statement.
The alligator, which was nearly 3.6m long, was “dispatched”, Captain Michael Mason of the Winter Garden Police Department said during a news conference on Oct 16. Asked if it had been euthanised, he said only that it was “removed as a danger to the public”.
Police first responded to the lake area – a known alligator habitat in central Florida – at about 5pm on Oct 16, he said.
“Lake Apopka has tons of alligators in it,” he said, “so it’s not uncommon to see alligators in this part of town.”
The Fish and Wildlife commission, which is investigating alongside police, said emergency personnel declared Hamilton dead at the scene. An alligator trapper was then sent to find the reptile.
It was not immediately clear what injuries Hamilton sustained.
Lake Apopka, which is 24km to 32km north-west of Orlando, is Florida’s fourth-largest lake at roughly 12,130ha, according to the St Johns River Water Management District. In 2024, it had the 14th-largest alligator population among lakes in the state, with more than 4,600, The Palm Beach Post reported.
There are alligators in all 67 Florida counties, according to the Fish and Wildlife commission. It estimates that the state has a healthy and stable alligator population surpassing one million.
Though there is a robust number of the reptiles throughout Florida, attacks on people are rare. They are more common in or around water, as they are not well adapted to capturing prey on land. They can, however, lunge at prey within a few feet of a shoreline.
“Local wildlife, respect it, keep your distance,” Mason said on Oct 16. An alligator “looks like it’s docile. It looks like your Florida emblem. But it can be dangerous”. NYTIMES

In the shadow of war, Israelis to decide if hard-right turn is permanent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
02:05:00 UTC
11:05:00 KST

In the shadow of war, Israelis to decide if hard-right turn is permanent
JERUSALEM – Three years after suffering their deadliest single attack, Israelis will deliver their verdict on veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in an Oct 27 election that could decide if the country moves definitively into hard-right nationalism.
The trauma of the Oct 7, 2023 Hamas attacks remains raw across Israel after it resulted in the deaths of more than 1,200 people.
Faded stickers bearing the haunting smiles of young people killed by Hamas cover station walls and lampposts, and at bustling restaurants, no one bats an eye as patrons dine with their assault rifles, now liberally allowed.
Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister who surveys show is in a tight race, is seeking a new mandate after leading a multi-front regional war in response to Oct 7, with Israel reducing Gaza to rubble, occupying part of Lebanon and, with American help, bombarding Iran.
The relentless Gaza campaign has brought pariah status to Israel in many once-friendly Western countries, and Netanyahu himself faces an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court.
Even if the public broadly has supported the war’s aims, the effects at home have been much more divisive, including emboldening Netanyahu’s far-right allies bent on reshaping Israel into a religious-nationalist Jewish state.
“I really think that these elections are about the future of the state in a literal sense,” said Gideon Rahat, a political scientist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and the Israel Democracy Institute.
Netanyahu’s government has ramped up settlements in the occupied West Bank where settlers armed with the blessing of far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir have been attacking Palestinians on their lands with only occasional pushback from the authorities.
“The state without a monopoly on the use of force is a failed state,” Rahat said.
Netanyahu, who turns 77 on Oct 21, has served as prime minister on and off for more than 19 years.
The wily political operator returned to power in December 2022 bringing in once-shunned ultra-nationalists and quickly tried to rein in the judiciary, which is examining corruption charges that could land him in jail.
The proposed reforms brought out some of the largest protests in Israel’s history in the months before the Hamas attack.
“Everyone in the country has a strong opinion about Netanyahu. People either hate him or adore him,” said Alon Yakter, a political scientist at Tel Aviv University.
“When you want to see who people vote for, the first question you have to ask is their emotional feelings about Netanyahu.”
Anti-Netanyahu in style, not stance
Seeking to unseat Netanyahu is an informal bloc of parties united mostly around their distaste for him.
Netanyahu’s most formidable rival, according to polls, is former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, who is in many ways his antithesis – a political novice who wants to unite centrists rather than rally a base, and a phlegmatic speaker with halting English and none of the American-raised Netanyahu’s flair for blistering, headline-grabbing speeches.
Eisenkot as well as other opposition leaders have zeroed in on why Netanyahu failed to prevent Oct 7.
Netanyahu has been rocked by reports he ignored warnings. He vehemently denies the charges, blaming security chiefs who he said failed to wake him up that morning.
Netanyahu “may have his perfect English, but even with perfect English he got us Oct 7”, Eisenkot, in Hebrew, told a security conference at Reichman University.
Eisenkot’s son died in the Gaza war – offering an unspoken contrast to Netanyahu’s son Yair, a globe-trotting social media provocateur.
The working-class son of Moroccan Jewish immigrants, Eisenkot would be the first prime minister of Middle Eastern ancestry, a watershed in a country politically dominated since its founding by an elite of European descent.
Opposition leaders have not criticised Netanyahu’s decision to wage war, likely a losing stance in a country where a recent survey found that only 21% of the population identifies as anywhere left of centre.
Eisenkot, as military chief during the 2006 Lebanon war, promoted the Israeli doctrine of using massive force even against civilian infrastructure when in areas used by militants such as Hezbollah.
The opposition has instead heavily focused on social issues including Netanyahu’s tight alliance with ultra-Orthodox Jews, a fast-growing segment of the population due to high birth rates that has promoted religious priorities such as keeping public transit closed on Saturdays.
Netanyahu, while personally secular, has allowed religious students to remain exempt from military service, a source of particular resentment when stretched reservists have served multiple tours.
Opposition figure Naftali Bennett, prime minister in a short-lived 2021-2022 government, has vowed to end all exemptions to military service and said social divisions were putting Israel on a “slow-motion suicide mission”.
Hardline appeal
While the opposition attacks Netanyahu over Oct 7, for some Israelis, the aftermath of the attack shows the government has brought stability.
While Israelis have died in Iranian and Hezbollah retaliatory attacks, fire has stopped from Gaza, even as Israel keeps striking the territory and Hamas remains.
Israel’s economy has boomed since Oct 7, with construction sites dotting the major cities and the stock market soaring, led by the technology and defence sectors.
Neriah Yarchi, 19, a barber from Bat Yam near Tel Aviv, came of political age after Oct 7. He said he would vote for far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who wants the “voluntary” removal of Gaza’s two million Palestinians.
“If Gaza had been ours, they wouldn’t have had a place to infiltrate from and there wouldn’t have been a massacre,” Yarchi said.
Netanyahu has sought to seize on his international notoriety, with his Likud party putting up posters of leaders including New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, an outspoken critic of Israeli policies, that read, “They want Netanyahu to lose. Don’t let them win.”
Netanyahu has also vowed loudly never to align with parties representing Arab Israelis, who make up around one-fifth of the population and who some expect to turn out in higher numbers after the intense anti-Arab stances of some of Netanyahu’s ministers.
Arab lawmakers broke precedent to be kingmakers in the 2021-2022 government.
If the new election’s results are as close as expected, it could take weeks or months to form a government. Eisenkot has said he would not ally with Arab parties or Netanyahu, but some critics do not believe he would refuse.
Uriel Reichman, a former lawmaker who founded the university bearing his name, told the conference addressed by Eisenkot that a Netanyahu triumph could permanently entrench Israel’s right-wing turn.
He drew a parallel to countries such as Turkey where an elected populist packs the government with loyalists and transforms once-independent institutions.
“Experience shows that once such a system is put in place, it would be extremely difficult to dismantle it,” he said. AFP

Iran says two tankers catch fire after hitting mines in Strait of Hormuz
The vessels, each carrying about two million barrels of crude oil, used an unauthorised route, the IRGC says.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has said two oil tankers, each carrying about two million barrels of crude oil, caught fire after hitting naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz.
The first tanker hit a mine, triggering an explosion and a “fierce fire”, the IRGC said on Saturday, while the second tanker hit a mine that engulfed it “in a massive blaze”, Iran’s official IRNA news agency reported.
Information about the ships’ names or the origin of their cargo was not immediately available.
IRNA said the vessels had switched off their positioning and radar systems and tried to use a route not authorised by Iran.
The IRGC also claimed that while one tanker tried to cross the waterway “with US support”, the second vessel was left immobilised.
Iran seized control of the Strait of Hormuz after the US-Israeli war on the country began in late February. Tehran has since demanded that all ships seek its authorisation before transiting. About one-fifth of global oil consumption transited the waterway before the war.
This week, IRGC naval commander Rear Admiral Ali Azmaei warned that any vessel that deactivated its navigation systems would be considered “hostile”.
The United States has imposed its own naval counter-blockade on Iranian oil exports.
Iran’s army earlier said that two tankers caught fire on Thursday and Friday in Tehran’s “prohibited zone” in the Gulf of Oman.
Maritime monitors also reported two tankers struck in Gulf waters off Saudi Arabia on Friday.
Last Sunday, six vessels were attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz, the most in a single day since the war began, according to security firm Vanguard, the International Maritime Organization and the UK maritime agency UKMTO.
Attacks around the waterway have surged over the past two weeks, with Iran saying it is stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions imposed last month.
Nearly 20.8 million barrels of oil passed through on October 8, but only 2.9 million on October 11, according to Kpler data.
The disruption has pushed up global energy prices and inflation.
US President Donald Trump has explicitly ruled out using a nuclear weapon against Iran. “I wouldn’t use nuclear,” he told the Newsmax news site in an interview on Thursday.
Trump said that he was also not considering putting troops on the ground in Iran. “No, I don’t see that, I don’t see it,” he said, adding he believes a deal to end the war will be reached after the November 3 US midterm elections.

The draft amendments were published in the Gazette of India on Oct 16 (AI image)
NEW DELHI: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has proposed two changes to food safety rules: prohibiting the addition of sucrose and fructose to products meant for babies up to six months and setting maximum residue limits for two pesticides in tea.The draft amendments were published in the Gazette of India on Oct 16. Currently, lactose and glucose polymers are the preferred carbohydrate sources in infant foods. Sucrose and fructose can be added when needed, but their combined amount cannot exceed 20% of total carbohydrates. The proposed amendment seeks to prohibit their addition in products for babies up to six months.
The proposal aims to limit early exposure to added sugars amid concerns over childhood obesity and related health risks. It also complements recommendations for exclusive breastfeeding during the first six months. A doctor said the restriction must be enforced at the licensing stage. “FSSAI should also consider extending the ban to products intended for children above six months, given concerns over obesity.
”FSSAI has also proposed maximum residue limits of 20 parts per million (ppm) for acetamiprid and 50 ppm for imidacloprid in tea.
Maximum residue limits specify the highest legally permitted concentration of pesticide residues in food and provide benchmarks. They do not indicate the amount necessarily present in a particular sample.One doctor said the proposed limits need to be accompanied by realistic assessments of consumer exposure. “Since tea is consumed several times a day, it is important to assess how much of these chemicals passes from the leaves into the brewed drink.”

Almost as soon as we notice something new, we start forming judgments about it. We can’t prevent…
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
01:52:50 UTC
10:52:50 KST

Almost as soon as we notice something new, we start forming judgments about it. We can’t prevent this from happening because we are judgmental beings by nature. We automatically evaluate everything (and everyone) we encounter, which means we judge some things to be good and others to be bad.
Our judgments would not be a problem if we allowed them to arise and then depart, but we also have a tendency to become attached to them. We feel that because our judgments follow from the unique beings that we are, we must also identify with them. We end up limiting our understanding of both world and self because we have already judged their contents in one way or another.
The consequence of this is that we tend to become stuck with a very narrow way of seeing the world, a way that follows directly from the particular attachments we have formed. We build our identities around this narrow view, which in turn keeps us trapped in an endless and unnecessary battle with suffering.

Chinese scientists develop new nanoparticles to make pesticides more efficient
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
09:47:52 CST
10:47:52 KST

HEFEI, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- A new study from the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science of the Chinese Academy of Sciences offers a new solution to one of agriculture's most persistent problems: pesticides that wash off crop leaves before they can do their job.
The study, published in the Journal of Controlled Release, drew inspiration from the tiny, hair-like structures that help bacteria cling to the human gut.
By mimicking this natural adhesion trick, the research team built rough-surfaced silica nanoparticles that grip leaf surfaces far better than conventional formulations, potentially cutting pesticide waste and reducing the need for repeated spraying.
According to the researchers, conventional pesticide spraying is remarkably inefficient. Leaf surfaces are coated in a waxy, water-repellent layer that causes spray droplets to bounce off. Rain washes away what does land, while sunlight and evaporation break down the active ingredients. Previous studies showed that as much as 90 percent of a pesticide may never reach its target, forcing farmers to spray again and again. This drives up costs and worsens pollution and ecological damage.
The research team turned to bacteria for the answer. Some gut bacteria have tiny, hair-like parts called pili. These pili work like little hooks. They grab onto surfaces so the bacteria don't get flushed away. The researchers copied this idea. They made tiny hollow silica particles and covered their surfaces with little spikes. Then they filled these particles with imidacloprid, a common insecticide.
Detailed analysis confirmed that when sprayed onto leaves, the spiky nanoparticles act just like bacterial pili. They dig into the waxy leaf surface and lock on, like tiny anchors. They also form hydrogen bonds -- weak chemical connections that work like tiny magnets -- which make the grip even stronger.
"This double grip helps the pesticide stay put, even in rain. The carriers also release the pesticide slowly and resist UV damage, making them even more efficient," said Wang Guozhong, a researcher at the institute.
The research team tested the new formulation on cotton, soybean and tomato leaves. After simulated rainfall, the amount of pesticide left on the leaves was more than 4.8 times higher than with a commercial imidacloprid product.
"Safety tests on plants and zebrafish showed no clear signs of harm, suggesting the new pesticide is environmentally friendly and could help pave the way for low-dose, high-efficiency, green pesticide products," Wang added. ■

However, implementation has often depended on whether schools have adequately trained teachers.
The proposed NCERT programmes are expected to focus not merely on whether a trainee can speak multiple languages, but whether the person has sufficient academic command to teach them in a classroom.The details, including how many languages a teacher can be trained in and the level of proficiency required in each, are still being worked out, sources said.
The academic pathway is also expected to extend beyond classroom teaching. Those completing the relevant postgraduate programme could qualify for school teaching, while students pursuing doctoral programmes could move into teacher education and research.The initiative is part of a wider restructuring after NCERT was declared an Institution Deemed to be University under the “distinct category” through a ministry notification on March 30. The notification has also asked NCERT to start research, doctoral and innovative academic programmes. The proposal could turn multilingualism from a curriculum principle into a teacher-workforce strategy.

IN BRIEF
- The challenges for Shoebridge started almost as soon as the 11-member party room chose him as its leader.
- He is facing a range of issues, from allegations against party members to the party's Ukraine policy.
Three weeks into the job, Greens leader David Shoebridge has gone from a public row over Ukraine to criticism from his own colleagues and now an inquiry into one of his senators.
Since Shoebridge was elected leader of the Greens at the end of September, he vowed to "beat down One Nation" and expose Labor's "failures".
Instead, the story has been one of ill-contained disarray, with one crisis tumbling into the next.
Political scientist Zareh Ghazarian of Monash University's School of Social Sciences told SBS News that the past weeks had been catastrophic for a party under new leadership, which had struggled to make ground amid the rise of One Nation.
"This could not have been a worse start to Senator David Shoebridge's leadership for the Greens," he said, adding that the Greens had needed an opportunity to stand out in a "positive way".

"That opportunity was there with a new leader, but these events and internal disagreements have taken their toll. It's been a very tough start to Senator Shoebridge's leadership."

A 'destabilising' debate

"One has been more focused on pragmatism and working with other political parties within parliament to achieve policy outcomes. The other has been more activist in its approach, with a stronger focus on changing grassroots behaviours and actions.
"Like other political parties, the Greens have internal divisions, and they can potentially be quite deep."

"This is occurring at a time when the Victorian Labor Party appears to be losing support, the Coalition appears to be gaining support, and One Nation is also polling strongly," he said.
"This election will be a real test.
"Any faltering by the Greens could prove costly because it is always difficult to win seats back once they are lost."
