====================================================================================================

The forgotten German who saved Jews in Japan - and the diary that resurfaced 80 years later
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
01:37:26 UTC
10:37:26 KST

Renate Quastler kept a tantalizing and expensive secret. She never told her family about the illustrated diary begun as a young girl in wartime Japan. Yet she never threw it away, either.
Renate was born in Stuttgart in 1933, the same year that Hitler came to power.
Six years later, her Jewish father, Ernst Quastler, her Christian mother, Else, and six-year-old Renate escaped Germany for Japan, where Ernst had been offered work by German industrialist Willy Rudolf Foerster, and where Renate kept her diary at the peak of the war.
More than eight decades later, after Renate’s death, that hidden diary would unexpectedly open a new chapter in the remarkable story of Foerster, and reopen questions about the German industrialist in wartime Tokyo whose rise and fall, and his role in helping Jewish refugees, are still being pieced together.
Handwritten in German, Renate filled more than 120 pages with drawings and watercolors, photographs, pressed flowers and plants, and the everyday observations of a Holocaust refugee child with no awareness of her Jewish identity.
Renate records the destruction of her family’s Tokyo home in the air raids of April 1945, both pleasant vacations and emergency evacuation in the mountain resort town of Karuizawa, postwar trips to barter for food, and then the bewildering new world of the American Occupation – Coca-Cola, nylon stockings, and jitterbugging.
Among the surviving memorabilia are even her commuter train passes, with the Quastler name printed in Japanese. And among the names in Renate’s diary is one that would reopen a nearly forgotten history: the wife of Renate’s father’s employer, Hideko Foerster.
Hideko came from a long lineage of doctors, and while the opposite in temperament to her headstrong husband, she was quietly self-assured with resources of inner strength to see her through a long life of unfathomable wealth and the complete dissolution of that fortune.
Her husband, Willy Rudolf Foerster, was a German anti-Nazi industrialist who built one of the country’s most successful foreign-owned manufacturing businesses, based in Tokyo.
Documents and photographs discovered by his biographer, Dr. Clemens Jochem, show that his factories employed more than a thousand people, including foreign workers from Korea and Southeast Asia and, astonishingly, a small number of Jewish refugees fleeing Germany and Nazi-controlled Europe – including Renate’s family.
Quastler was entrusted with a key position: he became Foerster’s Betriebsleiter (general manager).
Working closely with Tokyo’s Jewish Refugee Committee, Foerster helped Jewish families get employment, entry permissions, and other formalities they needed to reach Japan; in documented cases, he also paid their travel costs.
Jewish refugees were not hidden away at the margins of his enterprise. Some were placed in important managerial positions.
A trail of documents
The documented trail Foerster left behind is enormous and keeps on growing. Jochem spent more than a decade investigating Foerster’s story, working through thousands of pages of records discovered in archives in Japan, Germany, the United States, and Israel.
One document in particular caught his attention: a 1959 letter from Foerster to Fritz Bauer, the attorney-general in Frankfurt who played a crucial role in bringing Adolf Eichmann to justice, a key Nazi architect of the Final Solution.
Foerster provided Bauer with information about the wartime persecution of prisoners placed aboard German blockade-running ships in Japan. He also drew Bauer’s attention to what he believed was false testimony by former German diplomats that had obstructed efforts to clear his own name of Nazi associations.
In the letter, Foerster pointedly described how he had employed Jewish refugees fleeing Nazi persecution, making it unmistakable where he had stood during those years.
“I really was astonished,” Jochem recalled, “because if Foerster’s story was true, he seemed to be some sort of second Oskar Schindler.”
What began as curiosity became years of meticulous archival investigation.
In 2017, Jochem published his findings in The Foerster Case: The German-Japanese Machine Factory in Tokyo and the Jewish Relief Committee (Der Fall Foerster: Die deutsch-japanische Maschinenfabrik in Tokio und das Judische Hilfskomitee).
Jochem’s research also reconstructed the campaign that destroyed Foerster’s reputation and fortune. At the center of it was Adolf Hitler-appointed Josef Meisinger.
Infamously called the “Butcher of Warsaw,” Meisinger was sent to Tokyo in 1941 as a Gestapo and Security Service liaison attached to the German Embassy.
Foerster, who kept his distance from official Nazi circles in general, and Meisinger in particular, vehemently opposed National Socialism and, according to Jochem’s research, continued employing Jewish refugees.
That willingness to oppose authority was how Foerster’s daughter, Erica, now 85, remembered her father.
“My mother, Erica, always described him as someone who followed his own head,” Jesse Foerster told the Magazine. “If he felt something was wrong, he acted accordingly. She believed he knew that he was putting himself in opposition to the Nazi regime and that this could become dangerous for him. And even when his own situation became increasingly difficult, he continued.”
In May 1943, acting at Meisinger’s instigation, the Japanese arrested Foerster on accusations of spying for the Soviet Union. He was imprisoned and tortured for more than a year and forced during his captivity to surrender his business for a fraction of its value.
Released in June 1944, he was placed under house arrest. Hideko and several of Foerster’s employees were also arrested and detained.
The defeat of Nazi Germany and the subsequent Allied occupation of Japan under US general Douglas MacArthur did not restore Foerster’s standing, his property, and the recognition that he had actually opposed Nazism.
Instead, Allied occupation authorities classified Foerster as a Nazi, confiscated what remained of his extensive assets in Japan, and forcibly repatriated Willy, Hideko, and their two young children, Erica and Willy Jr., to Germany in 1947 – even though an internal US Counter Intelligence Corps investigation had reached a very different conclusion: “It is definitely established that he [Foerster] was anti-Nazi in fact and in action.”
Willy Foerster’s acts of courage
Yet even as Foerster was being stripped of what the Japanese had left him, his land, his farms, his family’s home and his factory, and forcibly deported as an ‘objectionable German’, testimony was accumulating that verified both his story and his acts of courage.
Jewish refugees and others who had known Foerster in Japan gave evidence on his behalf. Among them was Karl Rosenberg, a leader of Tokyo’s Jewish Refugee Committee.
Rosenberg helped Jewish refugees find employment in Japan and referred suitably qualified applicants to Foerster’s F. & K. Engineering factory.
One of Foerster’s Jewish employees was engineer Hugo Stern, who had made his way from Vienna through Shanghai to Tokyo. But his children, Ruth and Robert, were trapped in Nazi-controlled Vienna.
Stern’s wife had died in Shanghai, and almost his entire family was murdered in concentration camps.
“As far as I know,” Jochem told the Magazine, “he and his two children were the only survivors.”
In a surprising development this past August, alongside the separate discovery of Renate’s diary, Jochem uncovered Japanese Foreign Ministry records that document, month by month, Foerster’s efforts to rescue Stern’s young children, Ruth and Robert, and bring them safely to Japan to reunite with their father.
The Home Ministry approved the children’s entry on August 6; six days later, foreign minister Yosuke Matsuoka instructed the Japanese consul general in Vienna to issue their visas. Ruth and Robert subsequently reunited with Foerster’s employee, their father, in Japan.
It is not difficult to understand why, after the war, Stern was prepared to speak on Foerster’s behalf. Yet testimony from Stern, Rosenberg, and others did not restore Foerster’s name.
Paltry reparations
In 1963, Willy and Hideko Foerster were awarded 7,390 Deutsche Marks in damages ($1,853) – a worthless sum compared with the fortune confiscated in Japan, estimated at $88 million in wartime currency, or approximately $1.6 billion today. The family never recovered those assets.
Foerster nevertheless tried to begin again. In the early 1960s, he established Stahlbau Foerster in Bensheim, Germany, a similar engineering and industrial concern modeled after the one that had been so successful in Japan.
The new enterprise, however, never approached the scale of the business he had lost. On February 19, 1966, at the age of 60, Willy Rudolf Foerster died of a stroke.
“The judgment was not regarded by my grandfather as the final chapter in his effort to obtain justice, but as a first step,” Jesse shared.
For Jesse, recognition of his grandfather for Jewish lives is important, but, in his words: “I don’t regard it as something my family is owed. Against the enormity of what Jewish families lost in the Holocaust, I’m reluctant to make my own family’s losses the center of the story.”
The ‘Jewish consulate’ in Tokyo - With documentation by H.A. Straus and Chris Bock
Before the refugees began arriving, Tokyo already had a small community of European Jews established in business and professional life.
Among them were Ernst Baerwald, Heinrich Steinfeld, and Hans Alexander Straus. Baerwald had been in Japan for decades and was also well connected in Japanese society and the arts, while Straus worked for Columbia Records during the heyday of radio and Japan’s growing passion for Western classical music.
In 1933, as the first Jewish refugees from Germany began reaching Japan, the three men decided to organize help. Straus later described their work in his memoir chapter, “The ‘Jewish Consulate’ in Japan.”
Their roles evolved naturally: Baerwald handled financial matters, Steinfeld logistics, while Straus, whose work brought him into Japanese business circles, handled many of the government contacts.
Their principal means of helping Jews escape Europe was to secure these refugees from the Holocaust jobs in Japan. Employment was not merely what awaited a refugee after arrival; it was the way they could be given legal residency status in Japan.
“It was not easy to find work for Jewish refugees,” Straus recalled.
One remarkable case shows how the system worked.
In 1938, a Japanese industrialist approached Straus, looking for a specialist in armor plating.
The name supplied was Friedrich Ratsky – the identity used by Paul Patek, whose extraordinary escape from Europe would later become the subject of Chris Bock’s book An Ordinary Man.
Straus contacted the Jewish community in Vienna, offering Patek the prospect of an executive position with a Japanese company.
By the time the reply came, Patek was already on his way to Trieste to board a ship for Japan. He later told Straus that he had gotten him a job and helped him leave Austria “just in the nick of time.”
Karl Rosenberg, already established in Tokyo with the Swiss trading firm Liebermann-Waelchli & Co., would also become a central figure in the Jewish Refugee Committee. Rosenberg and Straus received applications from persecuted Jews in Europe and sought employers willing to give them work.
This is where Willy Rudolf Foerster became so important. His factories in Omori offered something desperately valuable: actual jobs for qualified refugees. Foerster could employ them and pursue the permissions necessary to bring employees and, in documented cases, their families to Japan.
The committee provided the network; established Jews in Tokyo made the connections; and employers such as Foerster provided the jobs that could become a route out of Europe.
How many families ultimately escaped Europe through this small circle of Jews already living and working in Tokyo remains an intriguing question.
Their children and grandchildren may still possess letters, photographs, diaries, and family stories that have never been connected to the Jewish Refugee Committee.
Renate Quastler’s diary has already shown what can surface after more than 80 years.
There may yet be other families who recognize a name, a photograph, or a fragment of their own history in this story and step forward to claim their place in it.
The surprise of Renate’s diary
The discovery of Renate Quastler’s diary was, in Jesse’s words, a “big, big surprise.”
Here was the childhood diary of a girl whose family his grandfather had helped bring to Japan, resurfacing more than 80 years later with references to his grandmother Hideko and evidence of a relationship between the two families that even their descendants are only now beginning to understand.
“I can’t wait to learn more,” Jesse said. “I’m nosy about that.”
Julie Quastler initially searched for family records regarding her Austrian ancestry and possible citizenship.
That search eventually led her to type the Quastler name into eBay, where she was astonished to find the $9,500 archive built around an illustrated diary belonging to her late aunt Renate – a diary Julie had never known existed.
Among the names in the seller’s description was the name Foerster. She barely knew who Foerster was.
But clearly the seller knew his Holocaust history and that he had stumbled upon an era in Japanese World War II history with evidence that Jews and even a non-Jewish German in Tokyo’s foreign community had actively played a role in saving the lives of Jews trapped in Europe.
One of the Jewish refugees was Julie’s grandfather, Ernst Quastler, standing next to his boss, Willy Rudolf Foerster, in a photograph at a company event.
“My heart was racing. I was absolutely stunned to discover my aunt’s illustrated diary on eBay – a diary I had never known existed,” she said.
Willy and Ernst’s grandfathers had worked closely together in wartime Tokyo. The diary and photographic evidence provided by the Quastlers show a relationship that extended well beyond the factory.
The very first image of her father, Imre, in the Quastler’s family photo album from Japan, shows his Lutheran baptism. Willy stands formally dressed with the family, and on the baptismal certificate his name appears as “Paten” – a German word that can mean godparent, godfather, or sponsor.
Was the baptism simply a reflection of Else’s Christian background, or did it also offer the family a way of obscuring Imre’s Jewish ancestry at a dangerous time? Imre himself didn’t know he had a Jewish father until his teen years.
The Quastlers stayed in Japan until 1951, and the Foersters were deported to Germany four years earlier. The families lost touch for the next 70 years. And now, the bridge comes through Renate’s diary, with vivid details of their bygone friendship.
She records the family spending eight days with Hideko Foerster at her home in Karuizawa in August 1947, during the same period when Willy was being forcibly repatriated to Germany as an alleged Nazi.
In 2019, Renate and Imre jointly signed a notarized declaration supporting Jochem’s research that showed Willy to have played a courageous and self-endangering role in helping their family escape Nazi persecution and reach Japan.
Imre gave the document to Jochem, who personally submitted it to Yad Vashem as part of the effort to have Foerster recognized as Righteous Among the Nations.
The $88 million question
Jochem submitted extensive paperwork to Yad Vashem after completing the research. Why then, despite the evidence assembled about his actions, has he not been recognized by Yad Vashem?
Dr. Joel Zisenwine, director of Yad Vashem’s Righteous Among the Nations Department, told the Magazine that a submission regarding Willy Rudolf Foerster had indeed been made, but that “the primary sources available are not sufficient to support recognition.”
Zisenwine emphasized that “the title requires active involvement in saving Jews from death or deportation, risk to the rescuer’s life, liberty, or position, no expectation of compensation or reward, and testimony or documentation establishing the nature of the rescue.”
Zisenwine left the door open. “If new testimony or evidence regarding this case becomes available, it can be submitted to the Righteous Among the Nations department for review,” he said. When a survivor’s personal account is unavailable, he added, supporting evidence may sometimes be found in archival primary sources.
The evidentiary picture today, however, is not the one Yad Vashem had beforehand. Jochem clarified that the notarized declaration he submitted in 2019 came jointly from Imre and Renate. And the silence surrounding Foerster was not as complete as it once appeared.
“There is one strand where it went differently,” Jochem told me. “The circle around Stern did engage, quite intensively and over years, with the German authorities to document the injustice that had happened in Japan.”
Now newly uncovered Japanese Foreign Ministry records add contemporaneous evidence of Foerster’s sustained efforts to bring Stern’s children out of Nazi-controlled Vienna and into Japan.
For Julie, the return of her aunt Renate’s diary has already changed the meaning of her family history.
She shared that what began as a records search connected with Austrian citizenship became “this rare opportunity to better understand Renate – whom I adored my whole life – while gaining insight into an extraordinary historical experience my family rarely discussed.
“I’m slowly discovering my own relationship to Jewish identity and history that was never part of my family’s conversations,” Julie added. “And if recovering Renate’s diary plays any part in Willy Foerster being honored as Righteous Among the Nations, I can’t imagine a more meaningful outcome.”
Jesse would agree.
“At one point, when I was preparing to bring more of my grandfather’s story into the public eye, COVID arrived, and the world suddenly had very different worries,” he told me.
“Later, when I felt that society might finally have entered a somewhat calmer period again and that there could perhaps be more space and attention for Willy’s story, October 7 happened – and with it another enormous tragedy.”
He found himself asking a question that kept his family’s historical grievance in proportion to suffering in the present: “How loudly would I have to shout in order to draw attention to something that happened so long ago, when you are looking into the eyes of people who are suffering right now?”
“I still feel that way,” Jesse continued. “What has changed is not my sense of proportion, but the fact that the story has suddenly begun to move again from the outside – especially through the rediscovery of Renate’s diary and the Stern documentation, and everything that has followed from it. And, of course, we are very happy about that.
“The historical classification of my grandfather’s story has become more important again, and perhaps the time is simply right.”
This most unexpected chapter in Willy’s story is unfolding generations later. The painstaking work of tracing the Jewish forebears whom he helped escape Nazi persecution and murder is allowing descendants who were not themselves raised as Jews to claim their place in their families’ Holocaust history.
And in recovering that nearly lost part of their inheritance, they are recovering Willy Rudolf Foerster’s story as well.
Hidden in plain sight
Nobody set out looking for Willy Rudolf Foerster.
Dr. Clemens Jochem certainly didn’t. His curiosity began much closer to home in Hamburg, with questions about his own German family and what had brought some of them to Shanghai during World War II.
Somewhere along that trail, he stumbled upon Willy Rudolf Foerster. What caught Jochem’s attention was the startling possibility that Foerster had helped Jewish refugees escape Nazi persecution – a figure with something of an Oskar Schindler-type story, but in Japan. That possibility sent him in an entirely new direction, and eventually into more than a decade of archival research.
One by one, following completely different questions from different corners of the world, we found Foerster – and eventually found one another.
Those of us who have become part of this team of fact-finding and verification are still somewhat awestruck by how it happened. In fact, the story of how this story came together is almost as remarkable as the history we were trying to uncover. We thought readers deserved to know that story, too.
I wasn’t looking for Foerster either. During my 30 years in Japan, I put down deep roots in Tokyo’s Jewish community and, as a journalist for The Japan Times, documented contemporary leaders, special occasions, and our holidays.
I knew the better-known history of Jews who found refuge in wartime Japan. But what had never occurred to me was to ask another question: Had Jews been living and working in Tokyo during the war?
The question surfaced unexpectedly back in 2019 while researching my memoir, The Wagamama Bride. Chabad House in Tokyo had recently purchased the Omori home of an elderly Japanese woman. I learned from the woman’s daughter that her late father had been a German Holocaust survivor. I couldn’t believe it.
Before World War II, Jews were typically ambitious and successful Sephardic businessmen. But Holocaust survivors who had actually made their home in Omori, that small corner of Tokyo precisely where Chabad had established its center? Unbelievable. That small mystery sent me searching.
By Googling “Jewish, Holocaust, Omori, Tokyo,” I stumbled upon the answer: Jochem’s book about Foerster mentions that during World War II he had a factory located less than 2 km. away from the current Chabad house.
What I discovered opened an entirely different window into Jewish life in wartime Japan. Foerster’s factory and engineering business had employed Jewish refugees who had escaped Nazi-controlled Europe.
BEHIND THEIR arrival was another largely forgotten story: Jews already established in Tokyo in the 1930s had organized to help persecuted Jews reach Japan, working through a Jewish Refugee Committee and seeking employers willing to give refugees legitimate work.
I contacted Jochem. Despite the distance between Hamburg and Israel – and a language barrier that kept much of our communication to emails, photographs, and documents – he generously opened up his research.
Together we sifted through the questions that arose as we tried to understand – and independently verify – the extraordinary story he had uncovered. My investigation became a 2019 Tablet article introducing Foerster’s largely unknown story in English.
People vested in the story began to reach out. In Germany, one grandson, Jesse Foerster, had already taken an active interest in his grandfather’s history, supporting Jochem’s research with photographs, family information, and whatever else might help fill in the missing pieces.
After reading the Tablet article, he reached out to me. Over time, Jesse contributed something no government archive could provide: family memories, photographs, and emotional insights that explain why setting the record straight about Willy Rudolf Foerster still matters nearly 80 years later.
Then, in Portland, Oregon, Julie Quastler’s own determined search into her family history led her to the astonishing discovery of her beloved aunt Renate’s illustrated childhood diary on eBay.
She recognized Foerster’s name and face from family photographs, became curious about her grandfather Ernst Quastler’s former employer, Googled him and found the Tablet article. Julie reached out to me, bringing another stream of family photographs, memories, and documents into the investigation.
Christopher Bock arrived from another direction. While researching the extraordinary wartime journey in Japan of his great-great-uncle Paul Patek for his book An Ordinary Man, he too encountered the Tablet article and contacted me.
His book paints a fascinating picture of daily life for foreign residents in wartime Tokyo, bringing to life both the privileges they enjoyed and the extreme dangers and persecution they faced during this volatile period.
NONE OF US could possibly have imagined that our separate searches would eventually bring us together around Willy Rudolf Foerster. We gratefully acknowledge the power of the Internet for making those connections possible – with, we like to think, a helping hand from Above.
Jesse expressed the unexpected gift of these connections beautifully when he said: 
“On a personal note: through the story and research, I’m now discovering the Quastler family history in a completely new way as well. For us, it is incredibly fascinating to see how these old connections between our families keep resurfacing after so many decades.
“I really hope our families will have the chance to meet one day. I think that would be something very special.”
The writer is the author of The Wagamama Bride: A Jewish Family Saga Made in Japan.
Dr. Clemens Jochem’s groundbreaking research into the Willy Rudolf Foerster story can be found here:
www.tabletmag.com/sections/news/articles/japans-oskar-schindler

A truck drove into a youth soccer game in Wichita, Kansas, leaving a six-year-old boy and a 35-year-old man dead, and 10 others hospitalized with traumatic injuries, police said on Saturday.
The injuries ranged from minor to severe, but none appear to be life-threatening, Wichita police Captain Aaron Moses said at a news conference. The two people killed were pronounced dead at the scene, he said.

The driver had a child playing soccer at the complex, but not on the field where the incident took place, Moses said. The truck involved had two juveniles as passengers, he said.
Emergency dispatchers started getting calls about the incident at 3:25 p.m. local time, Moses said.
"Today is a heartbreaking day for Wichita," Mayor Lily Wu said. "Families came to Stryker Sports Complex to enjoy a Saturday afternoon, watching their children play soccer, and no one could have imagined the tragedy that would unfold."

What is celebrated on October 18 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
04:35:56 EEST
10:35:56 KST

What is celebrated on October 18 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
On October 18, professional, international, and church observances are marked. In Ukraine, food industry workers and the Apostle Luke are honored.
On October 18, under the auspices of the UN, the European Day against Human Trafficking is observed worldwide; at the initiative of the WHO, World Menopause Day is held, and World Water Monitoring Day and International Necktie Day are also celebrated.
In Ukraine, Food Industry Workers’ Day is observed on the third Sunday of October. According to the new-style church calendar, Saint Luke the Apostle and Evangelist is commemorated, while according to the old style, Saint Martyr Charitina is remembered, UNN writes.
Food Industry Workers’ Day of Ukraine
An official professional holiday established by a decree of the President of Ukraine in 1995, observed annually on the third Sunday of October.
The event highlights the strategic importance of the food and processing industries in ensuring the state’s food security, the stability of the domestic market, and the expansion of the export potential of the domestic agro-industrial complex.
European Day against Human Trafficking
Launched by the European Commission in 2007 to unite the efforts of EU member states, law enforcement agencies, and civil society organizations in combating modern forms of slavery.
The event aims to raise public awareness of the risks of labor and sexual exploitation and recruitment via the Internet, as well as to strengthen the protection and social rehabilitation of affected persons.
UN reports sharp increase in human trafficking cases for online fraud28.07.26, 18:07 • 6049 views
World Menopause Day
The day was established by the International Menopause Society with the support of the World Health Organization.
The day aims to overcome the taboo surrounding age-related physiological changes in women’s bodies, expand women’s access to modern hormone replacement therapy, prevent osteoporosis and cardiovascular complications, and ensure a high quality of life in later adulthood.
World Water Monitoring Day
An international information and environmental program launched in 2003 by the U.S. Clean Water Foundation.
The event calls on citizens, volunteers, and scientists to conduct basic chemical and biological analyses of local bodies of water, drawing the global community’s attention to the problem of freshwater pollution and the need to preserve these resources.
International Necktie Day
A popular unofficial cultural holiday launched in Croatia at the initiative of the Academia Cravatica organization in 2003.
The accessory’s origins date back to the 17th century, when Croatian horsemen used silk neckerchiefs that later conquered Parisian fashion. The day promotes the necktie as an element of global business and social culture, elegance, and business dress code.
Commemoration of Saint Luke the Apostle and Evangelist
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic faithful commemorate Saint Luke the Apostle and Evangelist—one of Christ’s seventy disciples, a companion of the Apostle Paul, a physician by profession, and the author of the third Gospel and the Book of Acts.
According to church tradition, the Apostle Luke was the first icon painter, who created the first images of the Most Holy Theotokos, as well as of the Apostles Peter and Paul. He concluded his life of prayer and preaching with a martyr’s death in Greece.
According to the old calendar, the faithful commemorate Saint Martyr Charitina—a Christian virgin who suffered for her faith during the reign of Emperor Diocletian in the city of Amis.
Openly acknowledging herself as a Christian before the court, she endured severe tortures, during which she departed to the Lord with a prayer on her lips.

Venezuela sees nearly $97.4 billion oil investment over five years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Venezuela sees nearly $97.4 billion oil investment over five years
CARACAS – Venezuela expects almost US$76 billion (S$97.44 billion) of investment in its oil and gas sector over the next five years, acting president Delcy Rodríguez said on Oct 17, as the country seeks to draw private capital into a push to boost energy production.
Rodríguez gave the estimate during the closing of an energy conference in Maracaibo, capital of the oil-producing Zulia state, where more than 150 domestic and international companies gathered to discuss investment and the revival of production.
The acting leader said the government has signed 61 agreements under its revamped hydrocarbons framework and is negotiating another 44.
The projects are intended to combine foreign investment with Venezuelan capital and labour, according to Rodríguez.
The projected investments would generate more than 324,000 direct, indirect and induced jobs, she said.
The announcement highlights the scale of Venezuela’s ambitions as it tries to rebuild an oil industry that remains well below its historic output highs despite holding the world’s largest crude reserves.
Turning the commitments into production will require years of drilling and investment in deteriorated oil fields, power systems and other infrastructure.
The investment drive is increasingly intertwined with a US-backed effort to revive Venezuela’s vast but long-struggling oil industry.
Washington struck an agreement in August with North American Blue Energy Partners, covering 17 fields and as much as US$100 billion of planned investment.
The company said it aims to raise output to 500,000 barrels a day by the end of 2028 from about 200,000 currently.
Rodríguez said higher production in Zulia would eventually allow the state to become a producer of liquefied petroleum gas, first for domestic consumption and later for export.
The targets illustrate the scale of the challenge.
Chevron Corp, which recently expanded its development rights in the Orinoco Belt and updated terms for its Venezuelan ventures, said in September that the agreements opened the way for new investment but that many years of work remained.
The company said long-term growth would depend on continued reforms and cooperation between industry and government on infrastructure improvements.
Venezuela also faces constraints ranging from unreliable power and ageing production equipment to limited oil-field service capacity and shortages of experienced workers, all of which could slow efforts to bring new barrels online. BLOOMBERG

China’s ‘golden week’ holidays come at a cost
Unknown

10:30:06 KST

Advertisement
Opinion
China’s ‘golden week’ holidays come at a cost
A week of uninterrupted leave might look generous on paper, but it can conceal the working days shifted elsewhere to make it possible
4-MIN READ4-MIN
2
 Listen
Michael Han is assistant president and Shanghai general manager at Yuepu Technology Group. 
For iPhone users in China, the calendar has long presented a small but recurring problem. On a Sunday designated as a make-up workday, an alarm might remain silent. On a regular Friday converted into a day off, it might ring anyway.
Nearly 17 years after entering the Chinese market, Apple quietly updated its operating system in September to automatically recognise China’s official schedule of adjusted holidays and workdays. The fix is modest, but it points to a larger question: what happens when a society’s working week no longer matches the natural cadence of the days?
The issue transcends a foreign tech giant adapting to local rules. China’s holiday calendar is not a static record of dates but a dynamic mechanism for redistributing public time. By moving weekend leave to around national holidays, policymakers engineer longer continuous breaks at the expense of a predictable working week, effectively using time as an administrative lever.

The injuries ranged from minor to severe, but none appear to be life threatening, Wichita police Captain Aaron Moses said at a news conference.

Moses said a 34-year-old woman was driving the truck, which ended up in a field at the west end of the Stryker Sports Complex.

FSSAI cracks down on Priyagold biscuit maker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
01:23:39 UTC
10:23:39 KST

The FSSAI has taken legal action against three companies over serious violations of food safety standards
NEW DELHI: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has stepped up enforcement against major food companies, sanctioning prosecution against Priyagold biscuit maker Surya Food & Agro Ltd, Dodla Dairy Ltd and Ueir Organic Foods Pvt Ltd, while issuing notices to Nestlé India and Hindustan Unilever (HUL) over alleged labelling violations and misleading product claims.Action against Surya Food & Agro followed a consumer complaint that led officials to find bran meant for cattle feed being used as a fibre source in Priyagold biscuits.The gunny bags containing the material for the biscuits were marked for cattle feed. Inspectors also flagged deficiencies in plant hygiene, pest control, raw material storage and segregation, personnel hygiene and premises maintenance. The company’s FSSAI licence was suspended following the inspection, and the competent authority has now sanctioned prosecution. Attempts to reach the company for comment were unsuccessful.
FSSAI has issued notices to Nestlé India over its Nescafé ready-to-drink range, including Cappuccino, Choco Mocha and Chilled Latte, manufactured by Schreiber Dynamix Dairies and Lotus Dairy Products. The regulator flagged discrepancies between the front-of-pack description “Flavoured Milk” and the back label, which classified the products as “Proprietary Food – 1.12 Dairy Based Drink”.
Online listings described them as “Coffee Flavoured Milk” and carried claims about the goodness of flavoured double-toned milk, which FSSAI said were inconsistent with the declared product category. The companies have been asked to explain why action should not be initiated under food safety laws.A separate notice to Nestlé concerned its Resource Renal vanilla flavour powder, intended for dietary management of people with conservatively treated chronic kidney disease. FSSAI said the product lacked the required prior approval and that the prescribed vegetarian or non-vegetarian symbol was missing from the label.In a statement the company said, “FSSAI has sent a communication to Nestlé India concerning the label declarations/classification of the Nescafe Ready To Drink products. This does not relate to product safety or product quality. Mentioned products are safe to consume and meet all applicable food safety requirements.
We will be submitting our response to the authorities and will be engaging with them as per due process established under law.” Hindustan Unilever was issued notices over claims on Horlicks Women’s Plus Chocolate Nutrition Drink, including “Nutrition for Strong Bones” and “Clinically Proven to Help Improve Bone Strength in 6 Months”.In a statement to the press, the company spokesperson said, “Hindustan Unilever Limited is committed to providing safe, high-quality products that comply with all applicable regulatory requirements. Horlicks Women’s Plus and Mother’s Plus has been developed based on established nutritional science and is manufactured in accordance with stringent quality and safety standards. All product communication is developed in accordance with applicable laws, regulations, and governance processes. We will share all the scientific and regulatory evidence with the authorities as per normal process of review.”
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

Why is Hong Kong hosting the Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting? There is another agenda

As Hong Kong hosts the Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting on Tuesday, this two-part series examines the summit’s significance and its implications for Beijing on the global stage. In part one, Simpson Cheung and Alfred Lam explore how the event could elevate the city’s status as an international financial centre at a pivotal moment.
Beijing’s decision to have Hong Kong host the Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting this week is a deliberate move to galvanise the city’s standing as an offshore renminbi hub and showcase it as a safe harbour amid continuing geopolitical tensions, analysts have said.
About 500 guests, including finance chiefs and senior officials from the 21 member economies, are expected to attend the annual meeting on October 20 and 21, which Hong Kong will host for the first time. It will take place at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai.

The event would bolster its standing as an offshore renminbi hub and a wealth management capital, support the city’s economic development and underscore its importance to China’s development, he said.

China's Zhang wins world junior badminton women's singles title
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
08:57:28 CST
09:57:28 KST

CAIRO, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- China's Zhang Yixin came from a game down to defeat Japan's top-seeded Saki Matsumoto and win the women's singles title at the Badminton World Federation (BWF) World Junior Championships in Cairo on Saturday.
Zhang recovered from losing the opening game 9-15 to win the next two 15-10, 15-9 in a hard-fought 47-minute final, securing China's only gold medal in the five individual events.
"I'm extremely happy and excited because this is my first time competing at the World Junior Championships, and I've managed to win the title," Zhang told Xinhua.
"I think getting through this match was indeed very difficult. But I had prepared thoroughly beforehand, and my coach and teammates also gave me a lot of confidence and encouragement," she said.
She approached the final against the top seed as a challenger and remained calm under pressure. "I think it was mainly my mental strength. I had a very strong desire to win this gold medal for the Chinese team," Zhang said.
Matsumoto said she was able to dictate play in the opening game. "But in the second and third games, my opponent started getting used to my shots, and I was the one who made mistakes first. I think that's something I need to work on in the future," she said.
Yin Yiqing of China and Ip Sum Yau of Hong Kong, China shared bronze in women's singles after losing their semifinal matches on Friday.
In the mixed doubles final, Indonesia's Muhammad Luthfi Habibi and Dian Ramadhani Mukti defeated China's Feng Yilang and Li Menghan 17-15, 8-15, 16-14 in a closely contested 50-minute match, leaving the Chinese pair with silver.
Habibi explained that training with senior players had helped refine his playing style, adding that he wants to become a world champion at the senior level and an Olympic champion in the future.
"I think my performance today was fairly good overall, but I didn't make the most of some crucial points toward the end of the match," Li said, adding that Chinese players in all five disciplines had given their all and would continue to improve.
Chinese Taipei's Lee Wei-Ting and Chen Yu-Hsi, along with Indonesia's Raihan Daffa Edsel Pramono and Atresia Naufa Candani, shared the mixed doubles bronze medals.
Indonesia secured its second gold medal in men's singles, where Radithya Bayu Wardhana defeated compatriot Fardhan Rainanda Joe 15-9, 11-15, 15-8 in 47 minutes.
France's Mady Sow and India's Jagsher Singh Khangurra shared bronze in men's singles.
In women's doubles, Malaysia's second-seeded Genevie Lim and Low Zi Yu defeated Japan's Nijika Kamata and Shizuku Kashio 15-7, 9-15, 15-12 in a 41-minute final.
China's Shi Sichen and Xiang Yujin, along with South Korea's Choi Ye-da and Kim Min-chae, took bronze in women's doubles.
In the men's doubles final, Chinese Taipei's top-seeded Chen Ping-Hsuan and Lee Wei-Ting defeated Japan's Mahiro Oku and Masato Yamashiro 15-10, 15-9 in just 23 minutes.
Feng and Wei Jianzhen of China shared bronze in men's doubles with Njoto Michaelangelo and Yu Zhirui Jerry of Hong Kong, China.
Indonesia topped the individual-event gold medal standings with two titles, while China, Malaysia and Chinese Taipei claimed one each. China finished with one gold, one silver and three bronze medals, while Japan collected three silvers.
The individual championships followed the world junior team event, which China won earlier this month. ■

(IANS via Xinhua)
NEW DELHI, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- The death toll in Saturday's stampede in India's eastern city of Kolkata rose to 19, with 25 injured people receiving treatment in different hospitals and one in a critical condition, confirmed West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari on Sunday.
Most among the dead were women and children, he said while admitting that there were "some shortcomings" in the arrangements made by the organizers. Kolkata is the capital city of India's eastern state of West Bengal.
The stampede occurred at a religious event, locally called "Durga Puja", amid the ongoing annual festive season in the country. Thousands of people had gathered to take part in the celebrations when the stampede occurred. The mishap was partly blamed on heavy rains.
"This happened partly due to the rains, and there were also some shortcomings in the arrangements made by the event organizers," said the chief minister.
Meanwhile, media reports said that around 10 people, including the organizers and private security personnel, present when the mishap occurred were detained by the Kolkata Police for questioning. "Whoever is found negligent will face legal action," the chief minister said. ■

Crowd, rain or misleading announcement: What led to Kolkata stampede tragedy?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
00:51:06 UTC
09:51:06 KST

Several people reportedly fell down a flight of stairs near the exit and were trampled by those behind them
NEW DELHI: A sudden surge of people, heavy rain and alleged confusion over announcements and entry-exit routes are among the factors being investigated after a stampede at the Chorbagan Sarbojanin Durga Puja pandal in Kolkata killed at least 19 people and injured 25 others on Saturday evening.The incident occurred around 7.15pm on Maha Saptami, when a large crowd waiting on the narrow Radha Madhab Saha Lane to enter the pandal reportedly surged forward as a downpour began. Those already inside were caught in the rush, with people unable to move towards the exit as visitors ahead blocked their way. Several people reportedly fell down a flight of stairs near the exit and were trampled by those behind them.
A misleading announcement by the puja committee is also suspected to have added to the confusion, while the blowing of whistles by private security guards may have triggered a rush among visitors, according to CM Adhikari.
Crowd management and security under scrutiny
Kolkata Police are investigating whether lapses in crowd management, confusion over entry and exit routes, and heavy rain contributed to the tragedy, a senior officer told PTI. Eyewitnesses alleged that announcements about entry, exit and crowd movement were improper, leaving visitors confused during peak hours.Locals also questioned the police deployment at the venue, claiming that personnel were largely stationed near the VIP entrance.
"I have not seen adequate police presence this year. This resulted in the mismanagement," Chorbagan resident Sanghamitra Bhowmik told PTI.Another concern raised by locals was the alleged lack of administrative assistance in taking the injured to hospitals."There must be some lapses, but these should be probed. Whether lapses were on the part of the organisers or they had flouted the rules to erect the pandal will be checked," the police officer told PTI.A forensic team visited the site late on Saturday to collect evidence. Police are questioning the organisers and examining CCTV footage, while also seeking details of the security guards and other personnel deployed to manage the crowd. Officers who were posted at the venue will also be questioned as part of the investigation.
State orders safety review of pandals
Adhikari, who visited the injured at Kolkata Medical College and Hospital, said the incident had raised concerns about safety arrangements at crowded Durga Puja venues. According to hospital sources, 11 injured people were shifted to SSKM Hospital. The deceased included 13 women and a child, a source at the medical college said.The chief minister announced a high-level committee to inspect prominent pandals across West Bengal and review crowd management, exit routes, lighting and structural safety. The panel will be led by Disaster Management Principal Secretary Rajesh Sinha, Fire Services Director General Anuj Sharma and Additional Director General of Police (Law and Order) Javed Shamim.
Adhikari urged organisers to follow official safety recommendations, warning against elaborate themes that compromise visitors' safety. He also called for wider exits, better lighting and the removal of bottlenecks created by temporary rope enclosures. Where complex structures obstruct movement, organisers may be advised to restrict rituals to the inner sanctum and use LED screens outside.The state government has announced Rs 25 lakh in compensation and a Group D government job for the family of each deceased victim. A toll-free helpline, 18003455678, has also been set up to help people seeking information about those affected.

Across the US, ‘No Kings’ events seek to boost early voting for midterms
WASHINGTON – Carrying an umbrella painted with the words “vote, power, people”, retired teacher Sabine Carlson said the plan for the Oct 17 “No Kings” marches was clear.
“It’s great to voice your anger and we have long lists of complaints, but the most important thing of all is to go and vote,” said the 66-year-old Democrat from Washington’s suburbs.
At the demonstration near the country’s Capitol, Carlson joined one of the estimated 3,000 events organised by the prominent anti-Trump movement across the US on Oct 17.
Rather than holding massive marches, the latest “No Kings” events varied across the country – with honking convoys, concerts and neighbourhood gatherings.
It was the fourth iteration of the demonstrations since US President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025.
The stated goal of the event was to fire up voters just as Americans begin casting ballots in the midterm elections, where Republicans, who hold the majority in Congress, face fierce opposition.
Democrats are seeking to take control of Congress by campaigning on cost-of-living issues and an unpopular war in the Middle East.
Focused on early voting ahead of election day on Nov 3, the events ranged from New York, Los Angeles and other blue stronghold cities to small towns across the nation.
“It’s one of the most important votes and it’s really important to make people aware, and make sure they’re registered correctly,” Carlson said. “Don’t go to the wrong polling station.”
‘An act of joy’
Most areas of the US allow voters to cast their ballots ahead of time, sometimes weeks in advance.
Alma Couverthie, who oversees grassroots-organising efforts for democracy watchdog Common Cause, said the point of the “No Kings” rallies was “reclaiming voting for what it truly is: an act of power, an act of service, and an act of joy”.
Trump has openly criticised the practice of mail-in voting, and opponents have expressed concern that the administration will attempt to undermine the results – especially if Republicans end up losing, as opinion polls show is likely.
By advocating early voting, “No Kings” organisers hope to cut off the potential for any malfeasance.
“The best way to prevent any funny business from this administration after election day is to make sure that our turnout is massive, so clear and so overwhelming that our victory for democracy is impossible to question,” Couverthie said.
‘We want our country back’
One 52-year-old military veteran who joined the Oct 17 protest did so seeking catharsis from the current state of American politics.
“I am so disillusioned by what I thought I was serving versus what this country has become,” said the Virginia resident, declining to give his name.
“Over the last 18 months – I finally came to this conclusion about six months ago – I’ve been mourning my country.”
Carrying an umbrella with the message “Vote for humanity. End this circus now. We want our country back”, he said he hoped to see “a robust response come Nov 3 from the American people”.
Beyond Washington, like-minded Americans echoed his hopes and fears.
Outside a church in Gastonia, North Carolina, women carried signs that read “Honk for Democracy” and “Make a plan to vote!”
In Portland, Maine, demonstrators bundled up against the autumn chill waved the American flag and carried signs reading “Your Vote is Your Voice” and “No Kings, No Cowards Collins”, in reference to incumbent Republican Senator Susan Collins, who faces a tough re-election race.
In Wilton Manors, Florida, demonstrators were out in the sun, dressed in shorts and sunglasses and carrying signs reading “Enough is enough”.
“Trump is destroying America” and “Democracy not Autocracy”, said some signs in Atlanta, Georgia.
A man dressed as Uncle Sam at a protest in Kansas City, Missouri, stood near a sign reading “Uncle Sam Says Make American What Was Promised”.
In Houston, a large crowd marched through city streets carrying a banner that said “Resist All Corruption” and handmade signs reading “War Crimes Don’t Hide Sex Crimes” and “Rein in the Mad King Vote Blue”.
All across California – from San Diego to San Francisco and many points beyond – crowds filled the streets, including in Los Angeles, where protesters marched to city hall carrying signs declaring “No Kings” and at least one that added “No Idiots Either”. AFP

Trump’s Russia sanctions waiver called mistake by Republican Party allies

- Senators led by Ted Cruz and Thom Tillis urged Trump to keep pressure on Russia, saying the deal will not cut US prices much and may fund the war.
- Ukraine and Democrats also opposed the move, while Congress is unlikely to act soon because it is out of session until the midterm elections.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – US Republican lawmakers blasted President Donald Trump for waiving new tariffs and sanctions on Russia, prompting him to defend himself against members of his own party.
Republican Party critics said Trump’s decision trampled on the will of Congress, which overwhelmingly passed a sanctions law in September championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, and would aid Moscow’s war effort against Ukraine.
Trump issued the waiver shortly after cutting a deal with Russia on diesel exports aimed at lowering high fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections, in which the cost of living is voters’ dominant concern.
“It’s a very good decision. And it’s going to be a decision that’s good for the country and I think good for the world,” the President told reporters on Oct 17.
The decision by Trump threatens to open up a new rift between the White House and its congressional allies, with Republicans in serious danger of losing their majorities in the House and the Senate in the Nov 3 elections.
Earlier in the day, Senator Ted Cruz, a Texas Republican closely allied to Trump, said the administration should have found other ways to lower fuel costs, such as importing more from Canada or waiving renewable-fuel requirements.
“I wish the President hadn’t done it. I think it was a mistake,” Cruz said on Fox News, referring to Trump’s executive order late on Oct 16 waiving the Graham law. “The current path, unfortunately, just benefits Putin.”
At least eight Republican senators, along with several of their House counterparts, have spoken out against Trump’s diesel deal with Russia or the sanctions waiver.
“What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisers not understand?” Senator Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican retiring at the end of his term, wrote on Oct 17 in a social media post.
He said Trump could lower energy prices by addressing Iran rather than “doing a solid for Vladimir Putin”.
A bipartisan group of 12 senators sent Trump a letter earlier this week urging him to rescind his diesel deal with Russia and enforce the Graham law.
The Republican signatories included Tillis, Mitch McConnell, John Cornyn, Susan Collins, Alan Armstrong and Lisa Murkowski.
“Allowing Russian-origin diesel into global markets will offer limited to no relief to Americans,” the senators wrote in the letter, arguing that the revenue would help finance Russia’s war in Ukraine and deepen Moscow’s cooperation with China, Iran and North Korea.
Darline Graham, who was appointed to fill her late brother’s seat and is running for a full term, said she is proud of the Bill named after Lindsey Graham and plans to speak to Trump when he visits South Carolina next week.
“The President and I share the same goal, which is to end the war and get gas and diesel prices down. The sanctions Bill is one of the tolls he can use to do that. It’s up to him whether or not he chooses to do so,” she told local reporters on Oct 17.
“Personally, I would keep the pressure on Russia to end the war and get the gas prices down because I don’t trust Putin and I don’t trust Russia.”
While Ukraine has broad support on Capitol Hill, Congress is out of session through the midterm elections, so there is little prospect of immediate action to block Trump’s diesel deal.
His plan to return Russian diesel to US and global markets is expected to have little immediate effect on prices. A sustained resumption of Russian exports by the year end, however, could help shrink global supply deficits, provided Moscow can meet its commitments despite Ukrainian drone strikes on refineries.
Jeanne Shaheen, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, joined six other senators earlier in the week in a letter opposing the decision, saying Congress “explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine”.
“President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the US runs directly counter to that law,” Democratic senators Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal and Ron Wyden, and Republican senators Collins, Murkowski, Tillis and John Curtis said in a statement on Oct 18.
House lawmakers are also moving against the deal.
A group of Democrats and one Republican introduced legislation on Oct 16 to block Russian diesel imports, though passage would be difficult in the Republican-controlled Congress and could require overcoming a Trump veto.
Representative Don Bacon, a retiring Nebraska Republican, co-sponsored the Bill.
Representative Brian Fitzpatrick, a Pennsylvania Republican facing re-election in a contested seat, has separately said he would propose legislation barring purchases of Russian oil.
“Many of us won’t fund these things knowing he is propping up a dictator’s invasion and throwing an ally under the bus,” Bacon wrote in a social media post on Oct 17.
French Hill, a Republican lawmaker from Arkansas, said he has requested a classified briefing on the rationale behind the decision, arguing the US should be increasing economic pressure on Russia.
Democrats have almost unanimously opposed Trump’s overtures to Putin. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said in a social media post on Oct 17 that “there’s nothing America First” about the new diesel deal and criticised it for giving the Russian economy “life support” while “Americans need relief from skyrocketing prices”.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also criticised the waiver, saying it could mark the beginning of broader sanctions relief for Moscow.
“At the time when the Russians launched such a massive strike against our energy sector, in America, regrettably, a decision was made to completely ignore the Lindsey Graham law,” Zelensky wrote on Oct 17 in a social media post.
Tensions between Washington and Kyiv have risen since Trump announced the diesel deal last week.
Ukrainian defence officials said this week that connection speeds on Starshield, SpaceX’s military-grade satellite service, had been slowed. A US official said on Oct 16 that Trump had not ordered any limits on Ukraine’s access to the satellite technology.
“A US sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin – all of this only encourages him to keep attacking,” Zelensky said. BLOOMBERG

Two people, including a child, have been killed and several others injured after a vehicle drove directly onto a sports field during a youth football match in Wichita, Kansas, police confirmed.
The incident occurred at the Stryker Sports Complex when the driver of a black Chevrolet Silverado pickup truck breached the grounds while a match was in progress.
Wichita police confirmed that one child and one adult died at the scene, without immediately releasing their identities or ages.
Emergency services, including police, fire, and ambulance crews, arrived swiftly to treat multiple casualties and transfer them to area medical facilities.
"We have two fatalities confirmed here at the scene and multiple other casualties with individuals transported to area hospitals," Wichita Police Captain Aaron Moses told reporters at the site.
"The vehicle involved in this incident remained at the scene. The driver of that vehicle is currently in our custody. There is no additional ongoing threat to the public from that driver."
Driver detained
Authorities confirmed that two minors were inside the vehicle at the time of the incident.
Police have taken the driver into custody, though investigators have not released the individual's identity or stated whether the vehicle was driven onto the playing surface intentionally.
Wichita Mayor Lily Wu urged the public to stay away from the sports complex whilst investigators conduct their work, describing the incident as heartbreaking.
"My thoughts and prayers are with everyone affected, especially the children and families involved," Wu stated in a post on social media.
The area remained cordoned off on Saturday evening as forensic collision teams worked to determine how the pickup truck entered the playing area.

Zelensky criticises Trump’s waiver of sanctions on Russia as ‘wrong’
- Donald Trump waived planned US sanctions and tariffs on Russia, saying it was in America’s national interest. Volodymyr Zelensky called the move “wrong” and said it only helps Russia.
- Zelensky warned the decision will embolden Vladimir Putin and lead to more attacks on Ukraine. He said Russia hit more than 15 power sites and may target western Ukraine next.
- Russia praised the waiver as “a truly historic moment”. US critics said Trump was giving in to Putin, while the Graham Act could still be used to restore pressure later.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump’s decision to waive sanctions on Russia and tariffs on its goods days before they were to take effect, will embolden Moscow to keep attacking Ukraine, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct 17, predicting even more US sanctions relief.
“The decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me,” Zelensky wrote on X. “It definitely helps only the Russians.”
An executive order issued by Trump on the night of Oct 16 waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs – including duties on the country’s goods and penalties for buying its oil and gas – that had been scheduled to start next week under the legislation known as the Graham Act that he signed into law in September.
Trump said the waiver was in the national interests of the US.
The law is meant to increase pressure on Russia for its invasion of Ukraine that began in 2022. Trump, however, has been warming towards Moscow while publicly criticising Zelensky, including suggesting Kyiv needs a new leader.
Zelensky said the latest action emboldens Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“It only fuels their satisfaction and their desire to keep killing people,” wrote Zelensky, who said Russia struck more than 15 Ukrainian power generation and transmission sites on Oct 16. “This certainly does not stop the war.”
He accused Russia of planning to ramp up strikes in western Ukraine. “Is Russia preparing for this? I think so,” Zelensky wrote.
Russian envoy praises waiver
Russia’s investment envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, called the Trump waiver “a truly historic moment”, posting on X on Oct 16 that had the penalties taken effect, they could have effectively brought all economic cooperation between Russia and the US to a halt.
Weeks before US midterm elections in which Trump’s Republicans are battling to maintain their narrow grip on both chambers of Congress, the new measures could have risked further raising oil prices as Americans face increased costs largely due to the US-Israeli war with Iran, analysts said.
Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 in mid-September.
The legislation’s primary backer in Congress was the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, a South Carolina Republican. It would have imposed tariffs of up to 100% within 30 days on all goods brought into the US from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas, as well as any country that knowingly bought oil or gas 30 days after the law was enacted or was among the top five countries helping Russia evade sanctions.
Graham’s sister, Darline Graham, was appointed to fill his Senate seat after he died in July, and Trump endorsed her for a full term heading into the midterm elections. At a campaign stop on Oct 17, she did not directly criticise Trump for waiving sanctions, but said she would not have made that choice.
“Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia,” she told reporters, according to multiple news outlets. “Because I don’t trust Putin and I don’t trust Russia.”
China and India, which are among the biggest buyers of Russian oil, had raised concerns about the Graham Act.
Beijing said it “consistently opposed long-arm jurisdiction that lacks a basis in international law”, while India warned Washington that new tariffs could impact bilateral ties.
But the Graham Act also allows the president to waive sanctions by informing Congress that he has determined that they are not in the national interest. The Oct 16 executive order said the waiver will remain in effect until Trump or his top officials determine that “further action is appropriate”.
US Representative Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat, said Trump was giving in to Putin.
“Trump’s latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression,” Beyer said in a statement on Oct 16.
Lindsey Graham, who died in July, strongly supported US assistance to Ukraine. The passage of the bill named for him had provided hope of continued bipartisan support for Kyiv, wrote Zelensky.
But with Graham gone, the US under Trump will continue sanctions relief for Russia beyond the Oct 16 waiver and the diesel export agreement announced earlier in October, the Ukrainian leader predicted.
“I think the diesel deal and the move regarding the Lindsey Graham Act are not the end of it. Unfortunately,” wrote Zelensky, who lamented Graham’s absence. “It’s unfortunate because we all had great respect for Lindsey... It’s difficult without him, I’ll be honest.” REUTERS

Assistant treasurer knew about ATO's credit card ban plans months ago
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
23:58:19 UTC
08:58:19 KST

Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino concedes he knew of ATO's credit card ban plans in July
In short:
The assistant treasurer says the government knew in July the tax office was considering a credit card ban following the Reserve Bank's surcharge changes.
Outrage about the change from the business community forced the prime minister to step in.
What's next?
The issue has exposed tensions between the prime minister and the treasurer.
Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino has conceded the government knew the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) was considering banning credit card payments in July, months before the decision was made public.
The ATO's decision in late September to stop accepting credit card payments from December 1 sparked backlash from the business community.
That outrage eventually forced an intervention from the prime minister and the treasurer to underwrite the costs and allow credit cards to be accepted by the tax office until mid-2027.
Mr Mulino today said he and Treasurer Jim Chalmers were first made aware of the ATO's intentions months ago.
"In July, the government became aware that the ATO was looking at options and that at that point their preference was to not accept credit cards," Mr Mulino told ABC's Insiders.
"The indication we gave to the ATO was that they should continue to engage with the credit card companies, and that there should be a transition period."
The admission comes after the Australian Financial Review yesterday revealed the ATO had privately informed the government about its credit card ban and presented the government with options.
The ATO's decision followed changes from the Reserve Bank of Australia to scrap card surcharges from October 1, which the bank has said was "in the public interest" and was costing consumers about $1.6 billion a year.
Mr Mulino was asked why the government did not push for the ATO to continue accepting credit card payments from small businesses back in July.
"So, accepting credit card payments going on indefinitely, would have very serious fiscal ramifications for the budget, and that's why we always said that there should be a transition period,"
he said.
Small businesses were informed of the ATO's decision on September 30, a day before it was made public, and given a two-month grace period.
"But the transition period, as it turned out, from stakeholder feedback, wasn't enough. And so that's where the government stepped in," Mr Mulino said.
He was asked if he had any regrets about not stepping in earlier.
"We've changed our position. So I've listened to stakeholder feedback, as has the PM and the treasurer," he said.
"So, obviously we've changed tack and we've listened to feedback. And that's a sign of a government that is putting in place important big reforms."
Earlier this month, Mr Chalmers said he was informed by the ATO ahead of their decision, but did not give a specific timeline.
"The ATO made this decision late in September, not to accept credit card payments. Obviously, we were aware before then that they were grappling with this issue," he said.
Opposition says
Mr Mulino denied the government had a "hands-off approach", saying they "didn't get into all of the details" but insisted that the ATO should continue to negotiate with credit card companies.
Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson slammed the government, saying they "had three months to fix this" and "only stepped in when the backlash got too loud to ignore".
"At every point the Albanese government has failed to understand the implementation consequences of their higher taxes," he said.
He questioned Mr Mulino's assertion that the ATO made the call as an independent agency, only for the government to then fund the transition period for credit card payments.
"You can't claim it's somebody else's decision while you're the one paying for it," he said.
Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) chief executive Andrew McKellar said it was concerning these discussions were happening in July when businesses were only informed the day before it became public.
"Business wasn't made aware until just hours before the surcharge ban took effect in October," he said.
"This looks like a completely deficient policymaking process that took small business for granted."
The ATO initially defended its decision, saying it was not tenable for the agency to absorb the $200 million cost and that it would result in less revenue being collected and therefore less funding for government services.
Taxation commissioner Rob Heferen said the ATO "would have preferred to continue accepting credit cards" but that credit card companies did not offer a low enough rate.
Small businesses felt the move was a double standard, since they were expected to wear the costs of the RBA's surcharge changes themselves, and they also feared losing the ability to use credit card payments to the ATO as a tool to manage their cash flow.
Issue hints at leadership tensions
The debacle, and its timeline, has also exposed some tension between the treasurer and prime minister.
Mr Albanese said he intervened after receiving a text from ACCI's Mr McKellar the day before.
"My door is always open. Andrew did text me last Thursday morning, and by Friday morning we had an announcement," he said.
Mr Chalmers denied he was "rolled" and said he and Mr Albanese discussed the issue on the Wednesday prior.
Mr Wilson on Sunday suggested the prime minister "enjoys humiliating his treasurer" and described the relationship as a "psychodrama".
Industry Minister Tim Ayres denied there were underlying frustrations between the pair, and told News24 that Mr Albanese was "a remarkably collegial prime minister".
"This is a cabinet-style government that's working very well, it's very stable," he said.
"It's a real contrast to not just what's happening around the world, but a real contrast to what's happening on the other side of politics, which is a total mess."
Mr Ayres was asked if the government might permanently waive the ATO's credit card decision.
"I don't think that there's any prospect of this issue being managed that way. We've made a big decision to defer this question to allow credit card payments to continue being used," he said.
"There's a significant budget cost to that. It's the right call to make in these circumstances."
Mr McKellar said ACCI wanted a "permanent outcome".
"We think that will most likely involve a long-term solution for credit card payments to continue to be accepted, but let's not pre-empt those discussions," he said.
He said a key question was how that cost would be funded, and added it would be a welcome step if credit card companies lowered their fees.
"We don't want small business to be left carrying the can for this decision," he said.

Saudi Arabia reports incoming fire as Egypt weighs sending help

Riyadh leads a military coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government in its war with the Houthis, and a military spokesman for the Iran-backed group said on Oct 17 that dozens of Saudi strikes over the past day had killed and wounded “numerous” people.
Since Yemen’s conflict flared back to life in July after a years-long hiatus, Saudi Arabia has faced sustained Houthi missile and drone attacks targeting its oil installations, tankers and transit hubs, including one on Riyadh’s airport last week that killed 13 people.
A spokesman for the Saudi coalition said on Oct 17 that it had “intercepted and destroyed four drones over the past few hours in Riyadh, the Eastern Province and the South”.
The interceptions came as the President of Egypt, which is a member of the coalition, said he was willing to “carry out any measure to protect” Saudi Arabia if its leaders requested it.
President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said Egypt was not looking to intervene in regional wars, but added that it was “inconceivable” for Cairo to stand by while the kingdom was “harmed or its security and stability threatened”.
“I’m not talking about fighting anyone or attacking anyone,” he said. “We are speaking only about defence.”
Though Egypt is a member of the anti-Houthi coalition, its role has mostly concerned Red Sea maritime security rather than the fighting in Yemen. It and Saudi Arabia are historically close and have strategic economic ties.
Egypt’s Parliament will hold an emergency session on Oct 18 at Sisi’s request.
The repeated Houthi strikes have prompted foreign embassies to warn their citizens not to use Saudi airports or not to visit the country altogether.
The Saudi Education Ministry on Oct 17 announced the extension of remote learning measures for students in Riyadh and nearby Diriyah.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Oct 17 that Tehran supported a “comprehensive political process as the only practical and sustainable way to resolve” the conflict on the Arabian Peninsula.
He repeated Iran’s offer to mediate between the two sides.
Deputy Foreign Minister Saeed Khatibzadeh previously said Riyadh had not responded to Iran’s overture. But Yemeni Foreign Minister Afrah al-Zouba rejected Iran’s offer in a statement on X on Oct 17, saying “the Tehran regime is a party to the war against Yemenis, not a mediator”.
The Houthis are part of Iran’s “Axis of Resistance” against Israel and the US, but both they and Tehran insist the group acts independently.
Saudi Arabia has carried out daily air strikes on the Houthis in Yemen, where government forces are seeking to roll back gains the group made in a lightning offensive in September.
On Oct 17, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Riyadh had conducted 53 strikes on the Yemen capital Sanaa and six other provinces over the past 24 hours, with “numerous dead and wounded”.
A Houthi-affiliated news agency had earlier accused Saudi warplanes of targeting “civilian residences” in Dhamar and Taiz provinces, killing 12 people and wounding more than 30. It alleged that the strikes were carried out “using cluster bombs, which are banned internationally”. AFP

The Trump-appointed ambassador met Palestinian-Americans in the occupied West Bank town of Turmus Aya in September to hear locals’ testimony about their experiences with pogroms. In August, Huckabee called a days-long Israeli settler siege an “act of terror”.
The State Department criticised Friday’s attack using a cautious tone on Levine’s beating, stating condemnation of “criminal violence by any party”.
Israeli settlers have been involved in at least 170 pogroms against Palestinians since September 27, around the start of the olive harvest, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli group that monitors illegal Israeli settlements.
