Why a ‘killer switch’ to tackle Europe’s trade issues with China may not be so straightforward
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
23:30:00 UTC
08:30:00 KST

News analysis
Why a ‘killer switch’ to tackle Europe’s trade issues with China may not be so straightforward
- EU leaders backed new trade defence tools against China, including a possible “killer switch” to impose tariffs or quotas fast. The move follows a trade deficit of more than €360 billion and rising Chinese exports.
- The plan is still vague. There is no legal text, trigger or scope yet, and the European Commission is expected to propose ideas by the end of 2026. Many states may resist giving Brussels such wide powers.
- Support is growing in Brussels as chemicals, machinery and wind turbines face pressure from Chinese imports. The European Parliament called Chinese industrial policy “an existential threat to the EU”, showing the hardening mood.
AI generated
BRUSSELS – European Union leaders ended their summit in the late hours of Oct 16 with no deal on the Union’s future budget, but with a new and surprisingly strong resolve to adopt new defence tools to tackle a ballooning trade deficit with China.
Heads of state and government of the EU’s 27 member-nations approved a trade deal concluded in Beijing earlier in October, under which China voluntarily agreed to cut by almost half its exports of electric vehicles to Europe.
But the member-states still deemed this Chinese concession insufficient in addressing bigger trade questions, and they authorised the European Commission, the EU’s executive, to create “without delay” a toolbox of new trade defence instruments. That included a so-called “killer switch” provision that will enable the Commission to impose quotas and tariffs on products at a moment’s notice.
The Commission is expected to come forward with such proposals by the end of 2026. There is, as yet, no legal text, no defined trigger, no agreed scope and no answer to the question of what a trade “cut-off” would mean in practice.
Still, should the Commission gain such “killer switch” powers, the entire structure of Europe’s trade with the world could be revolutionised. And a trade war with China will be almost inevitable.
China loomed large at the EU leaders’ summit, as the European bloc faces a trade deficit of more than €360 billion (S$519 billion) with Beijing in 2026, or about €1 billion each day. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has long warned the Chinese authorities that such deficits are “unsustainable”.
Yet the latest EU statistics indicate that Chinese exports to the Union expanded by a further 25% during the first eight months of 2026. Europe’s car industry is no longer the primary concern; the continent’s chemicals and industrial machinery are now the latest sectors acutely vulnerable to what is described as a Chinese export onslaught.
A decade ago, the EU registered a yearly deficit of €71 billion in industrial machinery trade with China but enjoyed a surplus of €6 billion in trade in chemicals. Today, the machinery deficit has grown to €206 billion, while a gaping trade deficit has developed in chemicals, to the tune of €24 billion a year.
At the latest summit in Brussels, the seat of the European Commission, Belgium, Denmark, France and Germany backed the Commission’s determination to move fast on seeking to protect these sectors. EU anti-dumping investigations into chemicals, pharmaceuticals and machinery are expected within weeks, and an investigation into Chinese-manufactured wind turbines is not far off either.
In a joint letter released on Oct 5, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz argued that the Commission should be granted powers to, in the authors’ phrase, “cut off access to the European single market if needed if another trading nation deliberately ignores calls for the restoration of fair trade conditions”.
The proposed weapon could be deployed not only if trade in a particular commodity suddenly balloons and no action is taken, but also if another country were to use other coercion instruments – such as a cut-off in supplies of critical raw materials – in an effort to avoid serious discussions about trade imbalances.
If that happened, “the EU must be able to inflict damage comparable to that being done to us”, a German government official explained soon after the Franco-German proposal was released.
Challenges of a ‘switch’
EU officials are refusing to identify any country to which such a provision may apply.
Still, it is a legal necessity dressed as diplomatic courtesy: A China-specific regulation would be indefensible at the World Trade Organization and awkward for many European nations still hoping to maintain friendly relations with Beijing.
Yet nobody is fooled. The entire discussion about this “killer switch” provision – from subsidies and non-tariff barriers to overcapacity and dumping – amounts to the EU’s longstanding gripes against Beijing.
Currently, the EU’s powers of dealing with trade problems are cumbersome.
The Commission must start an investigation into alleged fair-trade distortion. The findings must be substantiated. And any measure taken against a nation exporting to the EU must be approved by a majority of the Union’s member-states.
Until now, China had little problem in rendering such European measures irrelevant, either by launching its own trade distortion investigations into European products entering Chinese markets, or by dangling economic favours to a number of individual European nations, in return for their pledge to veto Commission measures against Chinese trade.
But if the “killer switch” proposal is adopted, that will transform the entire trade debate.
The Commission will be able to dispense with most of the elaborate investigation procedure. And incoming goods in a particular sector could be immediately subjected to tariffs or blocked altogether without first asking for the approval of the EU member-nations.
This is, to all intents and purposes, a revolution in the way Europe does business.
Beijing seems to have understood the significance of this proposal; this is assumed to be the main reason why China offered a highly unusual voluntary concession on future exports of electric vehicles. However, the trade debate in Europe was never principally about cars; it was a template for broader discussions on China’s trade volumes.
So, while Beijing thought that its concession on cars was a one-off gesture to silence the debate, the agreement to limit the volumes of Chinese EVs sold in Europe encouraged EU member-states to believe that it was precisely the discussion about the “killer switch” that forced China into giving way.
The question now is whether a consensus really exists over the adoption of such a measure, and how quickly it can be implemented.
While the EU’s biggest economies support the “killer switch” suggestion, many governments may yet baulk at the idea of granting the Commission wide powers; the idea that the Commission can make such critical decisions without prior authority from member-states is controversial. So, all that has been agreed at this stage is that the Commission will come back with its proposals.
Then, there is the question of how quickly such measures could become legally enforceable. The guess in Brussels is that, even if new powers are adopted, the Commission will not be able to use them until the second half of 2027 because the necessary legislation will take time to be enacted.
Still, the anti-China mood is growing in Brussels. The European Parliament approved on Oct 7 by 454 votes to 86 – with 110 abstentions – a resolution calling Chinese industrial policy “an existential threat to the EU”.

People aware of the development said RSIIL, which has been blacklisted by NHAI from bidding for projects following non-performance, has submitted a bid for package-9. Officials said that though RSIIL has moved court against NHAI’s eligibility criteria, which exclude it from bidding, Delhi High Court has green-lighted NHAI’s evaluation of the bids. The matter is scheduled to come up for hearing next week.
Officials said they are confident of completing the process this month so that work can start in the next couple of months. They added that the construction work would take around two years. “These three stretches would be ready latest by December 2029. The Expressway project has faced delay due to several reasons, including Covid-19, delay in land acquisition and statutory approvals,” said one of them.People involved in the project said that apart from the three sections in Gujarat, one stretch each in Maharashtra and Rajasthan is yet to be completed. Western leaders back a two-state solution, but do Palestinians even want one? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
23:13:28 UTC
08:13:28 KST

You’d think that British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who just happens to be Jewish, would have heard the “From the river to the sea” chant, shouted by many of his citizens, at one of their almost daily anti-Israel protests.
The phrase, which represents the entire State of Israel, from the Jordan River to the Mediterranean Sea, means that any officially approved Palestinian state, to those protesters, would have to comprise that full area, including Judea, Samaria and Gaza.
That unnegotiable demand is not just coming from the shouters on the street. It is the final goal of Hamas, Hezbollah, Iran, and anyone who assumes leadership of Palestinians.
While some might be tempted to point to PLO head Mahmoud Abbas, arguing that he has advocated for a two-state solution, that contention is contradicted and completely undermined by the educational indoctrination given to Palestinian children who are taught, from an early age, that Israel is occupying Arab land and that the enemy must be eradicated.
So, for all intents and purposes, the spoken commitment of “From the river to the sea” wholeheartedly negates a two-state solution.
Nonetheless, for whatever reason, Miliband has said that “when it comes to the attempt to destroy the two-state solution, this party, this movement, this government says, ‘we will not let you succeed.’”
My question is, how do you square those two things – a growing protest movement that insists the State of Israel must be entirely replaced by a Palestinian one, with no Jewish presence, and a government minister who assures everyone that no one will succeed in extinguishing the aspiration of a two-state solution?
Unless I’m wrong, each of those concepts is diabolically opposed to the other. One supposes the good will of both sides, endeavoring to commit to peaceful coexistence and ready to make whatever compromise it takes for the sake of ending the long-standing conflict.
While the other immediately dispenses with all pretense, publicly declaring that there will be no compromise, no attempts at sharing the geographic area, and no getting along with those they clearly despise.
So, where do you go from there? Because Miliband and his government are, essentially, pushing a policy that’s being drowned out by the voices on the street who are, in no way, supportive of the idea.
Of course, Miliband is not alone. He shares the company of UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, along with an overwhelming majority of UN member states.
Leaders from France, Canada, and Australia are also on board with the two-state solution. And shockingly, the official policy of the US agrees with that position.
Needless to say, many Arab states, such as Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Morocco, the UAE, Qatar, and Egypt, support the idea as well. Those Arab League members base their assumption on pre-1967 borders, with east Jerusalem as the capital of a Palestinian state.
So what we’re witnessing is a stalled status quo, paralyzing the possibility of all progress, because while a significant part of the global leadership still promotes a two-state solution, the ones who would be instrumental in approving such a deal are laser-focused on the whole pie, and not just one piece.
How can there be any resolution to one of the world’s biggest conundrums when two sides are dug in deeply, believing that their particular philosophy is the only proposition that is acceptable?
That leaves us with only one conclusion. This falls into the category of unsolvable problems that are simply too complex and too emotionally charged to figure out.
When coming to that obvious reality, it’s tempting to ask ourselves why, then, would someone like Miliband, and all the others, continue to back a losing proposition, knowing, in advance, that the likelihood of its implementation is zero?
Here is a speculative answer. The whole concept of a two-state solution is very compatible with the social construct of virtue-signaling. That is because the idea of two states for two peoples sounds reasonable, moral, ethical, and even noble. It plays into the idea that there can be an equitable solution for both sides, resulting in a real win-win situation.
The cost of indoctrination
What is missed by those leaders, who are clearly attempting to inflate their own goodness, is the vast reservoir of hatred and contempt, welling up inside of the individuals who have been part of a centuries-long experiment of indoctrination, from cradle to grave.
The toxic and lethal education they received, both at home, in school, and at their mosques, did the trick, painting Jews as demons who must be eradicated at all costs. Losing one’s life for the sake of diminishing their numbers is the greatest sacrifice that can be made.
Consequently, it’s no wonder that such a society, dedicated to the end of another one, cannot build anything productive or contribute to others through its own achievements and accomplishments.
Because when you are obsessed with destruction, the thought of rising to greatness is completely counterproductive and immaterial to the goal of finally doing away with an avowed enemy. It’s the reason that their youth will never live to inherit the realization of their dream, if that were possible.
Everything is secondary to eliminating the evil in their backyard, and that is the tragedy completely missed by world leaders who have spent decades trying to fit a round peg into a square hole.
So, if you think about it, the thing that is standing in the way of “peace in our time between Jews and Arabs” is the personal need of those in power to appear virtuous, magnanimous, and the ones who possess the highest moral standards.
By forcing the rest of us to cling to a losing prospect, precious time is wasted, young lives are snuffed out, and nothing moves forward. It is the ultimate prolonging of conflict, almost deliberately designed to remain the world’s thorn in the side, as useless and feigned efforts are expended to resolve the mother of all unescapable quagmires.
Don’t even bother asking the question of why they can’t see this for what it is, because they clearly are deeply invested in playing the game of who can appear the most civilized and principled exemplary figures, each vying for that top honor.
Yet, they are outed by the continuing conflict, which will only result in more bloodshed. And, sadly, there’s absolutely no honor in that!
The writer, a former principal of Jerusalem elementary and middle schools, was a member of Kibbutz Re’im from 1994 to 1999. She is the author of Mistake-Proof Parenting, based on the time-tested wisdom found in the Book of Proverbs, available on Amazon.

Democrats say Netanyahu is the problem - but their opposition to Israel runs deeper - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
23:13:26 UTC
08:13:26 KST

American Democratic establishment figures’ criticism of Israel has gathered around one name: Benjamin Netanyahu.
Party leaders, activists, and editorial boards repeat it until the alliance itself slips out of the sentence.
The focus buys time. It lets Democrats appease a radicalizing part of their base without saying how far that base has moved from even conditional support for the US-Israel relationship.
Senate majority leader Chuck Schumer gave the strategy its most formal version in March 2024. On the Senate floor, he said he believed Prime Minister Netanyahu had “lost his way by allowing his political survival to take precedence over the best interests of Israel.”
He called for Israeli elections. The speech treated a change of prime minister as the remedy for a strained alliance. A different man in Jerusalem, the argument ran, and the old partnership could resume its familiar pace.
Sen. Bernie Sanders went further the next month. Responding to Netanyahu, he said, “Do not insult the intelligence of the American people by attempting to distract us from the immoral and illegal war policies of your extremist and racist government.”
The objection had already left one man’s calculations and landed on the government as such. Policy, coalition, and character were folded into a single charge.
Activist groups had been writing that indictment for months. In June 2023, Jewish Voice for Peace described the Israeli government as “the most extremist, racist, homophobic, and far-right in Israel’s history.” The sentence does the work these campaigns need. It implies the problem can be voted out. Attaching a superlative to one government leaves the door open for a later government to be welcomed back.
That implication is the hedge. Leaders can tell older voters and traditional donors that they still support Israel and object only to its present prime minister. They can tell campus organizations and the progressive wing that they have broken with the man those organizations have spent years branding as the obstacle to justice. The two assurances occupy the same week and different rooms. Each audience hears what it came to hear.
The arrangement holds only as long as Netanyahu remains available as the villain. His coalition partners supply ready language about extremism. His long tenure supplies a story about one politician clinging to power. A Democrat can point at Jerusalem and say the difficulty sits there, in a single career, and that a different Israeli government would restore the old terms.
Many Democrats still expect those old terms to return. Criticize the government of the day. Vote for aid. Affirm the alliance in a speech. Move on. The formula belonged to a party whose disagreements with Israel concerned settlements, timing, and tone, and whose voters still treated a Jewish state as a settled fact. Support came with arguments. It did not come with a question mark over the state’s existence.
Rejection of the Jewish state
A large and growing part of the Democratic base has left that settlement. For many activists, the objection is Israel; it is Zionism; it is the idea that a Jewish state should exist in any form. Encampments after October 7, 2023, made the demand public. Chants rejected a Jewish state “between the river and the sea.” Organizations that began with a cabinet ended with a country. The prime minister’s name remained useful. The country has become the target.
Surveys have tracked the same movement for years among younger Democrats, whose sympathy for Israel has fallen well below the levels their parents reported. Party leaders know the numbers. They also know that saying them aloud costs a coalition that still includes pro-Israel voters, Jewish communities, and members of Congress who will not abandon the alliance. Silence about the shift, paired with volume about Netanyahu, has been the working compromise.
So the Netanyahu frame continues and postpones the admission. Support that remains intact only until the loudest faction demands something more extreme is support on a timer. The faction has grown more maximalist with each cycle.
Conditional language about occupation gave way to language about an illegitimate state. Calls for a ceasefire gave way, in some quarters, to calls for the end of the state conducting the war. Each step was described as a response to the current government. Each step survived the news cycle and hardened into doctrine.
The choice will come. A party either grounds its support for Israel in principle, in the legitimacy of Jewish self-determination and in the reality of a democratic ally under attack, or it ties that support to the mood of a wing that has turned uncompromising. There is no stable third position in which leaders condemn a prime minister forever and never answer the people who condemn the country. Coalitions can delay a reckoning; they cannot cancel one.
Netanyahu will not be prime minister forever. Israeli politics has removed him before and can remove him again.
His departure will not retire the argument; it will end the postponement. A successor will still lead a Jewish state. That state will still control territory won in wars it did not start, still face groups sworn to its destruction, and still elect governments that American activists dislike. The adjectives will transfer. They already moved from earlier prime ministers to this one, with barely a pause for the difference between their records.
On that day, Democrats will have to answer a plain question. Were they drawing a line around one man, or were they moving, quietly and for years, toward a break with the alliance itself?
The voters who treated Netanyahu as a convenient objection will still be in the coalition. The voters who want the alliance intact will still be there, too. Neither group will accept the old double message once the named obstacle is gone. A new prime minister cannot do the work a party declined to do with its own base.
The Jewish state will remain after this prime minister, as it remained after the ones before him. American leaders who spent the Netanyahu years treating him as the whole issue will then have to say what they actually support.
The delay is the policy. The day Netanyahu leaves office, the policy expires. What remains is the argument they have been postponing, and it will be harder to hide.
The writer is a certified interfaith hospice chaplain in Jerusalem and the mayor of Mitzpe Yeriho.

Roundup: Firefighters battle multiple wildfires in Southern California under red flag warnings

Firefighters put out hot spots along Avenida Calita during the Norte Fire in San Juan Capistrano, Orange County, California, the United States, on Oct. 17, 2026. Firefighters are battling multiple wildfires across Southern California on Saturday as red flag warnings remain in effect amid critical fire weather conditions. (Photo by Qiu Chen/Xinhua)
LOS ANGELES, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Firefighters are battling multiple wildfires across Southern California on Saturday as red flag warnings remain in effect amid critical fire weather conditions.
A fast-moving wildfire, dubbed the Norte Fire, has burned 570 acres (about 2.3 square kilometers) near San Clemente and San Juan Capistrano as of Saturday morning, with only 5 percent contained, according to the Orange County Fire Authority.
"Crews worked throughout the night to attack the fire and strengthen containment lines," the agency said in an update on X.
Six homes have been damaged or destroyed, the agency said, adding that the cause of the fire remains under investigation.
Evacuation orders were issued for multiple neighborhoods in the area, affecting approximately 16,000 residents as of Saturday.
The Henderson Fire, the largest of the four wildfires currently burning in Southern California, has scorched 3,132 acres and is 35 percent contained, according to the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (Cal Fire).
The blaze was first reported Thursday afternoon in San Diego County.
Overnight, firefighters constructed handline along the southern portion of the fire in the heavily vegetated riparian area of Las Pulgas Canyon and worked to extinguish hot spots, Cal Fire said in an update on Saturday morning.
Crews will focus on the northern portion of the fire, extinguishing hot spots along the perimeter and within the interior, it added.
Relative humidity is expected to recover this evening, helping reduce fire activity. However, grasses and other vegetation remain extremely dry and will continue to pose a fire risk until significant, soaking rainfall occurs, according to the agency.
The Bryson Fire, which started on Thursday, has burned 147 acres in Malibu, Los Angeles County, with 52 percent contained.
Fire officials said that more than 700 personnel had been assigned to the fire as of Friday night. Crews will focus on mopping up hot spots identified during an infrared flight, reinforcing existing containment lines and building additional ones.
The smaller Peak Fire has burned 43 acres so far in Los Angeles County and is 41 percent contained.
A heat advisory issued by the National Weather Service remains in effect until 8 p.m. local time Saturday for parts of Southern California.
Red flag warnings across much of the region prompted Southern California Edison, the area's primary electric utility, to implement public safety power shutoffs, leaving more than 90,000 residents in Los Angeles and Ventura counties without power, local television reports said. ■

SC: No need for nod to prosecute govt official seeking bribe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
23:00:01 UTC
08:00:01 KST

The court stressed that the statutory protection is meant only to prevent persecution of officials for decisions made in discharge of their duties
NEW DELHI: In a significant ruling relating to Prevention of Corruption Act, Supreme Court has said that the shield of prior sanction from higher authorities to prosecute a public servant is not available if they are caught demanding bribes. The court stressed that the statutory protection is meant only to prevent persecution of officials for decisions made in discharge of their duties.The ruling was given by a bench of Justices SVN Bhatti and N V Anjaria while interpreting Section 17A of the Act, which was inserted in the statute in 2018 and prohibited police or investigating agencies from conducting without official approval any inquiry or investigation into alleged offences committed by public servants while discharging their duties.Dismissing an appeal by a Rajasthan police constable challenging an FIR and chargesheet against him for allegedly demanding a bribe of Rs 1.5 lakh, the bench said the Section 17A shield cannot have an omnibus application to all public servants facing prosecution for criminal offences.
“The act of demanding a bribe is a pure criminal act, not connected with official functions and not relatable to or having any linkage with recommendation or decision of the appellant in his capacity as public servant,” the bench said, accepting the arguments of Rajasthan additional advocate general Sansriti Pathak.
Writing the judgement, Justice Anjaria said, “In the facts and circumstances of the case, therefore, the act of the appellant does not fall within the protective umbrella of Section 17A of the Act. It could not be said that the proceedings were vitiated for want of sanction.”

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said in a statement that the diplomats' tour had not been coordinated with the military and that no IDF soldiers were present at the time of the attack, because the call was routed to a divisional operations room handling reports from security personnel rather than civilians.
Israeli police said that they had opened an investigation and notified the Israeli Foreign Ministry to help locate the diplomats who were attacked, collect statements, and identify the attackers.
"Israel Police condemns violence of any kind and will pursue these investigations to their conclusion, bringing to justice everyone involved in such incidents," the police statement said.

Demonstrators face off with law enforcement officers during a protest in Paris, France, Oct. 17, 2026. PARIS, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said Saturday that about 550,000 people took part in the protests across France.
Speaking on French media BFMTV, Nunez condemned the violence that occurred during the gatherings, noting that there have been approximately 400 arrests, and 60 members of the internal security forces were injured on Saturday.
According to French media reports, the demonstrations brought together farmers, climate activists, trade unions and students, expressing demands on fuel prices, the cost of living, education and public services.
Nunez reported numerous attacks on public buildings, police stations, and businesses during the demonstrations, referring to intrusions or attempted intrusions at city halls in Marseille, Lille, Calais and Angers, as well as actions at prefectures, notably in Bordeaux.
He also said that opportunistic offenders took advantage of the demonstrations to loot shops in several cities.
The protests disrupted public transport. The Paris public transport operator RATP announced on its website that the services on more than 10 metro lines in Paris had been temporarily suspended and several stations were closed.
The Louvre Museum announced a limit on the number of visitors on Saturday, while the Orangerie Museum admitted only visitors with reservations.

Macron also expressed his support to the law enforcement officers, saying that "we will stand united against those who sow chaos, whose only goal is to tear down our institutions and who prevent others from peacefully expressing their grievances." ■

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Oct 18, 2026
Mass protests in France spiral into worst riots in years
Rioting erupted in cities across France on Oct 17 as demonstrations against rising living costs and declining public services spiralled out of control in some of the worst violence the country has witnessed for decades.
While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully in street marches in scores of cities, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets and attacked police vehicles and officers.
In Limoges, the city hall was set ablaze as Marseille black-clad protesters broke in and defaced the building with anarchic graffiti. In Lyon, protesters torched the city’s tourist office.
‘You can’t die like this’: flydubai pilot recalls attack in first interview
The captain of a flydubai flight whose co-pilot attacked him with an axe in an alleged bid to bring down the plane said one thought kept running through his head as the harrowing ordeal unfolded: “You can’t die like this.”
Indian pilot Smit Machchhar recounted the “traumatic” experience to Sky News Arabia in his first interview since the incident late in September in which he, passengers and other crew members were credited with averting disaster on the Tel Aviv-bound flight.
With his head and one hand bandaged and glasses perched on his nose, Machchhar spoke from his hospital bed in the UAE.
Haaland brace extends Man City’s winning start in Premier League
Erling Haaland struck twice as Manchester City defiantly extended their blistering start to the Premier League season with a 3-2 win against Ipswich on Oct 17.
Phil Foden put City ahead in the first half at the Etihad Stadium before Daizen Maeda grabbed a shock equaliser for Ipswich.
Haaland netted before the interval and struck again after the break to take his tally for the season to 12.
It was City’s second win since the club were found guilty of more than 100 breaches of Premier League financial regulations in September.
Reporter who saw Covid-19 pandemic coming has died
Helen Branswell, a leading reporter on infectious diseases who wrote with foresight, urgency and clarity about the emerging danger of the Covid-19 pandemic, ahead of the vast majority of journalists and even many medical experts, died on Oct 13 in Ottawa. She was 69.
Her death, at a hospital, was from complications of a recurrence of breast cancer, her sister Brenda said.
Branswell “saw the pandemic coming well before anyone was paying attention”, Ashish Jha, the White House Covid-19 response coordinator in 2022 and 2023, said on social media.
Alberta support for Canada rises ahead of separation referendum
Support for Alberta remaining in Canada gathered pace ahead of a referendum on whether the province should begin a legal process to separate from the country, according to a poll from Abacus Data.
The survey of 1,021 eligible voters, released on Oct 17, found 68% of Albertans would vote to remain in Canada, up from 64% in September. Support for beginning a legal process that could ultimately lead to separation was unchanged at 24%, while the share of undecided voters or those planning not to vote fell to 8% from 12%.
Albertans will decide on Oct 19 whether to remain a Canadian province or to set the stage for a second, binding vote on secession. At stake is the future of Canada’s largest oil-producing province, which pumps more than 4 million barrels a day, most of it for export to the US.

Prices of 137 cancer drugs to fall by up to 70% from November 9
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
22:02:18 UTC
07:02:18 KST

This follows a nudge by Supreme Court, flagging the huge gap between price to retailer and MRP of medicines billed to patients
In good news for cancer patients, prices of 137 drugs are set to be reduced by up to 70% from Nov 9, with govt capping trade margins by 30%. Drug prices regulator National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) Saturday notified the 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs to address the issue of excessive trade margins, invoking Paragraph 19 of DPCO, 2013. Significantly, patented drugs are also included in the list.The trade margin rationalisation at 30% of MRP, excluding GST, corresponds to a mark-up of 42.9% on price to stockist/price to distributor (PTS/PTD), according to the minutes of the NPPA meeting accessed by TOI. Simply put, PTS/PTD is the first point of sale of the drug.
This follows a nudge by Supreme Court, flagging the huge gap between price to retailer and MRP of medicines billed to patients, in certain cases of 10 times.The MRPs of certain drugs — including pertuzumab + trastuzumab, atezolizumab, teclistamab, inotuzumab ozogamicin and daratumumab — are up to Rs 5 lakh per vial/pack.All manufacturers will be required to inform NPPA of their revised prices within seven days of publication of the gazette notification. Manufacturers will be req-uired to display the price lists on their website and widely disseminate them to all retailers and hospitals, with the latter also required to display the revised prices on their websites prominently.
The authority approved the calculation of the revised MRP based on PTS/PTD for March 2026 as the reference month.NPPA said patient assistance programme quantities may be excluded from the calculation of PTS/PTD and MRP for trade-margin capping only. These programmes, where drugs are supplied free of cost, are typically run by MNCs.As a substantial supply of anti-cancer drugs is directly made to hospitals and medical institutions, they shall be responsible for ensuring revised prices of such drugs from the date of implementation, NPPA said. State drug controllers will take necessary steps to ensure compliance by manufacturers, dealers including retailers, hospitals and medical institutions, it added.In a bid to tighten rules further, NPPA said uninterrupted availability of the covered formulations needed to be ensured. Any manufacturer intending to reduce monthly production levels would have to obtain permission.
Consumers can use the Pharma Sahi Daam app and NPPA website to check revised prices of drugs, an official release said.In 2019, the MRP of 526 brands of non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines was reduced by up to 90%, NPPA said. The present exercise extends this approach to a larger set of drugs, based on the list recommended by an expert committee under Directorate General of Health Services.

====================================================================================================

Mothers and fathers may pass along different kinds of sexism to their kids, new research suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
22:00:34 UTC
07:00:34 KST

A new study published in Sex Roles suggests that 8-year-old children’s views about women tend to mirror their parents’ sexist attitudes. Fathers’ hostile sexism and mothers’ benevolent sexism were most consistently linked to their children’s views, hinting that mothers and fathers may play different roles in passing these beliefs along.
Psychologists often divide sexism into two distinct categories: hostile and benevolent. Hostile sexism involves openly negative feelings toward women, particularly those who are perceived as challenging male power. Benevolent sexism is more subtle, as it involves idealizing women who conform to traditional gender roles and believing that they are delicate and require men’s protection.
Research suggests that benevolent sexism, despite its polite surface, can reinforce an unequal division of household labor and limit women’s career ambitions. Parents appear to be one source of children’s ideas about gender: a 2002 meta-analysis found that parents with more traditional views about gender tended to have children with more traditional views.
Studies of whether parents pass on hostile and benevolent sexism specifically have mostly involved teenagers. A 2012 study, for example, found that mothers who endorsed more benevolent sexism tended to have teenage daughters who did too. Some theorists had argued that benevolent sexism only emerges in adolescence, but a 2020 study co-authored by Hammond, which introduced the stuffed-toy task used in the new research, found that children as young as 5 already agree with both hostile and benevolent ideas about women.
Parental sexism may also show up in everyday interactions: research covered by PsyPost in 2023, led by Overall, found that mothers and fathers higher in hostile sexism were less responsive toward their young children during family interactions.
To build on this line of inquiry, researchers Oksana S. Voznyuk, a PhD candidate at the University of Auckland, Nickola C. Overall, a professor at the University of Auckland, and Matt Hammond, an associate professor at Victoria University of Wellington, set out to test the direct intergenerational links between parents and children. They wanted to see if mothers’ and fathers’ specific sexist attitudes predict their children’s agreement with similar statements.
“In the big picture, we wanted to investigate why gender gaps persist worldwide, even as generations of women and men have been fighting for gender equality,” Voznyuk, Overall, and Hammond told PsyPost. “We thought that an overlooked process that may contribute to this slow progress toward gender equality could be the transmission of sexist beliefs intergenerationally – from parents to their children.”
The research team collected data from 175 family groups, each consisting of a mother, a father, and their 8-year-old child. The families lived in New Zealand and were part of a larger study that began when the children were 4 or 5. The children were fairly evenly split by gender, with 51 percent being girls and 49 percent being boys. Parents filled out standard questionnaires designed to measure their levels of hostile and benevolent sexism.
To assess the children’s attitudes, the researchers used a specially designed laboratory activity that young kids could easily understand. An experimenter introduced each child to a stuffed toy named Feppy, explaining that the toy was a visitor from far away. Feppy then made a series of statements about men and women.
Some of the toy’s statements reflected hostile sexism, such as saying that women get upset easily over jokes. Other statements reflected benevolent sexism, such as claiming that men need to protect women from danger. The children were asked to indicate whether Feppy was “sort of” or “really” right or wrong about each statement. On average, children rated Feppy’s hostile statements as sort of wrong and its benevolent statements as sort of right, and boys and girls gave similar answers.
When the researchers analyzed the responses, they found distinct patterns connecting the parents’ views to their children’s views. Because both parents’ attitudes were analyzed together, each link held even after accounting for the other parent’s views. Fathers who expressed higher levels of hostile sexism tended to have children who also agreed more strongly with hostile gender attitudes. This link was present regardless of whether the child was a boy or a girl.
A different pattern emerged for benevolent sexism. Mothers who endorsed benevolent sexist beliefs were more likely to have children who agreed with benevolent gender attitudes. Just like the link between fathers’ and children’s hostile views, this connection applied to both sons and daughters. Fathers’ benevolent sexism, by contrast, was not linked to their children’s benevolent attitudes.
The researchers also found that a mother’s hostile sexism was linked to her child’s views, but only for sons. The authors note the reason is unclear, but one possibility is that mothers higher in hostile sexism parent boys differently, for example by being more controlling with sons.
“The big takeaway from our findings is that children learn from the attitudes, behaviors, and everyday conversations they see at home, and the messages we send about expectations for women and men, or girls and boys, likely have a lasting impact,” the researchers noted. “This matters because those beliefs can shape everything from career opportunities to romantic relationships later in life.”
“One surprising outcome was that mothers and fathers may play unique roles in passing along sexist beliefs,” the researchers explained. “These differences may be about the roles that fathers and mothers play. Fathers who agree with hostile sexism believe that they should be the authority in the family, and they may use more controlling parenting behavior and express hostile sexism by behaving aggressively toward mothers. These behaviors can show children that men should have power and authority and therefore socialize children’s hostile gender beliefs.”
The authors suggest that mothers who endorse benevolent sexism might actively teach these values to their children, as these beliefs often appear socially acceptable or positive on the surface. “Mothers who agree with benevolent sexism may be more likely to hold traditional homemaker and caregiver roles,” the team added. “This may give them more opportunity to model and teach children ideas about protecting and valuing women who fit traditional expectations of what good girls and good women should be like.”
To ensure these links were not driven by other factors, the researchers adjusted their statistical models for the parents’ education levels, employment status, perceived socioeconomic status, and whether the mother or father was the primary caregiver. They also controlled for the children’s age and their “theory of mind,” which is the psychological term for a person’s ability to understand that other people have their own separate thoughts and feelings. Even with these adjustments, the connections between the parents’ and children’s sexist attitudes remained, and incidentally, parents’ hostile sexism was linked to lower theory-of-mind scores in children.
“The most important note is that this research is not about blaming parents, but about recognizing that we all play a role in transmitting and reinforcing gender beliefs,” the researchers emphasized. “Small changes may make an important difference. Many of us have internalized sexist attitudes to some extent, and often we don’t even know what they are, their impact, or how we display them. This research is a good reminder that the little things we say and do can shape how children think about women and men.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The links were modest: the correlation between fathers’ and children’s hostile attitudes, for example, was about 0.29, on a scale where 1 would mean a perfect match.
“As with most research about beliefs and attitudes, the effect size of parents’ sexist beliefs on children’s beliefs is relatively small,” the researchers pointed out. “Children are likely to have many experiences that contribute to their beliefs about women and men, but as children’s first and often most long-term role models, parents are likely to be particularly impactful influences in children’s development of sexist attitudes and an important intervention point.”
The study relies on observational data, meaning it cannot establish a direct cause and effect. There is also a possibility that children influence their parents’ views over time as they express their own ideas about gender. Additionally, the stuffed-toy task was developed with U.S. children, and one hostile item had to be dropped for poor fit with this New Zealand sample. All of the families were mother-father couples in New Zealand, so the patterns may differ in other family types and cultures.
Future research will need to explore these dynamics in single-parent households, families with LGBTQ+ parents, and across different cultural contexts.
“We believe two main directions are important for the next steps in this research,” the researchers said. “The first is to investigate whether children’s gender attitudes are related to negative outcomes for children’s wellbeing and their social, emotional and educational development.”
They suspect these attitudes could affect how children see themselves, how they do in school, and how they get along with peers. “The second is to investigate how parents are passing down their beliefs – are parents modeling traditional gender roles at home, treating sons and daughters differently, or shaping how children dress and behave in a way that communicates these gender beliefs?” they added.
The authors argue that because children’s early beliefs about gender may shape their later interests, schooling, and relationships, efforts to reduce gender stereotypes in childhood will likely need to engage parents as well as children.
The study, “Intergenerational Links Between Parents’ and Children’s Hostile and Benevolent Sexism,” was authored by Oksana S. Voznyuk, Nickola C. Overall, Matthew D. Hammond, Rachel S. T. Low, Annette M. E. Henderson, Valerie T. Chang, and Myfanwy Christensen.

Internet is fundamental right of all, even children: Supreme Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
21:54:56 UTC
06:54:56 KST

It said the efficacy of such restrictive measures remains far from established in countries which have imposed them.
NEW DELHI: Raising citizens’ right to access and use of internet to the level of fundamental right, Supreme Court has held that even children are entitled to that right and said it does not endorse imposing in the name of safety a blanket ban on children accessing internet. At the same time, it favoured restricting access to content that is inherently harmful to kids.A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K V Chandran said that right to access and use of the internet is part of Article 21 (right to life and liberty) and Article 19(1)(a) (freedom of speech and expression). The internet is “priceless” as it provides access to information and education to all in even remote areas, where it is often the only source of learning for many children. Noting that the SC had earlier refrained from expressing a definitive view on whether the right to access the internet is, by itself, a fundamental right, the bench said, “...we have no hesitation in saying that the right to access and use the internet is a fundamental right of every individual under Article 21 read with Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.”
SC: Internet’s value priceless, efficacy of curbs not provedSC said, “Our children, irrespective of their age enjoy the same rights, and to deny the same altogether would be as absurd as saying children below a certain age do not have a conscience worth protecting or freedom of speech worth expressing.”
The order was passed on a public interest litigationfiled by NGO ‘Just Rights for Children Alliance’, which highlights continued lapses by intermediaries in tackling child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) despite SC’s 2024 judgment in this regard.
Agreeing with its plea, SC said there has been “no progress worth the name” in the last two years.Acknowledging that there has been “a growing yet short-lived tendency across the globe in the recent past to limit the access of children below a certain age to the internet, more particularly to social media platforms,” SC said, “we too gave this our anxious consideration, and only thereafter, we decided consciously not to endorse the same”.It said the efficacy of such restrictive measures remains far from established in countries which have imposed them.“... Children do not cease to use the internet merely because the law prohibits them from doing so ... They move to other platforms and websites that are unregulated and even more unsafe,” SC said.“All that we are trying to say is that any blanket restriction on access to internet by children is nothing more than unproven measures of proven disproportionality. No jurisdiction has, so far, been able to demonstrate that children are any safer on account of such measures,” it said.It said some age-based restrictions and safeguards should exist for the safety of children online.

Israeli charity Save a Child's Heart marks 30 years, 9,000 children treated
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
21:40:53 UTC
06:40:53 KST

The Talmud teaches that whoever saves a single life is considered to have saved an entire world. If that’s the case, Save a Child’s Heart (SACH) can be credited with saving some 9,000 worlds.
SACH is Israel’s leading practitioner of medical diplomacy.
Founded in 1995 by the late Dr. Ami Cohen and headquartered in the Sylvan Adams Children’s Hospital at the Wolfson Medical Center in Holon, it provides free cardiac surgery for children with heart ailments regardless of their religion, ethnicity, or nationality.
This includes children from countries that do not have diplomatic relations with Israel, as well as youngsters from countries that are sworn enemies of Israel.
To date, over 9,000 children from more than 75 countries have been brought to Israel for treatment. Each child is accompanied by a family member or nurse from the child’s home country.
In addition, medical personnel from third-world countries are brought to Israel to train in all aspects of cardiac surgery so that children with heart problems can be treated closer to home.
SACH teams frequently travel abroad to evaluate children with congenital and rheumatic heart diseases, and often perform urgent surgeries when the child’s condition is so serious that immediate treatment is required.
'We are celebrating 30 years of saving worlds'
SACH volunteers and supporters met last Friday with President Isaac Herzog at his official residence to celebrate the 30th anniversary of SACH’s founding.
Those who attended, along with the aforementioned, were medical personnel, ambassadors, and other diplomats from some of the African countries from which children have been brought to Israel for surgery; representatives of African hospitals whose cardiology pediatricians were trained in Israel; representatives of international foundations that fund SACH; and mothers with children who recently underwent successful surgeries and who will soon be returning home.
Simon Fisher, SACH executive director, described the children who had been treated by SACH over the years as “living miracles,” adding: “We are celebrating 30 years of saving worlds.”
He emphasized that, from a small group of dedicated professionals, SACH had grown to global proportions. He explained that “a child in need is part of our collective responsibility.”
Herzog, who has long been familiar with the work done by SACH, said that the organization deserved a Nobel Peace Prize and pledged to do everything he could to bring that about.
He declared that he was honored to host a milestone anniversary of “a remarkable Israeli humanitarian organization of which we’re very proud.”
Herzog characterized SACH’s achievements as “the triumph of human kindness that connects a wide heart of human effort.”
But it is more than simply healing a diseased heart, he pointed out. “From Iraq to the Palestinian Authority, all have been welcomed with wide open arms – simply because they are children in need.”
Herzog saw the effects of this a year ago when he paid a state visit to Zambia and met with adults who had been healed in Israel as children and were leading fruitful and meaningful lives.
“Few things leave me prouder to be Israeli,” he said. “This is the essence of doing good in the world. This is something the international community should bear in mind when they accuse us of something else.”
In closing, Herzog implied that SACH received its inspiration from the biblical Noah: “One man who braved the current and ultimately saved the world.”
SACH co-chair Robert Baruch noted that over the years, SACH has given thousands of children a second chance of life, and has not been deterred by the child’s place of birth.
Children come to Israel as the hope of families who cannot find treatment at home, he said. “It’s a reminder of what can happen when people decide to act. The impact of SACH is far greater than its size.”
Mega philanthropist Sylvan Adams, together with a group of other philanthropic families living in Israel, established the Sylvan Adams Children’s hospital within the Wolfson Medical Center in Holon and shared some of his own SACH experiences.
The first time he visited, which was over a decade ago, he was on a tour. A SACH staff member asked him whether he would like to spend a few minutes watching open heart surgery being performed.
He agreed, and was so fascinated by what he saw, that he sat for hours, and instantly became a donor. The children’s hospital which bears his name came into being because before that, there was no children’s hospital in Holon. Since its inception, he has visited many times.
On that first occasion, he saw the surgeon being assisted by a doctor from Tanzania. What amazed him was that the two were conversing in Hebrew.
One per cent of all children are born with heart defects
Adams was shocked to learn that 1% of all children are born with heart defects, which makes SACH’s work all the more vital.
During his visits he has witnessed children from Gaza coming with their parents and sometimes even accompanied by their physicians. They were always treated with dignity – even after October 7, he said.
Along the entrance to the main building in the presidential compound, there were tall round tables bearing enlarged photographs of children who came with hope and left healed. Alongside each photograph was a round vase filled with white tulips.
When the petals of a tulip first open, they form the shape of a heart. The message, though subtle, was clear.

Cost of living protests hit Belgium, Italy, Portugal and France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
21:02:26 UTC
06:02:26 KST

Cost of living protests hit Belgium, Italy, Portugal and France
Hundreds of thousands take to the streets for separate demonstrations, putting pressure on governments across the EU.
Hundreds of thousands of Europeans have taken to the streets in separate, uncoordinated demonstrations to protest against the rising cost of living in their countries.
Saturday’s wave of unrest in Belgium, France, Italy and Portugal has put pressure on governments across the European Union.
France experienced one of its most turbulent days of protests in decades, with more than 550,000 people joining demonstrations, according to the Ministry of Interior, and police facing off with protesters across the country.
The marches, which followed weeks of student protests, degenerated into clashes, looting and fires after violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, luxury boutiques and supermarkets, and attacked police vehicles and officers.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said 1,200 people were arrested and 150 police officers were hurt. “It’s a miracle the toll wasn’t higher,” he said as he visited officers deployed in central Paris.
Dozens of shops were looted in Paris, Marseille, Nice, Nantes, Bordeaux, Limoges, Lille, Toulouse and Strasbourg, the French news agency AFP reported.
Whole streets in the capital “have been devastated”, Paris Mayor Emmanuel Gregoire said.
A fire set by masked protesters in Limoges largely destroyed the more than 140-year-old town hall, while city halls in Marseille and Lille were broken into and vandalised. In Lyon, protesters torched the city’s tourist office.
President Emmanuel Macron said on X that those responsible would be “prosecuted and punished”.
In Belgium’s capital, Brussels – which has already seen weeks of protests by students against university registration fees – police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters, whom they accused of launching missiles at them and setting fires.
In Liege, a smaller city east of Brussels, police also deployed water cannon to break up demonstrations. Police did not say how many people attended.
Meanwhile, in the Portuguese capital of Lisbon, an estimated tens of thousands of protesters marched against the cost of living crisis, low wages and an inability to access housing in major cities. House prices in Portugal have more than doubled since 2017, while rents for new leases have increased nearly as much.
Portuguese Parliamentary Affairs Minister Carlos Abreu Amorim said on Friday that the “government will not yield to shouts from the street”. Protesters said their leaders are “out of touch” with the problem.
Italy
In Milan, rioters clashed with police, looted stores and set property on fire in the city centre, emptying Piazza del Duomo and a luxury arcade that would usually be full of shoppers.
A march against wars and rising living costs began peacefully, but masked protesters threw stones, paving blocks and other objects at riot police and set fire to barricades made from bar tables.
Police used water cannon and tear gas to disperse the crowds.
At least two police officers were injured, and about 50 demonstrators, many of them minors, were detained, the Italian LaPresse news agency reported.
Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni condemned the violence.
“Demonstrating is a right. Setting our cities ablaze is not,” she wrote on X, blaming “hooligans who exploit demonstrations to sow chaos”.
Milan’s centre-left mayor, Giuseppe Sala, said “the reasons for the protests were understandable. The violence against law enforcement and serious damage to the city are not justifiable.”
In Bologna, police also reported that, alongside peaceful rallies, protesters threw stones and clashed with officers.
French protests spill over
Although protests in the other countries did not reach the same scale as the rallies in France, they may be a sign of discontent spilling over, Alberto Alemanno, professor of EU law and policy at HEC Paris Business School, told Al Jazeera.
“France is the epicentre of this movement … and there are signs now that this is spreading beyond France,” Alemanno said.
He said Saturday’s protests may not be the last in many of these countries and new hotspots could emerge.
In Greece, Germany, and Austria, the “early stages” of a movement are emerging, with mobilisation expected “in the coming week”, he said.
They are not a single movement, he explained, but several protests happening at the same time, with some “shared grievances”: underfunded education, rising living costs and, for students, uncertain prospects after graduation.
The unrest comes at a crucial time for Europe, Alemanno said, as the continent prepares for an “unprecedented super-cycle of national elections” in the coming 12 months, with votes scheduled in Spain, France, Italy and Poland.
“Inevitably, all these protests, all these mobilisations, are going to be at the centre of the political conversation,” Alemanno said.

NEW DELHI: Two months after students of National Law School of India University (NLSIU), Bengaluru, opposed his presence on the campus, CJI Surya Kant addressed them at the convocation ceremony and said the legal profession is not for the faint-hearted as it demands intellectual independence coupled with fairness and hearing a person before judging.Delivering the ‘Presidential address of the Chancellor’ on Saturday at the convocation, which was postponed after students and alumni of NLSIU opposed his presence, CJI Kant said the university, regarded as ‘Harvard of the East’, has “witnessed its fair share of quad parties and impromptu flash mobs in the courtyard!” Shifting to the serious task, he said the legal profession demands not only the mastery of statutes but also the courage to defend what is just, and the humility to listen to the voices that get drowned in cacophony.
CJI Surya Kant at NLSIU said legal profession demands humility to listen to the voices that get drowned in cacophony.“This intellectual independence also calls for fairness: hearing before judging, distinguishing a person from a position and disagreeing without denying another person’s dignity,” he said.
He said the purpose of legal education is to enable law graduates to explore the situations beyond criminal and constitutional laws and gain experience from myriad real-life situations where many comprehend the world very differently than ourselves.
“Law will challenge your patience, test your ethics, and call upon the deepest reserves of your courage. But it will also reward you with the singular joy of service – the serene satisfaction of righting a wrong, the pride of defending liberty, and the honour of upholding the Constitution,” he said.Advising the students on the challenges that lie ahead of them in the challenging legal profession, the CJI said, “As you leave this campus, you step not only into a profession but into a calling.”

Mass protests in France spiral into worst riots in years

Mass protests in France spiral into worst riots in years
- Mass protests over rising living costs and poor public services turned violent in France, with attacks on city halls, shops and police, and about 1,200 arrests, said Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu.
- Macron and Lecornu vowed to punish the rioters and said violence would not change policy, while protesters said most marches were peaceful and blamed troublemakers for the damage.
- The unrest spread across Europe, and France’s police response faces scrutiny after injuries, including a teenager who lost a hand, and claims that officers are under severe strain.
AI generated
FRANCE – Rioting erupted in cities across France on Oct 17 as demonstrations against rising living costs and declining public services spiralled out of control in some of the worst violence the country has witnessed for decades.
While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully in street marches in scores of cities, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets and attacked police vehicles and officers.
In Limoges, the city hall was set ablaze, as Marseille black-clad protesters broke into City Hall and defaced the building with anarchic graffiti and, in Lyon, protesters torched the city’s tourist office.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the government would not be “intimidated” by violence, and blamed the unrest on the “far-left” and criminals just months before a presidential election next year.
“To those who clearly want to use this violence as a ‘warm-up’ before the presidential election, I say clearly – We will not let ourselves be intimidated. No one will impose their political agenda through violence,” he wrote in a post on X.
Some 1,200 people had been arrested as part of the protests, Lecornu said while visiting the sites in the evening.
Around 550,000 people had participated in the demonstrations across the country, he said. The CGT union estimated protesters at 800,000 people.
French President Emmanuel Macron vowed to prosecute and punish people who had performed such attacks.
“We will all stand united against the sowers of chaos, who only seek to undermine our institutions and prevent those who peacefully express their demands from doing so,” he wrote in a post on X.
Belgium, Portugal and Italy also faced smaller-scale protests on Oct 17 as living costs rise in Europe, while protesters in Albania again rallied against perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards.
Protesters said most people had marched peacefully, and put much of the violence down to troublemakers who had set out to cause damage and clash with the police. Many held signs bearing slogans against the police, the president and the wealthy.
“We are fighting because the cost of living is too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to protest, and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions,” said Lola, a 19-year-old protester in Paris.
Tear gas, fire and looting
Most protests kicked off around midday, with some beginning before the official start of the demonstrations.
In some parts of Paris, police fired tear gas rounds as they retreated in the face of mostly young protesters, many of whom were dressed in black and wore hoodies, masks and goggles to protect against tear gas.
Rioters tried to break into the Galeries Lafayette department store, smashed up banks, ransacked a Lacoste store as well as other boutiques, and looted a mobile phone shop. Protesters had been setting objects ablaze all day, including numerous cars.
In protests partly inspired by those in France, several hundred mostly young people protested in Brussels, and some clashed with police. Belgian student groups have said they are protesting against rising education costs and reforms they fear will make higher education less accessible.
In Albania, police fired what appeared to be rubber bullets at protesters during a fifth day of mass student demonstrations calling for Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama to step down.
In Portugal, tens of thousands took to the streets of Lisbon following days of unrest to protest against housing and other living costs. Housing prices in Portugal have doubled since 2017, fuelling one of the worst affordability crises in Europe.
In Italy, a march against high costs of living in Milan degenerated into disorder, with police clearing the central cathedral square with tear gas. Police in Bologna used water cannons to try to disperse crowds and made seven arrests after another protest turned violent, the ANSA news agency reported.
French police response under scrutiny
The protests in France began in September, at high schools in Paris’ working-class northern suburbs, where anger over teacher shortages and shabby facilities evolved into a broader movement focused on inequality, public spending and living standards.
In Paris on Oct 17, protesters in high-visibility vests blocked streets, recalling the Yellow Vest movement that marked French President Emmanuel Macron’s previous term in office.
The protests on Oct 17 eclipsed the size of the crowds at the peak of the Yellow Vest movement, though they were far lower than the levels seen at the protests in 2023 against Macron’s pension overhaul.
Macron is entering the final stretch of his presidency, facing a fragmented political landscape and growing pressure over the economy.
France’s efforts to reduce public debt have failed to reassure investors, pushing government borrowing costs to their highest levels in over two decades.
Police tactics have drawn criticism following injuries among demonstrators, including a teenager who lost a hand after picking up a stun grenade. The police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen allegations of police violence.
Lecornu said more than 150 police officers had been injured in the Oct 17 protests, but did not say whether any protesters had been hurt.
Nunez said one person lost his hand in clashes with police on Oct 17. French media reported he had tried to pick up a stun grenade.
The UNSA police union posted a video on X showing crowds attacking police vans with clubs and bricks in multiple locations. The union warned the government police forces were at breaking point.
“Today again, in every corner of France, our colleagues are being used as punching bags. Pelted with stones, injured, trapped in real ambushes,” the union said. “Let everyone take responsibility: this cannot go on indefinitely. The rope is stretched to its maximum.” REUTERS

Prominent Guatemalan anti-corruption lawyer killed in shooting

Prominent Guatemalan anti-corruption lawyer killed in shooting
GUATEMALA – Guatemalan lawyer Juan Francisco Solorzano Foppa, known for his high-profile fight against corruption in the Central American country, died after being shot on Oct 17 by two men while visiting a sports centre, a crime condemned by President Bernardo Arevalo.
Solorzano Foppa, 43, was a former prosecutor who denounced wrongdoing by some of Guatemala’s most powerful politicians, business leaders and companies, and in 2023, briefly joined the defence team of a prominent journalist.
Shortly after the attack, Guatemalan police reported that they had detained two men and seized a carbine-style firearm and a motorcycle. Police said the arrests and weapon seizure were in connection with the case.
“I strongly condemn the cowardly murder of former prosecutor Juan Francisco Solorzano Foppa. Both the direct perpetrators and those who ordered the crime must face the full weight of the law,” Arevalo posted on his official X account. He said he had instructed the government to coordinate with the relevant authorities to solve the crime.
“Those who believe that terror can intimidate the people of Guatemala and the government I lead are mistaken. In honour of Foppa, in honour of our homeland, in honour of justice.”
Foppa was known for his anti-corruption work as head of the Criminal Investigations Directorate in the Public Prosecutor’s Office, and later as head of Guatemala’s tax authority, the SAT, from 2016 to 2018, when he helped prosecute dozens of powerful Guatemalan business figures and recover unpaid taxes.
In 2025, Foppa alleged a connection between the Barrio 18 gang and the National Unity of Hope party, as well as links between criminal gangs and the judicial system.
In 2023, he briefly joined the defence team of Guatemalan journalist Jose Ruben Zamora, who has become an international symbol of resistance to the criminalisation of journalism and erosion of judicial independence in Central America.
Foppa had to leave the Zamora case after being accused by the Public Prosecutor’s Office of obstructing the proceedings and destroying or concealing information, a charge he denied but ultimately accepted as part of a plea agreement, saying he did not believe he would receive a fair trial.

tob.studio’s timber bike station in germany resembles stacked log pile
the bike station integrates e-bike charging stations, repair facilities, and digital information, as well as public amenities including an accessible toilet and shower.
prefer designboom on google
LOG PILE GEOMETRY SHAPES TIMBER CYCLING HUB by ToB.Studio
Designed by ToB.Studio, the Burgsinn Cycling Rest Station establishes a public service hub along the D9 cycle route in Germany, positioned at the transition between the town and surrounding landscape. Drawing visual cues from local forestry history, the compact building reinterprets the form of stacked timber logs. Its solid volume features carved-out niches that accommodate sheltered seating areas, entrances, and service points beneath a broad overhanging green roof.
rough-sawn larch cladding wraps bike station’s exterior
The station, designed by ToB.Studio architectural practice, provides a range of amenities for cyclists, pool visitors, and local residents, including e-bike charging stations, a repair and wash area, digital information displays, and an accessible toilet and shower. The structure is built using a prefabricated timber frame according to Design for Disassembly principles, utilizing reversible mechanical connections to facilitate future maintenance and material-specific recycling. Constructed with locally sourced untreated larch cladding, wood-fiber insulation, and a membrane-free wall assembly, the building rests on a single reinforced-concrete slab that functions as the foundation, flood barrier, and finished floor surface.

name: Bike-Station

19 killed in Kolkata stampede; CM Suvendu announces jobs, Rs 25 lakh for kin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

05:25:51 KST

Adhikari added that a fact-finding committee would be constituted to investigate the incident
NEW DELHI: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Saturday announced a compensation of Rs 25 lakh and a government job for the family of each person killed in a stampede at the Chorbagan Sarbojanin Durga Puja pandal in north Kolkata.The state government will also bear the entire cost of medical treatment for the injured and provide Rs 5 lakh to each of them, Adhikari said, adding that a fact-finding committee would be constituted to investigate the incident."This is a tragic incident. 19 people have lost their lives, 17 of whom died on the spot... 25 people have been injured; 24 of them are out of danger, while one remains in critical condition," the chief minister said. He added that the government was making every possible effort to assist the affected families and that he had personally met relatives of the deceased.
'Appropriate measures against those who failed to manage crowd'
Adhikari said the state government would seek the intervention of the Chief Justice of the Calcutta High Court to constitute a fact-finding committee, which would include special task force (STF) and forensic teams. The investigation would examine the circumstances leading to the stampede and identify those responsible for the crowd management arrangements.
Kolkata Police's Anti-Rowdy Section (ARS) has collected CCTV footage from the site, which will be examined as part of the investigation."We will check the footage and take appropriate measures against those who failed to manage the crowd. That could be a member of the puja committee, a homeguard, a temporary worker, a policeman, or a private company security guard. Nobody will be spared," Adhikari said.He said the state government was making arrangements for postmortems in accordance with the law and that six of the deceased had been identified so far. Officials were also coordinating with the families of the victims.The chief minister said the families who had met him had expressed faith in the state government. He added that the Prime Minister's Office had sought a report from the chief secretary, which had been submitted, and that the Centre and the state were working together to provide assistance.
'Some attempting to politicise this, but it will be to no avail'
Adhikari also criticised the previous state government over its handling of past tragedies, accusing some people of attempting to politicise the current incident."Everyone is well aware of the role of the previous government in similar incidents that occurred in the past. Some are attempting to politicize this, but it will be to no avail. I have met with the families of the deceased, and they have explicitly stated that they have full faith in the Chief Minister and the government... The PMO also requested a report from the Chief Secretary, which we have submitted. The Prime Minister has announced relief and compensation. The central and state governments are working together on this..." he said.Referring to other incidents, Adhikari said 13 people had died due to electrocution during the 2025 Puja season amid heavy rain. He also referred to a devastating flood in north Bengal that killed 100 people, questioning the previous chief minister's response to those tragedies.
'An announcement by the organisers' led to the rush
The stampede occurred on Saturday evening, on Maha Saptami, at the Chorbagan Sarbojanin Durga Puja pandal in north Kolkata. At least 19 people died and 25 were injured after a crowd surge amid rain, according to officials.A police officer said people waiting outside the pandal rushed forward as it began raining, causing some to fall on the road and triggering the stampede. Adhikari said an announcement made by the organisers of the community Durga Puja had led to a rush among revellers, resulting in what he described as a "painful incident".Officials of the organising club, private security guards and personnel on duty were detained for questioning, he said. The administration also advised several crowded theme-based puja pandals to temporarily close following the tragedy.
Union home minister Amit Shah, who had arrived in Kolkata and was scheduled to visit pandals on Sunday, cancelled his programmes following the incident. President Droupadi Murmu, Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Shah and former chief minister Mamata Banerjee expressed condolences over the deaths.PM Modi announced an ex gratia payment of Rs 2 lakh for the next of kin of each deceased person and Rs 50,000 for each injured person. The state government has also launched a toll-free helpline to provide information related to the stampede.

France in flames: Historic city hall collapses as riots spread | Watch
